en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Great Commentary on the Path of Purification (Second Part)
12. Explanation of the Exposition of the Supernormal Powers (Iddhividha-niddesa-vaṇṇanā). Commentary on the Discussion of the Higher Knowledges (Abhiññā-kathā-vaṇṇanā): 365.
By way of commentary, demonstrating that [this] is proximate and evident to the immediately preceding discussion of concentration, [the author states]: "This is the development of concentration."
He said: Having stated, "An effort must be made to accomplish the higher knowledges (abhiññā)," he spoke the passage beginning with "For thus" in order to show the specific purpose therein.

Although the state of greater stability and the ease of developing insight (vipassanā) are indeed benefits of developing concentration (samādhi), nevertheless, the five mundane higher knowledges are manifest as the benefits of the aforementioned development of concentration.
"Renowned" (paññātā) refers to the state of having attained benefits by means of those very [powers]; it refers to a state of greater stability through the fourteenfold taming of the mind.
Mastery over the mundane higher knowledges (lokīyābhiññā) is itself mastery over concentration;
and thus, because of the statement, "One who is concentrated understands things as they really are," it is said that "one will accomplish the development of wisdom with ease."

Therefore, since through the development of concentration one gains the benefit of greater stability and the development of wisdom succeeds with ease, we shall begin the discussion of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) first;
the intention is that this is done even though the occasion for the development of wisdom has already arrived.
The connection is that the five mundane direct knowledges were spoken of by the Blessed One. It is not merely the four jhānas alone that are [meant] here in this teaching.

It is not only the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) that is to be accomplished; rather, there is also something else. This is stated for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma in a progressively higher and more refined manner.

"The transformation of supernormal powers" (*iddhivikubbanam*) refers to the act of abandoning one's natural form, which is known as supernormal power. This is said because of the preeminence of the power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) among the various types of supernormal powers.
Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as "the supernormal power and the transformation. [The word] *vikubbanassa* is used separately...
The inclusion [of these] should also be understood by the reason already stated. Formless attainments do not occur by means of the space-kasiṇa;

and as for the light-kasiṇa, it is included within the white-kasiṇa, which is why it was said, "within the limits of the white-kasiṇa," since the intended method is the taming of the mind through the sequence of the kasiṇas beginning with conformity.
However, both of these must certainly be employed for the purpose of creating space and so forth. "Eight and eight."
In each of the kasiṇas as described above, there are eight attainments. "In forward order of the kasiṇas" means according to the sequence of the kasiṇas;
and that sequence should be understood by way of the teaching. However, "in forward order of the jhānas" may also be understood by way of practice.
"Ukkamana" means leaping over; "ukkantika" is simply the state of leaping over. "Jhānukkantika" refers to the leaping over of jhānas; therefore, it means "by leaping over the jhānas."
This is the meaning. From the perspective of the transition between factors and the transcendence of factors:

the mind must be thoroughly tamed so that one may enter the meditative absorptions (jhānas) wherever and whenever desired for the sake of their bliss, and for the sake of clearly discerning those objects.
For it is in this way that his mastery over them is successfully achieved.
366. Regarding the statement "he attains jhāna": does he attain all four kinds of jhāna, or only one at a time?

In this regard, if he were to attain all four, there would be no distinction based on the transition between factors (*aṅga-saṅkantito*). However, if he attains them one by one, there is a distinction based on the transition between objects (*ārammaṇa-saṅkantito*).

This fault does not apply, because their distinction is established through the influence of mental application (*ābhoga*). For when, having applied the mind solely in conformity with the *kasiṇa*, [he proceeds...]
When one attains the jhānas in various kasiṇas without shifting the factors [of the jhāna], that is "conformity with the kasiṇa" (kasiṇānuloma).
But when one attains the jhānas by employing the shifting of factors, then "shifting of factors" (aṅgasaṅkanti) is to be understood.
By this method, the mutual distinction between conformity with the kasiṇa, the shifting of objects, and so forth, should be understood. This is conformity with the kasiṇa.
The intended meaning is that it is called "the taming of the mind.
"In the same way" (tatheva) is the word *tathā* used for the purpose of concluding the statement: "in sequence, even eight times, a hundred times, or a thousand times among the eight kasiṇas.
And here, the sequence is in reverse order; therefore he said, "by way of reverse order."
This is the meaning here: first one enters the jhāna in the white kasiṇa, then in the red kasiṇa, and so on, up to the earth kasiṇa.
"Entering again and again" expresses the frequent practice, as stated by the words "a hundred times, a thousand times."
"In that very same place" means in the earth-kasiṇa itself. "Thereafter" means at the time immediately following emergence from the third jhāna.
"That very same" refers to the earth-kasiṇa itself. "Then, from the base of nothingness" means:

having emerged from the attainment of the base of infinite space—which had proceeded in the space cleared by removing the earth-kasiṇa—and without attending to the base of infinite consciousness, but rather leaping over it, [one attends] to the consciousness of the aforementioned base of infinite space.
In the absence [of the earth-kasiṇa], one enters the base of nothingness that has been set in motion.
Since the space-kasiṇa derived from the removal of the earth-kasiṇa belongs to the same category as the earth-kasiṇa, it is said, "without skipping over the kasiṇa.
Alternatively, the "skipping over of a kasiṇa" here refers to bypassing any one among the eight kasiṇas; thus he says, "without skipping over the kasiṇa."
Regarding the term *jhānukkantika* (skipping meditation), here the intended meaning must be excluded by means of restriction.

Having stated "thus the kasiṇa" and so forth to show the actual nature of the skipping, he spoke again—"thus the water-kasiṇa, etc.… should be practiced"—extending that same method to the remaining kasiṇas together with their supports.
Therefore he said, "by this method," and so forth. Just as...

The progression through the jhānas based on the earth-kasiṇa and so forth was demonstrated by way of the first jhāna; in the same way, that [progression] based on the second jhāna and so forth should also be shown as appropriate.

"That very same" refers to the first jhāna itself. Even in the progression through the kasiṇas, the application based on the water-kasiṇa and so forth should be made according to the method already stated, and likewise, those based on the second jhāna and so forth should be applied as appropriate.

From the red kasiṇa to the base of nothingness: one who adverts to the red kasiṇa and brings it before oneself, through the removal of that kasiṇa, enters the jhāna of the base of infinite space by not attending to the space where the kasiṇa was removed;
then, making the disappearance of the consciousness that previously occurred there its object, one enters the base of nothingness.
The others are the remaining fine-material-sphere jhānas.
For there is no shifting of factors in the immaterial jhānas, nor do they occur with the earth kasiṇa as their object.

As for what was said regarding the shifting of factors and objects—namely, "having discarded the blue kasiṇa, [one attains] the base of infinite space," and so on—that was stated according to what is actually found [in practice], by way of a figurative expression (pariyāya).

It should be understood thus. However, in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), just as the transformation of factors (*aṅga-saṅkanti*) is found only in the fine-material jhānas, so too the transformation of the object (*ārammaṇa-saṅkanti*) is found only in the immaterial jhānas.

For the transformation of the object consists in the occurrence of that very same jhāna upon a different object. Therefore he said: "The attainment of the same single jhāna upon all the kasiṇas is called the transformation of the object."
Just as it cannot be said that the phrase "in all kasiṇas" includes the space and consciousness kasiṇas as well—

since here only eight kasiṇas are attained— likewise it cannot be said that all immaterial jhānas constitute "one jhāna," because the taming of the mind is intended to be achieved through eight attainments.
Therefore, it should be understood that the transition of factors and objects is stated by way of the immaterial jhānas according to a figurative method (*pariyāya*).
For instance, with reference to the base of infinite consciousness—which has as its object the first immaterial-sphere consciousness in the space revealed by the yellow kasiṇa—it is said:
"Having attained the base of infinite consciousness from the yellow kasiṇa. This same method applies to the remaining two cases as well.
The meaning should be understood as follows. Regarding the phrase "by way of skipping" (*ekantarikavasena*): elsewhere the word *antara* has a different sense.
That which is simply an interval (*antara*) is *antarika*; that in which there is an interval occurring at single intervals is *ekantarika*, namely the attainment of jhāna, and it is by way of that.
Just as there is a difference among the factors and the object when they occur together, so too is there a difference by way of the manner of attaining [the jhānas].
However, that distinction arises by way of the surmounting of those lower factors and objects; thus it is said:

"The transition occurs by skipping over factors and objects alternately. When the factors have been defined as "this jhāna has five factors" and so forth, and the objects have been defined as "this is the earth-kasiṇa" and so forth, [the transition occurs] by bringing them together.
Since there is no distinction in the process of defining [the factors], this method is not adopted in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
And having done so, even though skipping over jhānas and so forth—in reverse order, in both direct and reverse order, and by skipping every other one—is possible, it has not been mentioned;
for even without those methods, the taming of the mind is accomplished, and thus [this] was omitted to avoid prolixity.
Or it should be understood that these [details] have not been included in the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā).

367. "One who has not developed what was to be developed" means one who has not performed the preliminary work regarding the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and direct knowledges (abhiññā). Regarding this, some say it refers even to one who lacks the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya).
"Initial work" (ādikamma) is the first stage of yoga practice; one who possesses this is an "initiate" (ādikammika), meaning one who has not previously cultivated familiarity.
"Devoted to meditation" means one who is intent upon the practice of development; therefore, he says "the practitioner of yoga" (*yogāvacara*). Even the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa* is a burden:

the practice within the *kasiṇa*-mandala according to the method of avoiding faults and so forth, until the arising of the learning-sign (*uggaha-nimitta*), is called the preliminary work for the *kasiṇa*, and that indeed is a burden, let alone the transformation of psychic power (*iddhi-vikubbanā*)—this is the intended meaning. "The production of the sign" refers to the production of the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*). That...
"Having increased" means having increased both that sign and the meditation. For the increase of the sign cannot be attained without meditation.

Since there are many who, having attained access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), are unable to reach absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*), he said, "The attainment of absorption is a burden.
Alternatively, "the attainment of absorption" refers to the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
He speaks of realization. He says, "The supporting condition for the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) is one thing, and that for the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) is another;

thus, even for one whose mind is fully subdued, the transformation of psychic power (*iddhivikubbana*) is called a burden. "Quickly perceiving" (*khippanisanti*) means the act of perceiving—that is, seeing with the eye of meditation (*jhānacakkhu*) the objects of meditation such as the earth-kasina—and so forth.
One who possesses this is "one who quickly perceives"; one who enters into meditation more swiftly. The state of being such is "the state of quickly perceiving" (*khippanisantibhāva*).
Therambatthala is the place where the Elder Mahāmahinda and others descended, which is covered by ambatara trees.

The passage beginning with “Therefore” was spoken to show this point: just as warriors roam about taking up stainless swords, lances, and so forth for the sake of conquering their adversaries, so too must a bhikkhu employ the stainless meditative absorptions (jhānas) and direct knowledges (abhiññās) for the sake of conquering the defilements (kilesas).
"Being a support" here is intended to mean the allaying of another's misfortune.
For that is more weighty than even the quality of being quick to respond, because it must be performed as an accomplishment of an urgent task and because it is difficult to bring about.
Although this is established by the example of the Elder Rakkhita alone, it is further elucidated by the protection afforded during the rain of embers, which is even more weighty than that.
“...for the Giribhaṇḍavāhana festival... the Elder [acted] thus,” he said.

The so-called Giribhaṇḍavāhana festival is a great island-wide offering beginning from Cetiyagiri, extending across the entire island and out into the ocean for a distance of one *yojana*. “Having fashioned the earth”:
as soon as the shower of embers unleashed by Māra reached even a mere spark’s distance from humans, he immediately [stretched it out] in the sky.
Having created the earth.

"Due to powerful prior application" means due to those great resolves (*mahābhinīhāra*) which serve as the cause for the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and so forth, which have a more substantial material basis.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the Chief Disciples and so forth," certain other Great Disciples are included. This is the sequence of development (*bhāvanānukkama*).

The aforementioned taming of the mind. Regarding the phrase "the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and so forth," it should be understood that by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhānañāṇa) and others are also included, not merely the remaining direct knowledges (abhiññā).
For even among disciples (sāvaka), the knowledge of what is possible and impossible and other such powers succeed to a certain extent.
Therefore—because for one who has fulfilled the prior causes, the direct knowledges [arise] without the aforementioned sequence of development.
They succeed for one [who possesses these], but not for another; therefore. "By means of heating the fire, pounding, and so forth" means by means of heating, pounding, and so on, applied to the fire.

And by the word "and" (*ca*), it includes even the pounding of lac and so forth, though not explicitly mentioned, as in the case of lac-makers and others. "By way of zeal (*chanda*)... and so forth" means:

"If supernormal knowledge (*abhiññā*) is accomplished for one who has zeal, it will be accomplished for me too"—thus taking the desire to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) as the head and the primary burden.
This is by way of entering the jhāna after making the first [jhāna] the forerunner, or after generating desire for it, or after making that the portal for its development.

This same method applies to the remaining [jhānas] as well. The phrase “by way of mastery over adverting and so forth” is said with reference to the attainment of preeminent mastery in all eight attainments. And that is indeed from the standpoint of a beginner.
He says, "Not by way of having performed the preliminary work," [adding] "The prior cause... is sufficient.

For one who is endowed with a prior cause, it is intended that while mastery must indeed have been practiced to a high degree (*sātisaya*) in that very jhāna which is made the basis for producing the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), this need not be the case for all [jhānas].
This is because of the statement, "by one who has practiced mastery in the fourth jhāna alone," [which implies that] the formless attainments (*arūpasamāpatti*)...
They say that [these powers] succeed even without direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). If that was said with reference to one who is endowed with past causes, it is indeed appropriate;
but if it refers to another, it is merely their own opinion. "In what way" (*yathā*) means by whatever manner or method.
"In this" (*ettha*) means in this accomplishment of the supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).
368. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that very same place. "In accordance with the method of the text" (*pāḷinayānusārena*) means by following the course of the text;

the meaning is: by following the sequence of the commentary on the recitation. Having stated, "He dwells having attained the fourth jhāna," he says, "the yogi who has attained the fourth jhāna," because the word "he" (*so*) was used.
Regarding the phrase "when [the mind] is thus concentrated" (*evaṃ samāhite*), the word "thus" (*evaṃ*)—

It is said, "‘Thus’ is an indication of the sequence of the fourth jhāna," for the purpose of illustrating the attainment of the fourth jhāna-concentration established through the successive order of attaining the three lower jhānas. It is an illustration both of the fourth jhāna and of the sequence of its attainment;
that is, it is an illustration of both the concentration of the fourth jhāna and the specific order of attainment by which that concentration was acquired.

This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “By this... it is stated. Although the word “thus” (evaṃ) indicates the attainment of the fourth jhāna together with the attainment of arrival, nevertheless, because the concentration of purity of mindfulness (satipārisuddhisamādhi) alone is the primary factor as the basis for supernormal power (iddhi), he said:
“concentrated by means of the concentration of the fourth jhāna. [The phrase] “by way of the state of purity of mindfulness and equanimity” (upekkhāsatipārisuddhibhāvena)...
Because of the presence of the purity of mindfulness produced by equanimity (*upekkhā*).

For when the purity-equanimity (*pārisuddhi-upekkhā*)—which is purified of all opposing states and secondary defilements (*upakkilesa*), and which remains unoccupied even with regard to the opposing factors—is present, the fourth jhāna and its associated mental states become perfectly pure and exceedingly clear; however, the teaching there is given under the heading of mindfulness (*sati*).

To the question "In what way?", he says: "By way of the purity of mindfulness and equanimity. He further says: "It is precisely through the purity [itself] that there is a specific mode of occurrence due to a specific condition;
this is 'radiance' (*pariyodātatā*), just as the brilliance of well-polished gold results from its rubbing.
Therefore, it is said: 'Because of its purity, it is radiant; it is luminous.'"
"By the destruction of the conditions for pleasure, etc. means by the suppression, respectively, of the conditions for lust and hatred that are pleasure and joy, and pain and grief.
For it has been said: "Pleasure is a condition for joy; joy is a condition for lust;
pain is a condition for grief. Just as lust and the others are called "stains" (*aṅgaṇāni*) because they are impurities and filth of the mind...
They are called "defilements" (*upakkilesa*) in the sense of defiling; thus he said, "Because it is free from blemish, it is devoid of defilement.
Therefore he said, "For by means of a blemish that mind becomes defiled," the meaning being that it is oppressed and tormented.
"Because it is well-developed" means because it has been thoroughly cultivated by bringing it to a state of proficiency. Therefore he said, "Having attained mastery."
The meaning is that it has attained mastery through the fivefold or fourteenfold taming by means of adverting and so forth.
For a mind that abides under control is said to be "well-massaged" like leather due to its attainment of proficiency, and "well-processed" like lac.
"Capable of work" (*kammakkhama*) means capable of performing works of supernormal power (*iddhi*), such as transformation and so forth. And "both of those" refers to...
The pair: softness and wieldiness.
In the passage beginning with "I do not," the word *na* has the sense of negation. "I" (*aham*) is the Teacher referring to himself.

"O monks" (*bhikkhave*) is an address to the monks. "Another" (*aññam*) means other than the consciousness that is about to be described. "Even a single dhamma" (*ekadhammam pi*) means even a single dhamma possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"I do not perceive" is the connection [of the sentence]. This is the meaning here:

"Monks, even when looking with the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), I do not perceive even a single other thing which, when developed by attaining mastery and made much-practiced through repeated performance, thus reaches a state of especially refined pliancy and becomes fit for action."
And it becomes workable. He says this because "this mind" is evident both to himself and to them.
Just as the aforementioned qualities such as purity do not disappear, so too is the mind well-developed.
In that regard, it is said here that it is "steadied" and "attained to imperturbability"; thus he says: "In these [qualities] such as purity..."
"Because they are established, they are steady; because they are established, they have reached imperturbability.
Just as softness and wieldiness characterize the attainment of mastery, so too the attainment of mastery is characterized by softness and wieldiness.
Or, because they abide under their own control due to their state of softness and wieldiness, they are said to be "steady. For just as a fruit is determined by its cause, [so too is this].
In this way, the cause is determined by its fruit; thus, "attaining imperturbability" (*āneñjappatti*) refers to remaining steadfast through an unshakable state.

And since that [steadfastness] arises through the stability of associated states and through being rendered unworkable by opposing factors, it occurs by the power of the faculties such as faith (*saddhā*);
therefore, the summarized meaning is stated as "because they are embraced by faith and the other [faculties], they have attained imperturbability."

To explain this, it is said: “Saddhāpariggahitaṃ hī” (for it is embraced by faith), and so forth. Therein, “embraced by faith” means that this mind—thus well-developed and having attained mastery—is embraced by the faith that occurs in the realization:
“This leads exclusively to the direct realization through higher knowledge of those states that are to be realized through higher knowledge”;
it is supported by the aforementioned power of faith.
"By lack of faith": by means of that lack of faith which is its opposite, it does not waver, does not shake, and does not tremble;
rather, it stands firm precisely because it brings about further distinction.

The meaning in the phrases "sustained by energy" and so forth should be understood by this same method. However, this is the distinction: "sustained by energy" refers to the means for achieving mastery and subduing [the mind].
"Supported by energy": it is supported by energy in the aforementioned frequent practice of development.
"Encompassed by mindfulness": it is supported by mindfulness—which effects non-forgetfulness and investigates the courses of wholesome states. "Encompassed by concentration":
it is supported by concentration, which accomplishes non-distraction in that very same state. "Encompassed by wisdom": [it is supported] by that...
It is supported by wisdom characterized by the discernment of phenomena that are helpful or unhelpful for meditation.

"Attained to illumination" means accompanied by the illumination of knowledge. For, seeing the side of defilement as it truly is through knowledge—which has become an illumination and is nourished by the aforementioned concentration—one overcomes it by being terrified and shrinking away from it.
One is not overcome by that. Therefore he said: "He does not waver due to the darkness of the defilements.

By this, he shows the power of moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) which is embraced by knowledge. "Endowed with the eight factors" refers to being concentrated, purified, and cleansed by the concentration of the fourth jhāna.
“Being without blemish, being free from defilements, pliancy, wieldiness, stability through the attainment of imperturbability,
and these factors of a concentrated mind”— having thus taken these eight factors individually rather than taking the phrase "in a concentrated mind" merely as a description of its state,
[the mind] is endowed with these eight factors. "Capable of directing itself" means for the purpose of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) and so forth.

It is capable of being directed toward the resolution (abhinīhāra) and fit for application toward that [goal]. Therefore he said: "for the direct realization through higher knowledge of those states that are to be realized through higher knowledge.
Granted that the attainment of the first jhāna occurs only after the hindrances have been suppressed, yet when applied thought (vitakka) and the rest are stilled...
And although there is likewise the attainment of the second jhāna and so forth, nevertheless, they are not as far removed or departed from those [hindrances] as they are from the fourth jhāna.

Because of its complete liberation from the hindrances and so on—which cause agitation and mental effort characterized by the mind’s turbidity—its purity and luminosity are appropriate; thus he said, "from the hindrances... purified."
"Conditioned by the attainment of jhāna" means having the attainment of jhāna as their cause; that is, those things that arise depending upon the attainment of jhāna. "Evil" means base or inferior.
"Belonging to the sphere of desire" means belonging to the range of desire, having descended through the power of desire—those [thoughts] occurring in such a manner as:
"Oh, may the Teacher himself, after repeatedly questioning me, teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus! and so forth.
[This refers to] conceit, deceit, fraud, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "covetousness and so forth," those very same [defilements] are included.

Furthermore, covetousness here is not suppressible by the first jhāna; conceit and the others should be understood as being associated with it, because the phrase "due to the conditions for the attainment of jhāna" continues to apply.
However, those that are suppressible are already included by the mention of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). But how [is this] by the first jhāna?

"Do they disappear here without being suppressed? This was said by way of the practice of effacement (*sallekha*), on the basis that "all wholesome states are the opposites of all unwholesome states," in order to show that jhāna is not something to be clung to (*aparāmaṭṭha*).
However, those [defilements] referred to here by the phrases "covetousness and so forth within the sphere of desire" include anger, its conditions, sensual lust, ill will, and the rest.
Based on their own intention, they reject the reading "of the conditions for the attainment of jhāna" and claim that the reading should be "of the opposites to the attainment of jhāna.
However, this is merely their own opinion, as such a reading does not exist at all.

Furthermore, it is illogical to speak of the removal of the hindrances and their associates—which are the opposites to the attainment of jhāna—and then subsequently urge the disappearance of their non-existence.
"But surely this meaning is not found in the Anaṅgaṇa-sutta and the Vattha-sutta, because only gross evil qualities are intended there?
True, that is so; however, since what is stated here is by way of one who has attained the fourth jhāna, only those subtle [qualities] are included.
The reference to those suttas here is made on the common ground of their being "stains" (aṅgaṇa) and "defilements" (upakkilesa). Likewise...

For it is said, "according to the Suttas," and not "by way of the Suttas. This must certainly be accepted as such, because even for some who have attained jhāna, there still exists the occurrence of the sphere of desire (icchāvacara).

"By approaching the state of being a basis for success" means by approaching the state of being a foundation (padaṭṭhāna) for the basis of success (iddhipāda). "By the fulfillment of development" means...
Because of the perfection of the development of the resolve through the absence of anything further to be done;
and because of the attainment of a refined state—meaning by virtue of having been brought to a state of excellence for that very reason, and in the sense of being insatiable.
Both of these are statements of the cause for stability, [resulting] from the attainment of a refined state once the development is perfected.
“‘Steadfast’ (ṭhite): ‘Attained to imperturbability’ (āneñjappatte) is a qualification of that steadfastness. Therefore he said: ‘Steadfast in such a way as to have attained imperturbability.
In this alternative, both ‘steadfast’ and ‘attained to imperturbability’ together constitute one factor, while ‘concentrated’ (samāhite) is another single factor.
It is with reference to its distinction from the first alternative that he said: ‘Thus it is endowed with eight factors.’”

Commentary on the Discourse on the Ten Attainments (Dasaiddhikathāvaṇṇanā) 369. “In the sense of accomplishment” means in the sense of being perfected. “In the sense of acquisition” means in the sense of reaching.
“That” refers to the desired object. “Is accomplished” means it is brought to completion. Here, “renunciation” (nekkhamma) extends from the going-forth (pabbajjā) up to the jhānas and the paths.
“Ijjhati” means it is attained. “Paṭiharatīti pāṭihāriyan” means it is called a miracle (pāṭihāriya) because it carries away (harati) and removes (apaneti) its opposite;

therefore, it is a miracle. It carries away its own opposite, thus it is “paṭihāriya”; renunciation and so forth are themselves the “paṭihāriya,” and that which is a *paṭihāriya* is a *pāṭihāriya*, just as in the cases of “vekataṃ” and “vesamaṃ.”

"In the sense of succeeding" means in the sense of accomplishment. "By the perfection of means" means for one who possesses the right means; the meaning is "one who undertakes in accordance with the proper method. "Succeeds" means it brings forth [its fruit]. "Virtuous" means virtuous by way of moral conduct (ācāra-sīla). "Of beautiful character" means one whose nature is excellent by way of the ten courses of wholesome action (dasakusala-kammapatha);
or, he is "virtuous" through the perfection of virtue, and "of beautiful character" by way of the remaining bases for meritorious action such as generosity (dāna) and so forth.
"Paṇidahissati" means he will aspire.

"Ijjhanti" means they increase; the sense is that they reach their peak. For *iddhi* is spoken of in the sense of success, attainment, achievement, accomplishment, and growth—especially distinguished success.
"That is tenfold" refers to all types of *iddhi* brought together here according to the method of enumerating their meanings.
This was said in order to demonstrate supernormal power (*iddhi*). It is called "resolution" (*adhiṭṭhānā*) because it possesses the resolving or fixing upon states such as multiplicity and so forth.
It is called "transformation" (*vikubbanā*) because it possesses the performing of various creations consisting of the manifestation of forms.

It is called "mind-made" (*manomayā*) because it is produced by means of the mind of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). It is called "the expansion of knowledge" (*ñāṇavipphārā*) because it possesses the forcefulness or momentum of knowledge.

Through the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphārā*). They go toward the noble ones, thus they are "noble" (*ariyā*). Psychic power born from the ripening of karma from any source whatsoever is "kamma-vipāka-born.

Psychic power produced by preeminent merit is "the psychic power of one possessing merit. It should be understood that this is the distinction between these two: kamma-vipāka-born psychic power exists from birth onwards, whereas the other exists whenever there is the time for the ripening of merit. [The latter] is produced through the science of *āthabbaṇa*.
Consisting of clear knowledge (*vijjāmayā*). Right application (*sammāpayoga*) is the employment of means, the undertaking of the method.
370. "By nature one" (*pakatiyā eko*) means one by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāvena*). "Many" (*bahukaṃ*) means much.

Having shown the manifoldness of what is to be resolved upon by means of that [term] which has no fixed limit, he says "or a hundred," etc., in order to show it again by way of a definite limit. "He adverts" (*āvajjati*).
He applies himself with an effort known as preliminary work (*parikamma*) toward the form to be manifested; he attends to it by means of that preliminary mental attention (*manasikāra*).

"He resolves with knowledge" means that having performed the preliminary work in such a manner, he resolves upon the many forms intended through the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*);
because the state of multiplicity is attained simultaneously with the resolving consciousness, this is the knowledge of the supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) that brings about multiplicity.
And while causing it to proceed, one is said to "resolve" (*adhiṭṭhāti*) in that manner. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
The word *evaṃ* has the sense of "manner"; by it, all modes of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) are included.
"By way of resolution" means because it is accomplished by way of the resolution described thus: "one resolves with knowledge."

371. *Pakativaṇṇan* means the natural configuration, one’s own ordinary form. *By way of the transformation consisting in the relinquishing of one’s own natural form* means by way of the transformation of form, such as the form of a youth, which is preceded by the relinquishing of one’s own natural form.
372. *From this body*: what is called "this" is the bhikkhu’s physical body (*karajakāya*), spoken of as such because it is present to direct perception.

*Another body*: another body made of supernormal power (*iddhimaya*). Precisely because it possesses a form made of supernormal power, it is "material" (*rūpin*). By means of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
It is "mind-made" (manomaya) because it is produced from the mind. "By way of production" means by way of being brought forth.

For just as the mind-made body is produced through the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa), so too its occurrence is "mind-made psychic power" (manomayiddhi). This same method applies to the remaining types as well.

If this is so, how is it that only this specific one is called "mind-made psychic power"? It should be understood that this is a conventional usage (ruḷhī), just as in the expression "the mind-made selfhood" (manomayo attabhāvo).
Or, for example, as the designation "cow" applies to a lump of matter possessing horns and so forth.

Alternatively, it should be understood that when this creation has emerged from within and is entirely similar to the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimat*), the application of the term "mind-made" (*manomaya*) is particularly evident because its state of being produced by the mind is clearly manifest;
it is not so [evident] in other cases such as the powers of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) or transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*), which possess different designations.

"Prior to the arising of knowledge" means either prior to the arising of the knowledge of the path to Arahantship during the moment of insight (vipassanā), or even prior to that, starting from the moment of taking rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) for one in their final existence. "Or afterwards" means until the parinibbāna of the aggregates.
"Or at that very moment" means at the time when the path arises. The "distinction produced by the power of knowledge" is like the place where the sun has risen.

And just as there is the capacity to produce light on all sides, so too, through the power of that very knowledge, there arises a specific excellence characterized by the complete fulfillment of the abandoning of what is to be abandoned and the developing of what is to be developed. As for the "bases," they are mentioned by way of being free from obstacles.
"By the contemplation of impermanence" means by strong insight that contemplates formations as impermanent. For one who has commenced insight...

For at the moment of the aforementioned insight, as well as before and after it—in the section on miscellaneous comprehension—the meaning of the abandoning of the perception of permanence is accomplished. This same method applies everywhere.
Granted that the intended meaning is indeed revealed even by this brief exposition, it becomes even clearer through a detailed exposition; therefore, he says, "it should be explained in detail."

“Even while still in the womb”: this is a genitive used in a sense of disregard (anādare). “In the manner stated”: in the manner stated in the story of the Elder Bākula, beginning with the words “of one in his final existence.
“Having made it a load of wood”: having placed the load of wood on the cart; the meaning is, having loaded it. “Having abandoned”: having discarded.
“At the base of the cart”: near the cart. “Haunted by fierce yakkhas”: to be frequented by cruel yakkhas.
For the city of Rājagaha was possessed by yakkhas.
"From concentration" means from the first jhāna and so forth. "Before" refers to the moment of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna).

"After" refers to the conclusion of the practice of the attainment (samāpatti). "At that moment" refers to the moment of having entered the attainment. "The distinction produced by the power of serenity" (samatha) [is thus explained].

The distinction—consisting of the suppression of the hindrances, the transcendence of applied thought (*vitakka*), and so forth, as well as the endurance of the perils of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha*)—is produced by the power of concentration (*samādhi-teja*) in each respective *jhāna*.
"In the Pigeon Cave" (*kapotakandarāyaṃ*) means in a forest monastery of that name. "On a moonlit night" (*juṇhāya rattiyā*) means on a night possessed of moonlight.

"With freshly grown hair" (*navoropitehi kesehi*) is an instrumental case used to indicate a characteristic state (*itthambhūta-lakkhaṇe*). "Of which" (*yassā*) refers to the blow. "Of that" (*tassā*)...
Because the state of being quick to attend [to others] had reached its highest excellence, the Elder entered attainment at the very moment the yakkha struck him;
thus it is said, "he offered attainment at the time of the blow.
However, in the Pāḷi it is stated: "He was seated, having entered a certain concentration. But these elders, at the very moment of emerging from attainment...
They say that he gave him a blow.
"The Elder Sañjīva" refers to the Great Elder who was the second chief disciple of the Blessed One Kakusandha.
For that venerable one, wherever he sat—in the forest or elsewhere—he would very easily enter into the attainment of cessation (nirodha).

Therefore, one day at the foot of a certain tree he entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); it was with reference to this that it was said, “having attained cessation,” and so forth.
He did not burn even a mere thread of cloth; what need is there to mention his body?
For that very reason, the elder was known as “Sañjīva. This is his—meaning, of this venerable elder Sañjīva, who...

The absence of the danger of fire during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—this is to be construed as "the supernormal power (*iddhi*) resulting from the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphārā*).
But how can there be the occurrence of the expansion of concentration during the attainment of cessation? To this he says: "Because of the successive... [and so on] ...being produced.
"Of the goods first set aside" means of the goods set aside at the very beginning; for at the time of taking them up, [they were placed there].
The very last one is grasped. "By way of a time limit" means by way of a time limit established prior to entering the attainment, thinking, "I shall emerge after such a length of time has passed.
"Terrified, they cried out" means that in the darkness of night, seeing a form, they imagined, "A *pisāca* demon is rising up!
[He was] completely covered with such a quantity of goods, yet remained unperturbed, [thinking], "Oh!"...
“Of great power! Oh, what a dweller in solitude!”—thus [he spoke] with faith directed toward the Elder.

“A cauldron of boiling oil”: by means of the term for the receptacle (*ādhāra*), he refers to that which is contained within it; the intention is that he poured the boiling oil from the cauldron using the cauldron itself. “Whirling about”: moving upward without clinging to anything whatsoever.

“Together with her retinue”: accompanied by five hundred women as her retinue. “He suffused the king with loving-kindness”: he touched the king through the attainment of directed loving-kindness (*odissaka-mettā-samāpatti*). “To shoot”: to pierce. “To remove”: to withdraw the armor from his body.
375. "In regard to the repulsive, etc. means in regard to the undesirable, etc. For what is undesirable is repulsive (*paṭikkūla*), and even what is unpleasant is called "repulsive.
By the word "etc.," one includes the non-repulsive and so forth. "Therein" means in regard to the repulsive object. "Equanimous" means equanimous by way of the sixfold equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*).
"Therein" means in regard to the basis that is divided into the repulsive and non-repulsive. "Mindful" means through the attainment of the fullness of mindfulness (*sativipula*).
“Mindful” (satimā). “Clearly comprehending” (sampajāno) means one who acts with clear comprehension through the attainment of the full expansion of wisdom (paññā).

“This” refers to this mastery over the mind (cittissariyatā) of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavā), established by the attainment of the supreme path, which consists in dwelling with the perception of non-repulsiveness toward objects that are repulsive and so forth. Therefore he said:
“Of those who have attained mastery over the mind... it is said.”

In regard to an unattractive object designated as "sentient being," one should apply the following: either the pervasion with loving-kindness (*mettā*), or the attention to elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) through reflection according to the elements, or the attention to elements regarding things such as excrement.

"He dwells perceiving no repulsiveness" means that, through the desire for their welfare and by reflecting on the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), he dwells in his postures without perceiving repulsiveness. Regarding the attractive...

Regarding the objects such as relatives and friends: "merely a portion of impurity consisting of hair and so forth" refers either to the pervasion of the foul (*asubha-pharaṇa*) or to the attention directed toward the foul (*asubha-manasikāra*).
In that context, the word *iti* has the sense of "the collection of material phenomena is impermanent," and so forth; therefore, the construction is:

"or one who attends to them as being impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change. Regarding "the repulsive and the non-repulsive": this refers to desirable and undesirable objects taken together.
Having grasped [the object], he speaks. This same method applies to the other case as well.

Or, regarding that which first appears to beings as repulsive but later appears as non-repulsive, and that which first appears as non-repulsive but later appears as repulsive—the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), if he so desires, may perceive either of these two as non-repulsive according to the method described.
"Or he should dwell perceiving repulsiveness"—this is called noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*).

"Having seen a form with the eye": by means of the visual consciousness capable of seeing forms—which is conventionally designated as "the eye" in the sense of being its instrument—or having seen a form by means of the eye as the instrumental cause, or as the door [of perception]. Neither...
"He is glad" is a negation of the joy based on household life, not of the feeling of joy associated with the side of renunciation.

"Six-factored equanimity" refers to the equanimity of mental neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*) which occurs at the six sense doors; it is named "six-factored equanimity" because its characteristic is the non-abandonment of its naturally pure state throughout the course of the six desirable and undesirable objects. Regarding the meaning as it has been stated:
To support this from the Pāli, the words beginning with "of the analytical knowledges" (*paṭisambhidāya*) and so forth were stated.
Regarding "of birds, etc.," the word "etc. includes gods and others. Furthermore, regarding "such as traveling through the air," the word "etc.
includes the purification of the eye and other such qualities. Even though [the state] has been produced by wholesome kamma, it is experienced through the influence of unwholesome ripening.

"Of those fallen into the states of misery" (vinipātikānaṃ) means because they have fallen from a happy existence. "Jhāna" is said with reference to jhāna that has attained direct knowledge (abhiññā).

As for "or insight" (vipassanaṃ vā), it is stated because even insight, when it has reached its peak and is accompanied by uplifting rapture (ubbegapīti), is sufficient to cause one to leap into the air.
"Of the beings of the first eon" (paṭhamakappikānaṃ) should be understood as a qualification of "of certain humans."
"Evamādīnaṃ" (of these and so forth): by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of Punabbasu, Mātā, and others is to be understood.
377. "Vehāsaṃ": this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative, or it denotes continuous connection.

For a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), having placed the Wheel-treasure in front and ascended from his own palace, proceeds through the air alone, keeping Sineru to his right, throughout the entire Cakkavāḷa world-system.
"Anusaṃyāyati" means follows along. "Assabandhā" refers to horse-keepers, those who provide fodder for horses; likewise for "gobandhā" (cow-keepers).

Since there would be excessive prolixity if the expansion of the supernatural power (*iddhi*) of wheel-turning monarchs and others were detailed, [the author], while intending to show the characteristic of the power of one possessing merit by stating, "It is a specific success when the equipment of merit has reached maturity," nevertheless mentions the case of Jotika and others.
The passage beginning with “And here” was stated in order to show a portion of the power of merit (*puññiddhi*).
Therein, “a mountain of gold” (*suvaṇṇapabbata*) refers to a mountain made entirely of gold; it is said that no trace of its removal is visible at the spot from which it has been taken.

“A furrow as wide as a plowshare” (*ekasītāmatta*): here, a *sītā* is a path made by a plow for the purpose of tilling. A *tumba* is a measure of capacity (*āḷhaka*). “Fourteen paths” (*cuddasa magga*) means fourteen tilled furrows.

378. *Vijjaṃ parijapitvā* means having recited one’s own spell (*vijjā*), such as the *Gandhārī-vijjā*, which has been mastered through practice, by reciting it according to the sequence of the mantra.
379. *Sammāpayogena* means by means of a proper method; that is, by undertaking the application of the principle in such a way that the desired goal is accomplished.
*Tassa tassa kammassa* refers to the specific action intended to be performed. And here, *tattha*... [the rest of the passage].

In this context, even in the exposition of this tenth supernormal power (*iddhi*)—defined as "success in the sense of accomplishment through the condition of right application"—it is "similar to the preceding text.

This means it is similar to the expositions of the supernormal powers such as the "emanation of concentration" (*samādhivipphāra-iddhi*). The phrase "by way of forming the wagon-array and so forth" connects to the idea that there is a specific manifestation produced by way of arranging the wagon-array (*sakaṭabyūha*), the wheel-array (*cakkabyūha*), the lotus-array (*padumabyūha*), and others.
The work of crafts includes mathematics, music, and so forth. The work of medicine includes surgery and so forth. Regarding the three Vedas, beginning with the *Iruveda*:

because the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) alone is included in such passages as “having been one, he becomes many,” it is said that “only the supernormal power of resolution has come down.
However, in this context—meaning in this matter consisting of the benefits of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), or in this matter consisting of the various kinds of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).

380. Regarding the phrase “a single mode of knowledge” (*ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu*) and so forth, the word *vidha* has the sense of a “division” (*koṭṭhāsa*), as in “he displays various military arrays” (*vividhampi senābyūhaṃ dasseti*). In this context, both meanings are applicable; thus he says:

“‘Of the modes of success’ (*iddhividhāya*) means ‘of a division of success’ (*iddhikoṭṭhāsāya*) or ‘of a variety of success’ (*iddhivikappāya*). For success (*iddhi*) is one division among the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), as will be explained.”

"And with many varieties through their divisions. "By way of the aforementioned types" means by way of the fourteen types of mental subduing already mentioned, and by way of the types such as concentration (*samāhitatā*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "for the supernormal power (*iddhividhā*)," he says "for the sake of attaining the supernormal powers" because it is a term expressing the accomplishment of that purpose.
"Having withdrawn from the kasiṇa object"—this refers to the preliminary minds (*parikammacitta*) that serve as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
This was stated by way of having a common mental continuum, not because the preliminary consciousness has the kasiṇa as its object.
"He directs it toward the modes of supernormal power" means he causes it to proceed by way of being oriented toward the modes of supernormal power that are to be accomplished.

For that very proceeding of the preliminary consciousness in the form of "May I be many," and so forth, is its "directing" (abhinīhāra), and it is also the directing toward the modes of supernormal power.

Likewise, because the various kinds of supernormal power (iddhividha) proceed from such an inclination, "inclination" here refers to the preliminary-work consciousness in the context of supernormal power;
thus he said, "it makes the mind inclined toward and leaning toward the supernormal powers to be attained.
Showing that "attaining," "touching," "realizing," and "reaching" are merely synonyms, he said, "the meaning is 'it reaches'. "Assa" means "of the various kinds of supernormal power."

The particle *pi* in the phrase "even one" (*ekopi*) has the sense of a collective totality (*sampiṇḍana*), taking into account the multiplicity that is about to be described. Its counterpart is expressed as:

"Having been even one, he becomes manifold; having been manifold, he becomes one. Furthermore, this refers to the attainment of oneness occurring in the interval while he remains after having manifested multiplicity.
However, the attainment of oneness through his own inherent power occurs according to the specific limitation of time.

Here, this [term] is not intended because it lacks the state of being fixed or constructed. Some say that even that is indeed "the power of psychic success" (*iddhānubhāva*) because it is established by way of a previously determined time limit.
Alternatively, the particle *pi* here is used out of place; the connection is: "having been one, he becomes many, and having been many, he becomes one.
In this interpretation, the particle *pi* refers to the state of oneness that is about to be mentioned.
Having stated, “the meaning is ‘a collective sense’,” everything beginning with “for he” and so forth should be explained as appropriate.

To show the purpose for the creation of many [forms], it was said, “in the presence of many,” and so forth. Therein, “in the presence of many” means in the vicinity of the many [beings] created by himself;
the intention is that he is surrounded by them. The word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative.
By this, such phrases as "desiring to speak on the Dhamma" and so forth are included. This should be connected by supplying the words: "It becomes thus for one who is resolved through knowledge. 381.

*Bhūmiyo* (planes) means that psychic powers (*iddhi*) exist therein; [here] they refer to the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). The locative case in *ettha* (therein) expresses the sense of cause. From seclusion...
The stage that has arisen is the "stage born of seclusion. For the first jhāna is "born of seclusion" because it arises from the seclusion of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

The stage consisting of rapture and pleasure is the "stage of rapture and pleasure. For the second jhāna is both the stage consisting of rapture and pleasure and that in which rapture and pleasure have arisen, by way of concentration.
The same method applies to the two stages above as well. "For the attainment of success" means for the acquisition of success (*iddhi*). "For the obtaining of success" means...

"By repeatedly obtaining supernormal power (iddhi)" means for the sake of its frequent practice. "By the transformation of supernormal power" means by means of supernormal power producing various forms;
the sense is "by the supernormal power of transformation. "By the diffusion of supernormal power" means by means of supernormal power producing various benefits.
"By mastery over supernormal power" means for the sake of attaining mastery such as rapid attainment and so forth. "By fearlessness regarding supernormal power" [means...]
Because of the removal of the opposites of supernormal power (*iddhi*), because of the absence of defilement, and because of being thoroughly confident.
Now, let the fourth jhāna be the ground for supernormal power, since it is to be accomplished by being established therein; but how are the others?
To this he says, "And here," and so forth. Therein, the connection is that the three jhānas should be understood as the ground of equipment (*sambhāra*).

In the third jhāna, it is by means of the pervasion of bliss; in the first and second, it is by means of the pervasion of rapture and the pervasion of bliss acting as causes—this is the application according to what is appropriate.

And here, "pervasion" refers to the nourishment of the mental body (nāmakāya) co-nascent with the conditions for jhāna, etc., through the influence of the exceptionally refined rapture and bliss resulting from the well-developed state of the jhāna, and of the material body (rūpakāya) through the [material] phenomena originating therefrom.
It is the state of being suffused with more sublime forms. Therefore the Blessed One said: “He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses [the body] with rapture and pleasure.
“Perception of pleasure” means perception accompanied by the pleasure of jhāna. “Perception of lightness” means perception accompanied by the lightness associated with that [jhāna].
“Having entered” means having penetrated; for in those jhānas, there is a perception associated with an exceptional degree of lightness.
It is said that the yogi, causing happiness to proceed by way of continuity, becomes as if he has entered into it; this is a description given by way of its characteristic of perception (*saññā*).
For lightness associated with jhāna, even without supernormal power (*iddhi*), reaches a measure sufficient to cause one to leap into the air.

And by the mention of "lightness" (*lahubhāva*) here, "pliancy" (*mudubhāva*) and "wieldiness" (*kammaññabhāva*) are also included. Therefore, he said: "having become light, pliant, and wieldy in body."
"By this method" means: by means of attaining the third jhānas, the body of name-and-form reaches a state of ease and lightness;
when the mind is thus subdued, the fourth jhāna leads to the attainment of psychic power with ease—this is "by this method.
For the stages of equipment, which serve as the foundation for the natural plane, are like the base of the foundation-pit for a city wall.

382. In the exposition of the bases for spiritual power (*iddhipāda*), "four" is the numerical limit. Regarding the term "bases for spiritual power" (*iddhipāda*): here, it is called *iddhi* because it succeeds (*ijjhati*);
the meaning is that it is accomplished and brought to fruition. Alternatively, it is called *iddhi* because by means of it beings succeed, become successful, and reach excellence.
According to the first sense, it is a "base for spiritual power" (*iddhipāda*) because it is the very foundation of spiritual power; the meaning is that it is a constituent part of spiritual power.
In the second sense, it is the "basis" (pāda) for success (iddhi), hence "basis of success" (iddhipāda). "Basis" (pāda) means a foundation or a means of attainment; this is the meaning.
For by means of that, one goes to and reaches success, which is designated as successive distinction. This, first of all, is the method of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
In this context, the first sense of the word *iddhi* is stated as the agent (*kattṛ*), and the second as the instrument (*karaṇa*). As for the word *pāda*:
The word *karaṇa* has only the sense of an instrument. It is stated that *iddhi* (success) is that which is to be attained, not that which is currently being accomplished;

and since the *iddhi* to be attained stands in grammatical apposition with the "foot" (*pāda*), which is the instrument for attaining it, one cannot, according to the first meaning, say: "the foot of success is simply success itself" (*iddhi eva pādo iddhipādo*).
Likewise, success—counted as growth—is that which is to be accomplished by means of the instrument of the act of succeeding, [just as it is] by means of the instrument of the act of attaining.

Regarding the term *pajjitabba* (to be understood): since it is impossible for two [words] functioning as instruments (*karaṇa*) not to share a common substratum (*asamānādhikaraṇatā*), one cannot, in the second sense, state that "a foot of success is a 'success-foot' (*iddhipāda*).

Therefore, in the first sense, a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*) is appropriate, whereas in the second sense, a genitive compound (*sāmivacanasamāsa*) is not. Thus, in the first sense, "a foot of success is a success-foot," and in the second sense...

The compound *iddhipāda* is appropriately analyzed as "the foot that is itself success" (*iddhi eva pādo*), or as previously stated, because the foot is the factor that succeeds, the part that succeeds, and the means for making it succeed.
It is "caused by desire" (*chandahetuka*) by way of the desire belonging to its preceding stage; it is "predominant in desire" (*chandādhi-ka*) by way of the desire associated with it.

Furthermore, the predominance of the co-nascent desire should be understood precisely by way of the prior formative volition (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*). Alternatively: "If a bhikkhu makes desire his dominant..."
From this passage—"Having performed [this], one attains concentration; one attains one-pointedness of mind;

this is called *chandasamādhi* (concentration through desire)"—it is understood that the compound *chandasamādhi* is stated by eliding the word *adhipati* (dominant influence), thus meaning "concentration dominated by desire.
However, according to the method of showing the meaning of the word *adhipati*, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) states: "Caused by desire..."
Or it is said: "Concentration is predominant over desire. For this very reason, he says: "Having made desire the dominant factor," and so forth.
Some say that "predominant" means "consisting of energy. However, the inclusion of the term "predominant" (padhāna) is for the purpose of excluding conditioned formations (saṅkhāra).

Alternatively, it is called a formation (saṅkhāra) because it constructs various specific qualities; thus, all energy is a formation. Among these, [the first] is distinguished by its accomplishment of the four functions.
The inclusion of the term "exertion" (*padhāna*) is for the purpose of excluding other factors; the meaning is that they are "exertions" because they are preeminent or supreme.
However, since the fourfold energy (*vīriya*) is intended here, it is expressed in the plural.

As for the explanation of the meaning of "basis of psychic power" (*iddhipāda*) by taking the word "basis" (*pāda*) to mean "means" (*upāya*) through the application of a compound such as "a basis of psychic power is a *iddhipāda*," that [explanation] pertains to the stage prior to their acquisition.

It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the state of the *iddhi* as the agent (*kattṛ*) and the state of the *iddhi* as the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because it is taught in the Abhidhamma by way of the "basis of *iddhi* consisting of desire" (*chandiddhipāda*), and so forth;

thus, it refers to the state of the *iddhi* as the agent for the growth to be accomplished by the bases of *iddhi* such as desire, and the state of the *iddhi* as the instrument of desire and the others.

In the case of the "basis of *iddhi* consisting of energy" (*vīriyiddhipāda*), the term "energy" (*vīriya*) occurs twice in the phrase: "endowed with energy, concentration, and the volitional formation of striving" (*vīriya-samādhi-padahāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgataṃ*).
In this context, the first is a qualification of concentration: "concentration dominated by energy" (*vīriyādhipati samādhi*) means "energy-concentration" (*vīriya-samādhi*).
The second shows the factors of possession. For indeed, in all cases there are only two factors of possession: concentration and the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*).

While desire and the others are qualifications of concentration, the volitional formation of striving is qualified by the word "striving" itself and not by desire and the others; therefore, the state of being dominated by energy is not mentioned here.

The "determination factor" (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) has been explained. Furthermore, since energy (*vīriya*) is mentioned by the term "determination factor" as a factor of possession precisely because it stands distinguished from concentration (*samādhi*), there is no mention of a possession of two types of energy.

However, since concentration is distinguished by zeal (*chanda*) and the other factors, and the determination factor is likewise associated with that very [concentration] thus distinguished, [it is not redundant].
And because there are other qualities as well, the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) are taught by way of the specific factors of concentration.
Furthermore, the state of being a "specific factor" for desire and the others occurs through their respective roles as supports.

Alternatively, by the phrase "or else" and so forth, it is stated that desire and the others possess the status of "bases of psychic power" in the sense of being means (*upāya*), even though the word *pāda* (foot/base) also carries the sense of a support (*nissaya*).

For that very reason, in the *Abhidhamma*, within the *Uttaracūḷabhājanīya*, it is stated that desire (*chanda*) and the others alone constitute the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), beginning with: "The four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power consisting of desire," and so forth.

Furthermore, in the *Pañhāpucchaka*, although the summary is made by stating: "The four bases of psychic power: here, a bhikkhu [possesses] concentration through desire (*chandasamādhi*)," and so forth, the state of being wholesome (*kusala*) and so on is analyzed again specifically for desire and the others. This is solely for the purpose of demonstrating the basis of psychic power as a skillful means (*upāyiddhipāda*).

For in the Suttas and in the Abhidhamma, the demonstration of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) by way of their support (*nissaya*) has been made; otherwise, their fourfold nature would not exist.

383. "The eight beginning with desire" means: desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi*), energy-concentration (*vīriya-samādhi*), mind-concentration (*citta-samādhi*), and investigation-concentration (*vīmaṃsā-samādhi*);
thus there are eight beginning with desire. Although here, in all four instances, concentration is indeed simply "concentration," nevertheless...
Concentration accompanied by the desire to arouse supernormal power (*iddhi*) leads to the attainment of supernormal power, but not concentration alone.

The same applies to energy-concentration and the others. Therefore, these four types of concentration together with desire and the rest, as well as the four factors beginning with desire themselves—making eight in total—are called "supernormal powers" (*iddhi*), because they are reached by means of them, or they themselves proceed toward the attainment of supernormal power.
They are called "factors" because they bring about success. Therefore, it is said: "they lead to the attainment of psychic power (iddhi).

As for the passage in the Pāḷi beginning with "desire is not concentration," although desire and the other factors produce psychic power only when accompanied by concentration, this nevertheless shows their status as individual factors.
The intention is that they must be joined together, and not function individually.
"Niyutta" means precisely "joined," not "detached. 384.

"Anonataṃ" means not bent down; the meaning is that it is not sluggish because it is exerted by energy. Therefore he said, "It does not waver in indolence," which means it does not fluctuate on account of indolence.
"Uddhaṃ nataṃ" means elevated, that is, agitated and distracted.
"Not haughty" means not elevated; "not distracted" means concentrated. Therefore he said, "it does not waver through restlessness.
"Not bent forward" means not inclined by way of attachment; it is unattached. "Not bent away" means not turned away by way of departing—that is, not averse due to anger.
"Not bent aside" means not crooked; it is undefiled. [By way of] view...
“Not dependent” (*anissita*) means not dependent by way of the basis [of the notions] “I” and “mine.
“Unbound” (*appaṭibaddha*) means not fettered by way of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*). Lust (*rāga*) is merely attachment; however, desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) are a heavy defilement.
For in that case, even an object standing at a distance remains truly bound. “Completely liberated” (*vippamutta*) means liberated in a specific sense. Of the jhānas...
He said "in sensual lust" because it is the opposite of sensual lust.

"Dissociated" means secluded from defilement, or not bound by the four bonds (yoga). "Made free from boundaries" means that one has practiced in such a way that no boundary of defilement exists even slightly.
"Attained to unity" means having reached one-pointedness, being perfectly concentrated.
For that very reason, it does not waver from the various defilements—that is, from defilements of diverse natures.

This is the meaning: [it is] the sign of indolence and so forth. The meaning of the immovability of this consciousness is indeed established, because it has been shown by way of illustrating the attainment of imperturbability (*āneñjya*).
It is stated again in connection with the demonstration of the stages, trees, and footprints of psychic power (*iddhi*): "These..."
The phrase "the roots are indeed [the factors]" is stated again for the purpose of showing their nature as roots.
"The former" refers to the method previously shown in six ways, beginning with "because they are embraced by faith and the rest. "This" refers to the method now shown in sixteen ways.

He says, "for the sake of non-confusion regarding both," because confusion does not arise concerning what has been shown in both the *Suttanaya* and the *Paṭisambhidānaya*, whereas it would if they were not shown.

385. “By means of knowledge he resolves”: here, in order to show the method of resolution, he cites the statement he himself made previously—“How, then, does this come to be so?”—namely, “having entered upon the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge and having emerged from it.
Regarding this, some say that one enters the four jhānas in succession and emerges from the fourth jhāna; however, that...
This is inappropriate. For the taming of the mind is for the purpose of attaining jhāna at will, and only the fourth jhāna serves as the basis for the direct knowledges (abhiññā), not the others.

"Having performed the preliminary work" (parikamma) means that here, having emerged from the foundational jhāna, the very act of thinking with a sense-sphere consciousness (kāmāvacara-citta) such as "May I be one hundred," etc., constitutes the performance of the preliminary work; likewise, the adverting of the mind is simply the act of adverting (āvajjana).
The word *api* (also) in the phrase "the second time also" has the sense of inclusion; by it, the meanings "the third time also" and "even more than that" are indicated.
For just as with the development of the jhānas, so too is the development of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). The expression "once or twice" should be regarded as a mere illustration.
"Having the sign as its object" means having the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) as its object. Regarding the term "preliminary consciousnesses" (*parikamma-cittāni*): here...
The state of having a hundred objects for each preliminary consciousness (parikamma-citta) should be understood from its proceeding with the thought, "May I be a hundred.

The same method applies here regarding the thousand objects. "By way of appearance" means by way of the appearance imagined by oneself. "Not by way of designation" means not by way of the designation "being" (satta).
That resolving consciousness (adhiṭṭhāna-citta) is "like absorption consciousness"—the inclusion of the word "like" (iva) refers to the direct-knowledge consciousness (abhiññā-citta).

This is stated because of its similarity to the first arising of the jhāna-consciousness, not because it possesses absorption (appanā). Regarding the phrase "possessing the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacaracatutthajjhānika), this means having the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere; it is associated with that.
If this is so, how is the statement in the *Paṭisambhidā*—"having adverted, he resolves by means of knowledge"—to be understood? To this he says: "And whatever... and so forth.

"In that case too" means even in the case of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*). "He adverts" refers to the textual phrase "he adverts much"; this is stated by way of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) alone, not by way of actual adverting.

"Having adverted, he resolves with knowledge" is stated by way of the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*), not by way of the knowledge associated with the preliminary-work consciousness or any other sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) knowledge; for [the latter] does not [possess such power].

“Such power exists. Therefore—meaning because the resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) occurs solely through the knowledge of direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) that has reached absorption (*appanā*)—he said, “He adverts to much,” and so forth, showing that this is the sequence of resolution.
Therein, “by way of establishing” means by way of producing. “For the purpose of demonstrating bodily witness” means:

it is not merely a matter of words; rather, because he has personally realized this meaning with his own body, he is a “bodily witness” (*kāyasakkhī*), and thus it is for the purpose of demonstrating such a witness.
*Kokanada* is a specific term for a lotus, as in the expression “*kokāsaka*. It is said that this lotus has many petals, is endowed with excellent color, and is exceedingly fragrant.
*Pāto* means early in the morning. This is the meaning here:
just as the lotus known as *kokanada*, at dawn—the time of the sun’s rising—becomes bloomed, fully opened, its fragrance undiminished, and radiant.

Thus, one beholds the Perfectly Enlightened One, Aṅgīrasa—fragrant with the scent of his body and the scent of his virtues, glowing with his own brilliance like the sun in the autumnal sky—and seeing him with rays of light streaming from his limbs, one realizes:
"This teaching has practice as its essence; practice is rooted in the study of the scriptures (pariyatti), and you have [neglected] the study of the scriptures."

One who is incapable of learning [the rules] is therefore "incapable"—this is the intended meaning. It is not called "incapable" in the sense of being disqualified from the status of a resident, because the primary factor here is the act of striving itself.

The term "bhikkhu" is used according to the conventional designation for one who has gone forth, or by reference to a future state of being a bhikkhu, just as it is said, "The Buddha went to Rājagaha.
*Pilotikakhaṇḍa* means a well-purified piece of cloth. It is called *rajoharaṇa* (dust-remover) because it removes dust.
Having manifested [the form], he gave it; for he had previously performed meritorious deeds (*pubbe katādhikāra*) toward that end.

Indeed, emerging wisely (*yoniso ummujjanto*), he acquired the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) and the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), thinking, "This is the fault of the individual existence (*attabhāva*). Then, by means of the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpapariggaha*) and so forth, he applied his knowledge to the five aggregates (*pañcasu khandhesu*).

Increasing insight (*vipassanā*) through the sequence beginning with the contemplation of the aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*), he proceeded through the stages of knowledge such as the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*).

He brought insight (vipassanā) close to the stages of conformity (anuloma) and the lineage-knowledge (gotrabhu). The verses spoken preceded by the emission of light are called "obhāsa-gāthā" (verses of illumination).
"In the discipline of the Noble One, lust (*rāga*) is 'dust' (*raja*); it is not, however, the [physical] pollen that is called 'dust.
Why? Because it causes the defilement of the mind. This term 'dust' is a designation for lust. They are stained by this—that is, by this dust known as lust. "Having utterly abandoned" means...
"By means of the supreme path, specifically for the sake of abandoning. "They dwell as wise ones" means that they dwell having become wise abandoners.
"In the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is free from passion"—that is, one from whom the dust of lust and other defilements has been entirely abandoned. For thus they say:
"When the mind is defiled, young men are defiled;..."
“When the mind is pure, they become purified—thus it was said by the Great Seer.

Although the Noble Path has already been explained through the inclusion of the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), [the author] speaks of “nine supramundane states” (*nava lokuttaradhammā*) in order to include both the fruits and Nibbāna, owing to their commonality in being unsurpassed.

Regarding the phrase “he covered his hand”: it means he placed his hand over [the bowl] in the manner of covering its opening; thus he is said to have “covered his hand. Alternatively, *hatthaṃ* is used in the accusative case with the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is, “he covered it with his hand.”
“Sahassakkhattum” means “a thousandfold. For even when one manifests oneself a thousand times by means of a single act of consciousness, it is as if one were manifesting oneself a thousand times.
Although there is no repetition of the action itself, the phrase “sahassakkhattum” is used to show that the purpose of that number is achieved.
“In a mango grove” (ambavane) means in a monastery built within a mango grove. “Delightful” (ramme) means beautiful. Up to...
The construction is: "He sat down for the announcement of the time.
"Without specifying" means without making a specification by way of complexion, limbs, body parts, requisites, particular actions, and so forth.

"Of various colors" means of diverse forms, in the various ways mentioned regarding complexion and the rest. "With hair mixed with grey" means hair intermingled with white hairs (*palita*). [This refers to] those with half their hair the color of night and half their hair the color of pale yellow, and so on.

"Of a certain complexion" refers to one whose robe is thus half-black. *Padabhāṇa* (recitation by word) is the reciting of the text according to the meaning of the words and according to the progression of the discourse.
*Dhammakathā* (discourse on the Dhamma) is the speaking of the Dhamma by way of exposition (*parikathā*) and so forth.

*Sarabhañña* (chanting by tone) is the vocalizing of the discourses and other texts with melodic intonation. "Others too" means others besides those modes already mentioned, such as long, short, thin, thick, and so on.
"In various ways": they become exactly the kind desired; in whatever manner they are desired, they become precisely that way.
For however many specific qualities—such as color and so forth—are desired in them, they possess those very same qualities.
Even though they are thus divided into many different forms, by taking them as an object according to their color, one single resolving consciousness (adhiṭṭhānacitta) [arises].

It proceeds. For this is its power: just as a single volition produces a personal existence (attabhāva) possessing various distinctions, therein the aspiration for existence (bhavapatthanā) becomes a specific condition for the kamma.
