And if it is argued that the ripening of kamma (kammavipāka) is inconceivable, it should be understood that here too the preliminary consciousness (parikammacitta) is a specific condition, and the sphere of psychic power (iddhivisaya) is inconceivable.

“This is the method”: this method, which was stated regarding the manifestation of many forms by means of the formula for resolution beginning with “having attained the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge,” applies to the other resolutions as well.
Having thus shown the general rule by way of extension, he says “But this is the distinction,” etc., in order to show the specific difference in its own form.
It has been said. Therein, the connection is with the words "by this bhikkhu, desiring.
"They will know me" means they will know me as "one possessed of psychic power. "In the interval" means precisely within the limited period [of time].

The passage beginning with "the foundation jhāna" is stated for the purpose of showing the manner of performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*); the rest, however, is clarified by way of extension (*atidesa*). Thus...
"Not making" means not making a resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) in the interim, thinking "I shall be alone.
By the phrase "according to the time limit previously determined," he shows that when one makes a resolution such as "I shall be a hundred," it must be done precisely by way of a time limit.
One becomes alone by oneself because the resolution has subsided. And here, regarding the preliminary work and the resolving consciousnesses...

One possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*) becomes himself the object by way of his own beauty. Among these, the preliminary consciousnesses (*parikamma-citta*) have as their object that which is present in a continuous stream (*santatipaccuppanna*).

They say that the consciousness of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-citta*) has as its object that which is occurring at that very moment (*sampativattamāna*), because the act of resolving lasts for only a single thought-moment (*ekacittakkhaṇika*). 387.
It is not appropriate to connect the word "manifestation" (*āvibhāva*) with the word *hoti* mentioned below, because [the former] is in the accusative case.

Because it has been so stated, and because the word *gacchati* (goes), which will be explained in that same way, intends the manifestation of both oneself and others, the noun-phrase depends upon a verb-phrase;
thus, having joined it with the verb *karoti*, which expresses the general sense of "doing," he says: "he makes manifestation" (*āvibhāvaṃ karoti*).
The same method applies here to the term *tirobhāvaṃ* (disappearance). If this is so, how [should one understand] the passage in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*? This is the objection.
He said, “For this very reason,” and so forth, with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*).

Although it is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* as “they become manifest, being unobstructed by anything,” and so on, that too was said with reference to this very same making manifest and making invisible.
The remaining words are synonyms for those two. “Darkness” refers to the darkness of night, or even during the day, that which is located within caves, grottoes, and the like.
*Andhakāram*: darkness. *Paṭicchannam*: concealed by walls, doors, and so forth. *Anāpātham*: not come within the range [of vision] due to distance, extreme subtlety, or other such factors.
*Ayam*: this one, the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*). One should connect the passage by transforming the grammatical case, as follows:
"so that he himself or another, even if concealed or standing at a distance, may be seen. *Ālokajātam*: become light, or having light produced.

388. But this "miracle" refers to the miracle of manifestation (*āvi-bhāva-pāṭihāriya*). As for the question "By whom was it performed before?", having asked about the body-witness (*kāyasakkhī*) therein and shown that "the Teacher is indeed the body-witness," he said "by the Blessed One.

To clarify that meaning, he spoke the passage beginning with "For the Blessed One... The connection is made by bringing in the phrase "the residents of Sāvatthī saw"; likewise, "as far as... [and so on].

“He showed Avīci. When the lower and lower celestial palaces among those situated in space are being crowded out by the upper and upper palaces acting as obstructions, the space occupied by them is said to be “crowded out”;
thus it is said, “having cleared away the space as if in two ways. This is the meaning:
that the Teacher performed the miracle of manifestation (*āvi-bhāva-pāṭihāriya*). [This concludes] the recollection of the practice of previous Buddhas.
For the purpose of preserving the lineage of the Buddhas. The passage beginning with "With one foot" and so forth is a demonstration of the three strides.
He provides a method—that method by following which he established the path of recitation.
The one named Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika was the younger brother of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.
"Having burst forth through Mount Sineru" means having burst forth while making that mountain visible to the assembly. "It" refers to Mount Sineru.

The miracle that makes the world-space, numbering many hundreds of thousands, and the world of beings dwelling therein open is called the "Opening of the World. "Mahābrahmā" refers to Sahampati Mahābrahmā.

Behold how the fruit of the unerring practice ripens: having first intimidated them with the fear of hell, one entices them with the bliss of heaven by means of the Teacher’s method of gradual instruction; yet this is not done by causing them to become inclined toward the attainment of heavenly success alone.

Just as the light-kasiṇa must be attained for the purpose of manifesting light in the process of making oneself visible, so too the blue kasiṇa must be attained for the purpose of manifesting darkness in the process of making oneself invisible.
Although this is not explicitly mentioned in the text, it is certainly implied.

The meaning of "the open" (*vivaṭa*) and "the covered" (*āvaṭa*) is already established by the very statement itself. Alternatively, this meaning is simply stated as being included within the white kasiṇa (*odātakasiṇa*), namely, the light kasiṇa (*ālokakasiṇa*).
"Darkness" (*andhakāra*) means possessing darkness. 390.
"The rest" refers to Elder Iṭṭiya and others.

391. "Manifest" (*pākaṭa*) means that which has a manifest possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*); thus it is "manifest. That which is both manifest and a marvel (*pāṭihāriya*) is a "manifest marvel" (*pākaṭapāṭihāriya*).

"Not manifest" (*apākaṭa*) means that the possessor of psychic power is not manifest here; thus it is "not manifest. That which is both not manifest and a marvel is a "not manifest marvel" (*apākaṭapāṭihāriya*).

This distinction exists solely due to the manifest or non-manifest status of the possessor of psychic power, not because of the marvel itself; for there is no such thing as a marvel that is not manifest.
"Superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) means that "human state" (*manussadhamma*) refers to the ten courses of wholesome action;
[superhuman] is what is above that human state. A miracle consisting of supernormal power is a "miracle of supernormal power" (*iddhipāṭihāriya*).

"In the courtyard" (*āḷinde*) means in front. "With spaces" (*okāsehi*) means by scattering. "A supernormal mental formation" (*iddhābhisaṅkhāra*) means the application of supernormal power. "He performed" (*abhisaṅkhāsī*) means he formed; the sense is that he did it.
"Through the keyhole" means through the opening made by a key. "Between the door-panels" means between the two parts of the door frame.

"Disappeared" means wishing to vanish. Having acted in such a way that the Brahmā Baka was unable to disappear, the Blessed One himself vanished by passing beyond the range of perception for him and the entire host of Brahmās.
Thinking, "Let there be no opportunity for the host of Brahmās to say, 'It is impossible to know whether the ascetic Gotama exists or does not exist in this place,'" he spoke this verse:

"I have seen the fear in existence. In this context, "I have seen the fear in existence" means: having seen the fear consisting of birth, old age, and so forth, within *bhava*, which is the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).

And having repeatedly seen both this threefold existence of beings—consisting of sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth—and those seeking non-existence (*vibhavesinaṃ*), who are searching for and pursuing non-existence, [I saw that] they were still within existence itself.

"I did not welcome existence" means that through craving and views, I did not welcome or grasp at any kind of existence. "And I did not cling to delight" refers to craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).
"He did not approach; he did not seize"—this is the meaning. 392. "Without clinging" means that by moving through penetration, he does not cling to anything such as walls.
"Having performed the preliminary work by adverting" means that having adverted to that which he wishes to go beyond, [he thinks] "Let there be space, let there be space."

Thus, by one possessing psychic power who has performed the preliminary work (parikamma): the terms "cavity" (*susira*) and "hole" (*chidda*) are stated in the masculine gender with reference to the surrounding wall and the mountain.
A cavity is an opening that extends vertically; a hole is one that extends horizontally.
"Having performed the preliminary work on any kasiṇa whatsoever" means on any kasiṇa among the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*) and so forth.
Having entered a jhāna and performed the preliminary work (parikamma), one should resolve: "Let there be space. Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Mastery over the eight attainments (samāpatti) alone is the measure. Therefore, whatever one wishes for, that very thing comes to be.
By this [method], one performs emerging and submerging in earth, enters the water-kasiṇa attainment, and creates earth within water and so forth.
It is implied that the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa (pathavīkasiṇa) is not to be desired as an absolute necessity.
"This" refers to the attainment of the space-kasiṇa (ākāsakasiṇa), which must necessarily be mentioned because it is appropriate for performing miracles such as passing through walls and so forth.

And having done so, just as there is the statement, "making what is covered open by means of the space-kasiṇa," likewise [there is the statement] by means of the earth-kasiṇa: "Having been one, he becomes many..."

The state of being [described] by the words "he becomes," and so forth, as well as what was stated in the miscellaneous method (pakiṇṇaka-naya) such as "he desires to travel on foot after having fashioned earth in the sky or in water"— all that is established.
With the intention that "there is no fault," it is like making something firm, as if it were well-bound by being bound twice over.
Having said this, in order to show the absence of any further purpose, he stated, "having entered [the attainment] again," and so forth.

Because it has been resolved upon, it indeed becomes space; thus, even if something such as a mountain were to appear in the interval, because that too has been resolved upon with the thought, "let it be space," it indeed becomes space.
This too is merely a hypothetical assumption of an impossibility, for there is simply no appearance of such a thing.
The words beginning with "in between" (*antarā*) were spoken in order to show that [the earth] does not exist.
393. "Having delimited" means having delimited the desired location by means of knowledge. "Therein" refers to that resolve upon the state of water in the earth;
this is the textual passage (*pāḷi*) that clarifies the aforementioned practice. Regarding the subsequent phrase, "therein this is the textual passage":
The meaning should be understood in this same manner even regarding places where [the water] has arrived.
"He" refers to the possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*). It is said, "having fixed a time limit, he resolves," which means that he resolves after having established a boundary for the duration.

"Natural water" is water that is not supernaturally created. 394. "Contrary" refers to that water which, when stepped upon, does not sink underfoot; this, however, should be understood here as the manifestation of earth by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), in the sense of the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*). "Earth-kasiṇa" refers to the jhāna of the earth-kasiṇa.
395. *Pallaṅka* means a cross-legged posture with the thighs bound all around.

Since a bird whose wings are clipped or whose wings have not yet grown cannot fly, the word *sakuṇa* (bird) is specified by the term *pakkhī* (winged one) in the text; thus it is said, "a bird endowed with wings.
*Having performed the preliminary exercise* means having performed the preliminary exercise [with the thought], "Let there be earth."
"In the sky, in the atmosphere" means in the sky known as the atmosphere. For wherever there is no obstruction, that is called "space.
And this possessor of psychic power does not travel in the space near the earth;
rather, he travels where it is beyond the range of birds, and such a place is called "the atmosphere" in the world.
Therefore it was said: "In the space designated as 'the atmosphere'.
"The Elder" refers to the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya mentioned previously. "Attaining the attainment" means attaining the attainment once again.
[Objection: Is not his mind already concentrated? [Response: Indeed, the mind of one possessing psychic power (*iddhimat*) that proceeds by way of a miracle (*pāṭihāriya*) is absolutely...
The intention is that it is indeed in a state of concentration (*samāhita*), and not, as at other times, in a state of non-concentration (*asamāhita*). However, that is merely the Elder’s opinion.
For previously, having attained the earth-kasiṇa (*pathavīkasiṇa*) and resolved upon the earth, he went;

but now space (*ākāsa*) is required, therefore he must attain the space-kasiṇa (*ākāsakasiṇa*). Thus he said, "Even though," and so forth. Regarding the miracle of passing through walls (*tirokuṭṭapāṭihāriye*):

"One should proceed in the manner already stated" means that just as in that case a wall or similar object becomes space through the act of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), so too here one should go having made mountains, trees, and so forth into space by means of resolution.
Alternatively, "in the manner stated for the miracle of passing through walls" refers to: "But if that bhikkhu, having resolved... [and so on].
By the method stated there, beginning with the words "As he goes," etc.,

this shows that even if another mountain or tree were to arise along the way by the power of a *nāga* or other such beings— thinking, "By the power of his previous resolve alone, it is impossible for another mountain or tree to arise"—
any obstruction created by them does not constitute an obstacle to his journey.
He makes himself visible in a secluded place suitable for practice. He becomes manifest, [thinking], "This ascetic is one who travels through the air.
(396) The mention of forty-two thousand *yojanas* is made according to the conditions of the first eon;
however, thereafter, due to the gradual rising of the earth, it may be reduced by several *yojanas*, or perhaps slightly increased.
It was stated thus because there is nothing deficient or not conforming to the calculation.

"By producing light simultaneously over the three continents" means that when they stand in the middle of whichever continent, they produce light by setting out toward the eastern continent and rising over the western one at that same moment.
Or, it is by surpassing other lights, and because [the beings] possess great psychic power and are difficult to see.
They possess great power through the allaying of the cold-fever of sentient beings and through the nourishing of medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest trees.
"Touches" means he makes physical contact. "Wipes" means he rubs by moving his hand here and there.

"By means of the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge" means by means of whichever jhāna serves as the basis for direct knowledge. By the word "eva" (only), he excludes any specific distinction regarding the basis-jhāna.
There is no formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For this very reason it was said: "There is no fixed rule here regarding the attainment of the kasiṇa.
The meaning is that, as in the miracle of passing through walls and so forth, there is no fixed rule here such as "one must enter jhāna in this specific kasiṇa and then make a resolution.
For indeed, in the Pāḷi, without referring to any particular attainment, it says: "Here, that possessor of psychic power... and so forth.
It has been stated. Regarding "within arm’s reach of the moon and sun": this refers to the orbs of the moon and sun as thus described.
"A visible form within arm’s reach" means a visible form situated within arm’s reach, or a visible form that is within arm’s reach.
The construction is: "or, having extended his hand, he touches it."
It was stated that there is an increase of the non-clung-to (*anupādinnaka*) based upon the clung-to (*upādinnaka*).

However, by way of logical reasoning (*yutti*), here the shadow of an increase of the clung-to is also seen. Just as there is a diminution of the clung-to when it is made smaller than itself, an increase is likewise possible.
This occurs together with its own basis, just as in the case of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s subduing of Nanda and Upananda.
In order to bring forward the Theravāda and demonstrate that meaning, the passage beginning with “The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said” was commenced.
The intention is: “Is it not so? Indeed, it is so,” for two negations lead back to the original state.
As for the statement, “At that time it was great, like that of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna,” this is by way of showing the meaning as it has been specified.
It has been stated that even the reduction to a minor status is obtainable here.
[In] the commentary on the story of the taming of the Nandopananda nāga, he looked according to the practice of the Buddhas, thinking:
"Does he possess the necessary potential (upanissaya)? [He saw] the mundane characteristic of confidence in the Triple Gem.
With reference to the entry into the Teaching, he said, "one who lacks faith. The intention is that such a person should be separated from wrong view and established in confidence.
Therefore he said, "Who indeed... might separate him?
"On that day" refers to when the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, was proceeding toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

That portion of the day. "They prepared the drinking grounds" means that they sprinkled and swept the place where he sat to perform his meal, and they prepared it by bringing forth the food implements and other such things.
"By means of the three kinds of dancers" means by means of the three types of dancing women:
those who were brides, those who were maidens, and those who were courtesans. "Looking on" means...
"Looking" means observing; "examining" means scrutinizing.
"One above the other" means from summit to summit. "By the state of existence" means by way of the term *bhavana*. "By enjoyments" means by the bodily enjoyments.
"Upside down" means with the face turned downward. "Having seized" means having completely taken over, so that not even a portion of the Tāvatiṃsa realm remains.

"Sineruparibhaṇḍa" means the girdle of Sineru. It is said that around Sineru, at a distance of five thousand yojanas both in thickness and in width, there are four terraces established by nāgas, garuḷas, kumbhaṇḍas, and yakkhas for the protection of the Tāvatiṃsa realm;
these are designated as such because they share the common characteristic of being terraces (paribhaṇḍa).
Having brought them together, it is called "the surrounding ornament" (*paribhaṇḍa*). It is said that by those [mountains], half of Sineru was encompassed.
"Having abandoned his own form" means having made the human appearance disappear. "It afflicts" means it produces a mere sense of exhaustion.
"Having abandoned his own form" means having abandoned the naga-form through the manifestation of a subtle body. He opened his mouth.
“I shall crunch the ascetic right in his mouth. The words “to the east and to the west” are said because the Nāga was lying down in that manner.
He said, “Pay attention,” for the purpose of establishing mindfulness thoroughly.
“All the miracles from the beginning” refers to the miracles performed by the Elder at that time. “But this occasion,” however, refers to this specific cause for emitting the breath through the nose.
"Anubandhi" means he pursued [him] out of fear, thinking, "It is not possible to strike back at this ascetic of such great psychic power.

"Ekapaṭipāṭiyā" means by a single succession; the sense is "without interval. "Ayameva" refers to that very growth of the non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) which occurs depending upon the clung-to (upādinnaka).
In such a miracle as this extension of the hand and so forth, the reasoning is indeed appropriate.
Because derived matter does not arise from mind or from temperature. Alternatively, "derived" (upādinnam) is intended to mean the entire [body] bound by the faculties.
Even so, its growth in that manner is not tenable; therefore, growth should be understood according to the method already stated.
Although the derived and the non-derived occur as if mixed within a single continuum, [they remain distinct].

In terms of its essential nature, it remains entirely unmixed. In this regard, just as when a measure of milk (*āḷhaka*) is mixed with many measures of water, although the milk is completely intermingled and remains suspended throughout the whole, nevertheless the milk does not increase there;
only the water increases. Even so, although the clung-to (*upādinna*) and the unclung-to (*anupādinna*) are intermingled...

Although it proceeds as if [it were] so, nevertheless that which is clung-to (upādinna) does not increase; rather, by the power of psychic potency (iddhānubhāva), that which is mind-born (cittaja) increases, and following that, that which is temperature-born (utuja) increases—this is how it should be understood.
"He" refers to that possessor of psychic potency (iddhimā). "Having done thus" means having extended his hand in the manner described, or having those [beings] come within the reach of his hand.

Having established [the foot]. The manner of placing the foot and so forth should also be understood according to the method already stated. There is yet another possessor of psychic power (*iddhimā*).
"In the same way" means as before, prior to performing the miracle. "This is comparable to that" means:
just as when many various moon-discs are seen in various bowls filled with water, there is no obstruction to the movement and so forth of the moon-disc, nor to those of the many [reflected moons].

Individual vision succeeds; this miracle is like that because there is no obstruction to the movement and so forth of the moon and sun, and because for many possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*), the application of psychic power (*iddhi-payoga*) succeeds exactly as desired—this is the intended meaning. 397.

"Having made a delimitation" means having made a delimitation by way of inclusion (*abhividhi*), not by way of a boundary (*mariyāda*). For in this way, he exercises mastery with his own body even in the Brahma-world. "The text" refers to the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-pāḷi*.
Regarding the phrase "he exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world":

here, what is intended is neither merely going to the Brahma-world, nor merely the act of going to the Brahma-world, but rather something else besides that. The expression "as far as the Brahma-world" is an illustration of a distant limit;
therefore, even after saying "if he should wish to go to the Brahma-world," one must also show the other case by saying, "even nearby, or far away."

The passage beginning with “he resolves” (*adhiṭṭhātī*) and so forth has been stated. Herein, the word *pi* (also/even) has the sense of inclusion; therefore, it should be understood that this includes everything remaining to be accomplished through the supernormal power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāniddhi*) that was not explicitly mentioned, and not merely what was already stated.

By the phrase “at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle,” etc., it is shown that the triple stride is produced by the supernormal power of resolution; elsewhere, however, it is characterized by its specific qualities and benefits. One should understand how these two do not contradict one another by investigating them accordingly.
“Blue-water source” (*nīlamātikā*) means a source of blue-colored water.

“The Great Bodhi” (*mahābodhi*) refers to the Great Bodhi tree at the Aparājita throne. “When the thought arose, he brought it near” means that immediately upon the arising of that thought, he contracted both the earth and the ocean and placed them near the Great Bodhi.

“On the day of the festival” (*nakkhattadivase*) means on the great festival day. “Moon-cakes” (*candapūva*) refers to cakes resembling the moon, shaped like the lunar disc. “He made them just enough to fill a single bowl” means he made them such that, by their size and form, they would fit entirely within a single bowl.
In the *Kākavaliya-vatthu*, the phrase “the Blessed One made it little into much” should be brought in and connected [to the context].

To show that story in brief, however, it was said: “It is said that the Elder Mahākassapa... and so forth. “By means of attainment” (*samāpatti*) refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

“On the bank of the Ganges” refers to the bank of the river Ganges on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. “He gave them a perception” means he gave them a perception such that they saw the ghee exactly as it had been resolved upon.
“Of him” means that he sees the form of whichever Brahmā he desires to see.

“Hears the sound” means that with the divine ear-element, he hears the sound of the Brahmā. “Understands the mind” means that by means of the knowledge of penetration of minds, he understands the mind of the Brahmā.
“By way of the body born of karma” means by way of the material body composed of the four great elements. “Mind... [The text continues: ...mind... [as before].
Regarding the phrase "he transforms it," what is that consciousness, or how is it transformed? He says: "Having taken the foundational jhāna-consciousness, he applies it to the body.
But how does he apply it to the body? He says: "He makes it conform to the body.
Furthermore, in order to cut off the path of verbal expression—lest one should be confused by the literal sound—he says: "It is slow-moving. "He makes" means...
The connection is as follows: bodily movement is indeed slow, because it has the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its condition;
this is the intended meaning. This is the sense here: a yogi, wishing to move with his visible body, directs his mind accordingly;
having entered the foundational jhāna and emerged from it, he performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*), thinking, "May this mind move slowly, just like the body."
Thus, it is with reference to the performance of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) that it is said,
"having taken the mind of the foundational jhāna. However, having performed the preliminary work and entered [jhāna] again, one who resolves by means of knowledge projects that mind onto the body,
making it follow the body and move slowly.

“Perception of pleasure” (*sukhasaññā*) means perception accompanied by pleasure; it is expressed by way of its primary characteristic (*saññāsīsenā*). “Lightness-perception” (*lahusaññā*) means perception [characterized] by lightness.
But how can there be the occurrence of the perception of pleasure together with the mind of psychic power (*iddhicitta*)?

To this he says: “The so-called ‘perception of pleasure’ is perception associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*). Or, "perception of pleasure" (*sukhasaññā*) means perception that is known as pleasure. For this very reason he says: "Equanimity..."

"Indeed, it is said that what is peaceful is happiness. Thus, showing that the dissociation of the mind and mental factors from the extremely heavy hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and from the gross, unpeaceful states such as applied thought (*vitakka*), etc., is the cause of lightness, he said: "That very [perception]... should be understood...
"Of one who has entered into that" means of one who has attained that perception of happiness and lightness. "His" refers to the practitioner (*yogin*). "The desire to go" [is the desire to depart].

"Only this much is the measure here": in this context, regarding the movement by means of the visible body, the measure is simply the preliminary work and the acts of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) undertaken with the intention of going toward that place one wishes to reach; by that much alone, the journey succeeds.
Therefore, the arrival at the desired destination occurs even without the creation of a path or the resolve involving wind. Now...
To make this same point more evident, the passage beginning with "For when there is mindfulness" was stated.
"Having taken up the body" means having taken up the material body by means of the preliminary-work consciousness (*parikamma-citta*) through the act of making it its object.

"He applies it to the mind" means he applies it to the foundational jhāna-consciousness (*pādaka-jjhāna-citta*), thinking: "May this body become like this mind," thereby bringing it into the same category as that [mind].
He makes it so. Therefore he said: "He makes it follow the mind, moving swiftly. "Mind-going" refers to the activity of the mind.
This, however, is the miracle of the transformation of the body by means of the mind. "Mind-going itself" means having a movement identical to that of the mind.
But how can the body, which functions slowly, have a movement identical to the mind, which revolves rapidly? It is not [so].
In every respect, it shares the same destiny. For just as when the mind transforms itself according to the body, the mind does not in every respect share the same destiny as the body;

for at that time, the mind does not proceed by way of the moment of material phenomena—which possess a heavy mode of existence—without having ceased its own moment established by its own intrinsic nature. [One might think: "Let this mind become like this body."

However, because the body—which is slow-moving—follows the resolution, the mind, proceeding by way of continuity in conformity with the body's movement until it reaches the desired location, is said to have been "directed" by the body's movement.
This occurs even more so through the perception of ease and lightness when one resolves: "May this body become like this mind."
Just as for one who has not cultivated the bases of psychic power, movement is slow;

but when the body proceeds in such a way that it reaches the desired place in only a few light mental moments rather than slowly, then that body is said to be "transformed by the course of the mind," though not by reaching the desired place in a single moment of consciousness.
And by doing so, even this simile—“Just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm, or bend his stretched arm”—is established in its literal sense. This must certainly be accepted in this way;
otherwise, it would contradict the readings of the Suttas and Abhidhamma, as well as the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā.

There would be a contradiction, and the natural law (*dhammatā*) would be subverted. For in the passage, “Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single dhamma,” the inclusion of the word “another” (*añña*) refers to material phenomena (*rūpadhammā*), because they do not turn over quickly.
Furthermore, in the Abhidhamma, only material form is stated as the prenascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), and it is that alone which is the postnascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*).
And wherever phenomena arise, [it is only material form that serves as such a condition].
They break up right there and then. There is no movement to another location, nor does their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) become otherwise.
Indeed, it is not possible for anyone by the power of psychic potency (iddhi) to alter the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) of phenomena;
however, it is possible to alter their state of existence (bhāva). The phrase "in all three moments" is also said with reference to the commencement of motion, not the completion of motion.
They say: "The Elder" refers to one elder among the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā*s. "Here" refers to the passage spoken after analyzing this miracle.
"Going himself" is what is understood [from the text], because it is stated: "He goes to the Brahma-world.
"Of the eye, ear, and so forth" means of the limbs such as the eye, ear, and so on; for it is likewise stated: "with all his limbs and members."

The meaning is "possessing all limbs and members. By the phrase "there is no serenity," it should be understood that the absence of the faculties of existence and life is also stated. "By way of inclination" means by way of desire. "Another as well" means he performs other actions besides those performed by the Blessed One.
And herein, this is the power of the Buddha: if there were diversity among the manifestations created by disciples.
[Objection: "It does not exist. But how is it that what was stated below—"if, however, one wishes to make them of various colors," and so forth—is possible? [Response:

That was stated on the grounds that for one who performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) in such and such a way and then resolves (*adhiṭṭhāti*), those specific qualities such as color and age are accomplished in accordance with that preliminary work.
However, in this case, regarding the created form (*nimmita-rūpa*) as it has been resolved, if the disciple [thinks], "These specific qualities..."
If one wishes, "May they be so," it does not succeed; however, for Buddhas it succeeds—this is the meaning shown here, and thus there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Now, regarding those fourteen miracles analyzed by way of showing the meaning of the text as "He exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world," such as "He resolves that what is distant be near," and so forth—it is the culmination of these [that is described].
The passage beginning with “And here” is commenced in order to demonstrate the miracle of mastery over the body (*kāyena vasavattanapāṭihāriya*).

In that context, the word “which” (*yaṃ*) is a reference to the action; by it, [it refers to] that which is the seeing of form in the phrase “he sees form,” that which is the hearing of sound in the phrase “he hears sound,” and that which is the knowing of the mind in the phrase “he understands the mind”—thus, [the action] has as its agent the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds.
It should be understood that he clings to the activity of seeing, hearing, and knowing. This same method applies to the subsequent terms such as "he settles upon" (santiṭṭhati) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *yampissa*: *yam* means "whatever," and *assa* refers to the yogin; thus the connection is "the resolve of this [yogin].

As for the word *kho* in the expression *yañca kho*, it has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) or a distinctive qualification (*visesa*). By means of that, it is indicated that this alone [is the resolve] here, among the miracles of mastery over the body (*kāyena vasavattanapāṭihāriyesu*).
This explains that it is more excellent. Why? Because it gives rise to doubt in some Brahmās, who wonder, "Is this one possessed of psychic power, or is this one a created being?
Furthermore, it should be understood as more excellent precisely because it is specifically called "mind-made" (manomaya) through its resolution (adhiṭṭhita).
Therefore he said: "To this extent, one is said to exercise mastery over the body."
If this is so, why are the remaining [powers] included here? To this he says: "The remainder... has been stated.

(398) This is the distinction: although these two types of supernormal power (*iddhi*) are indeed accomplished by means of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), nevertheless, this which is now being described is the distinction—the specific difference—between them. "Having abandoned one's natural form" means one's own...
"Having abandoned and removed his natural form" means not showing it to others. "The form of a youth" means the shape of a youth.
"He shows" means that, transforming himself in that way, he displays it within himself. The same principle applies to the phrases "the form of an elephant," and so forth.
"He shows even an elephant" means that he displays himself having become an elephant, or he displays an elephant externally. It is for this very purpose [that the text says]:
For here, instead of saying "he shows the appearance of an elephant," it is said, "he shows even an elephant.

As for what some say—that the statement regarding the seeing of elephants and so forth externally contradicts the state of supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) because of the phrase "having abandoned his natural form"—that is incorrect.
Why? Because "abandoning one's natural form" refers to one's own ordinary physical appearance.
It is the non-seeing of others, not the total cessation of himself.
This being so, when one does not show oneself but shows an elephant externally, what contradiction is there in saying, "Having abandoned his natural form, he shows an elephant"?
However, for one who becomes an elephant in form by himself and then shows an elephant externally, it is indeed appropriate [to say that he has abandoned his natural form].

It does not exist. For this very reason, it was said: "It is stated by way of seeing elephants and so forth externally. And by taking it thus, there is no contradiction with the nature of the supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*).

Furthermore, in the Pāḷi, in such passages as "he goes in the form of a young boy," the particle *vā* is used in the sense of indefiniteness; its purpose is to show that each one [of the forms] is produced individually.

However, in the passage beginning with "even an elephant," the sense is one of conjunction (*samuccaya*), for the purpose of showing that many things—elephants and so forth—are not to be made into one simultaneously.
The word *pi* has been mentioned. Therefore, in such cases as “he shows even a hand,” the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated for the second [case].
The manifestation of the form of a youth by one possessing psychic power (*iddhimant*) to others is the creation of the appearance of a youth;
nothing new, such as a basis like earth and so forth, is produced here. Because there is no purpose in the restriction of a *kasiṇa*, [it is not included] among the earth-*kasiṇa* and the rest.
It is said: "from a particular object. Or, even though the basis is being produced, it is accomplished according to the requirements by means of the earth-kasiṇa and so forth;
thus, there is no purpose here in restricting it to the kasiṇas.
For one wishing to show the form of a youth, one might show a blue color, or any other color such as yellow and so on. That being the case, the blue and other kasiṇas [are suitable].
The rule regarding the *kasiṇas* is that they must be attained; this same method applies to the rest as well.
When one has thus resolved, some—on the basis of the earth-*kasiṇa*—claim that such things as "having been one, he becomes many" constitute a "manifestation.

They argue that this contradicts the description of the *kasiṇas* given here in the section on "transformation," where it says: "from any one of the objects, such as the earth-*kasiṇa*," and so forth.
They have misgivings; thus it should be understood that "this is not a dwelling place.
Because it is desired by oneself through the power of creation (*nimminitabbabhāvena*), it is one's own form as a youth, but not one's own form as a youth from the time of one's own childhood.

This principle applies universally even to forms such as those of *nāgas* and so forth; therefore, when some say, "This does not seem to apply to the creation of *nāgas* and the like," that should be regarded as refuted.

The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "externally also" (*bahiddhāpi*) includes the internal as well. This is the meaning here: the passage beginning with "he shows even an elephant" refers to the internal;

and the statement regarding the seeing of elephants and so forth externally is likewise intended, and not merely in the sense of seeing the forms of boys and so on internally, as in the passage beginning with "the form of a boy. As for the method of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vidhāna*) that should be stated here:
That has already been explained above. 399.
"The body" refers to one's own physical body (*karajakāya*).

"In the manner already stated" means that after performing the preliminary exercise by thinking, "Let this body become hollow," one then enters the foundational jhāna, emerges from it, and proceeds according to the method described above.
"Another body" refers to whatever mind-made body one wishes to create. "From muñja grass" means from muñja reed-grass.
"A stalk" refers to its shaft. "From a sheath" means from a sword-sheath. "From a basket" means from a box; some also say it means from a snake's slough.
"He draws out" means he lifts up. "He would draw forth" means he would pull out.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Supernormal Powers is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the twelfth chapter. 13.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Direct Knowledges (Abhiññā).

Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Ear-Element (Dibbasotadhātukathāvaṇṇanā). 400. *Tattha* means in the exposition of the divine ear-element. For by way of exposition, the method for producing the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) is set forth in the Direct Knowledge Section of the Canon (*Abhiññāpāḷi*).
Here, the Direct Knowledge Section is spoken of under the heading of the direct knowledges themselves. Therefore he said: "In those that follow..."

"And in the three higher knowledges. The phrase "after that" is stated with reference to the Teacher’s sequence of teaching and his own sequence of recitation, not the sequence of practice. For those who practice do not practice according to this very sequence.

"In all places" means in the *Dibbasotadhātu* (Divine Ear Element) text and in the texts on the remaining higher knowledges—in all such instances. "Therein" is used as a particle for introducing a statement.

This is merely a particle, or it refers to the reading as previously stated. "Because of its similarity to the divine" means: they exist in the divine realm, thus they are "divine"—namely, the ear-element of the devas;
because of its similarity to that divine [ear], it is so called. Now, in order to clarify that similarity to the divine, the passage beginning with "of the devas" is stated.
Therein, "produced by karma of good conduct" refers to the excellence consisting in abundance of faith, purity of view, seeing the benefits [of virtue], and so forth.
They were produced by well-performed conduct (*sucarita*), that is, by meritorious karma that generates rebirth among the gods.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "bile, phlegm, blood, etc.," diseases such as those caused by wind (*vāta*) are included. "Unobstructed" (*apalibuddha*) means unafflicted.

Because they are unafflicted by bile and the other humors, and because of the loftiness of their karma, they should be understood as being free from defilements (*upakkilesa*). For karma that is devoid of the fault of defilements—
Just as a crop free from weeds and other defects yields an excellent, unblemished fruit, so too does this [consciousness] yield an unblemished, exalted fruit.
By way of figurative designation (*kāraṇūpacāra*), the fruit is spoken of in that manner, just as one says, "white" or "white ripening.

By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even at a distance," it includes the capacity to receive even a subtle object. The "translucent ear-element" (*pasādasotadhātu*) refers to the four great elements...
The ear element has the characteristic of clarity.
Since all development of the wholesome succeeds precisely through the exertion of energy, it is the development of energy;

or, since the development of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) is endowed with the formations of striving, it is especially the development of energy. That which is produced by the power of that [development] is "produced by the power of the development of energy."

The ear-element consisting of knowledge is the "knowledge-ear-element. "Just like that" means it is similar to that very [divine ear] because it is free from defilements and because it is capable of receiving objects even when they are distant or subtle.
"Obtained by way of the divine abiding" means obtained by way of the four planes known as the divine abidings; for this reason, it is [called] such.
He speaks of the divine state (*dibbabhāva*). Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated above. "Because it is dependent upon the divine abode" means:
because it proceeds by depending on the divine abode known as the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), which has reached its highest excellence through the possession of the eight factors;
or [it means] the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna associated with oneself, which is included within the divine abode.
The meaning here should also be understood as "being dependent" in the sense of being supported by a basis (*nissaya-paccaya*). "In the sense of hearing" means in the sense of apprehending sound.
For hearing is the perception of sound and the comprehension of its specific nature (*sabhāva*) exactly as it is.

Although there are other meanings of the verbal root *dhā*—such as "maintaining a nature" and so on—the Teacher’s teaching on the elements (*dhātu*) was for the purpose of demonstrating the emptiness of self (*atta-suññatā*); thus he said, "and in the sense of being devoid of a soul (*nijjīva*)."
The function of the ear-element is the reception of sound and its role as a condition for the determination of sound.
Since the purification of knowledge occurs precisely through the removal of defilements, he said, "unblemished by defilements. "Human" means belonging to humans;
it refers to the fleshly ear-element, distinguished by its specific function, which is the grasping of objects such as those that are distant or otherwise beyond the reach of the divine ear.
"Exceeding the human [realm]" means that by this [state], one has transcended what is human; thus he said: "by hearing sound after having transcended the human vicinity.
In this context, "human vicinity" refers to a place frequented by humans, the intended meaning being the range of objects normally perceivable by the ear-door.
Thus he said: "by hearing sound. "Divine" means included within the divine world.
Furthermore, since these sounds specifically belong to the devas, he says, "the sounds of the devas. Those belonging to humans are *mānusā*; [he says] "those humans.
Thus, because only the sounds of devas and humans are included, it is called "a partial inclusion" (*padesapariyādāna*);
the meaning is that it is a grasping of one part. "Dependent on the body" means dependent on one's own physical frame. This is a complete inclusion (*nippadesapariyādāna*).
Because it encompasses, without exception, all sounds—distinguished by categories such as those with consciousness and so forth—by means of grasping their differences in location.
This is the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*). "By the mind of preparatory concentration" means by the unique mind of concentration that constitutes the preparation;
the meaning is: by the mind concentrated through momentary concentration occurring by way of the preparation for the knowledge of the divine ear.

They say that what is called "access concentration" (*parikamma-samādhi*) is the stage of access to the divine ear-element (*dibba-sotadhātu*). However, it should be understood that this is spoken of by way of various acts of adverting the mind.
The sound of lions and so forth was mentioned first for the purpose of showing all coarse sounds;
for it is said that even at a distance of three *yojanas*, the roar of a maned lion can be heard. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the sounds of clouds, tigers, and others are included.
The summary should be understood as follows: And here, just as the attention directed toward a coarse sound is solely for the purpose of showing the means for attending to a subtle sound—
since the apprehension of a subtler sound is accomplished through the power of developing the apprehension of sound— so too,
it is shown that by following the apprehension of a nearby sound, the apprehension of sounds that are increasingly distant is also successfully achieved.
With the words “In the eastern direction,” etc., the method of attending to sounds according to their directional relations is commenced.
Therein, “the sign of sound” (*saddanimitta*) refers to the sound itself as the sign of sound, because it serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge;
or else, it refers to that gross or subtle aspect of sounds which is obtained by taking [each] successive [part] as its basis—that is the sign of sound. For this very reason, he said:

“‘The sign of sounds’: as for what was said, ‘the sign of sounds should be brought to mind for both coarse and subtle sounds,’ that is for the purpose of showing the presence of the coarse and subtle even in those things conventionally designated as coarse and subtle.

And all of that should be understood as being for the purpose of demonstrating proficiency in knowledge regarding the subtle. This is because the sign of sound lacks an intrinsic nature in the present.”
Some maintain that the position “sound itself is the sign of sound” is the one that accords with reason;
however, this is not so, because both gross and subtle sounds must be apprehended right there by means of knowledge whose object is color, just as colors such as blue and yellow are.
And here, what is intended by the term “sign of sound” is its gross or subtle state. “Of that” refers to one who practices according to the method described above.
"Those sounds" refers to those sounds, ranging from the coarsest upwards, which have been successively adverted to by the meditator as they become increasingly subtle.
"Even for one whose mind is ordinary" means even for the mind that was functioning prior to entering the foundational jhāna.
"The mind of preparatory concentration" refers to having entered the foundational jhāna for the purpose of producing the divine ear-element.

The connection is as follows: for the mind of momentary concentration that has arisen through the performance of preliminary work (parikamma) by taking sound as its object, these [signs] become exceedingly clear because they have been previously rubbed away by knowledge (ñāṇa).
"Among those sounds" refers to those many sounds mentioned for the purpose of showing the range of the preliminary work.
"A certain one" refers to that single sound upon which his frequent attention proceeded by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*).
"Beyond that" means beyond the arising of absorption (*appanā*). "In that stream" means in that stream of knowledge.
"Has entered" means that from the moment the absorption consciousness arises, the divine ear element is included within it, and he becomes a possessor of the knowledge of the divine ear.

The meaning is that once [the divine ear] has arisen, one need not desire further application to its development for that purpose. "That" refers to the divine ear-element (*dibbasotadhātu*). "Possessed of firmness" means having attained firmness, having reached a state of strength.
It should be developed by means of the object of the foundational absorption (*pādakajjhāna*). To the question "How much? he says:
"Having delimited it by the measure of a finger's breadth, thinking 'I hear sound within this distance. Of the foundational absorption...
For when one enters the foundational jhāna while attending to the kasiṇa-sign as the object, thinking, "Let it pervade this much space," the kasiṇa-sign remains pervading that same extent of space.
Having emerged from that attainment, he adverts to a sound occurring there; because his meditation has been well-developed, he perceives a certain sound therein.
Immediately after the adverting consciousness has arisen directed toward that object, four or five impulsion moments arise.
Among these, the last is the supernormal power consciousness; for the other [the meditator] must again attain the foundational jhāna.

For this very reason, he says with apprehension: "Even when a sound enters within the space touched by the object of the foundational jhāna, one still hears it. And here, the mention of "one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths," etc., is...
This was said with reference to subtle sounds.
"Hearing thus" means: having mastered direct knowledge (abhiññā) through hearing by repeatedly discerning [the sounds] in this way, he hears the sounds exactly as they are produced.
"Separately" means: even when those sounds occur together, he hears them individually.
When there is a desire to define [the faculties] by way of their respective bases.
The commentary on the discussion of the divine ear-element is finished.
Commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds.
401. *Pariyāti* means he knows by discerning through the distinctions of those possessed of lust and so forth. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'he discerns.
For those verbal roots whose primary meaning is 'going,' their meaning is also 'understanding.
Regarding the phrase "of other beings," the word *para* here has the sense of "another"; thus he said, "of all beings except oneself. For indeed, that which is not another is oneself.
That which is not-self is "other. Here, "beings" (*sattānaṃ*) refers to those who exist (*satta*) within form and the other aggregates.

Since this designation is conventionally established for the continuum of beings possessing consciousness, even those devoid of desire and lust are called "beings," either because they were once such or by way of their past state. "Pun" refers to hell;
those who "go" (*galanti*) or fall into it are "persons" (*puggalā*), namely, evildoers. The others [also] are [included] in *saṃsāra*.
Because they do not transcend that very nature as long as they are wandering in *saṃsāra*, they are called "persons" (*puggala*) precisely in the sense of individuals.

Alternatively, according to etymologists (*nerutta*), they are called "persons" because they fill (*pūraṇa*) various groups of beings through rebirth in this or that place, and because they fall away (*galana*) due to impermanence.

In the phrase "for this [is]... (*etañhi*), the word "for" (*hi*) has the sense of a reason; for it is because "this knowledge of the penetration of others' minds" [arises] by way of the divine eye-knowledge...

"Success!"—this refers to the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), which serves as the preliminary exercise (*parikamma*) for the arising of this knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*).
Therefore, the construction should be made thus: "by a bhikkhu who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye and who desires to produce the knowledge of others' minds.
As for "heart-matter" (*hadayarūpa*): it is not the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), but rather the lump of heart-flesh. That which is externally shaped like a lotus bud...
It is said that [the heart-base] is like the interior of a kosātakī fruit, for it is now in dependence upon that [fruit] that the blood mentioned here remains.
As for the heart-base (hadayavatthu), it functions in dependence upon this blood. But how, by seeing the color of the blood with the divine eye, does one seek after the formless mind?
To this he says, beginning with "When, indeed," and so forth. But how [does one know] the occurrence of consciousness accompanied by joy and so on?
Is it that blood produced by karma (*kammaja*) attains various colors? Or who says, "That blood is produced solely by karma"?
For even the fourfold continuity-form (*catusantatirūpa*) is found therein. Therefore, it is said: "This form is originated by the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya-samuṭṭhāna*)," and so forth.
Even so, must that which is not mind-born (*acittaja*) therein not possess the aforementioned distinctions of color? It must possess them.
Because they follow after those [other] material phenomena in the continuity of consciousness.

For just as, in the case of walking and so forth, the material phenomena born of mind (cittaja-rūpa) are followed by those born of temperature, karma, and nutriment—otherwise the body’s arising in another location would not even be possible—so too here, the material phenomena born of mind proceed while following after the other material phenomena in the continuity of consciousness.
It is precisely the attainment of a change in color in the eye during moments of passion or anger.
And this should be regarded as an illustration of that meaning.
"By one seeking" means by one who first sends forth knowledge through inference and thus investigates.

For a yogi desiring to produce the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) must, according to the method explained below, attain the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) endowed with the eight factors.

Having made it capable of being directed, and having attained the knowledge of the divine eye, he increases the light and, by means of the divine eye, perceives the color of the blood flowing in dependence upon the heart-flesh of another;
by seeing that color, he knows: "Now this person's mind is accompanied by joy," or "accompanied by grief," or "accompanied by equanimity."

Or, having determined [the object] by means of grasping the method, one should enter the foundational jhāna, emerge, and perform the preliminary work (parikamma) with the thought, "I know this person's mind.
One should proceed in the same manner, entering and emerging from the foundational jhāna again and again for a hundred times or a thousand times.
Thus, by means of the divine eye, through the procedure of seeing the color of the blood in the heart and so forth—

For one who is practicing with the thought, "Now, knowledge of penetration into others' minds will arise," mind-door adverting consciousness arises taking as its object that state of consciousness which was previously determined [by the practitioner] as being present at that time. When that has ceased, four or five impulsion moments (javana) occur.
Of these, the first three or four are known by the designations "preliminary work" (parikamma) and so forth, and belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
The fourth or fifth absorption consciousness belongs to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and is the fourth jhāna.
Among these, the knowledge that arises together with the final absorption consciousness is "knowledge of others' minds" (cetopariyañāṇa).
For that [knowledge] proceeds by directly penetrating and clearly discerning the other person's mind in whatever way the preliminary work (parikamma) was performed by him.

Just as the knowledge of the divine eye [perceives] form, and the knowledge of the divine ear [perceives] sound, so too, beyond that, there is the determination of states such as "with lust" and so forth by means of sense-sphere consciousnesses, just as there is the determination of colors such as blue and so forth.

Furthermore, the method for consolidating the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) once it has been attained is exactly like the method for its initial attainment; to show this, it says: "Therefore, by that... pe..."
"It should be made firm" is what was said.
"When it has thus become firm," and so forth, is the demonstration of the benefits of its becoming firm.

"All sense-sphere consciousness" refers to the fifty-four types of sense-sphere consciousness. The word "all" should also be brought over to the phrase "fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousness."

It should be connected [to the previous context]. By this, it is meant that there are fifteen types of fine-material-sphere consciousness (*rūpāvacara-citta*) and twelve types of immaterial-sphere consciousness (*arūpāvacara-citta*).
"He understands" means he knows by way of the modes such as "with lust" and so forth; the intention is that he penetrates them through direct perception.

This discussion of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is from the perspective of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*); therefore, supramundane consciousness (*lokuttara-citta*) is not mentioned here. For even that is [treated] by the one above.
Or, a noble one understands the mind of an inferior person who is his equal; thus, he understands even the mind of one who is equal.
Therefore, he said, “or a supreme mind,” and so forth. “Transmigrating” means approaching by means of knowledge.

For when one knows a certain mind and, without preparatory work (parikamma), knows another mind, one is said to be “transmigrating from mind to mind. Therefore, he said, “even without seeing the physical heart.”
For the method of seeing the heart-form and so forth is stated with reference to a beginner. Therefore he said, "And although this has been stated," and so on.
"Anywhere" means in either the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) or the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokāra-bhava*).

"One who has not made a fixed application" (*akatābhiniveso*) refers to one by whom no fixed application—consisting of the practice of higher knowledge (*abhiññānuyoga*)—has been made; the meaning is "of such a beginner. This discourse [begins with] "light..."
The discourse on preliminary preparation is stated by the passage beginning with “having increased,” and so forth.
“The remainder” refers to what has been left unsaid. To show, by way of analysis, that which was stated without analysis, he said:
“Wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is free from lust. For that [consciousness] possesses the conditions of wise attention and the state of being caused.
Because there is no possibility of association with greed (*rāga*), it receives the designation "free from greed" (*vītarāga*).

Since the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses lack association with greed, they possess no state of being "with greed" (*sarāgatā*); yet, because they are caused by that [greed], they might be considered "accompanied by it," and thus they possess no state of being "free from greed" either.
Therefore, it is stated that "in this dyad, inclusion is not appropriate," as only the state of being free from both [greed and its accompaniment] is logical.

"...are going. If this is so, does one thereby attain a partial knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*)? One does not, because those [states] are included within the interval between [the wholesome and unwholesome].

However, regarding those who maintain that even in the absence of opposition, the mere lack of association is the criterion here—just as in the case of certain indeterminate states—and who thus claim that even other unwholesome minds are free from lust, it was with reference to them that he said: "But some elders..."
"Those [factors] too are included. In the "Duo with Hatred" (sadosaduka) as well, the meaning should be understood according to this same method.

"By way of individual application" (pāṭipuggalikanayena) means by way of specific distinction; the meaning is that, unlike in other unwholesome states of consciousness, there is the presence of delusion (moha) alone, unmixed with greed (lobha) and hatred (dosa).
Regarding those things termed "unwholesome roots," it is "with delusion" (samoha) because it is accompanied by delusion according to the first method.

In the second method, however, because of the restriction of the subsequent and preceding words as "together with delusion" (*saha eva mohena*), the distinction between the two methods should be understood.

"Accompanied by sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddhānugata*) refers to the fivefold wholesome consciousness with prompting (*sasankhārika-kusala-citta*) that has proceeded—that is, arisen—in accordance with the sloth and torpor associated with itself, by way of following after it; [this occurs] through the contraction of the object.
Because it proceeds [in that manner]. It should be understood as being accompanied by restlessness according to the method already stated;
moreover, it is the consciousness associated with restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata-citta*), or that in which restlessness occurs having become firmly established through a specific condition.

It has attained greatness because it is capable of suppressing the defilements, because its fruit is vast, and because its continuity is long; or else, it is so called because it is possessed of great, sublime desire, energy, mind, and wisdom.
"Attained" (*gata*) means "practiced" (*paṭipanna*); "lofty" (*mahaggata*). "The remainder" (*avasesa*) refers to the limited (*paritta*) and the immeasurable (*appamāṇa*).

"With-surpassable" (*sauttara*) means together with those capable of surpassing oneself. "Crossed over" (*uttiṇṇa*) means "surpassing" (*uttara*); because they transcend the world by way of not being included within it, they are "supramundane" (*lokuttara*).
For that very reason, "there is nothing superior to this" is "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*). [This occurs] by means of that which has attained the characteristic of close contemplation (*upanijjhāna*).
It is "concentrated" (*samāhita*) because it is properly placed (*sammā-āhita*) by means of concentration (*samādhi*).

This refers to: wholesome sense-sphere consciousness that has attained liberation by way of its own factor (*tadaṅga-vimutti*); sublime consciousness that has attained suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*); path-consciousness that has attained eradication-liberation (*samuccheda-vimutti*);

fruition-consciousness that has attained tranquillization-liberation (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*); and both of these [path and fruition] which have also attained escape-liberation (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).
Granted that some reviewing consciousnesses and so forth have Nibbāna as their object, they do not, however, attain the liberation of escape because they lack the corresponding function.
[This applies] in every way, both according to the classification of "with lust" and so on found in the Canon, and according to their internal subdivisions.
The commentary on the discussion of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds is finished.

Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Recollection of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 402. One recollects past lives; or, the recollection of that [past life] is "recollection of past lives" (*pubbenivāsānussati*).

Because it arises in dependence upon that [recollection] as its support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) and other conditions, the meaning stated briefly as “the knowledge which is in the recollection of past lives, for the sake of that” is explained.

Having first shown the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), he spoke the passage beginning with "past lives" (*pubbenivāso*) in order to demonstrate the mindfulness and knowledge regarding them.
In that context, because of the statement "even a single birth," the word "previously" (*pubbe*) is intended here as referring to the domain of past existences;

thus he said, "in past births. The term *nivāsa* (dwelling) is derived from the root meaning "to dwell" (*vas*), functioning as a noun denoting the act of dwelling; furthermore, the phenomenon that dwells is distinct from the aggregates (*khandha*).
He said, "They do not exist," referring to them as "the aggregates that have been lived through" (*nivutthakkhandhā*).

Here, "having been lived through" means having occurred within one's own continuum; and being such, they have been experienced, undergone, and proceeded—that is, having arisen there, they have simply vanished.
Thus he said, "Lived through means dwelt upon, experienced, having arisen and ceased within one's own continuum. In this way, it is by way of phenomena included within one's own continuum...

Having explained the meaning of the word *nivāsa*, he now speaks of it without distinction, saying "or the dhammas inhabited (*nivuttha*)," and in order to clarify that, he says "by way of inhabiting the range (*gocara-nivāsena*)," and so forth.

For even those things that have become one's range (*gocara*) are called "inhabited" when they have been cultivated through the cultivation of the range and experienced by way of being made the object (*ārammaṇa*).
These, moreover, are twofold, according to whether they are the range of one's own consciousness or the range of another's consciousness.
To show both of these, the passage beginning with “of oneself” was stated.

Therein, after saying “cognized by one’s own consciousness,” the statement “delimited” means that those phenomena which have been dwelt upon through the dwelling in their respective objects are not merely consciousness by virtue of being consciousness alone;
rather, they are [delimited] according to previous distinctions such as birth, name, clan, complexion, gender, food, and so forth.
It is stated for the purpose of illustrating this meaning: "Having been grasped by discerning wisdom (*paññā*) through delimitation, this very knowledge likewise grasps it through delimitation.
Alternatively, the connection is: "Or, they are known even by the consciousness of others. The meaning is: not only by one's own consciousness, but also by the consciousness of others. Here too—
The word “delimited” (*paricchinna*) should be brought forward and connected [to the previous phrase] as: “or, they are delimited by the consciousness of others who have cognized them.
And the purpose for including that [word] should be stated in the same manner already explained.

Furthermore, because those [beings] were cognized and delimited by others in very many births, they have even attained final nibbāna (*parinibbuta*). For, at that time, of those who were the cognizers...
Since their past activity is also known by following the continuity of the present stream, the phrase "in the recollection of those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth (chinnavaṭumaka), etc.
is stated in order to show the past lives that constitute the object of the knowledge of recollecting past existences (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) to its full extent.

"Chinnavaṭumaka" refers to the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas; the recollection of them is "the recollection of those who have cut off the cycle of rebirth. By the word "etc.," the recollections of the Pacceka-Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddha are included.
They say that [these beings] were still grasping. However, all those who had severed the cycle of rebirth (vaṭumaka) have attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue.
The "recollection of them" means the recollection of their practice; that practice, in brief, is characterized by the grasping of the six objects of consciousness.
These [objects] are here included by way of the grasping of what was cognized by the consciousness of others. They...
"These are the domain of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones alone, not of others," he said, "for these are obtained by the Buddhas alone.

For it is not the case that the Blessed Buddhas of the past did not thus see, did not thus develop the path, did not thus realize the fruits and Nibbāna, and did not thus discipline those to be disciplined;
for in this regard, there is always the range of knowledge for others as well. By which...
"By means of mindfulness, one recollects past lives"; this should be connected by bringing in the phrase "that is the recollection of past lives.
"In many ways" means manifold, by way of various types of existence, birth-origins, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and so forth.
"By means of modes" means together with the aspects of name, clan, and so on; and here the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahayoga*). "Expounded" means by way of teaching.
Therefore he said, “described,” which means “elaborated. Regarding the term “dwelling” (*nivāsa*), it is a general designation that includes its specific subdivisions;
thus, showing them by grouping them according to the desire for detailed analysis, he said, “the continuum dwelling here and there.
This recollection belongs only to a disciple, not to the Teacher; as it was said: “by way of the succession of aggregates and by way of death and rebirth-linking.”
"Or" (*vā*). "The sequence of the aggregates" (*khandha-paṭipāṭi*) refers to the order of the aggregates. And that indeed proceeds by way of a reverse order starting from the moment of death.
However, some here say: "The sequence of postures is the sequence of the aggregates. "Following along, following along" means following along, following along by the course of knowledge.
"Forders" (*titthiya*) means those of other sects; they are proponents of karma and proponents of action.
The ascetics and so forth. Excluding the Chief Disciples and the Great Disciples, the other disciples of the Teacher are ordinary disciples.

Since in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and others among the non-Buddhists, the recollection of only forty eons of world-dissolution and evolution is mentioned, he says "not beyond that" and, stating the reason for this, says "because their wisdom is weak," and so on. By this...
This shows that application to insight (vipassanā) is the specific cause for the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa).
Regarding the phrase "strong foundation" (balavapaññatti), here the discernment of name-and-form (nāmarūpapariccheda) and so forth alone should be seen as the cause of strength for wisdom;
this is their common cause in this context. "So much" refers to a hundred thousand aeons, plus one, and two incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) aeons.
By the power of time alone, the application of merit and knowledge of those great disciples, chief disciples, and paccekabuddhas— each according to their respective order—

was completed as the perfections of disciple-enlightenment and paccekabuddha-enlightenment. If the distinction of the super-knowledge (abhiññā) and wisdom of these various noble ones is limited by the duration of the period for accumulating the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), then it follows that even for the Buddhas there would be a limitation of their range of objects (visaya).

He said: "But for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a limitation. Because of the statement, "As far as the knowable extends, so far extends knowledge," there is no limitation whatsoever regarding the range of the super-knowledge (abhiññā) of the Buddhas, just as there is none for their omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
In that regard, whatever they wish to know, they certainly know it. Alternatively, even though there is a limitation of time, [there is no limitation of object].
Because the equipment for great enlightenment is preeminent due to its being embraced by skill in means and causes, there is no limit to the power of the manifestation of the perfection of wisdom;
how much less so for the super-knowledge-wisdoms produced thereby? Thus he said, "But for the Buddhas, there is no limit.
This refers to the limitation of time, such as "there have been this many incalculable eons in the past."
There is no [distinction] of time, just as in the case of the knowledge of future states regarding the future.
Having thus shown the recollection of past lives of the six types of persons by way of the division of time, he now says "And the sectarians...
and so forth, in order to show it by way of the grasping of objects, the distinction of power, and the mode of occurrence. "By way of death and rebirth-linking" means...

Having observed the death (cuti) of oneself or another in this or that individual existence (attabhāva), one grasps [the process] solely by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), without touching upon anything in between.
To clarify this same point through both negative and positive concomitance, the passage beginning with "For those...
was stated. That ordinary disciples (pakatisāvaka) also transmigrate by way of death and rebirth-linking is according to the method explained below.

“‘Because it is defined by power’ (balavapaññattā)”: this is to be clarified by way of the cause; for there is no purpose in showing the intermediate state when one is observing the transition by way of death and rebirth-linking.
However, it is mentioned here for the purpose of demonstrating the power of knowledge.
That [intermediate state] is indeed evident; just as, for example, at the time of midday during the autumn season, in a room four *aratnis* high...
It is a world-established fact that for a man with eyes, visible forms are indeed quite manifest within his house;

yet it may be that those forms—distinguished as being more subtle, concealed, and so forth—are beyond his range. However, there is no such thing as the knowable (ñeyya) being beyond the range of the Buddhas when they desire to know it;
rather, it is illuminated by the light of their knowledge like an *āmalaka* fruit upon the palm of the hand.
It becomes as clearly manifest and distinct as if it were right before one’s eyes, because the cognitive obscurations (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*) have been thoroughly abandoned.

Regarding the phrase "having abbreviated like a formulaic passage (*peyyāla-pāḷi*)," just as those reciting a formulaic passage abbreviate by taking only the beginning and the end—saying, for example, "the first jhāna...
[pe] ...the fifth jhāna"—and do not recite every single word, so too [one remembers] many tens of millions of eons.
Having condensed [the explanation]: "Whatever they desire" means that in whichever aeon (*kappa*) or whichever existence (*bhava*), whatever they wish to know;
entering by means of knowledge precisely into those things they wish to know, they proceed by way of the movement of knowledge, like the leaping of a lion, like the falling of a lion’s stride.
This refers to one who has practiced the piercing of hair-tufts (*vālavedha*) by placing the tip of a hair split a hundredfold against another tip.
"Like Sarabhaṅga" means like the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga. It does not cling because it has not reached the stage of a "lakkha" (target).
It does not become dispassionate because of its mode of transcending and passing beyond.
It appears as similar to the glow of a firefly due to the extreme feebleness of the power of that knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Having offered [the oblation], the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) becomes manifest. This same method applies to the others as well.
"Similar to the light of a lamp" means similar to the ordinary light of a lamp. "The light of a torch" is the light of a large firebrand.

"The light of the medicinal-star" refers to the light of the star named *osadhi*—so called because its abundant light is sustained by it—or because it provides auxiliary power to medicinal herbs. It is similar to the orb of the autumnal sun.
