Because it completely dispels darkness regarding its own object;
because it does not let go of the succession of the aggregates, like walking on the tip of a staff;
a *daṇḍakasetu* is a bridge made with a single wooden pole for crossing over small streams; one that can be traversed by four or five people.
A *jaṅghasetu* is a crossing constructed by spreading planks on a surface and hammering in wedges;

it is like a footpath (*jaṅghamagga*), a crossing suitable for the passage of a foot-soldier (*jaṅghasattha*). A *sakaṭasetu* is a crossing suitable for the passage of a cart; it is like a cart-road (*sakaṭamagga*).
A path to be traversed by a large body of foot-soldiers is a great foot-path (*mahājaṅghamagga*). [It may be traversed] by many, or by twenty, or thirty...
Or, a road that must be traveled together with carts is a "cart-road.
But in this context, it refers to the section concerning the cultivation of concentration indicated for the disciple under the heading of "mind," namely: "Cultivate the mind and wisdom. 403.
*Tasmā* (therefore) means because the recollection of past lives intended here pertains to disciples; *evaṃ* (thus) means in the manner [described].
They recollect [the Buddhas] in this way by one who desires to recollect them.

Regarding the phrase "having attained the four jhānas," it is stated because of the gladdening of body and mind through the appropriate *pīti* (rapture) and *sukha* (bliss) in the three lower jhānas; otherwise, one would have to attain only the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).
That sitting posture in which the commencement of the recollection occurs while seated is the very last one mentioned here.
"Sitting" (*nisajjā*). "Then, the arranging of the seat" (*tato āsanapaññāpanaṃ*): the connection is that one should bring to mind the prior arrangement of the seat before sitting down.
This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. Regarding "the time for eating," etc., by means of the term "time," he refers to the duty performed at each respective time.

"The time for worshipping at the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard" (*cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavandanakālo*) means the time for worshipping the shrine and the Bodhi-tree in the shrine courtyard and the Bodhi-tree courtyard.
“Throughout the entire day and night” is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
“Some task”: by this much, namely, by the attainment of the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).

For the foundational jhāna, like a whetstone for a knife, brings about a state of sharpening for both mindfulness and wisdom. That which belongs to it—by attaining that [jhāna]—reaches the highest degree of refinement.
[They] exist. Therefore he said: "It becomes manifest like a lamp lit," meaning in a place of darkness.
"In the previous existence" means in the existence immediately preceding this present existence.

"Name-and-form that has proceeded" refers to the name-and-form that has proceeded by way of its own conditions. And in that case, having first adverted to the form, the name should be adverted to. First...

Others say that after attending to the name, one subsequently attends to the form. "It is possible" means it is capable. "The wise one" refers to one who has performed the requisite work for this development of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

"Another has arisen"—this is said with reference to the fact that another rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*) has arisen from a previous kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), because it belongs to the intermediate state of the present duration (*addhāpaccuppanna*).
Otherwise, within a single existence as well, only various [successive] mind-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arise.
And that which has ceased is without rebirth-linking. Therefore it was said:
"All those aggregates (khandhas) that have ceased for one dying here, or for one remaining here, are alike in having gone without rebirth-linking."

"That place" (*taṃ ṭhānaṃ*) means that location where [the consciousness] was deposited. "Dense" (*āhundarikaṃ*) means a crowded place, covered thickly on all sides and above. "Like blinding darkness" (*andhatamamiva*) means like the gloom of pitch-blackness.

"For the sake of the pinnacle of a gabled house" (*kūṭāgārakaṇṇikatthāya*) means for the sake of the peak of the gabled house. Knowledge of the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ*) is like the central pillar (*kaṇṇikā*) of the gabled house;
the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) occurring at the moment of death in a previous existence is like the great tree; and what is connected to it is like the branches and foliage.
In this existence, the rebirth-linking consciousness is like the axe-blade; the preliminary development (*parikamma-bhāvanā*) is like the woodcutter's workshop;
and the basic jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna*) is like the workshop itself—thus should the application of the similes be understood. There is also the simile of the wooden wedge:
"Just as when a strong man, splitting a large log for the purpose of cooking rice and so forth, splits it down to its bark and sapwood..."

It should be understood according to the method stated in such passages as: "Unable to split a large log with a damaged axe blade, he did not lay down his burden," and so forth. Likewise, it is like the simile of the hair-cutter.
There is no knowledge of past lives because there is an absence of the objective condition consisting of the phenomena that resided in past births. That...
The knowledge that occurs from the final sitting onwards until the moment of rebirth-linking,

which is associated with the concentration functioning as the preliminary exercise for the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*), is "knowledge of preliminary-concentration" (*parikamma-samādhi-ñāṇa*).

Their statement that this is not applicable with reference to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) implies that if this knowledge of the past is intended, it is meant to belong to the fine-material sphere.

It is not logical [to claim] that access-concentration knowledge (*parikamma-samādhi-ñāṇa*) belongs to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), for there is nothing found in either the Canon (*pāḷi*) or the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) stating that a fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) consciousness arises by taking as its object the aggregates occurring prior to the immediately preceding death-consciousness. The construction is:
"of those impulsions (*javana*) which are the preceding ones. However, when it is absorption consciousness (*appanā-citta*), [it is different].
The connection is thus: "This is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

Although it has been shown that this knowledge occurs by taking as its object the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that occurred at the moment of death in the immediately preceding existence, that should be regarded as merely an illustration, since it demonstrates the common nature of such knowledge. For, starting from that name-and-form, all...
Past aggregates and everything connected with those aggregates constitute past lives;

thus, the knowledge that proceeds by way of penetrating this is the knowledge of recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa*). Therefore it was said: "By means of that knowledge, through mindfulness associated with it, he recollects his manifold past lives."
404. "Even a single birth" (*ekampi jātiṃ*) means even a single existence (*bhava*).

For here, what is intended by "birth" is a continuity of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) produced by a single karma, delimited by grasping and casting off, and comprising a variety of internal phenomena.

Therefore he said: "even a single... [up to] ...continuity of aggregates. "Falling away" (*parihāyamāno*) means wasting away or perishing. "An eon" (*kappa*) refers to an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).
However, in terms of its actual meaning, "time" refers to the conditioned phenomena occurring at that moment; it is by way of these that its diminution is to be understood.
The same principle applies here to the phrase "an expanding aeon of evolution" (*vivaṭṭakappa*).

As for the sense in which "time is spent"—as in such passages as "Time devours all beings, together with the creator"—where the destruction of time itself is spoken of, that is not intended here, as it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

*Saṃvaṭṭanaṃ* (contraction) means destruction; *saṃvaṭṭo*. That which remains for a period after contraction is *saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*. "Because it has that as its root" means because it has that as its precursor.
*Vivaṭṭanaṃ* means manifestation or arising, or else expansion;

thus, *vivaṭṭo*. When the contractions are to be discussed according to the sequence of the boundaries of contraction—namely, the fire-contraction (*tejosaṃvaṭṭo*), the water-contraction (*āposaṃvaṭṭo*), and the wind-contraction (*vāyosaṃvaṭṭo*)—[the following applies].

Some say that by not stating it thus, the statement "dissolution by water, dissolution by fire, or dissolution by wind" is intended as a sequential teaching on the great elements of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭaka-mahābhūta*).

Others say it is a sequence of dissolutions (*saṃvaṭṭānupubbī*). "Dissolution by water" (*āposaṃvaṭṭo*) means dissolution through water. "Dissolution-limit" (*saṃvaṭṭasīmā*) means the boundary of dissolution.
"It dissolves" (*saṃvaṭṭati*) means it perishes. "Always" (*sadā*) means at all times; the meaning is: during all three periods of dissolution.
Regarding the phrase “a single Buddha-field,” in order to define and demonstrate what is intended here, it is said: “A Buddha-field is of three kinds,” and so forth.

To whatever extent the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of rebirth—intensified by the fruit of his merit—causes the earth itself to tremble by its own inherent force, all that is called the field for the production of the Buddha-sprout.
He said: "The field of birth extends as far as ten thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa). Regarding the phrase "its power prevails":

here, a possessor of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind, standing in any world-system included within the field of his command, performs a protective chant (paritta) for his own sake;
even if he goes to another world-system right there, he remains one for whom the chant has been performed. Or else, in that [other] place...

When a protective chant (paritta) is recited for the benefit of all beings while standing within a single world-system (cakkavāḷa), the power of that protection must indeed reach all those beings within the field of its command;
for therein, the deities must accept the protection for their own sake.
This refers to that specific field where one who claims to make themselves known by voice and to manifest their own form simultaneously proclaims it.
The Blessed One said: "Or as much as he might wish. "Where" means in whatever field of objects, infinite and immeasurable.
Whatever the Tathāgata wishes, that he knows, because the Buddha’s knowledge functions in dependence upon mere intention.
"Establishing" means evolving, coming into being.

405. “Gokhāyitakamattesū” means at the time when [the food] is the size of what is to be eaten by a cow. “Yam” refers to the time at which. The connection is: “And the deities who subsist on flowers and fruits are reborn in the Brahmā-world.

“Etesaṃ” refers to the beings mentioned by the words “those who subsist on rain,” and so forth. “Tattha” means in the Brahmā-world; and that should be understood as the Brahmā-world of Limited Radiance (Parittābha) and so on.
Having stated “by way of having attained jhāna,” he now shows the possibility of attaining jhāna.
“Then indeed,” etc., was said. They are called *lokabyūhā* because they push together and gather the world.
It is said that upon seeing them, people—whether standing or sitting here and there—are moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and, overcome with agitation, assemble in places near them.
They have “loose hair” (*muttasirā*) because their hair-knots have been released, and because their hair is being tossed about here and there.
With disheveled hair, they wore extremely hideous disguises due to their hearts being filled with sorrow from the fear of the world’s destruction.

“Mārisa” is a term of address used by the gods out of affection. But how do these beings know of the emergence of the aeon? The teachers say it is because they are impelled by the natural law (*dhammatā*).
Some say it is by seeing such signs. Others say it is because they have been urged on by the deities of Brahmā.

“Loving-kindness and so forth” refers to the sense-sphere merits consisting of the mental application of loving-kindness and the like. “In the world of the devas” means in the world of the devas of the sense sphere.
It is said that for the devas, because of their familiarity with grasping the wind that has a pleasant touch, the jhānas arise easily in the wind-kasiṇa;
therefore it is said, “having performed the preliminary work on the wind-kasiṇa, they attain jhāna. “But others besides those” refers to those bound for the states of deprivation (āpāyika).
He spoke with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Therein" means in the world of the gods (*devaloka*).
"A second sun" refers to a second solar disk (*sūriyamaṇḍala*). "The seven-sun [sutta]" refers to the *Sattasūriyapātubhāva-sutta*.
"The natural sun" refers to the solar mansion (*sūriyavimāna*) that arose prior to the time of the world's dissolution (*kappavuṭṭhāna*). However, at the time of the world's dissolution...
Just as other deities of the sense-sphere realm, so too the Sun Deity, having produced jhāna, is reborn in the Brahma-world;
however, the solar disk continues to revolve, becoming even more radiant and more majestic.
Others say that after it has vanished, another entirely new one arises. [The rivers] Ganges, Yamunā, Sarabhū, Aciravatī, and Mahī.
These are the five great rivers.
"Sources" refers to their places of origin. "Haṃsapāta" refers to the Mandākinī.
"Does not stand still" means it does not remain stationary.

"Pariyādinnasinehaṃ" means that its moisture is completely exhausted. That element of water by which the element of earth remains bound together and consolidated here and there comes to total exhaustion through the manifestation of six suns.
Just as this Cakkavāḷa [world-system] is consumed, so too are hundreds of thousands of kotis of Cakkavāḷas; this is due to the arising of the great clouds of destruction.
Starting from that point, all that has been stated here regarding the emergence of the eon is extended by analogy to that [other world].

"Having been destroyed" means having been cut off. "The mass of formations" refers to the various types of formations consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives. "Through the complete exhaustion of all formations" means through the exhaustion of those formations that are to be consumed by fire.
Being itself a part of the mass of formations, it [the ash] also—due to the absence of fuel—is [exhausted].
"Having consumed it without remainder and having extinguished it," he said, "ghee... [etc. ...is extinguished.
(406) "After a long period of time" means after the passing of a long duration reckoned as incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*) of dissolution and stabilization.
"From the trunk of a palmyra tree, etc."—by the word "etc.," one includes trees such as the *sāka* and *sāla*. "It makes a solid mass" means:
Without allowing it to disperse, he makes it compact. Therefore he says "encircled" (*parivaṭuma*), meaning delimited by its circular nature.
"That" refers to the water. "Of him" refers to the wind. "He gives an opening" means that just as he makes it dense and compacts it, so too he provides an interval therein.
"Being exhausted" refers to the wind which previously existed as a single mass reaching as far as the Brahma-world.
The construction is: "As it is being dried up and going toward total exhaustion, the Brahma-world appears. By "Brahma-world," he refers to the plane of the first jhāna.
"In the upper region of the four sense-sphere heavens" means in the place where the four [heavens], such as the Yāma heaven and so forth, are established.
However, the places where the abodes of the Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa devas are established [are elsewhere].
Because of their connection with the earth, they do not yet appear.
"They obstruct" means they cause cessation in such a way that [the light] does not scatter below.
"Those produced earlier" is a demonstration of the possibility of the exhaustion of the lifespan; by this, [it refers to] two or four...
This shows that they are reborn at the beginning of eight eons. "From there" means from the Ābhassara Brahma-world;
for both the Parittābha and Appamāṇābha realms are included by the term "Ābhassara.

The statement, "They are self-luminous, moving through the sky," is said because of the great power of the merit of access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*). "Making morsels" means making them into mouthfuls.
They say [it means] "making a plunder," that is to say, committing a looting.
"Joyful and delighted" means exceedingly joyful, with hearts overflowing with elation. "They give it a name" means they designate it as such in common usage.

Regarding the phrase "Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavat mountains," one should here add "the islands and the oceans. For he will say later: "In the lowest places there are oceans; in the level places there are islands. "Mound upon mound" means rising high and high.
*Atimaññanti* means they despise them after having surpassed them; the meaning is that they treat them with contempt.

*Tena eva nayena* means by the very same method as that stated in the passage beginning, "some are handsome. *Padālatā* is a species of creeper so named. They say that the *pārāsava* species of it is called *gaḷocī*.
*Akaṭṭhe eva bhūmippadese paccanako* means ripening spontaneously on unploughed ground. *Akaṇo* means free from broken grains (*kuṇḍaka*).
"Like the jasmine flower known as *sumana*": it is like the jasmine (*sumana*) flower. "Whatever its taste" means that which has whatever taste;
*odana* (boiled rice), meaning "possessing such a flavor"—this is the sense.

Having consumed the "taste-earth," the "earth-crust," and the "ground-vine," they remain dispelling hunger just as if consuming ambrosial food, increasing the essence alone through the nutrient channels.
The excretions do not arise from the subtlety of the substance; rather, it is precisely because of its subtlety that they become the fuel for perception.
However, when boiled rice is consumed, even while increasing the bodily fluids, it releases an excretion due to the grossness of the substance, thereby producing urine and feces;
thus he said, "From that time onwards, urine and feces are produced. Regarding previous existences:
By the power of the jhāna associated with the conventional practice, as long as the force of the suppression of sensual lust within the continuum of beings was not stilled,
the male and female faculties— which serve as the supporting conditions for powerful sensual lust— did not manifest. However,

when that [suppression] was interrupted and powerful sensual lust found an opportunity, then those [faculties], which are its supporting conditions, appeared within the personal existences of those beings.
They were born. Therefore it was said: “For a man... appears. For that very reason he said: “There, indeed,” and so forth.
“Of one who is by nature lazy” means of one whose disposition is indolent because of taking rice for the sake of the following day instead of taking it immediately.

“Lamenting” means grieving after. “We would authorize” means we would permit. “No” refers to us. “Properly” means exactly as is fitting. “To be censured” means worthy of censure, blameworthy. “To be reviled” means to be despised.

The construction is: "This Blessed One alone is capable of exercising encouragement and restraint. "He delights" means he causes them to rejoice and be satisfied properly through the bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).

"A world-cycle conducive to turning away from existence" (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) comprises sixty-four intermediate eons (*antarakappa*); some say it comprises twenty intermediate eons. The remaining *asaṅkhyeyya*s are equal in duration to that [first one]. 407.
"By great torrents" means by large streams of water for washing, as thick as the trunks of palm trees. "From all sides" means...
"Completely": from the very bottom of the earth upwards.
For by that water which sustains the earth, the earth, mountains, and so forth, wherever they are touched, simply dissolve like salt crystals thrown into water;

therefore, some say that together with the water sustaining the earth, it becomes one and the same water. Others [say] "the mass of water that sustains the earth and the mass of earth that sustains the water..."
They say that after completely destroying the mass of wind, it remains everywhere as a single unified stream;
this is correct. Regarding the phrase "in the three Brahmā-worlds," this refers to the Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara Brahmā-worlds.
This was stated because [the text] began with the words "but this is the distinction"; otherwise, one would have had to say "in the six Brahmā-worlds."
It may be so. "Subhakiṇha" is a designation for the plane of the third jhāna by way of its highest limit.
For even in the cases of the limited foulness and the measureless foulness, the water stands having reached them. The same principle applies here as in the previous passage:

"it stands having reached the Ābhassara [brahmās]. "That" refers to that water which destroys the aeon. "Followed by water" means followed or pervaded by water. "Having overcome" means having caused it to melt away.
"This is one incalculable" means that this constitutes one incalculable of the aeon known as the period of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*).
408. It is said, "Then the fine dust," because once the coarse dust has departed, the fine dust dependent upon the earth departs as well.
The connection is with the word "arises. "Great trees standing on uneven ground"—this is the first [point].
This was said with reference to what ought to be raised up.

Even the Cakkavāḷa mountain and even Sineru mountain—by the very overturning of the great earth, the wind lifts up both the Cakkavāḷa mountain and Sineru mountain and hurls them into the sky. These are the Cakkavāḷa mountains and so forth.

"Having struck" (*abhihantvā*) means having collided. "Mutually" (*aññamaññaṃ*) means having collided by way of mutual contact, such as the world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), Himavat, and Sineru of one world-system with the world-systems, Himavat, and Sineru of another world-system.

"The entire realm of formations" (*sabbasaṅkhāragataṃ*) refers to the water that supports the earth and the wind that supports that water; having destroyed all that realm of formations, it [the fire] itself...
It perishes because there is no cause for its continued existence. 409.

Even if the spontaneous cessation of formations (*saṅkhāra*) is causeless due to the absence of a cause for destruction, there is no cessation of the continuum (*santāna*) devoid of a cause, as is the case with the bodies of sentient beings.
The receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) likewise undergoes destruction accompanied by a cause.
"Is it to be so?"—with this he asks for the cause: "For what reason does the world thus undergo destruction?

The other replies, "By way of the unwholesome roots," showing that just as the world first expands through the power of the merit of those beings reborn therein, so too it contracts through the power of their demerit.
For, according to the predominance of lust, hatred, and delusion respectively, [the world contracts].

The intermediate aeon of disease (*rogantara-kappa*), the intermediate aeon of weapons (*satthantara-kappa*), and the intermediate aeon of famine (*dubbhikkhantara-kappa*)—these three types of intermediate aeons arise during an incalculable aeon while the world is in the process of expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyi*).

Thus, showing that these three aforementioned contractions (*saṃvaṭṭa*) occur precisely through the predominance of lust and the other [defilements], he said: "In the unwholesome roots," and so forth. *Ussannatara* means exceedingly.
When the fault (*dosa*) is predominant. Since destruction by a more pungent alkaline solution is appropriate for a fault that is more predominant—just as it is for a greater fault—it is said:

"When the fault is more predominant, it is destroyed by water. The intention is that fire-likeness is appropriate for a fault resembling manifest bile (*pākaṭa-sattu*), while alkaline-solution-likeness is appropriate for passion (*rāga*) resembling unmanifest bile (*apākaṭa-sattu*); thus, "when the fault is more predominant... [it is said].
The intention of the statement by some, "by fire when passion (*rāga*) is more prevalent, and by water [when it is more prevalent]," should be understood as follows:
since passion occurs most frequently among sentient beings, the destruction of the world happens many times over due to passion.

Having thus explained the contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*) and so forth as an incidental discussion, the passage beginning with "even when recollecting his former births" is now commenced in order to show the manner of their recollection according to what was specifically assigned.
"In that eon of dissolution" (*amumhi saṃvaṭṭakappe*) is stated because this [period] is taken from the beginning of the Pāḷi account of the eon of dissolution.
For even therein, his wandering through states of existence (*bhava*) and so forth for some time is found.

Or rather, it should be understood as showing that his rebirth occurred while the eons of dissolution were proceeding through the various states of existence. Alternatively, "in that eon of dissolution" means:
Here, the word "vā" (or) should be understood as being elided; by its sense of non-restriction, the inclusion of the other incalculables is thereby established.

In the phrases "in a [particular] existence," etc., this refers to: either in a realm of existence such as the sensual realm (*kāmadhātu*); or in a mode of birth such as the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*); or in a destination such as the gods (*deva*);
or in a station of consciousness such as "those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions"; or in an abode of beings (*sattāvāsa*); or in a class of beings such as the Khattiyas.

Or: "I was" (*āsinti ahosim*). By the word "or" (*vā*), he indicates "or beauty" (*vaṇṇasampattiṃ*) as well as "or ugliness" (*vaṇṇavipattiṃ*). "Food consisting of fine rice and meat" refers to the time of being a householder;

"one who eats fallen fruit" refers to the time of being an ascetic and so forth. "Worldly" (*sāmisā*) refers to joy and other states based on household life; "unworldly" (*nirāmisā*) refers to those based on renunciation. By the word "etc. (*ādi-*) there is an inclusion of the bliss born of seclusion, the bliss born of concentration, and so on.
Having shown the recollection of everything according to one's desire through the passage beginning with "I was there," he now [explains] the meaning in another way.
The phrase beginning with “apicā” (furthermore) was stated in order to show this. Therein, “amutrāsiṃ” (I was there) is a general designation, or it is an ellipsis for a specific analysis;

that is to say, “amutra amutrāsiṃ” (I was here and there). Regarding the phrase “recollection as far as desired for one who is ascending in due succession,” here “ārohantassa” (for one who is ascending) means for one who is ascending through past lives by means of knowledge in reverse order. “Paccavekkhaṇaṃ” (reviewing) [is what follows].
It is the reviewing of what has been recollected again and again, not the act of recollecting itself. The word *iti* indicates the meaning already stated.
Showing that this refers to the person as appropriate rather than according to a fixed sequence, he says: "by way of name and clan," and so forth. "By beauty, etc.
means by way of the delimitations of beauty, nutriment, feeling, and life-span. In the phrase "he is fair-skinned," the word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or the sense of "manner."
By this, it is shown that such and other [kinds] constitute this variety.

The commentary on the discourse concerning the knowledge of recollecting past lives is concluded. Now begins the commentary on the discourse concerning the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
"Death" (*cuti*) means passing away (*cavana*). "Rebirth" (*upapāta*) means arising (*upapajjana*). This locative case is used in the sense of proximity;
what is meant is that it refers to the vicinity of the moment of death and the vicinity of the moment of rebirth. For this reason, he will later say: "But those who are near to death," and so forth.
Since the passing away and rebirth of beings are known by the knowledge of the divine eye alone, he says: "for the purpose of the knowledge of the divine eye."
...is what is meant. Regarding the phrases “resembling the divine” and so forth, whatever needs to be said has already been stated above.
However, this is the distinction: there, in reference to the term “ear-element” (*sotadhātu*), it was spoken using the feminine gender; here, it should be spoken using the neuter gender.
Furthermore, while there was no purpose for the apprehension of light (*ālokapariggaha*) there, there is one here; thus it is said: “by the apprehension of light.”

It is called "divine" (*dibba*) because it possesses great radiance; the meaning is that it is so called because it is to be attained through the assistance of the light of the *kasiṇa*, and because it itself possesses the quality of spreading the light of knowledge. For even that which has great radiance is called "divine," as in such passages as "this divine mansion.
It is called "of great range" (*mahāgatika*) because its movement is worthy of honor; the meaning is that its activity is marvelous. For its [activity] is indeed marvelous.

It occurs because one sees forms that have passed beyond walls and so forth. The phrase "because it resembles the divine eye" is a comparison with something inferior, since this [knowledge] possesses greater power even than the divine eye of the deities.

Therefore, for a practitioner performing the preliminary work to obtain the divine eye, the desire for its victory—meaning the overcoming of its opposites—is what is called the aspiration for it; and one who has obtained the divine eye...

And because this knowledge of direct higher knowledge (abhiññāñāṇa) is established as having the nature of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) by way of the meanings comprised by the terms "victory over the abodes" (vihāravijaya), "desire for victory" (icchā), "discourse" (vohāra), "splendor" (jutī), and "going" (gati)— such that one possessing psychic power (iddhimā) may engage in discourse characterized by giving and receiving, like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and others,
through the capacity to receive the words of deities and the bestowing of Dhamma— those learned in grammar [should understand it] in those respects.
Thus it is said, "They maintain that the word *divu* has these meanings; all of that should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*).
"In the sense of seeing" means by way of the state of seeing forms (*rūpa*). For beings see forms with the eye.
Just as the physical eye (*maṃsacakkhu*), when presided over by consciousness, functions as if pointing out what is even or uneven, this [divine eye] does not function in that way. But this—
Because it performs the function of the eye even more excellently than that [physical eye], it is said: "It is also called 'eye' because it acts like an eye by performing the function of the eye.
To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly as "because it is the cause for the purification of view," the passage beginning with "For he who...
was spoken. One grasps at the view of annihilation because one does not see rebirth elsewhere, thinking, "This being is annihilated right here."
"Likewise for the others" means that one who gains [wrong views] adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings, like a proponent of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppattika*).
"The sons of the Buddha see indeed" is an emphasis on the latter term, not an emphasis on the former term.
For in this way, there is established no contradiction with the *Jayaddisa Jātaka* and other such texts.
“Human” (*mānusaka*) means belonging to humans; it refers to a visible object (*rūpārammaṇa*) that has become the sphere of experience for human beings.
However, because one sees other kinds of forms—such as those that are divine, concealed, or extremely subtle—it is called “beyond the human” (*atikkantamānusaka*).
And such a form is indeed said to have transcended the human domain (*manussūpacāra*); thus he said: “by seeing a form after having transcended the human domain.”
Having thus shown it by way of the object, he now says "or human" and so forth to show it by way of the subject.
Even there, the surpassing of the fleshly eye should be understood as occurring through the surpassing of its function.
By means of the divine eye—that is, by means of the knowledge of the divine eye—it is not possible to see [it], because the moment is exceedingly brief and exceedingly subtle.
Of certain types of matter. Furthermore, the present matter is the object of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), and that [matter] serves as a pre-arising condition (*purejātapaccaya*).
However, there is no occurrence of the sublime consciousness (*mahaggata*) without the preliminary work of adverting (*āvajjana*);

nor is it possible for matter to become an object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) while it is actually arising or while it is dissolving. Therefore, "matter at the moments of death and rebirth [is seen] by the divine eye..."
"It is impossible to see [them]"—this is well said. If the knowledge of the divine eye has only visible form as its object, then why is it said that "he sees beings"?
It is stated thus because, for the most part, it sees the forms contained within the continua of beings.
Alternatively, some say it is stated by way of conventional designation (vohāra) because it serves as the cause for the apprehension of "beings. These are intended as those who are passing away.
The connection [is as follows]. "Of such a kind" means that they are not those who possess the moments of death and rebirth;
this is the intended meaning. He said, "because it is associated with the outflow of delusion," meaning that karma which has delusion as its decisive support is inferior and yields inferior fruit.
"In the opposite of that" means in the opposite of that state of being despised and so forth; that is, in what is not despised, not reviled, not disregarded, and not held in contempt.
The meaning is "to be esteemed. "Suvaṇṇa" means having a beautiful color; "dubbaṇṇa" means having an unattractive color.

This quality of being beautiful or unattractive occurs, respectively, because of the presence or absence of the underlying support (upanissaya) of non-hatred in one's karma; thus he said, "because it is associated with the outflow of non-hatred," and so forth.

One who has gone to a beautiful destination is a "Sugata"; thus he said, "in the state of a Sugata," meaning reborn in a happy destination (sugati). [They are] those whose inclination is free from greed.

He said, "Beings who are generous and free from stinginess become fortunate and successful through karma supported by non-greed," thus stating, "or because they are endowed with the outflow of non-greed, they are wealthy and possess great riches.
He said, "those who have gone to a miserable destination are 'gone to a bad state' (duggatigate).
Beings whose inclinations are characterized by greed are greedy and stingy; through karma supported by greed, they are miserable.
“They are poorly endowed,” he said; this refers to those who, due to being possessed by the outflow of greed (*lobha-nissanda*), are destitute and lack food and drink.
“Accumulated” (*upacita*) means performed in such a way as to bring about a fruit. For an action is “accumulated” when it is performed in the manner that makes it capable of yielding a result.
By the words “passing away” (*cavamāna*) and so forth, the function of the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*) is stated; thus, by means of the object, he expresses the activity of the subject.
“By the former” means it is said with reference to the phrases beginning with “with the divine eye. Here, in the word “by the former” (*purimehi*), the particle *ca* is indicated as being elided.

Therefore, the meaning is that the function of the divine eye is described by these [phrases]—namely, “with the divine... sees,” and so forth—as well as by the phrase “beings passing away,” and so on.
“But by this phrase” refers to the sentence: “he understands beings according to their deeds. “Here, the bhikkhus” [refers to...]
The intention is that in this Dispensation, there is a bhikkhu who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye.
Having stood after seeing beings in hell directly through his attainment of the knowledge of the divine eye, he attends to them in this way:
having entered the foundational jhāna out of a desire to know the karma that leads those hell-beings to hell, and having emerged from it...
He attends to it by way of preliminary work (*parikamma*). The passage beginning with "What indeed... is a demonstration of the method of attention (*manasikāra-vidhi*).
Having thus performed the preliminary work, entered the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna*), and emerged from it, adverting (*āvajjana*) arises taking that [jhāna] as its object;
when that has ceased, four or five impulsion moments (*javana*) run their course, and so forth—all of this is explained.

It is exactly as stated. As for the statement, "There is no separate preliminary work," this is said with the intention that there is no separate preliminary work for the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) apart from the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa). And this must be accepted;
otherwise, the sublime state (mahaggata-bhāva) of the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds would not even exist. The same applies to the seeing of devas.
This is the method. Furthermore, the mention of hell-beings and devas here should be regarded as merely illustrative.
For one who possesses the divine eye and so desires may proceed in this very same way even with regard to those in other destinies. Thus he will say:

"By the mention of the states of misery (apāya), the animal realm is indicated," and "By the mention of the happy destinies (sugati), the human destiny is also included. That [kamma] which leads to hell...

“Having that kamma as its object” means that which has that kamma as its objective support (*ārammaṇa*). By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “in the Phārusaka Grove, etc.,” the inclusion of the Cittalatā Grove and so forth is intended.

“And just as for this” indicates that just as there is no separate preliminary work (*parikamma*) for this knowledge of rebirth according to kamma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), so too there is none for the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*); thus he demonstrates the absence of a separate preliminary work. He states the reason for this: “They have the divine eye as their basis.”
"For these [are the reasons]," it is said. Herein, this is the intended meaning:

just as one who has attained the divine eye, having increased his light toward the hells and other realms, sees beings such as those in hell and knows, exactly as they are, the karma conducive to hell and so forth previously accumulated by them—through such an undertaking and through the corresponding attention when the mind is fully prepared—in the same way...
When one desires to know the future personal existence of whichever being it may be immediately following [the present], one directs light specifically toward that being;
having seen by means of the knowledge of rebirth according to karma (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) the karma accumulated in the past or even now that brings about that existence,
and when one desires to know the future personal existence to be produced by that [karma], one does so with a corresponding undertaking and with that [knowledge].
And when the mind has been thoroughly refined by attention, he knows [the future] as it truly is. This same method applies to subsequent future existences as well.

This is called the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*). Since these two are accomplished only when the divine eye-knowledge (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) exists, and not when it is absent, it is said: "These two succeed together with the divine eye."

"Bad conduct by way of body" (*kāyaduccarita*) should be construed thus: it is "badly conducted" (*duṭṭhu caritaṃ*) by way of the body, or it is "badly conducted" because it has arisen from the body due to its being rotten with defilements (*kilesapūtikattā*). Here, "body" (*kāya*) is intended as the physical body (*copanakāya*).

Unwholesome bodily action (*kāyakamma*) that occurs by way of bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) is "bad conduct by way of body. Regarding "the others," this refers to verbal and mental misconduct. In whichever continuum (*santāna*) the kamma [occurs]...

Because that which has been accumulated through kamma does not lose its status as being liable to result even when there is an internal interruption [of the continuum], it must be said that the person remains possessed of it; thus he says: "Possessed means having become endowed with.

By the phrase "having become desirous of harm," it is meant that they do not act like parents who desire the welfare of their children, or like teachers and preceptors who desire the welfare of those dependent on them, but rather act as reproachers and slanderers.
He shows that they do not exist. "By the destruction of qualities" means by the demolition of existing qualities; the sense is "by their ruin.
But is it not the case that even an accusation based on the final ground (antimavatthu) is merely the destruction of qualities? That is true.

However, here "qualities" refers specifically to the distinguished superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), such as the jhānas and so forth; therefore, the destruction of virtue (sīla) is mentioned separately.
Therefore he said, "There is no ascetic practice for these," and so forth. By "ascetic practice" (*samaṇadhamma*), he refers to the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃyama*).
"Whether knowing" means either knowing the noble state (*ariyabhāva*) of the one whom he reviles; or "not knowing" means not knowing it.
In this context, both knowing and not knowing are irrelevant; the noble state alone is the criterion. Therefore he said, "In both ways..."

"It is indeed an insult to a noble one (ariyūpavāda). However, they say that for one who does not know "a noble one" and who proclaims the absence of noble qualities there with a mind free from hatred, there is no destruction of those qualities; thus, for him, it is not an insult to a noble one.
Yet, it is curable by means of asking for forgiveness; it is not incurable like an immediate offense (ānantariya).
"It is tormented" means it is pained; the meaning is that it gives rise to a painful feeling. "That" refers either to the elder or to that action.
Knowing full well, the elder asked, "Friend, do you have a firm footing?

The other replied, "I am a stream-enterer," because the realization of truth is established within the Dispensation. Feeling compassion for him, the elder revealed himself, saying, "One whose taints are destroyed has been slandered by you."

"If the monks in that monastery are junior" means if they are of younger standing. "Even when not asking for forgiveness in their presence" means even when it is impossible to ask for forgiveness face-to-face; alternatively, the reading is *akhamante* (if they do not forgive). This should be understood with reference to one who is a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
"The place where the couch of the Parinibbāna [is located]" is said with reference to the place where worship is performed.

"Those who have undertaken actions" (*kammasamādānā*): "undertakings" (*samādānāni*) in the sense of what is to be undertaken; those who possess such undertakings, i.e., actions, are "those who have undertaken actions. By way of wrong view...

Regarding "undertakings of action" (*kamma-samādāna*): either by including it within the sense of "cause," those who, through wrong view, cause others to undertake actions are "those who undertake actions of wrong view.
Demonstrating this meaning, he said, "by way of wrong view," and so forth.

The passage beginning with "endowed with virtue" (*sīla-sampanno*) is stated with reference to one who possesses the Path and whose faculties are fully matured. [This refers to] the stage of the highest path.

But there is nothing at all that needs to be said [further]. "Another" refers to arahantship. "Endowed with such [a state]" means: just as that [arahantship] is necessarily bound to occur, so too is this.

In the passages beginning with "without abandoning that speech," one is said to abandon speech when saying, "I shall not speak such speech again," referring to the reviling of noble ones; likewise, one abandons mind when thinking, "I shall not give rise to such a mind again."
By reflecting, one is said to abandon the mind; by resolving, "I will not again adopt such a view," one is said to abandon the view.
One who does not act thus neither abandons nor relinquishes it.
"As he was brought, so he is placed in hell" means that just as he was brought by the guardians of hell and placed in hell, so too is he in hell.
The meaning is: "It has indeed been set aside. There is no evil that should not be done by way of wrong view, since even the state of being a rotten stump in saṃsāra occurs because of it;
thus he said, "Bhikkhus, faults have wrong view as their supreme.
"Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata’s body stands with the conduit to existence cut off: this very body and, externally..."
In such passages as "and name-and-form," the word *kāya* here refers to the five aggregates; thus he says: "With the breaking up of the body" means the relinquishing of the appropriated aggregates.
Since for one who has not yet abandoned lust, what follows after death is precisely the appropriation of the form of another existence, he says:
"After death" means at the grasping of the aggregates produced immediately thereafter. That by which one remains...
"The body breaks up by way of its very cessation" is why he said, "with the breaking up of the body, that is, with the cutting off of the life-faculty.
It is *ayo* because happiness (*sukha*) comes from this; thus he said, "merit is called *aya*. It is *āya* because happiness comes from this;

it is the means for accomplishing happiness such as meritorious deeds. Therefore he said, "or because of the absence of the arrival (*āya*) of happiness. It is *iti* because one tastes or relishes it.
Regarding "iron is its gratification," he says: "iron is what is perceived as gratification.
In the phrase "of the nāga kings, etc.," the word "etc. includes the supaṇṇas and others. "Like the asuras" means like the *peta*-asuras.
"He" refers to the host of asuras. "From all elevations" means from all elevations of excellence. "By way of the opposite of what was stated" means...

“Because it is well-conducted, or because it is beautiful conduct due to its blamelessness”—this is by way of the opposite meaning of the phrases such as “by bodily misconduct,” etc., which were previously stated.

It is called a concluding statement (*nigamana-vacana*) because it is a restatement of the very meaning already expressed. This is the summary meaning here: “With the divine eye... he sees”; this is the aforementioned summary meaning in this context.
412. "Having the kasiṇas as its object" means having the kasiṇas as its object by way of all eight kasiṇas. "In every respect" means in this manner of every variety:
"by the fourteenfold taming of the mind, by the possession of the eight factors, and by the securing of the ground, the foot, and the root.
It is capable of being directed toward the knowledge of the divine eye; it is fit to be sent, worthy of being dispatched.

"Having made it near" means it should be made proximate to the arising of the knowledge of the divine eye. In that regard, having made access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) more proficient, one should expand the object.
Therefore he said: "Having made it the domain of access concentration, and having expanded it, it should be established.
"Therein" refers to that expanded kasiṇa object. "Absorption" (*appanā*) refers to absorption by way of jhāna.

For absorption does not succeed by way of direct knowledge for one who has not performed the preliminary work (*parikamma*). Therefore he said: "It has the foundational jhāna as its support" (*pādakajjhānanissaya*);
the meaning is that it has the foundational jhāna as its object. "Not supported by the preliminary work" means that the kasiṇa-object of the preliminary work is not a prop for it.
If that were the case, there would be no seeing of forms. "In these" refers to those [states] already mentioned.
Regarding the three kasiṇas beginning with the fire-kasiṇa: "having produced" means having produced it by means of the arising of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*).
For the appearance of the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) occurs together with the occurrence of access concentration. "Therein" refers to the description of the kasiṇas.
Only the form within [the kasiṇa] should be seen, not externally, because [seeing it externally] would become a cause for falling into distraction. Of the preliminary work (*parikamma*):

"The turn passes away" means that here, what is called "preliminary work" (*parikamma*)—namely, the access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) having the aforementioned kasiṇa as its object—does not occur for one who perceives what has become form (*rūpagata*).
Furthermore, the perception of what has become form occurs by way of the light of the kasiṇa, and the light of the kasiṇa occurs by way of the preliminary work;
thus, because that twofold preliminary work does not occur, neither of those two arises. Therefore he said: "From that..."
“The light disappears; when that has disappeared, even the visible form is no longer seen. The stage for the preliminary work (*parikamma*) of seeing the visible form has passed;
because the preliminary work has passed, there is no knowledge with the kasiṇa as its object, and thus the visible form is not seen.
To the question, “How then should one proceed? he says, “Then by this,” and so forth. Thus, in due order...

By repeatedly entering the basic jhāna and emerging from it, and by frequently pervading [the mind] with light, the light becomes firmly established and long-lasting. When this is so, one continues to see forms there for a very long time.
Therefore it is said: "In this case, light... [is present]."
Showing that this same point should be illustrated by the simile of the grass torch, he said, "As a grass torch at night," and so forth.
Therein, "entering again and again" means repeatedly attaining the foundational jhāna.
"The persistence of the light within its delimited extent" refers to the light that has become stable remaining within whatever area was delimited when the kasiṇa was expanded.
Having pervaded that much, it remains fixed.

"Not come within range" is said with reference to what is capable of coming within range. However, as for [objects] such as those gone inside the belly, since that capability is absent, they must indeed be distinguished by that [absence].
"That very same" refers to the divine eye itself. "In this regard" means among these consciousnesses that arise taking visible forms as their object.
"Capable of seeing form" means capable of discerning form according to its intrinsic nature, like eye-consciousness.
"Preparatory states of consciousness" refers to the preparatory states of consciousness known as adverting and preliminary work.
For even when these take an object, they do not function by discerning it exactly as it is, just like the adverting and receiving consciousnesses.

This, moreover, is the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). "An obstacle" means something that creates an impediment. "One who has strayed from jhāna" means one who is intoxicated by jhāna, having fallen into madness through the medium of jhāna-cultivation.

"One should be heedful" means that, without falling into complacency by thinking, "The divine eye has been attained by me," one must remain heedful by means of application to insight (*vipassanā*) or by means of the realization of the truths (*saccābhisamaya*).
By the passage beginning with “By one who wishes to see thus,” both the preliminary work consisting of various acts of adverting and the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhuñāṇa*) are shown;
however, the sequence of its arising is not shown. To demonstrate that, the passage beginning with “In this regard, this... was stated.
Since it follows the method explained below, it is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the discourse on the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings is finished. Commentary on the miscellaneous discourses (Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā): 413.

*Iti* means “in this way,” that is, by the manner just described. By this, [the text] refers to the sequence of the Pāḷi as it has been shown, beginning with “When his mind was thus concentrated... and so forth.
And he refers back to the method for explaining its meaning. Just as the Noble Truths are included within the [Four] Truths, so too are the aggregates of clinging included within the aggregates.

Regarding both of these, he—by means of his self-arisen knowledge—has known, understood, penetrated, and proclaimed them exactly as they are, with pre-eminence, in terms of their intrinsic nature, their origin, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them.

"The Blessed One alone is to be praised for his realization of the five aggregates," thus he said, "the knower of the five aggregates. The connection is with the phrase "having known what is to be known.
"In these" refers to the five direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). Since the ancillary knowledges are included by the mention of those [five] themselves, it is stated as "five.
Therefore he said, "For in these," and so forth.
In this context, "accessory knowledges" (*paribhaṇḍañāṇāni*) means surrounding knowledges.

For just as the surrounding regions of Sineru—those peripheral zones established for its formation which are called "girdles" (*mekhalā*)—are so designated, even so these [knowledges], being established through the accomplishment of the divine eye, are called its accessories.
Regarding the phrase "brought here": here, "here" refers to the scriptural passages as they have been shown.

This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). However, in other contexts such as the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta*, mind-made knowledge (*manomaya-ñāṇa*) is also mentioned separately as a direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "in these": does this refer back to the triads or to the objects? What is the case here? If it refers to the triads, that is incorrect;
for direct-knowledge consciousnesses do not occur within the [nine] triads. If it refers to the objects, that too is incorrect.
For it is not appropriate to refer to one thing while intending another. Let it be as you wish regarding the triads;
has it not been stated that "the direct knowledges do not occur among the triads"? This is not a contradiction, because by the term "triads," only the objects are being grasped.
Or alternatively, let it be the objects; has it not been stated...?
“Is it not improper to refer to one thing while intending another? This too is not a fault, for the reason is exactly as stated above.
414. Even though there is no difference in the objective basis (*vatthu*), there are seven types of objects distinguished by way of plane, time, and continuity.

For this distinction is taken here according to the triads; since the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) lacks the Path as its object, the triad here concerns that which has the Path as its object.

It is not obtained. "That" refers to the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*). Regarding such statements as "having made the body dependent upon the mind," that which ought to be said has already been explained above.
"Obtained through application" (*upayogaladdha*) is a term meaning "obtained by means of application. It is expressed in the accusative case as "he transforms the body" (*kāyaṃ pariṇāmeti*).
Therefore, he says "from the object of the material body" (*rūpakāyārammaṇato*), the meaning of which is "from the object of the beauty of the material body" (*rūpakāyassa vaṇṇārammaṇato*).
“That very same mind” means that very same foundational jhāna-consciousness which was mentioned in the context of transforming the mind by means of the body.

Having established the relic-shrine at Rāmagāma, he brought the relics for the remaining seven shrines by means of his psychic power and performed the great enshrinement of the relics in the pavilion on the ground-floor chamber at Rājagaha. “These perfumes,” etc., refers to the present perfumes and so forth.
Even after taking it up, their future form—endowed with specific qualities such as non-decay—is the object of the resolving consciousness, because the resolution is directed toward the future.
The "Vattaniya Monastery" is a monastery in the Viñjhā forest. "Curd-essence" (*dadhirasa*) means whey;
for one who resolves upon it, the future color of curd becomes the object. [This is] an object of the present.
It exists because it serves as the object for the present material body (*rūpakāya*).
"Of one's own body and mind" means of one's own body and of the mind.
(415) Sound is limited because all material form belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). "Only what is existing" means only that which is currently occurring.
416. "The mind of a stream-enterer" means the unique mind of a stream-enterer.

The same method applies to the cases of the once-returner and so forth. It should be understood as far as the arahant: "The once-returner does not know the mind of the non-returner; the non-returner [does not know] the mind of the arahant.
"Of all" means he knows the minds of all noble ones (ariya), let alone those of the non-noble. Furthermore...

"And the higher [state], such as that of a non-returner (anāgāmin) and so forth, knows the mind of the lower [state], such as that of a once-returner (sakadāgāmin) and so forth"—this is the connection.
He asks, "How can a present object be an object? with the underlying intention that while knowing the past and future minds of another is possible, knowing a present one is not. The other [responds]:
In order to demonstrate where [the classification] applies, he first analyzes and shows the present by saying, "The present is threefold," and so forth.
Therein, "attained to arising, presence, and dissolution" means having reached arising, presence, and dissolution;
the meaning is that it is included within the three moments. It should be understood that within this interval there are one or two hundred thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).
The meaning is that the series of material phenomena occurring within this interval should be understood as one or two series.
It is like someone entering a small inner room from a place of light, or even better, like someone already sitting there:
as long as the material object remains manifest, half the time consists of non-manifest series and half the time consists of manifest series; taking both together, they are called "two series."
This has been stated. However, this is not common to all; for some, it becomes manifest even quickly.

Thus, the inclusion of the word "one" was made in the phrase "one or two series of moments" (*ekadvesantativārā*). Alternatively, one or two series of moments should be understood as those arising from extremely subtle conditions such as earth and so forth.
A "water-line struck on the bank" refers to a streak of water near the shore that has become turbid. "Until it becomes clear" means...

It does not become completely clear until the turbidity has vanished. However, some explain the meaning here as follows: "As long as the water-line on the foot that was stepped upon with a wet foot on the near bank has not become clear, nor subsided, nor been stilled.

These specific points of time mentioned are stated according to the differentiation of the action; they are not exactly equal to one another, but rather possess a state of being deficient or excessive.
They are to be seen as two or three impulsion-moments (*javana-vāra*) by way of sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) impulsions, and not by way of other types of impulsions.
For these do not have a fixed duration; the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth that occur immediately after them are also to be regarded as included within that same period.
"Both of those" refers to the pair of material and immaterial continuities (*rūpa-arūpa-santati*).
"Delimited by a single existence" means delimited by rebirth-linking and death. That collection of phenomena included within a single existence is to be called "the present by duration.
"Mind" refers to consciousness together with its associated mental factors. "Phenomena" refers to objective phenomena.
Alternatively, "mind" refers to the mind-base (*manāyatana*), and "phenomena" refers to the immaterial aggregates, beginning with feeling. Both of these—
"Present" (*paccuppanna*) means that, being present in terms of time, both of these [the object and the consciousness] exist; this is the meaning.
"Consciousness" (*viññāṇa*) refers to consciousness accompanied by attachment (*nikanti-viññāṇa*), for it is bound to that present [object] by way of desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*).

"Rejoices" (*abhinandati*) means he rejoices through the rejoicing of craving and views. Being thus disposed, due to the absence of full understanding of the basis (*vatthu-pariññā*), he is swept away by those present phenomena.

It is dragged along by craving and views. And here, since it is stated regarding the twelve sense bases that "this is the present," one understands that the desire and lust occurring therein has the "extended present" as its object, not the "momentary present.
Demonstrating this, he said: "With reference to which it is said in the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*... 'it is swept away. "And the present..."

Regarding the passage, "He who discerns the Dhamma here and there," it should be understood that here too the mind of insight (*vipassanā-citta*) is present by moment (*khaṇa-paccuppanna*), while the phenomena to be discerned are present by duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*). Otherwise, insight itself would not be possible.
It was not stated that "momentary presence has come down in the Canon" because, according to that [definition], making it an object is not mentioned in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

"Some" refers to the inhabitants of Abhayagiri. "Consciousness arises at a single moment" is a demonstration of the logical principle that it is possible for another's consciousness to arise at the very same time as the arising of the supernormal (iddhi) consciousness.
"Just as in space," and so forth, is an analogous illustration. However, that statement of theirs is incorrect.
Why? Because, other than in the sequence of the path and its fruition (maggaphalavīthi), advertence (āvajjana) and impulsion (javana) do not occur in an undesirable state [simultaneously].
The statement "because it would result in having various objects" is a logical argument.
If this is so, one might ask: "How then does the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) have a present object? To this he says: "But as for the present by way of continuity," and so forth.
The intention is that the "present by way of duration" (addhāpaccuppanna), however, should be illustrated by a single cognitive process (javanavāra), not by the entire duration of the present.

In this context, the passage beginning with "Tatrāyaṃ dīpanā" (Herein, this is the exposition) is an exposition of the mode of occurrence of the consciousness of psychic power (*iddhicitta*) by way of demonstrating that the impulsion series (*javanavāra*) belongs to the present of duration (*addhāpaccuppanna*). "The others" refers to the advertence (*āvajjana*) and preparatory (*parikamma*) consciousnesses.

And here, although the phrase "some" (*keci*) intends the residents of Abhayagiri, they do not admit a moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) for consciousness; therefore, [the text says] "at the moment of stability... [and so forth].

Nor could it be said that "he penetrates [it]. Likewise, for those who claim that "the mind of this person and the mind of another arise simultaneously," their statement that "he penetrates it at the moment of its stationing or at the moment of its dissolution" is inconsistent.
For that which arises during those two moments cannot be simultaneous with the other's mind.
"It is called 'arising'. Furthermore, during the moments of its persistence and dissolution, that which is arising attains a portion having a present object and a portion having a past object.

And as for what was said—"When one thinks, 'I shall know another's mind,' and adverts to the minds of a great multitude by way of a mass"—here, "the great multitude" (mahājana) in actual fact refers to "others," meaning many individuals (*aneka-puggala*). Thus, "of others... [the text continues].
If one were to say, "I shall know the mind," it would have to be stated as the occurrence of adverting (*āvajjanappavatti*).

Furthermore, even if "of another" (*parassa*) were understood to mean "of the multitude" (*mahājanassa*), even then it would be improper for one person to penetrate the mental aggregate of that single individual after having adverted to it. For adverting to a collective mass is not the same as adverting to a single part;
therefore, regarding the phrase "in the minds of the multitude" (*mahājanassa citte*) by them...
The statement beginning with "when [the mind] is adverted" and so forth should not be said.
As for what they say—"because the consciousness of the possessor of psychic power and that of another arise at the same moment"—in this regard, the following intention might be appropriate:
one who has attained the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariyañāṇa), desiring to know the mind of another, [enters] the foundational jhāna...

Having entered and emerged from that attainment, and without making a distinction between past and so forth, one performs the preliminary work by means of the commonality of mind, thinking, "I know this person's mind, I know that person's mind.
Then, having again entered the foundational jhāna and emerged, one adverts to the mind by way of that same commonality;
immediately after three or four such preliminary acts, one knows it through the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa).
One penetrates and discerns another's mind just as one sees a visible form with the divine eye.
Beyond that, however, there occurs the determination of whether the sense-sphere minds are "with lust" and so forth, just as there is the determination of colors such as blue and so on.

In this context, the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*), which adverts to the mind of a being whose heart-base has been seen by the divine eye and who has appeared before it, becomes directed toward that mind by way of the commonality of mental states.

Taking the existing consciousness as its object, it adverts to that consciousness. The preliminary exercises proceed by taking each respective existing consciousness as their object through the commonality of being "consciousness," thus functioning as the preparations for knowing the mind.
However, the knowledge of penetration into others' minds arises in the very same moment as that [other person's] existing consciousness, piercing and discerning it.
In this context, because the processes beginning with adverting occur as "consciousness" (citta) by way of unity through the grasping of the continuity of the stream,
and that very consciousness is what is discerned by the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa),
there is no diversity of objects for the adverting and impulsion moments in any place other than the path and fruit sequences, owing to their occurrence in an identical mode.

It is established that the preliminary work (parikamma) having a present object is a condition for the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) having a present object by way of the condition of repetition (āsevana-paccaya).
Thus, the triad concerning the past is appropriately formulated.

Otherwise, if "present" were used here to refer to the present as a continuity (santati-paccuppanna) or the present as a temporal duration (addhā-paccuppanna), then there would be a lack of distinction regarding the present nature of the past and the future.

[It] would follow [that this is so]. And that being the case, it ought to be stated: "A present state is a condition for a present state by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya)," yet that has not been stated. [Rather, it is said: "A past state is a condition for a present state by way of proximity-condition.
Previous past aggregates are conditions for subsequent present [aggregates]."

Because of such statements as, “Immediately after the aggregates... [and] adaptation to change-of-lineage,” it is understood that the four immediately preceding past aggregates are indeed "past" within the context of the present of duration and the present of continuity.

Furthermore, nowhere in the Canon is it stated that the term "present" (paccuppanna) occurring in the Abhidhamma mātikā has the meaning of both the present of duration and the present of continuity. Therefore...

By means of these, it is stated that for one possessing supernormal power (*iddhimant*), both their own and another’s arising of consciousness are objects of the knowledge of penetration of minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) because they have the present as their object.
However, when one applies attention (*ābhoga*) by thinking, "I know whatever thought has arisen in this person;

I know whatever will arise," and then performs such acts as entering the foundational jhāna, then there are the acts of adverting and preliminary work (*parikamma*), as well as the knowledge of penetration of minds.
They have only past and future objects as their objective referents, because the differentiation [of the object] is effected by the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) itself.
However, those who hold that "one possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*), desiring to know another's mind, adverts;
the adverting consciousness, having made the present momentary state its object, ceases together with it. Thereafter, four or five impulsive moments (*javana*) arise, the last of which..."

"Based on this statement— 'The consciousness of psychic power (*iddhicitta*) and the remaining [consciousnesses] belong to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*); for all of them, that very same ceased consciousness becomes the object,

and they do not have different objects because, by way of duration, they have the present as their object'— it follows that although advertence (*āvajjana*) and the impulsion (*javana*) moments have objects that are both present and past, there is no state of having different objects."

Even when one adverts to minds that have not yet arisen— whether one, two, four, or five mind-moments in the future— there would be no diversity of objects for the adverting and impulsion consciousnesses,
despite their respective objects being future, present, or past. Therefore, when one adverts to four or five mind-moments in the future,
the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), which has the present moment as its object, arises immediately after the preliminary work (parikamma) whose object was the future.

They say, "It is established. Their doctrine is not [correct], because these questions—"A state with a future object is a condition, by way of the condition of repetition, for a state with a present object;

a state with a present object is a condition, by way of the condition of repetition, for a state with a past object"—have not been raised, and because it is stated in the enumeration that "there are three in the case of repetition."
It is not established. For there is no such thing as a non-repeated (anāsevana) state that is exalted (mahaggata) in wholesome functional (kiriya) consciousness.

Furthermore, the status of this [past] as a support for the adverting (āvajjana) and impulsion (javana) moments is not established by the statement that their object is "present-at-the-moment" (khaṇapaccuppanna) and has ceased;

for if one were to grasp [the object] without making the distinction between "that which has occurred" and "that which will occur," there would be no grasping of the future by the adverting consciousness, and in the absence of that...

This was stated specifically with reference to the fact that even for the javanas there is an absence of grasping [the object] while it is still occurring. For at that time, adverting (āvajjanā) proceeds by taking as its object precisely that consciousness which has become manifest immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Thus, if the state of having a present object were attributed even to the knowing consciousness (jānanacitta), there would be the fault of the two—adverting and knowing consciousnesses—occupying the same place simultaneously;

and furthermore, if adverting and penetration occurred within a single portion of the "heap" [of moments], there would be the consequence of adverting and knowing occurring simultaneously for each moment as it arises.
Furthermore, because it would entail the fault of advertence (*āvajjana*) and the impulsive moments (*javana*) having different objects (*nānārammaṇa*),

the statement that "the mind of the present moment is the object of the knowledge of penetration into others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*)" is rejected as improper. Having thus rejected it due to the aforementioned fault,

and having seen that there is no state of having different objects because the object is the present in terms of duration (*addhā*) and continuity (*santati*) according to time, [one understands] the relationship between advertence and the impulsions.
The state of being present is said to be the condition of having a ceased object. Even that statement the proponents of the former view would not accept;

for if that were the case, then—as in the passage "adverting [is a condition] for the wholesome" (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.417)—since a proximate condition would be established for something included within another term, it would follow that "adverting with a present object is a proximate condition for aggregates with a past object."
And it should have been stated that [it is] a condition, yet it was not so stated.
But why has the fact that knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) has the present as its object been investigated in this way?
Is it not the case that "a past state is a condition for a present state; a future state is a condition for a present state by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya)"?

In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of these [terms], it is said: "Past aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of supernormal powers, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of the destination according to karma, by way of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) for adverting (*āvajjanā*);

future aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of supernormal powers, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of future states, by way of being an object-condition for adverting. This is stated in the "arisen triad" (*uppanna-ttika*).

And having included the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) by stating, "Unarisen aggregates and arising aggregates are related to the knowledge of supernormal powers, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of future states,

and advertence by way of object-condition," [the text] then provides the analysis for the statement "A present state is related to a present state" as follows: "Present aggregates are related to the knowledge of supernormal powers..."

Because it is stated [in the Paṭṭhāna] that "advertence is a condition for its object by way of object-condition," and because in the section on arisen states it is stated only as much as "arisen aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of supernormal powers and for advertence by way of object-condition," it is understood that the knowledge of others' minds does not operate with respect to a present consciousness.
For if it were to operate there, then just as in the previous cases, the mention of the knowledge of others' minds would have occurred in the other cases as well.
"Should it be formulated? It is true that it should be formulated; however, it is understood from another portion of the text that it has been abbreviated by way of showing the underlying method:
"A state with a past object is a condition, by way of object-condition, for a state with a present object; a state with a future object is [a condition] for a state with a present object;
a state with a present object is [a condition] for a state with a present object."

For in their respective analyses (vibhaṅga), it is said: "By means of knowledge of penetration into others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), one knows the mind of one possessed of a present mind that has past objects;
present aggregates with past objects are a condition for the advertence (āvajjanā) of knowledge of penetration into others' minds by way of object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya);
by means of knowledge of penetration into others' minds, one knows the mind of one possessed of a present mind that has future objects."
Present aggregates with future objects are related to the adverting of knowledge of others' minds by way of object-condition;
through knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of one possessing a present mind that has a present object.
Present aggregates with present objects are related to the adverting of knowledge of others' minds by way of object-condition.

The statement, “It is a condition,” refers to the fact that the knowledge of penetration into others’ minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*) occurs with a present object. It should be understood that this investigation was undertaken for that very reason. 417. “Of those two”:

the genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), meaning “among those two kinds of knowledge. The intention is that the mind itself is the object for the knowledge of penetration into others’ minds.
Therefore he said: “It does not know any other aggregate (*khandha*) or anything connected to an aggregate. In this context:
Name, clan, and so forth are bound up with the aggregates (*khandha*). If this is so, how can it be said to have the Path as its object? He says:
