"But because it has as its object the consciousness associated with the Path, it is called 'having the Path as its object' in a figurative sense (*pariyāya*). The intention is that the object is merely volition (*cetanā*) itself;
for it is thus that it is called "knowledge of rebirth according to deeds" (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*). In the phrase "among those things bound up with the aggregates," here even *nibbāna* [is included].
It is indeed bound to the aggregates (khandha). They say this because it is made an object by the aggregates. For thus it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:

"The Buddhas of the past cultivated the path, realized the fruit, and attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue"—this is also [an example] through the recollection of one's previous births (*vaṭumaka*) and through the reviewing of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna.
"Of immeasurable object. In this context, the reviewing of the path and fruit occurs within the knowledges regarding the path and fruit through the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
And the reviewing of Nibbāna occurs within the knowledges regarding immeasurable states that have Nibbāna as their object.
Thus, the reviewings of the path and so forth establish the fact that the knowledge of recollection of past lives has an immeasurable object.

These [factors] should be understood. For it is stated that "immeasurable aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of recollection of past lives by way of object-condition," but it is not stated that "Nibbāna" is so.
Therefore, even when the function of reviewing the path and fruit is said to be performed by the knowledge of past lives itself, one cannot say that there is a reviewing of Nibbāna.
However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), its having Nibbāna as its object is demonstrated.

If it is argued: "The expression 'wholesome aggregates' (*kusalā khandhā*) is a plural designation referring specifically to the knowledge of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*), the knowledge of past lives (*pubbenivāsa*), and the knowledge of future states (*anāgataṃsa*); it does not refer to the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya*) or the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga*).
Therefore, it does not prove that these [latter two] have the four aggregates as their object," we say: No. For elsewhere it is stated:

"The aggregates devoid of applied thought but accompanied by sustained thought (*avitakkavicāramattā khandhā*), as well as sustained thought itself, are the objects of the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of future states."

Because it is stated: "It is a condition by way of object-condition," and "Aggregates accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, as well as applied thought itself, are a condition by way of object-condition for the knowledge of penetration of minds, the knowledge of recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of future states," it follows that even when referring to the knowledge of penetration of minds, the plural designation is used;
this meaning being established, it is the same for the knowledge of destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*).

Is it not the case that, because [the four aggregates] are not mentioned in such passages as “the aggregates consisting of mere investigation without applied thought, and investigation itself,” the status of having the four aggregates as its object is not established? No;

for there is another reason for their not being mentioned therein. For by means of the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*), the four aggregates associated with karma are grasped under the heading of "karma.
Indeed, just as the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*) [grasps the mind] by way of previous preparatory work, [so too does this knowledge grasp the aggregates].
It clarifies the mind by way of the classification into "without applied thought" and so forth, and the classification into "with lust" and so forth;

it does not clarify such classifications [as those mentioned]. Rather, it clarifies the aggregate as a whole by way of its function as kamma. Therefore, that [classification] was not stated in the formulation of distinctions such as "the aggregates without applied thought but with sustained thought, and sustained thought," nor because it does not have the four aggregates as its object. This, however, is its...
Some say it is not a cause. Even there, they indeed recite: "of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of passing away according to karma, and the knowledge of the future.

For that [knowledge] is not incapable of making manifest the classification of kamma—such as the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome—just as it is for the distinction between states with applied thought and so forth.

Indeed, even the manifestation of the distinction between misconduct and good conduct consists in the manifestation of the specific distinctions in the association with greed and so forth, or non-greed and so forth.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated only this much: “The knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa*) is not an object that can be described at the time of recollecting names and clans.
However, name and clan are designations established by convention (*sammutisiddha*), which are bound up with the aggregates (*khandha*);
they are the meaning of the expression, not the expression itself. “This is our position (*khanti*) in this matter” is the teacher’s own opinion. As for what was said:
“Not the phrasing”: the explanation for that is “For the phrasing,” and so forth. 419.
“He will be reborn in the sense-sphere realm” refers to the knowledge of knowing the aggregates at the moment of rebirth. 420. “In this”:
in this investigation of objects regarding the super-knowledge knowledges (*abhiññā-ñāṇa*) by way of the triad of internal objects. “If it has an internal object... [and so on].
Regarding what was stated in the ancient commentary by taking "internal object" and "external object" together as one—that is, "at times...

it indeed occurs"—the meaning is that this was said with that specific intention. For there is no such thing as an "internal-external" category existing separately, nor is that taken as a single combined object.
If this is so, then the triad is not fulfilled, because [an object] not included within those two terms [would remain unaccounted for].
This is not so, because there is no third distinct meaning; rather, it is because the presentation of the triad has as its object the differentiation of modes.
For thus it is said in the Commentary: "Those very same phenomena, though of three kinds. The meaning is: "those very same phenomena, in their threefold division by way of internal and so forth.
Here, the expression "of three kinds" (*tippakāre*)—rather than saying simply "those very same phenomena"—is based on the differentiation of modes.
This is stated for the purpose of showing that "this is the teaching of the triad. For while the teaching of the wholesome triad and so forth is based on distinctions such as the class (*jāti*),

association (*sampayoga*), abandonment (*pahāna*), the plane of training (*sikkhābhūmi*), object (*ārammaṇa*), classification (*pabheda*), determination (*niyama*), and time (*kāla*)— as appropriate for those phenomena—

this [present teaching] is not based on distinctions of class and so forth, nor is it based on distinctions of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth, as is the case with the teaching of the "visible" triad, the "root" dyads, and so on.
Rather, it is based on a distinction of classification.

For the five aggregates themselves are called "internal" when they are included within one's own continuity (*santati*), "external" when they are included within the continuity of another, and "both internal and external" when both are considered together.
Therefore he said: "With the exception of matter not bound to the faculties and Nibbāna, all phenomena..."
“[They] may be internal, may be external, or may be both internal and external. Now, one might ask:
“Is it not the case that there is no third category here, because there is no other entity [besides these two], and because no other mode has been mentioned? This is not so.

For although all phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhammā) are indeed included by the two terms alone—since the second term functions to include those not already included by the first term—...

They have been grasped; however, because the third term is stated by way of grasping those phenomena taken separately by each [of the first two] together as one, there is indeed a third category. For a whole is not identical to its parts;

yet, it is impossible to grasp phenomena that have distinct bases as one without relinquishing the distinction of their respective foundations. Therefore, at one time [they are] internal, and at another time...
It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the time of external knowledge.
The commentary on the exposition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the thirteenth chapter.
14. Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregates; Commentary on the Discussion of Wisdom (Paññākathā). 421.
"In every aspect" means: the aspect of access, the aspect of absorption, the aspect of mastery, and the aspect of the surmounting of applied thought and so forth.
By way of all modes of development, such as the mode of dispassion toward form and so forth, the fourteenfold mode of thorough taming of the mind,
and the mode of attaining the fivefold benefits;
and by the phrase "immediately after that," meaning according to the sequence of the teaching and the sequence of practice, of that concentration...
“Immediately following. The connection is: “Wisdom should be developed by a bhikkhu endowed with the development of concentration.

Because it was taught so very concisely as “Develop wisdom,” or because it was stated in the commentary on the verse so extremely briefly as “the sword of insight-wisdom well-sharpened on the whetstone of concentration,” this is that wisdom.

To begin with, it is not even easy to understand [them] by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). However, since the method of cultivation (*bhāvanāvidhāna*) has not been shown, it is all the more difficult to cultivate them;

such is the connection [of the text]. In the sense of "inquiring," it is a question (*pañha*); action (*kamma*), activity (*kiriyā*), or performance (*karaṇa*). A question itself as the action is "question-action" (*pañhākamma*), meaning the application of inquiry.
“What is wisdom? is a question concerning its essential nature (*sarūpapucchā*). “In what sense is it called wisdom? means:
by depending on what denotable meaning does the term “wisdom” function?

Furthermore, as to how this wisdom is to be known—by way of its intrinsic nature, its function, its mode of manifestation, and its proximate cause—it is asked: “What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?”
"How manyfold? is a question concerning classification. But why are questions regarding defilement (*saṃkilesa*) and purification (*vodāna*) not included here?

It is said: first, in the case of supramundane wisdom (*lokuttara-paññā*), there is no defilement at all; and since that is absent, how could there be a question of purification? Therefore, both of those are not included.

However, in the case of mundane wisdom (*lokiya-paññā*), those two are already contained within the very section on the methods of cultivation (*bhāvanā-vidhāna*). Thus [they are not treated separately].
They are not taken separately because they are included within the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path;

or rather, they should be understood according to the method already stated regarding the development of concentration, and thus they are not mentioned here. Since practice occurs only when there is a visible benefit, he asks:
"What is the benefit of the development of wisdom?"

422. *Tatra* means "in that" or "regarding that" question. *Vissajjanam* means "explanation. For a matter that has been asked remains hidden because it has not been disclosed, as if placed in a closed fist; its explanation is the "answer" (*vissajjana*) because it makes the matter manifest.
Although this is indeed a direct question regarding the nature of wisdom (*paññā*), it is nevertheless an elucidation of the intrinsic nature of those things that possess distinctions.
Since it occurs precisely by way of showing the analysis, the analysis must first be shown in its entirety.

And in order to show, through that demonstration, "this is the danger," it was said: "Wisdom is of many kinds," and so forth. Therein, "of many kinds" means manifold according to the categories of wholesome (*kusala*) and so on.

"Of various types" means diverse according to the distinctions such as that which produces meaning (*atthajāvika*), and according to the distinctions such as knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*).

"All that" refers to that entire classification of wisdom (*paññāvibhāga*) without exception. "One would not accomplish it" means that here the intended sense is the cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*) together with the cultivation of insight (*vipassanābhāvanā*);
for by that [cultivation], the tangle of craving (*taṇhājaṭā*) is disentangled, yet one would not accomplish that [disentanglement].

For if the various divisions of wisdom were to be explained exhaustively, then the entire section on the bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), beginning with "the basis of knowledge as a singlefold," [would have to be included] in the *Vibhaṅga*.
Furthermore, the various classifications of wisdom (paññā-pabhedo) found here and there in the Suttantas would have to be brought forward and answered;
and if that were the case, there would be no room at all for answering this specific method for the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā-vidhi) intended here.
Moreover, regarding this [method] which concerns the spheres of the possible and the impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna), the variety of kamma, the variety of fruition (vipāka), and so forth—
The differentiation of the occurrence of wisdom (paññā) should also be explained by classifying it appropriately according to its various fruits and non-fruits.
However, if that were to be explained, it would lead only to distraction, as is the case with matters outside one's scope.
Therefore he said: "And further, it would lead to distraction. [This refers to] insight-knowledge associated with wholesome consciousness.
Here, by the inclusion of "wholesome" (kusala), both kinds of the indeterminate (abyākata) are excluded;

likewise, it refutes the wrong view that occurs in the form, "there is defiled wisdom" (saṃkiliṭṭha-paññā). By the inclusion of "insight-knowledge" (vipassanā-ñāṇa), all other wholesome wisdoms are excluded. 423.
"Distinguished by the modes of perceiving and cognizing" means preeminent by way of the modes of perceiving and the modes of cognizing. Since—

Knowing in its various modes is the state of knowing; it is the mode of grasping an object. For that [mode] is common to them [the five aggregates], whereas the mode of perceiving (sañjānanā) and so forth is not.

In the phrase "yellowish," the word *iti* has the sense of "etcetera" (*ādi*); by this, it includes the modes to be grasped by perception (*saññā*), such as "red," "white," "long," "short," and so on.
Regarding the phrase "mere perceiving": here, "perceiving" (*sañjānanam*) refers to—“blue”...
"Yellow," and so forth, refers to the knowing that takes as its sign (saññānimitta) an object—whether it actually exists or not.

For this [perception] has the function of making a sign as a condition for subsequent recognition. By the word "only" (*matta*), in the sense of excluding qualifications, it excludes the modes of cognizing (*vijānana*) and fully understanding (*pajānana*);
by the word "just" (*eva*), it indicates that these two distinctions never exist in this [perception].

It comprehends. Therefore it is said: “Impermanent, suffering,” and so forth. In that context, since perception (saññā) is unable even to perform the function of consciousness (viññāṇa), how could it perform the function of wisdom (paññā)?
Thus it is stated that “it is not able to bring about the penetration of the characteristics,” but it is not stated that “it brings about the manifestation of the Path.
Consciousness, while occurring with respect to an object, does not [penetrate] in the same way that perception does.

It proceeds by way of perceiving blue, yellow, and so forth; however, it proceeds while also knowing other specific distinctions therein—thus he said, "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*), and so on. But how does consciousness bring about the penetration of the characteristics?
By the path shown by wisdom (*paññā*). For, having penetrated the characteristics many times through insight (*vipassanā*) that has the characteristics as its object, [one attains penetration].
Because it occurs with proficiency once it has been penetrated, insight can arise even through a consciousness dissociated from knowledge by virtue of familiarity—
just as, when reciting a well-mastered text, the sections that have been learned by heart are no longer consciously perceived.
And the phrase "penetration of the characteristics" is stated merely with reference to taking the characteristics as objects.
It is not a penetration. "Having ascended" means having applied oneself through the sequence of the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*).
It is unable to bring about the manifestation of the path because its intrinsic nature is non-enlightenment.

"By the method stated" means that by the method stated regarding consciousness, one knows the object and brings about the penetration of its characteristics. However, by its own unique power, which is not shared with others...
Having exerted itself, it brings about the manifestation of the path.
Now, in order to establish the aforementioned meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with “Just as” (*yathā hi*) was stated.

Therein, “one whose intelligence has not arisen” (*ajātabuddhi*) refers to one whose intelligence regarding conventional usage (*byavahāra*) has not yet been produced. “Enjoyment and use” (*upabhogaparibhoga*) means that which is worthy of enjoyment and use, [referring to] the objects of enjoyment and use.
"Fit for acquisition" is the meaning. "Cheka" means of great value. "Kūṭa" is a counterfeit coin made of copper, bronze, and so forth. "Addhasāra" means worth half [its face value].
The word *iti* has the sense of "etcetera"; by it, there is an inclusion of items such as those worth a quarter, a third, or more than a quarter.
He displays them in their various forms, both such as the Indra-net, the *ajāti*-flower, and so forth, and such as the *cheka* and so forth.

The passage beginning with "Perception, indeed... is a correlation of the similes. Perception is said to be like a child’s seeing a kahāpaṇa coin because it grasps the object as a mere lump without making distinctions.

For it is described as "having its proximate cause in the appearance of the object as it presents itself. Consciousness is like a villager’s seeing a kahāpaṇa coin because of its capacity to grasp specific details within the object.

It has been stated. It should be understood that wisdom (paññā) is said to be like a money-changer’s view of a coin because it awakens to every particularity of the object without exception. By the phrase “knowing in its various modes,” it is shown that wisdom is the awakening to objects of knowledge (ñeyya-dhammā) exactly as they are, insofar as those objects are each of various modes.
For it has likewise been stated: “All phenomena (dhammā) in all their aspects...”
"It comes within the range of the gateway of knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.

"In which" means in which arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*). "There it does not exist unilaterally" means that in that arising of consciousness, wisdom (*paññā*) does not exist as an absolute certainty;
for wisdom does not arise in those states of consciousness that possess two roots or are rootless (*duhetuka-ahetuka-cittuppāda*). "Inseparable" (*avinibbhuttā*) means unseparated.
"By those two" means by perception and consciousness. For just as pleasure is not invariably inseparable from rapture, so too perception and consciousness are not invariably inseparable from wisdom.
However, just as rapture is invariably inseparable from pleasure, so too wisdom is invariably inseparable from perception and consciousness.
Therefore, among these three states which are thus inseparable, of them...
The statement "separation is difficult" is illustrated by the example of three people looking at a coin.
To show their very state of having a difference that is difficult to discern through another mode of expression, it was said, beginning with "Therefore he said," and so forth.

In that context, even regarding material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), for instance, when the water of various rivers or various oils are poured into a single vessel and churned, one cannot say, "This is from such-and-such a river..."
Having distinguished [them] by saying, "This is water; this is such-and-such oil," it is difficult to show them in their own form;
how much more so, then, in the case of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*)? Demonstrating this, he said, "Of those immaterial things, mind and mental factors," and so forth. 424.

The intrinsic nature (*sako bhāvo*) of phenomena, and that which is the common nature (*samāno bhāvo*), is the "individual essence of phenomena" (*dhammasabhāva*). Therein, by the first [term], the specific characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*) such as hardness and contact are [indicated].

The first [characteristic] is grasped, and by the second, the common characteristics such as impermanence and suffering. Wisdom is defined as having the characteristic of penetrating both of these according to reality;
thus it is said: "Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating the intrinsic nature of phenomena (dhammasabhāva).

Just as the light of a lamp dispels external darkness that conceals objects like pots and cloths, so too does wisdom dispel the darkness of delusion (moha) that conceals the aforementioned intrinsic nature of phenomena.
Its function is to dispel. For the light of wisdom arises only by dispelling the darkness of the heart as it arises;

for that very reason, it stands present in the manner of non-delusion regarding the true nature of phenomena (dhamma-sabhāva), and thus it has non-delusion as its manifestation (asammoha-paccupaṭṭhāna).
Alternatively, being itself the cause, it brings about non-delusion as its fruit; in this way too, it has non-delusion as its manifestation.
Because it is insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) that is intended here, it is said that "concentration is its proximate cause.
For thus the Sutta passage, "One who is concentrated understands things as they truly are," has come down as the supporting authority.
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Divisions of Wisdom* (*Paññāpabhedakathāvaṇṇanā*)
425. The "penetration of the individual essence of phenomena" (*dhammasabhāvapaṭivedha*) is the unique characteristic of wisdom;
no subdivision of it can be found on that account. Therefore, it is said: "First, it is of one kind by way of the characteristic of penetration of the individual essence of phenomena.

That which is called the "world" (*loka*) is the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), in the sense of breaking up and falling away. Because they are included within that, or because they are known therein, they are called "mundane" (*lokika*).

In this context, they are "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) because, by virtue of being unincluded [in the mundane], they have transcended and crossed over the world. For even the supramundane [states] associated with the Path must be developed.
Since the method of insight (*vipassanā*) is indeed applicable to that [supramundane state], there is no contradiction in using the term "supramundane.
They are "with taints" (*sāsava*) because they occur together with the taints while taking the self as their object; yet, in terms of actually making [the self] an object, this is not the case.

"Of these, the taints (*āsava*) do not exist; thus they are 'taintless' (*anāsava*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the dyads such as "dissociated from taints" and "with taints" should be understood.
"By way of the discernment of name-and-form" means by way of the discernment of name and by way of the discernment of form.
It is "vision" because it first sees *nibbāna*; and the associated states are "present therein" because they have it as their support, while it itself—
Or, it is called the "ground of seeing" (*dassanabhūmi*) because it arises and becomes manifest, yet does not appear like Nibbāna; thus, it is the first path.

As for the remaining three paths, however, since they arise by way of development (*bhāvanā*) regarding that very same phenomenon already seen by the first path, and do not see anything previously unseen, they are called the "ground of development" (*bhāvanābhūmi*)—that is, development and ground in the sense already stated.
In this context, wisdom (paññā) is said to be twofold, by way of the plane of seeing (dassanabhūmi) and the plane of development (bhāvanābhūmi).

That which is produced by reflection (cintā) independent of hearing (suta) and so forth is "wisdom born of reflection" (cintāmayā). Likewise for "wisdom born of hearing" (sutamayā) and "wisdom born of development" (bhāvanāmayā).

The suffix "-maya" should be applied to each [term] individually. Skill in gain (āya) and growth is "skill in gain" (āyakosalla); skill in loss (apāya) and decline is "skill in loss" (apāyakosalla); [skill] in means (upāya)...
Skill in producing each respective purpose is "skill in means" (*upāyakosalla*); thus, the term "skill" (*kosalla*) should be connected to each individual instance.
That which has internal adherence (*abhinivesa*) as its mode of proceeding is "internal-adherence" (*ajjhattābhinivesā*).
In this same way, "external-adherence" (*bahiddhābhinivesā*) and "dual-adherence" (*ubhayābhinivesā*) are to be understood.

426. "Associated with the mundane path" (*lokiyamaggasampayuttā*) means associated with the arising of mundane wholesome consciousnesses that are connected to the path; specifically, it refers to those associated with the path included within the fourfold purification beginning with the purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).
He says "associated with the path" because a designation applied to a whole may also apply to its parts.
Alternatively, it is stated thus by taking the term "path" (*magga*) as applying individually to right view and the other factors.

It is said that "even though there is no difference in the nature of the Dhamma, because of the mere difference in the application of terms (*padatthāna*), it is difficult to explain [the distinction]," and thus it is stated: "But in meaning, this is both mundane and supramundane.
Even in the case of the pairs such as "dissociated from the taints" (*āsava-vippayutta*) and "with taints" (*sāsava*), the distinction lies solely in the apprehension of dissociation and so forth;

in meaning, wisdom is indeed both mundane and supramundane—hence he says, "The same method applies. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the pairs such as "subject to the flood" (*oghanīya*), "dissociated from the flood" (*ogha-vippayutta*), and "subject to the flood" (*oghanīya*) are included.
The inclusion should be understood as follows: there are four path-consciousnesses associated with the first jhāna, and likewise four for each of the second and subsequent jhānas;
thus, among these sixteen path-consciousnesses, sublime wisdom is not included here because it is insight-wisdom that is intended.
(427) "By way of one's own reflection" means: in the accomplishment of various blameless aims without the instruction of another.
"By means of one's own reflection on the means" means by way of one's own ingenuity. "By way of what has been heard" means by way of the instruction of others as it was heard.
"In whatever way" means for one who applies himself to meditation either after hearing the instruction from another or without having heard it.

The phrase "having reached absorption" is stated in order to show that which consists of meditation that has reached its culmination; it does not mean, however, that "only those consisting of meditation have reached absorption."
"In those prescribed by yoga" means: prescribed by wisdom, transformed by wisdom, and accomplished through skillful means (*upāya*).
"In the spheres of action" (*kammāyatana*): here, action itself is the sphere of action; or, it is called a "sphere of action" because it is both action and a source of livelihood (*ājīva*).
This same method applies to the spheres of craft (*sippāyatana*) as well. Therein, action is twofold: inferior, such as the work of a carpenter and so forth, and superior.
Agriculture, trade, and so forth. Craftsmanship (*sippa*) is also twofold: inferior, such as the craft of basket-making, and superior, such as arithmetic and calculation.

Knowledge (*vijjā*) is the field of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*). That should be understood as being strictly righteous, similar to the *nāgamaṇḍala*, protective charms (*paritta*), dice-rolling (*phudhamanaka*), and incantations (*manta*).
Now, some wise men, like Bodhisattvas, [establish] these for the comfortable dwelling of humanity.
Those who desire [to learn] do not see others performing [the acts], nor do they take up what has been done, nor do they listen to those who are speaking.

Rather, they perform them through their own natural inclination and reflection; even those things performed through one's own natural inclination and reflection by the wise become exactly like those performed by others after they have learned them from others.
“Kammassakata” means the knowledge that understands: “This action is one’s own property; this is not [the property] of others.
“Saccānulomika” means insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). For it is called “conforming to the truths” because it conforms to the penetration of the truths.
Now, in order to show the manner in which this [knowledge] proceeds, it is said: “‘Form is impermanent,’ or…” and so forth. Therein, by the word “or” (*vā*),...
It should be understood that by the sense of "indefiniteness," the characteristics of suffering and non-self are also included;
this is not because they lack the quality of being immediate. For whatever is impermanent is suffering, and whatever is suffering is non-self.

"That which is of such a nature" refers to that whose essential characteristic has been explained above. "Conformable patience" and so forth are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*), for it is that [wisdom] which was described above.

It is "conformable" (*anulomika*) because it conforms by way of seeing the sense-bases of action (*kammāyatana*) and so forth as non-opposing, and likewise because it does not oppose the truth of the path, the ultimate truth, and Nibbāna through its conduct for the welfare of beings.

It is "acceptance" (*khanti*) because one is able to endure and see all these reasons. It is "view" (*diṭṭhi*) because one sees. It is "inclination" (*ruci*) because one finds it pleasing. It is "wisdom" (*muni*) because one understands.

*Muti*. It is called *pekkhā* because it sees (*pekkhati*). Since those phenomena, such as the bases of action (*kammāyatana*), when being contemplated by this [wisdom], endure contemplation, it is "acceptance through contemplation of phenomena" (*dhammanijjhānakhanti*).
"Obtains without having heard from another" means that one obtains it while reflecting by oneself, without hearing the instructive words of another.
"This is called" means this is called wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayā paññā*).

Furthermore, this [wisdom] arises only for those well-known Bodhisattvas. Even among them, the knowledge conforming to the truths (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) arises only for two Bodhisattvas who are in their final existence;
all other wisdom arises for all those of great intelligence who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*).
"One acquires it by hearing from another" means that the sense-bases of action (*kammāyatana*) and so forth are being performed or have been performed by another.
Whether it be obtained by seeing, or by hearing another person speaking, or by learning in the presence of a teacher—it should be understood that all such [wisdom] is indeed "obtained from another.
"Of one who has attained" means of one possessing meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); this is merely an illustration.
Here, the wisdom of insight and the path is intended by the term "wisdom consisting in development" (*bhāvanāmayā paññā*).
“Limited-object” and “lofty-object” refer to the wisdom spoken of [in that context]. “Worldly insight” refers to the wisdom of worldly insight.
As for “supramundane insight,” that wisdom which has been described as having an immeasurable object because it occurs with reference to Nibbāna—that is supramundane insight;
this is said with reference to path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*). For that [path-wisdom], although it does not grasp at the impermanence and so forth of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*),...
It is called "insight" (vipassanā) because it specifically sees the characteristic of suchness (tathalakkhaṇa) either for the fulfillment of the function of insight or for Nibbāna.

Although the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa) has an immeasurable object, it does not receive the designation of "insight" because it occupies the position of the adverting consciousness (āvajjana) for the Path.

"Gain" (*āya*) means that by means of this [wisdom] these [benefits] come; it is increase. Skill in that regard means skill, proficiency, and expertise in that which is characterized by the abandonment of what is harmful and the arising of what is beneficial.
To demonstrate that absolute skill in gain according to the text itself, it is said: "These states," and so forth.
Therein, "this is called" refers to the non-arising and abandoning of these unwholesome states, and the arising and maintenance of wholesome states.
Wisdom (paññā) is what is called "skill in acquisition" (āyakosalla).

Because it is devoid of acquisition, which is characterized by growth, it is "loss" (apāya), meaning non-growth. In that context, "skill" means skillfulness or proficiency regarding that loss, which is characterized by the destruction of benefit and the arising of harm;
thus, it is "skill in loss" (apāyakosalla). To demonstrate that as well by way of the canonical text (pāḷi), [the Buddha said] "These phenomena," and so forth.

It has been said. Regarding that, it is stated: "That which is wisdom (paññā) concerning the non-arising and cessation of these wholesome states (kusaladhammā), or the arising and persistence of unwholesome states (akusaladhammā), this is called skill in the unfavorable (apāyakosallaṃ).
Now, let skill in the favorable (āyakosallaṃ) be wisdom; but how does skill in the unfavorable become known as wisdom? One considers thus: "The capacity for producing the unfavorable..."
“...there might be skill regarding the decline [of unwholesome states],” but that is merely his opinion. Why? For it is only one possessed of wisdom who understands:
“When I attend in this way, unarisen wholesome states do not arise and arisen ones cease;
unarisen unwholesome states arise and arisen ones increase. Having understood this, he—regarding the unarisen...
He does not give rise to what is unwholesome, and abandons it when it has arisen. He gives rise to what is wholesome when it has not yet arisen, and brings it to full development once it has arisen.
Thus, skill regarding the unfavorable is also wisdom.
"In all instances" means in all cases. "Of those various states" refers to the states of benefit and happiness for beings in their respective circumstances. "Arising at that very moment" means...
It is that which occurs at that very moment for the purpose of remedying an urgent task or when fear has arisen.

It is called *ṭhānuppattika* because its arising (*uppatti*) is dependent upon a specific occasion (*ṭhāna*); thus, it is that which arises immediately from the occasion itself. *Tatrupāyā* means those which serve as the appropriate means (*upāya*) for each respective task to be performed.
"Having grasped" means having grasped by way of discerning, "This is form; this much is form," and so forth.
"Having grasped both" means having discerned both internally and externally in successive order.
Alternatively, it means having grasped all five aggregates simultaneously with the thought, "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation."
Having grasped [them] without differentiation. This, however, is the application of insight for a bhikkhu of great merit who possesses sharp insight.
428. "Taking the truth of suffering as its object" means making the truth of suffering the object;
and knowledge that proceeds by way of destroying the delusion that conceals it is "knowledge of suffering. "Taking the origin of suffering as its object"—here too the method is the same. Likewise...
The same applies to the remaining two lines as well. For the knowledge of review (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) is indeed knowledge that occurs with reference to the Four Truths;
the third, however, is path-knowledge (maggañāṇa), while the other truths are clearly insight-knowledge (vipassanāñāṇa).
To explain in detail, by means of the canonical text itself, the meaning briefly stated as "knowledges that have reached differentiation regarding the meanings and so forth," [the author says]:
The passage beginning with “For this has been said” has been stated. Therein, “knowledge regarding the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning” (*atthapaṭisambhidā*):

that knowledge which has reached distinction regarding the meaning and is capable of observing, clarifying, and defining the various classifications of meaning—this is called the analytical knowledge of meaning.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. For [it is] that which is capable of observing, clarifying, and defining the various classifications of the Dhamma...
Knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding phenomena (*dhamma*) is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding linguistic expression, which is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the differentiation of language (*nirutti*), is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*), which is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the differentiation of ingenuity, is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). These [analytical knowledges] consist of the differentiation of language and ingenuity, along with their respective objects.
The meaning and so forth should be understood by distinguishing them through such categories as being "arisen from conditions" (*paccayuppanna*).
Even *nibbāna* is called "the goal" (*attha*) in the sense that it is "approached" or "attained" by following the cause that brings about its realization.

By the phrase "whatever has arisen from conditions," the suffering and other truths mentioned in the sections on the Truths, Causes, Dhamma, and Conditions are included. In the sections on the Truths and Conditions:

The five meanings should be understood according to what is stated in the Pāḷi as follows: Nibbāna; the meaning spoken in the section on the scriptures (pariyattivāra); and in the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya, "result" (vipāka) and "functional" (kiriya). It "burns," thus it is "vidahati";
this etymology is common to the causes that produce [results] and so forth. To clarify its specific meaning, however: "it causes to proceed" or "it reaches."
Thus it is said. Among these, the first meaning is to be understood as applying to those things excluding the Path.
For while spoken words convey their meaning by way of making it known, the Path brings one to Nibbāna; therefore, in that case, the latter meaning applies.

Indeed, Nibbāna is the meaning to be attained (*pattabbo attho*), spoken meaning is the meaning to be made known (*ñāpetabbo attho*), and the other is the meaning to be produced (*nibbattetabbo attho*); thus, it is threefold.
By the phrase “Whatever cause produces a fruit,” the [factors] beginning with origination (samudaya) as they appear in the sections on the Truths, Causes, Dhamma, and Conditions are included;

the Path (magga) is included in the sections on the Truths and Conditions; and that which is spoken of in the section on the Discourses (pariyatti) and as wholesome and unwholesome in the Abhidhamma-Bhājaniya—thus, by way of these very terms stated in the Pāḷi, five factors are to be understood. Among those, the Path...
The cause should be understood as threefold: that which brings about attainment, that which makes known what has been said, and that which produces the other [result].

And here, because volitional activities (kiriya) are without fruition (avipāka), their status as "dhamma" is not mentioned. If that is so, should their status as "attha" (meaning/object) also not be stated, since they are not fruitions?
No, because they possess the state of being produced by conditions. If this were the case, would it not follow that wholesome and unwholesome states also possess the status of "attha"?

Why is this? There is no fault here because it has not been prohibited. However, because the result (vipāka) is manifest due to its status as the primary cause, their nature as *dhammas* alone was stated.
If it is argued that their nature as *dhammas* follows from their being conditions for functional states (*kiriya*), there is no fault here because it has not been prohibited.
Yet, because they lack the causal status that constitutes the connection between karma and its fruit, their nature as *dhammas* was not stated. Furthermore, "this..."

It should be understood that the specific nature of the meaning and the phenomena (*atthadhammatā*) has not been explicitly stated for those who possess the analytical knowledges of phenomena and meaning (*dhammattha-paṭisambhidā*) while reflecting merely upon the wholesome and unwholesome, as well as resultant and functional states, without making the distinction: "this is the condition; this is the conditioned.

For the phrase "this indeed is the meaning" refers to the connection that the meaning—which was explained by way of the fivefold division of meaning and phenomena—is precisely what is shown here in the Abhidhamma after having been analyzed.

Regarding the phrase "in the expression of the linguistic designation of phenomena" (*dhammaniruttābhilāpe*): here, taking the word *dhamma* to signify intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), he says "the linguistic designation of intrinsic nature," which means an unerring linguistic designation.
Therefore, he says "non-deviant usage"; the meaning is that it is a verbal usage with a fixed relationship for the purpose of making known this or that specific object.
"In its expression" (*tadabhilāpe*) refers to that which is designated as the linguistic designation of intrinsic nature.
It is for the purpose of expressing that which is unerring in its conventional usage. Now, this natural language (*sabhāvanirutti*) is the Māgadhī tongue.
In terms of its meaning, the teachers maintain that it is a "name-designation" (*nāmapaññatti*). However, others argue:

if natural language were of the nature of a designation, then it would follow that the designation itself is what is to be expressed, not the speech; yet there is nothing to be expressed other than the speech itself.

There is something that must be uttered. Now, if it were to be understood or expressed by means of terms such as "contact" (phassa) and so forth, then since meaning (attha) and phenomena (dhamma) would also have to be understood, they too would consequently fall into the status of being linguistic expressions (nirutti).

This point is shown by the fact that "contact" (*phassa*) is a natural linguistic expression (*sabhāva-nirutti*), whereas "contact, contact" (*phassaṃ phassā*) is not a natural linguistic expression. Furthermore, such a kind of non-expression does not exist.
It exists. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows: it is the utterance, that is, the vocalization, of that very natural language which consists of speech.

For one who reflects by taking that sound of natural language as an object, the knowledge that has reached differentiation regarding that vocalization of natural language is the *niruttipaṭisambhidā*. Thus, this *niruttipaṭisambhidā* has sound as its object.

Because it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "It has name as its object, not the concept as its object," they say that after the ear-consciousness process—which has the sound of etymological analysis (*nirutti*) as its object—the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*) subsequently arises in the mind-door.

Furthermore, the statement, "The analytical knowledge of language has the present as its object," is said with reference to the subsequent cognition that occurs after having grasped the sound of the words. Thus...
Otherwise, it would follow that one present object is being described as another present object.

However, just as the knowledge of the divine ear (*dibbasotañāṇa*)— being a condition for the determination of the distinctions between sounds such as those of humans— is the revealer of each respective sound,

so too [the knowledge of language] is the condition for the determination of correct and incorrect linguistic expressions, having as its object the sounds of linguistic expressions that possess their own intrinsic nature in the present.
When that knowledge which analyzes [language] is called the "analytical knowledge of language" (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), there is no contradiction with the Canon.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that one cannot speak of "reviewing while taking as an object that sound which is natural language" or "engaging in review that has present sound as its object.
For that knowledge, while indeed analyzing natural language, immediately follows the reviewing of each respective sound.

Because it arises precisely by breaking through and penetrating the etymological analysis (*nirutti*) as the cause for determining each respective distinction, it is said to "have reached distinctions.
"Knowledge in all cases" means knowledge regarding every object; the intended meaning is that it is "all-knowledge. Therefore he said: "having knowledge as its object..."

"Knowledge. Or, "in all respects" (*sabbattha*) means: because it occurs in relation to all [categories] beginning with meaning—whether three or four—or because the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*), being a wholesome functional state, exists as both the phenomenon (*dhamma*) and the meaning (*attha*), it occurs in only three; thus it is called "knowledge in all respects.
Therefore he said, "or in those aforementioned," and so forth. Therein, "by way of its own range, function, and so on" refers to its own range (*sagocara*).
And by way of function (*kicca*) and so forth, it is the knowledge that "this knowledge has arisen making this its object, and it functions by means of this specific function.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*), proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), plane (*bhūmi*), and others.
For this very reason, he said: "These knowledges illuminate this meaning," and so on.
429. "They go to analysis" means they attain the capacity to understand, as it truly is, the various specific distinctions among objects that are divided into many different types.

The mention of the Elder Ānanda is made to exclude—by way of an exception—the meaning shown by the general rule that "the Great Disciples have gone to analysis on the stage of those beyond training" (asekkha-bhūmi).

This refers to the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). On the stage of those still in training (sekha-bhūmi), the attainment of analysis has a limited scope; on the stage of those beyond training, it has a vast scope.
He said, "Attainment (adhigama) means the reaching of Arahantship," or rather, this was said with reference to a preeminent attainment.
For even though those who are still in training (sekkha) have reached these [analytical insights], there is an attainment of their clarity through the reaching of Arahantship.

However, just like prior application, the reaching of Arahantship is indeed a condition for the clarity of the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) even for one who is already an Arahant; thus, it applies to all five.

The causality should be applied according to the circumstances through the purification of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of both those in training (*sekkha*) and those beyond training (*asekkha*).
Since they encompass the meaning and the doctrine without exception, it is the domain of the Buddha’s word alone that is shown by the terms "the scriptures" (*pariyatti*) and so forth.
He said: "Recitation of the text is mastery; hearing its meaning is 'hearing'; and the desire to know it thoroughly and completely is 'inquiry' (*paripucchā*)."
"Discourse on the determination of knotted passages (*gaṇṭhipada*) and meaning-passage (*atthapada*) in the Canon, the Commentaries, and so forth":

the meaning is that this is a detailed discourse providing a definitive conclusion regarding those points difficult to understand, both in terms of the literal meaning of the words (*padattha*) and their underlying intention (*adhippāya*).
For a word whose meaning is difficult to understand is a "knotted passage," while a word whose intention is difficult to understand is a "meaning-passage. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),...
It includes the paths of discourse connected with the aggregates and so forth.
One who possesses going and returning together with the application of development is called *gatapaccāgatika*; the state of being such is *gatapaccāgatikabhāva*.

The meaning is: one devoted to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) from his dwelling place as far as the village where he seeks alms, and from there back again to his dwelling place. [This continues] until one reaches the vicinity of the *anuloma* and *gotrabhū* stages.
He speaks of the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*). For that indeed proceeds in proximity to them.
"In wholesome works" (*satthesu*) means in blameless texts that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings. Likewise, "in the fields of craft" (*sippāyatanesu*); here too it is the same.

In ancient times, there were one hundred regional languages and one hundred modes of expression for the one hundred kings. In the *Dhammapada*, the Chapter on Pairs is called the Chapter on Similes (*opammavagga*).
Some say that in the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa*, there is the *Yamakavagga* and the *Opammavagga*; others say [there are more].
"Abounding in learning and inspired eloquence" means those who are well-versed (*bahussuta*) and possessed of ready wit (*paṭibhānavant*).
"All" refers either to the five mentioned previously or the eight mentioned later. At the conclusion of the *sekha-phala-vimokkha*.
These exist as the liberation belonging to the fruit of one in training (sekha).

Because the powers such as the knowledge of what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhānañāṇabala) and so forth are more manifest among all the Buddha-qualities by virtue of their respective functions, it is said, "like the ten powers";
or else, all other specific qualities of the Blessed One, such as omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), are likewise exclusively the liberation belonging to the fruit of one beyond training (asekha).
**Commentary on the Definition of the Ground, Root, and Body of Wisdom (Paññābhūmi-mūla-sarīravavatthānavaṇṇanā)** 430.
"By this wisdom" means by insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*). It is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because it serves as the basis for its occurrence through the grasping of characteristics and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of nutriment and the rest should be understood. But why are these many phenomena considered to have the nature of a ground?
Are they not grasped? Surely the purpose is accomplished even by one among the aggregates and so forth? No;

the inclusion of the triad beginning with the aggregates must be made for the sake of favoring three types of beings. Otherwise, the favor that is common to all would not be effected. For beings are of three kinds:
those deluded regarding form, those deluded regarding the formless, and those deluded regarding both. Among them, for the sake of those who are deluded regarding the formless—
The analysis of the aggregates (*khandha*) is fourfold because it classifies immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).
For those who are confused regarding form, the analysis of the bases (*āyatana*) is eleven-and-a-half-fold because it classifies material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).

For those, however, who are confused regarding both, the analysis of the elements (*dhātu*) is twofold because it classifies both types of phenomena. Likewise, according to the distinction of faculties (*indriya*), there are those with sharp faculties and those with medium faculties.

Sentient beings are of three types: those with dull faculties (*mudindriya*), those who prefer concise treatment (*saṃkhittaruci*), those who prefer intermediate treatment (*majjhimaruci*), and those who prefer detailed treatment (*vitthāraruci*).
It should be understood that for their sake, the aggregates and so forth are taken up in due order.
As for the mention of the "faculties" (*indriya*), although these factors indeed exercise sovereignty and dominance over co-nascent phenomena just as a lord does, that [sovereignty] of theirs—

It is established by the very nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*); herein, no one possesses mastery. This is for the purpose of easily grasping the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) through the statement, "These are empty, they are not subject to one's will.
Furthermore, these four kinds [of truths] are beneficial only when seen as the cause of occurrence, cessation, and both;
not otherwise. Thus, the pair beginning with the Truths is mentioned. By the word "beginning" (*ādi*), this same [principle] applies to the phenomena included therein as well.

The method is to be applied as follows: it is the "root" because it serves as the foundation. For when mindfulness exists, this wisdom is born from that root within both purification of virtue and purification of mind;
it does not exist when mindfulness is absent. It is the "body" because it is to be fully developed.

For while this wisdom proceeds by way of a continuous stream, these five purifications—beginning with purification of view—are its constituent parts, corresponding respectively to the feet, hands, and head.
They should be understood as "the body" by way of characterizing the whole.
431. Regarding the phrase "the five aggregates": here, "five" is a numerical limit; by this, it shows that there are neither fewer nor more than that.
"Aggregates" (khandhā) is an indication of phenomena that have been delimited. And because the word "aggregate" (khandha) here has the sense of a heap (rāsa).
As in the case of expressions such as “a great mass of water,” therefore, having grasped all form— distinguished by its divisions of past and so forth—
as a single unit through the intellect in the sense of a heap, the compound “rūpakkhandho” (form-aggregate) should be understood as a coordinate (samānādhikaraṇa) compound,

meaning “the aggregate that is itself form. However, when the word *khandha* is used in the sense of a portion, as in expressions such as “we will pay the debt in three installments,” [it is a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound].
Does it follow that even *nibbāna* would have the status of being another aggregate (*khandha*)? It does not so follow, because of the absence of distinctions such as past and so forth.
For there is no distinction of past, future, or present for *nibbāna*, which is a single, permanent reality. In the first sense, the meaning is "a heap of matter" (*rūpa-rāsi*);
in the second sense, it is "a portion of matter" (*rūpa-koṭṭhāsa*). The same method applies to the "aggregate of feeling" (*vedanā-khandha*) and the others. But why are these [aggregates]...

Are the aggregates taught as exactly five and in this very order? It should be understood that this is because they are presented by way of the analogy of the vessel, the food, the condiment, the cook, and the eater; and also because they are taught according to their relative grossness and their degree of defilement.

Furthermore, having considered their status as the root cause of disputes, their role as causes for saṃsāra, and their nature as causes for kamma, feeling and perception are extracted from the aggregate of mental formations and taught separately as distinct aggregates.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Aggregate of Form (Rūpakkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā) 432. *Tattha* means "among those five aggregates. *Yaṃ kiñci* ("whatever") is an expression used to include everything without exception.

*Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ* ("having the characteristic of being affected") is a restriction intended to prevent over-extension (*atippasaṅga*). For, by the use of the word *yaṃ* together with the word *kiṃ*, which denotes an indefinite sense...
When there is an excessive extension [of the term], the word "changing" (*ruppana*) prevents that; by this, the inclusion of matter (*rūpa*) is made exhaustive.
"By cold and so forth" means by cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so on. This instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause.

"That which has changing as its characteristic" is *ruppanalakkhaṇa*. "Dhamma itself" is *dhammajāta*. And here, "changing" occurs upon the encounter with opposing conditions such as cold and so forth.
"Dissimilar arising. But is it not the case that even for immaterial phenomena, dissimilar arising is obtained when there is a convergence of opposing conditions?
True, it is obtained; however, it is not more manifest. For here, "changeability" (ruppana) is intended in its most manifest sense, because of the perception of cold and so forth.
If this is so, how is the designation "form" (rūpa) applied in the Brahma-world? Even there, it certainly exists, because it does not transcend that intrinsic nature.
Or it is the designation "form" (*rūpa-saññā*) by way of being a supporting condition (*anuggāhaka-paccaya*).

Others maintain that "being formed" (*ruppana*) is that state which, upon the encounter with opposing conditions, becomes the cause for a dissimilar arising within one's own continuity even as it is breaking up.

In this view, "form" (*rūpa*) is so called because it "forms," meaning it brings about change; whereas in the former view, it is "that which is formed. This refers to the occurrence of change through impact.

Some say that the word *ruppana* (being affected) is conventional (*nirūḷha*). On this view, there is no possibility of applying the designation "matter" (*rūpa*) to non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), because they lack the quality of impact (*saṅghaṭṭana*).
Others say that "being affected" means resistance (*paṭighāta*). "Having made all that into one" means he speaks while keeping the sense of a "heap" (*rāsa*) in mind.

Regarding the phrase "due to the distinction between the primary elements (bhūta) and the derived matter (upādāya)": here, because it exists dependent upon them, the derived matter is called "derived" (*upādāya-rūpa*). The primary elements are "derived" (*upādāya*) in the sense that they are themselves derived [from causes], but they are not themselves derived by those [elements] or by anything else.
Granted, the primary elements have already been analyzed through their verbal definitions and so forth in the *Catudhātuvavatthāna* (The Analysis of the Four Elements);

however, since this section concerns the analysis of the characteristics and other attributes of phenomena according to their intrinsic natures, it is said: "In the *Catudhātuvavatthāna*, the characteristics, functions, and manifestations..."
“...have been stated. In that context, because the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) has not been stated, he says, “But as for the proximate cause,” and so forth.
And its non-statement should be understood as being because it has already been explained by way of another method in the passage concerning the conditionality of each respective meaning.
“All four” means all four elements. It is only when the earth element is embraced by the water element, sustained by the fire element, and expanded by the air element [that it exists].

"Proceeding, not otherwise"—this means it has the remaining three elements as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*); and since the others are likewise, he says, "having the remaining three elements as its proximate cause.

"Of twenty-four kinds" is a limitation by number for the purpose of excluding [the categories of] power-form (*balarūpa*) and so forth. Regarding that which must be said therein, it will be made clear later.
It is called the eye (*cakkhu*) because it sees (*cakkhati*), [referring to] matter (*rūpa*) which, being presided over by consciousness, experiences [objects].
The meaning is "it is as if. For this word *cakkhati*—as in "he tastes honey" (*madhuṃ cakkhati*) or "he tastes the sauce" (*byañjanaṃ cakkhatī*)—has the sense of relishing.
Indeed, it has been said: "The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and exults in forms.
And in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) it is also stated: "Its function is to attract among forms. Even though...

It should be understood that because the terms for the ear and so forth are conventionally established in reference to their respective objects such as sound, the word *cakkhu* (eye) occurs only in the sense of seeing, just as the words *paṅkaja* (mud-born) and others occur in reference to lotuses and the like.
Alternatively, the meaning is that it "sees" (*cakkhati*), insofar as, presided over by consciousness, it becomes as if clearly announcing or speaking out what is even or uneven.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is said: "It makes manifest... (*vibhāveti*).
And so it is said. This is stated on the grounds that since roots have multiple meanings, the sense of "manifesting" (*vibhāvana*) is also possible for the word *cakkhati*.
It is called the ear (*sota*) because one hears by means of it, or it itself hears when presided over by consciousness.
It is called the nose (*ghāna*) because one smells by means of it, or it itself smells. Because swallowing is rooted in the apprehension of taste, the flavor of food is the cause of life.
Because it craves for that [taste] due to its inclination toward it, it is called "tongue" (*jivhā*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*niruttinaya*).
The body (*kāya*) is the source—that is, the place of origin—of base, tainted phenomena (*sāsava-dhamma*).

Among the nose, tongue, and body, which do not serve as causes for the supreme states (*anuttariya*) but are produced by karma rooted in sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), and among which the body is a specific condition for sensual lust, the body is so designated because it is specifically a condition for the tainted states.
For it is because beings, relishing the pleasure of touch, engage in sexual intercourse.

Alternatively, the four aggregates based on the faculty of the body are specifically called "with-outflows" (*sāsava*) because they serve as the cause for the powerful outflow of sensual desire and so forth;

thus, the body (*kāya*) is said to be the "source" (*āya*) of those base phenomena that possess outflows. It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it causes what has entered the heart to undergo a transformation of color (*vaṇṇa-vikāra*); it is like a form.
"Manifests" means it shows as if with a physical form; or, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *rūpa* should be understood here in the sense of "manifesting.
It is called *sadda* (sound) because it resounds; or its meaning is that it is uttered, or it resounds through its own conditions, being brought to a state perceivable by the ear.
It is called *gandha* (odor) because it makes itself known (*gandhayati*), that is, it indicates its own substrate.
It makes manifest what is unmanifest, such as declaring, "This is fragrant," or "This is foul-smelling";

or it is like one who slanders by saying, "There is this here," regarding hidden flowers, fruits, and so forth—this is the meaning. It is called *rasa* because beings taste (*rasanti*) it; the meaning is that they relish it.
The faculty of a woman is the female faculty (*itthindriya*); likewise for the male faculty (*purisindriya*). They live by means of it, along with the co-nascent phenomena (*sahajātadhamma*).

That which is life is itself the faculty of life, the *jīvitindriya*. That which is both the heart and the physical basis (*vatthu*) is the "heart-basis" (*hadayavatthu*), or rather, the basis for the mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) located in the heart.
Because it consists in the act of moving the body and because it makes one's intention known, it is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*).
Because it consists in the act of uttering speech and because it makes one's intention known, it is called "vocal intimation" (*vacīviññatti*).
Vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*). Because it lacks solidity (*viggaha*), it does not resist being struck; it cannot be cut or broken.

Or, it does not "sound" (*kāsati*) but shines (*dibbati*), thus it is *akāsa*; *akāsa* itself is *ākāsa*. That very thing, in the sense of being devoid of beings and life-force, is the space element (*ākāsadhātu*).
"Of matter" (*rūpassa*) refers to produced matter (*nipphannarūpa*). Lightness is buoyancy (*lahutā*). It is specified as "of matter" because it is itself unproduced (*anipphanna*). This...
The method is the same for the remaining terms as well. However, this is the distinction: that which is fit for action is *kammañña*; the state of being so is *kammaññatā*.
Accumulation (*caya*) and occurrence (*pavatti*) at the beginning and above [respectively] constitute *upacaya*. Occurrence connected by way of preceding and succeeding moments is *santati*.
The state of that which is impermanent and subject to destruction is *aniccatā*. That which is made into a morsel is *kabaḷīkāra*; that which brings [nourishment] is *āhāra*.
Thus, first of all, derived matter (upādāyarūpa) should be understood according to the meaning of its term.
As for the sequence: because they serve as the support for all material phenomena and constitute their root, the primary elements (bhūtarūpa) are listed first.
Among the others, the five beginning with the eye are [listed next] because, by virtue of being internal, they constitute the root of what is designated as the "personal body" (attabhāva).
These have been listed at the beginning. In order to show that these four—form and so forth—are the objects of those respective sense-faculties, they are listed here.
However, the tangible (phoṭṭhabba) is not included here because it is a non-derived form (anupādārūpa) and is already included by the mention of the primary elements (bhūta).
Immediately following that, for the purpose of showing how this personal existence (attabhāva) comes to be designated as "woman" or "man" by means of these [faculties], [the faculties are listed].
The two faculties of female and male have been taught. Next is the life-faculty, for the purpose of showing that it receives the conventional designation "one lives by means of this.
Next is the heart-base, for the purpose of showing that, depending upon this, consciousness occurs and the accomplishment of one's own welfare and so forth takes place.
Next are the two types of intimation, for the purpose of showing that all bodily and verbal activities occur by means of these.
The space element is taught for the purpose of showing the delimitation of this material body and its directness;
the lightness and other qualities are taught for the purpose of showing its occurrence of pleasure, its arising, and so forth;
and it should be understood that edible food is mentioned at the end for the purpose of showing that this entire continuity of the fourfold stream of matter is supported by it.

433. Now, in order to define the derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) as they were enumerated above by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), the passage beginning with “therein, that which has the characteristic of being sensitive matter capable of being struck by form” is commenced.
Therein, “therein” means among those derived material phenomena. Striking against form, or of form, is “striking by form” (*rūpābhighāta*);

that which is worthy of this is “capable of being struck by form” (*rūpābhighātāraha*). Whether there is striking by form or not, it is of such a nature that it belongs to the four primary elements (*bhūta*).
"Transparency" (*pasāda*) means the clarity of the primary elements (*bhūta*) capable of being struck by visible forms; the meaning is that the eye has such a characteristic.

Since the eye's transparency functions as the striking of visible forms only when accompanied by other conditions, and not in isolation, the state of being "capable of being struck by visible forms" is mentioned to show that its very nature is the authority [for its definition], rather than the actual striking of visible forms—just as wholesome and unwholesome states are defined as "capable of producing result" (*vipākāraha*).
And "impact" (*abhighāta*) is the mutual facing of the sense-object and the sense-faculty, which, by being situated in a suitable location, is like a physical impact.
This occurs either of the eye in relation to the visible form, or of the visible form in relation to the eye. Therefore he said:
"That eye which is non-demonstrable and impinging, [impinges] upon a visible form that is demonstrable and impinging," and "in whatever eye..."
"Does visible form that is non-manifesting and impinging strike against, or is it struck by, visible form that is manifesting and impinging?

and so forth. Furthermore, sensual craving and form-craving—which serve as the causal basis for the production of a personal existence (attabhāva) consisting of either complete or incomplete sense bases—are worthy of the designation "desire to see," etc., because they involve the aspiration for existence within those respective sense bases.

The second method is stated in all instances. In that context, "having the desire to see as their source and karma as their origin" means those [visual objects] for which the desire to see is the source and karma is the origin.
The clarity (*pasāda*) of such material phenomena (*bhūta*) is the desire to see... [and so on] ...clarity;
such is the characteristic of the eye. For craving, which is the fundamental cause of each respective existence, [resides] therein.

Since even the sense bases and objects that are destined to arise in that existence are said to be fit for the designation of "desire for sight" and so forth regarding sensual craving and the rest, "desire for sight" (daṭṭhukāmatā) means the wish to see;

its meaning is "craving for form" (rūpataṇhā). In this context, once the prior arising has occurred, there is nothing further to be said regarding the desire for sight and the accumulation of karma that produces those respective individual existences at the moment of their formation.
However, it should be understood that the very state of not having been eradicated by the Path is the cause.
Since it has not been cut off by the Path, when the cause is obtained, it arises and becomes a condition for its own fruit;
thus, being actually present, its "arisen-ness" (uppannatā) and "existence" (atthitā) are spoken of by way of synonyms. [As it is said: "While developing the Noble Eightfold Path..."

It is said [in the Suttas]: "One who cultivates the path causes evil, unwholesome states that have arisen to vanish right then and there," and "If sensual desire is present within oneself, one understands: 'There is sensual desire in me,'" and so forth.
Its function is to attract a person or consciousness toward visible forms. It is manifested as a state of being a support, because it serves as a condition of dependence (nissaya-paccaya).
The primary proximate cause for this [eye-sensitivity] is the primary elements born of kamma rooted in the desire to see;

for it is made the immediate cause by those elements whose clarity constitutes the eye. And here, the preceding definition of the eye has been stated by way of the common kamma that produces each respective individual existence (*attabhāva*), because no specific distinction of cause has been mentioned.
However, by way of the unique kamma produced through the thought, "May my eye be of such-and-such a kind," [the following definition is given].

They say it is "the second. However, although there is a commonality among the five in their state of being translucent (*pasāda*), the former [eye] was mentioned first by way of the function of translucence known as the illumination of its own respective object.

Although there is a commonality among them in their state of being kamma-results, or in their unity, the second [ear] should be understood as being distinguished by way of showing its distinction from its own specific cause. [This applies to] the ear and the others.
The meaning should be understood according to the method already explained regarding the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth.
Here it is asked: "Do the faculties such as the eye arise from a single kamma, or from various kammas?

The ancient masters say: "In both ways. In that regard, first, concerning their arising from various kammas, there is no need to state a distinction between the eye and the other faculties, because the cause [is the same].
Because they are distinct. But if they arise through a single act of karma, how is there a distinction between them? It is precisely because their causes are distinct.

For craving, which consists of the aspiration for this or that state of existence, being itself diverse in form due to its longing for the sense bases included within those respective states of existence, establishes the diverse differentiation of the karma that produces those respective states of existence by way of being its decisive support (*upanissaya*).

For, having been infused with a specific quality at that time, it produces a manifold result of distinguished nature—as if it had itself assumed many forms—by virtue of its capacity for such [production].
And here, this "capacity" should not be understood as something other than the state of being capable;

it is merely the fitness for the production of a distinguished result in that which has been infused with a specific quality by means of a particular cause. And this is the connection with the distinction of a single action having multiple faculties as its cause.

It will follow from what follows by way of reasoning and scriptural authority. Furthermore, it is stated that a single wholesome consciousness is the cause for the production of sixteen types of resultant consciousnesses and so forth.
Even in the world, it is observed that a single grain of rice is the cause for the production of fruits ranging from fully developed grains to underdeveloped grains;
so what need is there for such deliberation on reasoning? For the fruit of karma consists of the eye and other faculties, as well as the maturation of karma.
"It is exclusively within the domain of the Buddhas' knowledge.
(434) "Some" refers to certain members of the Mahāsāṅghikas. Among them, Vasudhamma says: "In the eye, fire is predominant;
in the ear, air; in the nose, earth; in the tongue, water; in the body, all [elements] are equal. Regarding the eye and the other [senses]:
By saying "the predominance of fire and so forth" means showing that it is the predominance of those [elements] which serve as its support;
thus he said, "The sensitivity of the elements predominant in fire is the eye," and so on. As for the statement "the body belongs to all," what is the distinction here?

Is it not the case that the sensitivities of the elements predominant in fire and so forth belong to all beings alike? True, this is so; however, this expression "of all" refers to those who are similar.
This meaning is illustrated because it is stated by way of precluding a state where one [element] is in excess of the others while they are functioning together.

For it is evident that even when two or three elements are in excess—as in the case of each being individually excessive—the sensitivity of the body does not arise, due to the deficiency resulting from the aforementioned excess of one over the others, such as fire and so forth. Therefore:

The term "all" (*sabba*) here should be understood as indicating the state of equilibrium, in the sense that the sensitivity of the body arises through the equal proportion of all four primary elements (*bhūta*).

Regarding the phrase "of fire and so forth": according to the former view, this refers to the light-form of fire (in the form of a lamp), the sound of air, the odor of earth, and the taste of water (in the form of saliva); and according to the latter view, it should be applied accordingly.

The meaning is that it is so called because it is assisted by the qualities (*guṇa*) of this or that primary element (*bhūta*), and because it must be aided in the apprehension of visible forms and so forth.

Their tenet is that the capacity of the eye and other faculties to illuminate visible forms and so forth exists only when they are accompanied by cooperative causes such as light, and that the state of being a cavity is a quality (*guṇa*) that serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for ear-consciousness.
However, since a cavity lacks the nature of a primary element (*bhūta*), it is apprehended according to the circumstances, unlike fire and the other elements.
Alternatively, according to the intention of others—that even an aperture (*vivara*) is a quality of the primary elements (*bhūtaguṇa*)—the connection is to be made as follows:

with the respective qualities of each element, namely, with light-form for fire, with the sound designated as "space" for the aperture, with odor for air, with taste for water, and with tangible form for earth; thus, it should be applied accordingly.

"By way of showing the predominance of form and the rest": the first proponent said, "Form and the rest are their qualities," because he saw these specific associations: that in fire, form is luminous; in air, sound is heard by its own nature; in earth, there is fragrance such as the sweet-smelling;
and in water, there is a sweet taste. It is for him alone... [text continues].
