He provides the reply with the words beginning, “We would wish,” and so forth. By this very method, the refutation of the second proponent also occurs.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the passage beginning, “But if they should say,” was spoken in order to refute the doctrine of Kaṇāda—who asserts that the eye and other sense faculties are produced by fire, space, earth, water, and air, which possess specific qualities such as form—and to overturn his position. Regarding the taints (*āsava*):

If it is argued that even though a scent is perceived in earth associated with water, it is unlike that from cotton, and therefore the scent of the cotton does not attain a state of superiority—this is not so, because it is not overwhelmed.
For earth associated with water is overwhelmed by the water, whereas the cotton-earth is not;
thus, it must possess a superior scent due to that very [earth]. This is also the case with earth associated with hot water.
And if it were thought that fire is perceivable as something great, then its color would also be perceived as radiant, just like its touch;
consequently, in warm water, the color of the cold water—which is not connected with fire—would disappear.
Therefore, because of the absence of both [these qualities], the status of visible form and so forth as specific qualities of fire and so on is negated. By that negation, [the argument is refuted].
“The reason ‘because fire and so forth are not supported by qualities such as visible form’ has been refuted.

Thus, through this sequence, the absence of both [fire and its qualities] becomes the cause for abandoning the conceptualization of distinctions; therefore he said, “Therefore, one should abandon it,” and so forth.

Even within a single aggregate, visible form, taste, and the rest are dissimilar; what need then be said regarding the eye and other distinct aggregates, even in the absence of specific primary elements?
The illustration of visible form, taste, and so forth was stated in order to demonstrate this.

If there is no distinction among the primary elements (*bhūta*), what then is the cause for the distinction between the eye and the other sense organs? To show that, it was said: "That which [is the cause] of one another," and so on.
Even a single kamma, when produced through the aspiration for existence as a being endowed with the five sense bases, serves as the cause for the distinction between the eye and the other organs.
It should be understood that this is stated both as "not common to one another" and as "a specific type of kamma.
For it does not serve as a condition for the ear by the same specific quality through which it is a condition for the eye, because it has attained the status of being a different faculty.
This is evident from the statement: "At the moment of rebirth-linking, sublime volition is a condition for the kamma-produced material phenomena by way of kamma-condition."
It is understood that at the moment of rebirth-linking, a single volition is the kamma-condition for all the material phenomena produced by past karma (*kaṭattārūpa*) that exist at that time.
For if there were the arising of faculties through various volitions, the material phenomena produced by past karma would then result from both limited (*paritta*) and sublime (*mahaggata*) kamma.
Furthermore, a single rebirth-linking is not produced by multiple kamma-formations.
Thus it is established that the arising of multiple faculties occurs through a single kamma.
435. That which has a non-adherent support is "anallīnanissaya"; this refers to the object consisting of visible form and sound.
The supports for odors and tastes adhere to the supports of the nose and tongue; thus, they are "adhered-to" by way of their supports. Tangible object (*phoṭṭhabba*) itself...
Because it is an entity dependent upon and attached to the body. Another method [of explanation]:

the eye and ear grasp objects without reaching them (*appatta-visaya-aggāhakāni*), because they serve as the cause for the arising of consciousness even when the object is at a distance or beyond [the organ]. Some maintain that the ear also grasps objects by reaching them (*sampatta-visaya-aggāhī*).
If the ear were to grasp only what it reaches, then sound produced by the mind (*cittaja-sadda*) would not be an object for auditory consciousness; for [sound] does not exist externally [to the ear].
There is the arising of mind-originated [sounds]. And in the Pāḷi, the state of being an object of ear-consciousness is stated for sound-objects without distinction.
Furthermore, there would be no delimitation by direction or location for sound, because it must be apprehended precisely in the location of its own perceiver, just like a fragrance.
Therefore, sound remains right where it has arisen; if it comes within the range of the ear, it enters the field of perception.
Is it not the case that sounds such as those of a washerman are heard after a long time by those standing at a distance?

No, because there is no difference in the apprehension of sounds according to whether they are distant or near, provided the sounds are equally manifest. For just as, in the case of the sound of speech, there is no apprehension of specific forms for those standing far or near when the sound is equally manifest, yet there is indeed apprehension;
so too, in the case of the sound of a washerman and others, [the sound] of one who is near is apprehended from the beginning right up to the end.
When the sound has gradually become manifest, or when it has reached its end after being distant, or even when it becomes manifest through its accumulation in the middle,

there arises for one who grasps a conclusion— specifically for one whose ear-consciousness process has already passed— the overestimation (adhimāna) that "I heard it late," even though the sound was actually heard quickly.
Furthermore, that sound, at the moment of its own existence, is dependent solely on that very place where it arose.
It comes within the range of the ear. If there were no propagation of sound in all directions through a succession of material elements (*bhūta-paramparā*), how could an echo arise?

It should be understood that even a sound situated at a distance serves as the condition for the arising of an echo elsewhere and for the movement of vessels and so forth, just as a magnet is the condition for the movement of iron.

436. Although the eye has already been analyzed by way of its characteristics and so forth, the passage beginning with “The eye, moreover, here” is commenced in order to analyze it by way of its location and so on.
In this context, the connection is: “the eye stands accomplishing [its function]. The particle *ca* (moreover) has the sense of distinction;
by means of it, it illuminates the specific quality of the eye that is about to be stated. “Here” (*ettha*) means among these five derived material phenomena as they have been described.
By the phrase "in the place where the shape of the body arises," he excludes the remaining black circles (*kaṇhamaṇḍala*).

It exists pervading the seven layers of the eye-film like oil, receiving assistance from its own four supporting elements (*dhātu*), and being sustained and surrounded by the life-force, color, and other qualities dependent upon them;
it is produced by the three types of continuity-forms arising from temperature, mind, and nutriment.
It remains supported [by the physical eye]. By the expression "pervading the seven layers of the eyelid," he shows that the eye consists of many constituent parts (*kalāpa*).
As for the phrase "in size, the measure of a louse's head," this is said because it functions in a location the measure of a louse's head.

It serves as the physical basis (*vatthu*) for eye-consciousness by way of being its support (*nissaya*), and it serves as the door (*dvāra*) for the mental processes beginning with adverting and receiving, and ending with the registration consciousness.

From the place of assembly. Now, this eye, though it is multiple due to its division into bases—and even therein, because each one consists of many groups—is spoken of as "one" by way of a general description, owing to the unity of advertence (*āvajjanā*) and because it performs its function for only one [object] at a single moment.
But even so, how can there be the performance of a function for only one among many? That which is clear therein...
It should be understood that having been offered as a sacrifice, it becomes the support for consciousness, just as a particular tangible object serves as the objective field for body-consciousness.
In the word *manupassati*, the letter *m* functions to join the words; alternatively, *manu* means a mortal (*macca*).
A finger-ring is that which pierces the finger.
Because of its inclination toward unevenness, the eye is like a snake delighting in the holes of an anthill;

because of its inclination toward hollows, the ear is like a crocodile delighting in a water-hole; and because of its inclination toward space, the nose is like a bird delighting in the cloudless sky.

Showing that the tongue should be viewed as like a dog delighting in a village due to its inclination toward the village, and the body as like a jackal delighting in a raw charnel ground due to its inclination toward what is clung-to (upādinnaka), he said: "The skin...
should be seen. And this was stated because the inclination of the eye is like an uneven inclination; or else, it is by way of the inclination of the person possessing eyes.

The eye should be seen as having a crooked inclination. This same method applies to the others as well. Furthermore, all the aforementioned conceptual proliferation (papañca) should be understood as applicable to the ear and the other senses according to their respective cases. 437.
"Eye-impact" (cakkhupaṭihanana) refers to the striking against the eye or the impact upon the eye; that which has this as its characteristic is [the "eye-impacting"].

It has the characteristic of impinging upon the eye. Here, "impinging" is precisely the aforementioned striking. Its state as an object is its conditionality as an objective support (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*).
Granted that this is indeed its being a field of activity (*gocaratā*), nevertheless, there is this distinction between an "object" (*visaya*) and a "field of activity":

for visual consciousness, it consists in not having another purpose and in frequenting that [object] predominantly. Regarding what is to be said concerning its state as an object, that will be discussed further on.
It will become manifest. However, regarding bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) and so forth:
the state of a woman, or that by which the mind and the designation "woman" come to be, is "femininity" (*itthibhāva*).

That which has this as its characteristic mark is "characterized by femininity" (*itthibhāvalakkhaṇa*). For that very reason, the continuum (*santāna*) associated with that [characteristic] is called "a woman."

It is said that "it is as if making [her] manifest" because its function is to manifest her as a woman (*itthī*). The female sex characteristics (*itthiliṅga*) consist of the circularity [of the body], and the lack of distinctness in the hands, feet, and so forth.

The female sign (*itthinimitta*) consists of the lack of distinctness in the flesh of the breasts, the absence of facial hair, the binding of the hair, and the wearing of garments, because these serve as conditions for the perception of her as a "woman.
Even at the time of childhood, [these are present] by means of well-formed pestles, mortars, and so on.

Play, spinning thread with clay paste, and so forth, constitute *itthikutta*—the meaning is "female activity. The manner of going to places that are not clear [for such acts] and so forth is *itthākappa*.
According to another method: the female organ is the *itthiliṅga* (female characteristic). The female sign is the intention for sexual intercourse.
The manner of going to places that are not clear, sitting, eating, consuming food, and so forth, is *itthikutta*. The female physical form is *itthākappa*.

And although these female signs and so forth arise through their respective conditions such as karma, they generally arise in a continuum accompanied by the female faculty (*itthindriya*) assuming those particular forms;
thus, taking the female faculty to be their cause, it is said: "It has the manifestation of being the cause for female signs, characteristics, postures, and deportment."
Furthermore, the status of these as faculties (*indriyatā*) is stated on account of their predominance (*adhipatibhāva*), which is designated as their causal state (*kāraṇabhāva*),

specifically regarding the female sex-mark (*itthiliṅga*) and so forth; for within the continuum (*santāna*) conjoined with the faculties, the material conditions for the appearance of the female sex-mark and so forth do not arise otherwise,
and because the apprehension of "woman" occurs due to those material phenomena being its conditions.
However, because within the group of nine derived material phenomena (*bhāvadasaka*), the femininity faculty (*itthindriya*) is neither the producer,

nor the sustainer, nor the supporter of those material phenomena, nor of other groups of material phenomena, it is therefore not stated in the Canon as a "faculty-presence-non-disappearance condition" (*indriya-atthi-avigata-paccaya*) for all the material phenomena in that group— as the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is— or for the material phenomena of other groups— as nutriment (*āhāra*) is. This is because...

Furthermore, the gender marks and so forth are dependent on other conditions; therefore, even in material phenomena produced by the mind or by dead matter that resemble them, their particular shape is seen wherever its predominance exists.
This same method applies to the masculinity faculty as well. As for what is dissimilar in this case, it should be understood according to the method already stated.
Since these two do not arise together in a single continuum—"in whom the femininity faculty [exists]..."
Because of such statements as, "When [the life-faculty] arises, does the masculinity faculty arise for that person?
No," it should be understood that even for a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), only one [faculty] exists at a single moment.

To show that the claim of those who say, "The nature of matter (*bhāvarūpa*) functions in only one part of the body," is also incorrect, he states: "Both of these... [etc. ...are indeed pervasive. If—
Thus, in order to dispel the apprehension that there might be a confusion [of locations] with the body-sensitivity (*kāyappasāda*), he says: "And not by the body-sensitivity," and so forth.

Its meaning is as follows: although, because it pervades the entire body, it does not incur the designation "located in a place where the body-sensitivity is absent," nevertheless, because its physical basis (*nissaya*) is distinct from that [of the body-sensitivity], it also does not incur the designation "located in a place where [the body-sensitivity] is located."

And this is precisely the non-figurative (nippariyāya) explanation here. By the phrase “like visible form, taste, and so forth,” he shows that even when they share a common basis (*nissaya*), there is no confusion among mental phenomena (*nāma*) because their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) differ;
how much more so, then, when their bases and intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*) are distinct? 439.

“The characteristic of maintaining co-nascent material phenomena” means the characteristic of maintaining those material phenomena that have arisen together with itself. This refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

Because they are exclusively born of kamma, the fact that even those [material phenomena] which must be maintained are themselves born of kamma is established by the very mention of "conascent" (*sahaja*); therefore, the term "born of kamma" (*kammaja*) was not included.

Although material phenomena born of kamma last for only their own respective moment, they are "maintainers" (*anupālaka*) insofar as they serve as the cause for the continued occurrence of that [body];
thus, their characteristic is the maintenance of conascent material phenomena. For it is not the case that kamma alone can be the cause for the persistence of those things born of kamma.

It is worthy [of the name], just as food is for the things born of food and so forth. Why? Because of its non-existence at that very moment. "Of them" means of the co-nascent material phenomena (*sahajarūpa*).
"Causing to proceed" means maintaining. "Establishing" means being the cause of their persistence.

Its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) is those elements (*bhūta*) which are to be maintained and caused to proceed by way of its own preservation; thus it is the "proximate cause of the elements to be maintained. "In the sense of the characteristic of preservation, etc. means...

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes the function of maintaining (*pavattanarasa*) and so forth. "Only at the moment of existence" means only at the moment when those things to be maintained exist.
If there were nothing to be maintained, such as a lotus and so on, what would water maintain?

If the persistence of things born of karma does not occur without a cause for persistence, one asks: "What is the cause for the persistence of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*)? To this he says: "Of its own accord," and so forth. If the duration of things born of karma...
Since it is bound to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), why does it not persist at all times? To this he says, "Not from destruction," and so forth.
This is because it accomplishes the respective functions such as preservation. And that accomplishment is due to its being a condition for the specific state of being alive.

For materiality bound to a faculty differs from the materiality of the dead; and among those [types of matter], that which is born of karma (*kammaja*) and that which follows upon it—such as that produced by temperature (*utusamutthāna*) and so on—[are distinguished].

There is a distinction based on the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*); it should be understood that the life-faculty is the cause not only for momentary duration, but also for the non-interruption of the continuity [of existence].
Otherwise, death due to the exhaustion of the lifespan would not be possible.
440. How is it to be understood that the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is the characteristic support for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)?

From scripture (*āgama*) and from reasoning (*yutti*). The scripture is as follows: "That material form depending upon which the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) proceed, that material form is a condition for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the states associated with them, by way of the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*)," and so forth.
If this is so, why is it not stated in the *Rūpakaṇḍa* (the Section on Matter)? The reason for its non-mention there is as follows: [text continues]

There is another reason. What is it? It is the difference in the teaching. For while visual consciousness and the others have the eye and so forth as their bases exclusively, mental consciousness does not have the heart-basis as its base exclusively.
And it is on account of this dependence that the teaching regarding the number of bases and so forth proceeds, such as:
"There is material form that is the base for visual consciousness; there is material form that is not the base for visual consciousness," and so on.

Furthermore, since that [heart-base] is exclusively dependent upon the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), even when pairs such as "There is matter that is the base for mind-consciousness" and so forth are stated, there cannot possibly arise corresponding pairs of objects (*ārammaṇa*) and so on.
For it is not possible to say: "There is matter that is the object of mind-consciousness; there is matter that is not the object of mind-consciousness."
If the pairs of bases and objects were of different destinies, the teaching would not be of a single flavor;
and it is the Teacher’s intention here to teach a teaching of a single flavor. Therefore, the heart-base was not mentioned there; it should not be understood that it is because it cannot be found.
The logical reasoning (yutti) should be understood as follows: in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), the two elements have as their support derived matter that is produced (nipphanna).

In this context, since the sense-base of visible form and so forth, as well as nutritive essence, are seen to function even outside what is bound to the faculties, their status as supports for those faculties is not tenable.
Furthermore, since the female and male faculties are seen within a continuum that lacks both of them—namely, the two [sexual] elements—their status as supports is not tenable.
And since the life-faculty has other functions, its status as a support is also not tenable.
Thus, by way of elimination (*pārisesato*), it is understood that the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) is their support (*nissaya*).

For it can be said that the two elements have as their support the accomplished derived matter (*nipphanna-upādāyarūpa*), because in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*) their mode of occurrence is bound up with matter.

Indeed, whatever has a mode of occurrence bound up with matter is seen to have accomplished derived matter as its support, just as in the case of "the eye-consciousness element. [This applies] "in the five-aggregate existence."

And this qualification is made by way of the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). However, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) does not exist at all in the four-constituent existence (*catuvokārabhava*).

[Objection: But would this not result in a contradictory reason (*viruddho hetu*), since it is established by way of its dependence on a faculty (*indriya*) as well? [Response: No, because it is not contradicted by what is observed (*diṭṭhabādhanato*).
For it is observed that, just as in the case of eye-consciousness, the two elements do not conform to the dullness, sharpness, and so forth of their physical bases (*vatthu*).

For in the text, its status as a faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya) is not stated; therefore, its status as a faculty-support (indriya-nissaya)—which consists in conformity with that [faculty]—is contradicted.
Let it be granted that the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is the support for the two elements and for derived matter (upādāyarūpa);

however, how is it known that this [base] is produced by kamma (kamma-samutthāna), has a specific function, and resides precisely in the region of the heart? It is said: because it is a physical entity that serves as a base (vatthurūpa).
Like the eye, which is produced by kamma, it likewise has a specific function; the meaning is that it is the "basis-materiality" (*vatthurūpa*) because it serves as the support for consciousness.
It is understood that this [heart-base] is established therein because the heart becomes exhausted when one applies the mind with earnestness, attends with full attention, and thinks about something.
"Of those very elements" refers specifically to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
It is "manifestation as carrying" (*ubbahanapaccupaṭṭhāna*) because, by virtue of its state of dependence, it stands ready as if carrying [the body] upward after having lifted it.
The rest is exactly according to the method explained below.

441. Those things of which "forward movement" (*abhikkama*) is the first are "forward movement and so forth" (*abhikkamādi*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), backward movement, bending, stretching, lifting up, lowering down, and so on are included.

All activity is encompassed. That which has as its source the consciousness that initiates those actions such as approaching and so forth is "originated by the consciousness that initiates approaching and so forth";

this refers to the air element (*vāyodhātu*). Showing that the specific mode of form which serves as the cooperative cause for the functions of the co-nascent material body—namely, stiffening, supporting, and moving—is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*), he says: "Approaching and so forth... bodily intimation."
But whose shape and movement is it? It belongs to the mind-born great elements that have a predominance of the air element.

What is that capacity? It is their being mind-born and their being derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). Alternatively, it should be connected thus: "the shape and movement of the air element is co-nascent... [etc. ...a condition.
If this is so, then the status of intimation (*viññatti*) as derived matter would not be tenable; for it is not...
Derived matter has a single primary element as its support. For it is said, "derived matter of the four great elements";
this is not a fault, because a transformation belonging to the four occurs even for one among them, like property held in common by four.
And because the aggregate (kalāpa) has the air element in excess, the designation "of the air element" is not contradictory. Such is the state of being in excess.
And it is by way of its capacity, not by way of its measure; otherwise, its existence as an inseparable entity would not be tenable. Some say it is [the capacity] of the air element alone.
According to their view, it is difficult to establish that intimation (viññatti) is derived matter (upādāyarūpa), for the modification of one thing cannot belong to four.
However, this [intimation], immediately after the perception of the color of the quivering [body] during the movement of the hand and so forth, is not perceived by an interval...
It is apprehended by the impulsion of the mind-door (*manodvāra-javana*). There is some modification distinct from the mere appearance of quivering.
And how is it known that its apprehension occurs immediately after the apprehension of that [quivering]? It is because of the apprehension of the intention (*adhippāya*).

For the apprehension of an intention—such as "I think he is making this"—is not observed in cases like the swaying of trees, which are devoid of the modifications of intimation (*viññatti*), whereas it is observed in cases such as the movement of the hand.
However, it has been seen. Therefore, it is understood that there exists some modification distinct from the appearance of quivering which indicates the intention (*adhippāya*).
And a cause that indicates does not indicate the object to be indicated merely by its existence; rather, it indicates only when it has itself been apprehended.
Thus, the apprehension of the modification is also understood through inference immediately following the apprehension of the appearance. For they say thus:
“Sounds that have not attained the status of being objects do not convey meaning at all;
it is not from their mere existence that they reveal meanings when they are not known.

If the apprehension of a modification alone were the cause for the apprehension of intention, why would there be an apprehension of intention in the case of those for whom no linguistic convention has been grasped?

Is it not so? It should be understood that not only the apprehension of modification (*vikāra*) is the cause for the apprehension of intention (*adhippāya*), but rather the apprehension of a previously established relationship (*sambandha*) is also its decisive support (*upanissaya*).

It has been stated that stiffening, supporting, and moving occur through the air element (*vāyodhātu*) accompanied by informative modification (*viññatti-vikāra*). Do all air elements perform all those functions? This is not so.

For the air element produced by the seventh impulsion, having received the supporting condition from the air elements produced by the preceding impulsions, causes the mind-born materiality to move by acting as the cause for its arising in a different location; the others do not.

However, the others assist it by performing mere stabilization and maintenance. "Movement" is simply arising in a different location; thus, the status of the agent is attributed to the sign (the cause).
It should be understood as "superimposed. Otherwise, the insentience (*abyāpāratā*) and momentariness (*khaṇikatā*) of phenomena would not be possible.
Here, the commentary provides the illustration of a cart that must be pulled by seven oxen.

However, when the mind-born materiality (*cittaja-rūpa*) moves, the temperature-born, karma-born, and nutriment-born materiality (*utu-kamma-āhāra-ja-rūpa*) also moves because of its connection with it, like a dry lump of cow dung thrown into the current of a river.
Because it is stated that the apprehension of intimation (*viññatti*) occurs immediately after the apprehension of the appearance of movement.

Are only those wind elements (*vāyodhātu*) that cause motion accompanied by the transformation of intimation? This is not so; it should be understood that even those wind elements produced at the first impulsion (*pathamajavana*) and so forth—which are unable to move [the body] in that way, but merely perform the functions of stiffening and supporting—are indeed accompanied by the transformation of intimation. By which...

This [being] desires to initiate the forward movement and so forth in that particular direction, because there is a manifestation directed toward it. For intimation (*viññatti*) is a manifestation concomitant with intention.
And by establishing it thus, the statement that even the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) originates intimation is well-founded.
This is because the intention of the possessor of that [consciousness] is understood by way of grasping the aforementioned manifestation.
It is said: “Its function is to manifest intention.

Because it is a modification of the air element (vāyodhātu) which serves as the cause for the movement of the body, intimation (viññatti) is described, in a figurative sense, as having the manifestation of being the cause of bodily movement as its proximate cause.
And it is said that its proximate cause is the air element originated by consciousness because of the predominance of the air element’s functional activity.

The connection is as follows: because it is the cause for making known one’s intention by means of bodily movement—that is, by means of bodily movement acting as the instrument—it is called "bodily intimation" (*kāyaviññatti*). This is the meaning here: it intimates, thus it is "intimation" (*viññatti*).
What does it intimate? Intention. By what means? By the body. Of what kind? By that which is moving. In the second method...
But that which is made known by the body as described above is bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). The rest is exactly according to the method already stated.
A particularity of speech capable of making the meaning understood is vocal expression (*vacībhedo*); by this term, one excludes the sounds of wind, forest trees, rivers, and so forth.
Its originating cause is the consciousness that brings it about; thus, it is "originated by the consciousness that brings about vocal expression" (*vacībhedappavattakacittasamuṭṭhānā*).

The earth element (*pathavīdhātu*). Showing that the specific mode of form which serves as the cooperative cause for the function known as "striking"—which is the basis for the production of syllables within that [earth element] reckoned as appropriated—is called "vocal intimation" (*vacīviññatti*), he says: "Vocal bhedana... vocal intimation.
Now, the question "Of what, then, is the modification of form? and so forth, is to be understood in the same manner as was stated regarding bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*). This...

However, there is this distinction: just as it was stated there, "immediately after the apprehension of the appearance of vibration," so here it should be applied as "immediately after hearing the sound being heard.
Furthermore, because of the absence of stiffening (*thambhana*) and the other [preliminary stages] here, the method beginning with "arisen from the seventh impulsion" is not applicable.
For the sound arises together with the striking (*ghaṭṭana*), and that striking is indeed found even in the first impulsion and those that follow.
Impact (*ghaṭṭana*) is the mutual arising of material groups in closer proximity due to conditions;

motion (*calana*) is the successive arising of even a single [group] in different locations—this is the distinction between them. And just as motion is the function of the air element, so too is impact that of the earth element.
For this very reason it was said: "The earth element is the condition for the impact of what is clung-to."

The rest is exactly as previously stated. The passage beginning with “Just as” (*yathā hi*) and so forth clarifies how bodily and vocal intimation (*kāyavacī-viññatti*) are to be apprehended by means of inference.

For instance, having seen forms such as a cow’s head and so on that have been hoisted up and bound, one apprehends—via the mental-door process (*manodvāra-vīthi*) which occurs immediately thereafter and whose internal sequence is not consciously perceived—the mode of recognition of the water-accompanying characteristics of the cow’s head and so on, and thereby apprehends the water.

Thus, having grasped the sounds of the phonemes as they are articulated with such vibration, there occurs a grasping of the modification accompanied by intention, through the mental-door process (manodvāra-vīthi) that follows immediately thereafter—though its interval is imperceptible—and which is supported by the acquisition of the previously established relationship. 442.
It delimits visible forms, or it is itself delimited by them, or it is merely the delimitation of visible forms.
The delimitation of matter; that is its characteristic, thus it is "characterized by the delimitation of matter.
For this space element acts as if it were delimiting each respective cluster of matter. Therefore he said: "Its function is to manifest the boundaries of matter.
But in terms of its actual meaning, since it is apprehended merely as the delimitation of matter, it is therefore said: "It is manifested as the boundary of matter."
In whatever aggregate there is a delimitation of the primary elements, that [delimitation] has the state of being untouched by those very [elements] as its manifestation.

For even though the primary elements of one aggregate are touched by the primary elements of another aggregate, that which constitutes the delimitation—namely, "space is the limit of form consisting in the distinctness from each respective element"—is indeed untouched by those [elements].
Otherwise, there would be no such thing as delimitation.
Because those primary elements (mahābhūta) have attained a state of pervasion. Non-pervasion, indeed, is non-contact. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"It is not contacted by the four great elements. Or else, it is manifested as having the nature of cavities and apertures by way of the ear-cavity, the mouth-opening, and so forth.
It is stated that the delimitation of those material phenomena is obtained precisely there, by way of their state of being delimited.

“Having delimited form as its proximate cause. By the phrase “by which [it is] delimited,” etc., he shows that the space element is the cause for the non-confusion of various groups (kalāpa) with other groups. 443.
Non-sluggishness means lack of heaviness. Dispelling means distracting or removing; this is the meaning. Non-stiffness means...
Non-rigidity (*akathinatā*). It is the state of being non-opposed in all activities precisely because of one’s own pliancy (*mudubhāva*). For that which is pliant is not obstructed by anything.

Regarding the three instances [of the prefix *a-*], some say that the negative particle (*a-*) signifies the arising of the opposites of heaviness and so forth, as it is the opposite of the causes such as sluggishness (*dandhatā*).

Others, however, say it is used in the sense of "negating the existence" (*sattāpaṭisedhe*). It is the state of being wieldy (*kammaññabhāva*), characterized by suitability for the activities to be performed with the body.
"Of this" means its characteristic is the state of being wieldy (*kammaññabhāva*) conducive to bodily activity.
Since "unwieldy" is called "weak," wieldiness is said to be manifested as the state of non-weakness.
Because lightness and the others do not abandon one another, their diversity is difficult to discern; thus, they are described by means of their respective specific modifications.

In order to demonstrate that variety, it is said: "Even though this is so. Alternatively, *dhātukkhobha* refers to the agitation of wind, bile, and phlegm, or the state of transformation of the elements such as taste (*rasa*).
Although described in two ways, in meaning it should be understood as the transformation of the elements themselves, such as the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) and the rest.
The opposing conditions consist of unsuitable climate, nutriment, and lack of mental composure. And these [conditions] lead to their respective transformations.
They are described as such because they function as specific conditions; however, without distinction, all are conditions for all.

For they do not abandon one another, possessing mastery over them—such as in the case of supernormal powers (*iddhi*) or polishing—as in the manner of softening. Here, the mention of well-polished leather, refined gold, or the taking up [of materials] is merely an illustration of a form similar to softness and adaptability;
it is not what is intended here, because [the elements] actually possess both softness and adaptability.
For lightness and the other [qualities] do not occur in a material continuity that is not bound up with the sense faculties (*indriya*).

Nor do they exist even in a material existence (*rūpa-bhava*) bound up with the sense faculties, because of the absence of disturbances of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*) such as rigidity and so forth. Some say:

"When such a disturbance of the elements exists, there ought to be lightness and the others, which are produced by conditions opposed to it. That is not a valid reason. For the arising of a phenomenon that opposes something does not depend on the presence of an opposing factor that must be pacified.

If that were so, there would be an absolute absence of bodily lightness (*kāyalahutā*) and the other [characteristics] in the arising of functional consciousnesses (*kiriyacitta*) accompanied by roots.

Why, then, do lightness and the others not exist in material phenomena born of kamma (*kammajarūpa*)? Because they depend upon present conditions; otherwise, lightness and the others would have to exist at all times.
444. *Ācaya* means an accumulation, or a slight accumulation; it is an accumulation as if from here and there, coming according to its respective conditions.

Or, "accumulation" (ācaya) refers to both [growth and decay]; taking those two together, that which has accumulation as its characteristic is "characterized by accumulation" (ācayalakkhaṇo). The accumulation of matter (rūpa) is its first arising and its increase;
this is because the prefix *upa-* indicates the sense of "first" or "initial," as seen in such expressions as "prepared beforehand" (*upa-ññatta*) or "sprinkled beforehand" (*upa-sitta*).
"From the prior limit" (*pubbantato*) means from the initial portion, that is to say, from the state of being future. Regarding material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) as they are arising...
Arising is like causing something to emerge from the future moment; thus it is said to have "the function of making emerge.
Likewise, because it is grasped as if presenting [them] by saying, "These are material phenomena," it is said to have "the manifestation of presenting.
The state of having the manifestation of fullness should be understood by way of this meaning: "Accumulation is the piling up on top. "The characteristic of occurrence" refers to material phenomena.
It should be characterized as "occurring. Its function is to connect continuously, meaning its activity is to bind [phenomena] one after another in succession.
For that very reason, because it is to be grasped by way of non-interruption, its manifestation is non-interruption.
"Both" refers to both accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*). "Of birth-form alone" is a designation for the arising of material form itself.

If this is so, why was it taught by way of analysis? He says: "Because of the diversity of modes" (*ākāranānattato*). The meaning is: because of the difference in the modes of occurrence of the form of birth (*jātirūpa*).
The reason for teaching by way of analysis according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*) will be made clear further on. But how is this to be understood:

that the distinction of the form of birth is due to the diversity of its modes of occurrence, and not due to a difference in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)? [The answer is: "From the exposition" (*niddesato*).

In order to show this, he says, "But because... and so forth. Therein, "of the bases" (*āyatanānaṃ*) refers to those which, because they are the primary accumulation among the eleven and a half material bases (*rūpāyatana*), are called "accumulation" (*ācaya*).
That very same thing is "growth" (*upacaya*), taking the prefix *upa-* to mean "first" because it is the state of initial arising.
However, that which is "growth" (*upacaya*) by way of being an accumulation on top of those very things as they arise is "continuity" (*santati*), by virtue of its uninterrupted succession.

Because it is a state of arising (*uppattibhāva*). Alternatively, that arising which is characterized by the initial state of the accumulation (*ācaya*) of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is "accumulation" (*upacaya*), because there is a further heaping up (*cayatta*) of those very things as they arise therein; the meaning is "growth. Accumulation is arising characterized by the state of growth;
that itself is "continuity" (*santati*) because it is a state of arising in the form of a continuous succession. Therefore, he said: "In the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) also," and so forth.
In this regard, what is stated by the phrase "that which is the accumulation (*ācaya*) of the sense-bases (*āyatana*)" and so forth? What kind of meaning is expressed by this exposition?

The accumulation is expressed by means of the sense-bases. For accumulation, increase (*upacaya*), and continuity (*santati*) are indeed called "accumulation" insofar as they constitute the state of being produced;

thus, because accumulation and the others are manifested through the sense-bases, the accumulation is expressed by them. This is precisely by way of the expression "the accumulation of the sense-bases," and so on.
"Sense bases (āyatana) are of a nature to accumulate and are subject to arising"—thus, by means of accumulation, the sense base is described as having that very nature.
For arising is the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), not a "material form" (rūpa-rūpa).

The ripening of material form is the agedness of material phenomena. "Having the function of bringing near" means having the task of bringing about dissolution. "Even when their individual essence (sabhāva) has not departed..."

Even though the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) characterized by hardness and so forth has not disappeared. For aging occurs at the moment of stability, and yet at that time the phenomenon does not abandon its intrinsic nature.
The state of newness is the stage of arising; because it is grasped through the absence of that [newness], it is said: "having the manifestation of the departure from the state of newness.
The phrase "of immaterial phenomena" is stated because their aging is very well concealed. This applies to material phenomena as well.

For momentary aging (*khaṇika-jarā*) is indeed concealed, which is also called "uninterrupted aging" (*avīci-jarā*). "This transformation" refers to the transformations such as brokenness (*khaṇḍicca*) and so forth;

for that [transformation] is not found among formless phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*). It should be connected thus: even for that which is called uninterrupted aging, this [visible] transformation does not exist.
There is no interval (*vīci*) in this aging, hence it is "uninterrupted aging" (*avīci-jarā*); the meaning is that because of its perpetual state, the intervening aging is difficult to discern.
They are characterized by "breaking up" on all sides in every way; thus, they have the characteristic of disintegration (*paribheda-lakkhaṇa*). "Permanent" (*nicca*) means stable.

However, because matter is subject to momentary dissolution, it is "impermanent" (*anicca*) due to that breaking up which renders it not permanent. The state of being impermanent is "impermanence" (*aniccatā*).
Furthermore, it is said that this [impermanence] occurs because matter, having reached the stage of stability, seems to sink down through its nature of destruction.

“Having the nature of decaying”: because it is apprehended precisely through the mode of exhaustion and passing away due to the state of dissolution of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), it is therefore said to be “manifested as exhaustion and passing away. 445.

“The characteristic of nutritive essence (*ojā*): here, the essence of the nutrient that follows throughout every limb and member is that which provides support and strength, residing in the primary elements (*bhūta*).

The specific quality is nutritive essence (*ojā*). It is called "edible" (*kabaḷīkāro*) because it is made into mouthfuls. It is called "nutriment" (*āhāro*) because it is taken in; the meaning is that it is swallowed after being made into mouthfuls.
This, however, was stated to show that this nutritive essence has a physical basis. Only by obtaining external nutriment as a condition does internal nutriment produce matter;
and since it brings that matter into being, it is called "nutriment. Therefore, he said: "Its function is the bringing of matter."
For that very reason, by producing the eightfold material qualities beginning with nutritive essence (*ojā*), its manifestation is the supporting of this body.

Since the function of nutritive essence in taking up material food depends on external factors, it is said to have "the object to be taken up as its proximate cause" (*āharitabbavatthupadaṭṭhāna*). 446. Regarding "material quality of strength" and so forth:
there is what is called strength in this body, there is what is called origination, and there is what is called disease.
There is birth, because of the statement, “birth, being born”; since it cannot exist without those four great elements, the intention is that it must be a derived form (upādāyarūpa).
“Of some” refers to the residents of Abhayagiri. “Rejected”:
here the rejection should be understood as follows—torpor is not material form at all, because it is taught among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
For that which is taught among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is not material form (*rūpa*), just as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is not.
However, it might be argued that torpor (*middha*) is of two kinds: material and immaterial. In that case, is it the immaterial kind that is taught among the hindrances as "not material form"?
That is not so, because there is no qualifying statement. Torpor has not been specifically distinguished and taught among the hindrances; therefore, [the reference] is to torpor...
Even by postulating a twofold nature [of middha], it is not possible to negate its status as an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*). For one can indeed say:
"That middha which was postulated as distinct from the immaterial [hindrances] is also an hindrance because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is middha, just like the other middha.
If it is asked, "Let it be an hindrance; what is the contradiction? [the answer is: An hindrance must be abandoned. Having abandoned the five hindrances...
“Surely you are a sage, a perfectly awakened one; there are no hindrances in you,” according to these words. Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is not to be abandoned:

“Which phenomena are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation? They are: the wholesome in the four planes, the resultants in the four planes, the functional-undetermined in the three planes, as well as form and Nibbāna. These phenomena are neither to be abandoned by vision... [and so forth].
Because of the statement, "It is not to be abandoned by cultivation.

Nor is the abandonment of defilements that have that [matter] as their object intended here, because—as in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it"—the abandonment of sensual desire and so forth in that manner is not what is intended.
Therefore, torpor is not matter. If you do not accept that torpor has the nature of matter, [then...]

How can there be sleep for the Blessed One? For if it is asked why torpor (*middha*) is called "sleep" (*niddā*)—since it is analyzed in the *Vibhaṅga* as "that which causes one to fall into sleep" and so forth—it is because torpor is not itself sleep;
rather, it is analyzed as "sleep" due to its being the cause of sleep, just as [the term] "feminine gender" and so forth are used.
Even so, since the Blessed One lacks torpor, which is the cause of sleep, how can there be sleep for the Blessed One? [The answer is: Sleep [occurs] for the Blessed One due to an ailment of the body.
Not by drowsiness. And it cannot be said that such [drowsiness] does not exist, because of the statement: "My back aches; I shall stretch it.
Nor is there a restriction here that drowsiness alone is the cause of sleep; rather, the restriction is that sleep itself is the cause of drowsiness.
Therefore, there is another cause of sleep as well. What, then, is it? It is bodily illness. By this—
It is said: “The Blessed One had a bodily ailment of drowsiness (niddā), not of torpor (middha).
Furthermore, it cannot be said that the Blessed One was without drowsiness, because of the statement: “I recall, Aggivessana... [omission] ...that I slept during the day.
For this reason also, torpor is not material form, because of the mention of its association [with mental factors]. For it is said: “The hindrance of sloth and torpor...”
“By the hindrance of ignorance, it is both a hindrance and associated with a hindrance,” and so forth.

Nor can it be concluded here that [the object] exists according to its availability, because—just as in the case of the expressions “a pebble or a clod of earth” or “a school of fish moving or standing”—the state of being material form (*rūpa*) is not well-established. For if its state of being material form were established, then the condition of existing according to availability would be possible.
"One should apply [the analysis]": for this reason as well, matter is not [associated with] torpor, because it arises even in the formless realms (*ārūpya*).

And this has been stated in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the passage: "Dependent on a state that is a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), a state that is a hindrance arises, but not by way of the pre-existent condition (*purejāta-paccaya*)," namely:

"In the formless realm, dependent on the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), there arise the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*thina-middha-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of restlessness (*uddhacca-nīvaraṇa*), and the hindrance of ignorance (*avijjā-nīvaraṇa*)."
...arises,” and so on in detail. Therefore, that which is rejected in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*)—namely, that “torpor (*middha*) is not matter”—is indeed rightly rejected.
“In the others” refers to the material qualities such as strength (*bala-rūpa*) and so forth.
Even in the case of a disease originating from kamma, it is a disturbance of the elements (*dhātu-kkhobha*) produced by an incompatible condition (*visabhāga-paccaya*).

The proximate cause is even more so for the other [the immaterial]. And since that [cause] exists only during the moments of change, presence, and dissolution of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), it is said:
"The form of disease is indeed included by the inclusion of aging and impermanence.

It is also included by the inclusion of accumulation and continuity, because there is no arising of matter apart from those two. Furthermore, birth is nothing other than the state of being derived (*upādāvatthā*).

It does not exist at all. "Origin" (*sambhava*) is a specific mode of manifestation of the water element that serves as a condition for the ripening of the faculties in certain beings within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*);
therefore, it is said: "Materiality of origin is already included by the inclusion of the water element.

What is called "bodily strength" (*kāyabala*) is, in its actual meaning, a specific mode of manifestation of the air element, because it is the state of its expansion. Hence, it is called "vital strength" (*pāṇabala*).
They say so; therefore he says, "The nature of strength is indeed included by the inclusion of the air element.
But why is their negation performed out of order? It is because they do not exist separately; thus, it is done for the purpose of showing disregard due to their non-apprehensibility.

Alternatively, the negation of torpor was placed first because it is a "great question" (*mahāpañha*). Following that, it should be understood that the absence of the others is stated by way of reverse order.
The word "iti" (thus) should be connected with the phrase "twenty-eightfold"; that is to say, it is twenty-eightfold according to the sequence stated here.
Furthermore, its completeness should be understood as being exactly according to the method presented in the Pāḷi, while its lack of redundancy has already been demonstrated.
447. That by which a collection of associated states is led forward and established is a cause (*hetu*); in the sense of being a root, it refers to greed and the rest.
And because such a cause as non-greed and so forth does not exist, it is "without cause" (*nahetu*). It is "causeless" (*ahetuka*) because it has no cause;

the meaning is that it does not arise together with a cause, being the opposite of that which possesses a cause. Being precisely causeless due to its dissociation from a cause, it is "dissociated from cause" (*hetuvippayutta*).

For even though there is no difference in the nature of the phenomena (*dhamma*), a teaching in two parts occurs according to the needs of those to be trained, through a distinction in terminology; thus, it is expressed by way of the two terms.
This has been said. Because it exists dependent upon conditions, it is "with conditions" (*sappaccaya*).

It is "mundane" (*lokiya*) because it is joined to the world by its own conditions, or because it is known [in the world]. They flow up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) or up to the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*); thus they are "taints" (*āsava*).

That which is "with taints" (*sāsava*) means that which is to be clung to by the taints. By the word "etcetera," [the categories] "fettering" (*saṃyojanīya*) and "flood-producing" (*oghanīya*) are included.

The inclusion of such terms as "conducive to yoga," "conducive to the hindrances," "defiled," "clung to," "non-mental," "dissociated from mind," "not belonging to the fine-material sphere," "not belonging to the immaterial sphere," "not included [in the mundane]," "undetermined," "not leading to liberation," and "impermanent" should be understood in this way.

That wherein the conceit "I am" is established is the self (*atta*); it is the personal existence (*attabhāva*). Those things that function with reference to or directed toward that self are "internal" (*ajjhatta*).

"Phenomena bound to the faculties": among these, that which is internal consists of the eye and so forth. However, according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, "internal" (*ajjhattika*) means simply "internal" (*ajjhatta*);
this was said with reference to the meaning "it occurs in dependence upon the personal existence (*attabhāva*)," as in the expression "a Vinaya follower.
The remainder is twenty-three-fold. Regarding the phrase "because it is external to that":

It is stated [thus] because of the absence of internal characteristics. "By way of impact" means by way of the contact between that which possesses the object (the sense faculty) and the object itself.

The remainder consists of sixteen kinds. "Because of being contrary" means because it should not be grasped by way of impact. "Because of having a nature difficult to penetrate" means because its nature is hard to discern due to its subtlety.
"It is not near to knowledge" means it is distant. Thirteen [bases] end with the heart-base.

"By its own intrinsic nature (sabhāvena) alone" means that it should be grasped by discerning it through knowledge—such as hardness and so forth—by its own intrinsic nature, rather than by way of "the delimitation of matter," "the alteration of matter," or "the accumulation of matter.
The remaining tenfold [classification] is [to be understood] by its opposite nature, because it cannot be grasped by its own intrinsic nature.
This is because the ear and the other [senses], like the eye, possess a translucent intrinsic nature (pasannasabhāva).
Thus, showing that they serve as conditions for the apprehension of their respective objects, he said: "The eye-faculty and so forth... [the] sensitive matter.

"Because of being contrary" means because of having a nature opposed to them. "In the sense of predominance": here, first, the five beginning with the eye possess predominance over the five consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness, because those consciousnesses follow along with the keenness or dullness of the faculties; [likewise] of the two faculties, the female and the male...
In its own function, it [the life-faculty] maintains the co-nascent material phenomena. Both of these have already been explained above.
"Because of being grasped" means because of being seized. For that which is produced by kamma is, as it were, seized by kamma through the thought "This is my fruit," since it is not rejected.
448. "Of the triads beginning with 'visible' and 'kamma-born'" refers to the triad beginning with "visible" and the triads beginning with "kamma-born."
"Coarse" (*oḷārika*) refers to the twelve kinds of coarse material form (*rūpa*). "Material form" (*rūpa*) refers to the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).

"With visibility" (*sanidassana*) means together with demonstration (*nidassana*), which is defined as the state of being visible; "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) means together with opposition (*paṭigha*), which is defined as the state of being obstructive.
Thus, that which is both with visibility and with resistance is called "with visibility and with resistance. In this context, that which has the state of being visible...
It exists; that is "with visibility. The state of being the objective domain of eye-consciousness is precisely what constitutes the state of being visible.

Although this [quality] is not other than the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is stated as if it were something else—by way of distinguishing the sense-sphere of form from other phenomena—as "with visibility" (*sanidassana*), meaning together with visibility.
For among phenomena that have become unified through their commonality of being "phenomena" (*dhamma*), that specific distinction which effects differentiation is [here expressed].
Therefore, it is appropriate to employ the metaphorical designation (*upacara*) as if it were something else. For in this way, there arises an understanding of a specific meaning.

That which is the state of being turned toward one another—the mutual falling [upon each other]—of those things that have arrived through their own nature and through dependence, is the state of resistance (*paṭigha*).

By means of this, there occurs the arising of a modification in the eye and other sense-faculties when they encounter objects accompanied by other conditions for modification, such as mental activity (*byāpāra*).
The remaining elevenfold materiality is gross. For it is "non-demonstrable" because it lacks the quality of being visible; it is "with resistance" in the manner already stated;
and by the negation of both, it is "non-demonstrable and non-resistant. Regarding the phrase "born of kamma":

herein, there are nine kinds of materiality—namely, the eight faculties and the heart-base—which arise exclusively from kamma; and furthermore, among the nine kinds of materiality that arise from the four origins, that which is born of kamma.
They say that form is indeed ninefold; likewise, even the eighteenfold [form] is "born of kamma" (*kammaja*) because it arises from kamma.
For whatever has been born, is being born, or will be born—all that is called "born of kamma," just as [the term] "milk" is used [to refer to all states of milk].

"Born of other conditions than that" refers to what is born from conditions other than kamma, namely, those born of temperature (*utu*), mind (*citta*), and nutriment (*āhāra*). "Not born from anything at all" refers to...

He speaks of characteristic matter (*lakkhaṇarūpa*). The two types of intimation, sound, the space element, and the triad of lightness and so forth—these fifteen kinds of matter are mind-born (*cittaja*).
The space element, the triad of lightness and so forth, and the nutrition-born inseparable material phenomena—these twelve kinds of matter are nutriment-born (*āhāraja*). Herein, sound...

Having included the thirteenfold materiality arisen from temperature (utu) and born of temperature (utuja), the remainder should be understood according to the method already explained under "born of kamma" (*kammaja*).
The term "tetrad" (*catukka*) should be applied separately as follows: by way of the tetrad beginning with "seen" (*diṭṭha*), etc.;

by way of the tetrad beginning with "visible form" (*rūpa*) and "form" (*rūpa*), etc.; and by way of the tetrad beginning with "base" (*vatthu*), etc. Namely: that visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) which one has seen, which one sees, which one will see, and which one might see;
All that is called "seen" because it does not transcend the nature of what is seen, just as [the term] "milk" [is used for what has been milked]. This same method applies to the others as well.
"Being the object of seeing" means being cognizable by eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*). "Being the object of hearing" means being cognizable by ear-consciousness (*sota-viññāṇa*).
"The triad of odors, tastes, and tangibles" refers to this triad: odor, taste, and tangible. "Touched" (*muta*) means having touched.
Because it is to be grasped by touching. Therefore he said: "Because it is the object of the faculty that grasps what is present.
What is this so-called "tangible" (phoṭṭhabba)? It is the triad of the earth, fire, and air elements. But why is the water element not included here?
Is it not the case that coolness is grasped through touch, and that is the water element? True, it is grasped, but it is not the water element.
What is it then? It is simply the fire element (*tejodhātu*). For when the state of heat is weak, there arises the perception of cold. Indeed, there is no such quality as "cold" existing in itself;
rather, it is merely a misconception of coldness due to the weakness of the state of heat.

If one asks how this is to be known, it is because the perception of cold is unstable, just as [the perception of] the further shore and the near shore [is unstable]. For instance, when people are standing in the sun during the hot season...
To those who have entered the shade, there is a perception of cold; yet to those who have emerged from within the earth’s womb right there, there is a perception of heat.
For if coldness were the water element, it would be perceived together with the state of heat within a single group (kalāpa);
however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, it is understood that coldness is not the water element. And this [demonstrates] the inseparable functioning of the primary elements (bhūta).

This is the superior argument for those who desire it; and even for those who do not desire it, this remains the superior argument because the commonality of function among the four elements has been established by showing their activity within a single group (kalāpa).
Furthermore, for those who claim that "the characteristic of the air element is coldness," this very same argument serves as the rebuttal.
For if the air element were coldness, then [there would be no heat] in a single group due to its state of heat.
If coldness were co-existent [with the air element], it would be perceived; yet it is not perceived. Therefore, it is understood that the air element is not coldness itself.
As for those who hold the view that the water element is fluidity and that this is apprehended by touch, they should be told:
"The venerable ones' assertion that even the state of fluidity is touched is merely a matter of overestimation, like [the notion of] shape. For this has been said by the ancients:
“Touching the three elements that coexist with the liquid element, this world conceives the thought: ‘I am touching liquidity.
Just as one grasps shape by means of the mind while touching the elements, so too does one perceive.”
‘I touch it directly’—in this way, fluidity is to be known.
“The rest” refers to the twenty-one kinds of material phenomena remaining after setting aside the seven kinds of material phenomena already mentioned, such as visible form and so forth.
“Of consciousness alone” means of mental consciousness alone. By this restriction, [it is shown that] even the sense-base of visible form and the others are cognizable by mental consciousness.
"Because there is no fixed rule [regarding the knower], it is not of the nature of a cognizer"—this shows the absence of confusion.
Furthermore, "derived matter" (*nipphanna-rūpa*) here is called "matter-matter" (*rūpa-rūpa*);

that which among the twenty-eight kinds of matter is described as "derived," that alone is "matter" because it possesses the characteristic of matter. Matter is "that which is subject to change" (*ruppana*); since this [derived matter] has that [characteristic], it is matter.
Just as [one says] "the enemy" (*ari-sasa*), or as one says "blue cloth" due to its connection with the quality of blue;

so too, this term *rūpa* occurs by conventional usage even when it does not possess that intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is stated as "matter-matter" (*rūpa-rūpa*) by distinguishing it with another word for matter, just as in the cases of "sesame oil" or "suffering-suffering.
The meaning is: matter is that which has the intrinsic nature of being affected (*ruppana*). If this is so, [what of] the space-element and so forth?
How is it "matter" (*rūpa*)? Because it possesses the state of being delimited and subject to change—characteristics belonging to produced matter—it is called simply "matter.
It is called a "base" (*vatthu*) because the mind and mental factors dwell there and proceed therein; it is the support for the mind and its associated states.

Form. That, moreover, is sixfold. Among these, heart-form is merely a *vatthu* (base) because it serves as the support for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
It is not a *dvāra* (door), unlike the eye and other [senses] which are supports for others.

For just as the eye and so forth serve as doors for the occurrence of receiving and the other [mental processes], the heart-base does not do so. Therefore it is said: "But that which here is heart-form..."

That [base] is the object, not the door. The two types of intimation (viññatti) are doors because they function as the doors for kamma; they are not bases because there is no arising of consciousness dependent upon them.

The sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa) is both a base—for eye-consciousness and so forth that are dependent on themselves—and a door—for the receiving consciousness and so forth that are dependent on something else.
The remaining twenty-one kinds of materiality are the opposite of what has been stated.
Neither a site nor a door. 450.
"Born from one" (*ekaja*) means born from one [condition] alone. But is it not the case that there is no arising of a dependently arisen phenomenon from a single condition?
True, there is not; however, the intended meaning here is "from one among the conditions that produce matter. For the arising of matter [does not occur]...
It depends on a condition other than that which produces material form. The same method applies to the cases of "born from eggs" and so forth.
"Of these" means by way of these various classifications. "Born of karma alone" means born solely from karma. The same method applies here to "born of mind alone.
"Born of mind and temperature" means born at times from the mind and at times from temperature; thus it is born from both mind and temperature.
And that which is born [from the heart-base] should be seen as such. That "twice-born" means it is born from two. The same method applies to both [the following cases] hereafter.

Regarding the phrase "only the sound-base": some say that the sound-base born of mind is exclusively with intimation; however, the Ancients maintain that there is also non-intimated sound, namely the sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought (*vitakka-vipphāra*).

Relying on the statement in the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*) that "the sound produced by the diffusion of thought is not cognizable by the ear," one must accept the arising of mind-originated sound even without manifest intimation (*viññatti*).

For manifest intimation—referred to in the phrase "manifest intimations of body and speech"—does not arise together with a sound that is not cognizable by the ear; such being the case, [mind-originated sound arises independently].
There must also be a set of nine sounds produced by the mind (*cittaja*).
However, this position was rejected by the compilers [of the commentaries], who considered it a direct contradiction to say, "there is sound, yet it is not cognizable by the ear.

Others, however, do not reject the position of the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* (Great Commentary) but instead explain its intended meaning. How so? "The movement of the tongue, palate, and so forth, is originated by applied thought (*vitakkasamuṭṭhita*)."
In the Sutta it is said: "Having heard with the divine ear the subtle sound coexistent with intimation (*viññatti*), he announces it";
and in the Paṭṭhāna, the status of gross sound as an object-condition for ear-consciousness is stated.

With this intention, it is said that the sound produced by the diffusion of applied thought (*vitakka*) is not cognizable by the ear-consciousness. That [sound] consists of four [elements]. "The remainder" refers to the inseparable material phenomena (*avinibbhogarūpa*).
It includes the space element.
As for characteristic-form (lakkhaṇarūpa), however, it is not born from anywhere;
that is, it is not born from any condition, nor is it born of itself, because there is an absolute absence of anything that is born by itself without conditions. How, then, is this to be understood?
Is it not the case that characteristic-form (*lakkhaṇarūpa*) is not born? Because it lacks characteristics.

For while the bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth, which possess arising, have characteristics such as birth (*jāti*), birth and the others do not have [such] characteristics in this way. Therefore, it should be understood that birth and the others are not born.
But could it be that birth and the others do have characteristics such as birth? That is not so; why? Because if that were the case...

Because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavaṭṭhāna*). For if birth and the rest possessed birth and so forth, then those [secondary births] would also possess birth and so forth, and those too would possess birth and so forth;
thus, an infinite regress would indeed follow. Therefore, it is well said: "Birth and the rest are not born. Hence he said:
"For there is no arising of arising; and for that which has already arisen, there is merely the maturation and dissolution."
"The other two" means aging and death.

Therein, by the phrase "there is no arising," he states that there is an absence of aging and death for that which has not arisen. By the mere apprehension of the thought, "If there is no arising, from where could aging and death come?
he also indicates the absence of arising for aging and death. If this is so, how can there be a statement regarding birth as being born from something?
He asks, "How? and says, "That which also... and so forth. Therein, "because it was seen at the moment of the efficacy of the function":

those mental states and so forth which are the productive conditions for material phenomena such as the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*), possess a specific moment characterized by their state of being a condition—namely, the moment when their activity toward the production of those [phenomena] has not yet ceased—at which time the visible-object base and other phenomena are arising.
This is stated with reference to the fact that phenomena are perceived by way of their state of transformation;

for the sake of those persons to be trained, the Pāḷi authorizes that birth arises from some condition, just as it does for the mind-originated [matter] and so forth in the case of intimation and the like.
This is the summarized meaning here: at the very moment when those conditioning phenomena by which material form and the rest would arise attain the state of being conditions, [birth occurs].
Since form and the other aggregates are perceived prior to that [moment of birth] and are not perceived after it, they are understood to arise from that;

in this way, birth (*jāti*) should also be understood. If, in this manner, the fact that birth arises from something is established in its direct sense (*nippariyāyato*), then why was it stated "by way of the individuals to be guided" (*veneyya-puggala-vasena*)?
This is not so, because [birth] is perceived as a modification (*vikāra-bhāva*) of the phenomenon (*dhamma*) currently arising.
For if birth were perceived as a phenomenon (*dhamma*) in its own right, its state of being born from something else would be primary;
however, it is not perceived in that way, but rather as a mode of transformation. Therefore it was said:
"by way of the individuals to be guided. At that time, it seems, such a thought arose in the minds of the listeners: "This birth is the source of all phenomena, and itself..."
"Just as for those who propound primordial nature (*pakati*), it is not born from anything—that is their 'primordial nature'";

in order to refute this false grasping of theirs, the Teacher taught by dividing [the process] into two—accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*)—and established that [aging-and-death] is born from some condition.
However, aging-and-death is not [taught as such] because it is not seen at the moment when the conditions (the phenomena) exercise their functional efficacy. If this is so, how...

Is it said that "aging-and-death is dependently arisen"? Because aging-and-death consist in the ripening and dissolution of dependently arisen phenomena, they occur when those [phenomena] exist, not when they do not. For what is unborn does not ripen nor does it dissolve;
therefore, with reference to birth as its condition, it is stated figuratively in the Suttas that "aging-and-death is dependently arisen."

However, as for the specific modes of occurrence of material phenomena during rebirth-linking and the course of existence— classified according to the various modes of birth (yoni) through conditions such as karma within the realms of sense-desire existence (kāmabhava) and so forth—
it should be understood that this will not be stated here, as it will be revealed later in the discussion on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
Thus ends the commentary on the introductory exposition of the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*).
**Commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregate of Consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*):** 451.
By means of the two phrases beginning with "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*), which indicate an exhaustive inclusion without remainder, the manifold variety of what is felt (*vedayita*) is shown.

When it is being explained, it indicates the meaning of "heap" (*rāsa*). That which has the characteristic of being experienced—the experiencing of the flavor of an object—is "that which has the characteristic of being felt" (*vedayitalakkhaṇa*).

The intended meaning is that all those classes of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) [are included]; or else, what was previously stated in the discussion on the aggregate of form (*rūpakkhandha*) should be brought forward and connected here by virtue of the context.
"Having made them into one" means all of them, distinguished by such divisions as past and so forth.
Having unified that through the intellect (*buddhi*), such is the arising of that which stands as a mass. Its characteristic is "perceiving" (*sañjānanalakkhaṇa*);

that is, it is that which has the characteristic of perceiving—the cognizing of an object distinguished as blue and so forth—by way of generating a perception (*saññā*) such as "blue," "yellow," "long," or "short.
It is the act of forming (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*), the exertion (*āyūhana*), the engagement in activity, and the application (*abhisandahana*).
Or rather, since volition (cetanā) is predominant in both cases, the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is thus described as having "the characteristic of forming" (*abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa*).

For indeed, when the Blessed One was analyzing the aggregate of formations in the *Suttantabhājanīya*, he explained it solely as volition, beginning with the words: "volition born of eye-contact," and so forth.
Just as a man measuring an object to be measured with a nāḷi-measure... [by which]...

It grasps the object by way of a mode distinguished from the mode of perceiving; since this act of cognizing—designated as the apprehension of the object—is its characteristic, it is "characterized by cognizing.

The other aggregates, such as feeling and so forth, are easy to distinguish from consciousness because they arise simultaneously with it and because they can be differentiated according to their own specific classes and types.
In order to support with a Sutta the meaning already stated as "having the characteristic of cognizing" (*vijānanalakkhaṇa*), the passage beginning with "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) was spoken.

To show that this—namely, the phenomenon possessing its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*)—is merely a process occurring according to conditions, it was stated as "having the characteristic of cognizing" by way of an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).
There is no so-called agent whatsoever apart from the intrinsic nature of phenomena; therefore, [it refers] to that very [nature].

To show its status as an agent, it is said, “it cognizes. That which is consciousness in the sense of cognizing is itself the mind (*citta*) in the sense of thinking and so forth, and the intellect (*mano*) in the sense of mentation;
