thus he makes it understood through its synonyms as well. To this extent, consciousness has been analyzed by way of its aggregates, its divisions, and its synonyms.
*Jāti* (birth) is so called because here similar forms arise even from dissimilar things; it is a common form.
Although this *jāti* is indeed manifold and of various kinds, the author, showing only that which is intended here, says: "Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Therein, it is wholesome in the sense of being wholesome (*kusala*). What is this so-called sense of being wholesome? It is the sense of health and the sense of blamelessness.
The sense of having a pleasant result (*sukha-vipāka-ṭṭha*). For wholesome (*kusala*) is also spoken of in the sense of health, as in such passages as, "Is it well with you, sir? and so forth.

It is also spoken of in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja-ṭṭha*), as in such passages as, "But what, venerable sir, is wholesome bodily conduct? That bodily conduct which, O Great King, is blameless," and so forth.
And it is also spoken of in the sense of having a pleasant result, as in such passages as, "Monks, it is because of undertaking wholesome states... and so forth.

For a wholesome state of consciousness (*kusalacitta*) is "healthy" (*aroga*), "faultless" (*anavajja*), and "of pleasant result" (*sukhavipāka*) because it is the opposite of the mental diseases such as lust (*rāga*) and the rest—which are by nature faulty—and because it ripens into a pleasant result. As for its etymological meaning:
it is called *kusala* because it shakes (*salati*), moves, and destroys blameworthy, evil states (*pāpadhamma*).
They are called *kusā* because they lie in a loathsome manner; that is, those of evil nature (*pāpadhammā*). One who mows (*lunāti*) or cuts these *kusa* grasses is "skilled" (*kusala*).

Alternatively, knowledge is called *kusa* because it thins out or diminishes what is loathsome; that which is to be reaped, grasped, or set in motion by means of that [knowledge] is "skillful" (*kusala*).
Or, just as *kusa* grass mows the area of the hand on both sides, so too does this [skillful state] [mow away defilements] by way of what has arisen and what has not yet arisen.
It reaps and cuts away the side of defilement belonging to both parts; therefore, it is *kusala* because it reaps like a sickle (*kusa*).
Alternatively, it is *kusala* because of its flowing toward (*salanato*) and warding off (*saṃvaraṇato*) base, blameworthy states.

For, by means of wholesome states, unwholesome states are prevented from occurring at the six doors, including the mind, through the obstruction of their activity and the induction of their non-occurrence.
They are restrained and covered. Or, it is called *kusala* because it shakes (*salati*), makes tremble, and removes what is blameworthy (*kucchita*) or evil-natured (*pāpa-dhamma*).
Alternatively, *kusā* refers to hatred, greed, and so forth, because they sharpen (*sānato*), whet (*nisānato*), and excite (*tejanato*) those evil-natured states such as the taking of life.
For it is through the influence of hatred and the rest that volition attains a state of sharpness, whereby the taking of life and other such acts become greatly reprehensible. These...

It is *kusala* because it mows and cuts away the *kusa* grass [of evil]. Alternatively, the faculties such as faith that proceed by way of the performance of merit are called *kusa* because they cut away, bring an end to, and destroy what is contemptible (*kucchita*).
That which is to be obtained and set in motion by means of these is *kusala*.
Or, "ku" refers to the ground; that which is similar to it by way of being its foundation—namely, one's own basis—is [denoted by the prefix *su-*]. Thus, it is *kusala*.
They are called *kusā* because they burn away and destroy the continuity of both form and formless phenomena, both now and in the future.
Like those [reeds], they are *kusala* because they mow down—that is, cut off—their own support.
For wholesome states (*kusaladhammā*), when accomplished through application, utterly sever form and formless phenomena by preventing their further occurrence.
"Not wholesome" (*na kusala*) means unwholesome (*akusala*); the meaning is that it is the opposite of the wholesome.

For when the meaning of the term "unwholesome" is explained by way of its constituent parts through the negation of "wholesome"—namely, as that category of phenomena which is not healthy, not blameless, does not have a pleasant result, and is not produced by skill—this is the meaning demonstrated.

Thus, it is also shown that "unwholesome" (*akusala*) means that which does not have the nature of flowing away from what is vile, nor the nature of mowing down the weeds (*kusa*), nor that which is to be practiced by means of weeds or with weeds, nor that which is like a reaper who mows weeds; this is the meaning demonstrated here.
Furthermore, in this context, the wholesome (*kusala*) is the direct opposite of the unwholesome, because it serves as the antidote to the diseases of the mind and so forth.

It has also been explained by way of synonyms such as "health" (aroga) and so forth; therefore, it is said that "the unwholesome is the direct opposite of the wholesome," meaning it is the adversary of the wholesome.
Furthermore, this should be understood as being according to their respective order, in terms of the relationship between that which abandons and that which is to be abandoned.

"Indeterminate" (abyākata) means not declared [as either wholesome or unwholesome]; the meaning is that it is not stated as having the nature of being either wholesome or unwholesome. In that regard, the state of being wholesome...
The meaning is that it has the ripening of blameless happiness. It is stated that the unwholesome state has the ripening of blameworthy suffering;

thus, it is meant that [the indeterminate] is not described by way of either of those two. By this very same principle, its not being described by way of health or sickness and so forth should also be understood as having been illustrated.
Furthermore, here, because "indeterminate" is stated after saying "wholesome" and "unwholesome," it is not described by way of the states of wholesome or unwholesome alone.

It is cognized, not by way of another mode of manifestation. Furthermore, "not being stated" here should be understood as referring to those phenomena having a nature distinct from both [of the aforementioned modes], and not merely as a matter of their not being so stated.
For it is in this sense that they are called "characterized by non-resultant-ness. 452. Regarding "by way of distinction of plane":
a plane (*bhūmi*) is that wherein phenomena exist; it is a station (*ṭhāna*) and a state (*avatthā*). A state, moreover—
For it is grasped as the place of occurrence for those possessing states, just as a location is grasped; thus there is an easy comprehension of them.

In this context, the mundane plane (*bhūmi*) should be understood by way of its location (*ṭhāna*), while the supramundane is by way of its state (*avatthā*). Alternatively, the mundane may be understood by way of both location and state, whereas the supramundane is by way of state alone.

Regarding the term "belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara*): here, "sense-sphere" (*kāma*) refers to two kinds of sense-spheres—the sense-sphere of objects (*vatthu-kāma*) and the sense-sphere of defilements (*kilesa-kāma*).

Among those, "object-desire" (*vatthukāma*) refers specifically to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*), because they are desired; "defilement-desire" (*kilesakāma*) refers to craving (*taṇhā*), because it desires.
Where these two, acting together, move about—that is the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). But what is that? It is the elevenfold existence of the sense-sphere (*ekādasavidho kāmabhavo*).
Since [the mind] mostly moves about and functions there, it is called the "sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*); this is the meaning of one instance of the word *avacara*.

Having performed an elision (*lopa*). In this way, those pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*) are also to be understood by making the elision: craving for the fine-material is "fine-material" (*rūpa*), and craving for the immaterial is "immaterial" (*arūpa*).
Alternatively, sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*) is "sensual" (*kāma*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound.

That in which one moves about is a "sphere" (*avacara*); the sphere of sensuality is "sensuous-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*). In the same way, the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere are also to be understood. It transcends the world (*lokato uttarati*).
Because it is the supramundane (lokuttara) that is intended here as the wholesome (kusala). As for the other [type], it is "supramundane" because it has transcended the world (loka).

Regarding the phrase "by way of the distinction between joy, equanimity, knowledge, and formations": first, the distinction between joy and equanimity is appropriate, since they possess distinct intrinsic natures (sabhāva).
But how is there a distinction between knowledge and formations? This is not a fault; "the distinction between knowledge and formations" means the distinction consisting of knowledge and formations.
And because he is the one who causes their existence or non-existence. "Sobhanaṃ mano" means a beautiful mind; or, that which has a beautiful mind is "sumano.
The state of being *sumana* is *somanassa*, which, by conventional usage (*ruḷhi*), refers to mental pleasant feeling.

From the moment of its arising until its dissolution, it is accompanied (*sahagata*), occurring together, and associated (*sampayutta*) with *somanassa*; this is the meaning. This is the state of being accompanied by *somanassa*.
And this [distinction] should be understood by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*). For when the object is desirable, the consciousness is accompanied by joy (*somanassasahagata*).
But surely, a desirable object is the basis for greed; how then can there be wholesome (*kusala*) consciousness therein?

This is not an absolute rule, because wholesome consciousness arises even toward a desirable object by way of mental application (*ābhoga*) and so forth. For one who, through such means as the conjunction with the wheel of the fourfold success (*catusampatticakka*), ...
There is a proper application of the mind; the mind is fixed upon performing what is wholesome, thinking, "Only the wholesome must be done by me.
Having turned away from the occurrence of the unwholesome, it is directed solely toward the performance of the wholesome, and it is practiced through constant repetition.
Consequently, even with respect to a desirable object, his mind is associated only with non-greed and other such factors, not with greed and the like.

"Associated with knowledge" (*ñāṇasampayutta*) means being endowed with knowledge in its various modes. Here, it should be understood that "modes" refers specifically to simultaneous arising (*ekuppāda*) and so forth.
In this context, the causes for being associated with knowledge are the ripening of karma, the ripening of rebirth, the ripening of the faculties, and the distancing of the defilements.
For one who teaches the Dhamma to others trains them in blameless crafts, fields of work, and branches of science.
One performs such things as these that lead to wisdom; by virtue of the support of that kamma, when a wholesome consciousness arises, it is associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
Likewise, for one who has been reborn in a world free from affliction, by depending on that rebirth, [the consciousness] is associated with knowledge.
For this has been said: "For him, while there in happiness, the words of the Dhamma float up; slow, O monks, is the arising of mindfulness."

“Then that being very quickly partakes of distinction. Likewise, for one who has attained the group of fifteen factors, wholesome states arising by depending on the maturation of the faculties are associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*).
However, for one by whom the defilements have been suppressed, [wholesome states] arise associated with knowledge by depending on the distance from those defilements.
And this has also been said: “From yoga, indeed, [bondage] is born...”
“Abundant, the non-yoking, the abundant destruction. Or else, *saṅkhāra* is the conditioning consisting of the mental application (*cittapayoga*) produced by self-exertion or the exertion of another;
that which lacks this is *asaṅkhāra*. That which proceeds together with such *saṅkhāra* is *sasaṅkhāra*.
It is *ñāṇavippayutta*, meaning dissociated from or devoid of knowledge. And here, “dissociation” refers to [the absence] of knowledge.

It should be understood that non-existence is simply non-occurrence. It is called *upekkhā* because it looks on (*upekkhati*); even while experiencing, it looks upon the object with equanimity, meaning it is established in a state of neutrality.
Alternatively, it is *upekkhā* because it is an experience (*ikkhā*) that has approached (*upetā*) pleasure and pain without opposition.
Or else, it is so called because it arises through the absence of partiality toward objects that are desirable and undesirable.
It is called *upekkhā* because it looks at and experiences [the object] with equanimity; that which is accompanied by this is "accompanied by equanimity" (*upekkhāsahagata*).
All the rest is exactly as explained below.
Having thus enumerated the eight wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-kusala-citta*), in order to now show the manner of their occurrence, [it says]: "When..."

The passage beginning with “*Hī*” has been commenced. Therein, regarding the phrase “the excellence of the recipient and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) includes the excellence of the teacher, the time, virtuous friends, and other such factors.

Regarding the phrase “or any other cause for joy,” the inclusion of the word “any other” refers to an abundance of faith, purity of view, seeing the benefits of wholesome action, being reborn with a joyful mind, and the eleven bases for the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*).
“Dhammas” is a collective term for [the nine bases of right view] beginning with “there is sacrifice.

Regarding the phrase “proceeding according to the method beginning with,” it should be understood that by the word “beginning” (ādi), not only the nine bases of right view such as “there is sacrifice” are included, but also those things that serve as the basis for the investigation-of-dhammas enlightenment factor and so forth.
“Having placed before” means having made them the precursor; and this is by way of being a co-nascent precursor.
This is because, as in the passage beginning “mental states are preceded by mind,” it is association (*sampayoga*) that is intended.

"Not sinking" means not becoming discouraged or shrinking back from the performance of meritorious deeds due to pride, stinginess, and so forth; by this, he demonstrates his state of being free from attachment and the like.

"Unprompted" means not urged by anyone else; for this shows the practice of merit arising from one's own initiative (*sarasato*). By contrast, the phrase "by others" demonstrates the prompting of others (*pākaṭussāhana*).
“Giving and so forth” refers to these ten meritorious deeds beginning with giving (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), and ending with the rectification of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*).
Alternatively, “giving and so forth” refers to those consisting of giving, virtue, and meditation (*bhāvanā*), because the other seven are included therein.

They are called “meritorious deeds” (*puñña*) because they purify the mental continuum (*santāna*) in which they arise, or because they produce a venerable fruit of existence (*bhava*). [The word] “his” refers to that person who possesses the volition of merit (*puññacetanā*).

"Amuttacāgatā" is the state of a mind that is still attached to the object to be given. By the word "etc. (ādi), it includes such things as a lack of resolve regarding the undertaking of virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi).
"That very same [state]" is said because of its similarity to the state accompanied by joy (somanassa) and so forth;

for even when things are similar, they are conventionally referred to as "that very same," just as one says, "that is the same partridge," or "those are the same medicinal herbs. Regarding this meaning, for one who is sluggish...
Regarding the meaning consisting of the exertion and application of the mind: "this" refers to the word "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*).

"Of the prior application" means of the mental application that proceeds by way of rousing [the mind] after it has been diverted from the contraction occurring during the performance of meritorious deeds.

And here, the inclusion of the word "prior" is stated with the intention that such a volitional formation becomes a "formation" (*saṅkhāra*) by virtue of being a prior accumulation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) that has proceeded in that manner.

It is not because that volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*) belongs to a prior time. The mention of "the fool" (*bāla*) is for the purpose of showing the impossibility of right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) proceeding by way of the method beginning with "there is what is given" (*atthi dinnaṃ*).

The mention of "suddenly" (*sahasā*) is for the purpose of showing the absence of despondency and encouragement. The intention is that they perform merit devoid of joy (*somanassa*). [This is] by way of the absence of causes for joy.

This should be regarded as a mere illustration; for even mental formations such as those directed toward a neutral object, as well as the mind itself, are indeed causes for being accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
The words "Thus" and so forth constitute the conclusion. This eightfold wholesome sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacara-kusala-citta*) has visible form as its object.

It should be understood that, having taken any one of the six objects—up to a mental object (*dhammārammaṇa*)—as its support, [this consciousness] arises by way of bodily action and so forth through the three doors, such as the body door, immediately after the functional mind-consciousness element (*kiriyā-manoviññāṇadhātu*) accompanied by equanimity and rootless (*ahetuka*).

In this context, when the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge produce a rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) with three roots, then sixteen resultant consciousnesses (*vipākacitta*) bear fruit. When...

However, when it is double-rooted (*duhetuka*), there are then twelve [types of consciousness], excluding those with triple roots (*tihetuka*). As for rootless (*ahetuka*) rebirth-linking, it does not produce triple-rooted states at all;

however, when giving a double-rooted rebirth-linking, twelve [states] ripen, and when giving a rootless rebirth-linking, eight [states] ripen. But a triple-rooted rebirth-linking never occurs through double-rooted [consciousness]. "Eight..."
The statement, "They bear fruit," is said with reference to the rebirth-linking [consciousness] produced by a productive kamma (*janaka-kamma*).

However, according to the statement, "A root-cause-accompanied life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is a condition for a root-cause-free life-continuum by way of proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*)," even a resultant consciousness accompanied by root-causes can indeed occur for one whose rebirth-linking is root-cause-free. And in this position, by means of a powerful condition...
It should be understood that when it arises without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*), it is weak, whereas when it arises with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*), it is strong.

However, according to those who maintain that the state of being without volitional effort or with volitional effort belongs to the result (*vipāka*) by way of its arrival, one should apply the formula: "twelve and eight [kamma] yield results.

Thus, yielding results in these three ways, this [kamma] brings about rebirth in a happy destination within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara*), as well as the attainment of wealth in both happy and miserable destinations.

It produces [results]. For even that collection of enjoyments which arises for nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others, resembling the excellence of divine enjoyment, is the fruit of wholesome karma belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) alone.
This is because there is no desirable fruit for unwholesome karma.

The word "but" (*pana*) in the phrase "but the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacaraṃ pana*) indicates a distinction. By this, it is shown that whereas in the sense sphere [the results] are of the defilements...
That [previous knowledge] effects only the abandoning of the factors associated with it, but this is not so; rather, this effects the abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
Or, just as that [knowledge of the contemplation of feelings] is divided eightfold according to the classification of feelings, knowledges, and formations, this is not so;

rather, it is otherwise than that—this indicates the distinction that will be explained. Furthermore, this [knowledge of the contemplation of mind-objects] has a basis, is subject to the taints (*sāsava*), and is free from the hindrances (*vinīvaraṇa*).

It should be understood as "belonging to the fine-material sphere" (*rūpāvacara*). For by the phrase "having a physical basis" (*savatthukaṃ*), it excludes that which belongs to the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*);

by "with taints" (*sāsavaṃ*), it excludes the consciousness of the first path; and by "free from hindrances" (*vinīvaraṇaṃ*), it excludes the two types of consciousness associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).
In some cases there are five jhāna factors, in some four, in some three, in some two, and in some others two more.

Thus, in order to explain in detail the meaning stated in brief—that [the first jhāna] is fivefold according to the distinction of jhāna factors and modes—the passage beginning with "That is to say" (*seyyathidaṃ*) is commenced.
Regarding that, whatever needs to be said has already been stated below in the discussion on the jhānas.

This [jhāna], being exclusively consisting of development (*bhāvanāmaya*), takes as its object the earth-kasiṇa and so forth according to the method already described, immediately following wholesome states associated with knowledge as appropriate.

It arises; however, it should be understood that this [meditation], divided into categories such as inferior and so forth, produces rebirth respectively in all sixteen Brahma-worlds, beginning with the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārisajja).

The formless-sphere (arūpāvacara) is to be attained by means of the complete transcendence of the perception of form and so forth. Of the four formless [attainments]... by those consisting of equanimity and concentration...

"By means of the four formless jhānas. Here, this is the genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental. Or else, it refers to the "yoga"—that is, the application or classification of yoga—of the formless states (*arūpa*) by way of their objects and so forth, together with the associated mental factors;
it is "by means of" that. "In the manner stated" means in the manner stated below in the discussion on the formless attainments (*āruppa*).
"The first" refers to the first wholesome consciousness of the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara-kusala-citta*). "The second, third, and fourth" follows the same pattern here as well.

This is the method. These [states], being exclusively born of development (*bhāvanāmaya*), take as their objects, respectively, the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa, the consciousness of the first immaterial attainment, the state of non-existence, and the base of nothingness;

they arise immediately after wholesome states associated with knowledge accompanied by equanimity, and bestow rebirth-linking and the course of existence (*pavatti*) as resultants in the four immaterial Brahma-worlds. As for the rest here:
What needs to be said has already been stated above. The supramundane (lokuttara) is to be attained through the succession of purifications of the aura.

What should be said regarding that will follow later. "By association with the four paths" means by association with these four noble paths, from the path of stream-entry up to the path of arahantship.
And all four of these, being composed of development (bhāvanāmaya), are indeed [supramundane].
Taking Nibbāna as its object, it arises under the names "emptiness liberation," "signless liberation," and "desireless liberation";
it should be understood as that which turns back rebirth in the seven states of existence and so forth. Its nature is twenty-one-fold;
this is the intended meaning according to a method that is neither too concise nor too detailed.
453. Regarding the phrase "only pertaining to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*): here, other schools maintain that unwholesome states also exist in the fine-material and immaterial spheres;

thus, the inclusion of the term "sense-sphere" is for the purpose of negating their opinion. Furthermore, the restriction is intended to show that even though [such states] arise in the exalted planes (*mahaggata-bhūmi*) and even when they yield resultants during the course of existence (*pavatti*) in the fine-material realm, they are exclusively sense-sphere states. If...
Thus, for what reason is it said that [the consciousness] belongs only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*)? The reason for this has already been stated. How was it stated?

"Sensual craving (*kāmatanha*) is 'sensual' (*kāma*) by the elision of the latter member of the compound; it 'frequents' (*avacarati*) therein, thus it is a 'sphere' (*avacara*); the sphere of sensuality is the 'sense-sphere' (*kāmāvacara*).

For here, being the object of sensual craving is stated as the cause for the state of being a sense-sphere consciousness, just as being the object of craving for the fine-material and immaterial realms is the cause for those respective states.
“Of the existence pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. This must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, the characteristic of pervasiveness would not hold.

For if one were to establish the planes (bhūmi) by way of the states that can be taken as objects (ālambitabba-dhamma), then there would be no inclusion of those states that are objectless (anārammaṇa).
Alternatively, if it were by way of the giving of result (vipāka-dāna), even so there would be no inclusion of those states that are non-resultant (avipāka). Therefore...

That [classification] should be applied to those states included within the world (*pariyāpanna*) by way of their objects; however, for those not included (*apariyāpanna*), their supramundane nature (*lokuttaratā*) should be understood from the fact that they have transcended the world, and their unsurpassed nature (*anuttaratā*) from the absence of anything superior.
Furthermore, "included" (*pariyāpanna*) means having entered (*āpanna*) by being delimited by craving which acts as a delimiter; the sense is that they are grasped. Is it not so?
And here, what is craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*)? It is craving that has phenomena of the sense-sphere as its object.
What are those phenomena of the sense-sphere? [Are they] the objects of craving for sense-pleasures? [Is there] the fault of mutual dependence? This is not so;

because of their inclusion within the eleven bases beginning with Avīci, all craving is taken as being of the nature of craving for sense-pleasures, and phenomena of the sense-sphere are [defined] by way of being the objects of that same-natured craving.

Because it is to be characterized. In the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa* as well, the statement "having its range therein" (*etthāvacarā*) should be understood as being said with reference to the state of being an object for sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*), which is delimited by the Avīci hell and the Paranimmitavasavatti realm. And that craving has that as its sphere should be understood through its inclination toward that [sphere].
"Threefold from the root" means the three unwholesome roots, beginning with greed; by way of these, [craving] together with them is also threefold.

This is the meaning. For these [three] are called "roots" (mūla) because they are like roots insofar as they are the causes for being well-established. That which has greed as its root is "greed-rooted" (lobhamūla).
This designation is made by way of the specific [factor], just as one says "the sound of a drum" (bherisadda) or "a barley sprout" (yavaṅkura). Likewise for "hatred-rooted" (dosamūla).
That which has delusion alone as its root and nothing else is "delusion-rooted" (mohamūla).
"By way of the classification of joy, equanimity, views, and formations":

here the word "classification" (*bhedato*) should be applied individually to each term—namely, by way of the classification of joy and equanimity, the classification of views, and the classification of formations. What needs to be said regarding this has already been stated according to the method explained below.
"Associated with views" (*diṭṭhigatasampayutta*): "views" (*diṭṭhigata*) is simply "view" (*diṭṭhi*), just as one says "excrement-thing" (*gūthagata*) or "urine-thing" (*muttagata*).

Alternatively, it is called "view-position" (*diṭṭhigata*) because it is merely the course taken by a view that grasps things erroneously; there is no objective reality here that possesses such an intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, because it consists in the dogmatic adherence that "only this is true, all else is false," it occurs only together with greed (*lobha*), not with hatred (*dosa*).

The passage beginning with "When indeed" (*yadāhi*) and so forth shows the mode of occurrence of minds rooted in greed. "Wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) refers to wrong views such as annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

For beings whose minds are distorted by that [view], having rejected the next world on the grounds that "the sphere of living beings is only this much, as far as the range of the senses extends," they fall into a state of reckless indulgence in sensual pleasures, thinking, "There is no danger in sensual pleasures. Thus they engage in them in whatever way possible.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes such wrong views as: "This path was ordained from of old for those traveling to the world of the gods;

by it go those with sons, free from sorrow. Animals and birds see it, and therefore they even engage in sexual union with their mothers"—thus including the view that seeing the face of one's son is the path to heaven and liberation.

In the phrase “in matters of sensual pleasure” (*kāme vā*), the word *vā* has the sense of non-restriction; by this it is meant that for Brahmins, the taking of gold alone is blameworthy in the context of taking what is not given, while other such acts are blameless.
Likewise, lying for the sake of one’s elders, cattle, oneself, one’s life, or marriage is blameless, whereas other such lying is blameworthy.
Sowing dissension for the sake of one’s elders and so forth is blameless, while other such acts are [blameworthy].

It is blameworthy. It includes such wrong graspings as the belief that stories of the Bhārata war, the abduction of Sītā, and so forth, serve to pacify evil. "Blessings seen, etc. refers to blessings seen, heard, or sensed.
"By way of natural sharpness" means by way of greed or false resolve, being naturally sharp and cruel. "By way of dullness" means slow and not sharp.
However, such [false speech] occurs either through one’s own or another’s instigation; thus he says, "by one who is instigated.
Alternatively, by the word "or" (*vā*), the inclusion of false speech and so forth that proceeds in such a manner when stealing another's goods should be understood.
Or, it refers to sensual pleasures (*kāmānaṃ*) being experienced. By the word "or," [it includes] that which belongs to another, or that which is not as intended.
The phrase "having obtained, that should be grasped" includes the act of grasping and so forth.
It is of only two kinds because there is no division based on associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*).

If this is so, why is it said, "accompanied by mental displeasure and associated with aversion"? It is for the purpose of characterizing that consciousness by means of its specific, non-common factors.

"In killing living beings, etc. means in killing living beings and so forth. By the word "etc.," taking what is not given, false speech, slander, harsh speech, idle chatter, and ill will are included.

He says, "at the time of sharp or dull occurrence," with the intention that a mind proceeding while being sharp by nature is indeed *asaṅkhāra* (without volitional effort), whereas the other is *sasaṅkhāra* (with volitional effort). However, that which proceeds while being dull is, without exception...

It is not possible to discern it as "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) alone. It should be understood that it is described in such a way because whatever proceeds with volitional effort and application is necessarily weak.
A consciousness rooted solely in delusion is extremely deluded due to its lack of other roots, and it is restless due to its association with doubt and restlessness.
It is accompanied by equanimity alone; it never possesses natural sharpness.

For what kind of function would there need to be natural sharpness, or a necessity for exertion, in the case of these two types of consciousness which operate by way of creeping along and wavering over the object?
Therefore, there is no differentiation of formations (*saṅkhāra*) therein. [This is not the case] in other unwholesome states of consciousness.
Even though restlessness (uddhacca) is found elsewhere, it is especially strong here; for that very reason, it occurs as the predominant factor among the associated states.
It is for this reason that this [state] is distinguished by restlessness and described as "associated with restlessness" (uddhaccasampayutta).
For indeed, in the Pāḷi, restlessness is mentioned here in its own form; thus, by way of its unique and predominant factor, it is rooted in delusion (mohamūla).
It should be understood that it is stated to be twofold: "associated with doubt" and "associated with restlessness.
Lack of ascertainment is doubt; distraction is lack of tranquility, meaning instability.

This twelvefold unwholesome consciousness, having taken any one of the six objects as its support, arises immediately after a functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and rootless.

It should be understood that [kamma] arises by way of bodily action and so forth, and by way of both the courses of action— such as killing living beings— and as kamma itself, through the three doors beginning with the body-door, as appropriate. Among these,
with the exception of that accompanied by restlessness, the remaining elevenfold [unwholesome consciousness] brings about rebirth-linking in all four states of misery.
It gives rebirth-linking; it also gives process-result even in a happy destination. However, that which is accompanied by restlessness gives only process-result. Here it may be asked:

What is the reason that the weakest [kamma], associated with doubt, gives rebirth-linking, while the stronger one, accompanied by restlessness, does not give it because of the presence of resolution (*adhimokkha*)?
[The answer is: Because it is not mentioned among those [kinds of kamma] to be abandoned by vision (*dassanena pahātabba*). This...
For if it were to give rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it would have to give it in the woeful states;

and if it were to do so, it would have been stated that what is to be abandoned by vision leads to the woeful states, yet it was not so stated. Therefore, it does not give rebirth-linking; however, its giving of resultant [kamma] during the course of existence (pavatti) cannot be denied.
In the *Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga*: "Knowledge associated with restlessness is the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*)."
"Knowledge regarding its result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)," according to this statement.

Others, however, say: "The restlessness-accompanied [consciousness] arising in an ordinary person (puthujjana) gives both types of result, because of the presence of its companions that are to be abandoned by vision;
it does not do so for one in training (sekkha), because of the absence of those [companions]. This point here must be investigated: for which [type of consciousness] is there the giving of a result?

It has been stated; what is that? Is it something to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or not? What is the point here? If, first of all, it were to be abandoned by cultivation, then in the *Paṭṭhāna* [the section on] the asynchronous kamma-condition for that which is to be abandoned by cultivation would have to be mentioned.

If, on the other hand, it is not to be abandoned by cultivation, then in the "Triplet of What is to be Abandoned by Seeing" (*dassanena-pahātabba-ttika*), it would be included under the category of "neither to be abandoned by seeing nor by cultivation" (*nevadassanena-nabhāvanāya-pahātabba*).
It may be said that it ought to be stated in the *Vibhaṅga*.
If it were not stated there because its nature is contrary to that [classification], would it then follow that it is "not to be stated" (*navattabba*) in that triad? It does not so follow. Why?

Because the twelve unwholesome consciousness-arisings mentioned in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* are already included under two categories; therefore, there is nothing remaining to be shown by way of analysis.

Because there is necessarily no arising of any such consciousness, just as in the "Triplet of What Has Arisen" (*uppannattika*) the state of being "inexpressible" regarding the past and so forth was not mentioned,
so it is here as well. Alternatively, even though it cannot be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because it exists in the worldling (*puthujjana*),
it is designated by the term "to be abandoned by cultivation" due to its commonality with those states whose intrinsic nature is to be abandoned by cultivation, and because it is reprehensible.

Since it exists, there is no fault of having to state that it is "inexpressible. And because it is not to be abandoned by development in the direct sense, its status as a kamma-condition occurring at a different time is also not mentioned.

Even in the case of restlessness-accompanied [ignorance], which is a condition to be abandoned by vision, the act of vision merely provides a deficiency of its auxiliary factors; it does not bring about the state of non-arising for any actual entity whatsoever.
"Of that which has been brought about" (*tassa āpādito*) expresses the necessity of abandoning it through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) exclusively.

Alternatively, the statement regarding what is to be abandoned by vision (*dassanappahātabba*) is made with reference to the state of leading to the states of misery (*apāya*); since that [state] is absent here, this specific classification is stated.
(454) With reference to the word "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*), the neuter designation beginning with "the indeterminate result" (*abyākataṃ vipākaṃ*) is employed.

Therefore, it is stated that [the indeterminate] is twofold with reference specifically to the indeterminate. Otherwise, since material form and Nibbāna are also indeterminate, it would have to be said that it is fourfold.
The fact that resultant [kamma] belongs to the sense-sphere and so forth should be understood in the same manner as explained for wholesome [kamma].
Its state of being rootless (ahetukatā) is according to the presence of associated roots, not according to the root that produces it.

For although the state of being accompanied by roots (*sahetukatā*) of a result-of-maturation (*vipāka*) is established by way of a root-possessing kamma, it is nevertheless spoken of only by way of its associated roots;

otherwise, even those [consciousnesses] devoid of roots would fall into the category of being accompanied by roots. Why, then, is the result-of-maturation of that which is accompanied by roots itself devoid of roots?
The reason for this has already been stated. Furthermore, among the five types of sensory consciousness, there is merely the striking against the object.
Just as association with non-greed and the other [wholesome roots] is impossible, so too it is in the case of the very weak and weaker functions of receiving and investigating;
thus, their lack of roots should be understood from the impossibility of the arising of such roots.
Because it lacks the specific function of reflecting that is distinct from mental consciousness, the element consisting of mind alone is called the "mind-element" (manodhātu).
Its characteristic is the discerning of visible form by being dependent on the eye; thus, it is "characterized by the discerning of visible form dependent on the eye.
In this context, by the term "dependent on the eye," other consciousnesses that have visible form as their object are excluded.

By the inclusion of the term "discerning," contact and other factors dependent on the eye are excluded. By the inclusion of both "eye" and "visible form," [the distinction is made] in terms of the support and the object.
And one should cause consciousness to disappear because its existence depends upon both [factors].

For if there were no such thing as the eye, even blind people would see forms, yet they do not see them. And if there were no such thing as form—such as blue and so forth—it would not be subject to spatial and other restrictions; yet such restriction certainly exists.
Furthermore, it is stated that the mind has an object of apprehension (*ārammaṇa*) exclusively; therefore, [consciousness disappears] "by means of the object."
The doctrine that "mind proceeds without the appearance of blue and so forth" should be understood as a false doctrine.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," and so on.
But why is there this difference in phrasing here? Because even a single eye is a condition for consciousness, whereas form...
The phrase "only many in combination" is used for the purpose of showing this specific distinction.
But what is the reason that even a single eye is a condition for consciousness, whereas visible form must be many? It is because of the specific nature of their respective conditions.

For the eye, in being a condition for eye-consciousness by way of the conditions of support (*nissaya*), pre-existence (*purejāta*), faculty (*indriya*), and dissociation (*vippayutta*), acts as a condition through its mere existence (*atthibhāva*).
It exists because when that [condition] is present, it comes to be; and when it is absent, it does not exist.

Therefore, it is said that this [conditioned state] has that [condition] as its condition by way of the presence and non-disappearance conditions (*atthi-avigata-paccaya*). Furthermore, its dependence on that [condition] should not be understood as clinging to it in part, because it is formless (*arūpa*);
rather, it is by virtue of its existence being bound up with that [condition], just as students, subjects, and men are dependent upon their teacher, king, and master respectively.
The other conditions, however, should be understood according to their respective specific characteristics. This state of being a condition is not impossible in a single instance;
thus, since even a single eye can be a condition for consciousness, it is expressed in the singular as "dependent on the eye" (*cakkhuñca paṭicca*).
As for visible form, although—like the eye—it is a condition by way of the prenascence, presence, and non-disappearance conditions, it occurs earlier.
Because it is beneficial at the very moment it exists; nevertheless, it becomes a condition only when many [factors] are combined, by way of being an object (ārammaṇa).

For that consciousness which functions discerning a causal phenomenon—whether it be of an intrinsic nature or merely a conceptually constructed form—is, due to its own nature of having an object, [the primary factor] even though other things also possess the status of being conditions.

Because it must cling to something and is incapable of occurring without an object, that which is to be clung to is called an "object" (ārammaṇa). Since its acquisition of the condition of being an object occurs through the apprehension of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) in whatever way it may be,
therefore, when eye-consciousness arises directed toward a visible form, it proceeds only by making manifest that form's intrinsic nature.
And for him, whose functioning is dependent on the sense faculties, there is the apprehension of the objective nature of the object;

this occurs neither by way of the color belonging to one or two *kalāpas*, nor by way of the color belonging to only a few *kalāpas*, but rather by way of the color that has entered the range of perception in accordance with mental application (*ābhoga*).
Thus, showing that many material phenomena (*rūpa*) indeed serve as conditions for consciousness through their collective operation, the Blessed One said: "In regard to forms..."
He indicated this by means of the plural form "and [the others].
But as for what was stated—"The visible-object base is a condition, by way of object-condition, for the eye-consciousness element and for the states associated with it"—how is that so?
That too refers to whatever kind of visible-object base serves as an object-condition for eye-consciousness...
This was said with reference to exactly that kind [of object]. But what kind is it? "Aggregated" (samudita) is the meaning clearly evident here.

And by taking it thus, even what some say—that "eye-consciousness and the rest have the act of perceiving as their object by way of the perception of the sense-base (āyatana), and not by way of the perception of a substance"—is indeed appropriate.
Nor should it be suspected here that there is an object consisting of a composite whole (samudāyārammaṇatā).
This is because there is no enjoyment of the collection [of parts] as a whole. However, the color-phenomena (vaṇṇadhammā) when combined do serve as object-conditions (ārammaṇapaccaya).
But how can things that are individually incapable of being objects become objects when combined? Is it not the case that the blind, who are unable to see individually, cannot see even when combined?
This is not an absolute rule; for in cases such as carrying a palanquin, those who are individually incapable [of carrying it] [can do so when combined].

Because it is seen [only] through their collective capacity. Furthermore, since it is impossible to grasp the individual color of the hair and so forth at the place where they reside, yet it is possible to grasp their combined color at that very same place, their functioning in unison (*saṃhatyakāritā*) is even more clearly evident.
By this, [the following question is addressed]: Is the object of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) an atom-form (*paramāṇurūpa*), or rather a collection thereof? And so on.
It should be understood that the objection has been refuted. This same method applies to such passages as, “Dependent on the ear and sounds,” and so forth.
Thus, by virtue of its dependence on both [the sense organ and the object], the analysis of eye-consciousness has been made in terms of its support and its object;
likewise, this should be stated accordingly for ear-consciousness and the others.
"Having the mere form as its objective flavor" means that its function is to take only the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object.
By the word "mere" (*matta*), just as other objects are excluded, so too are certain specific qualities found within the sense-sphere of visible form itself excluded.
For eye-consciousness is not able to apprehend any quality therein other than the mere color. Therefore, he said:
The Blessed One said: "By means of the five kinds of consciousness, one does not cognize any phenomenon other than the mere impact [of the object].
Since eye-consciousness arises only with respect to a visible-form object when it arises, it is grasped as being directed toward that;
therefore, it is stated that its "manifestation is the state of being directed toward visible form. [This applies] to the immaterial phenomena that arise immediately after itself.

Immediately vanished immaterial states are helpful by providing an occasion for the occurrence [of the subsequent consciousness] through the conditions of proximity, contiguity, absence, and disappearance, like the supporting and objective conditions.
Showing that they are an immediate cause, he said: "It is the footing for the disappearance of the functional mind-element with visible form as its object.
The meaning should be understood in the same manner for ear-consciousness and the others as well.
Because it receives and, as it were, grasps the objects such as visible forms— which have been apprehended by eye-consciousness and the rest—
immediately after them without allowing them to fall away, it is said to "have the function of receiving visible forms and so forth.
It is "manifested as suchness" because it stands ready through that state of receiving.

Although its intrinsic nature is the cognition of any five or even just some of the six objects among the six objects, it is described as having the characteristic of cognizing the six objects because it does not transcend that nature,
or because the other objects are included within those very six. "Functions such as investigating" means either functions such as investigating and registration,
or functions such as investigating, registration, rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.

This is the intended meaning. The phrase “having the heart-base as its proximate cause” (*hadayavatthupadaṭṭhānā*) is stated because these two mind-consciousness elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) are invariably dependent upon the heart-base.
However, according to the method explained below, it is also appropriate to say that they have the departure of the respective immediately preceding consciousness as their proximate cause.
Regarding “its division,” this refers to that resultant mind-consciousness element which was stated to be “twofold.”
"Differentiation" means being twofold. "In an exclusively desirable object" means in an object that is exclusively desirable;

the sense is "in an extremely desirable object. "Both in the five doors and at the conclusion of impulsion": here, in the case of the five doors, its place is in the interval between the receiving consciousness (*sampaticchana*) and the investigating consciousness (*votthapana*);

elsewhere, it is in the interval between the impulsion (*javana*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). Thus, it has two places. For the other [type of registration], it also occurs at the time of investigation (*santīraṇa*) and registration of the object (*tadārammaṇa*).
It is exactly as previously stated; however, at the time of rebirth-linking and so forth, the interval between the death-consciousness and the life-continuum is for rebirth-linking;
the interval between rebirth-linking and adverting, or between registration-adverting and javana-adverting, or between determining-adverting and adverting, is for the life-continuum;
or the interval between registration and rebirth-linking, or between javana and rebirth-linking, [is for the life-continuum].
It should be understood that this refers to the state at the moment of death.
Regarding the phrase "in the six," the analysis here is to be understood according to the method already explained above.

Because of the powerful nature of the impact and friction of tangible objects—which serve as the physical basis for the body and are not very desirable—body-consciousness is associated with pleasure. This applies only to derived material phenomena (upādārūpa).

Because impact is weak, eye-consciousness and the others are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*). Therefore he said: "The rest are associated with equanimity. "The rest" refers to the sixfold [consciousness].

"Associated with non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion" means: non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are the "non-greed and so forth"; that which is associated with those resultant roots of non-greed and so forth is "associated with the resultant roots of non-greed and so forth.
"Like sense-sphere wholesome [consciousness], according to the divisions of joy and so forth" means as follows:
Sensuous-sphere wholesome consciousness is of eight kinds through the divisions of joy, equanimity, knowledge, and formations;

"in this way it is also" thus shows its similarity by way of that eightfold nature. It is indeed similar by way of being sensuous-sphere, by way of the low and so forth, and by way of arising in the various modes of birth;
however, it is dissimilar by way of associated states, by way of object, and by way of the mode of occurrence. Likewise...
For wholesome kamma occurs by way of doors, but this [resultant consciousness] does not, because resultants do not produce intimation.
However, by way of the doors of arising, there is indeed a distinction in its occurrence, since great resultants can occur by way of the object (tadārammaṇa) in the five doors and the mind door.
Just as the wholesome is fivefold by way of destiny (gati), so too is it [fivefold] by way of stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti).
And it is sevenfold; this [consciousness] is not so, because it arises only in a portion of that.

Therein, in order to show its distinctness by way of object and by way of the mode of certain occurrences, the passage beginning with "But as" was stated. "In the six objects" means in the six objects distinguished as limited and so forth, past and so forth, internal and so forth.
"By way of arrival and so forth" means by way of the condition of arrival (*āgamana-paccaya*). Therein, according to the opinion of certain teachers, in the mouth...
It is "without volitional effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) like the movement of the reflection of a face when the surface of a mirror moves;
it is "with volitional effort" (*sasaṅkhāra*) like the result of wholesome karma that is accompanied by volitional effort—thus according to the manner of its arrival.

However, according to the opinion of certain teachers, that which arises through powerful, manifest conditions such as karma is "without volitional effort," while that which arises through weak conditions is "with volitional effort."
Thus, it is by way of condition. Regarding "associated states" (*sampayutta-dhammā*): this refers to those associated states explicitly mentioned in the text (*pāḷi*).
For it is by way of them that there is no distinction between the wholesome and the resultant. Regarding "without effort" (*nirussāha*):

here, "effort" (*ussāha*) is a functional activity (*byāpāra*) characterized by the capacity to produce a result within a continuum where ignorance, craving, and conceit have not been severed; since that [activity] does not exist in resultant states, they are "without effort. In the wholesome states...
However, since these [mental factors] exist even during the occurrence of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), they are accompanied by effort (*saussāha*).
Because greed and so forth are exclusively reprehensible and have unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) as their cause, they possess no result of ripening (*vipāka*).

Likewise, because non-greed and so forth are by nature exclusively blameless, and because their cause is the opposite of those [reprehensible states], there is likewise no state of unwholesome ripening; thus he said.

“Unwholesome resultant [consciousness] is exclusively rootless. Just as the wholesome resultant mind-consciousness element is twofold—accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity—due to the presence of a distinction in feeling when the object is extremely desirable or moderately desirable, there is no such distinction in feeling when the object is extremely undesirable or moderately undesirable;
thus, the unwholesome resultant mind-consciousness element [is not twofold].
It is stated as "sevenfold" because it is indeed one [type of consciousness]. For if there were a distinction of feeling therein, then displeasure (aniṭṭha) would necessarily have to be present;
and yet, mental grief (domanassa) does not arise without aversion (paṭigha).

The fact that body-consciousness is accompanied by pain (dukkha-sahagata) should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated regarding wholesome resultant [consciousness]. Equanimity (upekkhā)...

"Inferior" means that because it is the result (*vipāka*) of exclusively inferior unwholesome (*akusala*) karma, even though equanimity (*upekkhā*) is [normally] neutral, it is indeed inferior due to its nature as suffering (*dukkha*).
Therefore, he said: "It is not very sharp, like suffering. Just as suffering is extremely sharp and pungent, this is not so;
nevertheless, it proceeds precisely with the nature of suffering. For the result of unwholesome karma is never without suffering. This is the state of equanimity.

This should be understood as being like the equanimity of a weak man, who is unable to strike back when being oppressed by a powerful person and is thus subjected to the suffering inflicted by him. "In the others" refers to the wholesome resultant states.

"Fine-material-sphere" refers to the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere. For this is the discussion of resultants. "Like the wholesome" refers to the wholesome consciousness of the fine-material sphere.

It is not like that; for the resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) is not similar to other wholesome states. Furthermore, these are relative terms, namely "wholesome" and "resultant.
Therefore, just as when it is said, "He attends upon his mother," it is established even though "his own mother" is not explicitly stated, so too here:
the meaning is "like one's own wholesome state. This refers to similarity with the wholesome.
And here [the distinction] should be understood by way of the factors (dhamma) and by way of the object (ārammaṇa).

For those factors such as contact (phassa) and so forth that are found in the wholesome (kusala) are also found in the resultant (vipāka). And in whatever object the wholesome occurs, in that very same object this resultant also occurs.
However, regarding the fifth jhāna consciousness that has attained direct knowledge (abhiññā), there is no resultant at all for it.
Why does it not exist? Because it is impossible and because it constitutes a benefit (*ānisamsa*).

For if that were to give its result (*vipāka*), it would have to give only a fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) result. Indeed, karma belonging to one plane does not give a result belonging to another plane.

Furthermore, since the state of having the "sign of the deed" (*kamma-nimitta*) as its object has been stated for fine-material-sphere results, such a result does not occur by taking anything else as its object. And its objects are limited (*paritta*) and so forth.
"That it does not exist" refers to the impossibility [of its arising].

However, there is indeed a distinction between the result (vipāka) that has arisen and the wholesome (kusala), just as there is a difference in the acquisition of conditions for generosity and so forth within that same personal existence (attabhāva). To demonstrate this, he says: "But the wholesome... and so on.
It has been stated. Like the wholesome [consciousness], it is fourfold according to the distinction of its objects, such as space cleared from the kasiṇa and so forth.
The distinction in its occurrence is in the same manner as previously described, because it occurs by way of impulsion (javana) and by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and so on.
It is the fruit of the consciousness associated with the four noble paths, because it is the result of the wholesome consciousness associated with the four noble paths.
The meaning is: "because of being associated with the fourfold fruits of recluseship.

Although it occurs an unlimited number of times during the course of the path and during the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti)—occurring twice or thrice—it is said to "occur in two ways" because it occurs in two places.
"All" refers to the twenty-three types of sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) resultant consciousness and the five types...

Resultant consciousness of the fine-material sphere, fourfold resultant consciousness of the immaterial sphere, and likewise fourfold supramundane resultant—thus, all resultant consciousness, by a method that is neither too brief nor too detailed, is thirty-sixfold.
It is threefold according to the distinction of planes, because of the absence of the supramundane [in those planes]. For there is no supramundane functional consciousness at all.
Because it yields its result immediately. For it is said: "They call this concentration 'the immediate'.
Let it be granted for now that the unsurpassed wholesome state arising in those still in training (sekkha) is fruitful because it leads to another person’s existence;
however, why is it not accepted that the state arising in an Arahant is merely functional (kiriya), being fruitless because it does not lead to another person’s existence?
It might be so desired. If there were a repeated arising of that [consciousness], it would be only once that supramundane wholesome consciousness occurs.
For if it were to occur repeatedly, then even in an Arahant the path-consciousness would occur, and thus it would become a supramundane functional consciousness;
however, this is not the case because there is no purpose for it. Therefore, there is no supramundane functional consciousness. "Functional consciousness" (kiriyaviññāṇa) [refers to...].

And "mere functional consciousness" means a consciousness that occurs as mere function, without producing any result (vipāka) like wholesome or unwholesome [kamma], but remaining as mere function itself.
But why does this not produce a result? It is said:

for here, those two types of adverting consciousness, though occurring in a continuity where the root of existence (bhava-mūla) has not been severed, do so because they lack the quality of repetition (anāsevanatā).
Due to its weakness, like a flower lacking the potency of a seed, it remains fruitless.

Furthermore, that eighteen-fold consciousness which occurs within a continuity where the root of existence has been severed should be understood as not yielding fruit—just like the flower of a creeper whose roots have been cut.
Because nothing else can arise, it is by means of the functional cause (*kriyā-hetu*), namely non-greed and so forth, [that this occurs].
"It must come to be," he said, [meaning] "devoid of the causal factors such as non-greed.

Having preceded the eye-consciousness and so forth, its characteristic is the cognizing of objects such as visible forms; thus, it has the characteristic of cognizing visible forms and so forth prior to the eye-consciousness and the rest.

Furthermore, although this arises from mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*), because it lacks the specific function of reflecting (*manana*), it is merely mind (*mano-matta*), and thus it is the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
For it is not a condition for mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, will follow in the "Description of the Elements" (*Dhātuniddesa*).
Its function is adverting (*āvajjana-rasa*); that is, its function is to direct [the mind], or its function is to divert the stream of consciousness from its previous mode.

Its proximate cause is the interruption of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-viccheda-padaṭṭhāna*), meaning it is the basis for the interruption of the life-continuum stream. It has an unprecedented object and occurs only once.
Since it is unable to experience the flavor of an object in any way while it is occurring, it remains associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*) toward all objects, whether desirable or otherwise.

"Common" (*sādhāraṇā*) means shared by those in training (*sekkha*), those beyond training (*asekkha*), and worldlings (*puthujjana*). "Uncommon" (*asādhāraṇā*) means exclusive to those beyond training.
Its function is to determine (*voṭṭhabbanā-āvajjana-rasa*); that is, as if it were defining the object grasped by the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) at the five sense doors.
Its function is determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) because it determines; however, in the mind-door, its function is adverting (*āvajjana*), according to the method already stated.
It is manifested as suchness (*tathābhāva-paccupaṭṭhāna*) because it stands present in the five doors and the mind-door respectively by way of determining and adverting.

At the time of determining, it is the proximate cause for the three rootless resultant mind-consciousness elements whose function is investigating (*santīraṇa*); at the time of adverting, [it is the proximate cause for the fivefold sense-cognitions].
"Of any life-continuum whatsoever"—by this he means that the departure of any one of these is its proximate cause; thus he says, "the footing for the rootless [consciousness]... etc.
"Of an Arahant" is said because it is unique to Arahants alone. "In lowly objects" refers to such things as skeletons, the forms of hungry ghosts, or other unexalted bases.
"Having the function of producing a smile" means having the function of producing a smile itself. Likewise...
Indeed, that consciousness is called specifically the "consciousness producing laughter" (*hasituppāda*), not because other types of consciousness that produce laughter are non-existent.

For there exist twelve other limited wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) which, as appropriate, produce laughter for worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others;
however, this [specific] consciousness is devoid of investigative wisdom (*vicāraṇa-paññā*).
It arises producing a measure of mental joy (somanassamatta) in Arahants regarding limited and inferior objects.
It is stated in the Commentary that it also arises in the Blessed One; having spoken of his unimpeded knowledge regarding the past and so forth, [it says]:
"The entire bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these three qualities, is preceded by knowledge."
Some say that because of the statement, "it follows after knowledge," this must be investigated.

In that regard, although the Blessed One’s act of smiling occurs through a mind of laughter-arising consciousness, it is indeed "following after knowledge" because it conforms to the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the future, and omniscience.
Since this is the case regarding its being a following after knowledge, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the scriptures or the commentaries. And having established it thus:
In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: “At the conclusion of those cognitions, this consciousness arises. And this must necessarily be accepted as such;
otherwise, the arising of another rootless consciousness (*ahetuka-citta*) capable of originating intimation (*viññatti*) would not be tenable for the Blessed One.
For [intimation] does not arise from a consciousness that originates intimation once that intimation has already been produced.

The state of entering into the condition of bodily action and so forth is obstructed. This is because [the consciousness] arises exclusively in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), having the heart-base as its proximate cause (padatthāna).

This is the distinction here: while there is the capacity to produce a resultant [consciousness] upon the arising of both trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana), this capacity is absent upon the arising of Arahants.
Thus, in the wholesome functional consciousnesses (kusalakiriyaviññāṇa) within the mental continuum of both, it is characterized by their respective arising.

This is the distinction. By establishing it in this way, the undesirable consequence that wholesome and unwholesome states—even those without fruition—might possess the nature of functional (kiriyā) states due to a deficiency in conditions is averted.
The same principle applies here as well in the phrase "the distinction from the wholesome" [in the subsequent section].
455. All these wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states comprise eighty-nine consciousnesses, according to a method that is neither too concise nor too prolix.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). The "function" (*kicca*) of rebirth-linking consciousness and the others is simply their occurrence in the manner of linking to another existence (*bhavantara*) and so forth.
Since there is no other function for consciousness apart from that, he said, "they occur in fourteen ways. "By way of power" (*ānubhāvena*) means by way of capability.
For karma that has been performed and accumulated gives its result when the remaining conditions come together.
It is as if it were emitting its own majesty. "Among gods and humans" means among the gods of the six sense-sphere heavens (*kāmāvacara*) and among humans.

Regarding "kamma, the sign of kamma, and the sign of the destination": here, "kamma" refers to wholesome sense-sphere kamma that has been performed and accumulated, and which has found the opportunity to yield its result.
Therefore, he said "present. The "sign of kamma" is [the object] at the moment of accumulating kamma.

The objects of giving and so forth, which serve as conditions for volition (*cetanā*). The sign of destiny (*gatinimitta*) is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) included within whichever destiny one is reborn into. "The state of being a *paṇḍaka* and so forth" means the state of being a *paṇḍaka*, a *mūga*, a *mammana*, and so on.

For the weak—namely, the mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and lacking roots (*ahetuka*), which is the result of weak two-rooted wholesome karma—the weak... [etc. ...mind-consciousness element. Of these:

Of beings who have cultivated wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres. "Only the sign of the kamma" means only one's own kamma-object, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.

"Thus, firstly, here" means that here, in the exposition of the consciousness aggregate, the occurrence of the nineteen resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking should be understood thus, merely by way of showing their essential nature in brief. [This is further specified] by way of the classification of the existence-objects and so forth.
However, whatever is to be said regarding this matter will be addressed in the discussion on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
That continuum (*tanti*) follows in immediate succession for rebirth-linking consciousnesses (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*), as each one arises and ceases, being linked to the very next that arises.
"Of each respective [kamma]" means of whichever specific kamma it constitutes the result (*vipāka*).

Rebirth-consciousness [arises] for this or that [being]. "In that very same" means in that very same [object], such as karma and so forth. If karma is the object of rebirth-consciousness, then it is in that karma;
or if it is the sign of the karma (*kammanimitta*) and the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*), then it is in that sign of karma or sign of destination—this is the meaning.
"Of exactly that kind" refers to the nature of the rebirth-consciousness according to its cause and the remaining associated mental states.
And it is of that same nature. "Causing the cessation of the continuity" means causing the cessation of the continuity of the *bhavaṅga*.
[It occurs] in another arising of consciousness termed "adverting. Dreaming occurs only through a functional (*kiriyamaya*) state of consciousness; thus he said, "for one not seeing a dream.
It indeed proceeds even in immeasurable numbers, for it is called "life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga*) because it functions as a constituent part of the existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
It is said: "Of those very ones" means of those very [factors] that constitute rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Faculties" (*indriyāni*) refers to the faculties such as the eye and so forth. "Capable of grasping objects" means they are able to grasp objects such as visible forms.
For indeed, just as at the time of being in the mother's womb, even at the time of having emerged from it, the faculties are not yet performing their own specific functions.
However, they become functional only when they have gradually reached a state of maturity. For this very reason, it is said:
"Here, because of the full ripening of the sense bases. "Come into the range" means situated in a suitable location.

Depending on that very form situated in a suitable location, and having obtained the condition of impact (*ghaṭṭanā*). "Impact" means resistance (*paṭighāta*), by which—[in conjunction with] other specific conditions such as effort and so forth—...

The meaning is that there is assistance and impairment by way of the state of being desirable or undesirable for the object of the eye, which consists in the arising of a modification or the arising of something dissimilar.
"From that" means immediately after the impact. "By the power of the impact" means by the force of the impact.
"Vibration of the life-continuum" (bhavaṅgacalana) means the shaking of the life-continuum consciousness; likewise, through its occurrence twice, it is dissimilar [to the preceding state].

The meaning is "attaining the state of being a cause. For that [change] is called "movement" because it is like a movement, insofar as it serves as the cause for a different state of the preceding state of the mental continuum.

Let there first be an impact upon the sensitivity (pasāda) by way of the object's presence, since this is established by the natural law (dhammatā) consisting in the relationship between object and subject; but as for the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), which is dependent on something else—
How does the movement occur? It occurs due to the existence of a connection with that [object].
An example here is the movement of a fly sitting on one grain of sand when another grain of sand placed upon the surface of a drum is struck.

"That very form" refers to that very visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) which has come into the range of perception and serves as the condition for the movement of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). The life-continuum...
It proceeds as if severing the continuum of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), as though cutting it off.

Since the life-continuum arises subsequently to the occurrence of the object-reception, after having mentioned the five-door adverting consciousness—which performs the grasping of the object—one might expect that seeing and so forth should be mentioned next;

yet, instead of mentioning those, the mind-door adverting consciousness is taken up here because, in the summary list, both types of adverting consciousness are included under the common characteristic of being "adverting."
“Immediately after the adverting consciousness” means immediately after the five-door adverting consciousness.

For those who do not admit that the receiving and other process-consciousnesses exist—just as there is a heart-base—the textual tradition (Pāḷi) has been handed down in various places stating, “for the receiving eye-consciousness element,” and so forth.
Indeed, it is not possible to reject the textual tradition.
The phrase "if it is large" is stated because this refers to the occurrence of consciousness up to the point of the impulsion (javana).
For here, an object with a lifespan of fourteen mind-moments is intended by the term "large";
and that should be understood as entering the range of the senses after having arisen and passed away for two or three mind-moments.

"In the manner determined" means in the way determined by the process of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) as previously described. Since the processes of adverting (*āvajjana*) and determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) have already been mentioned, the term "the remainder" is used in the phrase "the remaining functional consciousnesses of the sense sphere.

By the word "or" in the expression "six or seven," it should be understood that "five" is also included; for at times such as when one is fainting from hunger, even five impulsion moments (*javana*) may occur.
“Those very same” refers to the twenty-nine sense-sphere javanas mentioned by the phrase “of eight,” and so forth.
The inclusion of the word “only” (eva) is for the purpose of showing that there is no other consciousness arising immediately after mind-door adverting apart from these.

The term “change-of-lineage” (gotrabhū) here includes the preliminary (parikamma) and purification (vodāna) stages that are conducive to change-of-lineage, but not the actual change-of-lineage itself.
Thus. "Resultant consciousnesses" refers to those resultant consciousnesses that proceed by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

"Whichever has obtained the necessary conditions" means whichever impulsion (*javana*)—such as a fine-material-sphere impulsion and so forth—has obtained the conditions for its arising immediately after the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) moment.
"Exceedingly great" means having a lifespan of sixteen mind-moments; for it is there, and not elsewhere, that the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa-citta*) arises.
"Vibhūtaṃ" means well-manifested, and that [object] belongs only to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), for it is there that its arising as an object occurs.

"At the conclusion of the sense-sphere impulsion" means precisely at the end of the sense-sphere impulsion. For that [impulsion], being produced by karma rooted in sense-desire craving, does not follow after sublime or supramundane impulsions, because it is not their producer and because it is dissimilar to them.
It is just like a young child who wishes to go out from his house.
It follows that which is its producer or similar to its producer, and not anything else; this case is likewise.

Even there, it is not from every [preceding] impulsion (javana) that every [subsequent] impulsion is determined as having that same object, because the object must be determined by the impulsion, and the feeling must be exchanged according to the object.

In this regard, the rule is as follows: immediately after any one of the functional (kiriya) impulsions associated with joy, rooted in greed and delusion, and pertaining to the limited (paritta) wholesome [category]—
When the object is very great, one of the five registration consciousnesses accompanied by joy arises with that as its object;

likewise, immediately after any of the functional javanas accompanied by equanimity—whether limited, wholesome, or unwholesome—one of the six registration consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity occurs.
"Of desirable objects, etc. means of objects that are desirable, desirable-neutral, or undesirable.
"By way of" (*vasena*) is the connection [to the preceding]. This is stated for the purpose of showing the transformation of feeling by way of the object.
"By way of previous karma" is said for the purpose of showing the distinction of that object-representation (*tadārammaṇa*).
