For it is not only the karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) which produces the object-representation; rather, other karma does so as well. However, that [object-representation] arises from an object-representation that is to be produced by the karma that bestows rebirth-linking.
“It produces even the disagreeable”: the phrase “by way of impulsion consciousness” is for the purpose of showing the necessity of the registration [consciousness].
For it has been said: “The registration must be determined by the impulsion. By the word “etcetera,” the rebirth-linking consciousness is included;
for that does not serve as a condition for a more superior registration of its own. Whatever condition is obtained...
"Occurs" means that whichever among the aforementioned desirable objects and so forth is present as a condition for the arising of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
"For some interval" means for some momentary interval. "Like water" means like water flowing against the current.
The expression "twice or once" is stated for the sake of euphony, just as in the case of "eight or ten" and so forth.

However, they explain that it occurs only twice. Because it is a resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*), because the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*) is remote, and because of the commonality of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)—such as its being the root-life-continuum and so forth—it is fit to proceed toward the same object as the life-continuum;

thus, since its object is the object of that impulsion (*javana*), it is called "having that as its object" (*tadārammaṇa*), by eliding one of the two *ārammaṇa* words. It is "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*).

And as in the case of "the mouth of the lip. Here, some maintain that because it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna*—“When the wholesome or unwholesome has ceased, the resultant arises by way of object-recollection (*tadārammaṇatā*)”—that object-recollection occurs only immediately after states possessing the nature of resultants (*vipākadhammadhammā*), they do not accept [it] immediately after functional impulsions (*kriyājavana*).
For an impulsion, being expansive, follows upon the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) like a boat following the current of a river.
However, for one possessing the sixfold equanimity, the impulsion of peaceful conduct and activity is like a leaf-boat in a river-current.
This [impulsion] is seen to be left unmentioned in certain contexts despite being applicable, due to some specific intention;

just as, for example, the *adhipati* (dominant factor) is not mentioned in the description of the unwholesome in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, even though it is applicable. And as for that leaf-boat which was illustrated, it too—
It is not the same as that which was illustrated. For the turning back and the movement of a boat and a leaf-boat against the current of a river are dissimilar;

thus, while it is logical for a boat to follow the river’s current and a leaf-boat not to follow it, here, however, the turning back and the movement of both functional and other types of javanas against the stream of the *bhavaṅga* are similar; therefore, it is illogical for this [the latter] not to follow it.
And the following [of the object] by another [consciousness] is not tenable. Therefore, it must be investigated.

The restriction "only the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga*) is used because the conclusion of existence is not intended here. Otherwise, there would likewise be no death even at the end of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*).
"Seeing and so forth" refers to seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. The word "iti" [is used to indicate the end of the list].

The word "etc. (ādi) has this meaning; by it, the inclusion of the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana-citta) and the others should be understood. From rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) there is only the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and from the life-continuum there is only the adverting consciousness (āvajjana);
thus, it is solely by way of the fixed order of occurring consciousnesses. "That too" (tampi) refers to the death-consciousness (cuti-citta).
Like the rebirth-linking and life-continuum consciousnesses, it is of exactly nineteen types, because there is no difference in its actual meaning (attha).

"In the states of existence, destinies, stations, and abodes" means: in the three realms of existence (*bhava*), the five destinies (*gati*), the seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and the nine abodes of beings (*sattāvāsa*).
However, that which is here without mind should not be included here, because this is a discourse on consciousness.
The word "here" (*ettha*) should be connected with the phrase "of beings wandering [in saṃsāra]. "Here" refers to those wandering in these [realms] according to the method already stated.
The intention is that among beings, whoever attains Arahantship does so by following right practice.
For that Arahant, the mind has indeed ceased, because of the state of being without rebirth-linking.
Thus ends the commentary on the section of the detailed exposition concerning the aggregate of consciousness.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Aggregate of Feeling (Vedanākkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā) 456. That which is gone toward, or proceeded toward, by means of feeling in the mode of experiencing is "the experienced" (*vedayita*).

The class of phenomena characterized as such is the "characteristic of being experienced. Since that, in its actual meaning, is simply feeling itself, he said: "The characteristic of being experienced is called feeling."

Alternatively, because "being felt" (*vedayita*) is its characteristic, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*) itself by way of a *aññapadattha* compound, relying on a distinction established through conventional usage;

thus he says: "That which has the characteristic of being felt is called feeling. The statement "it feels, it feels" is made according to the desire for verbal expression (*byāpani-icchā*) in order to show the frequent occurrence of feeling within its own object.
Apart from the phenomenon that is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*), there is no other agent.

The designation "agent" (kattuniddesa) is for the purpose of showing that [feeling] does not exist [as a self]. "Iti" has the sense of a cause in an unrestricted sense. "Kho" is a mere ornament of speech.
"Tasmā" is its restriction. This is what is meant: because it experiences the flavor of the object according to its conditions, it is therefore called "feeling" (vedanā).
“Associated with wholesome consciousness”: this should be understood as a characteristic mark of wholesome feeling.
Whatever wholesome feeling there may be, all of it is associated with wholesome consciousness; however, this is not for the purpose of demonstrating the establishment of its wholesomeness.
For the wholesomeness of wholesome feeling does not arise from association with wholesome consciousness, but rather from wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) and so forth.
Therefore he said, "by way of genus" (*jātivasena*). The same method applies to the unwholesome and so forth as well.

Just as they are threefold by way of genus through association with wholesome consciousness and so on, so too they should be understood as being eighty-ninefold, up to their association with the eighty-nine types of consciousness.

"By way of difference in intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvabhedato*) means: the sense is that this is stated solely by way of the distinction produced by their own intrinsic nature, without taking into account the distinctions obtained by way of their associated plane, object, and so forth.

Having stated "fivefold," the words beginning with "pleasure" (sukha) were spoken in order to demonstrate that fivefold nature. In this context, it is called *sukha* because it "pleases" (*sukhayati*);
the meaning is that it causes the body and its associated mental states to attain satisfaction.

Alternatively, it is *sukha* because it thoroughly consumes (*suṭṭhu khādati*) or carves away (*khaṇati*) bodily affliction. Others say it is *sukha* because it provides a comfortable space (*sukaraṃ okāsa-dānaṃ*).
It is called *dukkha* because it causes suffering; the meaning is that it afflicts the body and associated mental states.
Alternatively, it is *dukkha* because it eats or gnaws wickedly (*duṭṭhu*) at bodily pleasure. Others say it is *dukkha* because it is difficult (*dukkara*) to make room for it.
The literal meaning of *somanassa* and *upekkhā* has already been explained above. For *domanassa*, one should follow the method explained for *somanassa*.
This should be understood. But what is the reason that pleasure and pain are explained by dividing them according to whether they are mental or otherwise as "pleasure, mental joy;
pain, mental grief," whereas equanimity—both mental and otherwise—is stated as a single category?
Because there is no division. For just as pleasure and pain differ from one another in terms of being beneficial or harmful to the body, [equanimity does not].
They bring about both assistance and injury, whereas equanimity does not alter the mind in such ways; therefore, because there is no differentiation, equanimity is said to be of a single kind.
In this context, the way in which feeling is fivefold by way of its intrinsic differentiation is clearly evident when shown in the section on the course of existence (pavatti).

In order to show the place of its occurrence, the passage beginning with “therein” (*tattha*) is commenced. Regarding the phrase “by unwholesome resultant,” here too the words “associated with body-consciousness” (*kāyaviññāṇena sampayuttaṃ*) should be brought forward and connected.

Just as when one places a tuft of cotton-wool on the top of an anvil and strikes it with an iron hammer, the hammer passes through the tuft of cotton and strikes the anvil; so too [is this consciousness].
Friction is powerful; thus, because of the power of friction through impact, body-consciousness is accompanied by pleasure when the object is desirable or desirable-neutral.

It is accompanied by pain when the object is undesirable or undesirable-neutral; hence he said, "Wholesome... [up to] pain. The five resultant consciousnesses of the sense sphere are accompanied by joy by way of having karma as their object.

There are four resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere by way of kamma; the remaining thirteen are of the sense-sphere, eight are of the fine-material sphere, and thirty-two are supramundane.
These are associated with joy, respectively, by way of mental volition, object, basis, and so forth. Thus it is said: "Joy is associated with sixty-two types of consciousness."
Mental grief (*domanassa*) is associated with two unwholesome consciousnesses by way of mental formations, objects, and so forth.
"The remaining fifty-five" refers to the fifty-five remaining after setting aside the sixty-six consciousnesses already mentioned.

Among those, the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant [consciousnesses] are free from conceptualization regarding desirable and undesirable things, and are associated with pleasure and pain respectively.

Even though they are capable of arising, because the friction and impact between the two sets of two types of derived matter (upādārūpa) are weak—like that between two balls of cotton—the eight consciousnesses supported by the eye and the other sense bases are associated with equanimity (*upekkhā*) in all instances;
likewise, because pleasure and pain have strong conditions, and those [consciousnesses] lack such conditions. These [consciousnesses] arise in dependence on a new object and a new support.
The consciousnesses of adverting and receiving; the registration (voṭṭhabbana), which is the beginning of the commencement of functional activity and serves as the dissimilar immediate condition;
the unwholesome-resultant rebirth-linking and so forth, which serve as the decisive support for the fruit of the unwholesome due to the predominance of bodily pain;
and the sense-sphere wholesome-resultant consciousnesses that arise with desirable or neutral objects—all these are accompanied by equanimity alone.
They exist. Or rather, it is appropriate that there is a state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure toward desirable and undesirable objects when experiencing the result (vipāka) by way of kamma.

And while equanimity exists as the result, being neutral between pleasure and pain, one should understand that for wholesome-resultant [equanimity] there is a state of desirability, and for unwholesome-resultant [equanimity] there is a state of undesirability, by way of the kamma-object. As for the remaining [states]...
Furthermore, thirty-seven types of consciousness are associated with equanimity by way of being mental formations, objects, bases, and so forth;
thus, association with equanimity should be understood through these fifty-five types of consciousness.
The "specific characteristic" (salakkhaṇa) of phenomena is their intrinsic nature (sabhāva) not shared with anything else, and "experiencing" (anubhavana) is the common quality of all feelings.

Regarding the "general characteristic": in order to define it by means of its specific object, he says, "Pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing desirable tangibles," because there is no deviation from this definition.
"Intensification" (upabrūhana) means abundant nourishment or increase.

While this [characteristic] can indeed be found in mental pleasure as well, that [mental pleasure] occurs even through the influence of mental volitional formations (*cetobhisaṅkhāra*) accompanied by conceptualization (*savikappaka*).
But this [factor], because it is established by its own nature, is superior to that; thus he said, "its function is to nourish the associated states.
It is called *assāda* (gratification) because one relishes it; it is pleasant feeling. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent upon the five aggregates of clinging, this, bhikkhus, is called gratification in the five aggregates of clinging."
"Gratification. Because it is dependent on the body, its existence is bodily (*kāyika*); that very gratification manifests in such a way, thus it is "manifested as bodily gratification.
Its proximate cause is the body-faculty, because it does not have any other basis.
The characteristics and other qualities of suffering should be understood according to the method already explained.
Its characteristic is the experiencing of a desirable object, whether by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or by way of conceptual construction (*parikappa*).
Thus it is said: "Its function is the enjoyment of a desirable aspect, in whatever way.

This means that its function is the relishing of an object through a desirable aspect—whether it be as it actually is or not as it actually is—and its role is direct experience. "Its proximate cause is tranquility (*passaddhi*)."
This was stated based on the sutta passage: “With a tranquil body, he experiences happiness. However, that [happiness] should be understood by way of spiritual (nirāmisa) joy (*somanassa*).

The characteristics and other features of mental displeasure (*domanassa*) should be understood as the opposite of what was said regarding joy. Because mental displeasure arises in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), its proximate cause is invariably the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*);

this is its distinction from the former. Equanimity (*upekkhā*) has the characteristic of feeling or experiencing neutrality toward the object; it is so called because such experiencing is its defining mark.
It has the characteristic of feeling that is neutral. Precisely because it experiences what is neutral, its function is neither to over-excite nor to wither the associated mental states.
As for the phrase "manifested as a state of peace," this should be understood in reference to blameless, non-sensual equanimity (*upekkhā*), and not to all types of equanimity.
Thus ends the commentary on the section of the detailed exposition concerning the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-khandha*).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Aggregate of Perception (Saññākkhandhakathāvaṇṇanā) 457.

Regarding the phrase "perception has the characteristic of perceiving," whatever is to be said therein should be understood according to the same method already stated in the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandhaniddesa).
Granted that there is no consciousness dissociated from feeling, nevertheless, because it is distinct from feeling by way of its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva), for some...
Even though it is associated with feeling, it is dissociated from some [other factors]. However, such a thing does not exist for perception;
thus he said: "For that consciousness... [etc. ...not for perception.
"All" means belonging even to the four planes. Alternatively, just as feeling—due to its distinct intrinsic nature—is characterized by the act of feeling and so forth...
It has not been stated thus; rather, this [perception] has the characteristic of perceiving (*sañjānanalakkhaṇā*).
Having made the perception of an object distinguished by blue and so forth into "perception" (*saññā*), its characteristic is knowing; thus it is "that which has the characteristic of perceiving.
For it is said to have the function of re-cognizing (*paccābhiññāṇarasa*) because it perceives through recognition. Indeed, its task is to perceive again by means of a sign (*nimitta*).

It has the function of recognition (*paccābhiññāṇa*). Its occurrence should be understood at the time of recognizing by means of that mark (*abhiññāṇa*) after a carpenter has made a mark on a piece of wood.
Therefore he said, "This is that very same thing," and so forth. Furthermore, the condition for re-cognizing is the "condition for re-cognizing" (*puna-sañjānana-paccaya*);
that is, the sign itself is the "sign for re-cognizing," the making of that [sign] is the "making for re-cognizing," and it is that which constitutes the condition for re-cognizing.
Furthermore, the making of a sign (*nimittakaraṇa*)... [as before] ...is its function. Thus, its essential property (*rasa*) is the making of a sign as a condition for subsequent cognition.

The making of a sign for the purpose of subsequent cognition should be applied equally to all types of perception (*saññā*), whether it be that which makes a sign or that which cognizes by means of a sign.
The making of an insistence (*abhinivesakaraṇa*) refers merely to the insistence of perception in the form: "This alone is the truth."
It should be seen [as such], because its proximate cause is the object as it presents itself, and because its intrinsic nature is non-conceptualizing.
However, perception associated with knowledge follows knowledge itself; therefore, it does not produce misinterpretation nor does it grasp things erroneously.

By this very fact, it should be understood that because it is associated with concentration, it does not persist for long. Thus, [it is distinguished] from that which is associated with lust, views, conceit, and so forth.
The state of perception being a follower of lust and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the introductory exposition of the aggregate of perception (*saññākkhandha*).
Now follows the commentary on the discourse concerning the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
458. "The characteristic of making things relishable" means the characteristic of combining; therefore, formations (*saṅkhāra*) are said to have the function of accumulating.

For it is because volition (*cetanā*) is predominant that the phenomena of the formation aggregate (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) are described in this way. Thus he said: "But what is that? It is just the formations," and so forth.
In that context, "they form the conditioned" means they bring about their own fruit as something conditioned.
The meaning is that they "form" [them] in such a way that they are properly brought to completion. Regarding the phrase "manifesting as diffusion" (*vipphāra-paccupaṭṭhāna*):
here, "diffusion" (*vipphāra*) means the state of being expansive; therefore, the meaning is "manifesting with active effort" (*sabyāpāra*).

They are "determined" (*niyata*) because they necessarily arise whenever that particular consciousness arises. "They come with their own specific form" (*sarūpena āgatā*); thus it is said in the *Piṭṭhivattaka*.
They have been mentioned in their own specific forms as they appear in the Pāḷi. They are called "indeterminate" (aniyata) because they arise only occasionally and are not fixed.
Although they are indeterminate and do not arise together at once, they are said to be "thirty-six" because they possess the nature of arising within that same consciousness.
Therefore he said: "And even when they do arise, they do not arise all together."
459. "Touches" (*phusati*) is a designation for the agent. The reason for this has already been stated above.

Alternatively, contact (*phassa*) is that by means of which one touches; for the associated mental states, while occurring toward an object, act as if they are touching it by means of contact characterized by the act of touching.
Or, contact is the mere touching of the object; thus all three modes of grammatical derivation (*sādhana*) are indeed appropriate.

Regarding phenomena as states (bhāvadhamma), an expression that functions as an agent, instrument, or object is a figurative discourse (pariyāyakathā) because it superimposes those forms [of action] upon them;

an expression functioning solely as a state (bhāvasādhanavacana) is non-figurative discourse (nippariyāyakathā). Thus it is said: "having the characteristic of touching" (phusanalakkhaṇo). The passage beginning with "For this...

and so forth is an establishment of the aforementioned characteristics and other qualities. If this dharma is mental (cetasika), then being an immaterial phenomenon (arūpadhamma), how can it have the characteristic of touching, or possess such functions as impact (saṅghaṭṭana) and so on?
And because it "exists," having placed the internal accusation in his heart, he said, "Even though it is an immaterial phenomenon (*arūpadhamma*)," and so forth, for the purpose of clearing it away.
Therein, by the phrase "it occurs precisely in the mode of touching," he demonstrates that this is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of that phenomenon, even though it is immaterial.
And that occurrence of its mode of touching [is like] that of one who sees someone eating sour mangoes and the like.
It becomes clearly manifest in such instances as: the arising of saliva at the sight of another; the trembling of the body of a compassionate person upon seeing another being tormented;
the quivering of the legs of a timid man standing on the ground when he sees a man precariously perched on the tip of a tree branch;
and the stiffness of the thighs upon seeing something to be feared, such as a malevolent spirit (pisāca).
"By one side" means by one of its own sides, like two pieces of wood and so forth. "Even though not adhering" means even though not clinging together.
The commonality between contact (*phassa*) and visible forms and sounds is simply the lack of adherence and non-collision, not the state of being an object (*visaya*).
Just as visible forms and sounds are said to be "touched" and so forth even while not adhering to the eye and ear respectively, so it is with contact as well.
"Contacting, touching, and colliding with the object. Colliding (*saṅghaṭṭana*) is precisely the state of the convergence of consciousness, the object, and the sense base.
Therefore, it is said: "It causes the consciousness and the object to collide. It is described as having the function of colliding by way of its essential property (*rasa*).
Alternatively, because it is accomplished through the meeting of the sense base and the object, contact is "accomplished by colliding," and thus it has the function of colliding.

It has been said. Just as in such expressions as "two hands might strike each other," the striking of one hand against the other and the material phenomena (rūpa-dhammas) that constitute its specific qualities are to be understood, so too should the striking of the mind against its object and the single mental factor (cetasika-dhamma) that constitutes its specific quality be understood.
This is because of the statement, "The meeting of the three is contact" (tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso), which refers to the meeting of the eye, visible form, and consciousness, and so forth.
Because it is to be grasped, he says, "of that which is designated as the triad-conjunction," and so forth. The appropriate attention (*tajjā-samannāhāra*) is the cause of that contact;

it is the state of the faculty being directed toward that [object], the making of the object by adverting (*āvajjanā*), the preparedness and conditioning of the sense-field, and the making of the object for consciousness—this is the meaning. Just as...
Just as a flayed cow encounters nothing but suffering wherever it goes, so too, when there is contact, feeling necessarily arises.
And since feeling has the nature of a dart of suffering and the like, it is said: "But because it is the basis for feeling, it should be regarded as being like a flayed cow."
460. It binds together, connects, and sets in motion. Its nature is volition (*cetanā*), its nature is activity.

"Exertion" (*āyūhana*) means intending, moving. "Arranging" (*saṃvidahana*) means investigating. When volition, whose function is exertion, is active, all associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) become intent upon their respective functions;
thus it is said to accomplish both its own function and the functions of others. It is like an elder pupil among others.
Encouraging others to recite, she herself also recites. When the Great Carpenter has begun his carpentry work, the others do likewise.
"By way of instigation" means by way of showing respect; for she, being herself respectful, causes the associated mental states to be respectful as well.
Instigation should be understood here in the sense of application, not in the sense of the instigation of energy (*vīriya*).
461. *Vīrabhāva*: the meaning is that it is the quality (*dhamma*) by which one becomes a hero (*vīra*).
Or, it is energy (*vīriya*), exertion, the undertaking of various tasks, or striving (*parakkama*), because it is to be impelled or set in motion according to the proper method (*vidhi*).

*Upatthambhana* is the supporting, the upholding, or the providing of reinforcement for associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) by not allowing them to fall into the side of indolence (*kosajja-pakkha*); or it is the grasping [of them] correctly. It is the opposite of sinking (*saṃsīdana*).

The Dhamma is non-sinking; it is not merely the absence of sinking. Thus, because it stands as the state of non-sinking, it is said to have "non-sinking as its manifestation" (*asaṃsīdanabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna*).
It has "agitation as its proximate cause" (*saṃvegapadaṭṭhāna*) in the sense that it is the basis for the exertion of energy in wholesome activity preceded by the eight kinds of agitation.
"The path is to be traveled; the path has been traveled; the work..."
“[The task] must be done; the task has been done; a slight ailment has arisen; he has recovered from illness;
having recently recovered from illness, while wandering for alms in a village or town, he does not obtain a sufficient quantity of coarse or refined food;
[or] he obtains... [up to] a sufficient quantity”—these [cases] are stated together with their corresponding reflections.
The eight bases for the arousal of energy, or the reflections rooted therein.
462. The function of life is the preservation of the co-nascent states that must be preserved by itself;
and since this is their "living," it is said with reference to its status as their cause: "they live by means of it. That too...
Since its meaning is simply living, he says: "Or rather, it is merely living. (463) It "places" means it establishes.
Non-distraction (*avisāra*) is the very nature of not wandering away from itself.
Non-distraction (*avikkhepa*) is the state of non-wandering of the associated states. That state by which the associated states become non-wandering is "non-distraction."
It is "manifested as peace" because it stands present in the mode of pacifying the mind by being the opposite of distraction, which is characterized by lack of peace.
"In particular" means for the most part; for there is indeed concentration that is devoid of happiness.
By the illustration of the lamp's flame, he shows the state of stability in the continuity of concentration.
464. "They believe by means of this" indicates that faith is the condition for those phenomena occurring through the act of believing, by virtue of its sovereignty over them.
For when phenomena possess such a conditional relationship, there arises the conventional expression, "the person believes.
Believing (*saddahana*) is the conviction regarding the object to be believed; since this is its characteristic, it is called "characterized by believing" (*saddahanalakkhaṇā*).
"Characterized by conviction" (*okappanalakkhaṇā*) means having the characteristic of determining, thinking "it is thus," after having entered into [the object].

Its "function of clarification" (*pasādanarasa*) is that which, having dispelled the stain of turbidity, produces clarity for its associated mental factors or for the person themselves, making them free from agitation.
"Leaping forward" (*pakkhandana*) is the entering into the object by way of resolute confidence (*adhimuccanavasena*). "Non-turbid nature" (*akālussiya*) is the state of being untroubled.
The meaning is "a state free from turbidity. In objects that inspire confidence, unwholesome lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) and wrong resolve (*micchā-adhimutti*) are the opposites of confidence.

The term "confidence" (*pasāda*) refers specifically to a decisive conviction (*nicchaya*) directed toward its object, which is the antidote to those states; it does not refer to the mere mental factor of resolve (*adhimokkha*) included among the general mental concomitants.

The Three Jewels, karma, and the fruit of karma are the objects of faith (*saddheyyavatthu*). Associating with virtuous persons, hearing the true Dhamma, appropriate attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), and practice in accordance with the Dhamma are the factors [that lead to confidence].

The factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅgāni) should be regarded as being like a hand for grasping wholesome states, like wealth for bestowing all forms of prosperity, and like a seed for producing the fruit of the deathless. 465.
They are called "refuges" (saraṇa) because they exercise sovereignty over those phenomena that proceed as the act of taking refuge.

It shows the conditionality of mindfulness. For when there is such a state of being a condition for mental phenomena, there arises the conventional expression that "the person possessing it remembers.

Non-floating—meaning not allowing [the mind] to drift away like a gourd in water, but rather fixing it upon an object so that it remains motionless like a stone—is "remembering" (*saraṇa*), which is the act of making [the object] non-forgetful. It is the function opposed to confusion.
It is non-forgetfulness, not merely the absence of forgetfulness. Because of the statement, "with a mind guarded by mindfulness," it has the manifestation of guarding (*ārakkha*).
It is called *sati* because, coming from elsewhere, it faces toward the object of consciousness; thus, it is the state of being directed toward the object.

The body and so forth, which serve as the basis for mindfulness, are themselves the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) regarding the body and so forth; or else, preceding mindfulness itself is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for subsequent mindfulness.
466. In the phrase "by bodily misconduct, etc.," the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). "Is ashamed" (*hiriyati*) means one feels disgust in the manner of modesty.
"By those very things" means by bodily misconduct and so forth themselves. "Is afraid" (*ottappati*) means one is terrified.

Since modesty (*hirī*) feels disgust upon seeing evil states as if they were excrement, it is said: "Modesty has the characteristic of disgust for evil. Fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) [views them] as if they were hot.
It is said that one who is observing [an object] trembles at it; thus, "the characteristic of trembling is *ottappa* (moral dread).

"In the manner described" means by way of the mode of shame (*lajjā*) and the mode of trembling. *Hirī* (self-respect) has self-reverence as its proximate cause because it arises internally and has the self as its dominant influence.
*Ottappa* (moral dread) has other-reverence as its proximate cause because it arises externally and has the world as its dominant influence. This same point:
To make it more evident, the passage beginning with “one who has self” (*attānaṃ hi*) was stated.

Furthermore, the fact that moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) originate internally and so forth is stated because they are manifest in various contexts; however, there is never any dissociation between these two.

For there is no shameless state devoid of fear, nor is there a dread of evil that is not accompanied by shame. Regarding the term “guardians of the world” (*lokapālaka*), here [it refers to]: “Bhikkhus, these two... [and so on].
The scriptural passage, “Bright qualities protect the world,” refers to the predominance of the self (*attādhipati*).

Regarding the state of predominance over the world (*lokādhipatibhāva*), one should cite the scriptural passages: “Having made the self alone his own master, having made the world alone his own master.
(467) Since non-greed (*alobha*) is the opposite of greed, those phenomena associated with it, or the beings endowed with it, [are what protect the world].
Because of that, they do not become greedy; they themselves never become greedy at any time, or rather, it is simply the state of non-greediness in its essential meaning.

Therefore, it is said: "they do not become greedy," and so forth. "The same method applies" refers by extension to the application of the three factors of agency in the phrase "they do not become corrupt through that," and so on.

Non-covetousness (*agedha*) means the absence of coveting, the absence of longing. The state of being unattached (*alagga-bhāva*) is the absence of clinging (*anāsatta-tā*). Non-possessiveness (*apariggaha*).
It is the non-grasping of any object by way of the sense of "mine. That whose nature or intention (*adhippāya*) is not clinging is "one whose nature is unclinging" (*anallīnabhāva*).
For it is in this way that it accords with the simile. 468.
The state of being fierce is *caṇḍikka*, which is anger. Its opposite is *acaṇḍikka*, which is non-malice (*abyāpāda*). It is non-opposition.

"Without conflict" (*aviggaha*): a friend who is compliant and one who acts in accordance [with one's needs]. "The essence of discipline" (*vinayarasa*): the flavor of training. "Serenity" (*sommabhāva*):

the state of being refreshing by way of cleansing. (469) "Penetration according to the true nature" (*yathāsabhāvapaṭivedha*): the penetration of each and every intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena just as it is.
"Unwavering penetration" (*akkhalitapaṭivedha*): penetration without stumbling or failing. "Illumination of the object": the dispelling of the darkness of delusion that obscures it.
It is the manifestation of the object. It stands present in the manner of non-delusion regarding any object whatsoever;
or, because it is the opposite of delusion, it establishes the absence of that [delusion], thus it is "having non-delusion as its manifestation" (*asammoha-paccupaṭṭhāna*).
It is the "foundation" (*patiṭṭhā*) because it serves as the basis for all wholesome states by establishing the well-firm footing of all wholesome phenomena belonging to the four planes; it is not...

By means of establishing their state as wholesome (*kusala*). For if their wholesomeness were dependent upon the wholesome roots (*kusalamūla*), then, that being the case, there would be no conditionality by way of cause (*hetupaccayatā*) for the material phenomena (*rūpa*) originated by them.

Indeed, those [roots] do not establish the state of wholesomeness and so forth for those [phenomena], yet they are not non-conditions. For this has been said: "Roots [are conditions] for the states associated with roots..."
“And it is a condition, by way of root-cause, for the material phenomena originating from it.
Just as the state of being wholesome (kusala) is dependent upon wholesome roots, so too the state of being indeterminate (abyākata) would have to be dependent upon indeterminate roots.

If that were the case, the state of being indeterminate could not exist in rootless consciousnesses (ahetuka-citta), and in unwholesome states where there is only a single root, that [state] would lack the quality of being unwholesome; yet both [states] certainly do exist.
Therefore, the state of being wholesome and so forth is not dependent on roots; rather, it is dependent on wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and the like.
However, it should be understood that the roots are what establish their well-established nature. 470.
*Passambhana* is the subsiding of distress. The word "body" (*kāya*) denotes a collection, and that refers specifically to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).
He said: "And here, 'body' refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. For this very reason he said:
"In that context, what at that time is bodily tranquility? It is that which, at that time, belongs to the aggregate of feeling," and so forth. "Distress" (daratha) means agitation;
it is a designation for the defilements characterized by restlessness that are conditioned by mental displeasure, or for the four aggregates as they occur in such a manner.
The state of coolness, free from the burning and agitation [caused by] the crushing of the dart, is "coolness without agitation.
The defilements dominated by restlessness are the "defilements beginning with restlessness"; alternatively, it includes all defilements by taking restlessness as the first.
The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

Heaviness (*garubhāva*) is sluggishness; it is a designation for those [states] predominant in sloth and torpor, or for the four aggregates occurring in that manner. Non-sluggishness (*adandhatā*) is the opposite of sluggishness, not merely the absence of sluggishness.
Rigidity (*thambha*) is stiffness; it is the name for those [states] predominant in views and conceit, or for the four aggregates having those as their primary factors.
Because they crush out rigidity, they present themselves toward certain objects in an unimpeded manner.
Or, it is "manifesting as non-resistance" because it presents non-resistance toward the associated states therein.
"Wieldiness" (*kammañña*) means fit for action; "unwieldiness" (*akammañña*) is the state of being unfit for action, which is the unfitness for meritorious deeds such as giving and virtue.
In terms of its meaning, it consists of the defiled states such as sensual desire, or the four unwholesome aggregates that have those as their predominance.
The perfection of making an object the focal point (*ārammaṇakaraṇasampatti*) is the grasping of the object in its perfected mode by means of that very wieldiness (*kammaññabhāva*).
The remaining factors mentioned—sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and so forth—as well as the defilements associated with them, such as the other hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), are the obstacles.

They bring about clarity (*pasāda*) toward objects that inspire confidence because they cause the mind to proceed happily through the crushing of its fetters. It is like the purification of gold; just as...
Just as gold that is purified, free from dross, and fit for use in various ornaments, so too this [mind] is fit for the application of beneficial action through the departure of defilement.
The sickness of body and mind consists of lack of faith and so forth, along with the evil states associated therewith. The antidote to this sickness is...

The state of being free from illness is *agelañña*; these [faculties] have that as their characteristic, thus they are "characterized by the state of freedom from illness. Precisely because of the crushing of the aforementioned illness, there is no disadvantage (*ādīnava*) or defect in them;
nor do they proceed toward what is wretched (*ādīna*), thus they are "free from disadvantage" (*nirādīnavā*).

They present themselves in that manner, or they cause that [freedom from disadvantage] to be presented among the associated states, thus they are "presented as free from disadvantage" (*nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhānā*).
It has the characteristic of rectitude of body and mind because it is defined as the state of being straight in relation to both body and mind.
Its function is to crush out the crookedness of body and mind, which is reckoned as the curvature of a plough’s head, the crescent of a new moon, or the curve of a cow’s tail.
For that very reason, it establishes itself in every way through its state of non-crookedness.
Or, it is called "having the manifestation of non-crookedness" because it presents non-crookedness to the associated states.
Deceit (*māyā*) has the characteristic of concealing existing faults; craftiness (*sāṭheyya*) has the characteristic of making unreal qualities appear real.

These are the unwholesome aggregates that arise in such a mode, as well as the defiled states associated with them, such as deceit, craftiness, and so forth. And here, by means of mental tranquility (*cittapassaddhi*) and the rest...
The mind itself becomes tranquil, light, malleable, wieldy, proficient, and straight. However, through bodily tranquility and the other factors, the material body (rūpakāya) also becomes so.
For this very reason, the Blessed One has stated here that phenomena are twofold, but not in all instances.
471. *Chanda* is desire; it is the state of being interested in an object. In such passages as "desire is lust," however, it is also used to denote craving (*taṇhā*).

In such passages as “he generates desire and exerts effort,” energy (*vīriya*) is also mentioned; therefore, in order to distinguish it [from that], it is stated: “this is a designation for the desire to act.

The desire to act is called the wish to perform. And because a mental state (*cetasika-dhamma*) possesses an object (*sārammaṇa*), this wish to act occurs only by way of the desire to grasp an object of focus;
thus, its characteristic is the wish to take an object as one’s focus.
Chanda is said to have the characteristic of the desire to act. For this very reason, it is said: "Its function is the seeking of an object; its manifestation is the need for an object.
To the extent that this [chanda] has the function of seeking an object for itself, to that same extent it also belongs to the associated states because they share a single object.
For this reason, it is said: "In the grasping of an object, this is the stretching out of the hand of the mind."
...should be regarded as being like that. This desire, when arisen in regard to wholesome states, is called “wholesome desire” because it originates from wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).
472. Resolute confidence (*adhimuccana*) should be understood as a form of decision regarding the object, not as a form of serene clarity (*pasāda*).

For resolute confidence is simply the settling upon an object in whatever way it may be; whereas for one who lacks such confidence, [there is no such settling] regarding killing and so forth, or regarding giving and so forth.
Or because of the absence of [such] activity; however, faith (*saddhā*) is the resolution of confidence toward things that inspire confidence—this is the distinction between them.

As for determining (*voṭṭhabbana*), having proceeded by way of deciding upon the meaning as it has been investigated, it serves as a condition for subsequent mindfulness and wisdom to proceed in that same manner. If this is so, how is it in the case of those associated with doubt (*vicikicchā*)? For them too...
It should be understood that this is a condition for the mode of creeping along exclusively in one direction.
Non-creeping is the performance of an opposing action to the indecision—such as "I shall do" or "I shall not do"—that occurs in a child as it creeps here and there.
In those mental states where this resolve (adhimokkha) characterized by determination exists, the object-dhamma itself is the dhamma to be determined.

473. "Kiriyā kāro" (action is the doing) expresses that the word *kāra* has the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*). "In the mind, the doing" (*manasmiṃ kāro*) means the making of the object in the mind.

For by that [mental state] the mind is made to act upon the object because it is conjoined with the object; for that very reason, the object is also made the focus of the mind (*manasi karīyati*) by it.
"From the preceding mind" means from the life-continuum mind (*bhavaṅgamanas*). "Dissimilar mind" refers to the cognitive process (*vīthi*) and the impulsion (*javana*).
"Directs the mind" (*manasikaroti*) indicates, by way of the general term *manasikāra*, that which initiates the cognitive process (*vīthi*) and its impulsion (*javana*).
Because it is as if bringing the associated states toward the object, *manasikāra* is said to have the characteristic of "directing" (*sāraṇa*).
Its manifestation is the state of being directed toward the object by way of mindfulness’s quality of non-forgetfulness. As for *manasikāra*:
However, their distinction lies in this: [the former] has the state of being directed toward an object as its manifestation by way of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The statement that the factor which leads to the object is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) merely indicates that other types of attention are included within the other aggregates;

having thus indicated them, in order to show how they are subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*), the passage beginning with “that which leads along the cognitive process” (*vīthipaṭipādaka*) was stated.
474. "In those states" means in those mental states—the mind and mental factors—with which one is oneself associated and which have arisen.
Even though they lack an object, because they proceed with equanimity toward those [states] that are proceeding evenly, they are called "equanimity toward the middle.
"Characterized by even conveyance" means characterized by proceeding evenly—that is, without partiality—in their respective functions. By way of this state of equanimity...
For even while it is itself occurring, this [volition] causes the associated states to proceed in their respective functions;

just as a king, though sitting silently, causes his ministers—who are established in the Dhamma and intent on their duties—to proceed in their respective functions. Its function is to act as a condition for a state of proceeding that is neither sluggish nor agitated, and its essence is the prevention of deficiency or excess.
This is stated by way of its specific activity (kicca). If this is so, how is it with regard to co-nascent predominance (sahajātādhipati)?
That too is simply its function. As for the statement that it is the state of predominance (adhipatibhāva) over co-nascent phenomena, its occurrence in that manner is likewise its very function;

thus, there is no fault here. The intention is that "partiality" (pakkhapāta) refers to an occurrence as if through favoritism, such as thinking, "Let this have a lesser function, let this have a greater function"; [the predominance] acts as if cutting off such partiality.
By the phrase “they desire [it] among the indeterminate states,” it is shown that they desire it as a distinct mental factor (*cetasika*). Loving-kindness (*mettā*) is simply non-hatred (*adosa*);

for it is that very same state which is defined by such terms as “loving-kindness, the act of loving-kindness,” and so forth. As for equanimity (*upekkhā*), that which they conceive of as being together with loving-kindness is precisely the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
475. “The bases for bodily misconduct, etc. refers to the lives of others, the property of others, the wives of others, and so forth. “Non-crushing” is the state of being the opposite of crushing.

It should be understood that by means of the expression “the act of shrinking away from the bases for bodily misconduct, etc.,” it is actually the act of shrinking away from bodily misconduct itself that is stated.
For it would not be logical for the abstentions to have the non-performance of the bases for misconduct as their manifestation.

Now, the distinction between these is as follows: the contraction of misconduct through the influence of the virtues of abstinence (*soracca*), and the shrinking away from non-performance through the influence of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), such as by means of disgust and so forth.

(476) "Formations" (*saṅkhārā*) is said with reference to the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*); for it is those that are intended here, otherwise there would be thirty-eight.
It should be stated. Just as with the consciousness, so too its associated states are "with volitional formations" (sasaṅkhāra) in the second [jhāna];
thus he says, "In this case, the distinction is merely the state of being with volitional formations. The remaining factors are those mentioned in the first [jhāna].
Regarding the statement, "The remaining ones enter into association with the fifth," how is it in the case of those accompanied by compassion, gladness, and equanimity?

Why do they arise? Because they exist as preliminary stages (*pubbabhāga*). For it is only when [compassion and gladness] have reached absorption (*appanā*) that they are not accompanied by equanimity;
however, the teachers maintain that elsewhere they may also be accompanied by equanimity.
Through the settling of the mind, there occurs the manifestation of wholesome states pertaining to the fine-material and immaterial spheres, based on well-purified bodily action and so forth.

Since abstinences are impossible in sublime states of consciousness (mahaggata-cittuppāda)—neither by way of purifying bodily actions and so forth, nor by way of uprooting or pacifying misconduct and wrong livelihood—it is said, “excluding the three abstinences.

“From that” means from the mental factors mentioned in the first fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) state. “Those very same” refers to the mental factors mentioned in the fifth fine-material-sphere state.
If it is asked, "What is the distinction from the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara)? he says: "For the very state of being immaterial (arūpāvacara) is the distinction here.

Regarding the phrase "possessing the first jhāna" (paṭhamajjhānika), it means "having the first jhāna. The connection is that [the distinctions] should be understood in the same manner as stated for all four kinds of path-consciousness (maggaviññāṇa).
Regarding the phrase "in the path-consciousness distinguished by the second jhāna, etc.," the word "etc. (ādi) includes those possessing the third, fourth, and fifth jhānas.
He includes [them]. To the objection—“In the manner stated”—asking whether this is said without distinction, he says “Of compassion and gladness,” and so forth, showing that [distinction].

Therein, because the path-consciousnesses have Nibbāna as their object, while compassion and gladness have sentient beings as their object, there is no possibility of those two [latter] occurring therein.
Furthermore, among the factors of the path, due to the fixed order of the foundations and so on, there may at times be an absence of right intention.

However, it is not "certainty of abstinence" (niyataviratitā) because the Noble Path proceeds by way of the total eradication of bodily misconduct and so forth, rather than merely through the absence of abstinence. 478.
One who does not feel shame or modesty is *ahirika*—this refers to a person, the mind, or the aggregate of states associated with that [mind].
Although one should say *ahirikka*, the single letter *k* is elided, and thus it is called *ahirika*. "Na... [does not]"... [shame]... [is]... [ahirika].
"Ottappa" refers to the state that is the opposite of moral dread (*ottappa*). It means a lack of disgust and a lack of reproach; it is shamelessness (*alajjā*) and lack of moral scruple (*aviriḷā*).
"By those very things" means by bodily misconduct and so forth. "Fearlessness" (*asārajja*) is the state of being without fear. "Lack of trepidation" (*anuttāsa*) is the absence of agitation.

"By way of the opposites of what was stated" means that *ahirika* has the function of committing evil through the mode of shamelessness, while [the other] has the function [of committing evil] through the mode of lack of trepidation.
Lack of moral dread (*anottappa*)—in the manner already described—is manifested by the absence of shrinking away from evil; its proximate cause is a lack of reverence for oneself and for others.
Just as a village pig feels no disgust toward filth, so one feels no loathing for the defilements, which are filthy with impurity, because of a lack of shame (*ahirika*);
just as a moth feels no fear of fire, so one feels no terror of evil because of a lack of moral dread (*anottappa*). Thus, the detailed exposition should be understood by way of these opposites.
479. Regarding the passage beginning with "They are lusted after by that," whatever is to be said should be understood according to the method explained below.
"Lusted after" (lubbhanti) means they covet. "Deluded" (muyhanti) means they do not understand.
"Grasping at an object" (ārammaṇaggahaṇaṃ) is not merely making something an object; it is the non-relinquishing of an object through adhering to it by way of craving and the conceit "this is mine."
Attachment (*abhisaṅga*) is clinging by way of being directed toward [an object]. Non-relinquishment is not letting go, or rather, the state of being difficult to release.
Seeing gratification is the view of gratification; for it is said: "And for one who contemplates gratification, craving increases.
(480) The blindness of the mind is the non-perception of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) as it actually is. Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is the opposite of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Inability to penetrate is non-penetration (*asampaṭivedha*). Just as it is impossible for knowledge to penetrate the intrinsic nature of an object, so too the occurrence of delusion is the obscuring of the intrinsic nature of the object.
It manifests as wrong practice, or it is grasped as being the opposite of right practice; thus, it is said to "manifest as wrong practice. Of which...
It arises; its "darkness" (*andhakāra*) is that which causes blindness, and because it presents itself in such a way, it is said to have darkness as its manifestation (*andhakārapaccupaṭṭhāna*).

481. "Wrongly" (*micchā*) means contrary to the true nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena; the meaning is "as permanent," and so forth. "Improper mental fixation" (*ayoniso abhiniveso*) is fixation by means of an incorrect method, or fixation upon a wrong path.
"Misapprehension" (*parāmāso*) is the grasping of something external after having transcended the true nature of phenomena. This is by way of a perverted grasp.
“Only this is true, anything else is false”—this kind of dogmatic adherence is wrong adherence (*micchābhiniveso*).
That state by virtue of which the mind becomes agitated, or the states associated with it, is restlessness (*uddhacca*).
“Lack of tranquility” (*avūpasamo*) refers to a state of non-settling and lack of serenity. Its function is non-stability (*anavaṭṭhānarasa*), meaning its activity is to cause wavering.
"Bhantatta" means the state of wandering about. Regarding "the non-quiescence of the mind," the locative case is used in the sense of the purpose to be accomplished;

or else, the object which serves as the condition for non-quiescence is called "non-quiescence. Because unwholesome states are exclusively inferior, it is said that they are "base by way of being unwholesome."

483. "Lethargy and drowsiness (*thīnamiddha*) here are indeterminate; it is not pride (*māna*) and so forth"—this is the indeterminacy of lethargy and drowsiness, and it constitutes the distinction of this second unwholesome consciousness from the first.

"Lethargy" (*thina*) is the state of being congealed through lack of exertion and a tendency toward sinking; because the mind is joined with that, it is "lethargic," and its abstract state is "lethargy-ness" (*thinatā*).
"Drowsiness" (*middha*) is unwieldiness due to incapacity and exhaustion. Because of that very [drowsiness], the mental factors associated with it [are likewise affected].
Because one’s capacity for mental exertion (*medhitā*) is destroyed, it is called “torpor” (*middha*). Its characteristic is the absence of effort;
that is, its characteristic is the opposite of exertion (*ussāha*). The dispelling or casting away of energy is the “dispelling of energy” (*vīriyāvanodana*).
It stands present by way of causing the associated states to sink, or it brings about their sinking; thus, it is “manifested as sinking” (*saṃsīdanapaccupaṭṭhāna*).

Regarding the phrase "having the characteristic of unwieldiness" (*akammaññatālakkhaṇa*): while it is true that lethargy (*thina*) also has the essential nature of being unwieldy, there is this distinction here: lethargy belongs to the mind, whereas drowsiness (*middha*) belongs to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling. For thus it is said in the Pāḷi: "In this context, what is lethargy?
That which is the mind’s lack of fitness, its unwieldiness. In this context, what is drowsiness? That which is the body’s lack of fitness..."
The exposition of these [factors] proceeds with the words beginning, “unwieldiness” and so forth. *Onahanam* means the closing up, the shutting of the doors of consciousness.
*Līnatā* is the state of being sluggish; it is a contraction in the grasping of the object.

Since through *thina* (sloth) there is a stiffening of the mind alone, whereas through *middha* (torpor) there is a stiffening of the three aggregates—feeling and the rest—as well as of the physical body, therefore that [latter] is drowsiness and sleep.

"Manifests" (*paccupaṭṭhapeti*) refers to the manifestation of drowsiness and sleepiness (*pacalāyikā-niddā*). "Dislike" (*arati*) is the lack of inclination toward secluded lodgings and toward wholesome qualities.
"Stretching" (*vijambhikā*) is the occurrence of defilement that serves as the cause for the bodily languor known as stretching.

In the phrase "dislike, stretching, and so forth" (*arativijambhikādīsu*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes sloth (*tandi*) and other such factors. [This occurs] when there is a purpose to be accomplished.
This is a locative expression.
The remaining sixteen [factors] are fixed; however, conceit (*māna*) here is indeterminate, and thus there are seventeen altogether.
For in the *Paṭṭhāna*, in the passage: “Dependent on a fettered state, a fettered state arises by way of root-condition,” it occurs four times.
Regarding sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), repulsion (*paṭigha*) three times, conceit (*māna*), doubt (*vicikicchā*), and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*):
these three are shown as the tenfold fettering by means of the fetters of the once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*).

Having stated, "In dependence on the fetter of sensual lust, there are the fetter of conceit and the fetter of ignorance," it then says, "In dependence on the fetter of sensual lust, there is the fetter of ignorance."
Likewise, having stated, "Dependent on the fetter of conceit, there are the fetters of lust for existence and ignorance" (*Paṭṭhāna* 3.4.1),
and further stating, "Dependent on the fetter of lust for existence, there is the fetter of ignorance," the fact that conceit is not fixed is clarified by these applications.
For if conceit were fixed, there would be no occurrence of sensual lust devoid of conceit.

The same would apply to attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*). If this were so, then in the *Paṭṭhāna*, there would not be four instances of conjunction with sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), but only three;
nor would there be [a case] rooted in attachment to existence. Furthermore, the conjunction of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) by means of the fetters would then be eightfold rather than tenfold.
Yet, it is shown as being tenfold. This is by way of "lying down" (*seyyā*) and so forth.

Elevation (*unnati*) is the act of raising oneself up. Its function is grasping (*sampaggaha*) precisely by way of this upward lifting; it is not, like energy (*vīriya*), by way of exertion in the accomplishment of various tasks.
It should be understood that even in the case of self-depreciation (*omāna*), the grasping of oneself as inferior occurs by way of this very same grasping.
A "banner" (*ketu*) is called a lofty flag; however, here it means "like a banner," referring to a state of being most excellent and so forth.
It is called *ketukamyatā* because the mind desires that banner (*ketu*) which is designated as the state of being a banner.
That phenomenon by virtue of which there is this desire for the banner is *ketukamyatā*. Because it proceeds with the thought "I," its mode of occurrence is similar to that of views;

therefore, it does not arise in the same momentary consciousness as a view, and since it is dependent upon self-love (*attasineha*), it is said to have "greed dissociated from views" as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*).
In this context as well, the word "ca" (and) draws in *thīnamiddha* (sloth and torpor).

485. *Dussanti* means they become corrupted. *Caṇḍikka* is anger. Its function is to spread out according to its own mode of occurrence and by way of giving rise to unsightly crawling forms and undesirable appearances.
Its function is to burn its own support by causing the body to reach a state of putrefaction. *Dussana* (corruption).

He shows that it must not be accepted in any way whatsoever by stating that, at the time of enjoying oneself or another, [envy] is undesirable, and should be viewed as like putrid urine mixed with poison. 486.
Showing that the act of being envious toward the prosperity of others is "envy" (*issā*), he says: "The state of envying is envy. Envy (*usūyana*).
"Intolerance. "In that very place" means precisely regarding the prosperity of others. The function of envy (*issā*) is the opposite of delight;
it is not merely the absence of delight. Therefore, he says: "Its essence is non-delight. 487.
Having taken the word *macchariya* as it occurs in the sense of "one who possesses stinginess" (*macchara-yogena maccharī*), he says: "The state of stinginess (*macchara-bhāva*)."

Regarding “macchariya”: according to the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), however, the ancients say it is *macchariya* because one thinks, “Let this wonder (*acchariya*) not belong to others; let it belong to me alone.
That envy (*macchariya*) persists by exhausting the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and other qualities that are being described.
Its manifestation is contraction (*saṅkocana*); it manifests as contraction by making one’s own excellences non-common to others.
Bitterness of character is a state of harshness and irritability.
Self-accomplishment refers to one’s dwelling and so forth. (488) Regarding the term *kukata*: here, even that which has not been done is indeed *kukata*.

For people speak thus: "That which was not done by me is a *kukata*. Likewise, it will be said later: "Its function is to brood over what has been done and what has not been done. Thus, misconduct consists of both what has been done and what has not been done.

Regarding good conduct and misconduct: the mind that arises by way of remorse (vippaṭisāra) with respect to those two should be understood here as "misconduct" (*kukata*) because it is concomitant with them;
thus it is said, "the state of that is remorse" (*kukkucca*). Subsequent regret and vexation is "subsequent remorse" (*pacchānutāpa*).
This refers to the misconduct and good conduct distinguished by the manner in which they were performed or not performed.
Remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) is a deformed resort by way of lamentation.

Because it is caused by dependence on another, it should be regarded as like slavery. For just as when there is slavery, a slave is dependent on another, so too when there is remorse, one who possesses it [is dependent].
Indeed, he is not able to proceed toward the wholesome by his own nature. Alternatively, it is the lamenting over what has been done and what has not been done, whether unwholesome or wholesome.
Because of being dependent on both of those, one possesses remorse (*kukkucca*); thus, it is like slavery.

Regarding envy (*issā*) and the rest among the undetermined states, the word "only" (*eva*) should be supplied after "the very occurrence of sloth and torpor" (*thinamiddhasambhava*) and connected [to the sentence]. 490.
"Merely the duration of its occurrence" means merely the duration of a single moment (*khaṇa*). For it is said: "Like the persistence of the flame of a lamp in a windless place."

Because it is unable to serve as a condition for the stability of the continuum—unlike the stability of a well-polished gem—it is merely a condition for the occurrence of the mind, since it does not provide firm support due to the absence of certainty; hence he said, "weak concentration.
It is called "free from doubt" because it is difficult to cure, not because of the total absence of doubt.
“By way of being a disease” indicates its mere nature as such. It is called *saṃsayo* because it lies down (*seti*) by way of creeping about (*saṃsappana*), according to the expression “Is it thus?
Is it not thus? and so forth. Its function is to cause wavering; that is, it has the activity of making the mind waver among various objects.
For restlessness (*uddhacca*) wanders while remaining fixed upon the very aspect grasped by itself; thus it occurs by way of agitation toward a single object alone. Doubt (*vicikicchā*)...
However, even though it arises with respect to only one object among visible forms and so forth, nevertheless, because it looks toward another mode of apprehension—thinking, "Is it thus?
Is it not thus? Is this it? Is it something else?"—there is a wavering regarding multiple objects.
It presents indecision as its manifestation; thus, it is "presented as indecision. Of that which is non-conclusive...

It is "presented as apprehending in multiple ways" because it stands opposed [to its object] by way of apprehending the various intrinsic natures within the objective field (*ārammaṇa*). 491. Regarding "having beings as their objective field":

this means having the designations (*paññatti*) of beings as their objective field. Anticipating the objection, "But do not even resultant states have designations as their objective field?", he says: "For the resultants of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) have exclusively limited objects. This also applies to the abstinences (*virati*).

Regarding the statement "they do not exist in the resultants," he says, "For it has been stated that the five training precepts (sikkhāpada) are exclusively wholesome," having in mind the objection: "But surely there are also abstinences (virati) in some resultants. By this, he shows that abstinences do not exist in mundane resultants.

The word "of them" (tesaṃ) refers to the resultant consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere and so forth; for this genitive case is used in the sense of the relationship between that which is to be produced and that which produces it.

492. These are the rootless functional formations (*ahetuka-kiriya-saṅkhāra*). In this context, those associated with the wholesome resultant mind-element (*kusalavipāka-manodhātu*) are associated with the rootless functional mind-element;
those associated with the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (*somanassa-sahagata-santīraṇa*) are associated with the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppāda*);

and those associated with the investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā-sahagata-santīraṇa*) are associated with the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*). It is by showing this meaning that [the text] proceeds.

Having said, “being wholesome... [and so on]... while in meditative absorption,” the passage beginning with “but in the case of the two mind-consciousness elements” was stated to show the specific distinction obtained thereafter.
Because of the presence of energy (*vīriya*), concentration becomes powerful, considering that “the power of energy” is its constituent factor.

Since the function of abstaining is already fulfilled for Arahants by means of the abandonments through complete cutting off (*samuccheda-virati*) alone, the abstinences do not exist in functional consciousnesses (*kiriya-citta*).

He said, "excluding the abstinences," meaning that there is a distinction between the volitional formations (saṅkhāra) of sense-sphere functional states accompanied by roots and those of sense-sphere wholesome states due to the presence of abstinences;
however, among the sublime (mahaggata) states, even such a distinction does not exist. Therefore he said, "in every respect," which means in every way:
by way of the phenomena themselves, by way of their objects, and by way of the mode of their occurrence.
Thus ends the commentary on the introductory exposition of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
Regarding the commentary on the analysis of the past and so forth:

although the "Analysis according to the Suttas" (*suttantabhājanīya*) is included within the Abhidhamma, it follows the method of the Suttas; however, that which follows exclusively the Abhidhamma method is the "Analysis according to the Abhidhamma" (*abhidhammabhājanīya*). Therefore, he says: "by way of the analysis of the words in the Abhidhamma."
493. The connection is that the aggregates (*khandhā*) have been thus detailed by the Blessed One.
Therefore, the intention is: "We shall now provide a commentary on the aggregates by means of this scriptural passage as well.

In the phrase "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*), *yaṃ* is a general indication of non-specification, while *kiñci* is a non-specification that touches upon the various modes [of existence]. By both of these, [it refers to] the past... [or] the near.
Because it grasps everything—whether little or much, or of such-and-such a kind—that is worthy of being designated as neuter, pervading it all, he says:

"the inclusion of the remainderless. However, seeing that this [definition] would over-apply to other things also worthy of being designated as neuter, since it would extend beyond the intended meaning there, he uses the word "matter" (*rūpa*) in order to restrict that over-extension.
Showing that it has been so stated, he said: "‘Rūpa’ is for the purpose of restricting an over-extension.

Regarding the phrase *yaṃ kiñci*, by taking the word *yaṃ* as one word and the compound *kiñci* (the word *kiṃ*) as another word, it is stated "even by two words" because they indicate an unrestricted single meaning.
*Assa* means "of form" (*rūpassa*). He begins the classification by way of the past and so forth with the words "past, future, and present," etc.
494. Regarding the phrase "by way of extent (addhā), continuity (santati), time (samaya), and moment (khaṇa)":
here, it is understood from such suttas as "Was I indeed in the past extent?

that the word *addhā* refers to the period delimited by death and rebirth-linking (*cuti-paṭisandhi*). For likewise, in the *Bhaddekaratta Sutta*, the state of being past and so forth is expressed precisely by way of extent, in the passage beginning, "One should not pursue the past."
“Bhikkhus, there are three periods of time (*addhā*). Which three? The past period, the future period, and the present period.
However, when the period is delimited from the ultimate standpoint (*paramatthato*), it is stated as being delimited by a moment (*khaṇa*) according to the *Niruttipatha-sutta*.
For therein it says: “Bhikkhus, whatever form has been born... manifested—that is reckoned as ‘it exists’.”
The state of being present belongs to that which currently exists; prior to that and subsequent to it, the states of past and future are spoken of.

In other suttas, however, the temporal period (addhā) consisting of the past and so forth is for the most part defined by the limits of death and rebirth-linking; it is precisely this that is referred to here as "by way of the temporal period.
Cold is of the same nature as cold, and likewise, heat is of the same nature as heat. But as for that cold or heat which has entered into the body—
That which proceeds by way of continuity, neither deficient nor excessive, and uniform in aspect, is called "one season" (*utu*);

thus, the term "one" is used because the similar seasons (*sabhāga-utu*) are manifold. The same applies to nutriment (*āhāra*). "Arising from a single cognitive process and a single impulsion" is stated with reference to the five or six sense doors.
The discussion on continuity and time was set forth in the commentaries for the benefit of those practicing insight (*vipassaka*). [This is] the generator.
The cause (*hetu*) is the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka-paccaya*); its function is the production of those [resultants] and their support.

Just as the seed produces the sprout while the earth and other factors support it, so too does karma produce the resultant materiality born of past action (*kaṭattā-rūpa-vipāka*), while nutriment and the rest support it;
likewise for each group (*kalāpa*) and for the arising of consciousness, [the cause produces and the conditions support].

The functions of those [factors] that serve as conditions such as the immediate antecedent condition (*kamma-anantara-paccaya*), as well as the conascent (*sahajāta*), prenascence (*purejāta*), and postnascence (*pacchājāta*) supporting factors, should be applied according to their respective possibilities.

Thus, because temperature (*utu*) and so forth can be either homogeneous or heterogeneous, the division of the material phenomena originated by them into past and so on was stated by way of their continuity;
however, for karma that produces a single existence, there is no distinction between homogeneous and heterogeneous.

The statement "it does not exist" was spoken solely by way of its supporting factor (*upatthambhaka*), without specifying the division into past and so forth according to the continuity (*santati*) of the material phenomena originating from it.

However, when a change of gender occurs, then through powerful unwholesome [kamma], the male gender disappears, and through weak wholesome [kamma], the female gender becomes manifest. And through weak unwholesome [kamma], the female gender disappears.

Because even material phenomena originating from kamma (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) possess dissimilarity—since the male characteristic appears through the power of wholesome karma—their division into past and so forth is possible by way of their continuity;
however, because that [dissimilarity] does not exist at all times, it is not included here.

"At each respective time" (*tantaṃsamayaṃ*): that which has such and such a time, such as a single moment and so forth, is "at each respective time"; the meaning is "matter possessing such and such a time."
"Prior to that" means prior to the completion of those three moments. It is "future" because it has not yet arisen. "After that" means after those [moments].
It is "past" because the three moments have been transcended. That for which the function of cause and the function of condition have been completed is past.
It should be understood that the function of cause occurs at the moment of arising, and it is completed because the fruit has already arisen.

The function of conditionality exists in all three moments. "One's own function" (*sakicca*) refers to the specific functions of earth and the other elements, such as supporting, or of contact and the other mental factors, such as touching.
The moment of performing one's own function is the "moment of one's own function" (*sakiccakkhaṇa*). Alternatively, that which is together with its function is "with its own function" (*sakicca*);
the moment in which a form or a non-form possesses its own function is the "moment of one's own function," and at that moment it is present.

And here, in the discussion of the moment (*khaṇa*) and so forth, the statement "prior to that it is future, after that it is past" is used in its primary sense (*nippariyāya*), because—as in the case of the [three] periods of time (*addhā*) and so on—there is no difference [in the phenomenon itself].
For by way of the periods of time and so forth, different phenomena are found as past, others as future, and others as present;
but by way of the moment and so forth, there is no difference in terms of the phenomenon itself, only in terms of time.

The distinction is as follows: from the perspective of the literal sense (*nippariyāya*), [a phenomenon] is "future" prior to its arising, "present" during the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution], and "past" thereafter;
for there is no possibility of it being called past or future by any figurative method (*pariyāya*), such as in the case of the temporal present (*addhā-paccuppanna*) and so forth.
Having stated "the very method already explained" with reference to the internal and external distinctions mentioned below, one who is not satisfied with that—

Although the literal meaning of the word *ajjhattika* can be obtained there as simply "internal," nevertheless, there is indeed a difference in meaning between the terms *ajjhatta* and *ajjhattika*, as well as between the terms *bahiddhā* and *bāhira*.

For instance, the term *ajjhattika* applies to the eye and so forth belonging to one's own continuum, just as the term *bāhira* applies to visible forms and so forth; whereas the term *ajjhatta* refers to each individual sentient being.
The term "external" (bahiddhā) applies to the eye, visible forms, and so forth, precisely when they belong to another continuum, just as it does to things other than those;
therefore, to demonstrate this meaning, the passage beginning with “Moreover” (apicā) was stated. In that context, “here” (idha) means in this method of the Suttanta.

The intended sense is that even what is one’s own internal (niyakajjhatta) is not merely the "internal" (ajjhattika) previously mentioned, and even what belongs to another person (parapuggalika) is not merely the "external" (bāhira) previously mentioned.
496. The connection is that the distinction between the inferior (*hīna*) and the sublime (*paṇīta*) should be understood both figuratively (*pariyāyato*) and non-figuratively (*nippariyāyato*).
That very same form belongs to the Sudassī devas. "In which" means in whichever object-base (*ārammaṇa*).
