That object-base by taking which unwholesome resultant consciousness arises is "inferior" because of its undesirable nature. That which is wholesome resultant is "sublime" because of its desirable nature. For just as the unwholesome resultant...

Just as that which is undesirable arises only in what is undesirable and not in what is desirable, so too wholesome resultant [consciousness], being itself desirable, arises only in what is desirable and not in what is undesirable. For it is said in the Commentary:
"The five strands of sensual pleasure, born of unwholesome karma, are analyzed as undesirable; however, that which is born of wholesome karma..."
There is nothing that is not desired; all is indeed desirable. By way of wholesome kamma, the five strands of sensual pleasure are classified as desirable.
For there is nothing born of wholesome kamma that is undesirable; all is indeed desirable.
In this context, although there are certain pleasing things such as elephant-forms and so forth produced by unwholesome kamma, they are not [included here].
These very elephants and so forth become the causes of pleasure for them.

For whatever being, that which is produced by their own wholesome karma (*kusala*) becomes a condition for pleasure, while that produced by unwholesome karma (*akusala*) becomes a condition for suffering.
Therefore, the desirability or undesirability of things born of karma should be understood in relation to the being who performs the karma. Regarding this, it was said:
It has not been stated that "there is nothing born of unwholesome kamma that is undesirable," whereas it was stated that "there is nothing born of wholesome kamma that is undesirable.
By this, it will have been admitted that even what is born of unwholesome kamma can be beautiful and desirable for other beings;
however, what is born of wholesome kamma is desirable for everyone.
However, for some animals, a human form is unpleasant; seeing it, they flee.
And humans, seeing the form of a deity, are afraid. Even in their case, the resultant consciousness arising with reference to that form is exclusively wholesome-resultant;
yet because of the absence of such merit, they find no delight therein.
It exists. Furthermore, just as there is an absence of what is undesirable born of wholesome kamma, so too must there be an absence of what is desirable born of unwholesome kamma.
For even in the case of elephants and such, that which is born of unwholesome kamma is an object for the unwholesome resultants of humans;
however, that which is born of wholesome kamma during the course of existence is an object for the wholesome resultants. By means of a desirable object...
However, because it is mixed, it can be understood that a small amount of unwholesome kamma will not be the cause for the arising of a large amount of unwholesome result;
yet, since it is impossible to deceive the result, the definition of desirable and undesirable objects by way of their results is perfectly appropriate.
As for what was said, "the five strands of sense pleasure are undesirable," that was stated from the perspective of their common nature as forms and so forth.

This is stated by applying the designation of the "strands of sensual pleasure" (kāmaguṇa) to things similar to them because of their similarity to those strands. For indeed, only desirable forms and so forth are called "strands of sensual pleasure" in the Canon.

Alternatively, forms and so forth that are dissimilar to the strands of sensual pleasure are called "strands of sensual pleasure" just as there is the conventional expression "auspicious" for what is inauspicious.
Or else, all forms and so forth—whether desirable or undesirable—are indeed strands of sensual pleasure because they serve as the objective basis for craving. For it has been said:

“Forms in the world are lovely things, pleasant things,” and so forth. However, because they are exceedingly desirable, the desirable forms and so on are called *kāmaguṇa* (strands of sensual pleasure) in the Suttas.
Regarding the phrase “in the manner already stated”:
it has been shown that distance and proximity are determined by way of characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) rather than by way of location; therefore, he says: “In this context, even by way of location...”
“Nearness and farness should be understood by taking each [instance] in turn. In this regard, from what point on is matter called “near” by way of location, and from what point on is it called “far”?
For those discussing the natural state, twelve cubits is known as the range of hearing;
within that distance it is near, beyond that it is far. Among these, subtle matter is far.
That which is distant both by way of characteristic and by way of location remains distant; however, that which is near is near only by way of location, not by way of characteristic.
Gross material form, when near, is near both by way of characteristic and by way of location; when distant, it is distant only by way of location, not by way of characteristic.
But because it is stated as "derived from each respective [material cause]," one's own material form—
"Near" means that even for one who has entered another's belly, it is distant; for one who has entered the belly, it is near, while for one standing outside, it is distant.

Thus, the state of being distant or near should be understood by way of what is inside or outside of the inner chamber, the entrance hall, the courtyard, the monastery grounds, the boundary, the village, the field, the district, the kingdom, the ocean, and the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).
497. *Tadekajjhaṃ*: that together, as one. *Abhisaṃyūhitvā*: having gathered together, or having made a collection.
*Abhisaṅkhipitvā*: having condensed, having made an abridgment. By the phrase “all form...
is shown,” he demonstrates that the terms *rūpa* and *khandha* form a compound in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). For this very reason, he says: “Not from form... [and so forth].
"There is another thing called the aggregate of form.
One should supply and connect the words "the aggregates of feeling and so forth" by way of their being gathered into a heap.
Regarding the phrase "by way of continuity and by way of moments, etc.," there is no mention here of the division into past and so forth by way of duration (addhā) or time (samaya).
Because it is spoken of as having past and other states by way of its division into pleasure and so forth.

For it is not the case that pleasure alone becomes past and so on by way of time-period (*addhā*) and by way of occasion (*samaya*); likewise for pain and for neither-pain-nor-pleasure, which are divided according to their bodily, mental, and other natures.
Therefore, the aggregate of feeling deserves to be designated as having past and other states by way of time-period and occasion.
Because the aggregate must be delimited by those [factors], whereas when a portion of feeling is apprehended,
it deserves delimitation by way of its continuity and moment, since it is to be apprehended after being so delimited. However,
among the various types of pleasure and so forth within a single continuity, that specific variety which is apprehended as the object of delimitation is of a single mode and is manifest.

The continuity (santati) that arises with its corresponding door and object, and which proceeds through an uninterrupted conjunction with a single type of object that produces it, is fit to be called "delimiting";
thus, without mentioning any other distinction within it, it is grasped by way of its delimiting nature.
Alternatively, immaterial phenomena (arūpadhammā), which revolve rapidly, are delimited by the very act of their revolving.
"Arahantī" (the one who is an arahant) expresses the delimitation by way of the continuity and the moment alone.
For one who, even for a whole day, sees the form of the Buddha or hears the Dhamma, the feeling that arises together with faith and so forth is "present.
By the phrase "gone to the past, future, and middle," he shows the method stated by way of the function of the cause-condition.

499. Since the states of being accompanied by malice (*savyāpāda*), being accompanied by exertion (*saussāha*), and having a result of ripening (*savipāka*) are common to all three—wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth—it was said, “Because it is the cause of blameworthy action,” and so on, in order to show what is unique [to the unwholesome].
Therein, “because it is the cause of blameworthy action” means because it is the basis for contemptible actions such as the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*).

“Because it has the nature of the torment of defilements” means because it possesses a state of constant striving due to the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*). [This is contrasted with] the wholesome, which has a nature that is perfectly tranquil.

It is gross in comparison to feeling (*vedanā*). "With exertion" means with effort; by this, he speaks of its occurrence in such a way that it must necessarily be a result (*vipāka*), thereby stating its fitness for producing a result. "With energy" means with strength; by this, [he states] its capacity to produce a result.
"With a result" means because of the presence of a result; by this, [he indicates] the production of a result through the convergence of other conditions.
By these three terms, he demonstrates precisely the state of being subject to fruition (*vipākadhammatā*).

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows: it is "with activity" (*sabyāpāra*) because of the presence of bodily action and so forth; it is "with effort" (*saussāha*) by way of impulsion and exertion; and it is "with fruition" (*savipāka*) by way of the capacity to produce fruition.
Even though it does not produce fruition, functional (*kiriya*) consciousness is like the wholesome (*kusala*): it is indeed with activity and with effort.

And because it "is," without mentioning both of those [terms], in the section on the functional-indeterminate (kiriyābyākatavāra), it is stated simply as "with result" (*savipākato*). "With affliction" (*sabyābajjhatoti*) means "with suffering" due to the suffering of the defilements (*kilesadukkha*). "By way of the opposite of what was stated" means:
by way of the faultless functional cause, by the absence of the burning heat of the defilements, and by being non-afflictive (*abyābajjha*), thus having a tranquil course;
this is according to the inversion of what was stated for the unwholesome. "As appropriate" (*yathāyogaṃ*) means in accordance with the application (*yoga*).
"In three ways" means that whichever [reason] is appropriate for whichever [feeling], it is according to that; this is the meaning.

The resultant-indeterminate (vipākavyākatā) is grosser than the wholesome and unwholesome feelings by all three reasons. The functional-indeterminate (kriyāvyākatā) is grosser than the resultant-indeterminate because it possesses result, because its activity and effort are distinguished from those lacking result, or because it possesses activity and effort.
"By the stated method" means that the resultant-indeterminate is [grosser] than those wholesome and unwholesome feelings because it lacks activity, lacks effort, and lacks result.

They are subtle. They are functionally indeterminate (*kiriyābyākatā*) because they are not results (*avipāka*), or rather, because they possess activity and effort despite being distinguished from results by the absence of such results; this is stated as the opposite of what was said regarding the wholesome and unwholesome.

For results (*vipākā*), being cast by the force of karma and being the reflection of karma, are devoid of the activity of bodily action and so forth, and thus lack effort. Functioning states (*kiriyā*), however, possess effort and are of a nature that does not produce results. For those things that are of a nature to produce results are gross, like a pregnant woman.

“500. ‘From lack of gratification’ means from the absence of gratification, that is, from the rejection of pleasure. ‘With diffusion’ means with vibration; the meaning is ‘not tranquil. ‘From overcoming’ means from overwhelming. There is no neutrality in pleasure, but there is continuity in equanimity (*upekkhā*).
However, since qualities such as tranquility are found in all instances of both pleasant and neutral equanimity, [the text says] ‘according to what is appropriate.’”

It has been said. "By way of being manifest" means that it is to be known even by seeing whether one is happy or suffering, because its state is evident. That is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

(501) Furthermore, by the inclusion of both those who have not attained and those who have attained [jhāna], it should be understood that the grossness and subtlety of feelings have also been stated here by way of plane. The other is the feeling of one who has attained [jhāna].
"By way of being subject to the floods" means that it must be transcended by making the floods its object. Likewise for "subject to the yokes" and "subject to the ties."
In this context as well, "bond" (*gantha*) refers to the act of binding; that which is beneficial for it by way of being its object is "bondable" (*ganthaniya*).

In the same way, "hindrance-able" (*nīvaraṇiya*) and "clinging-able" (*upādāniya*) are to be understood. "Defiling" (*saṃkilesika*) means either being connected with defilement (*saṃkilesa*) or being worthy of defilement.
That [state] is free from taints (*anāsava*).
502. *Tattha* means "in that regard," referring to the aforementioned grossness and subtlety. *Sambheda* means "confusion.
One must avoid the fault of [confusing] those described as "gross" and "subtle" such that they do not again become subtle or gross by way of their genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

For instance, one must avoid attributing grossness to a feeling that is subtle by way of its genus, through the categories of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), person (*puggala*), or the mundane (*lokiya*).
To show this by way of the canonical text (pāḷi), the passage beginning with “For it has been said” was stated.
Regarding the phrase “so too pleasure and so forth”: here, unwholesome feeling is gross by way of its genus (jāti) but subtle by way of its intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

Wholesome feeling accompanied by jhāna is gross by way of its genus, but subtle by way of the person (puggala), considering it to be the feeling of one who has attained absorption; thus it should be applied in such ways.
“‘It should not be grasped’—by this it is shown that the four categories beginning with birth must be taken as entirely unmixed with one another.

Thus he demonstrates that there is no avoiding this confusion, nor is there any other way. Just as it was shown by way of the indeterminate, so too it should be shown by way of the wholesome and unwholesome;
and just as it was shown by way of birth, so too it should be shown by way of intrinsic nature (sabhāva) and so forth. This is the method.
With the words "in all cases," he refers [to the previous analysis].

Now, in order to show the relative grossness and subtlety of the unwholesome and other factors within each category—beginning with birth—relative to one another, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) is commenced.
By the phrase "because of burning its support" (*nissayadahanato*), [the text] indicates the manifest occurrence of cruelty accompanied by hatred (*dosa*).
[The text] shows this. "Fixed" means fixed by way of the fixed course of wrongness (*micchattaniyāma*);

having reached the state of an immediate result (*ānantariya*), it persists for an eon (*kappaṭṭhitika*) because its ripening lasts for an eon, as in the case of Devadatta and others. That which is unprompted (*asaṅkhārika*) is gross due to its natural sharpness.

That which is associated with views is gross due to its great blameworthiness. Furthermore, that which is associated with views and is fixed is gross; even more so than that is that which persists for an eon.
Then, as for "the unprompted," although all three types have been explained according to the method stated below, they are mentioned together here and should be applied individually.
Therefore he said: "The others are subtle. "Without distinction" means without differentiating between those accompanied by hatred (*dosasahagata*) and those accompanied by greed (*lobhasahagata*).

Unwholesome states have great results and are gross due to the predominance of hatred; likewise, wholesome states have small results. The unwholesome states are dull because of the dullness of hatred.
Those with little result are subtle. Likewise, those that are wholesome have much result.
The grossness and subtlety of the sense-sphere and other realms are due to their being objects of desire that are respectively gross or subtle; however, the supramundane is exclusively subtle.
Furthermore, he will explain the distinction between them later. "Also consisting of development" means [the path] consisting of development.
It should be understood that by means of this analysis, the analysis of those consisting of giving and virtue is also shown.

Regarding the phrase "those consisting of development (bhāvanāmaya) are also twofold-rooted," it is stated because at times during the periods when development is practiced or when it is proficient and powerful, attention may even occur with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta-citta).

As for the expression "in the resultant and functional feelings of their respective planes," here [the distinction is made] such as: "sense-sphere resultants are gross, while fine-material-sphere [resultants] are subtle," and so forth.

This should be carried on up to the fruit of arahantship. By such statements as "functional consciousness of the sense sphere is gross, functional consciousness of the fine-material sphere is subtle," and so forth, the sense-sphere consciousnesses should be carried on;

and by such statements as "those occurring in the mode of giving are gross, those occurring in the mode of virtue are subtle," and so forth, this should be carried on up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
And in order to show that just as this classification applies to the section on origin, it likewise applies to the sections on intrinsic nature and so forth:
“‘Dukkha, etc. was said.
Since this entire classification was stated based on the [three] characteristics (lakkhaṇa), he said, “And also by way of the bases (okāsa),” and so forth.

By the word “also” (pi) in the phrase “even pleasant (sukhāpi),” he includes the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling]. “In all instances” (sabbattha) means in all planes (bhūmi). “Accordingly” (yathānurūpaṃ) means...
Whichever feeling is obtained wherever it may be, [it is classified] according to that. "By way of the basis" means also by way of the physical basis upon which the feeling arises.
"Having a low basis" means that for one eating coarse grain (*kaṅgu*) while making a low basis—that is, a low object—the feeling is gross due to the lowness of the basis;
whereas for one eating fine rice with meat, it is subtle due to the excellence of the basis.

503. By the phrase "by way of the first method," he touches upon the entire course of the Pāḷi. "Heterogeneity" (visabhāgatā) is the state of not belonging to the same class by way of birth and so forth.
"Non-mixture" (asaṃsaṭṭhatā) is the state of having dissimilar functions by way of having painful fruition and so forth; it does not mean non-association (asampayoga).

If it were [non-association], then proximity would occur through the reverse of distance, whereby non-mixture would result in proximity; yet there is no association of one feeling with another feeling.

And regarding the commentary on the *Santika-pada*, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated: "by way of commonality (*sabhāgata*) and by way of similarity (*sarikkhata*).

Non-similarity is the state of having a dissimilar nature. "In all instances" means in all the sections that ought to be discussed according to the method explained for the distinctions between the gross and the subtle.
Commonality (*sabhāgatā*) is the state of belonging to the same category by way of birth and so forth; [while] by way of having a painful result and so forth—
However, similarity is the state of having an identical nature. Therefore he said: “But the unwholesome...
[etc. ...are near. Thus ends the commentary on the detailed exposition of the classification of the aggregate of feeling into the past and so forth.
Commentary on the Discourse Determining the Order and So Forth.
504. *Etanti* means "thus. *Atītādivibhāge vitthārakathāmukhan* means the introduction to the detailed exposition regarding the classification of the past and so forth.

*Ñāṇabhedatthan* means for the purpose of the various distinctions of knowledge. *Kamatoti* means according to the order of teaching; the meaning is "because of that reason by which this order of teaching was established. *Visesatoti* means by way of distinction;
the meaning is by way of the classification of the aggregates (*khandha*) and the bases of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*). *Anūnādhikato* means neither deficient nor redundant.
"By way of the five states. "By way of comparison" means by way of being comparable through similes. "To be seen in two ways" means it is to be perceived by knowledge in two modes.
"Because of the accomplishment of the goal for one who sees" means because of the fulfillment of the intended purpose for one who perceives it.
"By the discerning" means by the wise.
"Order of arising" means the sequence in which things arise according to their respective conditions. "Those to be abandoned by vision," and so forth:
those to be abandoned first were stated first, and those to be abandoned second were stated second; this is the "order of abandoning.
One should practice the purification of mind after having practiced the purification of virtue; likewise for those that follow—thus he said: "Purification of virtue... [etc.]..."
The "sequence of practice" refers to the stages that are progressively more refined, established in successive order; this is the sequence of the planes (*bhūmikkama*).
The "sequence of teaching" (*desanākkama*) refers to such passages as "the four foundations of mindfulness," because the foundations of mindfulness and so forth can arise even within a single moment.

Discourses on giving and the like are taught according to a progressive gradation; however, because there is no fixed determination regarding their origin and so forth, [no specific sequence is prescribed] for giving and the rest.

This refers here to the statement regarding the sequence of the teaching. For since the teaching beginning with "first there is the *kalala*" is given on the basis of establishing [the order] by way of their arising and so forth, it is stated precisely according to that sequence of arising and so on.

However, because it is impossible for numerous statements to occur simultaneously in the absence of such a defined sequence, they must be taught in some order of priority; therefore, by that [sequence],...
In that sense, the sequence of the mere teaching itself is to be understood as the "sequence of teaching.

By way of establishing priority and posteriority: the aggregate of form comes first, and then the aggregate of feeling; thus it is because they do not arise [simultaneously] by way of such establishment of priority and posteriority. By way of what is not to be abandoned:
among the aggregates, there are some for which there is no state of being abandonable at all, so how could there be a sequence of abandonment? [This applies to] mindfulness.

Indeed, their teaching would follow the sequence of abandonment because they are all to be abandoned. "Because it is not to be practiced" means that it is not to be practiced by way of right practice.
By the phrase "because they are included within the four planes," he shows that feeling and the other [aggregates] have indeterminate planes;
for a sequence of planes would only be possible in the case of those factors that have determinate planes.
"Without making a distinction" means without making a division or separation between form and so forth, but by grasping them together as a single mass.

"Fallen into the grasp of a self" means fallen into the flood of views known as the grasp of a self. "By seeing the resolution of the compact mass" means, while distinguishing the immaterial from the material, seeing the resolution of the compact mass within the collection of both material and immaterial phenomena. It is also the object of the eye and the other [senses].
By means of a part, he speaks of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) as a whole. The connection is as follows:
"That which here experiences the desirable and undesirable form is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha)"—thus he taught feeling as that which experiences desirable and undesirable forms.

This applies in all cases. Since even the desirable-neutral and undesirable-neutral possess the same essential nature as the desirable and undesirable, they are included by the very mention of "desirable and undesirable."

“Grasping” (gahaṇaṃ) should be understood. “Thus” (evaṃ) means by the method already stated. Because volitional formations arise with respect to an object that has been grasped through perception, he says, “in the one who forms [volitions] by way of perception.

He says, “the support for feeling and the rest,” because the status of consciousness as a support for its associated states is manifest, whereas that is not so for feeling and the others. “Mind precedes all phenomena...”
Because of the statement, “The states that follow the mind are the king who rules over the six doors,” consciousness is the dominant factor.

Regarding the aggregate of form, the expression “with taints and subject to clinging” is intended to exclude from the nature of the aggregate of form those states that are without taints (anāsava), not to exclude form that is itself without taints.

In the phrase “only those without taints are mentioned among the aggregates,” the word “only” (eva) is used in a sense of restriction; the meaning is that only those without taints are mentioned among the aggregates. However, here in the *Visuddhimagga*, all these are both aggregates (khandhā) and aggregates subject to clinging (upādānakkhandhā).
506. The grouping together, in one place, of all conditioned things by way of their commonality is the "grouping of all conditioned things by way of their commonality.

For all conditioned things, when grouped together by virtue of their commonality, constitute the five aggregates. In this context, those items belonging to the same category by virtue of a common characteristic such as "being subject to deformation" (ruppana) should be understood as "common" (sabhāga).
Among these, the function of conditioning the conditioned is predominant in volition (cetanā), whose essential nature is exertion (āyūhana).

That [aggregate] is called the "aggregate of formations" (*saṅkhārakkhandha*). Furthermore, other factors such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth—which lack specific characteristics such as being subject to change (*ruppana*)—should be understood as such by virtue of their commonality in forming conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-abhisaṅkharaṇa*).

However, it should be understood that the Tathāgata, who knows the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), did not speak of "contact-aggregates" and so on, because the individual natures of touching and the rest are not what is designated by the term "aggregate. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics..."
Or, by way of such suttas as, "Whether they be brahmins who hold to eternalism and proclaim the self and the world to be eternal,

all of them do so in dependence upon and based upon these very five aggregates of clinging, or upon one or another of them," it should be understood that the grasping after a self and what belongs to a self has this as its ultimate limit.
And by this [statement], as well as by the sutta to be mentioned later, [it is shown that] the aggregates...

Thus, depending on this, it is stated that a view arises—such as that which takes a limited object (*parittārammaṇa*) and so forth—which cannot be predicated [of anything], because there is no such thing as a dharma with intrinsic nature (*sabhāvadhamma*) other than the aggregates (*khandha*) and Nibbāna.
By the term "form" (*rūpa*), he refers to a collection of phenomena whose intrinsic nature is to be affected (*ruppanasabhāva*).

The same method applies to "feeling" (*vedanā*) and the others as well. This is because of such statements as "the aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandha*), "the aggregate of concentration" (*samādhikkhandha*), and so forth, and because of other [evidences].

He says, "Because others are included therein," in order to refute the objection that there are not only five aggregates, since the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth also exist as things denoted by the term "aggregate" (*khandha*).

It is said, "because it is a place of abiding," meaning it is like a dwelling place that serves as a locus for occurrence. [The three types of suffering] are by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*).

Feeling (vedanā) should be seen as the state of being afflictive. Perception (saññā), which grasps the forms of women, men, and so forth, and which is rooted in various types of conceptualization, is the origination (samuṭṭhāna) for suffering associated with passion and the like—such as the suffering of change.
Just as bile and the like are the proximate cause of a disease, perception is the origination.

Just as irregularity of climate, food, and lifestyle, or improper conduct, are the primary causes, the underlying cause (nidāna) is likewise [the source]. Mental factors (cetasika) are those that constitute limbs of the mind (citta).

Consciousness is said to be like a sick person. Just as the ointment applied by one suffering from leprosy leads to an increase in the disease, so too the activity of a fool through the formation of merit and so forth brings about the suffering of feeling, being similar to the use of unwholesome food.

"For the sake of feeling" means for the purpose of the intrinsic nature of feeling; the meaning is "for the attainment of the state of feeling. This is because it serves as the locus of the cause and as the support for nutriment.

And form is like a jailer and like a vessel. Perception is like an offender and like a condiment, because it acts as the cause for the production of feeling through the perception of beauty and so forth, and because it covers over the food of feeling.
The aggregate of formations is like a cause-maker and like a server, because it is the cause of feeling; and since it is the cook who generally serves the meal, [it is like a server].
The taking of the food-server: consciousness is said to be like the offender because it is to be afflicted by feeling, and like the eater because it is to be assisted by it.
508. “Bhikkhus, ‘five executioners and enemies with raised swords’ is a designation for these five aggregates subject to clinging.”
“Designation”: in the *Āsīvisūpama-sutta* (The Simile of the Venomous Snake), they are called “murderers”;
in the *Bhāra-sutta* (The Discourse on the Burden), it says, “‘Burden,’ monks, is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging”; and [in the *Mahānidāna-sutta*]:
“In the past, too, I was devoured by form in just this same way as I am being devoured by form now in the present. And if I...”
In the *Khajjanīya-pariyāya* (The Discourse on Being Devoured), it says: "If I were to delight in future form... for the duration of the future, I would likewise be devoured by that form, just as...

[I am now] being devoured," and so forth; thus, they are called "the devourers. In the *Yamaka-sutta*, it says: "He does not understand impermanent form, as it really is, as 'impermanent form,'" and so forth; thus, they are called "the impermanent, etc. Even though [it is said]: "But here, all these..."

It is said, “having been made into one, they are intended as ‘aggregates’ (khandhā),” but it should be understood that, by way of predominance, the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are to be seen as included therein.
For this is an investigation of the stages for insight (vipassanā).
In the passages beginning with “like a lump of foam,” the similarity of form and the other [aggregates] to a lump of foam and so forth is to be seen; just as a lump of foam...
It is substanceless and very weak, unfit for grasping; even when grasped, it accomplishes no purpose whatsoever.
It is full of holes and cracks, composed of many joints and connections, a dwelling place for many small creatures, built up layer by layer, falling apart in every part, and bound to break asunder.
Thus, form is likewise "substanceless" because it is devoid of any permanent essence, like the soft wood of a tree's pith; it is "very weak" because it is easily broken.
It should not be grasped as "permanent," or "stable," or "I," or "mine"; even when so grasped, it is not thus.
It is full of holes, a conglomeration of one hundred and eighty joints, an abode for many swarms of worms, and built up successively starting from the stage of the *kalala* and so forth;
it perishes in all its stages and must inevitably break apart. Thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
However, the relationship between the simile and the thing illustrated is stated solely in terms of the inability to withstand being rubbed.
Just as a bubble is insubstantial, extremely weak, unfit for grasping, and even when grasped achieves no purpose and does not endure for long—so too is feeling.
And just as a bubble [arises from] the surface of the water, a drop of water, or a film on the water...
Having gathered together and formed a bundle, it arises in dependence upon four causes, including the grasping wind. In the same way, feeling also arises in dependence upon four causes:
the physical basis, the object, the impurity of defilements, and the impact of contact.
For just as the wind produced by the falling of a drop upon the surface of water [stirs] the watery scum known as "water-impurity,"...

Having gathered [the moisture] together and formed it into a lump, it is called a bubble; likewise, contact—arisen when an object enters the range of the sense-bases—gathers the unceasing filth of the defilements by acting as a cooperative condition and produces what is called feeling (*vedanā*).
And this [feeling] is produced by the defilements, which serve both as its primary cause and as the relishing of the object, and thus belongs to the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭagata*).
This was said with reference to feeling (*vedanā*). Or, the four conditions were stated by way of the maximum limit;
however, they certainly arise even when fewer than these are present. Here, the relationship between the simile and the thing illustrated is expressed as a momentary state of delight.
Just as a mirage is without essence and ungraspable—for one cannot take it up to drink from or bathe in—it is like a vessel [that cannot hold water].
Or just as it is impossible to fill [the ocean], so too perception (saññā) is essence-less and ungraspable. And just as a shimmering mirage, appearing as if possessed by a surging force,
deceives the multitude, so too perception— occurring with respect to an object as "blue," "yellow," "long," "short," and so forth—
does not abide in the mere intrinsic nature (sabhāvamatta), but rather leads to false grasping such as "beautiful," "pleasant," and "permanent."
It deceives the world by appearing as a cause.

Just as the trunk of a plantain tree is pithless and unfit for grasping—for it cannot be taken and used for purposes such as rafters—and even if it were taken, it would not serve that purpose, yet it consists of a mass of many layers;
so too is the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

It is essence-less and not fit to be grasped. For it cannot be grasped by way of being permanent and so forth; even when grasped, it does not exist in that manner, and it is a conglomeration of many phenomena.
Indeed, the characteristic of contact is one thing, while that of volition and the others is another;
yet, having combined all of these together, they are called the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).
Just as a magical illusion is substanceless and ungraspable— for one cannot achieve any purposeful task by seizing it—
it is transient, appearing fleetingly, and deceives the multitude by presenting non-jewels and the like in the form of jewels and so forth;
even so, consciousness is substanceless, transient, and appears fleetingly, such that with that very same mind it seems to come and go.
It causes one to grasp [the object] by making it appear as if standing, as if sitting, and so forth; thus the mind is one thing when coming, and another in going and other such actions.
In this way, consciousness is like an illusion.
Furthermore, even the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are of an impure nature and so on, because they are the basis for defilement and impurity; thus, they are "impure" (asubha), etc.
They must indeed be seen; nevertheless, because in some instances a certain distinction is easy to grasp, he says, "And especially," and so forth.

In that context, since the four foundations of mindfulness effect the abandoning of the four perversions, their status as objects of observation is stated by way of their being perceived as foulness and so on within the aggregate of form and the other aggregates.

509. One is not oppressed by the aggregates because their true nature has been fully understood. Even one who practices insight does not encounter suffering when they fail; however, in the case of those whose taints are destroyed, it need not even be mentioned. For they will not be afflicted by the aggregates even in the future.

"He fully understands physical nutriment": because of the statement, "With the arising of nutriment comes the arising of form," one who abandons desire and lust for internal form also abandons desire and lust for physical nutriment, which is its source of arising.

This is full understanding by abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). However, when one comprehends internal material form, one also comprehends the physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) that serves as its condition;
this is full understanding by knowing (*ñāta-pariññā*). Furthermore, the observation of its arising and passing away should be connected with full understanding by scrutinizing (*tīraṇa-pariññā*).
Thus, as these three types of full understanding are accomplished, these [defilements] such as the perversions are dispelled; so it was said.
“He abandons the perversion that takes the foul as beautiful,” and so forth. In this context, he says “the bodily tie of covetousness” with reference to covetousness consisting of sensual lust.
For through the contemplation of the foul, there is the abandoning of sensual lust; or rather, he speaks of the abandoning of all greed by way of sensual lust.
One does not cling, one does not grasp, one does not give rise [to it].

Because it is stated that “feeling has contact as its condition,” the full understanding of contact should be applied according to the method explained for the full understanding of nutriment, beginning with: “While abandoning desire and lust for feeling, one also abandons desire and lust for the nutriment of contact, which is its condition.
By seeing feeling as suffering, one abandons the perversion that there is pleasure therein. For the sake of pleasure...
"There is the aspiration for existence" means that by abandoning craving for feeling, one crosses over the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*).
From that very fact, one becomes dissociated from the yoke of existence (*bhava-yoga*). And through the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*), one becomes free from taints (*anāsava*).

Seeing all feeling as suffering, one does not worry about suffering previously produced by oneself or others, nor about happiness that has been destroyed; therefore, [one abandons] "what is harmful..."
By abandoning the grounds for resentment through such statements as "He has done me harm," one breaks the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpādakāyagantha*).

Not grasping at the idea that "purity lies in a state of rebirth in a happy realm abounding in pleasure," but rather adhering to purity through things such as the cow-vow (*gosīla*) or the cow-life (*govata*), one adheres solely by way of the longing for pleasure;
thus, even while abandoning craving for feeling (*vedanā*), one does not take up the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
Mental volition is the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), while perception (*saññā*) is associated with it;

thus, one who sees perceptions as formations as non-self abandons desire and lust for mental volition, comprehends it, and brings it to completion—hence it is said: "He fully understands perception as formations...
etc., he fully understands. One who sees perceptions as formations as non-self [abandons] because they are rooted in the view of self.
Showing that all views are dispelled just as the view of self is, he said: "He crosses over the flood of views...
he does not cling to the clinging to a doctrine of self.
One who sees consciousness as impermanent, by means of the contemplation of impermanence, exerts himself in all three contemplations.
Through the full understandings, one fully understands the nutriment of consciousness. Specifically, herein one abandons the perversion that takes the impermanent to be permanent.
In this regard, because ignorance abounds in the grasping at permanence, there is a perception of solidity toward consciousness;
thus, by effecting the resolution of that solidity and viewing it as impermanent, one crosses over the flood of ignorance. Consequently, one is dissociated from the bond of ignorance.

And by means of the taint of ignorance, he becomes one who is free from taints. Since adherence to rules and observances arises through the very power of delusion, one who abandons that [delusion] "breaks the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances.
And as for this, monks, which is called "mind," or "intellect," or "consciousness"—therein the uninstructed person...
An ordinary person is not capable of becoming disenchanted, not capable of becoming dispassionate, and not capable of being liberated.
Why is that? Because for a long time, monks, this has been clung to, cherished, and adhered to by the uninstructed ordinary person, thinking:
“This is mine, this I am, this is my self,” and so forth.
According to the statement: "Just as one who views consciousness as permanent clings to the clinging of views, so too one who views it as impermanent does not cling to the clinging of views.

Thus, it is said to have great benefit because it serves as the means for dispelling the entire mass of defilements, such as the perversions; thus it has vast arising. "By way of the executioner, etc.
means by way of an executioner with sword raised, and so forth. "One might see" means by means of knowledge and vision.
One would see it through direct experience.
The commentary on the Description of the Aggregates is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourteenth chapter.
15. Commentary on the Exposition of the Bases and Elements;
Commentary on the Detailed Discussion of the Bases. 510.
Having stated "the bases" by way of enumerating the terms previously listed in the passage beginning with "The aggregates and bases," etc., [the text now proceeds].
By way of enumeration and delimitation, he says: "The twelve bases. What is to be said regarding that will be explained by himself later on.
"The eye-base," and so forth, is the demonstration of their specific nature.

"Meaning" (attha) refers to the literal meaning of a word; however, the "essential meaning" (bhāvattha) is simply the characteristic (lakkhaṇa). That literal meaning is twofold: the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) and...

"Common. In this context, the referent of the word "eye" (*cakkhu*) and so forth is uncommon, whereas the referent of the word "base" (*āyatana*) is common, because it is shared equally by all twelve.
Among these, showing first that which is uncommon, he says: "First, in its specific sense," and so on.

In that passage, "in its specific sense" means in the sense of a specific meaning; that is to say, in the sense of the words "eye" and so forth. He says "it relishes": the word *cakkhati* [is used here]; [as in] "he relishes honey," "he relishes the sauce..."
Because the meaning of *cakkhati* is "to taste" (*rasasāyana*), he explains the meaning by way of that [root].
From the statement, "But the eye, Māgandiya, delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and exults in forms," the eye relishes form.
Even though the ear and the other [faculties] possess the quality of delighting in sounds and so forth, it is [the eye] which—derived from the four great elements—[is being discussed].
It should be understood that the word "eye" (cakkhu) applies specifically to the eye-faculty because it is conventionally established in that very sense—

just as the word "cow" and so forth apply to cows and other animals— based on the specific meaning stated in the Pāḷi as "serenity" (pasāda), etc., and in the Aṭṭhakathā as "characterized by the sensitivity of the primary elements capable of being struck by visible forms," and so forth.
And by the phrase "he makes manifest" (*vibhāveti*), he states the meaning according to the word *cakkhati*, which is established by the characteristics of grammar.

For "he sees" (*cakkhati*) means "he explains" (*ācikkhati*), that is, he speaks clearly. Since explaining consists precisely in making known what is even and uneven—just as one who possesses eyes [sees]—it is said:
"the meaning is 'he makes manifest'. Alternatively, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, it has the sense of "making manifest."
And the word *cakkhati* should be understood [in this context].

At times such as when one is affected by passion or anger, matter undergoes a change of color—like the form of a chameleon or like the form of a leech—and it "makes manifest" (*rūpayati*) that which has entered the heart;
the meaning is that it makes it appear as if it possessed a physical body, as if making it visible. Alternatively, the meaning of the word *rūpa* is "extension" (*vitthāraṇa*), and extension...

"Manifestation itself," he says, "is the meaning of 'it manifests'. Alternatively, because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the word *rūpa* should be understood here as having the sense of "manifesting.

For the word *rūpa* when denoting "color," the etymology is "it colors" (*rūpayati*); for the word *rūpa* when denoting the "aggregate of form" (*rūpakkhandha*), the distinction is that it is "affected" (*ruppati*).
In the phrase "it is exemplified," the word *vacana* should be taken in the sense of "it is spoken" (*vuccati*).
And here, "sound" does not refer only to the sound of speech; rather, it refers to everything cognizable by the ear.
"Possessing sound" (*sappati*) means that it is made to possess sound through its own conditions; the meaning is that it is brought to the state of being cognizable by the ear.
"Indicates" (*sūcayati*) means that it makes manifest its own basis—which is otherwise unperceived—by way of odor, declaring: "This is fragrant," or "This is foul-smelling."

The meaning is that it is like one who slanders by saying of a hidden object, such as a flower or the like, "There is a flower here," or "There is a fruit such as a campaka," or "There are mangoes and so forth.
Because swallowing is rooted in the perception of taste, and because of its inclination toward the flavor of food which is the cause of life, it "invokes life" (avhayati);
thus, by way of its etymological definition (*niruttilakkhaṇa*), it is called the tongue (*jivhā*). [It is so called] because of the base, tainted phenomena...

"Body" (*kāya*) is mentioned specifically because it does not attain the status of being a cause for the unsurpassed [states] among those things produced by karma rooted in sensual lust, nor among the specific conditions for sensual lust—namely, the nose, tongue, and body. This is because the body is a condition for the outflows (*āsava*) to a much greater degree than the others;
for it is by relishing the pleasure of touch that beings engage even in sexual intercourse. "Place of arising" (*uppattidesa*) means the place of birth (*uppattiṭṭhāna*).

The meaning is: "the source of their arising. Alternatively, the four aggregates based on the body-faculty (kāyindriya) are specifically called "with-outflows" (sāsava) because they serve as the cause for the powerful outflow of sensual desire and so forth; thus, it means the place where those arise.
"He knows" (munāti) means that he cognizes the object just as one measuring with a nāḷi-measure or weighing with a great balance-scale.
The meaning [of *manas*] is as follows: it is called *mano* because it "thinks" (*manate*); that is to say, it knows various objects by way of delimiting them.
As for those which, by virtue of their specific characteristics, ought to be designated by the term "base" (*āyatana*), they are the eye and so forth, and thus have been so stated.
Therefore, other phenomena (*dhammā*) that constitute the domain of the mind (*manogocara*) possess the status of a single base solely by virtue of their common characteristic.

Having introduced [the term], it is explained as follows: Just as the preceding [objects] are manifest through the relations of object and subject—consisting of coarse things, objects, and mental processes—so too other domains of the mind (manogocara) are not unmanifest; yet they do not maintain their own intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
It is for the purpose of illustrating this meaning that the word *dhamma* is used. They are maintained (*dhārīyanti*) in the sense that they are determined by way of a common form (*sāmaññarūpa*).

Or [these are] mental objects (dhammā). For just as visible forms and so forth are cognized by eye-consciousness and the rest solely through their respective individual natures in an exclusive manner, these [mental objects] are not so;
rather, because they consist of manifold phenomena, because they are common [to all consciousness], and because they share a commonality of nature, they are cognized by the mind.
511. "Sena senā" means by their respective [groups]. "Uṭṭhahanti" means they exert themselves; "vāyamanti" means they strive, which has the sense of performing their own respective functions.

And in this context, regarding the term *āyatana*, in the expression "āyatanti ettha," the word *āyatana* has the sense of a locus (adhikaraṇa); in the second and third [instances], it has the sense of an agent (kattū).
"Te ca" refers to those mental states and mental factors (*cittacetasika-dhammā*). For they [arise] in relation to their respective doors and objects.
They come, they go, they proceed—thus they are called *āyā*. "They extend" means that because they have not previously arisen, they were dormant and unmanifest;
now, from the past onwards, they stretch forth, making them manifest; the meaning is that they cause them to arise. And this is the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
"It does not turn back" means it does not cease by way of non-arising and cessation. "Basis, basis" (*āyatanaṃ āyatanaṃ*) is a reduplicated expression.
This is for the purpose of showing that the designation "eye" and so forth is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) in relation to those [bases].

Having thus explained the meaning of the term *āyatana* by way of its distinct components, he now begins the passage starting with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) in order to show its meaning also by way of its figurative application (*pariyāya*). [The bases are] delightful because they are filled with excellent fruits and because they are free from danger.
They are said to "dwell therein" because they are as if dwelling there; hence he says, "because their existence is dependent upon them. Wherein gold, gems, and so forth [are found]...
They remain crowded together as if they were dwelling there; that region is their mine.

Thus, showing that the mind and mental factors [are present] in the eye and so forth—that these are their mine—it is said: “In the eye and so forth... the mine. Regarding the phrase “because of being dependent on that”:
here, the mind is not the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) for the mind-consciousness and other mental factors; therefore, its status as their door is [denied].

It should be understood as the state of dependence (*nissayabhāva*). Although consciousness and mental factors arise through the convergence of conditions while not having previously existed, they appear there as if gathered together in one place when obtained simultaneously; thus it is said: "because of their convergence by way of base, door, and object.
For there is no such thing as the existence of phenomena even in the future time. Therefore he said: "a heap..."
“There is nothing in the future. “From arising right there” means from arising within those very [bases] such as the eye.
This is stated by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), treating the eye and so forth—which serve as the conditions for arising—as if they were the place of arising.

For immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) have no actual place of arising in the primary sense (*nippariyāyato*). Or rather, it is because they serve as their support (*nissaya*) and object (*ārammaṇa*).

Therefore, it is designated as having arisen from that very source. For there is no relationship of support and supported even among material phenomena (rūpadhamma) apart from their status as conditions.

Hence he said: "by way of being the support and the object. Because the definition of a cause emphasizes its negative concomitance (vyatireka), he stated only "due to their absence, [the effect] is absent," and not "due to their presence, [the effect] is present."

“By the meaning as stated” means by the meaning expressed in the manner described: as in “it sees,” etc.; as in “because of entering (āyāna) from the sense bases (āyatana) and because of extending (tana),” etc.; and as in “the place of abiding,” etc.

Because of the great number of phenomena included within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), and because they mostly perform their function only when existing in plurality, there is the use of the plural designation: “they are both phenomena (dhammā) and a base (āyatana).”

513. It is a "characteristic" (*lakkhaṇa*) because it is characterized in such and such a way, or because it is that by which something is characterized; thus, it is intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "To that extent" means according to that measure;

by this, he shows the state of being neither deficient nor excessive. In this regard, since there is no phenomenon whatsoever apart from the twelve bases (*āyatana*), there is no objection regarding excess.
However, the possession of their own characteristics (*salakkhaṇadhāraṇa*) applies to all of them.
Regarding the "general characteristic" (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), he says, "For even the eye and so forth," etc., in order to show that a charge of deficiency could arise.
"Designated as the life-continuum mind" (*bhavaṅgamanasaṅkhāta*) means designated as the life-continuum mind that has proceeded after vibrating twice.
Since the arising of adverting (*āvajjana*) occurs only when there is the proceeding of the life-continuum by way of vibration, and not otherwise, it is also the cause of adverting.
Having said this, it was stated: “The so-called life-continuum mind... [is] the door of arising. “Unshared” means unshared by eye-consciousness and the rest.
Even though they are indeed unshared, it should be understood that the sphere of mental objects (dhammāyatana) is not included because the eye and the other [senses] are taken as doors.
Alternatively, it is called “unshared” with reference to its uniqueness in terms of being both a door and an object.
514. Inconsistency should be applied regarding the order of arising and so forth, based on the fact that they generally arise together.
For, as a rule, the eye-base and the others arise together for someone at some time. Thus it has been said:

"At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), eleven bases become manifest for someone," and so forth. Therefore, first of all, the order of the arising of the bases is not tenable.

There is no sequence of abandoning because the wholesome and indeterminate states are not to be abandoned; no sequence of practice because the unwholesome and certain indeterminate states are not to be practiced;

and no sequence of planes because eight of the eleven bases belong exclusively to the sense-sphere, while the others are included within the four planes, and some are even supramundane. Regarding the internal [bases]:...

By the word "first" (*hī*), he shows that among internal bases, those that are internal should be taught first because they possess the nature of being internal and the nature of being objects [of consciousness];
and among those which must be taught first, the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) was taught earliest because it is the most manifest. Then, regarding the phrase "the nose-base and so forth":
here, because they lack the quality of being of great utility, they should not have been taught earlier than the eye and the ear.
The intention is that because they cannot be spoken of simultaneously, they should be taught in a single sequence; thus, they are taught according to the order beginning with the nose (*ghāna*).
For even if they were taught otherwise, one could not object to it, nor can it be said that those things which ought to be understood have not been taught.

Alternatively, the eye and the other [senses] are mentioned first because they have present objects (*paccuppannārammaṇa*) and are therefore more manifest in terms of their objects; as for the mind-base (*manāyatana*),...
However, [the objects] from "some with past objects" … pe … down to "some with indeterminable objects" are stated later.
Even among those with present objects, the four types having derived matter as their object are stated first, followed by that having primary matter as its object.

Furthermore, even among those with derived matter as their object, the order of teaching for the eye and so forth is for the purpose of illustrating how they receive objects more distantly and more distantly, and more swiftly and more swiftly.
The pair of eye and ear is stated first because their range is distant; even there, the eye is stated first of all because its range is more distant.
For even when one sees the current of a river from a great distance, one does not hear the sound of the water striking against it.
Between the nose and the tongue as well, the nose is stated first because its activity is swifter, [perceiving] even that which is merely placed in front.
"The smell of food is perceived. Or else, their order of teaching follows their respective locations. For in this body, the seat of the eye is at the very top;
below that is the ear; below that is the nose; below that is the tongue; and likewise, for the most part, the body.
But the mind, because it is formless (arūpī), is mentioned last of all. This is because each [sense] has its own specific range of objects (gocara).
Since the external bases (bāhirāyatana) are stated immediately after each [internal base], this is the meaning already expressed; thus, the sequence of these [bases] should be understood in this way.
"Gocaravisaya" means that which has a range (gocara) or object (visaya); it refers to the mind (mano). But what is its range, its object?

It is the range and object of all five [bases], beginning with the eye. [The phrase] "from the determination of the cause for the arising of consciousness" refers to the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness and the rest.

"Because of their fixed nature and because of their state of having grammatical case-endings. By this, he states the reason for mentioning visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth immediately after the eye (*cakkhu*) and other [bases].
(515) "Because they are included" means because they are included by way of numerical grouping. "By way of genus" means by way of their commonality as the state of being an eye.

"Difference in condition" refers to the difference in karma and so forth; for [there is a distinction] between wholesome and unwholesome karma, which is divided into categories such as giving (*dāna*) and taking life (*pāṇātipāta*).
And due to the distinction between its internal and external conditions that act as cooperative causes, the eye-base becomes differentiated and dissimilar.

"The differentiation of destinies" refers to the distinctions among the various destinations such as hell and so forth, and the differences between those without feet and so on; or it is understood as the differentiation within those very destinies.

"The differentiation of classes" refers to categories such as elephants and horses, or kṣatriyas and so forth. "The differentiation of the individual continuums" refers to the specific stream of existence of each respective being.

The classification of individuals (*puggalabheda*). That which was stated as the infinite variety of the bases (*vatthu*) such as the eye, that itself is the classification of the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*), because it does not transcend such a variety. From that, the infinite variety of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) should be applied.
Since there is no supramundane consciousness (*lokuttara-citta*) devoid of jhāna, therefore, by way of the five jhānas, there are eight supramundane types of consciousness.
“They are forty” means that by adding those [forty] to the eighty-one mundane consciousnesses, he said, “and of one hundred and twenty-one varieties.

“Bases” (vatthu) refers to the bases such as the eye and so forth. By way of their variety, consciousness is of infinite variety. “Ways of practice” (paṭipadā) refers to the painful way of practice and so forth.
By the word “and so forth” (ādi), the inclusion of the predominance of jhāna, the planes, the objects, and so on, should be understood. Blue is the counterpart (sabhāga) of blue.

"Other" means of a different kind. "Condition" refers to karma and so forth. Within that, too, the distinction should be understood as being originated by the wholesome (*kusala*) and so on, and as being originated by the cold season and so on.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the distinction of realms of existence (*gati*) and classes of beings (*nikāya*) is included.

"By way of distinction of individual essence and diversity": the distinction of individual essence (*sabhāva-bheda*) consists of such things as "pleasant," "painful," and "neither-painful-nor-pleasant. The diversity (*nānatta*) consists of such things as "born of eye-contact" and "born of ear-contact."
516. To explain in detail the meaning stated in brief as "because of not coming and because of not going," the passage beginning with "for they...

was spoken. Because their own nature is non-existent at the prior and subsequent limits, they do not come from anywhere prior to their arising, nor do they go anywhere after their passing away; even during the moment they exist, they are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change due to their fleeting duration.
Therefore he said, “Then indeed,” and so forth. *Īhanā* (endeavor) is the striving by way of active movement; *byāpāra* (activity) is the engagement by way of reflection.
Demonstrating the activity therein, he said, “For it does not occur thus for the eye, visible forms, and so on. Demonstrating the endeavor, he said, “And they [do not]...,” and so forth.
However, both together constitute what is called *īhā* and *byāpāra*; this is a statement given in reverse order. It is the very nature of things (*dhammatā*).
It is the very nature (*sabhāva*), or the causal capacity (*kāraṇasamatthatā*)—the state of being doors and so forth in those things devoid of effort or activity—which is *dhammatā*.
And in this sense, the meaning of "yaṃ" is "yasmā" (because). In the previous [explanation], the word "yaṃ" is a qualification of the arising (*sambhavana*).
This is because of the statement: "Monks, 'an empty village' is a designation for these six internal sense-bases."
They are to be regarded as like an empty village. When an empty village is entered along with food and drink, whatever vessel one touches is found to be empty;
likewise, when these [aggregates] grasped as permanent and so forth are investigated thoroughly, they are seen to be empty indeed.
Therefore he said: "Because they are devoid of permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood."

It is said that visible forms and other objects are "afflictive" (*abhighātaka*) to the eye and other sense faculties by virtue of their capacity to give rise to covetousness and dejection within the doors of the eye and so forth.
There are six types of creatures: snakes, pythons, birds, dogs, lions, and monkeys. Their respective domains are uneven terrain, caves, the open air, villages, charnel grounds, and forests.

In this context, through the eyes and other faculties—which possess inclinations toward uneven terrain and so forth—their states resemble those who have grasped at phenomena existing in conditions similar to uneven ground, caves, the open air, villages, charnel grounds, and forests.
The similarity of visible forms and the other [sense objects] to poison and so forth should be applied because they are not delightful.
Thus ends the commentary on the introduction to the detailed exposition of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Elements (*dhātu*)
517. "Consciousness of the eye" (*cakkhussa viññāṇaṃ*) means the consciousness that has the eye as its cause.
Granted that visible forms, light, attention, and so forth are also causes of that consciousness, they are common causes; whereas the eye is the uncommon [cause].

This designation is made by way of the uncommon cause, just as one says "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout. For indeed, the eye is not shared with other persons, yet it is shared with respect to all visible forms such as blue and so on.
It is indicated by way of its state as a master. "Vidahati" means that it produces [the action] as if assigning it, saying, "In this and that manner you must proceed"; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, since the specific sense of the verbal root (dhātu) is illuminated by the prefix (upasagga), it is called a "root" even when the prefix is absent.

It should be understood that this word expresses that meaning. Since the establishment of verbal roots (dhātu) occurs in relation to the agent, the object, the state of being, the instrument, and the locus, all five of these meanings have been stated.

Because supramundane elements (lokuttara-dhātuyo) do not burn with the suffering of saṃsāra, but rather dispel it, they are specified as "mundane" (lokiya). "Vavatthitā" means established, or else, mutually unmixed.
The elements such as gold and silver refer to the rocks and so forth that serve as the seeds for gold and the like.

Regarding the phrase "according to what occurs" (*yathāsambhava*), some here explain the meaning as: "whatever purpose occurs in relation to the mundane and supramundane elements, [it is] in accordance with that.

This is incorrect, because it was stated specifically by qualifying them as "mundane elements. Furthermore, this inclusion of the phrase "according to what occurs" is made from the standpoint of their functional purpose (*atthavasena*).
This is stated by way of function, not by way of element. Granted that all five functions are desirable for all [faculties] such as the eye;
nevertheless, among the eye and the others, when there is a desire to express a factor in its capacity as agent (*kattūvacana*), it does not at that time have the status of an object (*kamma*).

But when there is a desire to express it as an object, it does not at that time have the status of an agent. The same applies to the remaining [faculties]; thus, the inclusion is made according to what is possible. Therefore he said:
“Thus, regarding the eye and so forth,” etc. (518).

They are called *dhātu*s because they bear (*dhārenti*) their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); here too, the grammatical derivation of the word *dhātu* should be understood as “that which bears is a *dhātu*,” taking the root *dhā* in the sense of “bearing.
Furthermore, this [root] has the sense of an agent (*kattuattha*), which is distinct from the former [sense of] “establishing” and “maintaining.”
Because they possess distinct natures. Furthermore, the primary meaning of the word *dhātu*—the mere maintenance of a nature devoid of a sentient being—is stated separately.

In the phrase "the elements (dhātuyo) like the elements (dhātuyo)," it should be understood that the word *dhātu*, which is conventionally established for men just as the word *sīha* is for a lion, is here applied metaphorically (*upacāra*) to the eye and so forth, just as it is established for the mineral constituents of a rock. Knowledge and the knowable are "knowledge-and-knowable" (*ñāṇañeyyāni*).
Their components are the elements (dhātu) that constitute those various divisions, which are the components of both knowledge and the knowable.

In this context, the division of knowledge is a portion of the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), while the division of the knowable consists of all eighteen [elements]; thus, the elements are merely the components of knowledge and the knowable.

Alternatively, the "knowable by knowledge" (ñāṇañeyya) refers to the unerring intrinsic nature (sabhāva) to be known by knowledge, which is what is expressed by the word *dhātu*; it does not refer to things grasped erroneously by views and the like.
The meaning is "that which is to be known" (*ñeyya*); the eyes and so forth are the constituent parts (*avayava*) of that object of knowledge (*ñāṇa-ñeyya*).

It should be understood that the word *dhātu*, which is conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) for tastes and other qualities that are constituent parts possessing dissimilar characteristics, is used metaphorically (*upacarita*) for the eyes and other such parts. Alternatively, it may be seen as being conventionally established for the eyes and so forth just as it is for tastes and the like.
By the phrase "this is a designation for that which is merely devoid of a soul" (*nijjīvamattass' etaṃ adhivacanaṃ*), [it is shown] regarding the referent of the term "merely devoid of a soul"...
This shows the conventional usage (*nirūḷhata*) of the word *dhātu*. "One who has six elements" (*cha-dhāturo*) means one for whom there are six elements.

That collection of phenomena which is called a "man" in the world is merely a collection of the six elements—earth and the rest—which are themselves devoid of a soul and consist of mere intrinsic natures;
the meaning is that herein there is no soul (*jīva*) nor any person (*purisa*).
519. Since the sequence of the eye and the other [faculties] was stated previously, here, in order to show the sequence of the three elements within each triad, he says:
"By way of the successive determination of cause and fruit. The successive determination of cause and fruit is simply their status as cause and fruit;

and the status of the mind-element and the mental-object element as causes for the mind-consciousness-element should be applied according to what is possible. [This applies to] the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*).

The resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*) is a condition for resultant mind-consciousness by way of proximity (*anantara*) and so forth, as well as by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). For other [types of mind-consciousness], all [elements] are conditions by way of decisive support.

Furthermore, the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*), whether co-nascent or non-co-nascent—such as feeling and the rest—is a condition for mind-consciousness by way of co-nascence and so forth, by way of proximity and so forth when not co-nascent, by way of decisive support, and by way of object (*ārammaṇa*) and so forth. Thus it is a condition for mind-consciousness.
Or, by way of the mind that has become the door. For even the mind that has become the door is called the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) in the Suttas;
thus, the status of that mind-element as the cause of mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) should be applied according to the circumstances.

In this context, "cause" (*hetu*) is intended in the sense of a condition (*paccaya*), and "fruit" (*phala*) is intended in the sense of what is produced by conditions; hence he says "the eye-element," and so forth.
520. "By way of all" means by way of the thirty-five elements previously mentioned, beginning with the light element (*ābhā-dhātu*).

Since that which lacks an ultimate intrinsic nature can never be included within things that possess an ultimate intrinsic nature, he says, "existing by way of their own intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato vijjamānānam*).

Because the various appearances of color, such as the radiance of the moon and the sun, are indeed forms, he says, "the light element is simply the form element" (*rūpa-dhātu*). They are bound up with form and so forth.

Having defined the "sign of beauty" (*subhanimitta*) as the mode of appearance that should be grasped by way of being an object for lust, the text uses a dependent construction instead of simply saying "only visible forms and so forth.
The second alternative is stated: even when it is not an object for lust, the wholesome-resultant object is the "element of beauty" (*subhadhātu*).
The word "the rest" refers to those associated with the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). "The mere cessation of two elements" refers to the mind-consciousness elements.
It is "mere cessation" because it is the state of cessation of the fourth immaterial-sphere consciousness-arising.

The mention of the two elements is made because, like the cessation of other consciousnesses, the cessation of the consciousness-element and the mind-element is accomplished through the power of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
The phrase "mere dharma-element" is stated because the dharma-element is included within the sense-sphere (*kāmadhātu*). "Associated with the sense-sphere" means...
Associated with sensual lust, or connected with the strands of sensual pleasure by way of making them its object.

"In this interval" means in that space delimited by the Avīci hell and the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven. They are called "those who range here" because, having plunged [into it], they move within the lower portion of that space.
Even though they may range elsewhere, they are included "here" because they are comprised within the aforementioned place.
The renunciation element (*nekkhammadhātu*) is simply the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) on the side of applied thought (*vitakka*).

"All wholesome states" (*sabbepi kusalā dhammā*) refers to all blameless states that occur from the performance of merit consisting in giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriya*), the performance of merit consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-puññakiriya*), and going forth (*pabbajjā*), up until the attainment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*).
The cruelty element (*vihiṃsādhātu*) is volition (*cetanā*) or the desire to harm others. Non-cruelty is compassion (*karuṇā*).

"Inferior" means despised; "superior" means esteemed. It should be understood that in the *Khandha-niddesa*, the phrase "neither too despised nor too esteemed—this is the intermediate" refers to the intermediate element (*majjhimā dhātu*) extracted precisely from the inferior category.
"Both" refers to the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) and the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
Although the consciousness element is analyzed by way of the sixfold consciousness element, nevertheless, by the inclusion of the term "consciousness element," [all seven are meant].

Because it precedes and follows that [visual consciousness], the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is already included; thus he said: "The consciousness-element is simply the seven consciousness-elements, beginning with eye-consciousness.

Because there are many eye-elements and so forth, and because each of these exists in various modes, the world is described as having "many elements" (*anekadhātu*) by way of those diverse elements (*nānādhātu*); thus he said: "It is merely a classification of the eighteen elements."

521. In many manuscripts it is written: "By way of the division into the eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element"; in some, however, it is written: "By way of the division into the eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element.

In this context, the intended meaning is not a connection with the word *dhātu* (element) alone for the eye and so forth, because what is being stated is the differentiation of that which has the intrinsic nature of cognizing.
And when a connection is made with the term *viññāṇadhātu*, two mentions of "mind" (*mano*) need not be made;

for there are not two mind-consciousness-elements (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). Alternatively, without inserting the mention of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) in between, one could say: "eye... pe... body, mind-consciousness-element, and mind-element," because there is no formation of a *dvanda* compound when the members are not of equal rank.
However, the reading here might be: "by way of the distinction of eye... pe... body-consciousness, mind, and mind-consciousness-elements."

Since those who mostly hold the doctrine of self proclaim the non-duality and permanence of each respective self, this exposition of multiplicity and impermanence serves to eradicate their perception of a "living soul" (jīva).

The teaching on the aggregates and bases is a concise exposition, while the teaching on the faculties is a detailed exposition; with reference to both of these, this [teaching] is neither too concise nor too detailed.
The teaching on the elements (*dhātudesanā*). The teaching on the elements as set forth in the Abhidhamma or in the Suttanta-bhājaniya is an extremely concise teaching;
the teaching that should be expounded by way of the many elements beginning with the light-element (*ābhādhātu*) and ending with the various elements (*nānādhātu*) is an extremely detailed teaching.
In relation to both of these, this [present] teaching is neither too concise nor too detailed.
Of that Blessed One. "Struck down by the splendor of the True Dhamma" means struck down by the power of the True Dhamma.

(522) "As a conditioned phenomenon" means by way of enumeration. "As a genus" means by way of the commonality of being an eye. Alternatively, "as a genus" means by way of the specific nature of the eye; thus he said, "eye-sensitivity.
It is reckoned as "twenty phenomena" by not breaking down [the category] into feeling and so forth.
