"By way of inclusion. Regarding the phrase "by way of the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousnesses": here, the term "remaining" is used in relation to the indeterminate;
however, the wholesome and unwholesome are not included at all.
(523) And those are the five elements beginning with eye-consciousness.

“Only by the immediately preceding and so forth” means by the immediately preceding condition and others. However, it has already been stated that the impulsion-consciousness-element is also a condition for the impulsion-consciousness-element by way of the repetition condition (*āsevanapaccaya*). By “mental-object element” (*dhammadhātu*), the co-nascent aggregates such as feeling and so forth are intended.
Therefore he said: “The co-nascent... [is] a condition. In the phrase “by the non-disappearance condition and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (*ādi*)— [...continues...]
The state of being a condition for the mind-consciousness element—whether as root, predominance, kamma, result, nutriment, faculty, jhāna, or path—is subsumed according to what is appropriate.
Therefore it is said: "It is a condition in many ways.

Furthermore, certain types of the dhamma-element—namely, subtle matter and the various modes of Nibbāna—are fit to be made objects of consciousness due to the absence of association, immediate succession, and so forth. This is for the purpose of [providing objects for] the five-door resultant and functional consciousnesses.

It was stated, “of a certain mind-consciousness element”; however, resultant [consciousness] associated with the mind-door also occurs taking a certain portion of the mental-object element as its object.

Alternatively, this phrase “of a certain mind-consciousness element” refers to all such [states] as sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, sense-sphere functional consciousness, the two types of direct knowledge, and the two formless-sphere [resultants].

This was stated with reference to the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); however, it is well known that for the supramundane mind-consciousness element, certain factors of the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*) serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).

In order to show the conditions for the eye-consciousness element and so forth—which exceed the aforementioned conditioning factors such as the eye—[the author] began with the words "not only" (*na kevalam*), etc.
Therein, "light and so forth" (*ālokādayo*) refers to light...
"Name" refers to light such as that of the sun. Its status as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) should be understood according to the method of the Suttas;
the same applies to the remaining factors. "Aperture" specifically refers to the ear canal. "Wind" is the air that carries odors. "Water" is the moisture that moistens the food placed in the mouth.
"Earth" is the earth element that serves as the support for the bodily sensitivity. The life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) occurs twice.
The life-continuum consciousness has stirred. In all instances, "attention" refers to advertence-attention.
Because the mode of appearance to be seen is being stated without distinction, he said, "all of them.

Since this is an investigation of the plane of insight specifically, it is qualified as "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*). Regarding the phrase "secluded from the past and future limits," here "the past limit" means...

The past time is called the "prior end" (*pubbanta*) and the future is called the "subsequent end" (*aparanta*). In both cases, conditioned elements (*saṅkhata-dhātu*) are devoid of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-vivitta*), because their intrinsic nature is not to be found.
Alternatively, the prior end of a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature is its arising, because it was non-existent prior to that;

the subsequent end is its passing away, because it is non-existent after that. Therefore, by the phrase "devoid of prior and subsequent ends," what is meant is the absence of production and the absence of destruction.
It is because it serves as a support (*nissaya*) for consciousness, just as the surface of a drum is for sound or as the eye-faculty is for consciousness.
The same principle applies to the surface of a mirror and so forth. "Press" (*yanta*) refers to a sugarcane press. "Oil-press roller" (*cakkayaṭṭhi*) refers to a sesame cake;
for although it is not actually a roller, it is called a "oil-press roller" because it resembles one, or it is stated thus with reference specifically to the roller itself.
By means of these similes, it demonstrates that when insentient things—such as a drum, a hide, a stick, and so forth—come together, there occurs the production of insentient sounds and the like;
likewise, when insentient things—such as the eye, visible forms, and so forth—come together, there occurs the arising of insentient eye-consciousness and the like.
Thus, it shows that cause and effect consist merely of elements (dhātu) and are devoid of an agent or an experiencer.
"Preceding and following attendants of one who is lifeless go forth"— the meaning is that certain lifeless things act as preceding and following attendants for any lifeless thing.

Alternatively, the mind-element itself, not overstepping its own moment, should be regarded as if it were a preceding and following attendant— due to its state of being immediately prior and subsequent in time—
even though no such intention to precede or follow exists in relation to eye-consciousness and the rest, which likewise do not overstep their own moments.

For, just as there is no simultaneous arising of various consciousness-elements because they lack a single simultaneous immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*), so too there is no immediate succession [of different types] because they lack mutual immediate conditions.
If such [succession] were possible, then even in the presence of the six objects, the apprehension of those six objects would occur even without attention (*manasikāra*);
yet this does not happen. Therefore, immediately after seeing and the other [sensory processes],...

Just as there is no hearing and so forth [immediately] after the absence [of the sense bases], neither do seeing and so forth arise immediately after the mind-consciousness element, nor does the mind-consciousness element arise immediately after seeing and so forth.

In this regard, it is logical that because the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and seeing and so forth have different objects, seeing and so forth do not arise immediately after the mind-consciousness element, nor do hearing and so forth arise immediately after seeing and so forth. [This applies to] seeing and so forth...

But is it not improper [to claim] that because the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) and the subsequent [consciousnesses] have different objects, no mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) arises immediately after the eye-consciousness and the others?
This is not so, because there is an established distinction between those with fixed objects and those with unfixed objects.

Furthermore, if any consciousness element were to arise immediately after seeing and the other [sensory processes], that too would be a consciousness element of seeing and so forth by virtue of being the door of seeing and so forth.

If that were so, it would not be the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); and consequently, just as the mental door’s engagement in the function of thinking does not relinquish its function of reflecting, so too the seeing-consciousness element would be reduced to not relinquishing its function of seeing.
Likewise, because everything immediately following that [seeing] would also be of the nature of seeing-consciousness, the groups of consciousness (*viññāṇakāya*) would no longer exist.
If it is argued that just as the mind-element (manodhātu) follows immediately after the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), and from that, the eye-consciousness and so forth arise;

and likewise, the mind-element follows immediately after the seeing-consciousness-element (dassanaviññāṇadhātu), and from that, the ear-consciousness and so forth arise—this is not so, because it would follow that the mind-element itself is the seeing-element.

For just as the state of the mind when it is undifferentiated is called the mind-element by virtue of being mere mentation (mananamattatā), so too [would it follow] for the state of seeing when it is undifferentiated.

The visual element (*dassanadhātu*) would consist merely in the act of seeing. And since that eye-consciousness has visible form as its object, there would be an absence of the engagement with objects such as sound;

consequently, auditory consciousness and the others would be impossible. Furthermore, consciousness would be directed solely toward the objective field of visible form, because it would follow—just as in the case of mental consciousness—that visual consciousness and the others must have the same physical basis (*vatthu*), whereas consciousness is dependent upon different bases.

It would not be so, and that is not tenable. Therefore, just as with pleasure and pain, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) should be regarded as the intermediary between the eye-consciousness and the others on one hand, and the mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) on the other.
Yet, unlike that equanimity (*upekkhā*), it does not possess the state of being neither-painful-nor-pleasant, nor is it characterized by non-seeing or non-thinking;

rather, its identity with mind-consciousness arises from the lack of distinction in its function of thinking. For the mind, while operating within the physical basis of the heart, [performs this function].

Having shown the object of consciousnesses dependent on other bases, it turns back and remains merely as heat and merely as conceiving, just like a fire that turns back after showing its object; and when arising upon the cessation of consciousnesses dependent on other bases, it arises merely as heat, just like a fire.
And these mere conceivings, which proceed in accordance with their conditions, constitute the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).

They are the limits. For the five types of sensory consciousness accompanied by perception of resistance have the mere function of impingement, because they are produced by the impact of the sense-faculties and their objects;
and for the mind-consciousness, which arises with the faculty characterized by mentation, there is a non-occurrence of reflection upon the object, because it lacks the capacity for such reflection.
Therefore, by the power of the friction and impact caused by that impingement, the characteristic of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) [is interrupted].

The mind, having been in a state of movement and turning back, being devoid of any specific reflection, produces a mere mentalizing (manana) at the end of its reflecting, which is conducive to the initial impact (abhinipāta).
Even seeing and so forth, not exceeding a second moment beyond the mere impact, is likewise devoid of the designations "reflection" and "mentalizing" because it conforms to itself [as mere sensing].
The mind-element (manodhātu), although comprised within the body of mental consciousness (manoviññāṇakāya) by virtue of its object and function,

produces— distinct through its specific modes of engagement such as seeing and so forth, yet similar to it in its nature as a state of mind— a mere act of thinking consisting of reflection and so on with respect to another object. Therefore,

because it serves as the exit and entry for the mind-door and functions as the reception of the object from another door and another range of attention for the five types of sensory consciousness, [it is distinguished from them].

These are described as preceding and following respectively according to their sequence. Now, although this [consciousness] possesses the nature of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), because it lacks the specific function of reflecting (*manana*) that arises from the mind (*mano*), it is called the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*) simply as "mind" (*manomatta*) due to its commonality with the state of being an element (*dhātubhāva*).
And for the same reason stated above, by eliding the suffix *-matta* and applying the meaning of "consciousness," it is also called "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*).

Its inclusion within the category of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) is indeed appropriate. However, it is called "mind-element" (manodhātu) for the purpose of distinguishing it from the other consciousnesses and their respective doors and objects.
But in the term "mind-consciousness element" (manoviññāṇadhātu), the mention of "mind" (mano) serves as a qualification of the consciousness element.
And when "mind-consciousness" is used to qualify the element, the mention of "mind" functions specifically as the door through which that consciousness arises.

It is not called "mind-element" (manodhātu) because it is worthy of the designation "door. For that [element] is included within the mind-door (manodvāra), whereas the consciousness-element of the mind (manoviññāṇadhātu)—which is the consciousness of the mind—is worthy of the designation "mind-door" because it precedes and follows seeing and so forth;

and because its function of reflecting (manana) is more specific than its function of cognizing (viññāṇa). Therefore, by means of the elision of the particle *matta*, it is termed "mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa) for the purpose of clarifying its insentient nature.
And it is called the "mind-consciousness element.

It should be regarded as like a dart and like a stake because of its association with the three kinds of suffering. "Associated with the darts and stakes of feeling" means because of its association with the darts and stakes known as feeling.
"Like those who are afflicted" means like persons who have become afflicted by that [feeling]. "Hope itself is suffering" is "hope-suffering," which is the frustration of hope.

Or it is suffering. For perception clings to even the foul and so forth as being beautiful and so forth; and it produces frustration for that [clinging] because the beauty and so forth desired by it are not accomplished.
A forest deer who perceives a grass-man as a man is one who grasps a sign that is not according to reality; perception is just like that, thus he said, "like a forest deer.
Since volitional formations (saṅkhāra) have action as their primary characteristic, he says, "because of casting [the result] into rebirth-linking," and so forth.
It has been said. "Because it is followed by the suffering of birth" means that it is accompanied by the suffering of birth produced by oneself;

for birth, conditioned by existence (*bhava*), is indeed the suffering of birth. Like a lotus, even a form appearing as a woman or the like—which is seen to be like a razor-wheel—produces various kinds of calamities.
All disadvantages are [rooted in] passion and so forth, as well as birth and so forth.
And [the conditioned] is an object, unpacified, and fearful. Because it is the opposite of that, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) should be viewed as the deathless and so forth.
The absence of definition is the absence of a restriction such as "this alone is the object for this [consciousness]"; by means of that, just as a forest monkey...
Just as someone, unrestrained by anyone, lets go of one tree branch he has grasped and takes hold of another,

letting go of that too to take another, wandering about without remaining fixed anywhere; so too, it is "unsteadiness" (anavaṭṭhitatā) when, having let go of one object grasped, one takes another, and letting go of that too, another— being incapable of proceeding without grasping an object.
And he shows that it is "equal to a monkey. A wicked horse-colt is one who, even when pierced by eight spears, follows a wrong path.
"Falling wherever it pleases" means because of its state of falling upon whatever desired object it wishes.
A stage actor is one who wears various costumes.
The commentary on the exposition of the bases and the givers is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth chapter.
16. Commentary on the Exposition of the Faculties and the Truths.

Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Faculties (Indriyavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā) 525. "Twenty-two" is the delimitation by number. "Faculties" (indriyāni) is the indication of the phenomena so delimited. "The eye-faculty," and so forth, is the demonstration of their specific nature.
In that regard, it exercises the function of a lord (indaṭṭhaṃ) at the eye-door; in its capacity as the eye-door, [it exercises this function] by means of those things associated with that door.
It is called the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) because it exercises lordship over itself and sovereignty over others.

For it makes itself conform to the apprehension of those visible forms, and they in turn conform to it. The same principle applies to the rest as well. Therefore, it exercises the function of lordship at the doors of the ear, nose, tongue, and body;
thus it is the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*). It exercises the function of lordship in the characteristic of cognizing; thus it is the mind-faculty (*manindriya*).
In the characteristic of femininity, the characteristic of being a member of an assembly, the characteristic of protection, the characteristic of pleasure, the characteristic of pain,
the characteristic of mental joy, the characteristic of mental grief, the characteristic of equanimity, the characteristic of resolve, the characteristic of exertion,
the characteristic of establishment, the characteristic of non-distraction, the characteristic of seeing, and in the occurrence of the thought "I shall know the unknown."

The faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is so called because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) in the state of "one who has already known" (*aññātāvibhāva*), which is the further thorough knowledge of those very phenomena already known, characterized by knowing.
"One should know" (*vijāniyā*) means one should understand. The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and from the plane" (*bhūmito ca*) has the sense of including what is not explicitly stated;

by this, it includes "only that much. We shall explain that "only that much" later. This is because [the faculty] exists even in those states that have not yet reached full comprehension (*asammasanupaga*).
The state of being visible is not included here.
"In the prior stage" means in the stage prior to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "Unknown" means not known, not attained.

It is "deathless" (*amata*) because, by virtue of its permanence, there is no death—that is, no breaking up—for it; or, because when this is attained, there is no more dying. It is so called because it is to be reached.

"And the state" (*padañca*) refers to the deathless state, Nibbāna. By the phrase "because it arises for one who has practiced in this way," he shows that this faculty is designated thus by way of its preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).
"From thorough understanding" (*ājānato*) means from knowing without overstepping the boundary seen by the first path.
That state by which the person possessing it, or the phenomena associated with it, become "those who have already known" (*aññātāvino*), is the state of "one who has already known" (*aññātāvibhāva*).

Because it arises as an actual state (*bhāvabhūta*) for one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) who knows that his task is finished, it is said: "because it arises for one whose taints are destroyed.
It is called a *liṅga* because it leads to or makes known (*gameti ñāpeti*); or else, it is a *liṅga* because by means of it something is marked (*liṅgīyati*).
What does it lead to, or what is marked by it? It is Indra, or [the state of] Indra. The *liṅga* of Indra is *indaliṅga*; the meaning of *indaliṅga* is its specific nature (*tamsabhāva*).
The meaning of "indaliṅga" is either the mark of Indra (the sense-faculty) or the meaning of the word *indriya* itself;
thus it is "indaliṅgaṭṭho. That which is prepared or produced is called "siṭṭha"; that which is bestowed by Indra is "indasiṭṭha. "Juṭṭha" means practiced or cultivated.

Since they are the marks of the "Indra" designated as karma, and are also bestowed by him, they should be associated only with those [faculties] born of karma, and not others. And these two meanings apply only to karma.
They are to be applied, and the others likewise to the Blessed One; thus he said, "according to what is appropriate. "By that" means by the Blessed One, because of his sovereignty over karma.
"In this" means among these faculties. They "indicate," "make known," or "reveal" through the success or failure of the fruit, because of the comprehension of the success or failure of the cause.
In such passages as "He cultivates that sign," even the making of an object [is implied].
When it was said that "cultivation has been explained," he said, "some [are for] cultivation by way of the object.

Although all [factors] are to be made into objects, the word "some" is used because those not to be contemplated are not to be cultivated due to the frequent attention paid to them; for in their case, there is merely reflective observation (*paccavekkhaṇā*).
In such passages as "of one cultivating that path," cultivation is stated to be *bhāvanā* (development); thus, those [factors] which are to be developed...
Referring to faith and the other [faculties], he said: "Some are for the sake of cultivation and frequenting.
Sovereignty (*ādhipacca*) is the state of being a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*).

And even though they lack the status of a faculty-condition, in the case of the female and male faculties, when they occur according to their respective conditions within a continuum accompanied by them, [other states] do not occur in any other mode.

The predominance [of the faculties] consists in their being followed by the gender and so forth. And in this sense, they are called *indriyas* because they "exercise power" (*indanti*), that is, they exercise supreme sovereignty.
According to the method shown for the eye and the others, the predominance of the others—such as vitality (*jīvita*) and so forth—in following those [faculties] should be applied accordingly.

Non-delusion itself is not four separate states; therefore, it is the intention that its characteristics and so forth should be understood as those explained in the discussion on the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*).
The remaining [characteristics] are presented there in the description of the aggregates (*khandhaniddesa*) by means of their characteristics and so forth, specifically as the immaterial.
526. The acquisition of the noble plane by beings is common to the Blessed One’s teaching and is the purpose of the words.

He said: "By means of the full understanding of internal phenomena," and so forth. Because the other faculties are also included within the personal existence (*attabhāva*), and because they serve as the root for the manifestation of that personal existence, the eye-faculty and the others are said to be "preeminently included within the personal existence";
thus it is stated: "The eye-faculty and the rest are included within the personal existence. In the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*, immediately after the female and male faculties...
Since the sequence for the teaching on the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) has already been stated, it is also said here:

"Then, the life-faculty. That [sequence] accords with the teaching in the *Indriyayamaka*. However, in the *Indriyavibhaṅga*, the life-faculty is mentioned immediately after the mind-faculty (*manindriya*);

it should be understood that it is placed in the middle of those [faculties] in order to demonstrate its role as the protector of both the preceding internal and the succeeding external ones. And that which...

"Whatever is felt, all that is suffering. This is for the purpose of making known that as long as the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), which sustains the two-fold state of existence, continues to function, there is no cessation of these feelings which are of the nature of suffering;
and by this, he makes known that the eye and so forth are to be fully understood because they are followed by suffering.
"For the purpose of showing the practice" means for the purpose of showing the preliminary practice (pubbabhāga-paṭipatti).

“Of that very same” means of the *anaññātaññassāmītindriya* itself. “Because it is to be developed immediately after that” is said with reference to the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) associated with the path of development; for development follows immediately after seeing.

Regarding the term “distinction,” here a distinction by way of intrinsic nature is intended, not by way of plane, person, and so forth; thus he says, “there is no distinction among the remaining ones.”
But is it not the case that the life-faculty has the characteristic of maintaining [the body] as its intrinsic nature, and therefore there is no distinction between its two types?
True, this is so; however, a distinction was taken for that [life-faculty] based on its material and immaterial intrinsic natures.

But since no such distinction exists for the others, their "non-distinction" was stated as the absence of any distinction. Is it not the case that here feeling and wisdom were mentioned by distinguishing them [from each other]?
No, because among the twenty-two faculties taught, both their differentiation and non-differentiation are intended.

(527) Although the eye-faculty and the others possess the status of being pre-arisen conditions (*purejāta-paccaya*) and so forth, it is said that "function" refers specifically to the function that must be accomplished by way of the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*), because that [specific function] is not shared with anything else and because it is the primary subject of this discussion on the faculties. Of itself...

The aspect of being sharp, dull, and so forth, is the "aspect of self" (attākāra); the causing of that [aspect] to follow along is the "causing of the aspect of self to follow along" (attākārānuvattāpana).

Therefore, he said: "the causing of the aspect of self—consisting of being sharp, dull, and so forth—to follow along. Alternatively, the causing of both what is designated as sharp, dull, etc., and the aspect of self to follow along is "the causing... to follow along.
Furthermore, by the separate mention of the "aspect of self" here, the inclusion of the manifestation of form and so forth should be understood. Of the eye-faculty...

For indeed, if the capacity for the manifestation of form—which is reckoned as the suitability for striking against form—were absent, the function of seeing by visual consciousness would never be possible.
This same principle applies to the ear-faculty and the others as well. It is the mind-faculty that exercises mastery over the others by virtue of its being their precursor;
it is not the others that do so for it. For even the faculties associated with it act only in accordance with its influence.
They accomplish their respective functions of the faculties by virtue of being mental factors (*cetasika*), but the mind-faculty (*manindriya*) does not do so under their influence;

for this [mind-faculty] possesses the quality of being the precursor (*pubbaṅgama*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the governing context—that [the function] must be accomplished through the status of being a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*)—continues to apply in all cases.
Even though there is no production (*anuppādana*) and no supporting (*anupatthambhana*) [of the subsequent state], the occurrence of those [subsequent states] proceeds by way of those conditions.
The state of being a sign (nimittabhāva) is conformity (anuvidhāna).
Pleasant and painful feelings, arising after having concealed and pervaded [the mind], overcome the co-nascent phenomena and overwhelm them;
they become manifest by themselves, and the co-nascent phenomena, through their influence, appear as if they have attained the state of pleasure or pain.

He said: "By not assuming their respective coarse aspects. One should apply [this principle] to the state of being neutral, as appropriate, even for that which is non-existent, unremoved, or associated with the unwholesome and its result.
Alternatively, it should be understood as the non-assumption of the aspects of existence and excellence by pleasures and pains of a similar kind.
"Overcoming of opposites" means the overcoming of opposites such as lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). "From the aspect of clarity," etc.
The functions of faith and the other [faculties] are, respectively, the attainment of the modes of seeing that are clear, grasped, established, and concentrated.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "ill-will and so forth," the higher fetters (*uddhaṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*) are included. Furthermore, the function shown belongs specifically to the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) when it is associated with the path;
for that very reason, when it is associated with the fruit, its function is the subsiding and abandoning of the respective fetters.

"It is shown" means this: for one who has performed all duties, because there is nothing further to be known, the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) is directed toward the Deathless alone and is a condition for its attainment;
it is not, like the others, occupied with other functions. Therefore he said: "and being a condition for the state of being directed toward the Deathless.
(528) The analysis by way of plane is of obvious meaning. Here it is asked: But why are there only these many faculties?

Are these alone what have been stated, and only these that have been stated? [They are stated] by way of the sense of predominance (*ādhipacca*); for "predominance" is indeed said to be sovereignty (*issariya*).
Why then is this predominance not found in other intrinsic phenomena (*sabhāva-dhamma*) as well, in respect of their respective functions and fruits?
For it may be that those things arisen from conditions (*paccayuppanna*) exist in dependence upon conditions; thus, [predominance] applies to both the fruit and the causal phenomena.
Is it that they follow one another and are to be followed? This is true; nevertheless, there is a distinction between them.

This very point has been shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) with the passage beginning: "For in the occurrence of eye-consciousness and so forth, the predominance of the eye and the other [faculties] is established.
Furthermore, regarding this designation of a "being" within the pentad of aggregates, its specific basis is the "six internal bases"; these, first of all—
They are stated first as "the eye-faculty... the mind-faculty" by way of their predominance (*ādhipaccatta*).
The two [female and male] states are for the purpose of showing that this personal existence (*attabhāva*) receives the designations "woman" and "man" on account of these.
And the state by which these acquired phenomena (*upādinnadhamma*) proceed is the cause of their persistence; this is for the purpose of showing that.

The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). This collection of phenomena, designated as a "being," proceeding by way of continuity, becomes defiled through these feelings; it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the pentad of feelings is presented.
Following that, for those desiring purification, the pentad beginning with faith is presented for the purpose of showing the equipment for cleansing.
These [factors]—the origin and the equipment for cleansing—are purified by means of these [five faculties]; having attained purity, their task is indeed finished.
The three faculties beginning with *anaññātaññassāmītindriya* are mentioned for the purpose of showing that [the noble persons] exist.
In all instances, the phrase "by way of predominance" (*ādhipaccattaṃ upādāya*) should be connected. Since the intended meaning is established by this much, others are not included.

Alternatively, these very same [faculties] are mentioned because they show the departure and so forth from both the process of existence (*pavatti*) and its cessation (*nivatti*). For, regarding the process of existence...
In particular, there are the six internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*), which serve as the fundamental support. As it is said: "The world has arisen in the six," and so forth.
Its arising is, for the most part, the manifestation of the mass of beings through the female and male faculties, by means of the signs of passion for objects that are discordant with one's own kind.
For this has been stated: "Great King, the descent of the embryo occurs through the conjunction of three things..."
“The mother is in her season, the gandhabba is present, and the parents have come together,” and so forth.

Its maintenance is by means of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), because it is to be sustained by that; hence he said: “life-span (*āyu*), stability (*ṭhiti*), subsistence (*yapanā*), maintenance (*yāpanā*),” and so forth.

Its enjoyment is by means of the feelings (*vedanā*); for it is through the influence of feeling that there is the enjoyment of all objects, whether desirable or otherwise. As it is said: “It feels, it feels... (*vedayati vedayatīti*).

“Monks, it is for this reason that it is called ‘feeling. Thus, fourteen faculties—from the eye faculty up to the equanimity faculty—have been taught with respect to their basis, origination, persistence, and enjoyment during the course of existence (*pavatti*). Just as these are presented in relation to the course of existence, so too are the others in relation to its cessation (*nivatti*).
For the five faculties beginning with faith are produced by depending upon the state of turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*).
The support is through turning back. Its arising is by means of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because it arises first by way of that turning back.

Its stability is by means of the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*), and its enjoyment is by means of the faculty of one who has known (*aññātāvindriya*), due to the full enjoyment of the supreme fruit.
Those whose taints are destroyed enjoy the bliss of Nibbāna through the mastery of their powers. Thus, too, these very same faculties have been taught.

To this extent, because the intended meaning has been established, there is no mention of others. By this very fact, it should be understood that their sequence of teaching has also been commented upon.
The commentary on the Exposition of the Faculties is finished.

Commentary on the Detailed Explanation of the Truths (Saccavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā): 529. Showing that even those [truths] mentioned by the word "truth" (*sacca*) alone, without being qualified by the word "noble" (*ariya*), are indeed the Noble Truths, he said:
"Truths means the four Noble Truths. For a general designation settles upon its specific instances.
And one who seeks a distinction must apply that distinction [to the specific term]. Alternatively, when the Noble Truths have been examined, the others are also effectively examined by implication;
thus, because they constitute the ground for insight (vipassanā) and are indeed the Noble Truths, the word "truths" was extracted and then specified as "the four Noble Truths."

"Sāsana-kkama" refers to the Noble Truths, or the teaching on the Noble Truths. For indeed, there is no word of the Blessed One that constitutes the entire Dispensation (*sāsana*) which is devoid of the Truths, since it proceeds by way of demonstrating both the path of progress and the path of cessation, along with their respective causes.

Therefore, it "proceeds" (*kamati*) within the Truths; or rather, the Dispensation—consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom—proceeds toward them by way of accomplishing its functions such as full understanding.

It proceeds; therefore, it is called *kama* because one goes (*kamati*) therein. What goes? The Dispensation (*sāsana*). The sequence of the Dispensation is the "sequence of the Dispensation" (*sāsanakkamo*);
the Truths are called the bases for the proceeding of the Dispensation, and that teaching is designated by that term.

"Thus" (*tathā*) means having that nature, namely the nature of suffering and so forth. "Not otherwise" (*avitathā*) means not having a different nature from that, being real in their nature as affliction and so on.
"Anaññathā" means being devoid of any other mode, free from modes such as non-affliction and so forth.

The sense of oppression is due to its being established through the state of suffering-as-suffering and the state of being the cause thereof. The sense of the conditioned is the state of being produced by conditions coming together and combining.

The sense of burning is the scorching by way of suffering-as-suffering and the state of being the cause thereof, or the association with the burning of the defilements. The state of being subject to change is twofold: by way of aging and by way of death.
The sense of change (*vipariṇāmaṭṭha*). Herein, the sense of oppression (*pīḷanaṭṭha*) is the mode of manifestation of suffering by its own essential nature;
the others are, respectively, the modes of manifestation through the seeing of origin, the path, and cessation. This is the distinction between all four.

Therein, *āyūhana*—the spreading out, the heaping up, and the production of suffering by way of delighting therein—is so called because the sense of "spreading" (*byāpana*) applies to the mode [of suffering].
It is called *āya* because it comes together (*samudayati*). The accumulation (*āyūhana*) of that suffering—its occurrence and manifestation—is its mode of appearing through its own inherent nature.
It is called *nidāna* because it deposits (*nidadāti*) suffering; the meaning is that it gives rise [to suffering] as if making one accept it, thinking, "This is that very suffering.
This is the sense of *nidāna*, which is the mode of appearing through the vision of suffering. By means of the suffering of saṃsāra...

The meaning of fetter (*saṃyojana*) is the state of binding. The meaning of impediment (*palibodha*) is that which obstructs the attainment of the path. These meanings of fetter and impediment are modes of manifestation revealed through the vision of cessation and the path.

It is called "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because beings escape from it, or because it itself is escaped from—being dissociated from all conditioned things by virtue of its nature as the relinquishment of all acquisitions (*upadhi*). This is its [meaning].

The mode of manifestation by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is its own specific characteristic; the other modes—seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment—or the modes of manifestation through the vision of origin, path, and suffering, consist in being undestroyed by the conditions of the syllables of origination.
"Emergence" (*niyyāna*) is the going forth from saṃsāra. This is its mode of manifestation by way of its own essence (*sarasa*). Through the cutting off of thorough ignorance (*paribodha*).
The attainment of Nibbāna is the meaning of the path as a cause, because the path has Nibbāna as its objective.
Its meaning as vision is the seeing of Nibbāna—or the seeing of the Four Truths—due to wisdom being predominant within it.

The meaning of dominance of the path is that the factors of the path exercise sovereignty over the associated mental states in the seeing of the Four Truths and in the pacification of the torment of defilements and suffering.

Or, because the path-factors, being specifically the objective support (*ālambana*) and the dominant influence (*adhipati*), are expressed by the term "dominant in the path" (*maggādhipatino*), that mode of theirs is the sense of dominance (*ādhipateyyaṭṭha*).
These are the modes of manifestation through the vision of the cause, the vision of origin, and the vision of cessation, which constitute the sense of dominance.

The connection is: "He spoke thus," and so forth. The "sense of clear realization" (*abhisamayaṭṭha*) is the sense of that which is to be clearly realized (*abhisametabbaṭṭha*). Of clear realization...
Alternatively, the meaning of "realization" (*abhisamaya*) is the object that has become the sphere [of realization]. Or else, the meaning of "realization" is the mode of occurrence of realization.
And here, it should be understood that this is shown by means of the affliction (*pīḷanā*) and so forth, which are to be realized.
530. *Kha* is wretched suffering; the meaning is that it is blameworthy and lacks essence.

In such cases as “samāgamo sametaṃ,” because the meaning of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not perceived when the word *āgama* alone or the word *eta* is used, whereas it is perceived when the prefix *saṃ-* is present, he says that [the prefix] “indicates conjunction.
This is established both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since its function of illuminating that meaning is proven.
The same method applies here to the phrase “uppannaṃ uditaṃ. As for the word *aya-*...
The word *hetu* (cause), even when established in the sense of "going," indicates a cause;

for it goes (*ayati*) or proceeds by producing its own fruit, or from it the fruit comes (*eti*), thus it is called *aya*. In the case of *samudaya*, the prefix *sam-* signifies the cause of arising through conjunction.
Here, it should be understood that even when used separately, prefixes indicate the meaning of conjunction or the meaning of arising along with the verbal root, as they serve to qualify the action.
“Cessation (nirodha) is the absence of obstruction here”—by this, he shows that Nibbāna is the state of being devoid of suffering.
When that [Nibbāna] is attained, there is an absence of obstruction for the person because of its attainment;

this is due to the achievement of a turning away (nivatti), which is the opposite of the obstruction consisting in the process of existence (pavatti). And in this sense, "the absence of obstruction here" means...

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) is thus a compound of words. Here, however, it refers to the absence of suffering for the person, not to the extinction of *nibbāna* itself. "Non-arising" (*anuppāda*) is itself "cessation"; thus it is "cessation as non-arising.

This excludes the word "cessation" when it signifies dissolution—meaning the non-occurrence in the future of existence and so forth, rather than destruction—and adopts instead the sense of non-arising.
In this context, the effect is metaphorically designated by the cause.
Having been made, it is called "cessation" by way of being a condition for cessation.

And there is a path for a person to attain the cessation of suffering. But is it not the case that since the attainment of the cessation of suffering is that very thing, it is not logical for that [path] to be the path for that very [attainment]?
No, because it is not by way of being the attainment of the person's realization; rather, by those [factors] he...
It is so stated because it is the means by which one attains those [states] that serve as its causes.
For although there is no difference in the actual realization itself, the exposition is made by distinguishing between the states that constitute the realization and the person who realizes them.
Alternatively, it refers to that fruit which is the culmination of the attainment of the cessation of suffering, and which is itself the attainment of the cessation of suffering.
The practice leading to the attainment of the cessation of suffering should be seen as being the very realization of that [cessation].

Regarding the statement, "The Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, penetrate [it]," the designation "Buddha" and so forth, which occurs at the time of penetration, is applied by way of metaphorical usage—just as in expressions such as "The Buddha went to Rājagaha"—where a future state is treated as if it were already present; thus, this designation is attributed even to the prior period.
It is said, "the Buddhas and so forth. For those Buddhas and others penetrate [them] by means of the four paths; therefore, they are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*).

Herein, the meaning of "Noble Truths" is that they are truths to be penetrated by the Noble Ones (*ariya*); thus, in the compound *ariyasaccāni*, there is an elision of the latter member of the first word (*ariya-paṭivijjhitabbāni saccāni*).
Indeed, because they have been personally realized and proclaimed by the Tathāgata, from that...
And thus, because they are not to be attained by others, those [truths] belong to him. Regarding the phrase "also because of the accomplishment of the state of an Aryan" (*ariyabhāvasiddhito*):

here, as before, one should understand that there is an elision of the latter member of the compound, such that the truths which accomplish an Aryan are "Aryan Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*). Regarding the phrase "also [as] 'Aryan Truths'":

here, they are "Aryan" (*ariyāni*) because they are to be sought after (*araṇīyattā*) due to their non-falsity, or because they are to be attained; or else, the designation "Aryan" refers to that which is non-deceptive.
They should be understood as established in their non-false nature.

532. "The characteristic of oppression" (bādhanalakkhaṇaṃ): here, "oppression" refers to the state of being the cause of the suffering of suffering, or the state of being afflicted by arising and passing away.
It is simply the frequent occurrence of suffering through birth and so forth within the various realms of existence, and through eye-disease and so forth.
It is the tormenting of the person; its function (*rasa*) is that very task, thus it has "tormenting" as its function.

It is manifested as the process of existence (*pavatti*), for having become the process within the cycles of wandering-on and turning-back—that is, within saṃsāra—it is grasped as such; thus it has "process" as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).

Suffering originates from this, it is produced, and by means of a prior existence, a subsequent existence is joined and proceeds in connection with it; thus it is "origination" (*pabhava*). "In this way, too, regarding the latent tendency of craving..."
"Because it is not removed, this suffering arises again and again"—thus, its repeated production is the non-interruption [of the cycle].

The obstacle is that which prevents escape from existence (*bhava*). Peace (*santi*) is the cessation of the continuity of all suffering by means of the destruction of craving (*taṇhakkhaya*) and so forth.

The "state of immortality" (*accuti-rasa*) refers either to the attainment of immortality or to the function of being non-decaying. And "function" (*kicca*) is like a function insofar as it is the absence of decay.
This has been stated by way of synonyms. Its non-falling away should be understood as the non-abandonment of its intrinsic nature and its immutability.
Because it is grasped without being apprehended as a sign due to the emptiness of the signs of the five aggregates, it has the appearance of the signless (*animitta*).

Its state of being the means for exiting from the prison of saṃsāra through the eradication of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) is its "leading out" (*niyyāna*). Its function is the abandoning of the defilements through the non-arising and cessation of all defilements.
It is called "manifesting as emergence" because it is apprehended as the emergence of consciousness from both its sign and its occurrence.
(533) A "māyā" is that which appears as gold and so forth when it is not gold and so forth; its falsity is stated because of the actual existence of the underlying object (*vatthu*).
However, a "mirage" (*marīci*) appearing as water is empty for those who have approached it, even though there is merely the substance of that [appearance].
"It is not seen" means it is said to be deceptive. A state that is devoid of rays, illusions, and selfhood is a state that is real, non-perverted, and true.

"Of noble knowledge" refers to the noble knowledge that apprehends things as they truly are; by this, both the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*) are included.
Their "state of being an objective field" should be understood as their being something to be penetrated and their being an object of focus. The characteristic of fire.
Heat. For that is never non-deceptive, contrary, or unreal with respect to the various types of fuel, such as wood and so forth.
The natural order of the world (*lokapakati*)—namely birth and so forth—as described in the passage, "Subject to birth, subject to aging, and likewise subject to death";
the horizontal length of certain animals; the vertical height of humans and others; and the culmination of growth.
They say that "the non-increase of what has been attained" and so forth are worldly conventions (*lokapakati*).

Among the terms *tatha*, *avitatha*, and *anaññatha* used for things that are real, non-perverted, and factual, the last is *tathatā* (suchness), the first is *avitathatā* (non-falsity), and the middle is *anaññathatā* (unalterability); this is their distinction.
Why was it said, "Nothing other than suffering is oppressive"? Is not craving (*taṇhā*) also a cause of suffering, just like birth?

Is it because it is an oppressor (*bādhikā*)? No; for it is taken separately by virtue of its being the source of oppression. For in this way, both the process of occurrence and the cause of that occurrence are understood without confusion.

Alternatively, just as with birth and the other [truths], suffering has the nature of being a basis (*adhiṭṭhānabhāva*), and its state of being suffering-suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) constitutes its oppressiveness;
it is not oppressiveness by virtue of being the source of suffering. Thus, craving is not taken separately by virtue of its being a source.
There would be the consequence of [other things] being obstructors. Therefore he said: "Nothing other than suffering is an obstructor. By the rule of being an obstructor means:
by the determination of being an obstructor in both ways—that suffering is exclusively an obstructor, and that only suffering is an obstructor; this is the meaning.

"By the rule of being an obstructor" refers to the rule regarding the obstructor and the state of being an obstructor. Just as the state of being an obstructor is restricted to suffering, so too is suffering...
And [it is] because of its necessity as an obstructive factor.

"Without that, there is nothing else": although the remaining defilements (*kilesa*), the remaining unwholesome states, the remaining wholesome roots subject to cankers (*sāsava*), and the remaining wholesome phenomena subject to cankers are causes of suffering, there is no state of being a cause of suffering for them without craving (*taṇhā*);
yet, even without those [other factors], craving [remains].

The state of being a cause of suffering exists both without wholesome states—namely, without the wholesome states of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) and so forth—and without unwholesome states—namely, without those of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth—because craving produces suffering.
"Certainty regarding the state of peace" (*santabhāvaniyāma*) means certainty (*niyāma*) in the state of peace or the state of peace itself; by that certainty regarding the state of peace.
"Because it is the state of being a vehicle for the straight" means that, by means of this twofold certainty, it is straight and possesses the quality of being a vehicle (*niyyānabhāva*).
This [path] is "true" (*taccha*) because it possesses the state of being true, unlike the wrong path which is perverted, or the worldly path which is uncertain;

thus, its state is the state of being true. Therefore, because of this state of being true, the state of being true, non-perverted, and real is stated in all instances according to a twofold fixed rule; hence he says, "Thus, through truth and non-perversion," and so forth.

534. *Niddhāraṇa* (selection) is the extraction of a meaning from among those meanings that can arise from the word *sacca* (truth), or, having stated the possible meanings, the extraction of the intended meaning;
this is the "door of meaning. In the phrase *viratisacca* (truth as abstinence), it refers to abstinence from false speech (*musāvādavirati*).

For the word *sacca* is not conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) in the sense of other types of abstinence. As for those who say, "Truth as abstinence is abstinence through undertaking (*samādānavirati*)," [they are referring to the same thing].

For them as well, truth as abstinence (*virati-sacca*) is not merely the act of undertaking [the precept], but rather the non-deception regarding that undertaking. Furthermore, that truth of promise (*paṭiññā-sacca*) is simply the abstinence from false speech.
The view that proceeds with the thought, "This alone is the truth; all else is vain," is "truth of view" (*diṭṭhi-sacca*) because it functions through an adherence to [that view] as "truth.
Nibbāna is the ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) because its nature is non-deceptive (*amosadhamma*). [The verse continues: "Non-deceptive by nature..."

For it is said: "The noble ones know Nibbāna as the truth"; and since the understanding of that [Nibbāna] and of the path leading to it constitutes penetration (*paṭivedha*), which is the cause for non-dispute, both are referred to as "truth" in this verse: "There is indeed one truth, there is no second;
in regard to which people do not dispute when they understand."

535. By the statement, “It is not possible that this [birth and so forth] should not come to be the Noble Truth of Suffering,” he shows the non-erroneous nature of birth and the rest as being the Noble Truth of Suffering, because they are exclusively of a harmful nature.
By the statement, “It is not possible that there should be another Noble Truth of Suffering,” he [shows] the status of the Noble Truth of Suffering...
He demonstrates the fixed nature regarding birth and so forth because there is no other possibility.

Even if someone were somehow to come with such a thought, it is said, "It is impossible that he would come thinking, 'I shall explain this... in order to show that there is no one capable of establishing his own doctrine through the proclamation of its principles or by making it known according to the Dhamma.
The "absence of a standing place" (*ṭhānābhāva*) here refers simply to the non-alterability of birth and so forth, and the non-existence of anything else that could possess such a nature.
Even if someone were to come, let them come; however, there is no standing place for them—this is the meaning of the sutta here. This same method applies to the second sutta as well.
Therein, it is through the acquisition of a personal existence (*attabhāva*) that beings attain birth and so forth, and these become manifest.

The first [truth] is so called because it is fully accomplished, directly perceived, and primary—since it was taught by the Blessed One first. The second is so called because it has that as its cause.
The third is so called because it is the pacification of that. The fourth is to be understood as that which brings about the accomplishment of that [pacification].
By the phrase "having this as the ultimate," he expresses the exhaustive inclusion of the processes of occurrence and so forth within the four noble truths.

For one desiring liberation, there is no other task to be performed beyond full understanding (*parijānana*) and so forth; nor is there any duty regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-ñāṇa*) other than this.

Furthermore, since the objects to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) and so on are limited to these alone, only four [tasks] are mentioned. It is stated that for those who see the danger (*ādīnava*) in craving, the objects of craving and so forth are limited to these very things.
Likewise, regarding attachment (*ālaya*), which consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), [it is limited to these].

It is said that for those who see the fault in suffering— whether that suffering is defined as all objects of sensual desire or as the three realms of existence— these [fetters] such as *ālaya* (attachment) and the rest reach their ultimate limit.
(536) "Because of its grossness" refers to the fact that the painful nature of birth and so forth is evident even to ordinary people.
It is stated [as such], not as a mode to be penetrated by noble knowledge (*ariya-ñāṇa*). "That" refers to suffering (*dukkha*). "Unmade" (*akata*) means unproduced;

the intention is that it has not been brought about by a cause. For when the cause is established, the fruit is necessarily established. By the phrase "nor does it come from what is unmade," he rejects the doctrine of no-cause (*ahetuvāda*).
By the phrase "not from the creation of a Lord (*issara-nimmāna*), etc.," he [rejects] the doctrines of Pajāpati, Puruṣa, Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), Time (*kāla*), and so forth.
He rejects it. Whatever else needs to be said here will be made clear later.

By the phrase "by suffering together with its cause," he expresses the intensification of the sense of urgency (*saṃvega*) produced by the vision of suffering. For, through the fact that suffering possesses a cause, a powerful sense of urgency arises, [realizing]:
"As long as this cause exists, so long will this suffering continue to occur without interruption. This is for the purpose of generating encouragement (*assāsa*).
He spoke of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) in order to produce consolation for one who has developed a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
For indeed, when the discourse on cessation is being spoken to one who is weary of the suffering of *saṃsāra*, it produces an exceeding measure of consolation. 537.
The connection is: "Those phenomena beginning with birth which were taught by the Blessed One. But why is illness (*byādhi*) not mentioned here?
Is it grasped? Because its existence is not universal. For instance, it does not exist at certain times or for certain people.
As it is said: "In former times there were three diseases: desire, hunger, and old age. It did not exist at all for those such as Bākula and others.

Or rather, it should be understood that "disease" is included here by the term "suffering. For in the ultimate sense, [disease] is physical [suffering] conditioned by the disturbance of the elements (*dhātu*).
"Suffering is disease. Having grouped the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhapañcaka) into a single portion, it is stated that there are "twelve things.

By grouping [craving] together as a unity through their commonality of being craving for sense-pleasures (kāmataṇhā), the "Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering" is grasped in a single form without mentioning the other internal subdivisions;
yet even this craving—whether accompanied by the view of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) or the view of annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi)—[is included therein].
They are described as being divided into three types: those devoid of wrong view, those consisting solely of the gratification of sensual desire, and those that are both.

Although they are spoken of collectively under the heading of the Noble Eightfold Path as the truth of the path, it is said "eight factors" because these phenomena are distinct by way of their intrinsic nature.
The commentary on the Exposition of Truth is finished.
The commentary on the discourse on the Exposition of Suffering;
the commentary on the Exposition of Birth.
"Becoming" (*bhava*) is a continuum of phenomena delimited by grasping and relinquishing; it is "in that becoming.

For it is called "birth" (*jāti*) because beings are born therein according to the divisions of womb, destiny, and so forth; or, birth is the class (*nikāya*) because beings of a similar nature are born therein.
Regarding the "characteristic of the conditioned," this refers to arising anywhere whatsoever. For it is "birth" in the sense of generating. It is "relinking" (*paṭisandhi*).
At the moment of rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). Regarding the term "just born" (*sampātijāto*):

here, with reference to the meaning of "being born," which is designated by the word *jāti* as the act of emerging from the mother’s womb, he says "in birth" (*pasūtiyaṃ*), meaning "in noble birth" (*abhijātiyaṃ*). That by which the designation of "Khattiya" and so forth arises is *jāti*;

it is the clan (*kula*). 538. One lies upon it, thus it is a "bed" (*seyyā*); those for whom the womb—designated as the "mother's belly"—is their bed are "those who lie in the womb" (*gabbhaseyyakā*).
[The first two] are egg-born and womb-born; the others belong to the moisture-born and the spontaneously born.

"This too" refers not only to the discussion immediately preceding it—namely, "only in the rebirth-linking aggregates"—but even more so to the discussion stated as "starting from rebirth-linking. Therefore he said:
"Birth is the first manifestation of this or that [aggregate]."

It is said to have "emerging" as its manifestation because it is grasped by way of emerging; it is said to have "variety of suffering" as its manifestation because it manifests the variety of suffering according to the classification that will be explained.

As for the questioner who asks, "But why?", his intention is this: "Granted that there is the suffering of birth in hell, which is exclusively painful, or even in other miserable destinies (duggati) since they arise from evil kamma; however, [why is it so] in those [realms] that arise from kamma conducive to happiness?"
"But how is it so in the happy realms? The other replies, "This birth is not called suffering by way of its intrinsic nature being suffering;
for there is no rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) whatsoever that is associated with painful feeling (dukkhavedanā). Rather, it is because it serves as the basis (adhiṭṭhānabhāva) for suffering.

Demonstrating this, he says, "Because it is the locus (vatthu) for manifold sufferings," and so forth. Even though it does not have suffering as its intrinsic nature, [it is called suffering] figuratively (pariyāyato).

“It is called ‘suffering’” means that it is stated as “the suffering of suffering” (*dukkhadukkha*) by qualifying the nature of suffering with the word “suffering,” just as one says “form-form” (*rūparūpa*).

“Because it is a cause for the arising of suffering” means because it is a cause for the arising of mental suffering (*cetasikadukkha*), such as thinking, “Alas, may this have been mine; alas, may that not have been so.

Because of the statement, “What is impermanent, that is suffering,” the formations belonging to the three planes are the “suffering of formations” (*saṅkhāradukkha*); regarding this, he states the reason.
“Because it is subject to arising and passing away. For that which is repeatedly oppressed is called suffering due to its nature of being unpleasant;
since the practice of insight (vipassanā) is intended here, the inclusion of the three planes (tebhūmaka) is made.
“Suffering of suffering” refers to the distress and despair of suffering. This is what is stated in the *Vibhaṅga* on the Truth of Suffering, beginning with “Birth, too, is suffering,” and so forth.

"By the Blessed One as well" means by the Blessed One who possesses unobstructed knowledge and mastery over the marvelous and immeasurable treasury of teachings. "By way of similes" means by way of similes such as the simile of the pit of glowing embers.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the white lotus and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) excludes a heap of jewels such as gems, gold, silver, and coral;
it also excludes a beautiful and pleasing couch made of eggs, sweat-born matter, or moisture-born matter; nor does it refer to a palace floor made of delightful jeweled pavement.
The inclusion of such places as the vicinity of a palace adorned with offerings of white-washed, polished flowers;
the secluded courtyard strewn with sand resembling a network of pearls; and the ground-level area whose soft, even surface is like a green woolen carpet, should be understood.
"Extremely crowded" means exceedingly congested. "Gloomy darkness" means thick darkness.
In that place crowded with various foul things such as bile, phlegm, pus, blood, excrement, and the stomach,
if the mother is twenty, thirty, or forty years of age, for that long it remains in extreme loathsomeness, resembling an unclean cesspool.
While putrid fish and so forth are not entirely comparable examples, because [the fetus] possesses some degree of removal of foul odors through the action of wind and other factors.
"Ten months" is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous duration; it is stated by way of the majority, since for some it is possible to remain there even longer than that.
He sits in the squatting posture (*ukkhuṭika*), with his two hands placed face down and joined together, being devoid of the actions of contracting or extending [the limbs].
Drawing toward oneself is *ākaḍḍhana*. Drawing from all sides, all around, is *parikaḍḍhana*. Shaking downward is *odhūnana*.
Shaking repeatedly after having set it down is *niddhūnana*. Here, the phrase "drawing and so forth" (*ākaḍḍhanādi*) is used because it is similar to drawing and the other actions.
The body within the womb is exceedingly delicate, like a fresh wound.
The phrase "it cannot endure even slight cold, etc. indicates his rebirth in the Sīta (Cold) hell and similar states;

for that [cold] stands before him as something exceedingly cold and exceedingly hot. "Scraping the body with adzes and the like, and pouring caustic" refers to the *khārāpaṭicchaka* (the caustic-receptacle).
By the phrase "in the place where suffering arises," he refers to the third whirlpool known as the womb-abode (*gabbhāsayasaññita*).
"Having turned over" means having turned over by way of being head-downwards and feet-upwards. This is the suffering rooted in childbirth;

oppressed by which suffering of death, beings who have reached that sensation forget even their course of existence for more than just a few months, as if they have plunged into a great darkness and a great abyss.

"Afflicting" (*vadhentassa*) means causing pain through lamentation, weeping, striking the head, and so forth. "Tormenting" (*ātāpanaṃ*) refers to the affliction caused by hunger, thirst, heat, standing, and the like; "scorching" (*paritāpanaṃ*) refers to the affliction caused by the five fires and similar practices.

"Of this" (*imassa*) refers to the sevenfold [suffering] already mentioned. "Of all" (*sabbassapi*) means of the entirety produced by the burning and crushing in the womb and other stages, as well as by the burning of the fires of hell.
It is the basis (*vatthu*) alone [that remains], because in its absence [the suffering] does not exist. For this very reason, he said: "If one were not born," and so forth.
541. *Vicittaṃ* means manifold or wonderful.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of birth (*jāti*).
Now follows the commentary on the exposition of aging (*jarā*).
542. Regarding the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*): it is said that "change while standing" refers to momentary aging (*khaṇikajara*).
It is called "reckoned as brokenness, etc. because it is designated by such terms as brokenness (*khaṇḍicca*), hoariness (*pālicca*), and greying of the skin (*valittacatā*).
This is manifest aging, known as the state of the aggregates being worn out. The ripening of the aggregates is the state of being worn out of the aggregates included within a single existence.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of aging.
543. The commentary on the exposition of death:
"The characteristic of the conditioned" refers to the momentary death known as the passing away of formations. With reference to this, it says:
The meaning is that what is called “death” in the passage, “Old age and death are comprised within two aggregates,” refers to momentary death.
“That” refers to manifest death, known as the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).

“Passing away” (*cavana*) has the characteristic of falling away (*cuti*) because it is to be characterized by such. It has the function of dissociation from the seven aggregates of beings as they have been acquired. As for “according to the place of rebirth”:

It is manifested as separation from one's destination because it is apprehended by way of separation from that destination; thus, it has "separation from destination" as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*).
"Of evil" means of what is associated with evil; the meaning is, of accumulated evil kamma. "The sign of evil kamma, etc.
refers to the unwholesome resultant object that appears at the time of death, known as the sign of evil kamma, the sign of the kamma itself, and the sign of the destination.
For one who sees that [vision], there arises great suffering as if actually experiencing it. "Bhaddassa" means of one who has performed auspicious deeds;

that is to say, of one who has done wholesome karma. Although for such a person only a desirable object appears, nevertheless, a great suffering based on separation from the beloved appears as the object. Indeed, a great suffering based on separation from the beloved [arises].
"It arises" refers to the statement: "for one who cannot endure separation from what is dear. "Without distinction" means in the common sense of both evil and good.

Although it says "without distinction," the further mention of "of all" is for the purpose of showing that this suffering exists even for some who have crushed their formations—the *khīṇāsava*—as well.
"With vitiated vital parts" refers to [the body] by means of the wind that severs the joints and ligaments.
Of the places where the vital organs are pierced.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of death.
Commentary on the exposition of sorrow.
544. *Soka* (sorrow) is, in its essential meaning, nothing other than *domanassa* (mental grief), because there is no separate mental factor [between them].

However, it is a specific variety of *domanassa*, owing to the presence of a specific mode of occurrence when directed toward a specific object. Therefore, in order to show that distinction by way of its characteristic and so forth, the passage beginning with "Even though this is so" (*evaṃ santepi*) was stated.
*Anto nijjhānaṃ* (internal brooding) is a burning of the mind. *Parijjhāpanaṃ* (tormenting) is distinguished from the fever of passion and hatred (*rāga-dosa-pariḷāha*).
Burning. Regret (*kukkucca*) is remorse occurring in the form of mental distress regarding what has been done or left undone, whether wholesome or unwholesome;

sorrow (*soka*) is remorse consisting solely of mental agitation regarding such objects as the loss of relatives. Although both have the manifestation of remorse, this is the distinction between them.
A poisoned arrow is a "poisoned shaft" (*visasalla*). Through sorrow, there also arise diseases such as dysentery; for one who is full of sorrow, the body—
"Before long it decays; overcome by powerful sorrow, one even reaches death"—thus he said, "And it brings about disease, aging, death, and dissolution.
This concludes the commentary on the exposition of sorrow (*soka*). Now follows the commentary on the exposition of lamentation (*parideva*).
545. *Vacīpalāpa* means verbal rambling; in terms of its meaning, it is simply sound. *Bhiyyo* means beyond sorrow and suffering, for lamentation (*parideva*) originates from sorrow.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of lamentation.
Now begins the commentary on the exposition of suffering (*dukkha*).

546. Although birth and the other [ten factors] are also suffering by virtue of being bases for suffering and by way of the suffering of suffering (dukkhadukkhatā) as appropriate, this [bodily pain] is said to be "suffering specifically" because it oppresses the body; thus he says: "It is stated as 'suffering' specifically. This concludes the commentary on the exposition of suffering.
Now follows the commentary on the exposition of mental grief (domanassa).
547. "The function of afflicting the mind" (*manovighātakaraṇa*) refers to the mind being distressed by way of association with ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

"Possessed of mental suffering" (*cetosukhasamappitā*) means those who possess mental pain (*cetasika-dukkha*). "They turn about" (*āvaṭṭanti*) means they roll face upwards; whichever direction they have fallen toward, they roll in that very same direction.
"They turn away" (*vivaṭṭanti*) means they roll by way of turning over. "They fall headlong" (*uddhaṃpādaṃ papatanti*) means...
They fall with their feet turned upwards. "They bring forth weapons" means they apply weapons to their own bodies by way of piercing and cutting them.
Thus ends the commentary on the description of grief (*domanassa*).
Now begins the commentary on the description of despair (*upāyāsa*).
548. *Dosoyeva*: the meaning is that it is the very mode of occurrence of hatred (*dosa*) by way of the exhaustion of body and mind;
for since it is an intense exhaustion, it is called "extreme exhaustion" (*upāyāsa*), just as an intense grasping is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). *Eko dhammo*:
one mental factor distinct from the fourteen unwholesome mental concomitants, which they call "despondency" (*visāda*). Because it succeeds through the act of sighing (*nitthunana*).
It has the function of belching, or its purpose is to produce belching in the body.

Having stated "because it is of the nature of the suffering of formations" (*saṅkhāradukkhabhāva*), he says "because it burns the mind and because it desponds the body" in order to show that this [suffering] is particularly prominent here.

And these—sorrow (*soka*), lamentation (*parideva*), and despair (*upāyāsa*)—[occur] both without and with the manifestation (*viññatti*) of the arising of a state of mental distress (*domanassacitta*), according to the conditions.

The phrase beginning with “And here” is stated in order to show the specific mode of occurrence. In that context, “like cooking” means like the cooking of a substance to be cooked, such as cloth, by means of dye and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of the means (upāya).

Commentary on the Exposition of Association with the Unpleasant (Appiyasampayoganiddesavaṇṇanā) 549. *Samodhāna* means meeting or coming together. It is manifested as the presence of various misfortunes, such as bodily suffering and mental distress; thus it is "manifested as the state of misfortune" (*anatthabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāna*).

The effort consisting of physical and verbal application directed toward those unpleasant things is "the exertion toward them" (*tadupakkama*); that which arises from this is "arisen from that exertion" (*tadupakkamasambhūta*).
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of association with the unpleasant.
Commentary on the Exposition of Separation from the Pleasant (Piyavippayoganiddesavaṇṇanā):
550. It stands as an affliction, thus it is "manifested as calamity" (byasanapaccupaṭṭhāna).
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of separation from the beloved.
**Commentary on the Exposition of Not Obtaining What is Desired** 551.
"Not obtaining what is desired" (icchitālābha) means the non-attainment of any object whatsoever that one desires for oneself. "And whatever [is desired]... [etc.]

For it is said: "he does not obtain. However, to show the failure to obtain what is desired when it has reached its ultimate limit, the Pāḷi explains this with the words "of beings subject to birth," and so forth;
to demonstrate that very point, the passage beginning with "Oh, alas! was spoken.
Regarding the phrase "a flood of desires," some say it means a lack of gain accompanied by desire. "Having the seeking after them as their function" refers to those things which cannot be obtained.
The flavor of seeking. Non-attainment is lack of gain.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of not obtaining what is desired.
The commentary on the exposition of the five aggregates of clinging.

552. "That which was stated here" refers to what was stated here in the Exposition of the Truths (Saccaniddesa) by way of its specific nature. "That which was not stated" refers to what was stated elsewhere—in such discourses as the Khandha-saṃyutta, the Bāla-paṇḍita-sutta, and so forth—but was not stated here by way of its specific nature.

Since all of that cannot be found apart from these aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha), it is said, "like fire for Indra," in order to show that suffering, which is dependent upon the aggregates, afflicts the aggregates themselves.
It has been said. Or, just as a target is the basis for the impact of a weapon, so too are the aggregates the basis for the suffering of saṃsāra.
And just as cattle are the basis for the affliction of gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like; just as a field is the basis for the growth of a mature crop;

and just as a village is the basis for the affliction of those who plunder it—so too, to show that the aggregates are the bases for the suffering of birth and so forth, [the text] says, “like a target,” and so on.
It has been said. Generally, those things in the world that cause affliction do not themselves depend on what is to be afflicted;

however, to show that these [beings] do indeed depend on what is to be afflicted, it is said, "grass, creepers, and so forth. Granted, in beginningless *saṃsāra*, there is no such thing as a "beginning" for anyone;
nevertheless, with reference to the continuum of aggregates (*khandhasantāna*) delimited by a single existence, it is said: "Birth is the suffering of the beginning."
For this very reason it is said: "Death is suffering at the end. Here, however, only the death of total annihilation is not intended.
Suffering that arises near to, close to death, is "death-bed suffering" (*māraṇantikadukkha*). "Burning" is the torment of the mind.
"Lamentation" is excessive, confused wailing. "Moaning" is internal brooding. "Each one" refers to birth and the other [stages of existence].
"Of each one" refers to each individual among those distinguished by internal differences, such as birth and so forth, or among the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
"Having condensed" means having grouped together, or having made a summary by means of a general designation.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of suffering.
Commentary on the Exposition of Origination (Samudayaniddesakathāvaṇṇanā) 553.
"Re-becoming" (*punabbhava*) means the act of making re-becoming; the latter member of the compound is elided.

Alternatively, just as one whose habit is eating cakes is called a "cake-eater" (*āpūpika*), so too those whose habit is making re-becoming [are called "re-becoming-makers"]. Or, it is that which deserves the fruit of re-becoming; or, that is its purpose.

It leads to renewed existence (*ponobhavikā*). Because it delights (*nandanato*) and because it causes passion (*rañjanato*), it is "accompanied by delight-and-lust" (*nandīrāgasahagatā*) due to its functioning without abandoning the state of delight-and-lust in all circumstances.
