And because beings take delight (*nandanti*) in various states of existence, even in the forms of worms, insects, moths, and so forth, and because they become impassioned (*rañjanti*) through such things as delighting in form, it is "rejoicing here and there" (*tatratatrābhinandinī*). Therefore he said: "by means of delight-and-lust..."
"Accompanied," and so forth. For this word *sahagata* has the sense of "having that nature.

Craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*) are to be understood according to their occurrence through the divisions of the realms of sensual desire, becoming, and non-becoming.

Without touching upon the specific divisions such as craving for sensual pleasure and so on, but by grasping them as a single entity solely by way of their common nature as craving, one brings them to a state of unity; for there is no similarity whatsoever between any sentient being and another.

The Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering is that which, by producing various diverse states through the accomplishment of corresponding kamma, possesses an exceedingly manifold nature and serves as the cause for all suffering.
But why is craving alone stated here as the Truth of the Origin? Because it is the specific cause. For ignorance [is the cause] regarding the various states of existence...
Concealing their own faults and increasing craving— which clings here and there to views and other forms of clinging—

the defilements such as hatred and the rest also become causes for kamma; however, craving, by aspiring toward the diversity of various existences, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, classes of beings,
families, enjoyments, lordships, and so forth, becomes the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the variety of kamma and enters into the state of being its companion.
It determines the diversity of existence and so forth; therefore, it should be understood that craving alone is called the truth of origination because it is the specific cause of suffering,
even though other causes of suffering— such as ignorance, clinging, and kamma— are mentioned in the Suttas and the Abhidhamma among the remaining defilements, unwholesome roots, and so on.
Thus ends the commentary on the discourse explaining the origin [of suffering].
Commentary on the Discourse Explaining Cessation (Nirodha-niddesa-kathā-vaṇṇanā): 554.
"Of that very same" means: by the same criterion as that by which craving was stated to be the truth of the origin, by that same criterion there is this restriction: "of that very same."
For when the cause of striving has ceased, all other causes necessarily cease as well;

thus, just as the subsiding of a disease occurs through the pacification of its symptoms, the cessation of the fruit occurs through the cessation of its cause. Therefore, it is said: "With the cessation of the origin, there is the cessation of suffering.
The phrase "and not otherwise" demonstrates the absolute certainty of the meaning as previously stated.

"Free from calamity" (*anupaddava*) means devoid of misfortunes such as being struck by insects or weapons. For that very reason, it is "firm" (*daḷha*) and "stable" (*thira*). Even if it is cut by the lopping off of branches and so forth, [it remains]. Regarding "underlying tendencies of craving" (*taṇhānusaya*), this refers to the underlying tendencies of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*). "Unrooted" (*anūhata*) means not destroyed.

Just as a lion, when an arrow is shot at its own body, displays its strength right there upon itself and not on the arrow, so too is the practice of the Buddhas directed toward the cause (*kāraṇa*) and not toward the fruit (*phala*). Furthermore, just as dogs, when struck by someone with a clod of earth, bark...
They eat the clod of earth but do not rise up against the one who threw it;

in the same way, those of other sects, desiring to extinguish suffering, devote themselves to the mutilation of the body rather than to the extinction of the defilements. To show this point, it was said: “Those whose conduct is like that of a lion,” and so forth. 555.
That by which the origin [of suffering] is detached from, dissolved, and cut off is called *virāga*, the Path. The act of detaching (*virajjana*)...

"Dissolution," "cutting off," and "dispassion" are what is called "abandoning. Therefore—because the term *virāga* (dispassion) and the term *nirodha* (cessation) are synonyms for abandoning—therefore [it is said].
It should be connected thus: "Through the uprooting of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), dispassion is without remainder; cessation is without remainder.
He speaks by including the terms "renunciation" (*cāga*) and so forth, saying that all of these [are synonyms]. Because Nibbāna is so described.
It is not merely the cessation of suffering; therefore, terms such as "the remainderless fading away and cessation of craving" are also synonyms for Nibbāna.
The passage beginning with "But because... establishes this very point. It demonstrates how terms such as "fading away" (virāga) are applicable to Nibbāna.
In that context, "having reached that" means having attained that Nibbāna by way of making it the object [of consciousness]. "Craving fades away" means...
By means of the Noble Path, craving is detached through the state of ultimate dispassion (*virāga*). "Ceases" means it is brought to cessation;
thus he explains that the terms *virāga* (dispassion) and *nirodha* (cessation) function as locative abstractions (*adhikaraṇasādhana*). "That very same" refers to Nibbāna itself.

"There are renunciation and so forth" means he speaks of the cause—renunciation and the rest—using the terminology of the result. Regarding the phrase "in the abodes of the strands of sensual pleasure," although some manuscripts write *kāmaguṇālayesu*, the reading *kāmaguṇālayādīsu* is the correct one.
556. The passage beginning with *tayidanti* is not an ancient reading; rather, it was brought from the *Saccatthadīpanī* and inserted later according to the method stated therein.
For indeed, the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, which were already mentioned previously, are stated once again.

Its "essence" (*rasa*) is providing consolation, as it acts like one granting relief to a mind weary of the suffering of *saṃsāra*. It has the characteristic of being the cause for the subsiding of all conceptual proliferation (*papañca*), such as lust and the rest.
It is "having non-proliferation as its manifestation" (nippapañca-paccupaṭṭhāna) because it presents non-proliferation. 557.
If the proposition "Nirvana does not exist at all" is made in a general sense, it follows that even the Nirvana intended by oneself does not exist;

if that were so, there would be a contradiction with one's own proposition. If, on the other hand, it refers to the Nirvana favored by others, then in that case, the [proponent's] thesis is not established.

Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished by way of its basis (*nissaya*). Regarding the phrase "because it is not perceptible" (*anupalabbhanīyato*): is this meant in terms of direct perception (*paccakkha*), or rather in terms of inference (*anumāna*)?

In the former case, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) due to the eyes and other faculties; in the latter case, the reason is unestablished for the opponent. Therefore, he said:

"No, because it is perceptible by means of a method (*upāya)," and so forth. In that context, [it is known] only by those Noble Ones (*ariya*) who have attained the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*).
They know the supramundane consciousness of others; and even therein, it is only the Arahant who knows all [minds], not everyone.
Likewise, Nibbāna is also attained by means of the right practice consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
This should be understood as a statement of the fact (*atthavacana*), not a statement of the method (*payogavacana*). That will become clear further on.
558. It should not be said that [it] does not exist; the intention is that it is apprehended by the Noble Ones (ariya).
That those whose minds are agitated by the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) attain Nibbāna through right practice is a principle established in all systems.

In this context, he speaks specifically from the standpoint of the Dispensation (sāsana), saying: "Because practice would result in deception. Therefore, he says: "If it were non-existent," and so forth. "Preceded by right view" (sammādiṭṭhipurejavā):
[It is] preceded by right view. And its being "preceded" is because it is the primary factor.

For it is that [right view] which first enters the teaching, not because it arises at the very beginning [of the path]. Nor is this right practice barren, because it leads to Nibbāna—that is, because it brings about the attainment of Nibbāna.
But according to your opinion, since Nibbāna itself does not exist, it would follow that [right practice] is barren.

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: "Because it brings about the non-existence of the aggregates" means that by way of cutting off the defilements through right practice, it brings about the non-existence of the aggregates;
the meaning is, "if you were to say, 'It does not result in barrenness'"; *na* is used in the sense of negation.
That which was asserted by you, who said "because it brings about non-existence," namely that the non-existence of the aggregates is Nibbāna—that is not so.
Why? Because even if the past and future were non-existent, there would still be no attainment of Nibbāna.
For if it were the case that the past and future aggregates do not exist, then upon their non-existence, Nibbāna might be said to have been attained; however, that [non-existence] does not occur.
It is not only for the past and future, but also for the present—that is, the non-existence of all aggregates belonging to the three times is Nibbāna. Not...
If it is argued that it is logical for Nibbāna to be the absence of a portion of those [conditioned phenomena] while they are present, then [Nibbāna] would not be non-existent;

and if it were non-existent, it could not be said to be "present. Thus, the claim that "it is present and yet does not exist" is a contradiction. Therefore he says: "No, because of their... [as found in the texts].
Furthermore, if Nibbāna were the absence of what is present, then when the Noble Path is present, at that time its—
If one were to hold that the aggregates (khandhas) are currently existing as the basis [of Nibbāna], then at that time there would be an absence of Nibbāna.

And if that were the case, it would follow that even at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), there would be no realization of Nibbāna; showing this, he said: "Because of the fault... while existing...
We do not say that Nibbāna exists for all [beings] simply because [the aggregates] are not currently existing. What then? At that time, during the moment of the Path...
Is it not the case that because the defilements do not occur, there is no fault, meaning the aforementioned faults are absent?

If Nibbāna is an absence—defined as the non-occurrence of defilements—then it follows that the Noble Path is rendered useless, since that absence would already be established prior to the moment of the Path.
Therefore he said, "Of the Noble Path," and so forth. Thus, this [argument] is not a valid reason, because it does not apply to Nibbāna.

[If that were so,] there would follow the unfindability [of Nibbāna], its mere non-existence, the fruitlessness of practice, and the attainment of Nibbāna in the absence of both the past and the future;
furthermore, the non-existence of present phenomena would be impossible, let alone the non-occurrence of the defilements, and the Noble Path would fall into meaninglessness.
Therefore, as for this [argument] intended to prove the non-existence of Nibbāna:
“The reason was stated as: ‘because it is unapprehendable, because it is devoid of the evil of existence, and because at that time the defilements are not occurring’;
this is not a valid reason, meaning it is illogical.

(559) “From the word ‘beginning’ (ādi-vacanato): by the word ‘beginning,’ the remainder of the passage from the *Jambukhādaka Sutta* and other [passages] regarding the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) [are included].”
It summarizes the canonical text for the exposition of the element (*dhātu*). For it is said in the *Jambukhādaka Sutta*: "Friend Sāriputta, 'Nibbāna, Nibbāna' is what is spoken of;

but what, friend, is Nibbāna? That which, friend, is the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—this is called Nibbāna. And therein: "What is the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)?"
“Element? It is said in the *Vibhaṅga* on the Bases: “The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion. Herein, this is the meaning:
Nibbāna is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhatā dhātu*), the phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is unconditioned.

Because lust and the other defilements are destroyed by resorting to it, it is therefore called the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion. And the phrase “by resorting to” means by [the cessation of] all conditioned formations.

The meaning is: by means of the path, for one who is disenchanted, who is inclined toward the dismantling of formations (*visaṅkhāra*), and whose mind has turned away through the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*).

For when that [Nibbāna] is being realized—having been attained and depending upon it as the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and upon it as the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) which serves as the foundation for the state of ultimate relief and for the state of the supreme goal where all formations are transcended—[it is realized].
Having been established, the path—consisting of destruction—destroys lust and the other defilements;

thus, in the absence of the realization of that [path], there would be no non-arising and no proceeding toward cessation for lust and the rest. Therefore, it is said that "by resorting to that [path], lust and the rest are destroyed.
This must be accepted unreservedly; otherwise, if the meaning of the scripture were taken according to the literal expression alone, many faults would arise.
In order to show that they attain [these states], it is said: "Even of arahantship," and so forth. For arahantship consists of the four aggregates headed by the supreme fruit;
thus, it is not logical to say that it is merely the destruction of lust and the other defilements. That too, indeed... is explained.

In this regard, just as arahantship is described in the Sutta as "the destruction of lust" and so on because it arises at the conclusion of the destruction of lust and the rest, so too... [is explained].

Because its meaning requires further interpretation (*neyyattha*). Thus, since it is by coming to nibbāna that lust and the other defilements are exhausted, nibbāna is defined as "the destruction of lust" and so forth;
one should understand that this sutta also has a meaning requiring further interpretation. The passage beginning with "And what more?
is commenced to show that many faults would follow if nibbāna were considered to be merely the destruction of lust and the rest.

In this context, "because of falling into faults such as being of limited duration" means that because [the path] falls into such faults as: being of short duration due to the mere destruction of lust and the other defilements;
possessing the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*); being attainable by its own inherent power even without effort; not being entirely liberated from lust and the other defilements;

being aflame; being suffering (*dukkha*); being unpacified; being manifold; being gross; and not being an object for the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) and the paths—these and other such faults would follow.
The destruction of lust alone is the "destruction of lust," not the destruction of hatred and the rest. Likewise for the destruction of hatred and so forth.

Thus, there is a destruction of lust distinct from the destruction of hatred, and a destruction of delusion distinct from them; there are three *nibbānas* consisting of the destruction of the three unwholesome roots, four [nibbānas] in the destruction of the four clingings, five in the destruction of the five hindrances, and six in the destruction of the six groups of craving.

Furthermore, there would be many *nibbānas*: seven for the destruction of the seven underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), eight for the destruction of the eight wrongnesses (*micchatta*), nine for the destruction of the nine rooted in craving (*taṇhāmūlaka*), ten for the destruction of the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*), and a distinct *nibbāna* for each of the destructions of the one thousand five hundred defilements (*kilesa*).
Moreover, the destruction of lust and so forth is something that even blind fools [can achieve].
It is "obvious" (*pākaṭo*), meaning it is easily understood even by animals such as leopards, deer, and monkeys; thus, Nibbāna is "gross" (*oḷārika*).

Because there is an absence of the destruction of defilements at the moment of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*), and because [defilements] have not yet been destroyed at the moment of the Path (*magga*), it is simply impossible for it to be made an object [of consciousness].
"Because of its being Nibbāna" means because of the state of Nibbāna, which is the ultimate destruction of lust and the other defilements. Therefore...
From the moment of its destruction onwards, the manifestation of lust and the other defilements no longer occurs;
yet that [destruction] cannot be defined as "this is it," because there is no object for the knowledge of the path and the fruit. Therefore he said:
"Because there is no such destruction. Furthermore—having seen the danger in lust and the other defilements even in the third existence after the final one, through the cultivation of jhāna...
Having suppressed those [defilements] and died with his jhāna unimpaired, he was reborn in the Brahma-world;
staying there for the full span of his life, even upon returning here, he became free from passion for sensual pleasures, went forth, and attained Arahantship.
And as for him who, having become disillusioned with passion and the like in his very first stage of life, suppressed them through jhāna and attained Arahantship in his final stage—of these two...
Because they do not arise from the moment of the suppression of lust and the other defilements onward, their non-arising is itself "cessation" due to its similarity to cessation.
They would thus be said to have attained Nibbāna; however, they do not [actually] become so. Therefore, such a destruction (khaya) cannot be Nibbāna.
For that too is associated with the defect of being merely temporary; thus he says, "And even if it exists," and so forth.

If, because of the word "destruction" (khaya), you imagine that Nibbāna is merely that destruction from which the non-arising of lust and the other defilements begins, then—since the term "destruction" is used in such expressions as "knowledge of destruction"—it would follow that the Path itself becomes Nibbāna, because lust and the others do not arise from the moment that [knowledge] arises.
Demonstrating this, he says: "And of the Noble Path," and so forth.

Just as those that have ceased do not exist, so too do those that have not yet arisen; thus, because they share the commonality of non-existence and are similar to cessation, non-arising itself is cessation—this is "cessation by non-arising" (*anuppattinirodha*).
This is indeed the mode to be exhausted by the Path, namely, the bringing about of the state of non-arising for that which is liable to arise;
therefore, it is called "destruction" (*khaya*). Distinguishing this from other forms of destruction, [the text says]: "of that which is designated as cessation by non-arising..."

"But [it is] for the sake of its destruction," he said. However, it is stated that the non-produced nature of that destruction serves as a proximate cause (*upanissaya*) by way of a figurative expression.

For Nibbāna, which is the object of the Path that brings about the destruction consisting in the cessation of non-arising, is to be described as being, in terms of its actual meaning (*atthato*), like a proximate cause for that [destruction].
"By way of a metaphorical designation for that" means by way of the conventional term "destruction," which is the fruit in terms of its actual meaning.
For a cause is often spoken of by way of its effect, as in the expressions “ghee is life” and “molasses is phlegm.
“Assa” means of Nibbāna. This is because, when the Blessed One reflects on it with such words as “This state, indeed, is very difficult to see,” it brings about a state of non-exertion in him.
For that noble eye, Māgaṇḍiya, which you lack—by which [eye] you [might see]—is not yours.
Because of the statement, "One should know health with the eye; one should see Nibbāna," it is to be seen with the noble eye.

560. If there is such a thing as Nibbāna, which is a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma) and included within the continuum of beings, then why is it not obtained as something common to all, like an alms-hall at a crossroads? To this he says: "Because it is to be attained by one who possesses the Path."
"Uncommon": because there is no prior limit—such as "it arose in the time of such-and-such a Perfectly Enlightened One"—it has no beginning.

"In the existence of the Path" means in the presence of the Noble Path; "because of its existence" means because it is found and can be attained. "Of atoms and so forth" refers to atoms, primordial matter, time, the primal person, and so on.
"The attainment of eternal existence" means the establishment of the state of being eternal (*sassata*). "Immovable eternity" (*kūṭaṭṭha-niccatā*).
For here [in this context], these are what is intended. "Due to the absence of a reason" means due to the absence of a probative reason for the arising [of those things].

"Those atoms and so forth are eternal" [is asserted] because of the eternity of *nibbāna*; thus, since they are dependent phenomena (*apekkhadhamma*), the definition of a reason (*hetulakkhaṇa*) is unestablished.

By the phrase "because atoms and so forth are unproven," he demonstrates that there is a non-establishment of the subject (*dhammi-asiddhi*) in the proposition "atoms and so forth are eternal," and consequently, the reason is unestablished in its locus (*nissaya-asiddha*).
561. "Because of the existence of the reasoning already stated": this is said with reference to the reason he himself has stated, namely, "because of having no origin.
Its state of having no origin is to be understood as its being without conditions; by that, there is an absence of its prior limit.

By the phrase "because of transcending the intrinsic nature of form," it is shown that just as material phenomena have the intrinsic nature of being subject to transformation (*ruppaṇa*), they possess spatial connection through their occurrence as aggregates due to their possessing resistance (*paṭighātavatā*).
And by this, he shows that for Nibbāna there is no resistance anywhere, nor is it localized;
for Nibbāna cannot be pointed out as being "in such a direction" or "in such a place," since it is indeed without a fixed location (*appatiṭṭha*).
By the phrase "not slack... because it is to be gone to," he demonstrates that Nibbāna is established through the direct perception (*paccakkha*) of the Noble Ones.
By the phrase “because of the word of the Omniscient One,” he shows that for others [the existence of Nibbāna] is established through inference;
and by both of these, together with the phrase “because it is not perceived,” he shows the non-establishment of that reason.

Having concluded the matter as it was begun—namely, that what does not exist in the ultimate sense is indeed non-existent—he states “For this has been said,” etc., showing the scripture that proves that point.
In this context, the four terms—*ajāta*, *abhūta*, *akata*, and *asaṅkhata*—are synonyms for one another.
Alternatively, it is "unborn" (*ajāta*) because, unlike feeling and the other aggregates, it is not born or produced by a causal complex consisting of the conjunction of causes and conditions.
It is "unbecome" (*abhūta*) because, being devoid of a cause, it has not itself come into being, has not manifested, and has not arisen.
Thus, because it has not been born and has not come to be, it is "unmade" (akata) since it has not been produced by any cause whatsoever.

Furthermore, the state of being born, having become, and being made belongs to conditioned phenomena such as form and so forth, but not to the unconditioned state of Nibbāna; it is for the purpose of showing this that it is called "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata).
Alternatively, it is "conditioned" (saṅkhata) in the sense of being made by conditions coming together and combining.

Likewise, because it is not conditioned—being devoid of the characteristics of the conditioned—and thus "unconditioned," and because its state of being produced has been denied through these various reasons, the term "unmade" (*akata*) is stated to show that it was not made by anyone, lest there be the suspicion:
"Could this have been made by a single cause, like the *prakṛti* of the proponents of *prakṛti*? Thus, it is also without conditions.
Similarly, in order to dispel the suspicion that "this has actually appeared as something that has come into being," it is said to be "unbecome" (*abhūta*).
Furthermore, to show that this state of its being unbecome and unconditioned is entirely characterized by the quality of non-arising, it is said to be "unborn" (*ajāta*).
In this way, the Teacher proclaimed here the actual existence of *nibbāna* in the ultimate sense; and while proclaiming it, he said, "I..."

The Lord of Dhamma, the Master of Dhamma—thus he did not proclaim [this] merely by his own authority; rather, out of compassion for those who take words as the ultimate, he proclaimed it through reasoning as well. As he said:
"If, monks, this were not unarisen, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned, then here for that which has arisen..."

“An escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned would not be discerned. But because, monks, there is that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned, therefore an escape from what is born, become, made, and conditioned is discerned.
The meaning of this is: monks, if the unconditioned element, whose nature is unborn and so forth, were not to exist, were not to be, [then an escape would not be discerned].
In this world, the escape from the conditioned— which consists of the five aggregates of form and so forth,
characterized by birth and other such qualities— namely its complete subsiding, would not be discerned, would not be found, and would not be possible.
For it is by taking Nibbāna as their object that the factors of the Noble Path, such as right view and the rest, completely eradicate all defilements.
In this context, the departure from all the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is understood as its escape (*nissaraṇa*).

Having thus demonstrated the existence of Nibbāna by way of contrast (*byatireka*), the passage beginning with "But because... is stated in order to demonstrate it again by way of agreement (*anugama*) and to provide a conclusion.
Its meaning should be understood in the same manner already explained.

And here, because of such passages as: “Conditionless phenomena are unconditioned phenomena. There is, monks, that sphere where there is neither earth... This state, too, is very difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions... And I shall teach you, monks, the unconditioned phenomenon and the way leading to the unconditioned. Through numerous scriptural passages, and specifically by this sutta passage, "Bhikkhus,
there is that which is unborn," the existence of the element of Nibbāna in the ultimate sense was proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One out of compassion for the entire world; therefore,
even for those wise ones who have deep faith in the Dispensation but have not yet personally realized it, there is no doubt whatsoever.

But for those individuals whose intellects are still to be led by others, this is an investigation through reasoning by way of determining the underlying intention here, for the purpose of dispelling their doubts: Just as the escape (nissaraṇa)—
which is the opposite of sensual desires and forms that are subject to being fully understood (pariññeyya), and which possesses a nature contrary to them— is recognized,
so too [is there an escape] by means of that which is the opposite of all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) in their own inherent nature.
There must be an escape by way of the state of being contrary to that [defilement]. And that which is the escape is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu).

Furthermore—insight-knowledge having conditioned phenomena as its object, as well as conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa), abandons defilements by way of their functional factor (tadaṅga-vasena), but it is not able to abandon them by way of their total eradication (samuccheda-vasena). Likewise, [knowledge] having conventional truth (saṃmuti-sacca) as its object in the first jhāna and so forth...
Knowledge abandons defilements only by way of suppression, not by way of eradication. Thus,
because knowledge that has conditioned phenomena as its object and conventional truth as its object is incapable of eradicating defilements through their total destruction,
it possesses an object whose intrinsic nature is the opposite of that noble path-knowledge which effects such eradication.
It must exist; that is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

Likewise, such statements as, "There is, monks, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned," which indicate the ultimate existence of Nibbāna, possess an unerring meaning because they were spoken by the Blessed One. For whatever has been spoken by the Blessed One—
That meaning is non-erroneous, just as it is in the case of "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are non-self";
likewise, in certain contexts, the word *nibbāna* has as its object the ultimate reality (*paramattha*) exactly as it is, because of the presence of figurative usage (*upacāra-vutti*).

This is established through reasoning by way of such examples as the word *sīha* ("lion"), and so forth, regarding the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Its existence must be understood.

Another method: if, however, Nibbāna were a mere non-existence, its profundity and other qualities—namely, that it is "profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise"—would not be possible. Furthermore, [the Buddha said]: "And that which is unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) for you..."

By such statements as, "Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma," and so forth, it would not be appropriate to speak of its being unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) and so on; nor would it be appropriate to speak of its being an indeterminate phenomenon (*abyākatadhamma*), as in, "Indeterminate phenomena are non-causal phenomena.
For there is no intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) whatsoever in non-existence (*abhāva*) by which it could be known through aspects such as being profound or unconditioned.
Non-existence is simply non-existence; how could it have a connection with states such as being profound or unconditioned?
Furthermore, this non-existence [of defilements] might be either one for all defilements throughout the mental continua of all beings, or it might be many.
If it were one, then once the non-existence of all defilements had been effected and realized by means of a single path, other paths and further paths would be rendered useless;
thus there would be no multiplicity of paths, and all beings would simultaneously attain Nibbāna.
[It] falls into [this error]. But it might be argued: "That which is designated as Nibbāna is simply the absence of defilements (kilesa);

however, that is not something to be produced by the paths, but rather something to be realized. If this were so, it would follow that the path is specifically useless, because the defilements have not been abandoned;
thus, there would not even be a single path. And if there is no abandonment of defilements, there can be no cessation of suffering.

What would be the purpose of the realization of the absence of defilements? Alternatively, since the paths have specific functions—such as the abandonment of the three fetters occurring within the mental continuum—the absence of defilements is distinct for each of the four paths.
This being the case, there can be no multiplicity without a difference in intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*);
therefore, that which is spoken of by way of the exhaustion of defilements must be the very phenomenon possessing an intrinsic nature.

If it is argued that because there is an absence of certain things, a metaphorical designation of differentiation is applied to that absence based on the differentiation of those things—then since those things possess their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), that absence would also have to be metaphorically designated as possessing an intrinsic nature.
And in that case, because they [the things] are subject to defilement and conditioning, that absence would also have to be metaphorically designated as being subject to defilement and conditioning.

If these [designations] are not accepted, then the metaphorical designation of differentiation based on the differentiation of those things should likewise not be accepted. Furthermore, what is merely metaphorical cannot be effective.
Multiplicity (*bahubhāva*) means, in its actual sense, for the sake of multiplicity. For water, when figuratively designated as "fire," does not burn or cook.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that this question regarding unity (*ekattha*) is untenable because non-existence (*abhāva*)—due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*asabhāvatā*)—cannot endure; for since non-existence is common to all [non-existent things], the designation of non-difference is appropriate.
As for unity, the faults have already been stated above; however, when multiplicity exists, it is according to the method already explained.

The nature of intrinsic essence (*sabhāvadhammatā*) is established. If it is argued that, even given this nature of intrinsic essence, just as multiplicity does not deviate from existence, so too existence would not deviate from multiplicity—and thus there would be the undesirable consequence (*pasaṅga*) of Nibbāna being multiple—[we reply: No, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence of the very non-existence of multiplicity.
For if, just as hardness does not deviate from existence, existence likewise did not deviate from hardness, then [existence would be nothing other than its specific quality].
If existence were present in all things, they would all become earth; how then could there be a plurality of existents?
Therefore, although multiplicity may depend upon existents due to the diversity of worldly conventions, existence itself does not depend upon multiplicity.
Thus, for Nibbāna—which exists as an existent—there is no plurality, because of the statement: "The goal is one, not manifold. And in that very same [state]...
The two—seeing and cultivation—are possible.
For those who have attained final Nibbāna, if there were a separate Nibbāna for each individual, it would have to be a Nibbāna determined by the continuity of a sentient being (*sattasantānaniyata*).

If that were the case, it would not transcend the defects such as being conditioned (*saṅkhata*); or else, the function of the Path would be the abandoning of defilements, and Nibbāna would simply be the non-existence of defilements.

And since there is no multiplicity of paths when it is a single unity—because there is no other function to be performed—the multiplicity of paths arises through the distinction in the abandoning of defilements by means of a specific realization, which occurs due to the varying degrees of proficiency of the faculties (indriya) regarding a single state (dhamma) to be realized by the paths:
namely, non-proficiency, proficiency, greater proficiency, and supreme proficiency. Thus, this [multiplicity] exists only if Nibbāna is a state possessing an intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma).
It might be so. Furthermore, the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the defilements (*kilesa*) must indeed be effected by the Path through the performance of its own function;
it is not something to be realized (*sacchikātabba*). For what is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of non-existence that it could be something to be realized?

If it were so, then Nibbāna—which is one and indivisible—would result in being something produced as the non-existence of all defilements by means of a single Path. Otherwise, if Nibbāna were to become fourfold according to the different Paths...

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of a fourfold state of being and the consequence of multiple types of Nibbāna; thus, because the function of the path is one, there would be a multiplicity of paths.

However, since their plurality is established by the aforementioned method as a distinction in realization within a single dhamma, the fact that Nibbāna is a dhamma possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhammatā) is proven.
Furthermore, it is called "destruction" (khaya) because it is to be attained through the destruction [of defilements].

For according to the statement, “Knowledge of destruction,” the noble path is called “destruction. Since this [Nibbāna] is to be attained and realized by means of that [path], it is therefore called “destruction.
Thus ends the commentary on the exposition of cessation.
Commentary on the Exposition of the Path (Magganiddesakathāvaṇṇanā) 562.

"Eight factors" refers to those mentioned in the Pāḷi, in the exposition of the Noble Truth of the Practice Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, beginning with "What is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is right view," and so forth; and it is precisely that [which is meant].

The intention is that the eight factors beginning with right view, which were mentioned here by way of recitation after being brought from the Pāli, have been explained according to their actual meaning (*atthato*), and not by way of the exposition of the Truth of the Path.
If they have been explained according to their meaning, he asks, "But for what purpose are they stated here?
and replies with the words "But here... and so forth. In that context, the phrase "occurring in a single moment" refers to mundane wholesome states of consciousness.
This was stated on the grounds that the abstinences (virati) occur only at different moments. However, the remaining path-factors (magga-dhamma) arise together even there.
"For the purpose of understanding the distinction" means for the purpose of understanding the specific mode of occurrence, such as the eradication of opposites.
He said "in brief" because a detailed discussion of the path will be made clear further on.

"Of one practicing for the penetration of the Four Truths" means: of one who practices by way of fulfilling the preliminary practice in its entirety, so that there may be the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Four Truths;
[he is called] a "yogi" because of the presence of the yoga consisting of the Noble Path.

Granted, when the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of ignorance is eradicated, not even a trace of the defilements associated with it remains; however, as for ignorance, by means of true knowledge (*vijjā*)...
It is called "the eradicator of the underlying tendency of ignorance" (avijjānusayasamugghātaka) for the purpose of showing its quality as the direct opposite.
The same principle applies to the subsequent mention of wrong intention and so forth.

Its function is the manifestation of the elements (dhātu), meaning its function is the manifestation of the ultimate truth, which is the task of discerning the Four Noble Truths. The mode of the path-factors in dispelling their opposites is preeminent.

By stating that "it manifests as something evident," although this refers to right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) having eradicated the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of ignorance (*avijjā*), it is nevertheless described as having the manifestation of destroying the darkness of ignorance.
Likewise, the phrase "one whose view is perfected" means one who has perfected the right view of the path (*magga-sammā-diṭṭhi*) in such a way that the underlying tendency of ignorance is eradicated.
Thus, the word "tathā" (likewise) refers to the meaning: "of the yogi who has thus entered upon the practice for the penetration of the Four Noble Truths."
It brings [the fruit] together. Its having Nibbāna as its object, however, is indicated by the very expression "associated with that.

"Destroyer of wrong intention" means it completely cuts off wrong intentions such as sensual desire-intention and so forth. "The essence of absorption" (appanā-rasa) means it functions by way of the arising of the path-consciousness directed toward the object of Nibbāna;
thus, its function is absorption.
"Seeing and thinking thus": this refers to seeing by means of right view in the manner already described, and applying the mind through right intention with Nibbāna as its object.

"Destroying verbal misconduct" means that it cuts off all four kinds of verbal misconduct. Because lying and the other [verbal misdeeds] have the functions of deceiving and so forth, they are harsh and unrefined; [this virtue] is their antidote.
Right speech has the nature of grasping associated states through its lubricating quality because it acts as an antidote;

thus it is said, "it has the characteristic of grasping. Since bodily activity originates something that is to be done and itself constitutes an origination or an effort, abstinence—designated as right action—is also said to have the nature of originating.
Or, it is the lifting up or arousing of associated states, like the lifting of a burden by means of bodily action.
"Of him" means of the practitioner (*yogin*). Because it is purified when that [wrong livelihood] exists, it is "become pure.

It is the purity or cleansing of a living being, or of associated states, or indeed of the livelihood itself—that is, the functioning of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). This refers to a right livelihood that is not censured by the Buddhas.

Right livelihood has the essence of the occurrence of a life lived according to the principle, because it is the cause for the maintenance of a right way of living; for once this [right livelihood] has begun to occur, wrong livelihood no longer occurs.
Right effort, which destroys all unwholesome states, is said to be the eradicator of laziness by way of seeing it as the direct opposite.

Its exertion is "exertion" (paggaha) even from the side of the defilements, in the sense of grasping hold [of the mind]. It is [also] the upholding of the body and so forth by way of maintaining aspects such as beauty.
Unwholesome aggregates preceded by perceptions of beauty and so forth are wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*); its destruction is the shaking off of wrong mindfulness.
"Non-forgetfulness" (*asammosa*) is the opposite of forgetfulness because it destroys it. "Establishment" (*upaṭṭhāna*) is the precise observation of the object according to its true nature.
It is specifically "manifested as protection" (*ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā*) and "by a mind protected by mindfulness" (*satārakkhena cetasā*), according to the scriptural statements.
"Mindfulness is the protection for a wholesome state of mind"—thus he said, "of one whose mind is guarded by mindfulness.
(563) "Of knowledge of the truths" means of the knowledge that proceeds with reference to the truths; it does not awaken all at once like the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*).
Rather, because it arises again and again, it is "subsequent awakening" (*anubodha*), which follows upon hearsay, modes of reflection, views, meditation, and acceptance.
Or, awakening (*bodha*) is subsequent realization (*anubodha*); that itself is knowledge, thus it is "knowledge of subsequent realization.

For one does not awaken to that through direct perception (*paccakkha*), but rather awakens by way of conceptualization (*kappa*) through means such as hearsay (*anussava*). "By way of function" means by way of full understanding (*parijānana*) and so forth.

Indeed, by performing those very functions, those [truths] become manifest to him just like the objects to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) and the rest. For, through the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*), from conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*)—
For one whose mind is being withdrawn [from the world], the knowledge of the path that arises takes as its object the escape from suffering—
the disintegration of formations— and thereby delimits suffering, abandons the craving directed toward suffering,
and realizes and touches cessation. Like the sun with its radiance, he develops that path which has arisen together with right intention and the other factors.
And it is not possible for knowledge that is still occurring without having released the formations to accomplish all this, because it has not emerged from the occurrence of signs.
Therefore, while performing these functions, that knowledge clarifies suffering and the other truths by way of turning away from delusion regarding them;
thus it is said, "it penetrates all four truths," the intention being that it does so through a single penetration.
If it is argued that the statement, "He also sees the origin of suffering," was spoken with reference to seeing at a later time (*kālantara*), we say no.

This is because this sutta was brought forward by the Venerable Gavampati Thera for the purpose of establishing that one who sees one [truth] necessarily sees the other three, within the investigation of whether one who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering, as expressed in such passages as: "Friend, does he who sees suffering also see the origin of suffering?
Furthermore, [this applies] to each of the truths individually.

Because it is applied to the seeing of the other three [truths] while they are being seen. Otherwise, if there were gradual realization (*anupubbābhisamaya*), since what was previously seen would not be seen later, one who sees the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth could not be connected with the seeing of suffering (*dukkha*) and so forth; yet that connection is indeed made in such passages as:
"He who sees the origin of suffering also sees suffering. This refers to mundane knowledge of the truths (*lokiya-sacca-ñāṇa*).
In that context, regarding mundane knowledge (*lokiya-ñāṇa*): "Overpowering by means of obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhānābhibhava*) refers to overpowering characterized as obsession;
it is by means of this [knowledge] that one turns back the obsession of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), because it sees merely a heap of pure formations (*saṅkhāra*).
This is according to the statement: "Kaccāna, for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, that which is called 'non-existence' in the world does not occur."

The vision of origination (samudayadassana), because it sees the uninterrupted succession of cause and fruit, turns away the view of annihilationism as it proceeds by way of overcoming the underlying tendencies (pariyuṭṭhāna).

The vision of cessation (nirodhadassana) turns away the view of eternalism, because it sees the cessation of the fruit through the cessation of the cause; this is according to the statement: “For one who sees the cessation of the world... whatever existence there was in the world, that no longer exists.”
Because it provides a direct vision of the agent, the vision of the Path abandons the view of non-action, such as: "There is no personal effort, there is no external effort, there is no human effort.
It also abandons [the views]: "There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings;
beings are defiled without cause and without condition," and "There is no cause... [no condition] for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause..."
The view of no-cause, such as "beings are purified without conditions," should be understood here as being included by the very mention of the view of non-action (*akiriyā-diṭṭhi*).

For that too is abandoned through the vision of the path to purification. Knowledge regarding suffering sees the state of impermanence and so forth in suffering—which is the fruit of its origin—and thus turns one away from error regarding the fruit.

The proponents of the Lord as cause (Issarakāraṇins) say: "The Lord sets the world in motion, prepares it, brings it back, and withdraws it. The proponents of Primordial Matter as cause (Padhānakāraṇins) say: "From Primordial Matter the world becomes manifest, and into that very same [matter] it dissolves.
[And they quote: "Time creates beings; Time withdraws creatures; Time keeps watch while others sleep; for Time is indeed difficult to overcome."
The *Kālavādins* (Proponents of Time) maintain that the world arises and passes away by its very nature (*sabhāva*), just as the sharpness of a thorn, the roundness of wood-apples and the like,
or the diversity of animals, birds, and reptiles [is inherent]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*),
they include those who hold that the world proceeds from atoms, that everything has been caused by past actions (*pubbekatahetu*), and that the world is predetermined (*niyata*).
The proponents of necessity (niyativādins) maintain that [the world] is like a gem that cannot be cut or split, and that there is no human effort (purisakāra) involved here.
As it is said: “They proceed by chance, they turn back by chance;
pleasure and pain come by chance; therefore, the multitude of beings is accidental.”

Those who advocate [theories] according to their own whims are called "fortuitous-originationists" (*adhiccasamuppattivādino*). Such instances should be understood as being included under the category of "causeless theories.
Like Rāma, Udaka, Āḷāra, and others, or like the Nigaṇṭhas in the formless realm, the grasping of liberation as occurring at the world's pinnacle is "grasping at apavarga" (*apavaggagāho*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the non-occurrence of effort and the state of one devoid of qualities [are also included].

The inclusion of such views as the persistence of one’s own individuality (*sakattani avaṭṭhānaṃ*), dwelling in the same world as Brahmā (*brahmunā salokatā*), proximity to him (*samīpatā*), union with him (*saṃyogo*), and the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*) should be understood.
Furthermore, herein, the non-occurrence of the primary [consciousness] refers to its lack of transformation or its non-manifestation due to states such as greatness (*mahatta*).
This occurs through the recognition of another person—the Primordial Nature (*pakati*)—as it manifests in the form: "I am one, and Nature is another."
It is said that when the undifferentiated apprehension of self, pleasure, pain, and delusion has ceased, the exertion described by the aforementioned method does not proceed;

this is "liberation," according to the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas). "Of one devoid of qualities" means devoid of the nine qualities of the self—namely, intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, effort, merit (*dhamma*), demerit (*adhamma*), and mental formations (*saṅkhāra*)—according to the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas). "Salokatā" is the state of being in the same world as Brahmā.
Proximity (*samīpatā*) is the state of occurring in close vicinity to that [object]. Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the attainment of oneness with it.

The pursuit of sensual pleasure (*kāmasukhallikānuyoga*) is the engagement [with objects] by holding the view that "there is no liberation without the gratification of the senses, the sight of one's children’s faces, and so forth.

Self-mortification (*attakilamatha*) is the belief that liberation comes through the practice of austerities such as fasting and plucking out the hair, as well as through self-torment via nakedness, the cow-vow, the dog-vow, and so forth.
"All this wrong grasp finds no footing when true knowledge is present"—recapitulating this very point, he spoke the verse beginning, "In the world, and in the origin of the world.
The commentary on the exposition by way of the function of knowledge is finished. 564.
"The remaining states": the remaining eighty-one mundane states among the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*).
By way of craving for sense-desires, existence, and non-existence, there are thirty-six modes of craving-conduct (*taṇhāvicarita*) consisting of twelve types;

these are stated according to the method found in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga* without taking account of the division by time. For if that division were taken into account, there would be one hundred and eight.

"Unmixed" means unmixed with anything else because it is a single unit; the intention is: "How could there be a differentiation included within that? [This refers to] the bases of psychic power such as investigation (*vīmaṃsiddhipāda*), etc.

Although the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā) differ in their functions, they are identical in essence; therefore, it is stated that they are subsumed under right view (sammādiṭṭhi), as they are included within its scope by way of right view.

The three types of renunciation-thoughts (nekkhamma-vitakka) and so forth are differentiated in the mundane moment through their association with non-greed (alobha), loving-kindness (mettā), and compassion (karuṇā).

At the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇe), because it effects the total eradication of greed, ill-will, and cruelty, it is called "the three" as a single unit. This same method applies to right speech and the others.
However, since right livelihood arises when there is the presence of fewness of wishes and contentment, their inclusion by means of that [right livelihood] should be understood.

Because they are not to be transgressed by the Noble Ones even for the sake of life in another existence, they are the virtues of right speech and so forth that are "dear to the Noble Ones" (ariyakanta).

By means of that "grasping" by which they are to be grasped with the hand of faith, that hand of faith is already grasped; therefore, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) and the power of faith (*saddhābala*), being not other than that, are said to be included therein.
Furthermore, since desire (*chanda*) is concordant with faith, its inclusion within that same [category] as the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chandiddhipāda*) is stated.
"Because of their existence" refers to the faculty of faith, the power of faith, and the basis of psychic power consisting of desire.
Because virtue exists through the presence of virtue, those three [factors] are included therein, as they are all comprised within the threefold virtue.

"Concentration of mind" (cittasamādhi) refers to the basis of psychic power consisting of mind (cittiddhipāda). For since concentration is spoken of by way of mind in the phrase "Develop the mind and wisdom," it is likewise appropriate to speak of mind by way of concentration. This is because of the development of the basis of psychic power consisting of mind.

However, since concentration (*samādhi*) is also predominant, it is not called the "basis of psychic power consisting of mind" (*cittiddhipāda*)—as is the case with the expressions for the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation (*vīmaṃsiddhipāda*) and so on—but is instead stated here as "concentration of mind" (*cittasamādhi*).
Because of the statement, "The body of one whose mind is joyful becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness;
the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," joy (*pīti*) and tranquility (*passaddhi*) are auxiliaries to concentration; therefore...
They are included by the inclusion of concentration (*samādhi*). Equanimity (*upekkhā*), however, is included because it assists concentration and because its function is similar to it.
Therefore, their inclusion under the heading of concentration should be understood.
The commentary on the analysis of those factors that are included is finished.
565. The truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is like a burden because it causes affliction; the meaning is that it must be cast off by way of its being something to be withdrawn.
It is like the taking up of a burden because it serves as the cause for the affliction arising in various states of existence (*bhava*).

It is like the laying down of a burden because it is the state of the subsiding of the suffering of the round of existence (*pavatti*). It is like a disease and like a famine because it is oppressive. [It is] the source of disease.
It has the characteristic of origin, like a good rain and like a timely rain. "Drought" (dubbuṭṭhī) means either a lack of rain or excessive rain.
It has the characteristic of peace, like the subsiding of disease and like a time of plenty, because it is a state of happiness;
for it is said: "Nirvana is the supreme happiness. It has the characteristic of cutting off the cause of suffering, like medicine and like a well-timed rain.

And because it is the means for the removal of that [suffering]. For the truth of the path has the characteristic of leading out. Suffering is like an enemy, a thicket of trees, fear, and the near shore, because of its undesirable nature and because it is accompanied by danger and peril.
"Enmity" (*vera*) means ill-will or the state of being an adversary.
The eradication of enmity is the pacification of enmity, which is loving-kindness (*mettā*). The means for the eradication of enmity are the bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
The explanation of the determination by way of analogy is finished.
566. This same method applies to the origin and the other [truths]. Herein, there is that which is the origin but not a noble truth;
there is that which is a noble truth but not the origin; there is that which is both the origin and a noble truth; and there is that which is neither the origin nor a noble truth.

This same method applies to the other two truths as well. Noble Truth (ariyasacca) is not [the object] to be fully understood, because it lacks the state of being conditioned or the state of being something to be abandoned, and because it is the state of the way-out (niyyāna).

"The other two Noble Truths," however, refers to the pair consisting of the Truth of Origin and the Truth of the Path. It may be that suffering exists by virtue of the suffering inherent in formations (saṅkhāradukkhatā); therefore he said, "by way of impermanence.
"By suchness" (tathattena) means by its true nature (tathasabhāva), that is to say, by way of being the state of what is to be fully understood. By this...
This demonstrates the meaning that regarding those two Noble Truths: "there may be suffering that is not a Noble Truth, and there may be a Noble Truth that is not suffering.
For when the words "suffering" and so forth are followed by the term "Noble Truth," they express the state of being something to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*) and so on.
Therefore, with reference to the word "suffering" independently of the term "Noble Truth," [it refers to] the states of the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*) associated with the Path.
The inclusion of the first term has been stated; however, with reference to the word *ariyasacca* (noble truth), there is an inclusion of the fourth term.

"In every way" means in every manner. The meaning is that, unlike the factors associated with the path and so forth which lack one or another factor, [the noble truths] possess all factors by way of both being suffering and being a noble truth. "The pentad of the aggregates of clinging."

Since it might be argued that craving (*taṇhā*) would also be included [in the category of origin], the phrase "except for craving" was stated in order to exclude it, because craving possesses the status of a separate Noble Truth (*ariyasacca*). Regarding the remaining defilements and so forth among the origins and other truths:

they are the "origin" in the sense of being the source of arising, but they are not the Noble Truth of Origin, as this is understood according to the interpretation of the Suttas. Cessation is the Noble Truth, not the origin. The other...
However, the two Noble Truths may be the "origin" (*samudaya*) in the sense of being conditions for their own respective fruits;

yet they are not the "origin" in the sense of that which must be abandoned for the sake of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In every respect, however, it is both craving-origination (*taṇhā-samudaya*) and a Noble Truth.
Furthermore, the states associated with the Path and the fruits of recluseship are [the origin] for the sake of whose abandonment the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
The holy life is lived according to that [state] such that there is neither origination nor the Noble Truth [of origination].
The cessation of formations and the attainment of cessation are cessation, but not the Noble Truth [of cessation]. Origination is the Noble Truth, but not cessation.

As for the other two Noble Truths, they may be considered cessation because of the presence of momentary cessation, yet they are not that [cessation] for the realization of which [the holy life is lived].
The holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of suchness. However, in every respect, the unconditioned element is both cessation and the noble truth.
The remainder is exactly as previously stated. Paths other than the noble path are paths, but not noble truths.
Cessation is a noble truth, but not a path. As for the other two truths, they may be paths because they are the way leading to the states of existence.

But it is not that for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One through cultivation—thatness—but rather, in every aspect, the path leading to cessation is both the path and the noble truth. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
The commentary on the analysis by way of the tetrad is finished.
567. “Empty” means empty of those things such as a feeler (vedaka) imagined by outsiders; this is the intended meaning.

For although suffering is indeed something to be felt, it is devoid of a feeler; rather, when it arises through its own conditions, there is merely the conventional expression that “one feels suffering.
This same method applies to the others as well.
By the restrictive term "only suffering" (*dukkham eva*), the meaning excluded is shown by the statement "no one is suffering.
When he says "only activity exists," he speaks with reference to the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).

Because the first two truths are comprised within the round of results and the round of kamma respectively, he states the essential nature of the truth of suffering as being the agent. For even the activity to be performed is devoid of an agent; it exists merely in itself...
It is a mere conventional expression to say that [the path] performs an action within the continuity of phenomena designated as suffering, which proceeds by way of conditions.

The same principle applies to the terms *nibbāna* and *gāmaka*. When it should be said "there is a path" (*maggo atthi*), one should understand that the absence of the vowel *o*—as in "there is a path" (*maggamatthi*)—is a grammatical elision. A *gāmaka* is one who goes to *nibbāna*.

Considering that the state of being subject to taints (*sāsavatā*) is foulness (*asubhatā*) in the sense of being a flow of the impurities of the defilements (*kilesa*), the cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*magga*)—being free from taints (*anāsavattā*)—are indeed beautiful (*subhā*).

Furthermore, while suffering (*dukkha*) and the other [truths] may, by way of synonym, possess the nature of origin (*samudaya*) and so forth, they do not possess the nature of cessation; nor does cessation possess the nature of suffering and the rest.
Therefore, because cessation is distinct from the remaining three, they do not coexist with one another; thus he said, "or empty of cessation," and so forth.
"Because of the non-existence of suffering in the origin": this is because there is no further becoming due to the craving that leads to renewed existence (*ponobhavikā taṇhā*).

Or, just as for the proponents of primordial nature (*pakativādī*), transformations exist by virtue of the non-transformed state of the primal nature, and having subsided previously, they remain as that very primal nature;
so too, suffering associated with the origin does not remain by way of the state of being the origin. Thus he said, "because of the non-existence of suffering in the origin."
The connection is with the phrase "due to the non-existence of the path and cessation.

Just as those who propound primordial nature (*prakṛtivādins*) maintain that primordial nature is pregnant with [all things] because its modifications (*vikāras*)—namely, the great ego (*mahāhaṅkāra*), the specificities of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and the gross elements (*bhūta*)—remain in the state of primordial nature itself, so too the cause is not pregnant with the fruit;
this is the meaning. Expounding upon the statement, "Because of the non-conjunction of suffering and its origin with cessation and the path," he said:

“‘The fruit is not inherent in its cause,’ and so forth. In this context, *samavāya* (inherence) is the relationship between things established as non-separate, which generates the conventional designation of the intellect here—such as “the cloth is in the threads,” “the jar is in the potsherds,” “the mat is in the *vīraṇa* grass,” or “the dyad is in two atoms.
By means of that inherence, the fruit—the dyad—is inherent in the two atoms, which are the causes, as if it were a single unified entity.
The proponents of the theory of inherence (*samavāya*) maintain that the effect— inhering within its own causes— extends from two atoms joined together and three atoms forming a triad,
all the way up to the masses of great earth, great water, great fire, and great air. However, according to those who speak thus,
a single effect of immense magnitude inhering within its immeasurable causes must be pregnant with its own constituent parts.
It is said that it is "not empty. Thus, here, because of the absence of a combination [of cause and fruit], there is no cause for the fruit; the meaning is that the fruit is empty of causes.
The commentary on the determination of emptiness is finished.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse explaining the description of the path.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Determination of the Singlefold, etc.
(568). "By way of the state of occurrence" means by way of the state of the occurrence of *saṃsāra*.

"By way of the division of the four nutriments" means by way of the specific conditions consisting of the four nutriments. By this [it is meant] the four specific nutriments beginning with physical food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*): the object to be swallowed, the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), ignorance (*avijjā*), and what is termed volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).

It includes both the specific phenomena that serve as its conditions—namely, the nutritive-essence octad (*ojaṭṭhamaka-rūpa*), feeling, and rebirth-linking consciousness—and the specific phenomena produced by them, which are comprised within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
This is because it is the cause of the suffering of the process of existence (*pavatti-dukkha*).
The distinction of delighting in form and so forth refers to the distinction of delighting in the aggregate of form and the other aggregates.

They say it is also by way of the objective field of visible form (*rūpārammaṇa*) and so forth. Because craving for visible forms (*rūpataṇhā*) and the others each have many subdivisions, there are six groups of craving (*cha taṇhākāyā*);
[the phrase refers to] their specific divisions. That which is grasped by means of the clingings (*upādāna*) is "clinging" (*upādi*), namely the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
Nibbāna is that which is the escape from them; its pacification is the peace thereof. Having taken that as the remainder [of existence] until the final consciousness, beyond that—

And because it is taken without remainder, the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining (*nirupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) are designated as two-fold.
Just as this distinction exists through conventional designation (*vohārato*), so too do the others; thus, in order to show some of them, it is said, "it is threefold," and so forth.
Otherwise, since Nibbāna is a single entity, from where could there be any distinction?
Regarding the classification by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*):

here they say that right view and right intention are insight, while the others are serenity. For their intention is that even moral discipline (*sīla*) is included under the term "serenity" because it is a support for serenity.
Alternatively, the path obtained by means of the two vehicles is stated as "serenity and insight" from the perspective of its arrival.
It should be seen. "This" refers to the Noble Path. "Possessing a portion" means being a part of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) and so forth.
For a "portion" (*padesa*) is that which is seen as a part, or that which is pointed out (*apadisīyati*) as a constituent member;

it is called "possessing a portion" (*sappadesa*) because it exists together with its own aggregate (*samudāya*), just as in the expression "dhammas possessing visibility" (*sanidassanā dhammā*). And such are the aggregates of virtue and the rest.
It includes all mundane and supramundane virtues (sīla) and so forth; since the noble path (ariyamagga) is supramundane, it constitutes a single part of that [virtue].

"By way of common genus" means by way of a common genus of virtue (sīlajāti), in the sense of the shared nature of virtue among the various divisions such as the abstention from verbal misconduct and so on.

Effort (vāyāma) is like a companion who leans forward, due to the commonality of its function of exertion (paggaha). Mindfulness (sati) is like a companion standing with his shoulder blades pressed together.
By way of commonality, it is because they both function to produce a state of immobility through the act of non-floating.

"Of the same genus" means that they belong to the same genus of concentration (*samādhi-jāti*) among the various divisions such as with-applied-thought-and-sustained-thought (*savitakka-savicāra*), and so forth. "By way of activity" means by way of an activity conformable to concentration. For this very reason, it is said:

"The four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are the signs of concentration; the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are the requisites of concentration. Thus, mindfulness (*sati*) and effort (*vāyāma*) [are included].
The state of being an accessory for the sign of concentration has been described.

"As if striking" means as if striking all around with a function similar to the function of wisdom—by way of [repeating] "impermanent, impermanent," and so on—and as if turning it over by way of [reflecting] "the impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror," and so forth; having thus taken hold [of the object].
Having inferred, wisdom penetrates that which has already been given. Although the two are simultaneous, the description of right intention as preceding is made by way of its being the condition.
"By way of genus" means by way of the same genus of wisdom, as in the phrases "knowledge regarding suffering," and so forth.
"By way of function": here, the activity similar to wisdom is called "function"; whereas previously, that which assists concentration was [so described].
The specific distinction here is that their functions correspond accordingly.

Because of the statement, “Bhikkhus, everything is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*),” all four are to be known directly through personal experience or known by means of distinguished knowledge; thus they are called "to be directly known.
(569) "Mutually similar" means having parts in common with one another; the meaning is that they have identical forms.
“Difficult to attain” means it is more difficult to reach, to accomplish, or to achieve; the meaning is that it is hard to acquire due to the failure of one’s power.
“A dart” (asana) refers to an arrow. “Should shoot” means he would hurl it. “With the tip” means with the tip of the arrow, or with the point of a hair.
“The tip” refers to the very tip of the hair. “Should pierce” means he would pierce by facing toward it.
The definition by way of the characteristics of oppression, origin, and the outlet is the definition of specific characteristics. "Profoundness" means being difficult to fathom;
thus, suffering and its origin are coarse. For even among animals, suffering is evident, as is their craving for food and so forth.
However, by way of the modes of affliction and accumulation, one discerns: "This is suffering; this is its cause."

They are "deep" because they cannot be fathomed exactly as they are. Because they are subtle and refined phenomena, cessation and the path are difficult to penetrate in the sense that their intrinsic nature is deep.
For this very reason, once the path has arisen, there is no lack of penetration regarding cessation and the path.
Since even Nibbāna must be attained by means of the path, it is designated as its fruit; thus he said, "by way of designating it as the fruit."

For this has been said: “Knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā). Since the Path also brings about the attainment of cessation, it is designated as the “cause”;

thus he says, “by way of designating the cause. And this too has been stated: “Knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā).”

The connection is: “In such ways as these, thus it should be understood. Therein, by the word *iti*, he shows the sequence of understanding. By the word *evaṃ* (thus) in the phrase *evaṃ-pakārehi* (in such ways), he indicates precisely that which serves as the cause for understanding.
The commentary on the determination of the similar and dissimilar is finished.
The commentary on the exposition of the faculties and the truths is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the sixteenth chapter.
17. Commentary on the Exposition of the Grounds of Wisdom;
Commentary on the Discourse on Dependent Origination.
“By this wisdom” means by this insight (vipassanā) as it has been attained. “In those that have become the ground” means in those things that have become the basis for its occurrence.

Granted that this designation “dependent origination” (paṭiccasamuppāda) and “dependently originated” (paṭiccasamuppanna) is established through mutual dependence—just like the designations “father” and “son”—nevertheless, they are fixed respectively upon the phenomena that are cause and fruit; thus [the text says] “both dependent origination,” and so forth.
It is stated by way of analysis. By the word "etc. (*ādi*)—that is, by the word "etc.

used in the phrase "the divisions beginning with dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppādādibhedā*)—it is intended that the remaining [factors] are included. Therefore he said: "The sequence for their commentary has now arrived.
Ignorance and the other factors constitute dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), not merely their arising (*samuppattimatta*). This meaning is established by this scriptural passage:

Having stated "For this has been said," etc., in order to show what is to be known, and then in order to show those things that have arisen dependently, the passage beginning with "But aging-and-death and so forth" is commenced.
Why, however, are the phenomena of dependent origination shown here in direct order (*anuloma*), while the dependently originated phenomena are shown in reverse order (*paṭiloma*)?
It is for the purpose of demonstrating immediately following that from which they have arisen as conditions.
"Not permanent, not eternal" means impermanent (*anicca*). "Conditioned by coming together and being produced by conditions" means conditioned (*saṅkhata*).
"Dependent on conditions, having relied upon a condition that is so worthy, arisen only in conjunction" means dependently arisen (*paṭiccasamuppanna*).

"Having the nature of wasting away" means subject to destruction (*khayadhamma*). "Having the nature of passing away" means subject to vanishing (*vayadhamma*). "Having the nature of fading away, having the nature of crumbling" means subject to dispassion (*virāgadhamma*).
It has the nature of ceasing; it is subject to cessation. Whatever else remains to be said here will be made clear later.
(571) "In this" means in these aforementioned passages from the Suttas. "In brief" means a summary of the meaning. "With birth as condition" means with conditions consisting of birth.
The ablative case (*nissakkavacana*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetumhi*). "That element remains as it is" refers to that which...
The specific conditionality of aging and death—namely, "with birth as condition, there is aging and death"—is this element, this intrinsic nature.
This was not produced by the Tathāgatas before their appearance, nor after their passing; it is known in the interim. It was not created by the Tathāgatas;
rather, for all time, aging and death that come into being do so with birth as their condition.

It remains exactly as it is. However, because he has fully awakened to it through his own independent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*) and because he proclaims, "This Dhamma has been realized by the Tathāgata," the Tathāgata is called the "Lord of the Dhamma" (*dhammassāmī*), not because he produced something previously non-existent.

Therefore it was said: "That element remains just as it is. Regarding the statement, "With that very [element] as condition for birth, there is aging and death": here, because there is no distortion (*vipallāsa*).
For one who understands this nature in this way, the fact that the cause remains established exactly as it is constitutes "the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*).
Alternatively, birth is the arising, the persistence, the occurrence, the accumulation, the conjunction, the obstruction, the origination, and the causal condition for aging-and-death;

the fact that it remains established through its state of arising and so forth is "the stability of phenomena. Thus, by way of the efficacy of the fruit, he speaks of the cause itself as "the stability of phenomena."
