Alternatively, it is called *dhamma* because it is maintained by conditions (*paccaya*). It is called *ṭhiti* (stability) because the fruit stands there, depending on that [condition] for its existence.
Thus, *dhammaṭṭhiti* means the stability of the *dhamma*. Or, *dhamma* means the cause; the meaning is "condition.

Since the very nature of the stability of the *dhamma* is not a nature other than the *dhamma* itself, it is *dhammaṭṭhiti*, which is the condition. Therefore he said: "In the discernment of conditions..."
“Wisdom is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa). The very stability of phenomena is the state of stability of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitatā).

That itself is the element (dhātu), because there is no otherness in this intrinsic nature or cause—namely, that “with birth as condition, aging-and-death comes to be”—and because there is an absence of that state in what is understood as “without birth as condition, aging-and-death does not come to be”;
thus it is the fixedness of phenomena (dhammaniyāmatā), the established state. Of the fruit...

When there is birth, there is the occurrence of aging and death; because it is established upon a cause, it is the "stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitatā*). When there is no [birth], there is no occurrence;
because it is fixed within a phenomenon, it is the "regularity of phenomena" (*dhammaniyāmatā*). In this way, one clarifies the cause by means of the fruit.
One fully awakens to that specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*)—which was stated in the passage beginning with "That element remains constant"—by making it manifest through direct perception.
One awakens; one penetrates according to reality. "Abhisameti" (one fully understands) is a synonym for that.
Speaking from the beginning, he "explains" (*ācikkhati*); the meaning is that he "indicates" (*uddisati*). Bringing that very indication to its conclusion, he "teaches" (*deseti*).

Making known the matter exactly as indicated by way of various methods, he "proclaims" (*paññapeti*). Establishing it by those very same methods, he "sets forth" (*paṭṭhapeti*) the matter exactly as it has been explained.
He reveals and analyzes by way of pointing back; for having made the meaning revealed and analyzed, he makes it plain by means of showing the reasons and the retention [of the teaching].
While making it plain, he says, "Behold! by way of conclusion, having rendered it thus directly evident. 572.
"The characteristic of condition" means the characteristic of the state of being a condition, or that which is to be characterized as a condition. Of the suffering of occurrence...

Its function is to bind one to suffering because it has the task of bringing about a continuity [of existence]. Its manifestation is as a wrong path because it serves as a deviation from the path leading to Nibbāna.

Furthermore, regarding this dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda): when a particular fruit is capable of arising through a certain number of conditions, it arises only through those conditions in their entirety;
there is no need for anything other than them. Thus he said, "only by those that are neither deficient nor excessive."

Just as eye-consciousness [arises] from the eye, visible form, light, and attention, by this production of respective fruits, he shows that the "suchness" (tathatā) of that completeness of conditions is their "other-dependence" (tapparatā). "Sāmaggī" means a coming together;
the meaning is a combination (samavāya). "From the absence of non-arising" means from the absence of non-occurrence. For when there is a completeness of conditions, if there is no arising—
There would be its falsity. "By conditions for another dhamma" means by conditions for another resultant dhamma.

"Because of the non-arising of another dhamma" means because no other resultant dhamma arises from that [set of conditions]. For there is never the occurrence of ear-consciousness through the eye, visible forms, light, and attention;
if it were so, there would indeed be what is called the "alteration" (vitathatā) of that causal complex. But this is not the case.

Because this exists, it is called "unalterability" (*anaññathatā*). "From conditionality" means from the state of being a condition. The same method applies here as well regarding "from the collection of conditions.
The term *idappaccayatā* is simply *idappaccaya* with the suffix *-tā* added to the word; there is no difference in meaning, just as *deva* is the same as *devatā*.
Alternatively, the suffix *-tā* is used in the sense of a collection: the collection of these specific conditions (*idappaccaya*) is "conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*).
Just as "a collection of people is a *janatā*. But is it not the case that when asked, "Is there, Ānanda, this condition for aging and death?
one should say, "There is"; and if he should ask, "With what as condition is there aging and death? one should say, "With birth as condition is there aging and death"?
[In this passage,] the word *kiṃ* (what) stands in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the words *jāti* (birth) and *paccaya* (condition).
Because the word *idaṃ* (this) is shown to have a common substratum [with its referent], the compound *idappaccaya* is seen as a *kammadhāraya* (descriptive determinative) compound;

for here, a question regarding the arising of aging-and-death from a condition of this [specific] thing—or from any other condition—is not possible, because its nature is already known and [such a condition] is impossible.
However, a question regarding the condition of aging-and-death itself is indeed possible.
Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with the word *paccaya*, the question "from what condition" (*imasmā paccayā*) is appropriate for the word *idaṃ*.

And that coreferentiality is found even in external-object compounds (*bāhiratthasamāsa*). Furthermore, when there is no desire to express a meaning other than the constituent members, a descriptive compound (*kammadhārayasamāsa*) is obtained.

But since there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) in a compound of genitive case-words (*sāmivacanasa-māsa*), how could a *kammadhāraya* (descriptive) compound ever be possible here? This is not so, because of the existence of another intended meaning.
For this is an intended meaning regarding dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) in the passage: "This-conditionality is dependent origination" (*idappaccayatā paṭiccasamuppādo*).
But in the passage: "With this as condition, there is aging-and-death" (*atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ*), it refers to aging-and-death.

This is a question concerning the mere condition (*paccayamatta*). Therefore, just as the word *idaṃ* (this) functions both as a qualifier of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and as a qualifier of the conditions to be inquired about, so too should a compound alternative (*samāsavikappa*) be applied here and there; thus, the demonstration of other compounds does not preclude the genitive compound (*sāmivacanasamāsa*).
Why, then, is a descriptive compound (*kammadhārayasamāsa*) not desired even here? Because [the meaning is] "dependent origination is the cause of those things that arise from causes."
Because this meaning is impossible in a *kammadhāraya* compound, and because this meaning is intended— namely,

"the condition corresponding to this [thing] which is itself according to its own conditions is 'idappaccaya'"— whatever meaning is grasped here by the word *idaṃ* is already grasped by the mention of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in the passage: "There is aging-and-death with this as its condition."
The word *idaṃ* (this) remains fixed upon the condition because it does not deviate from what has arisen dependently (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) and because nothing else can come about;
therefore, in that case, there is a *kammadhāraya* compound. However, since there is no reason here for the word *idaṃ* to relinquish its own meaning, it is simply a *sāmivacana* (genitive) compound.
Even so, it is not logical that the state of being a "conditioned by this" (*idappaccayabhāva*) should be identical to the "conditioned by this" (*idappaccaya*) itself.
Is it not the case that the state of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādatā*) does not arise from the state of specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*)?

This is not a fault, for this very meaning has already been stated as being non-different in essence. Alternatively, let the state of specific conditionality be "specific conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*).

Here, "state" (*bhāva*) refers to the existence of a cause with respect to its inseparable effect. For indeed, the term *idappaccaya* is conventionally established in the sense of birth and so forth. And that existence of specific conditions—
There is nothing other than specific conditionality (*idappaccaya*). If there were something else, it would be non-existent.
For that which exists cannot be other than what exists. Now, "existence" (*satta*) means being; that whose state is existence would have to be non-existence (*asa*).

For that existence is not different from its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), because it is distinct from existence itself. Therefore, the designation "existence" as the state of that which exists is not tenable.
Furthermore, "existence" (*saṃ*) does not become "non-existence" (*asaṃ*) through connection; how much less so through conjunction.

And since the apprehension of "being" when there is no being is a mistaken apprehension, there is no establishment of existence through such apprehension. Moreover, just as a youth cannot possess the nature of a lion through the conceptualization of similarity, non-existent things do not possess the nature of existence.
For the state of being a condition for this [effect] consists in the aforementioned existence, not in non-existence.

Nor does that [conditionality] belong to the entity itself; therefore, in order to show that this state of conditionality (*idappaccayabhāva*)—which is the very nature of the "this-condition" (*idappaccaya*)—is distinguished from other natures, it is stated as "the conditionality of this" (*idappaccayatā*) by qualifying it with "of this" (*imassāyam*). Thus, there is no impossibility of the state of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādabhāva*) existing within this conditionality.
Because it arises dependent upon this, it is called *paṭiccasamuppāda*.

Since that [term] also possesses the sense of a cause, the status of being primarily concerned with the cause must be applied to the words "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth in the same way, by taking them to mean "the dependent origination which is the cause of those things produced from a cause.
For it is said: "Monks, the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers, is endowed with the four grounds of self-confidence..."
The meaning expressed by this *Sīhanāda Sutta*—namely, that "he claims the bull’s place, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel;
when this exists, that comes to be," and so on, up to "thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering"—is as follows.
[This was said] by one who was asked: "What does your venerable teacher claim? What does he proclaim?"
By the venerable Elder Assaji:
“Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has stated their cause, as well as their cessation;
such is the teaching of the Great Recluse.”
It has been stated. By this it is understood that dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the cause of those things that arise from a cause.

What else needs to be said here will be made clear later. 574. "Dependent" (*paṭicca*) means relying upon this or that cause. "Correctly" (*sammā*) means without error, taking into account that the arising of the impermanent is from the impermanent.
For the arising of a fruit from a cause that is permanent would be erroneous. Therefore he said: "The sectarians... [etc. ...independent."

Their intention is that "arising" (*uppāda*) is a distinct mode characterized by conditions (*paccaya-lakkhaṇa*), as stated here in the phrases "from conditions" and "from moments," which is different from the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa*) spoken of as "arising is discerned.

Regarding that [mode] with reference to which they say, "birth and so forth are the causes of birth and so forth," that is merely their own opinion; for such a thing is devoid of the characteristic of production (*nibbatti-lakkhaṇa*).

Because of the non-existence of anything [of that nature]. Therefore he said, "That is not tenable," and so forth. "Because of the impossibility of profound methods" means because of the impossibility of profound principles (*naya*).

"Because of the corruption of the word" means because of the destruction of the word or because of the inappropriateness of the word. There is no sutta; for in such suttas as, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*)," only mere arising (*uppādamatta*) is proclaimed. For this alone—

The meaning has been shown below, and it is now shown here as well. That is merely its arising. "I dwell" (*viharāmi*)—the intention is that this was said during the period immediately following my initial full enlightenment (*paṭhamābhisambuddhakāla*).
Alternatively, "I dwell" is stated with a shift in tense; the meaning is "I dwelt" (*vihāsiṃ*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that dwelling in a particular place.

"By showing the mode of conditions" (*paccayākāradassanena*) means by the manner in which a conditioning phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*) is a condition for that which has arisen through conditions (*paccayuppanna*).
That is the mode of conditionality, the state of being a condition; it is by the seeing of that. However, here the state of being a condition for feelings is intended.
Therefore he said: "There is also feeling conditioned by wrong view," and so forth.

For one who sees the condition for feelings specifically, this dwelling is called a "partial dwelling" (padesavihāra), because it is considered a dwelling that sees only a portion of dependent origination.

The first dwelling of one who has attained full enlightenment is the mental attention to the *paṭṭhāna* (foundations) of infinite methods. For some, this is indeed the complete demonstration of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*).
However, this would entail a contradiction with the *Padesavihāra Sutta*, because that sutta demonstrates mental attention to the specific condition for feelings.
"The origin of the world" (*lokasamudaya*) refers to the collection of conditions beginning with ignorance, and not merely the simple arising of the world.
Therefore he said, "dependent origination in forward order" (*anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda*). "Non-existence" (*natthitā*) means absolute non-being;

the meaning is annihilation, which is the destruction of the continuity of beings. However, because it accompanies non-existence, the view of annihilation (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*) is intended here by the term "non-existence.
"Non-cessation of conditions" means the non-interruption of conditions. For just as the present pentad of effects depends upon the past pentad of causes...
Just as there is a pentad of causes, so too, by depending on this present pentad of causes, there will be a pentad of future fruits.
Therefore he said: "Because when the conditions cease, the fruits do not cease.

That profundity does not exist in the mere arising [of phenomena], because they are phenomena lacking intrinsic nature (asabhāva). The methods such as the method of unity (ekattanaya) apply to phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva).
He says, "The fourfold *nayacatukka* does not exist in the mere arising," because [the factors] might otherwise be obtained in some way even from the mere act of arising.

575. "In the same agent" (*samāne kattari*) means that the one who is the agent of the action of arising is precisely the same one who has become the agent of the action of conditioning; for example, "having bathed, he eats; having eaten, he sleeps."

“‘In the past time’ (pubbakāle): this is stated because the words *tvā* and *saddantānaṃ* mostly indicate the performance of an action at a prior time; it is not because the word *paṭicca* here has the meaning of a prior time.
For in that case, the demonstrative expression ‘dependent on the eye’ (*cakkhuṃ paṭicca*) would be consistent with that which is to be demonstrated.
Alternatively, although there is indeed simultaneity of both actions here, [this is said] with respect to the action of arising.”

Because the activity of being a condition was impossible previously, nevertheless, it is appropriate to speak of the causal activity as having occurred at a prior time, just as one speaks of the activity of the fruit.
Thus, the determination of cause and fruit is made clear here; therefore, taking the prior time established by conventional usage, it is said, "at a prior time.
"Effecting the accomplishment of the purpose" means effecting the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence.
For here, by "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), what is intended is the accomplishment of the meaning through the understanding of the sense of the sentence.
The word *paṭicca*, when employed, must be construed with the word "due to the absence of an agent" (*kattubhāvato*) which is implied for that which is expressed by the word "arising" (*uppāda*).
This is the meaning here in such passages as: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises."
In the case of the action of conditioning and the action of arising, consciousness alone is the agent; thus, identity of agent (*samānakattukatā*) is obtained.
However, in the expression “dependent origination” (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), because the word *uppāda* (arising) functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*), it denotes the action itself;
therefore, a verbal usage characterized by identity of agent is not possible. For this reason, he said: “it undergoes a change in its grammatical form.”

The meaning is that there is the application of an ablative case. And here, it is not an application of the *parāvara-yoga* (Pāṇini 3.4.20), as in examples such as “the mountain before reaching the river” (*appatvā nadiṃ pabbato*) or “the river after passing the mountain” (*atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī*);

nor is it an application of a characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇa*), a cause (*hetu*), and so forth, as in examples such as “fear arises upon seeing a lion,” “strength is born after drinking ghee,” or “the staff fell because [he] said ‘dha’.”

There is no difference in meaning here. For when the Great Sages stand having made all that is to be known directly manifest—as if an *āmalaka* fruit were in the palm of their hand—there is no opportunity for grammarians to find fault with their words. Or, let there be such fault;
for the word is established by its sentence-meaning, as in expressions such as "going after bathing" or "lying down after eating. Thus it is also.
And it does not accomplish any purpose. Even if the meaning of each individual word is obtained, the meaning of the sentence is not tenable;
therefore, the intention is that, like sentences such as "ten pomegranates," it is meaningless due to the lack of a connected meaning.
When a noun-word is uttered, even if [other] words are not employed, one should bring in verbal forms such as "exists" (atthi), "is" (hoti), or "is found" (vijjati).
He says, "We shall connect it with the word *hoti*," with reference to the method of what is to be connected.
"In these" refers to the terms for dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) as stated according to the exposition, the promise, the question, and the conclusion. And this is merely an illustration;
for in other instances as well, one "thoroughly and wisely attends to dependent origination itself, namely, to this specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*)."
In such passages as, "Dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). And this dependent origination, Ānanda, is profound," the word *saha* does not connect with even a single [other term].
It does not form a conjunction (*yoga*) because it has not been stated as having that kind of syntactical connection.

Furthermore, in the phrase "and there is no arising" (*na ca uppādo hoti*), the characteristic of production (*nibbatti-lakkhaṇa*) is not applicable to "arising" (*uppāda*) because arising is a phenomenon devoid of intrinsic nature (*asabhāva-dhamma*).
This was said with intentional meaning (*saṇdhāya*). For just as there is no destruction of destruction, so too there is no arising of arising, just as there is no destruction of arising.

If there were such a thing, then that arising by which an arising becomes "possessed of arising" would itself be possessed of arising, and thus one would fall into the fault of infinite regress (*anavaṭṭhāna*);
this is the very point that has been stated. Therefore he said, "If it were so," and so forth. If this is the case, how is it the origin?

Is it not the case that [the term] "occurs" (hoti) is used? This is not a fault, because the actual production (nibbatti) is not intended here. Thus, the meaning here is: "In this way, the origin, the manifestation, and the arising of the mass of suffering occurs.

However, in this context, since "dependent origination occurs" (paṭiccasamuppādo hoti) is taken as an exhortation regarding its existence, it is stated with the intention that "it occurs" and "it is born" may serve as an exhortation regarding production; hence it was said: "It is not the arising that occurs."

576. The conditions for these volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth are "this-conditionality" (*idappaccaya*), namely ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest; the state of those [conditions] is "this-conditionality" (*idappaccayatā*).
To the question, "What, then, is this state? he says: "And what is called 'state' (*bhāva*)," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:

in whatever manner ignorance and the rest are the causes for the manifestation of volitional formations and so forth, that specific mode of occurrence, that particular modification (*vikāra*) in ignorance and the rest, is designated by the conventional term "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
That is the conceit of those proponents. "From the statement of the cause" means from the statement of the state of being a cause. 577. "In this context" refers to the term *paṭiccasamuppāda*.

For those who do not understand the unerring meaning—that *paṭiccasamuppāda* is a cause possessing power (*sasattika*), to be understood through the primary sense of the word *samuppāda*—[they assume] elsewhere that the word *samuppāda* functions as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*).

Just as it was seen [in the previous context], so here too, the notion that arises—namely, that "only the arising is stated here by way of the shadow of the phrasing, and not the cause"—should be stilled and dispelled by grasping the meaning of this term *paṭiccasamuppāda* in the manner now to be explained.
The summary meaning of the verse beginning with "Dvedhā" (*In two ways*) is as follows: because the collection of conditioned phenomena proceeds by virtue of its own respective conditions...
It is "dependent" (*paṭicca*) because it must be understood through dependence, and it is "arising together" (*samuppāda*) because it arises simultaneously;

or alternatively, it is so called because it arises simultaneously without rejecting the collection of causes. Thus, this term "dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) should be understood in these two ways.
Therefore, even the conditioning state itself is called "dependent origination" by way of metaphorical designation as the fruit.
"By way of conditionality" means from the collection of conditions. "Occurrence" means that which has been produced. "A mass of phenomena" means a heap of phenomena arisen through conditions.

"Being realized" means being approached face-to-face by the course of knowledge; the meaning is "being fully understood. "For the welfare and happiness" means for supramundane welfare and for supramundane happiness.
It arises together [with the path], because it arises even at some time for each individual.
"By way of non-existence": because it does not arise without a cause or from an improper cause.
"It arises together" means it arises simultaneously, even as little as eight factors arising together. "Without rejecting" means without denying;
the meaning is that it is not separated from any collection of phenomena that serve as its own conditions. "Of that" refers to this which is called "dependent origination."
The collection of phenomena arisen through conditions has been stated; this collection of causes for it begins with ignorance (*avijjā*).

By the phrase “because of being conditioned by that,” he shows that the designation “dependent origination” (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is applied in dependence upon the conditions of dependent origination. Therefore, he says:
“Just as in the world,” and so forth. For just as in the world one says, “the bile is churned,” “sura is curd,” “tipusa is fever,” “phlegm is sugar,” and “life is ghee.”

And just as a condition is spoken of by way of the conventional term "fruit," so too it should be understood that dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for the fruit.
In the word *paṭicca*, he says "facing toward" (*paṭimukham*) and "gone" (*ito*) to show that the prefix *pati-* has the sense of "facing toward" and the root *ic-* has the sense of "going.
To the three challenges—"Facing toward what?", "Gone by means of what?", or "What is it that goes?"—he provides the latter [answer].
Explaining [the term], he says: "a collection of causes. For when that [term] is relinquished, the meaning is that "a collection of causes" refers to the convergence of conditions (*paccayasāmaggī*);
therein, because they face one another and are directed toward one another, this meaning is what is relinquished. "Combined" means gathered together and inseparable.
"That" refers to the collection of causes. The construction is: "it is said to be 'arising together' (*samuppādo*)."

"For manifestation" means for arising. Although in the text it is stated that "volitional formations have ignorance as their condition," thus presenting ignorance alone as the condition, nevertheless, ignorance is not the sole condition.

Rather, conascent factors such as the physical basis and the object, appropriate attention and so forth, and craving, clinging, and so forth, all act as conditions for the arising of volitional formations according to their respective roles.
They are indeed cooperative causes. Thus, formations and the rest are also [cooperative causes] for consciousness and the rest; hence he says:
"The collection of causes is demonstrated under the heading of each individual cause, such as ignorance.

"In the sense of producing a common fruit" means by way of being the producer of a fruit that is shared by those causal factors included within that collection. "In the sense of non-deficiency" means by way of being complete.

For if, within that collection of causes, this particular fruit were unique to some [causes] and were to be produced by those alone, then all those conditioning phenomena (paccayadhamma) would lack mutual dependence;
thus, because there would be no coming together face-to-face, the meaning of "dependent" (paṭicca) would not be fulfilled.
"Of the factors of the combination" means of those that have become members of the combination of conditions; the sense is "of the collections."
This genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). "Concomitance" (*sahitatā*) of resultant phenomena means their absence of separateness;
it does not mean mutual dependence as is the case with causal phenomena. Thus he says, "phenomena that exist in inseparable association with one another.

Here, the inclusion of the term "inseparable" (*avinibbhoga*) is for the purpose of encompassing material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) as well; otherwise, it would have been stated simply as "associated phenomena" (*sampayuttadhamma*).
579. *Paccayatā* means this collection of conditions beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*). *Aññoññaṃ* means mutually.

*Paṭicca* means depending upon, having obtained a cooperative cause. *Samaṃ* means not uneven, being without deficiency. *Saha* means together. *Dhamme* refers to the phenomena produced by their respective conditions.
Because it causes [them] to arise, for that reason also—and for that reason as well—it is called *paṭiccasamuppāda*.

The construction is: "spoken by the Blessed One, the Sage. By stating "not without dependence, but precisely through dependence," he shows that the word *eva* (precisely) in the verse is indicated as being elided for the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇattha*).
"A single part" means a portion of a portion of the aggregate of the fruit; the sense is "a fraction. "By way of prior and posterior sequence" means...
In successive order. All of this is stated with reference to the production of groups (kalāpa) of both material and immaterial phenomena.
"By one skilled in conventional expression following the meaning" means by one proficient in conventional usage that conforms to ultimate phenomena (paramattha-dhamma).
[The phrase] "by the first term" is the construction. "Of eternalism and so forth" refers to states of eternalism and so forth, or to the doctrines of eternalism and so forth.
Or: for even doctrines associated with eternalism are called "eternalism" and so forth, just as the teaching on suffering is called "suffering.

The same principle applies here to "annihilationism" and the rest. "Affliction" (vighāta) means destruction or abandonment. "The method" (ñāya) refers to the Middle Way practice, which is devoid of the two extremes.
"Of phenomena subject to occurrence" (pavattidhammānaṃ) means of those phenomena that have come into existence, namely the cycle of defilements and so forth. "Eternal... [text fragment]
The eternalist view (*sassatavāda*) proceeds in such a manner as: "The self and the world [are eternal]. The causeless view (*ahetuvāda*) proceeds in such a manner as:

"There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings. The view of irregular causes (*visamahetuvāda*) proceeds thus: "The world proceeds by way of primordial nature (*pakati*), atoms (*aṇu*), time (*kāla*), and so forth.
The doctrines of Īśvara, Puruṣa, and Prajāpati are doctrines of those who claim to have mastery (*vasavattivāda*). By the inclusion of the causeless view itself, [these are also subsumed].

And here, the doctrine of natural necessity (*sabhāvaniyati*) should be understood as including even the doctrine of chance (*yadicchāvāda*). However, some maintain that the doctrine of discordant causes, such as "the eye itself is the cause of the eye," is included within the doctrine of no-cause (*ahetuvāda*).

They say that the doctrine of God (*issarādivāda*) and others is subsumed under the doctrine of no-cause, while the doctrine that phenomena proceed by their own nature alone is called the "doctrine of mastery" (*vasavattivāda*). For what purpose would there be a collection of conditions?
The intended meaning (*adhippāya*) is thus connected [to the statement]: "It is elucidated by the term 'co-arising' (*samuppāda*).

Furthermore, in order to show the non-erroneous reason for this elucidation, it is said: "Because phenomena arise when there is a completeness of conditions. The word *vihata* means struck down or destroyed.

By the phrase "by way of each preceding condition," he shows the continuity of cause and fruit (*hetuphalapabandha*), which occurs without interruption and thereby turns back the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*).

Therefore he said, "Whence is annihilation? It should be understood that by the very statement of the absence of annihilation, he also demonstrates the non-existence of the doctrine of annihilation (ucchedavāda).
"In each respective combination of conditions" means in each respective concurrence of causes and conditions. "Without interrupting the continuity" means...
By means of not interrupting the continuum known as the connection between cause and fruit;

and by not falling into the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism—because of the occurrence and arising of those various conditionally arisen phenomena—the production of appropriate fruits from their respective conditions is intended here as the "Middle Way. [This applies to] the cycle of kamma and the cycle of kamma-result.
Furthermore, because of their difference in intrinsic nature and difference in time, the doctrine that "he who acts is he who experiences" is abandoned.
For the designation "agent" applies to the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome aggregates, while the designation "experiencer" applies to the occurrence of resultant aggregates.
Since the fruit arises in the very same continuum where the karma was produced, it is not the case that one person acts [and another experiences].
“The other experiences [the result]” is the abandonment of such a claim; for there is no destruction of what has been done, nor the arrival of what has not been done.

The terms “woman” and “man” are merely worldly designations (*janapadanirutti*). In this regard, because even the wise in the world do not say, “Bring the five aggregates,” or “Let name-and-form come,” but rather employ the conventional terms “woman” and “man,” therefore, “this is indeed a woman.”
This adherence belongs to those who have not fully understood the basis [of things], just as it happens for a person [who mistakes a mirage for water].

However, for one who sees and knows dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), there is no adherence to the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) regarding those phenomena as they occur in their various ways, because they are merely designations (*paññatti-matta*) based upon them.
Thus he said: "Non-adherence to local dialects. "By way of common usage" means by way of worldly convention (*lokasamaññā*).

“Not overstepping” means not transgressing. For when the word “being” (satta) is used, one should employ it according to worldly convention—without overstepping that convention—just as worldly people do, without making a distinction such as, “What is the being here?
Is it form, or is it feeling and so forth?”
Another method: it is "dependent" (*paṭicca*) because it is worthy of being understood.
For that which one understands and realizes leads exclusively to the subsiding of suffering. It "arises together" (*samuppāda*) because it arises correctly and simultaneously.
A causal phenomenon, when producing its own fruit, produces it in its entirety, not in a deficient manner. And those phenomena which it produces—
It produces all of them together, not one by one. Thus, because it is dependent (*paṭicca*) and it is an arising (*samuppāda*), it is called *paṭiccasamuppāda*.
Alternatively, having gone toward (*paṭimukhaṃ itvā*) [the conditions] in dependence, it produces [the effect] in combination without rejecting the completeness of the causes;
thus it is *paṭiccasamuppāda*. And this "going toward" [refers to] the condition’s status as a factor for the completeness of the causes with respect to the fruit.

It is simply arising. Regarding the phrase "without having rejected": the meaning is that it does not arise by itself, without that completeness of causes, without having attained the status of a constituent factor (*aṅga*).
By this, the multiplicity of causes is shown; by the word "conjoined" (*sahite*), the multiplicity of the phenomena produced by conditions is shown.
By both of these, the method of the Teaching to be explained later—beginning with "one [cause] is not [produced] from one"—is illustrated.

Alternatively, *paṭiccasamuppāda* means that having gone toward (*paṭigantvā*) a condition (*paccaya*) which is to be depended upon (*paccetabba*), there is the arising of a connected state (*sambandha*) not without that [condition].

Here, *paṭiccasamuppāda* should be understood as a cause accompanied by power, to be known from the word where the emphasis is on the "arising together" (*samuppāda*). In this context, when it is said "having depended" (*paṭicca*), one might ask what it is that is depended upon; therefore, he says "that which is to be depended upon" (*paccetabba*).
And because it is a phenomenon that serves as a condition, it is called "condition" (*paccaya*). Now he explains the meaning of the word *paṭicca* with the words "having gone back" (*paṭigantvā*).
This means having reached [the result] by way of the nature of the cause, through the process of attaining that [result]. How is it not without that?
Only when that [cause] exists, and only from the arising of its fruit, and not otherwise. And when it is absent, [it is so] from its cessation.
This is the meaning of the word *paṭicca* as the stability of conditions (*paccayaṭṭhiti*).

Therefore, this word *paṭicca*—just as the words "when this exists, this arises"—indicates, by way of expressing the locative and ablative cases, that the state of dependence of the possessor of the cause (the *hetumato*) upon the cause, which is denoted by the word "this" (*idaṃ*), is such that it looks toward the subsequent activity following the arising of the entity;
and it is by means of that very capacity [of dependence] that [the term *paṭicca* functions].

They speak of a cause (*hetu*). Thus, by means of the causal relation (*hetupaccaya*), which is to be expressed through the word "having gone" (*gantvā*), [the Buddha] stated the cause by way of its dependence on that very object to be known;
this dependence consists in the state of being contingent upon the cause, with regard to the subsequent action of simultaneous arising.
And having done so, he said: "Dependent on ignorance (*avijjā*), volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are dependently arisen," and so forth.
This is stated in the *Saṅkhāra-piṭaka*. Here, "capability" refers to the state of being the cause (*nidāna*) and so forth;

and that [capability] exists precisely as a reality with respect to the fruit that is invariably concomitant with it. Regarding the phrase "of the connection": by way of conformity to the fetters (*saṃyojana*), there is a connection through birth and so forth, which has arisen from conditions such as aging and death.
"Arising" (*uppāda*) means the act of arising. If this is so, how is the term "dependent" (*paṭicca*) employed?

Is it not the case that such verbal usage occurs when there are actions with a common agent at a prior time? [The answer is: This is true in instances such as “having eaten, he goes” (*bhutvā gacchati*) or “having ploughed, he sows” (*kasitvā vapati*);
however, this should be understood as being based on the majority of cases, since such usage is also seen where the times are different and where the agents are not the same.
First, regarding cases where the time is the same:
“Having destroyed the darkness, this sun has risen;
having shone forth with the radiance of beauty and wisdom, it has ascended.”—this is the example.
Some, however, cite: “He sleeps with his mouth open; he looks with his eyes rolled back. Others cite: “He studies while sitting; he speaks while standing.”

In this context, there exists a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority based on the expectation of an action that involves the presentation and subsequent display of an object; yet, because it does not characterize a distinct division [of time], it is not marked as such by some.

Furthermore, in the cases of "having sat down, he studies" (*nisajja adhīte*) and "having stood, he speaks" (*ṭhatvā katheti*), even though there is simultaneity, since sitting and standing can also occur prior to the acts of studying and speaking, a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority is possible.
Therefore, the previous examples alone are appropriate; for the cessation of that which is to be ceased occurs at the very same time as its arising.
At a later time, one says, "Having closed the door, he enters," or "Having closed it, he goes out. Some, however, cite the example, "The staff fell with a thud.
But the simultaneity of the sound produced by the impact with the impact itself and its co-nascent factors is [the point].
Since this is found here, therefore even in this case the previous examples alone are appropriate.

However, by the very desire to express the state of being a characteristic and a cause for the characteristic, the cause, and the action—namely, the desire to express the state of being a characteristic and a cause—the grammatical derivation of the word "nihantvāna" (having struck down) is intended as a time prior to the state of being a characteristic; and thus, the action of conditioning is [prior] to the action of arising.
The grammatical derivation of the word *paccaya* is established by its connection with the prefix *pati*. In that context, it is appropriate because it directly shows the agent (*kattā*).
But here, since that [directness] is absent, it is not appropriate, one might argue? This is not a fault. Here too, it is established through inference (*anumāna*).

The agent, beginning with aging and death, certainly exists, as seen in such usages as “having known [it] from the process of passing away” (*ñatvā kiriyato vayaṃ*); for it must necessarily be inferred.
Such a verbal usage is intended when the agent (*kattar*) is identical. However, when the agent is not identical, one should understand examples such as:
"Fear arises upon seeing a *pisāca*, and for him, having seen with wisdom, the taints (*āsava*) are utterly destroyed.
And just as in those cases there is the activity of a person—such as the act of seeing a *pisāca*—so too here, the activity of the condition (*paccaya-vyāpāra*) is its own...
The production of the fruit, and its simultaneous arising with that [fruit], is what is meant by "when the condition exists, due to the arising of the condition.

Thus, it should be understood that the term *paṭicca* (dependent) is established even in the absence of an agent, as it indicates the state of being the cause for the simultaneous arising of the condition.
If dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) were merely the arising of a dependent connection, how could the condition itself be called dependent origination?

This matter has already been discussed below. Furthermore, that which is intended here as the "cause" (hetu) is the causal factor—characterized by potency—that is revealed by the term *paṭicca* (dependent) among those things produced by conditions (*paccayuppanna*) which are revealed by the term *samuppāda* (co-arising).
It is spoken of in that way because its intrinsic nature is to be understood through words denoting exertion, owing to its being directed toward co-arising (*samuppāda*).
But what is the reason that the cause of co-arising is to be known by means of a word where co-arising is predominant, and not [by a word where the cause itself is predominant]?
"Is it thus that arising is with cause? It is said: because the condition for the suffering that has been seen has been clarified by the exposition of conditions. How so? As it is said:
"In this case, monks, a monk, investigating, investigates: 'Whatever this manifold [suffering] is...'"
‘Various kinds of suffering arise in the world, such as aging and death. Now, what is the source of this suffering? What is its origin? From what is it born? What is its provenance?

When what exists does aging and death come to be? When what does not exist do aging and death not come to be? While investigating thus, he understands: ‘This which is … [as before] … this indeed is the source of this suffering; this is its origin; from this it is born; this is its provenance. When this exists, aging and death come to be; when this does not exist, aging and death do not come to be.’”

“Suffering has birth as its source,” and so forth—this source of the suffering already seen is stated in the *Parivīmaṃsa Sutta*. And that source must also be understood through full comprehension. As it was said:
“Bhikkhus, before my enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this occurred to me.”
‘Alas, this world has fallen into trouble; it is born, ages, dies, passes away, and is reborn, yet it does not understand the escape from this suffering, from aging and death.
When, alas, will an escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be discerned? … Then, monks, through my thorough application of mindfulness…
"Through attention there was the breakthrough by means of wisdom: 'When birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death arises.

By such statements, the breakthrough consisting in the investigation of the conditions for suffering already seen is expressed. For the condition must be known, and the understanding of the escape from suffering depends upon that breakthrough.
And that which is to be known must be proclaimed; thus is the term *paṭiccasamuppāda* (dependent origination).
Whatever suffering is seen as manifested by the sound of its arising, that occurs only in dependence upon conditions and not otherwise; thus it is stated for the purpose of analyzing conditions.

For indeed, even though the primary factor is something to be known and proclaimed due to its desirability, it may be described as secondary because it must be understood through some specific distinction, just as in the case of the question: "Who is a stream-enterer?"
“For whom have the three fetters been abandoned?

Who is Devadatta, whose houses are higher?”—in this way, here too, in the sense of making known the condition and the conditioned, the condition is spoken of by way of the synonym “dependent” (*paṭicca*), because it is to be known through its own fruit by means of a specific capability within the exposition (*niddesa*). Its opposition [to the fruit] is established through that specific capability.

And this exposition beginning with “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise],” which demonstrates the conditions starting from the very root of the entire mass of suffering, concludes at the end by showing the eradication of that suffering through the word “thus”: “In this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering. Thus...

Having directed one toward the origination of those conditions as they have been stated, the conditions are thus concluded. In the *Paṭipadā-sutta* as well, after stating, "With ignorance as condition...
[and so on]... there is origination," it says, "This, monks, is called wrong practice (*micchāpaṭipadā*).
Now, suffering (*dukkha*) as apprehended by way of its state of being dependently arisen is not itself wrong practice; rather, it is that which constitutes the origination of suffering.
"Condition": Just as in the case of "five-factored right concentration" or "right concentration possessing five kinds of knowledge," where—

because the purpose of the teaching is the penetration of the factors and the knowledge— the penetration of the factors and the knowledge is effected by means of words dominated by "right concentration," so too here it should be understood that the penetration of the condition is effected by means of a word dominated by "co-arising."

581. As for the phrase "this *tantrī*," it refers to the connection [of the words]. "Laid down" (*nikkhittā*) means established; the meaning is "taught. It is called a *tantrī* because it extends (*tananato*) the intended meaning;
thus, it is a composition (*gantha*). Because the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa, when asked by [King Asoka], "Venerable sir, what is the doctrine of the Perfectly Enlightened One?
replied, "He is an analyst (*vibhajjavādī*), Great King," the disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One...

They are proponents of analysis (*vibhajjavādino*). For they reiterate what was taught by the Teacher through analysis regarding the nature of being subject to discipline and so forth, as well as the states of those things to be cultivated and not cultivated among mental joy and the like, and robes and the like. Or, they speak analytically regarding the doctrines of eternalism and annihilationism.

This is because they set aside those questions to be set aside, such as "Is the self and the world eternal? and because they distinguish between the eternal destruction of passion and the like, and the annihilation of bodily misconduct and the like.

And because of their verbal expression, they do not exclude the three questions—such as those to be answered with a categorical denial—and speak only of that which is to be answered by analysis (*vibhajja-vyākaraṇīya*).
The circle or assembly of those who advocate analysis is the "circle of the Vibhajjavādins" (*vibhajjavādimaṇḍala*).

Alternatively, they say that the assembly of the Blessed One, consisting of the Vibhajjavādins, is the "circle of the Vibhajjavādins. Or else, it refers to those who analyze both eternalism (*sassata*) and annihilationism (*uccheda*).

Because the Blessed One taught dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) as the middle way, without falling into extremes, and because his disciples followed that teaching, they are "proponents of analysis" (*vibhajjavādino*). The rest is as before.
"Having descended" means having plunged in; the sense is "having become a proponent of analysis. For one who is himself not a proponent of analysis...

One is considered to have entered the circle of the Vibhajjavādins merely by standing among those who advocate analysis, provided one does not misrepresent them by explaining meanings that are contrary to what has been taught by the Teachers.

This applies even when one asserts that ignorance is a cause and condition for both meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations, and when one speaks of the "person" (puggala) and other such views that are rejected in the *Kathāvatthu*.

"Deviation from one's own system" means by one who does not deviate in such a manner. "Without exerting oneself toward another system" means by remaining free from the activity of attributing faults [to it].
Some say this means "not gathering together another system with the thought, 'This sutta too must be accepted.
"Thus do I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that very same consciousness runs on..."
By saying such things as, "He transmigrates, not another," one indeed rejects the Sutta; likewise, by one who does not reject it [the following must be stated]:
"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not capable of being obstacles for one who indulges in them;
a transgression committed even in a dream constitutes an offense," and so forth.
To speak [contrary to this] is called "contravening the Vinaya"; by contrast, it is through being in accordance with it that one conforms to it.

For how can one who contravenes it—by interrupting the sequence of formal acts (*kamma*) and violating the true nature of the Dhamma (*dhammatā*)—possibly conform to the discipline (*vinaya*) regarding the defilements?

Regarding what has been stated in the Sutta, there are the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*); and regarding what has been stated in the Commentary, there are the four Great Authorities consisting of the Sutta, the Sutta-conformity, the Teacher’s tradition, and one’s own reflection.
By "observing. For by observing that [connection], one remains established in the Sutta and the Vinaya and does not overstep them.

"Dhamma" refers to the text of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). "Meaning" (*attha*) refers to its meaning. Here, the cause, or the causes and effects, is the "dhamma," while this effect is the "meaning.
Alternatively, "dhamma" refers to the nature of things (*dhammatā*). Just as some say, "From arising... [and so forth].
Misinterpreting the meaning of the Sutta passage, “Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise,
that element remains constant,” they falsely teach that the phenomenon of the mode of conditions— dependent origination— is eternal. Instead of teaching it thus,
one should explain it as having a fixed nature in relation to its own fruit, according to the method stated above.
And just as some wrongly grasp the meaning of dependent origination by saying "non-cessation, non-arising," and so forth, [the author]—
without adopting such a grasp— summarizes the unerring meaning according to the method already stated.

Having restated the meaning previously expressed as "ignorance regarding suffering and the rest is *avijjā*," he further explains it through other synonyms, beginning with "ignorance regarding the past," and so on.
By way of demonstrating. They say it is by way of demonstrating: "Formations are called 'existence' (bhava) by this method;
craving is called 'clinging' (upādāna) by this method," and so forth. "Naturally" means without reference to the aforementioned specific arrangement, but simply as such.
"Truth" refers to the Four Noble Truths. "Being" they say is the emptiness of a being (satta-suññatā); however, regarding formations that are empty of a being—
The conventional designation of "being," the accomplishment of the duties of a being, and the very mode of conditionality—this is the meaning of *paccayākāro* (the mode of conditionality);
here, the letter *ma* serves as a sandhi-conjunction. The meaning of *paṭiccasamuppāda* is the state of being a condition for their own fruit on the part of the conditioned phenomena themselves.
Therefore, because it must be explained according to the method already stated, and because it is difficult [to do so], I do not find a firm footing.
The meaning is: "I do not, by the power of my own knowledge, discover that method which serves as the foundation for that [teaching] which is easy to explain when one is established therein.
However, pointing out the basis [for his understanding], he said, "But this teaching...

and so forth. Here, "the teaching" (*sāsana*) refers to the Dhamma of the Pāḷi, or specifically to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*). For that is adorned with various methods of exposition, such as the direct and reverse orders.
Because it has not been interrupted and continues even today, it serves as a support; so too does the path of the ancient teachers, which is known as the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on that [text].
If one asks what the purpose is for generating reverence and inciting effort with the words, “Listen to that, being composed,” he says, “For this has been said,” and so forth.
“Making it a bone” means making it the essential meaning; or, it means having reached the state of a bone so that it may not be lost.
"Making it as if [it were] bone" means having made it into bone. "Successive" (*pubbāpariya*) refers to existence from an earlier time to a later time.
"Distinguishing" means that from the very first undertaking onwards, one attains a distinction in knowledge and a distinction in the destruction of the defilements at every moment;

this is the meaning. (582) "By way of the difference in teaching" means by way of the specific distinctions in the teaching. "By way of meaning, characteristic, and so forth, and by way of the singlefold, and so forth" means by way of meaning, characteristic, the singlefold, and so forth. "And the determination of the factors" means by way of showing the determination of the twelve factors, beginning with ignorance.
Because it is the root cause of the rounds of kamma, its result, and the defilements, and because it is mentioned first, ignorance is the root of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).

In this regard, one should not apply the analogy that "just as when the root of a creeper is seen, the clearing away of the creeper begins from there, so too when the root of dependent origination is seen, the teaching of dependent origination begins from there. It is not [so].
For there is nothing that the Blessed One has not seen; thus, it must be distinguished that "this is seen" and "this is unseen" does not apply to him, since he has seen everything.
However, from the very beginning, the teaching on dependent origination was presented starting from the root, just as one might pull up a creeper by its roots;

this is the commonality intended here. Alternatively, the commonality of showing the root and so forth should be applied according to the inclinations of those to be enlightened, or by way of the necessity of what must be made known to them.
“Of him”: “Monks, as that youth, with the passing of time and the ripening of his faculties, becomes endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure... which are alluring.
Having seen a form with the eye, he becomes infatuated with forms that are pleasing, and [averse] to forms that are unpleasing...”
He becomes afflicted with regard to form; he dwells with unestablished mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind;
and he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.
Thus, having fallen into attraction and aversion, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant or...
“Whether it be painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it”—thus it was said.
This applies likewise to the door of the ear and the other sense-doors. “He delights in it” means he rejoices by way of the presence of craving accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-taṇhā*).
“He welcomes it” means by way of powerful craving that issues in verbal expressions such as, “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!”
This refers to one who asserts "I" and "mine. From that state, there arises a powerful clinging (*ajjhosāya*) which persists because it is impossible to release;
even more powerful than that is craving (*taṇhā*), which constitutes grasping (*upādāna*). Here, craving is expressed by the term "delight" (*abhinandanā*);

by the word "delight" (*nandi*), it should be understood that all four kinds of grasping are included, both through their being the conditions for delight and through their states of delighting in craving and views, as well as through their inseparability from that delight.
And the statement beginning with "With birth as condition, aging-and-death" and so forth was spoken in that very same Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta.

Furthermore, regarding the nutriment-originated nutritive essence (*ojā*) within rebirth-linking, the process of existence, contact, and so on—which constitute the round of kamma-result—[it was said]:
"The four nutriments have craving as their source," and so forth. However, the other nutriments, which support the round of existence, arise from craving.
Since they do not exist when that [craving] is absent, it is appropriate to say, "they have craving as their source" (*taṇhānidāna*).
583. "From this and that" refers to from each of the fourfold teachings. It "leads to the penetration of the method" (*ñāyappaṭivedha*);
thus, "method" (*ñāya*) is the path, or rather, dependent origination itself is the method, as in: "The noble method has been well seen by his wisdom."

By way of the words. For, because he is perfectly auspicious (*samantabhaddaka*) and because [the truth] must be penetrated in such and such a manner, each respective teaching leads to his own penetration.
"Attainment of the fourfold profundity" means that he is established by having reached a firm footing in the profundities of the Dhamma, its meaning, its teaching, and its penetration.

The state of being universally excellent (*samantabhaddakatā*) and the attainment of elegance in teaching are common causes for all four types of teaching; therefore, wishing to state the specific cause, he says "specifically" (*visesato*).
"Of this" (*assā*) should be construed as "of this Blessed One’s teaching" or "of the teaching of this dependent origination" (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
The analysis of the causes for its occurrence refers to ignorance and the rest themselves, whose intrinsic natures have not yet been analyzed; thus, it is the cause.
Or [it is] the non-causality and causality of the primary elements (*pakati*) and so forth, as well as of ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth, which have been taken up.
In this regard, some are deluded and grasp what is not a cause as being a cause, while others do not perceive anything as a cause;

therefore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the occurrence of the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*) and so forth by means of their respective appropriate causes, and for the purpose of demonstrating the occurrence of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

The meaning is as follows: Ignorance (*avijjā*), which conceals the danger in the process of existence (*pavatti*), is the beginning; from that, volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) arise, and from those, consciousness (*viññāṇa*).

Thus, the teaching proceeds in direct order (*anuloma*) for the purpose of demonstrating the sequence of arising in the process of existence, and also for the purpose of demonstrating the successive order in which the individual selfhood (*attabhāva*) arises in various states of existence, such as those born from a womb. As for the others...
Even though that purpose is not possible for those [other knowledges], their activity does not have that purpose alone, because other purposes exist;
however, since this [knowledge] has that purpose alone, its having that purpose is stated.
For one who is reviewing, there is the preliminary penetration (pubbhāga-paṭivedha) consisting of the comprehension of the various conditions arising prior to full enlightenment.

This teaching in reverse order was set forth for the purpose of demonstrating that which has been realized—namely, the cause of aging, death, and so forth, such as birth and so forth—by following and tracking back from that [realization].
Alternatively, the connection is: "The teaching in reverse order was set forth by one who is looking back.
For even when teaching, the Blessed One, having looked back upon the world fallen into suffering, [proceeds] with the prior stage... [etc.]

"He taught for the purpose of pointing out" means: with the intention that "nutriment and craving belong to the present time, while formations and ignorance belong to the past," he said, "having carried it back as far as the past time.
Alternatively, nutriment is to be produced by craving and thus belongs to the future time;
craving and so forth are the present; and formations and ignorance are the past. However, the fruit is directly perceived.
Having shown this, it is said that the demonstration of the succession of causes and effects is appropriate by way of showing the source of that [suffering]:
the nutriments are produced by past craving and constitute the present time-period; craving and so forth belong to the past;

and formations and ignorance are even further back than that, stated for the purpose of showing the beginninglessness of saṃsāra. "As far as the past time-period" means as far as the more remote past.

“Appropriate”: The four nutriments that bring about the production of renewed existence in the future—regarding these, I do not say, “I eat them”… [as before] …“But if someone were to ask me, who does not speak thus, ‘Venerable sir, for what purpose is the nutriment consciousness?
this would be a fitting question, and there would be a fitting answer: ‘The nutriment consciousness is for the purpose of the production of renewed existence in the future.’”
This is because of the verbal expression [of desire], because contact and volition are associated with it, and because edible food is the cause for its occurrence.
For by means of that, there is the accumulation of sensual consciousness in one whose material body is supported by it and who desires it.
Indeed, it has been stated that food is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for faith and so forth, as well as for lust and so forth. Therefore, those foods are included within the cycle of kamma.
Regarding the phrase "the present time," in this context, only the former meaning is appropriate.
Starting from the past time with the passage, "Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations," and so forth,
[the Buddha] has ascended by way of demonstrating the causal relationship— both cause and effect— in succession, using the directly perceived foods as the basis for showing the source (nidāna).
The meaning is that this teaching proceeds for the purpose of demonstrating that [truth] to those who do not awaken without such turning back.

"From the origination of the causes of the future period onwards" means starting from the arising of those phenomena that serve as the causes for future existence. "For the purpose of demonstrating the future period" means for those who have not penetrated the future period.
The meaning is: for the purpose of demonstrating that [result] through the succession of cause and fruit by showing the present cause to those who do not see it directly.

And herein, from the beginning until the end, and from the end back to the beginning, the teaching that proceeds consists of twelve factors, and for that very reason, it has three connections and four summaries. From the middle until...

The teaching that proceeds from the beginning has eight factors, two connections, and three summaries. However, the teaching that proceeds from the middle until the conclusion has six factors, two connections, and three summaries. This is shown by such passages as:
"Bhikkhus, for one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that fetter, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging [arises]," and so forth, from the middle.
The teaching that proceeds from the beginning to the end has one connection and two summaries.

Thus, this teaching on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is presented with many factors. However, a teaching on dependent origination is indeed found even by way of a single factor. As it is said:
"In this regard, monks, the learned noble disciple attends thoroughly and wisely to dependent origination itself..."
"He acts thus: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. Monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises."

"Ādi. For here, the dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is stated merely as "with contact as condition" (*phassapaccayā*). By this it is understood that this is a "dependent origination consisting of a single factor.

In that context, "when this exists, that comes to be" means that when this condition—beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*)—exists, this result—beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*)—comes to be.
"With the arising of this, that arises" means with the arising of this condition, beginning with ignorance...
The meaning is: "This result, beginning with volitional formations (saṅkhāra), arises. By stating, "When this is absent, that does not come to be;

with the cessation of this, that ceases," the restriction regarding the first characteristic of conditionality is shown—namely, the absence of volitional formations and so forth when ignorance and so forth are absent, and the cessation of volitional formations and so forth through the cessation of ignorance and so forth.
"Only when this exists, not when it does not exist; only with the arising of this, not with its cessation.
Thus, it should be understood that this characteristic is stated here for dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) as including an internal necessity.

Furthermore, "cessation" (nirodha) refers to the non-arising and non-occurrence in the future through the attainment of dispassion (virāga) regarding ignorance and the other factors. For it has been said accordingly:
“With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance,” and so forth. Arising is the opposite of cessation;

since it is stated as being opposed to arising in the formula, “With the cessation of this, that ceases,” this shows that what is called “arising” is actually non-cessation, and that here it is also referred to as “existence.
For this very definition applies: “When this exists, that comes to be.”
By the other person who states, "With the arising of this, that arises," by means of a different method of exposition, the former [condition] is specified;
therefore, it is understood that the phrase "when this exists" is not spoken with reference solely to its continued presence, but rather to its state of not having been ceased by the path.
And because of the statement, "When this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this..."

By stating the exposition of cessation—which was indicated in two ways by the words "this ceases"—through the passage beginning, "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations," it is shown that cessation itself is what is meant; therefore, even non-existence is indeed cessation.
Thus, it is demonstrated that existence, which is the opposite of non-existence, is non-cessation. By that which is termed "non-cessation" (anirodha)...

It distinguishes arising by means of the state of existence (*atthibhāva*). Therefore, what is intended here as "arising" is not merely the acquisition of selfhood, but rather the state of existence characterized by non-cessation;
thus, this meaning is clarified. In this way, these two statements regarding the characteristics should be understood as purposeful through their mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified.
But what is this so-called "non-cessation" (anirodha), which is said to be existence (atthibhāva) and arising (uppāda)?

It is the state of not being abandoned; it is the state of the fruit not yet having been produced, and the state of being fit for the production of fruit because it has not yet been rendered unfit for abandonment. It is the state of those unwholesome states (akusala-dhammā) that ought to be abandoned by them not having been eradicated by the Noble Path (ariyamagga);

and as for those wholesome (kusala) and indeterminate (abyākata) states that are not to be abandoned, it is the presence of fetters (saṃyojana) toward them in those whose taints (āsava) have not been destroyed.

And [it is] because they are not exhausted. For dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) is the occurrence of the aggregates together with their fetters (*saṃyojana*), due to the fact that the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have not been eradicated. Thus it has been said:

"Bhikkhus, for that ignorance by which the fool is shrouded, and for that craving with which he is associated, this body has come into being. That very ignorance of the fool is unabandoned, and that craving is unexhausted. Why is that?"
What is the cause? It is because, monks, the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering;
therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool goes to a state of being, and being one who has gone to a state of being, he is not liberated from birth, aging, and death.

Thus it is said. However, for those whose fetters are exhausted, because of the absence of ignorance, volitional formations do not arise; and because of the absence of craving and clinging, grasping and becoming do not come to be. Thus the cutting off of the round is made known. Therefore he said:

“Indeed, Phagguna, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of the spheres of contact, there is the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling,” and so forth.
For it is not that the six sense bases and the rest do not function from the attainment of the highest path until final Nibbāna;
rather, their non-existence, their state of being expressible by the word “cessation,” and the fact that the fetters have been exhausted, is what is called “cessation. Furthermore—
Even an action performed long ago is called "fit for fruition" (phalāraha) precisely because its fruit has not yet been produced and because that which is fit for it has not been abandoned;

it is not so called because its fruit has already been produced, nor because that which is fit for it has been abandoned. Thus, the state of being fit for fruition—consisting of ignorance, volitional formations, and so forth, which are the conditions for the arising of the fruit—should be understood as "non-cessation" (anirodha) according to the method already stated. For it is by this very state of non-cessation that...
Without a fruit, [the effect] cannot come to be; that cause, even though past and so forth, is expressed by the phrase "when this exists.

For that very reason, the arising of conditions—which has not fallen into the state of non-occurrence for one whose holy life (*brahmacariya*) is unfulfilled—is stated as "with the arising of this," precisely because it does not disregard the distinction of time and does not turn back. Alternatively, when the remaining conditions have come together...
The state of being directed toward the arising of a fruit—whether that fruit is non-existent or already existent, let alone when it is actually present—is what is called "with the arising of this.
For at that time, because the fruit arises from it, the cause in that particular state appears as the very act of producing the fruit;
thus it is said to have "arisen" (*uppatita*). It should be understood that "arising" refers to being in that specific state, rather than to the cause being merely existent while not in that state.

In this context, by the word "when present" (*sati*), he shows the conditionality of dependent origination by stating its status as a condition through mere existence, thereby demonstrating its lack of agency.

By the word "arising" (*uppādā*), he demonstrates the impermanence of dependent origination by indicating its nature of coming into being, its non-existence at all other times, and its orientation toward the production of a fruit. Thus: "When present, not when absent; arising, not ceasing."
However, [the word *paṭicca*] demonstrates that dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) possesses the nature of being a cause,
an origin, a birth, and a source, as expressed by locative and ablative case endings with the sense of "cause" (*hetuattha*). Here,

the status of having the sense of "cause" in the locative case should be understood as occurring in that [locative] by which the existence of a fruit invariably concomitant with it is characterized, just as when wealth is not bestowed upon those who are poor.
“Poverty reached its full extent,” and “When the crop has ripened, a good harvest arises.

Even in the case of an ablative construction, it carries the sense of a cause (*hetu*), occurring both in the arising of a fruit from its source and in its natural occurrence, as in: “From the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*;
from the *abbuda* the *pesī* is born,” and “The Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat; the lake arises from the peak. [This applies] by way of ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the state of being formations and so forth, which are inseparable from that [ignorance], is characterized; and by means of ignorance and the rest, the formations and so forth come into being (*pabhavanti*) and are produced (*pakarīyanti*).

Thus, they are its "source" (*pabhava*) and its "nature" (*pakati*). Therefore, in order to illuminate this meaning, the locative case and the particle *nissaka* (the suffix *-to*) are employed in the sense of a cause, as in:
"When this exists, through the arising of this... (*imasmiṃ sati imassuppādā*).

And because here there is a detailed exposition of dependent origination—beginning with "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise," and so forth—which was briefly indicated by the formula "When this exists, that comes to be;

with the arising of this, that arises," it is understood that the aforementioned state of existence and the arising [of phenomena] constitute the causal status of those various dependently arisen states. For [the meaning of the formula] is not merely the state of being unceased...
Apart from the state of existence (atthibhāva)— which is characterized by an irreversible nature or the state of arising—
and which is explained by statements containing internal restrictions such as "only when present, not when absent" and "only when arising,
not when ceasing," there is no other so-called "conditionality. Therefore, the aforementioned state of existence and the process of arising constitute conditionality.

It should be understood [as follows]. For even those twenty-four conditions, beginning with the root-cause (hetu), that are mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna* should be understood as specific modes of this very same state of being a condition.
Likewise, this [condition] is expressed by such synonyms as "root," "cause" (*nidāna*), "origin" (*sambhava*), and "source" (*pabhava*);

and by such synonyms as "arising" (*uppāda*-ṭṭhiti), "stationing" (*ṭhiti*), "occurrence" (*pavatta*-ṭṭhiti), "sign" (*nimitta*-ṭṭhiti), "accumulation" (*āyūhana*-ṭṭhiti), "bondage" (*saṃyoga*-ṭṭhiti), and "impediment" (*palibodha*-ṭṭhiti).
And the meaning of "cause" has been explained; that too should be understood as being included right here.
(584) With reference to the word *mūlakāraṇa* (root cause), the neuter designation *akāraṇaṃ* is used, meaning "not a cause.
Showing that if it were not a cause, the Sutta would be contradicted, he cites the Sutta: "From the arising of the taints... (*āsavasamudayā*).
“Pariyāya” means a reason. In the discourse on the round of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), the status of being the head refers both to the round itself and to its cause, which is karma.
In that context, ignorance (*avijjā*) is also the cause of craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*);
since craving arises toward existence whose dangers are concealed by that ignorance, ignorance is specifically the "head," and is thus called the "root cause."
He said, "And so, monks, this is said," etc., [meaning] that one might grasp at permanence because no prior limit is known due to the absence of arising.
By this, he shows the meaning that the non-knowing of a prior limit is stated because there has been no previous arising before this point, owing to its being unknown.

585. When it is necessary to speak of the fruits as being caused by ignorance and craving, the expression “those going to happy and miserable destinies” is used for the sake of not contradicting grammatical rules.
For in a *dvanda* compound, that which is more venerable is placed first.

It is said that the Savaras kill a cow by repeatedly heating it over a fire, pounding it, and making it drink hot water, so that the meat does not stick to the bone; they then cut the meat from the carcass once it has been drained.

Therefore he said, "From the heat of fire," and so forth. In this context, just as the cow condemned to death, being overcome by ignorance, begins to drink the aforementioned hot water, so too does the worldling begin to perform the aforementioned karma that leads to an unhappy destination.
However, just as she, seeing the danger in drinking the hot water, begins to drink cold water out of craving, so too does the worldling...
Because ignorance is not exceedingly powerful, one perceives the danger in karma leading to a miserable destination and, by means of craving, undertakes karma leading to a happy destination.
