For in suffering, craving follows along with ignorance; in happiness, ignorance follows along with craving.
(586) In a certain sutta, it is said: “The teaching based on a single state”: among ignorance and craving, only a single state is the root.
"Of these" means rooted in a single dhamma; the meaning is that it teaches the exposition of dependent origination by making that one single dhamma the root therein.
"Upanisā" means that where the fruit depends upon (upanisīdati), it is the cause. "With ignorance as their proximate cause" (avijjūpanisā) means those for which ignorance is the proximate cause.
"Perceiving gratification" means because of the quality of being gratified within the objects consisting of the dhammas of the three planes that are subject to clinging.

It is characterized by pleasure and joy, being designated as gratification, for one whose nature is contemplation. It belongs to a fool because of the association with the characteristic of a fool due to the non-abandonment of ignorance (*avijjā*).
"Thus" (*evaṃ*) means because it is shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving (*taṇhā*).

"This body" (*ayaṃ kāyo*) refers to this conscious body consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*), which is directly evident both to me and to you. "With the six sense bases as condition, contact [arises]" (*saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso*).
Or, because it is called the cause of contact by way of its verbal designation, it is the "sixfold base" (*āyatana-ṣaṭka*). "Arisen" means produced.
"And externally, name-and-form" refers to the body together with consciousness externally, which consists of the five aggregates or the six bases.
"It is thus" means it is in this manner. One's own and others' five aggregates and twelve bases exist by way of being doors and objects.

The meaning is that the two are established as "name. Elsewhere, it is said that "contact arises dependent on a dyad," referring to visual contact and so forth arising dependent on the dyads of the eye and visible forms;
however, here it refers to the internal and external bases, which are called the "great dyad.
This is the intended meaning here: elsewhere, "dependent on the eye... [and so on].

In such passages as, "When there is form and eye-consciousness arises, the meeting of the three is contact," it is stated that visual contact and so forth arise in dependence upon the dyads consisting of the eye and forms... and so on, up to the mind and mental objects.
However, here, by the phrase "this very body," all remaining phenomena supported by the eye and so forth are treated as being themselves the supports for the eye and so forth.

Having taken the internal body, such as the eye and so forth, as a unity under the designation "internal sense base," and having stated that the external name-and-form consists of the objects such as visible form and so forth as a unity under the designation "external sense base," contact is said to arise in dependence upon those internal and external sense bases;
therefore, this is the "great dyad."
And having done so, this meaning—that for both oneself and another there are five aggregates and six bases—should be illustrated, as it has been said:
"For the eye and so forth, together with their supports, which are spoken of as 'this body,' are one's own five aggregates;
while the forms and so forth, which are spoken of as 'external name-and-form,' belong to others. Likewise, this body consists of one's own six internal [bases]."
The sense bases (āyatana) are, externally, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) belonging to others as "external.
Otherwise, if it were stated merely that "this body" refers only to internal sense bases, then only one's own internal sense bases would constitute one's own five aggregates (pañcakkhandha);
thus, an exposition by means of the five aggregates of both oneself and others would not be possible. "Only the six sense bases" means only the six causes of contact (phassa).
The fool experiences pleasure and pain through contact that has arisen from those bases which serve as its causes.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should connect [the passage] beginning with: "Or by one of these; for the wise man, O monks, who is hindered by ignorance and associated with craving...
In this sutta, indeed, volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) are treated as being dependent solely upon ignorance and craving.
By including consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases under the term "body," and by showing that contact within that body is dependent solely upon those six sense bases,
the Blessed One— by demonstrating the specific conditionality of feeling— has shown the dependent origination ending in feeling,
which for both the foolish and the wise is rooted in ignorance and craving regarding the past. Furthermore, for the foolish and the wise...
Showing the distinction:
"Monks, that ignorance by which the fool is shrouded and that craving with which he is associated—by means of these, this body has come to be.
That very ignorance of the fool is not abandoned, and that craving is not exhausted. Why is that?"
What is the cause? It is because, monks, the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering.
Therefore, with the breakup of the body, the fool becomes one who goes to a [new] body; being one who has gone to a body, he is not liberated from birth... [and so on] ...from suffering, I say.
Thus, having shown that craving—accompanied by ignorance—is the origin of feeling, and having established clinging and becoming as dependent upon it, [he says]: "one who goes to a body..."
By showing birth and so forth through the passage beginning with “it comes to be,” dependent origination is explained by way of its two roots starting from its origination from present causes;
and conversely, for the wise person, the reverse order of dependent origination is explained by way of those same two roots starting from the investigation of present causes until their exhaustion.

587. *Pūretum* means to increase or to accumulate; this is the meaning. Because ignorance (*avijjā*) is a specific condition for karma leading to miserable destinies (*duggati*), it is said that "it finds what is not to be found" (*avindiyaṃ vindati*).
Likewise, because it is not a specific condition for what is to be found (*vindiya*), it is also said that "it does not find what is to be found" (*vindiyaṃ na vindati*).
The *āyatana* (base) is the production—that is, the causing to arise—of eye-consciousness and the rest by making them dependent upon itself.
Because it has not been fully realized due to its very state of delusion, it makes [the meaning] unknown and unrecognized.

"It causes it to move within that which is devoid of an end" means: by means of the fivefold characteristics of etymological derivation (*niruttilakkhaṇa*)—namely, the addition of phonemes (*vaṇṇāgama*), transposition (*vipariyāya*), modification (*vikāra*), elision (*vināsa*), and the application of specific meanings of verbal roots (*dhātu-atthavisesayoga*)—one takes the letter *a*, the letter *vi*, and the letter *ja*, effects the elision of other phonemes, and the addition of a second *ja* for the [first] *ja*.
Having stated this, it was called "ignorance" (*avijjā*). After explaining the literal meaning, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (*apica*) was stated to show its essential nature (*sabhāva*).
Ignorance is said to be that which conceals these [bases and objects], because eye-consciousness and the rest are unable to know through ignorance, "This is the base; this is the object.
It is precisely because it conceals the essential nature of the bases and objects that ignorance and the other [factors] are so designated.

The concealment of dependent origination and of the dependently originated should be understood as the concealing of the state of being dependently originated and the state of being dependently arisen, such as aging, death, and so forth.
"Without rejecting" means without having rejected or without having repudiated. The meaning of "condition" (paccaya) is the sense of being helpful, just as alms-food and the like are for the body.
“They construct the conditioned” means they construct it in such a way that it becomes conditioned.

“Volitional formations arrived at by the word ‘volitional formation’” refers to those volitional formations conveyed by the term *saṅkhāra*. Although volitional formations conditioned by ignorance are also conveyed by the word *saṅkhāra*, they are mentioned separately because they are the primary subject of this teaching;
therefore, in the phrase “of two kinds,” by the word *saṅkhāra*—

Excluding the formative volitional activity (*abhisaṅkharaṇa-saṅkhāra*) among those things included under the term "formations" (*saṅkhāra*), the other formations mentioned by the word *saṅkhāra* should be connected [with the rest].
Alternatively, the phrase "formations mentioned by the word *saṅkhāra*" refers to the whole collection;

and here, a portion of that collection is taken up for exposition as "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance. Therefore, it is stated by way of including all formations that are to be explained.

It should be understood that "twofoldness" has been stated. By the passage beginning, "First the verbal formation ceases," etc., the formations of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), inhalation and exhalation (*assāsa-passāsa*), perception (*saññā*), feeling (*vedanā*), and verbal formations (*vacī-saṅkhāra*) are mentioned;

it is not the bodily volitions (*kāya-sañcetanā*) and so forth mentioned among the formations conditioned by ignorance (*avijjā-paccaya*). They are called "conditioned formations" (*saṅkhata-saṅkhāra*) because they are conditioned by their respective conditions. Even though [they] are produced by conditions...

Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*) are produced by karma that, as it were, turns toward them with the thought "this is my fruit," they possess a pre-eminent state of being conditioned among the resultant and kamma-originated materiality of the three planes;
it is with this intention that the *Aṭṭhakathā* states that those produced by karma have the nature of "volitionally conditioned formations" (*abhisaṅkhata-saṅkhāra*).
However, because there is no such passage in the *Pāḷi*, [the text continues]: "Those too... pe..."

"It is said that they are all included right here. All phenomena, including those originated by both [mind and body] and so forth, are described as "impermanent, alas, are conditioned things" (*aniccā vata saṅkhārā*).
It is called the "conditioning formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra-saṅkhāra*) because it conditions its own fruit.
Bodily energy that initiates bodily application is "bodily energy" (*kāyika-vīriya*). "Of the conditioning" (*abhisaṅkhārassa*) refers to the momentum of the application.
It conditions speech, thus it is the verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*). It is conditioned by the body, thus it is the bodily formation (*kāya-saṅkhāra*).
It is conditioned by the mind, or it conditions the mind, thus it is the mental formation (*citta-saṅkhāra*).

In brief, however, all these should be understood as "formations" (*saṅkhāra*) because they condition and are conditioned accordingly. By the word "said" (*vutta*), he refers to the meaning of "formation," the meaning of "condition," and so forth.
“Bows” (*namati*) means it inclines toward the object because of its exclusive focus upon that object. “Is agitated” (*paritassati*) means it thirsts; or, due to the torment of craving, it wavers.
“Grasps” (*upādiyatī*) means it takes hold firmly. “Exists” (*bhavati*) is said with reference to rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).

“Becomes” (*bhāvayati*) refers to kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*). “Death” (*cuti*) is the passing away of the aggregates; it is called this because “by means of this they die. Painful feeling is suffering by way of its arising.
Having established that "stability is suffering," it is said, "it digs in two ways. *Āyāsa* means exhaustion or dejection.
"Showing the method as it has been demonstrated" means the demonstration of the procedure exactly as it was set forth.
The word *kevala* is used to express "unmixed," as in "the *sālaya* plants are *kevala*," and it is also used to express "without remainder," as in "the whole of Aṅga and Magadha are *kevala*."
Therefore, it expresses the meaning in two ways. Therein, "of the unmixed" means of that which is devoid of pleasure; for there is nothing here that is free from arising and passing away.
"Of the whole" means of that which has gone to all states of existence and so forth, and of all times.
Regarding the phrase "from the singlefold characteristic and so forth," he shows that the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be applied separately to each term.
He said: "By way of its characteristic, etc. It has the function of deluding because it causes confusion regarding associated states or the person possessing them.
It has the manifestation of concealing because it is apprehended as the concealment of the true nature of the object.

It has the proximate cause of the taints (*āsava*) because of the statement: "With the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance. It exerts effort—that is, it performs an activity—for the purpose of producing rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

They "perform" [action], thus they have the function (*rasa*) of accumulating (*āyūhana*). Alternatively, accumulation is the act of forming a heap. Because its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is volition (*cetanā*), it is grasped as being volition itself;
thus, it has volition as its manifestation (*paccupaṭṭhāna*). It proceeds by way of being a precursor to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); thus, it has the function of being a forerunner (*pubbaṅgama*).
Since it is grasped as joining together with the previous existence, it has rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as its manifestation. Together with consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and mutually...

It has the function of association because it associates. Association (*sampayoga*) is a conjunction (*yoga*) that is equal (*sama*) in its modes. Non-separation (*avinibbhoga*) is the absence of being distinct.

It has the function of dispersing because matter disperses due to the absence of association; for it is precisely for this reason that rice and other grains, when being ground, disperse, become powder, and fall apart.
Since the mental state (*nāma*) may at times also exist as wholesome and so forth, [the term "matter"] is used for the purpose of distinguishing it from that.

It is stated as “having the manifestation of the indeterminate. Here, as in the phrase “insentient and indeterminate,” its indeterminate nature should be understood as being without an object (anārammaṇatā).
Its characteristic is that of striking (ghaṭṭana), or alternatively, its characteristic is the stretching (tanana) of the senses (āyāna).
It has the function of seeing because it performs the respective grasping of objects for vision. [It is said] “having the function of seeing and so forth.”
However, it is stated in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "The manifestation as basis and door belongs respectively to the consciousness element and the mind-consciousness element;
this is the intended meaning. Here, the mention of the "basis" refers to the pentad beginning with the eye.

Because unwholesome-resultant equanimity is undesirable, it is comprised by suffering, while the other is comprised by pleasure because it is desirable; thus they are said to have "pleasure and pain as their manifestation."
It has been said: Craving (taṇhā) has the characteristic of being a cause because it is the origin of suffering. From the statement, "It finds delight here and there," its function is delighting.
It is manifested as a state of dissatisfaction, for it is apprehended as the mind’s—or the person’s—state of not being satisfied with forms and so forth.
Its function is non-relinquishment, by way of the adherence to craving and views. Through its intensity, it becomes the clinging of sensual desire; the others [are likewise].

"Manifesting as view" means that craving has the manifestation of intensified view. The characteristics and other [aspects] of existence (*bhava*) should be applied according to the categories of kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*).

Regarding the phrase "by way of being delusion and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes lack of full comprehension (*ananubodha*) and the rest. It refers to the state of ignorance (*aññāṇa*) with respect to suffering and the other [truths].
"Wrong practice" (*appaṭipatti*) is wrong practice by way of the perversions (*vipallāsa*) such as perceiving the beautiful in the foul and so forth.
Alternatively, it is non-practice (*appaṭipatti*) by way of dissociation from views, and wrong practice (*micchāpaṭipatti*) by way of association with views.
"By way of door and object" means by way of the doors and by way of the objects, because [the mind] proceeds in the six doors and upon the six objects. However, this distinction is not...
Because it is found not only in ignorance, but also in other factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) among the immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), he says "in all [of them].

Regarding the phrase "by way of being a phenomenon subject to ripening (*vipākadhammadhamma*), etc.," the word "etc. includes such states as being neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee (*nevasekkhānāsekkha*) and being subject to fetters (*saṃyojaniya*). "By way of leading to the four modes of birth" means by way of producing an individual existence (*attabhāva*) included within the four modes of birth.

Regarding the phrase "as being the state of mundane classification and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) here includes such states as the indeterminate, the conditioned-with-cause, and the conditioned. Regarding the phrase "as being with-cause and without-cause and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the distinctions such as with-motivation and without-motivation.

Although name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is spoken of by way of the present time-period, nevertheless, since it must be understood by way of principle to include even that which belongs to the two other time-periods—just as the present is, so too are the past and future—it is said to be "threefold as past and so forth."
"From the place of meeting with those of similar birth" means because it is the location for the arising and occurrence of phenomena associated with consciousness.
The reading "from the primary elements, the sensitive organs, and consciousness" is appropriate; however, they read it as "from consciousness, etc.

Since the external sense bases are also included by way of the principle of "single remainder" (*ekasesanaya*), it should be understood that they are subsumed by the word "etc. "Neither of both spheres" means...
He speaks of the mind-base (*manāyatana*). For immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), there is no proximity or distance in terms of location, because they lack physical form (*aviggaha*);
therefore, it is not said that the object of the mind-base has either reached or not reached the mind-base. Regarding the phrase "of contact and so forth":

here, contact (*phassa*) is first of one kind by virtue of its essential nature of touching and its state of being worldly and subject to taints (*sāsava*). It is also divided into the categories of contact involving resistance (*paṭigha-samphassa*) and contact consisting of designation (*adhivacana-samphassa*).

It is twofold by way of being with cause and so forth. It is threefold by way of being included within the three realms of existence, by way of association with the three types of feeling, and by way of being without cause, with two causes, or with three causes.
It is fourfold and fivefold by way of the modes of birth and the destinations.

Feeling is singlefold by way of its characteristic of experiencing and by way of its state as mundane and subject to taints (*sāsava*). [It is also distinguished] by the division into the five-door and the mind-door.

It is twofold. It is threefold according to the distinction of pleasure and so forth. It is fourfold and fivefold by way of birth and destiny. It is sixfold according to the distinction of the six objects.
It is singlefold because craving is the origin of the world. It is twofold according to its association with or dissociation from views.

It is threefold according to the distinction between craving for sense-pleasures, for existence, and for non-existence. It is fourfold according to what is to be abandoned by the four paths. It is fivefold according to the state of delighting in form and so forth.
Craving is sixfold according to the division of the six groups of craving.

Clinging is singlefold because it is a state of firm grasping. It is twofold according to the division of craving and views. It is threefold because it serves as the decisive support for the three realms of existence (*bhava*). It is fourfold according to the division of clinging to sense pleasures and so forth. It is fivefold because it leads to rebirth in the five destinations.

Existence (*bhava*) is singlefold because it is mundane, subject to taints, and so on. It is twofold according to the division of karma-existence and rebirth-existence. It is threefold according to the division of sense-sphere existence and so forth.

It is fourfold by way of being conditioned by the four kinds of clinging. It is fivefold by way of leading to the five destinations. It is sixfold by way of the divisions of sense-sphere existence, kamma-existence, and so forth.

It is sevenfold by way of being comprised within the seven stations of consciousness. It is eightfold by way of the divisions of kamma-existence conditioned by the four kinds of clinging, and so forth.
It is ninefold by way of the divisions of sense-sphere existence and so forth.

Birth is of one kind there, by way of being the first manifestation in various states of existence. It is of two kinds, by way of being included within the aggregate of form and the aggregate of mental formations.
It is of three kinds, by way of being comprised within the three realms of existence. It is of four kinds and five kinds by way of birth and destiny.
In this same manner, the state of being of one kind and so forth should also be understood for aging, death, and the rest.

590. Since sorrow and the rest are also included, one should understand that the determination of the factors as "only twelve" is intended to prevent the contingency of an excessive number of factors.
For sorrow and the rest are not stated as being constituent factors themselves; rather, they are mentioned to show ignorance as the root factor by way of its result.
Indeed, these arise for the fool who is struck down by aging and death; thus, sorrow and the rest constitute the causes of aging and death.
It is stated [in the suttas], yet it is not said, "Touched by bodily painful feeling";
and in the sutta, suffering is included as the cause of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which is stated as a proof for its arising in one who is struck down by that cause, aging and death.
However, since the single summary of sorrow and the rest is made precisely by means of aging and death, their state of having birth as a condition is established.
This is appropriate. For if ignorance were the condition for aging-and-death alone, a single summary could have been made;
however, since aging-and-death as well as sorrow and the rest arise with birth as their condition, aging-and-death is taken there as the exclusive factor in the causal chain.
Sorrow and the rest, however, are non-exclusive because they are absent in the form-existence (*rūpa-bhava*) and so forth, and thus are mentioned only by way of their manifest result.

[Ignorance] is taken [as the first link] for the purpose of demonstrating ignorance. By this, since birth exists in the future, ignorance—which stands as the cause of the subsequent rebirth-linking—is demonstrated;
thus, the non-interruption of the wheel of existence (*bhavacakkā*) is shown.

Furthermore, the Sutta should be understood as proving precisely this point—that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and the rest—not merely that for a fool, sorrow and the rest have old age and death as their mere sign.
For by the expression “the uninstructed worldling,” it is shown that ignorance is the cause of sorrow and the rest; yet suffering is not suffering merely because it is the sign of aging and death.
Another method: aging and death are also a condition, otherwise the twelve links would not be complete.
Of what, then, are they the condition? They are the condition for sorrow and the rest. If this is so, why [does the Sutta] say, “With aging and death as condition, sorrow and the rest arise”?
Is it not stated that "with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, and so forth, come into being"?

Because those [sorrow and so forth] arise for one who is touched by other phenomena of suffering as well, therefore, even for one whose fetters are not abandoned, their status as having that [birth] as a condition is not certain;
thus, only the conditionality of birth is stated. Alternatively, by the mention of aging-and-death, the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is included.
For the ripening of the aggregates that have been grasped is the waning of the life-span; the ripening of the faculties is aging; and their dissolution is death.
And when there is an existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), the karma performed and accumulated therein—whether past or present—is the existence as karma (*kammabhava*);
since it produces rebirth-linking immediately after the moment of death through the presentation of that karma and so forth, the existence of rebirth is the condition for birth.
Therefore, aging-and-death is also dependent origination by virtue of its being a condition for birth.

However, because the fact that the rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is a condition for birth is already included in the statement "with existence as condition, birth [comes to be]," it was not stated as "with aging-and-death as condition, birth [comes to be]" due to the inclusion within the aforementioned method of exposition. Thus, the status of aging-and-death as a condition is established.
It should be understood that "the state of dependent origination" is established as consisting of twelve factors. Therefore he said, "only twelve," and so forth.
The phrase "this, first of all" is said with reference to the commentary on the meaning stated by the words "according to the different modes of teaching," and so on.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]."

591. "This, however" refers to what will now be explained. It is said "according to the method of the Suttantas" because in the Suttantas, ignorance is described as having four bases, beginning with: "And what, monks, is ignorance? It is lack of knowledge regarding suffering," and so forth.
However, in the *Nikkhepakaṇḍa*, based on the functions of that very same ignorance which was taught in the Suttantas in four places, it is further analyzed into eight bases.

Because it has already been stated, in order to provide an exposition by way of a commentary on that meaning, the passage beginning with “By way of the Abhidhamma method” was commenced, followed by “For this has been said,” and so forth.
[The teaching] should be analyzed without omission; for analysis is indeed the method of the Abhidhamma.
The phrase “ignorance regarding eight points” should be brought forward and connected [to the context]. “In the remaining points” refers to suffering and its origin.
And regarding the past and so forth. "By way of object" means also by way of making it an object. "Here" refers to this passage beginning with "ignorance regarding suffering.
"That" refers to ignorance (*avijjā*). "Arisen" means arisen without having been eradicated, let alone being present.
To show the mode of concealment mentioned here in the phrase "having concealed," [the text says]: "the characteristic of its own true nature..."
"...does not allow one to penetrate it," it is said. "Rasa" (taste) is the essential nature that is to be tasted and penetrated. "Sarasa" (own-taste) is its own taste.

"Yāthāvasarasa" (the essential nature as it truly is) is the taste existing exactly as it is; and that which is described by the phrase "the sense of oppression" and so forth, namely the divisions of the truth of suffering and the prior limit and so on—that very thing is the "characteristic of the essential nature as it truly is" (*yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇa*) because it is to be characterized. To penetrate that...
It does not allow one to know [them] through direct perception (*paccakkha*).

"Both" refers to the past and the future—the five aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*) of the past and the future. Alternatively, because it possesses the divisions of the past and the future, the present middle portion is itself the "past and future.
[This refers to] ignorance (*avijjā*) and these formations (*saṅkhārā*) among those phenomena that have arisen dependently according to specific conditions (*idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppanna*).
This is the demonstration of the mode of knowing through direct experience. "In this" means in these [truths] such as suffering and so forth.

Although ignorance also functions by taking suffering and the rest as its object, it nevertheless—just as it is unable to take cessation and the path as objects—functions for one who wishes to know them by way of concealing them, and with respect to what are not cessation or the path, by way of being the cause for grasping them as cessation and the path.
And it should be understood that this applies likewise to suffering and the other [truths], for they do not allow one to penetrate them as they truly are while they are occurring.
Thus it is said: "In this context, they are intended only in the sense of concealment.
Ignorance (*aññāṇa*) is the mode of non-seeing which has suffering and the rest as its object, and which serves as the condition for the blind crocodiles of greed and the other [defilements].

592. "Meritorious deeds, etc. refers to the formative volitions of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth. In this context, it is called "merit" (*puñña*) because it purifies one's own continuum by cleansing it of the fruits of demerit and of suffering and defilement. Alternatively, it is called "merit" because one performs meritorious deeds with the intention for welfare and happiness;

thus, by bringing that [intention] to fruition, it fulfills the aspiration of the agent, or it brings about a state worthy of honor (*pujja*). Thus, it is that which fulfills and that which produces what is worthy of honor.

And it should be understood as "merit" (*puñña*) according to the method of etymological derivation (*nirutti*). And because it conditions (*abhisaṅkharaṇa*) its own fruit, it is a "volitional formation" (*abhisankhāra*);

thus, it is a "meritorious volitional formation" (*puññābhisankhāra*). By the reverse of what was stated—that is, by contrast with merit—one should understand the "demeritorious volitional formation" (*apuññābhisankhāra*).
Because it is extremely remote from the opposites of concentration (*samādhi*), it does not waver; and being unwavering (*aniñja*), [it is called "the immovable"].

It conditions existence, thus it is the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*). That which proceeds by way of the body, or proceeds from the body, or is a formation of the body, is the bodily formation (*kāyasaṅkhāra*).

The same method applies to the verbal and mental formations as well. Therein, the first triad is taken according to such suttas as the *Parivīmaṃsanā-sutta*; for therein it says: "If one conditions a meritorious formation..."
It is stated [in the suttas] as: “Consciousness is directed toward merit,” and so forth. The second triad is according to the *Vibhaṅga-sutta*. For there it is said:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three formations. Which three? The bodily formation, the verbal formation, and the mental formation.

As for the passage beginning with “In detail, however,” etc., it is an exposition of the meritorious formations and the rest by way of their essential nature and their classification. It is precisely by way of cultivation (*bhāvanā*)...
"Arising by way of development, not by way of giving or virtue" indicates the basis for performing merit available therein.
And having established this, even immaterial-sphere volition is stated to "arise only by way of development.

As for those who say that the restrictive phrase "only by way of development" excludes the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), that is incorrect, because that too has ignorance as its condition.

This is because it is intended to be a state of meritorious volitional formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). Otherwise, the arising of a mind associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) would not be included among the bases for meritorious action (*puññakiriyavatthu*), and it is not logical to say that "it is wholesome but not a basis for meritorious action.

Regarding the phrase "killing living beings, etc.," the word "etc. should be understood as including not only the remaining unwholesome courses of action (*akusalakammapatha*), but indeed all unwholesome kamma without exception.
"But in the others," however, refers to the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) and so forth.

The statement "twenty volitions" is made for the purpose of showing the occurrence [of these formations] by way of the doors, since the wholesome and unwholesome volitions that give rise to bodily and verbal intimation (*viññatti*)—when they are occurring—are called "bodily formation" and "verbal formation" according to these doors. If this is so, why...

Addressing the objection that even wholesome volition pertaining to direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*), when occurring in such a manner, should be described as a verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*), he says, “direct knowledge volition,” and so forth.
“In this context” means in the inclusion of bodily and verbal formations, or in the inclusion of bodily and verbal volitions.
It is “not included” because it is not mentioned in the Commentary [with the statement]: “Direct knowledge volition is not a condition for consciousness.”
But why is it not so? Is it not the case that it too is wholesome (*kusala*) and of a nature to result in maturation (*vipākadhamma*)? True, this is so;

however, its wholesomeness and its nature to result in maturation are stated with respect to its occurrence as an active process within a continuum where craving has not been severed, not by way of actually producing maturation.
And were it to produce maturation, it would produce only that of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*). For karma belonging to one plane does not [produce maturation] on another plane.
"It produces a result" means that it would produce only an object similar to itself and one that is fixed (tiṭṭhānika).
This is because, in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*, it is stated that the fine-material-sphere resultant has an object similar to the kamma.

Furthermore, there is no fine-material-sphere resultant with a limited (paritta) or other such object, whereas the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) does indeed have limited objects and so forth. Therefore, it is understood that [the latter] does not produce a result.
Furthermore, the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are the benefits of the fourth jhāna concentration produced within the kasiṇas, as it is said:
"When his mind is thus concentrated," and so forth. Therefore, they are similar to the fruit of concentration, yet they do not themselves yield a fruit.
Just as the acquisition of requisites in that very existence is the benefit of generosity and virtue, these [higher knowledges] likewise do not produce a result of karmic ripening (*vipāka*).
The point that "just as there is no volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*), so too there is no volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*)" should be investigated;
for this was stated after extracting the factors associated with restlessness separately, saying: "Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*).

However, since that investigation has already been discussed below in the commentary on the Exposition of the Aggregates (*khandha-niddesa*) within the section on unwholesome states, it should be sought there.
They should be understood according to the method already investigated. Furthermore, regarding this point, some explain by way of analysis as follows:

even in the absence of [the specific] seeing and cultivation, for those worldlings and trainees who ought to possess seeing and cultivation through those [factors], at the time of their arising, those unwholesome states that can be abandoned by them are called "to be abandoned by seeing" and "to be abandoned by cultivation."
However, because ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) lack the practice of meditation (*bhāvanā*), there is no consideration regarding what is to be abandoned by meditation.
Therefore, even though their [defilements] are currently active and cannot be abandoned by seeing (*dassana*), they are not said to be "abandonable by meditation.

If they were so designated, then those abandonable by seeing would [in some cases] become objects, object-predominance conditions (*ārammaṇādhipati*), or decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for certain things abandonable by meditation at any time.
Could they be conditions? In the *Paṭṭhāna*, those states to be abandoned by seeing are not stated to be a condition for those to be abandoned by cultivation by way of any condition whatsoever.
However, because they can be abandoned by cultivation by those in training (*sekkha*) who possess them, they are "to be abandoned by cultivation.
For that very reason, they are "to be abandoned by seeing" for those in training, because they have been relinquished, cast off, and released.
Because they have been abandoned, relinquished, extracted, and thoroughly uprooted, they are not to be relished or rejoiced in.
Precisely because they have been abandoned, they do not produce joy—which is their cause—nor do they produce non-distraction; nor do they produce grief or restlessness.

Therefore, these [objects] do not possess for them the status of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) or a predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), nor the status of being a natural decisive-support-condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*).
They go away. For a noble one does not, by depending on what has been abandoned, give rise to defilements such as lust.
Indeed, this has been said: “Those defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry—those defilements he does not repeat, does not return to, does not go back to...
[and so on] ...by the path of arahantship... [and so on] ...he goes back to. And it is not by seeing ordinary worldlings that [the noble one returns].
It is possible to relinquish them; however, for the others, it cannot be said that they do not become conditions for one another by any means.
Thus: "One relishes and delights in views; taking those as an object, lust arises, and doubt, restlessness, and views arise.
Taking doubt as an object, doubt, views, and restlessness arise. This refers to views and doubt.
Because the state of being an object-condition for restlessness has been stated [in this context].

For here, "restlessness" is said with reference to a mental arising accompanied by restlessness. And having done so, in the exposition of the predominance condition, only this much is stated: "Having esteemed a view, one relishes it and delights in it; having esteemed it, lust arises, and a view arises."

It is not stated that "restlessness arises. Therefore, although those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation cannot be described as being past and so forth, among those ordinary persons (puthujjana) in whom such a state of being subject to non-arising has been induced by those two [paths], those that exist and can be abandoned by seeing—relative to that seeing—are "to be abandoned by seeing" (dassanena pahātabba). Those existing among trainees (sekkha)...
Those that can be abandoned by means of that cultivation, having regard for cultivation, are "to be abandoned by cultivation.

Among them, because those [states] to be abandoned by cultivation do not produce a result when deprived of their companions, the state of being a kamma-condition at a different time is not mentioned for volition to be abandoned by cultivation;
however, for those [states] devoid of the seeing and cultivation that ought to be relied upon...

Because the three fetters and the defilements associated with them have not been severed among worldlings (*puthujjana*), and because the desire, lust, and so forth toward their own possessions, as well as the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*), still have unexhausted companions, it is impossible to prevent the production of their resultants;
thus, the resultants of states accompanied by restlessness are mentioned in the *Vibhaṅga*. If this is so, [then...]

Does it not follow that unwholesome states—which lack the seeing and cultivation of what is to be looked upon—are "inexpressible" (navattabba) in terms of being abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation? It does not so follow;

for those things that are not to be abandoned are described as "to be abandoned neither by seeing nor by cultivation," and because unwholesome states possess a nature contrary to that which is not to be abandoned.
In this way, would it follow that those [states] in this triad should also be called "not to be designated"?
They do not so follow, because the twelve unwholesome consciousness-arising types shown in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa* are included under two terms.

For just as all conditioned phenomena are included by way of their nature (*dhamma-vasena*), so too, although past states are not included by way of time (*kāla-vasena*) in the "arisen triad," they are nevertheless called "not to be designated."
It was not stated [as a separate category] because there is no "inexpressible" (avattabba) among those things already included under the nature of mental states or matter;

likewise here, it should be understood that "inexpressibility" was not mentioned because there is no non-included "inexpressible" among those things already included under the nature of mental states.
For wherever there is some mental state that must necessarily be inexpressible, there exists for them a fourth category.

Just as in the previously mentioned passages, here too, regarding those mental states that must be analyzed and divided, he analyzes and divides them by saying, "They may be undeclared, or have a limited object," and so forth.
Because of their absence, they were not stated in the "arisen triad" (*uppannatika*), nor are they stated here in that way.

Alternatively, just as in the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) the three great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*) because they share the same nature as those things with resistance;
It has been stated thus: “For non-percipient beings, in dependence on one great primary element that is non-demonstrable and impinging, two great primary elements [arise];
in dependence on two great primary elements, one great primary element [arises].

In this way, could it not be said that the formations occurring in worldlings—which possess the same nature as those to be abandoned by cultivation—are themselves abandoned by cultivation? There is no possibility of such an objection being raised.

This being the case, it follows that even for worldlings, the desire and lust for one's own belongings—which are to be abandoned by cultivation—even while they are present, serve as a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) for desire and lust toward the belongings of others; and lust serves as a predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) for lustful views.
However, just as the three great primary elements do not exist in an ultimate sense within the sphere of visible form (*rūpa-dhātu*) because it is not a tangible object, [so too...]

Thus, for ordinary persons who lack the cultivation of such things worthy of regard, the desire-and-lust (*chanda-rāga*) and so forth toward their own belongings—which are with resistance (*sappaṭigha*)—are not, in the ultimate sense, to be abandoned by cultivation.

Therefore, it is not stated that those [states] to be abandoned by cultivation have the condition of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*). Nor is that which is to be abandoned by vision a condition, by any kind of conditionality, for that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
It has been said: "Those defilements which have conditions to be abandoned by seeing do not continue to occur after seeing has taken place.
However, in the case of restlessness-accompanied [defilement] even though it has conditions to be abandoned by seeing, seeing has merely rendered it deficient in its companions;
no aspect of it has been brought to a state of non-arising by seeing. Therefore, it is to be abandoned exclusively by cultivation."

Thus it has been stated. Therefore, for such a [state of mind], the statement that it produces a result when a companion is present, and the statement that it does not produce a result when one is absent, are not contradictory. Others, however, say:
"All this is merely the 'I-am-a-great-man' (ahopurisa) conceit of those teachers. Why? Because restlessness-accompanied [consciousness] is to be abandoned exclusively by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
For it was said by the Blessed One: "Which phenomena are to be abandoned by cultivation..."
“Is it to be abandoned by cultivation? “A state of consciousness accompanied by restlessness.

For if that were intended, then just as in the triad on past objects it was stated categorically that “there are none with future objects” and then explained analytically, so too here it would have been stated categorically that “there are none to be abandoned by cultivation,” and then explained analytically:
“That which is accompanied by restlessness may be abandoned by cultivation, or it may be so described.”
One might say this. Furthermore, the logical justification stated by the one who maintains that position—beginning with "if it were said," and so forth—is also illogical.
Why? Because it is precisely the state of being abandoned by vision that is intended for lust, views, doubt, and restlessness, which have objects to be abandoned by vision.
As for the inclusion of restlessness (*uddhacca*) in the Pāḷi [text], by means of that term...

Having stated that "the arising of consciousness has been explained," the reason for not including restlessness (*uddhacca*) in the exposition of the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) was given in order to establish that point;
yet even that is not a valid reason, because the *Paṭṭhāna* shows a text that is incomplete. For it is said:
"A past state [is a condition] for a present state; a future state [is a condition] for a present state by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*)."

In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of these [terms], having included the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariyañāṇa*), that which is obtainable in the analysis of "a present state is a condition for a present state" has not been mentioned.

This is because it is seen as the giving of a result (*vipāka*) by that which is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), while the presentment of assistance to that which is to be abandoned through vision (*dassana*) is what is intended here.

This must be investigated: Does ignorance and so forth, like the giving of gifts and the practice of virtue, become an auxiliary to that which is to be abandoned by cultivation by way of being a basis for the capacity to yield fruition at the very moment of their own arising;
or rather, do they act as an obstruction to the giving of rebirth-linking by karma, similar to the defilements? And in this regard, if it is the first alternative...

Because it is to be abandoned by vision once it has been abandoned, the state of being a functional (kiriyā) phenomenon belonging to what is to be abandoned by cultivation would follow for that which occurs in the continuum of a trainee (sekkha), just like giving and so forth occurring in a continuum where ignorance, craving, and conceit have been abandoned.

Alternatively, if the second [alternative] were accepted, it too would follow that it is to be abandoned by vision, because it does not transcend its own nature of leading to the states of deprivation (apāya);
therefore, according to the method investigated above, [this applies] to that which is accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca).
The determination of the meaning here should be understood by way of its non-contradiction with both the canonical text (pāḷi) and the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) regarding the giving of kamma-result.

"That too" refers to the volition of restlessness (uddhacca-cetanā). Regarding "in the state of being a condition for consciousness": it means in the state of being a condition for the complete resultant consciousness.
To show the reason why it was stated that there are "twenty-one types of volition" even if [restlessness] is to be excluded, he says:
"But all these [mental states] arise with ignorance as their condition. This shows that even volition associated with direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) functions as a condition.

If this were so, one might ask why it should not be stated that there are twenty-one [types of consciousness] together with the volition of direct knowledge; the answer is no, because the reason for not stating it in that way has already been given.

Furthermore, that same reason applies to the non-inclusion of the others as well. Thus, regarding the non-inclusion of a single type that is of the same nature [as the rest], it is in consideration of that specific reason [that they are excluded].

One [term] was not mentioned; by that reason, he shows that even what was mentioned should not be stated [in this context]. "This triad" refers to the triad of bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhārattika*).
"The former triad" refers to the triad of meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhārattika*). "Enters"—how does it enter?

For the meritorious volitional formation, which consists of the eight types of sense-sphere volition, may become a bodily formation for one who refrains from bodily misconduct, and [likewise] from verbal misconduct...

For one who is abstaining, there may be verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*); however, the thirteen types of volition (*cetanā*) that arise at the mind-door are both meritorious formations (*puññābhisankhāra*) and mental formations (*citta-saṅkhāra*).
Furthermore, non-meritorious formation (*apuññābhisankhāra*), by way of bodily misconduct, may be bodily formation during its occurrence;
by way of verbal misconduct, it may be verbal formation during its occurrence; and setting aside the two doors [of body and speech], it occurs as mental formation.
In the process occurring at the mind-door, there may be both the mental formation (*cittasaṅkhāra*) and the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*);

thus, the second triad is included within the first triad itself. Therefore it was said: "The conditionality of ignorance should be understood by way of the meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth alone in terms of their actual meaning."
593. "Because of the existence [of formations] when ignorance is present" means that because of the presence (*atthibhāva*) of ignorance, formations exist.
For indeed, when ignorance is absent, formations never come to be. Now, showing that presence of ignorance, he says: "Ignorance is unabandoned.
By this, the non-cessation through that path is here the presence of ignorance, not merely its current occurrence.

[The text] demonstrates this. This very meaning has already been clarified above. Furthermore, by the phrase “consisting of ignorance” (*avijjāsaṅkhāta*), it excludes the absence of knowledge and so forth.

For this negative particle *a-* is seen in such instances as “rootless phenomena” (*ahetukā dhammā*) and “a residence without a resident monk” (*abhikkhuko āvāso*) to indicate the exclusion of that connection.

Here, non-existence is indicated. In the case of “phenomena without conditions” (*appaccayā dhammā*), it indicates the exclusion of being related to those [conditions]. For that which is produced by conditions...
"Connected with conditions" means that here its state of being connected is illuminated by the fact of its arising without a suffix (*appaccaya*).

"Invisible phenomena" (*anidassanā dhammā*): this refers to the exclusion of their own specific nature. For "visibility" (*nidassana*) is the state of being visible. Furthermore, "eye-consciousness is invisible because it does not see":
this refers to the exclusion of its being an object of apprehension. Likewise for "outflow-free phenomena" (*anāsavā dhammā*). "Non-reactive phenomena" (*appaṭighā dhammā*),...
“Dhammas without an object” is used for the exclusion of that function. “Formless dhammas,” “non-mental factors” are used for the exclusion of that state.
For otherwise, it is explained here [in those cases] as something other than that. “A non-human being” is used for the exclusion of that mere state;
there is no mere humanity, but another similar [state] is indicated here by way of similarity. “One who is not an ascetic, though claiming to be an ascetic; one who has no son.”
Likewise, in the phrase "the non-arising of qualities expected to arise," it is censure that is understood here. In the phrase "Is your honor free from illness?
Is the maiden slender-waisted?", there is the non-arising of what was not previously produced. In the phrase "unarisen states" (*anuppannā dhammā*), there is the exclusion of things similar to them;
for past things have already arisen, and those things whose nature is to arise possess the state of having begun to arise through the production of a portion of their conditions.

Because that which is free from time exists, there is conformity with what has arisen; how much more so for those that are presently arisen? Thus, their dissimilarity [to the unwholesome] is understood here.
The phrase "states of one beyond training" (asekkhā dhammā) serves to exclude anything other than that finality. For it is this finality that is being elucidated here.
Since these meanings are impossible [in the case of the unwholesome], by way of elimination (pārisesa), they are understood as states that are the opposites of the wholesome.
Since ignorance (*avijjā*) is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*), it should be understood that the state which is the opposite of wisdom (*ñāṇa*) is non-knowledge (*aññāṇa*).

Having grasped [the world] through the perception of pleasure, the wise should perceive the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāradukkha*)—which consists of the suffering of pain, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations—as nothing but suffering; for by adhering to the perception of it as pleasure, craving proceeds therein.
[The text] shows this. "He undertakes" means he produces it. "Adorned by craving" means it is surrounded, encircled, or decorated by craving through such notions as "pleasure" or "beauty";
this is the meaning. For the fool, not knowing that craving is the origin of suffering, thinks:
"O, may I, after the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of wealthy kshatriyas," and so forth.
Being agitated, one conditions the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*). Or, "conditioned by craving" (*taṇhāparikkhāra*) means being an attendant (*parivāra*) to craving.

For the formations, having conditioned the eye and so forth, as well as visible forms and so forth—which are the bases for craving—and bestowing them upon those possessed of craving, act as attendants to that craving by bringing it near.
[This occurs] in specific destinies such as the Brahma-world and others. Terrifying to hundreds of bound animals...
The sacrifice such as the Vājapeyya and others. "Amaratapa" (the austerity of immortality) refers to the practice of difficult penances undertaken for the sake of not dying;

or, it refers to the observance of vows performed with the thought, "May I become immortal or a god, or some particular deity. Alternatively, because of its difficulty, it is "mara-tapo" (the torment that kills), and thus "amara-tapo" (the austerity that [leads to] non-death).
Just as the word "adiṭṭha" (unseen) is used for what is seen, the word "amara" should be understood here in the sense of "mara" (death).
The formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) is said to be like a precipice because it produces the suffering of falling into birth and so forth.
By the phrase "producing great fever," he shows that the fruit of merit is like a grass torch in the sense of its burning nature.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the expression "and its lack of satisfaction," he includes such things as being struck down, pierced through, and the crushing of limbs and members. "Having that as its condition" (*tappaccayaṃ*)—that...
The fruit of a happy destination, which is of the nature of suffering due to its liability to change, has as its condition the fruit of merit.
When this fruit of merit is grasped through its quality of being delightful and its quality of being pleasurable, it is like the edge of a sword smeared with honey or the flame of a lamp.
And the volitional formation of merit that aims at that [fruit] is said to be like licking the [honey] adhering to that [sword-edge]. "Happy is this young woman, soft and hairy... [and so forth].

Through such passages as "contact with the arm," it is shown that the enjoyment of certain sensual pleasures—by way of failing to perceive the foul nature of what is actually pleasant—is like a fool playing with excrement;
and because one is overwhelmed by defilements, being overcome by anger and lust, it is like eating poison when one wishes to die and lacks self-control.
This is loathsome and painful both at the moment of present action and at the moment of future fruition.

One undertakes an unwholesome volitional formation (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*). One should apply the analogy of playing with excrement for that which is accompanied by greed (*lobha*), and the analogy of eating poison for that which is accompanied by hatred (*dosa*).

Just as even a city of demons (*pisācanagara*), though full of danger, becomes a cause for the delusion of happiness due to the abundance of sensual qualities (*kāmaguṇa*), so too it is with the results of the formless realm (*ārūppavipāka*):
because they are continuous and their arising and passing away are not clearly perceived, their existence appears as a long-lasting continuum.

The fact that even those formations which undergo change and are of the nature of the suffering of change—though they cannot be grasped—are the cause for the perversions such as the notion of permanence, should be applied to the immovable formation (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*) in its similarity to a city of demons and in its similarity to proceeding toward it.
Furthermore, formations exist precisely because of the presence of ignorance, not because of its absence; thus, this is a brief summary regarding the conditionality of formations upon ignorance.
In order to support the point already stated through both positive (anvaya) and negative (vyatireka) reasoning, the scriptural passage beginning with "And this has also been said" is cited.
Therein, "the ignorant" (avidva) means those who lack knowledge. "Enveloped in ignorance" (avijjāgata) means possessed of ignorance;
the intended meaning is that their ignorance has not been abandoned.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Conditions in the *Paṭṭhāna* (594). *Tāva* is a particle that expects something further to be said; by it, he shows: "First, this is established—that ignorance is a condition for volitional formations—but this other thing must also be stated.
As for the phrase "this, however, must be stated," it refers to the following point:

This was said with a specific intention; to show that, [the author] asked, "Of which volitional formations (saṅkhārā) is ignorance a condition, and in what way?"—anticipating the doubt that it might apply to ignorance as well, given the multiplicity of both those things for which conditions exist and the ways in which they exist as conditions.
There are many volitional formations, such as meritorious volitional formations and so forth.
[Ignorance] has been stated. Ignorance is a condition for some [formations], but it does not function as a condition for all in the same way;
therefore, the meaning is that it must be explained how it serves as a condition for these formations. "Therein" means in that state of being a condition.

Although the question was initiated specifically regarding certain formations by the words "For which formations," etc., this [answer] is nevertheless a characterization of the whole by means of a part.
It must be stated that each of the twelve factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) functions as a condition for that which has arisen in dependence upon it;

in order to demonstrate this, or because ignorance was asked about as a condition, and wishing to answer by way of that context regarding the conditional nature of all conditioning phenomena (paccayadhamma),
he first shows the conditions according to the method of the Canon (pāḷinaya) with the words, "For by the Blessed One," and so forth.
"Initiated. The connection here is that twenty-four conditions were stated by the Blessed One therein.
The intention is that the status of ignorance and the other factors as conditions should be understood by way of those [twenty-four].
By the expression "it is both a cause and a condition," there is the inclusion of both a cause (*hetu*) and that which serves as a predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*) and so forth.
To prevent that [objection], he said, "Being the cause, it is the condition. Even so, the same fault would still follow;

therefore, he said again, "It is stated that it is a condition by way of being the cause. By this, he shows that here the word "cause" (hetu) does not denote the phenomenon itself, but rather the specific capacity of the phenomenon is what is grasped. For that word "condition" (paccaya)...
And with reference to their being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), it is stated: "It is both a cause and a condition; having been a cause, it is a condition.

Having done so, the text further on states, by way of various modes of assistance such as the state of being a cause, that each respective phenomenon is an assisting factor for the other, beginning with: "Roots are roots... [and so on] ...they are a condition by way of root-condition," and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Abhidhammaṭṭhakathā*.
However, by means of the exposition of the establishment of phenomena (*dhammapaṭṭhāna*)— such as "Whatever phenomenon stands or arises without excluding another phenomenon,

that is its condition," and "A phenomenon that is helpful in the sense of being a root is a root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*)— it is shown that there is no power of phenomena other than the phenomena themselves;
thus, the manifestation of the power of phenomena is accomplished by means of the phenomena alone.
It should be understood thus. Or, here too, by the phrase "it is both a cause and a condition," he demonstrates the functional capacity of a phenomenon (dhamma) by means of the phenomenon itself.

For the enumeration beginning with "cause-condition" (hetupaccaya) and so forth is not primarily concerned with the phenomenon itself—unlike the enumeration of the wholesome (kusala) and so on—but rather it is primarily concerned with the state of being a supporting factor for phenomena.
“‘The same method applies’—by this, he extends [the analysis] to the object and other conditions by way of their being that [very thing], as follows:

‘It is both the object and a condition, thus it is an object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya); it is a condition by having become an object; the meaning is: a condition by way of the state of being an object.
It is not merely a *kammadhāraya* compound.”
595. "A member of speech" (vacanāvayava) is said with reference to a member of proof (sādhanāvayava).
For proof, which has the nature of speech, is well-known and recognized in the world as "proof" because it makes known a meaning unknown to others.

Thus, those who speak according to the system (ñāyavādino) state that the definition of a member is proof having the nature of speech, and that words such as the thesis (pakkha) and so forth are members of proof.

"In such cases as ‘affirmation’ (paṭiññā) and ‘reason’ (hetu), etc. means: affirmation, reason, example (udāharaṇa), application (upanaya), and conclusion (nigamana). A reason is that which establishes the probandum through its similarity to the example.
And in such expressions as “the reason is dissimilar” and so forth, it refers to any cause characterized as a cause, or even characterized as that which brings about [an effect].
By the word “etc.,” there is the inclusion of that [type of reason] as well; however, the characteristic of an indicator (ñāpaka-lakkhaṇa) is—
It is included by the mention of the "members of speech" (*vacanāvayava*). Granted, the root (*mūla*) also has the characteristic of being a cause and is indeed a cause;

however, in this context, "cause" (*kāraṇa*) refers to the condition-cause (*paccayahetu*). The root is mentioned separately because it is the object of a specific type of cause, namely the root-cause (*hetuhetu*).
The word "goes" (*eti*) is a synonym for "proceeds" (*vattati*); and that is a term common to both arising and persistence.
For this very reason it is said: "It either persists or arises. For one kind of condition is contributory only to persistence, such as the post-nascence condition;
another is contributory only to arising, such as the proximity condition and so forth; and another is contributory to both, such as the root-cause and others.
And by the phrase "characterized by being contributory," it should be understood that a phenomenon demonstrates its capacity for contributing to another phenomenon. It impels (hinoti).

It is called a *hetu* (cause) because "it is established therein" (*patiṭṭhāti ettha*). For, due to the multivalence of verbal roots, the word *hi* should be understood as having the sense of "establishing," just like the word *mūla* (root).
Alternatively, it is a *hetu* because by means of this—acting as the basis for the kamma and carrying nourishment upward like a root—a tree reaches its fruit dependent on that condition;
it proceeds, comes into being, and attains growth and development. [It is] of itself...
It is called a *kāraṇa* (cause) because it produces a fruit (*phalaṃ karoti*). It is called a *nidāna* (source) because it lays down [the fruit], as if presenting it.
It is called a *sambhava* (origin) because the fruit arises from it (*etasmā*). It is called a *pabhava* (source) because the fruit originates from it (*etasmā*).

Through these terms—*paccaya*, *hetu*, and so on—it should be understood that they share the same meaning with the others. Nevertheless, while the word *hetu* refers to a specific kind of cause, the word *paccaya* refers to the general category of causes.

He says "in the sense of being the root," and so forth, in order to show this. Since the meaning of cause (*hetu*) and the meaning of condition (*paccaya*) have already been explained at length below, he says "In brief... the cause-condition" in order to present them concisely.
Just as seeds such as rice and paddy are the actualizers of the state of rice and paddy for their respective plants, [so too are] the bases for the radiance of gems and the like.

And just as blue and other colors establish the appearance of blue and so forth, so too the root-cause (hetupaccaya) establishes the state of being wholesome and so on for the associated states (sampayuttadhamma) as appropriate;
this meaning is shown by the passage beginning with "so sāliādīnaṃ. And the phrase "of the teachers" refers to the teacher Revata.
"This being so" means: if the root-cause is the establisher of the state of being wholesome and so on.
This being the case, it does not succeed, it is not accomplished.

Just as a wholesome or unwholesome cause is not sufficient for the state of wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of the matter originated by it, so too an indeterminate cause is [not sufficient] for the indeterminate state of the matter originated by it.

For that [matter] is indeterminate by its very intrinsic nature; thus he said: "For it does not establish their state as wholesome and so forth. This refers to the root-cause condition (*hetupaccaya*).
And since they indeed possess it, he said, "the condition is not absent. Now, in order to support that point with the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he said, "For this has been stated," and so forth.
"Without this" means: without this reason which establishes the state of being indeterminate (*abyākata*);
the intention is that the state of being indeterminate is established by its very own nature (*sabhāva*) because of its lack of a [separate] cause.
“Monks, for one who attends appropriately (*yoniso*), unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states increase.
Through such statements, it is established that the state of wholesomeness is dependent upon appropriate attention; thus he said, “The state of wholesomeness is dependent upon appropriate attention.
By this very same principle, the states of unwholesomeness and the indeterminate are also [established as being dependent].
It is thus shown that [wholesomeness] is not dependent on a cause, unlike the state of being unwholesome. However, some might think:

"Just as the state of being unwholesome belongs to the causeless cause by its very nature, so too the states of wholesomeness and so forth belong to the causes with causes by their very nature, while for other associated factors they are dependent on a cause.
To state the rebuttal to this, he said: "And if... and so forth. Wholesomeness may be non-greed...
Regarding the phrase "or it is indeterminate": if non-greed (*alobha*) were wholesome by its very nature, then because of that wholesome nature, it would not be indeterminate.
Conversely, if it were indeterminate, then because of that nature, it would not be wholesome—just as there is an absence of non-hatred (*adosa*) in that which has the nature of non-greed.

However, since it exists in both ways, therefore, just as in the case of associated factors such as faith (*saddhā*) and the rest, which exist in both ways, [the result] is dependent upon the cause (*hetu*).
One should seek the state of being wholesome and so forth, not by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*);

likewise, among the causes, the wholesomeness and so forth must be sought as dependent on something else, not as intrinsic nature. Thus, what was stated—that "among the associated causes, the state of being wholesome and so forth exists by way of intrinsic nature"—is untenable.
Furthermore, when that [wholesomeness] is sought, it is found to be dependent on such factors as wise attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*). Therefore, regarding the causes...

The intention is that it is established that even in the case of associated states, their status as wholesome and so forth is dependent upon wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and the like, rather than being dependent upon [karmic] roots.

By the phrase "like those with well-developed roots," he shows that they are called "roots" because they are like [the roots of a tree]. For this very reason, he says: "by means of establishing the state of being well-established."

This is explained in the section on the analysis of questions (*pañhāvāra*) in seven ways as follows: "A wholesome state [is related] to a wholesome state; a wholesome state to an indeterminate state; a wholesome state to both wholesome and indeterminate states;
an unwholesome state to an unwholesome state; an unwholesome state to an indeterminate state; an unwholesome state to both unwholesome and indeterminate states;
and an indeterminate state to an indeterminate state. Furthermore, that which was stated:
In demonstrating the function of a cause, it is said: "Roots are a condition, by way of root-condition, for states associated with roots and for the material phenomena produced by them.
In this context, the first word "root" (hetu) indicates the specific nature [of the cause] and is a designation for the conditioning state itself;

thus, it shows that its status as a root-condition consists in its being an assistance by way of its causal nature. The second [word "root"] is a qualification of that which has arisen through the condition.
This shows that the roots are not a condition by way of root-condition for any associated states whatsoever; rather, they are [a condition] only for those states associated with the roots themselves.

Now, since the word "associated" (*sampayutta*) is dependent, even though a second word "root" (*hetu*) is absent, because no other thing to be depended upon has been specified, the roots [are conditions] for those very things associated with themselves.
Is this meaning understood as "conditioned by way of root-condition" (*hetupaccaya*)? This is not necessarily so.
For when the word *hetu* (root) is used as a specific designation—as in the phrase "conditioned by way of root-condition"—it is restricted to that very context;

it does not then function as a qualifier for associated states. Thus, anything whatsoever, whether associated or unassociated, might be included. Is it not the case that, just as in the expression "the immaterial foods" (*arūpino āhārā*)...?

When it is said, “of associated states,” and “of immaterial faculties, of associated states,” even without the mention of nutriment by the second [term] and without the mention of faculty, only those associated with nutriment and faculty are included; might it be the same here as well?
No, because there is no state to be excluded that is not associated with nutriment or faculty. Because there is nothing to be excluded.
For in that [previous] case, although there was no mention of the second "nutriment" or "faculty," those associated with them were nevertheless included;
thus, it was not stated. Here, however, since there is something to be excluded, the second mention of "cause" must be made.

Even so, in the phrase "causes [are related] to those associated with causes," because no qualification is made—that "those associated with causes" refers specifically to those associated with a cause—the word could refer to anything whatsoever.
Does it follow that for any cause associated with a cause, that cause becomes a condition by way of the "cause-condition" (hetupaccaya)?
It does not follow, because the word "cause" is stated again as a specific qualification of the associated state for that very cause already indicated in its own right.
Indeed, it is for this very purpose that the term "cause" is included, even though the state of being associated with a cause is already established without a second word "cause."

Alternatively, since there is no second term "root" (hetu), it might be understood that [the root] is a condition by way of the root-condition (hetupaccaya) for those factors associated with the root, but not for the roots themselves;
therefore, that [term] was stated in order to preclude such an interpretation.
By this, it is shown that for all those factors which possess the state of being associated with the root, as well as for other roots, the root is a condition by way of the root-condition.

However, because the roots, jhāna-factors, and path-factors are independent of other phenomena by virtue of their being mere bases and so forth—and are not dependent in the same way as the nutriments and faculties are—therefore, the second mention of "root" and so on was made specifically for these.
The nutriments and faculties, however, are indeed dependent upon what is to be nourished and what is to be mastered;
therefore, even without a second mention of "nutriment" and "faculty," they [establish themselves] by themselves.
Since those [factors] which are to be brought forth and which are to be sought after have already become the nutriment-faculties,

and since other associated factors are also delimited therein, that [function] was not assigned there. And here, because the conditions arising from causes and the causes themselves— which serve as conditions— are delimited by the second mention of "cause" (hetu), there is no further specific function to be performed.

In the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), it should be understood that the second mention of "cause" (*hetu*)—in such passages as "wholesome causes [are conditions] for the associated aggregates"—has not been made.

596. "By way of being an object" (*ārammaṇabhāvena*) means by way of being a domain (*visayabhāvena*), that is to say, by way of being something to be taken as an objective support (*ālambitabbabhāvena*).

By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even having begun" (*ārabhitvāpi*), he shows this meaning: that one does not remain fixed upon any single thing whatsoever, such as the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) alone, but rather [takes whatever it may be].
Regarding the statement, “having taken the Dhamma as object” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.2), because it is stated without restriction that all bases of form (*rūpāyatana*)...

[and so on] ...and all bases of phenomena (*dhammāyatana*) function as object-conditions (*ārammaṇapaccaya*), there is no phenomenon whatsoever among the sixfold classified phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned, and whether manifest or designated—that does not serve as an object-condition. This nature of being an object-condition has been explained below.
Thus. "Having taken hold" means having grasped. Since there is no occurrence that does not have an object as its exclusive support, he said, "or having undertaken.
This [refers to the following]: a wholesome state [is the condition] for a wholesome [state]; a wholesome state for an unwholesome [state]; a wholesome state for an indeterminate [state];
an unwholesome state for an unwholesome [state], for a wholesome [state], and for an indeterminate [state]; an indeterminate state...
It should be understood as being of nine kinds in this way: indeterminate, wholesome, and unwholesome.
(597) "In the sense of being pre-eminent" means by way of being the foremost. For a state that serves as the counterpart to those [mental factors] dependent on itself is the *adhipati* (predominant).

It functions as the foremost among them. [The phrase] beginning with "What indeed is not accomplished for one who has zeal? refers to the decisive support (*upanissaya*) consisting of prior volitional formations.

When a thought-moment arises having been obtained, desire and the other [mental factors] proceed as the leaders and the foremost, accomplishing the associated states and bringing them under their control;
and the associated states proceed according to them, following after them by way of being inferior or superior.
