Therefore, they are the predominance conditions (*adhipatipaccaya*). An object that is to be highly esteemed [is also a predominance condition].
It acts as a condition for those states that are inclined, bent, and leaning toward it—namely, relishing, reviewing, the path, and the fruit—as if bringing them under its own control.
Therefore, this should be understood as the *adhipati-paccaya* (dominant condition) because it assists by way of being the master over those things dependent on itself.
*Chandādhipati* means a dominant factor consisting of desire; it is desire that is the primary force, desire that is the foremost.
This is the name for the desire for action (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) that arises at the moment of the arising of consciousness. The same method applies to the others as well.

But why is it that, whereas in the exposition of the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) it is stated, "roots [are conditions] for those associated with roots," it is not stated here, "dominants (*adhipati*) [are conditions] for those associated with dominants," but rather, "the dominant of desire (*chanda-adhipati*) [is a condition] for those associated with desire," and so forth?

Is it stated according to this principle? Because they do not exist simultaneously. For two or even three roots can function as root-conditions (*hetu-paccaya*) at one and the same moment, since they do not abandon their state of being supportive in the sense of being a "root.

However, the dominant condition (*adhipati*) is supportive in the sense of being "foremost," and many things cannot be foremost at one and the same moment. Therefore, even for those [roots] that arise together, there is no status as a dominant condition at one and the same moment.

Regarding the phrase "there is none," it was not stated as "the predominance [factor] for those associated with predominance," but rather in the manner beginning with "the predominance of desire for those associated with desire. "Whatever phenomenon" means whatever object-phenomenon.
"Making it venerable" means making it something to be honored, respected, relished, not forsaken, and not disregarded, by way of reverence, esteem, or appreciation. Those...

“Dhammas” refers to those various states that are to be respected. “Of those respective [states]” means of those various states which perform the function of respect. “By way of the predominance condition” means by way of the object-predominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipatipaccaya*).

This [predominance] is as follows: a wholesome state [is related] to a wholesome [state] by way of co-nascent and objective [predominance]; to an unwholesome [state] by way of the objective [predominance] alone; to an indeterminate [state] by way of co-nascent and objective [predominance];
and to both wholesome and indeterminate [states] by way of co-nascent [predominance] alone. Thus, from the wholesome roots...
“Fourfold: unwholesome states [condition] the unwholesome by way of co-nascence and object; the indeterminate by way of co-nascence alone;
likewise for the unwholesome-indeterminate—thus there are three rooted in the unwholesome. Indeterminate states [condition] the indeterminate by way of co-nascence and object;
the wholesome by way of object alone; likewise for the unwholesome—thus there are three rooted in the indeterminate. In brief, there are ten types.

The predominance condition (*adhipatipaccaya*). Herein, it should be understood that there are sevenfold co-nascent predominance (*sahajātādhipati*) and sevenfold object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*).
598. It obstructs, thus it is "intervening" (*antara*); the meaning is "that which separates. There is no intervening space for this, thus it is "immediate" (*anantara*);

and being both immediate and a condition, it is the "immediate condition" (*anantarapaccaya*). "The state of having no interval in respect to the object is the immediate condition; the state of having no interval in respect to time..."
They elaborate extensively with such terms as "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-paccaya*) and so forth, producing a fruitless proliferation of texts.

Whereas the "absence" (*natthi*) and "disappearance" (*vigata*) conditions are stated by way of their specific nature of providing space for the occurrence [of other states], the "proximity" (*anantara*) and "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) conditions are not so;
rather, these are stated by way of being causes for the determination of consciousness. To demonstrate that nature of being causes for the determination of consciousness, it says: "For whoever..."
The passage beginning with “This is... has been commenced. Therein, regarding the phrase “the mind-consciousness element,” etc., which refers to the determination of consciousness:

here, by the word “etc.,” one includes the determining consciousness immediately following the investigating consciousness, and the rebirth-linking consciousness immediately following the death consciousness.

This refers to the rule of immediate succession for whichever consciousness arises immediately after whichever [preceding] consciousness; that is, the specific condition of each respective cooperating cause for that particular consciousness.
This shows that it succeeds by the power of each preceding consciousness itself.

"By way of immediate succession in meaning" means by way of being immediately followed by some state or phenomenon (*dhamma*). "By way of immediate succession in time" means by way of being immediately followed by a temporal distinction.
"Of the teachers" (*ācariyānaṃ*): here too, this is said with reference specifically to the teacher Revata. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in that [context].
Regarding the state of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) due to temporal contiguity, or regarding that aforementioned contradiction:

as for the phrase "because it has been warded off by the power of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-bala*), here it is just as when a tree has been pruned, it does not flower even though it is capable of flowering;
yet, once the pruning is removed, it flowers precisely because of that same capacity. So too, in this case, by the power of cultivation...

The intention is this: it is the non-arousing by one who is indeed capable of arousing [the offense] due to having been restrained; and when that restraint has passed away, there is an arousing by virtue of that very same capability.
Furthermore, that statement does not mean there is no interval of time, because there is an intervening period of seven days and so forth.
It is precisely for this reason that we say, "there is an interval of time. But is there not some such thing as "time"?
Fearing that [the opponent] might say, "It does not exist in the ultimate sense (paramatthato)," he said:

"The difference... [is only] in the time-interval... such is the position. One should understand that the distinction here is to be recognized merely in the phrasing (byañjana), and not in the meaning (attha).

The intention is that there is a distinction merely in the verbal meaning, as in the case of terms such as *upacaya* (accumulation) and *santati* (continuity), but not in the thing to be expressed (*vacanīyattha*). For this very reason, the specific verbal meaning—

In order to demonstrate this, he said, "How," and so forth. Therein, the state of being an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) consists in the capacity for uninterrupted production due to the absence of any interval between the cessation of the preceding [moment] and the arising of the succeeding one.

Because there is no shape—as there is in the case of material clusters—and because there is no simultaneous existence of the condition and the conditioned, there is no distinction such as "this is below, above, or across" from that; rather, it is as if they were identical with itself.
The state of being a "contiguous condition" (*samanantara-paccayatā*) is the capacity to produce [a subsequent state] immediately after having brought it close.

Regarding this "capacity to produce," since phenomena (*dhammā*) are devoid of agency (*abyāpārattā*), one should understand that when a particular mode has ceased, or while it is present, those phenomena come to possess their respective specific qualities;
it is that very mode which is called [the contiguous condition]. And it is merely the occurrence of phenomena...
"Expression in terms of time based on [a sequence]" means that for one emerging from cessation,
for one passing away from the attainment of the fruit of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and for the prior death-moment and subsequent rebirth-linking moment,

there is no interval of time because of the uninterrupted succession of cessation and arising. Indeed, there is no occurrence of immaterial phenomena in between them upon which an interval of time could be based.
It would be said that the occurrence of material phenomena does not create an interval for the occurrence of immaterial phenomena, because they belong to different continua.
For the two continuities of the material and the immaterial, though they proceed by way of mutual assistance due to their distinct natures, remain separate.
And within a single continuity, that which occurs between the preceding and succeeding moments is included within that same continuity.

There is an intervening factor. Yet, there is nothing of that kind between the fruition attainment (*phalasamāpatti*) and the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*);
nor does non-existence act as an intervening factor, precisely because it is non-existent.

Therefore, just as in the case of one impulsion immediately following another impulsion, or one life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) immediately following another life-continuum, there is a state of non-interruption—a truly perfect non-interruption.
Likewise, the capacity for production should also be understood to apply to the deceases from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*).

Here, because the state of being a condition for arising is evident through the immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) and others, it is described simply as "the capacity for production. However, regarding present phenomena that are delimited by the past and future limits and do not receive the designation "arising," [this capacity is not applicable].

Since the status of being a condition such as the "proximity-condition" (anantara-paccaya) is stated in passages such as, “A past state is a condition for a present state by way of the proximity-condition,” it is understood that this [conditioning] does not belong to arising alone.
For the mention of the "present" is not indeterminate like the mention of "wholesome" and so forth;

otherwise, there would have been a mention of only those things possessing mere arising. And for this very reason, in the "Past Triplet," the sections on "Dependent" (paṭicca-vāra) and so on [are formulated accordingly].

"They do not exist. Its sevenfold classification should be understood as follows: "a wholesome state [is related] to a wholesome state; a wholesome state to an indeterminate state; an unwholesome state to an unwholesome state;
an unwholesome state to an indeterminate state; an indeterminate state to an indeterminate state; an indeterminate state to a wholesome state; and an indeterminate state to an unwholesome state."

599. Regarding the phrase "arising together with the state of arising," it should be understood that here too, by means of the conditionality of arising which is manifest, the conditionality of stability is also being demonstrated; otherwise, the illustration of the lamp would not be appropriate.
For a lamp is a condition for the persistence of light as well, not merely for its arising. This is because [the factors] are co-nascent with their conditions.
Being a supporting factor is the state of being a conascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*). "At the moment of descent" means at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
For at that moment, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) arises as if it has descended, as if it were coming from the other world and entering here into the mother’s womb and so forth;
therefore, that moment is called the "moment of descent. And here, by "form" (*rūpa*), only the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*) is intended.
For that name is a co-nascent condition for that [matter], and that matter is a co-nascent condition for that name.
"Mind and mental factors" refers to the four aggregates during the course of existence (*pavatti*), because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) there is no mind-originated matter.

"Material phenomena" is said with reference to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). Although it was previously stated that "at the moment of descent [into the womb] there is name-and-form," nevertheless, by that [statement]...

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of excluding [the possibility] that the state of being a co-nascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya) for material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) is not precluded at other moments; for "at some time" means "for some [phenomena] at some particular time.

By this, it is meant that certain material phenomena, acting as the physical basis (vatthu), exist for other material phenomena and for the basis itself during the course of existence (pavatti) at some moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
It precludes, where previously unprecluded, the status of the non-material phenomena (arūpadhammā) as being co-nascent conditions (sahajātapaccaya).
And having done so, instead of saying "at some time" (kiñci kālaṃ) or "at any time" (kismiñci kāle), it is stated by means of a change of case-ending (vibhattivipallāsa).
Therefore, *kiñci* is the singular accusative. In connection with the phrase "material phenomena" (rūpino dhammā), it is the nominative plural.
It arises. It should be understood that by the word "at the time" (*kāle*), it is indicated that this is the locative singular case in connection with that [arising].

Furthermore, while the preceding statement—"one aggregate and the basis are [the condition] for the three aggregates," etc.—would imply that the basis, being accompanied by name, is the condition for name, the latter [statement] shows that the basis alone may also be so described.
The conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) should be understood as ninefold: a wholesome state for a wholesome [state], for an indeterminate [state], and for a wholesome-indeterminate [state];

an unwholesome state for an unwholesome [state], for an indeterminate [state], and for an unwholesome-indeterminate [state]; and an indeterminate state for an indeterminate [state], a wholesome-indeterminate state for an indeterminate [state], and an unwholesome-indeterminate state for an indeterminate [state].
600. The state of being a support for that which supports oneself is *aññamañña-paccayatā* (mutuality-conditionality). For this reason, the example of the tripod has been shown.
Furthermore, this state of being a support should be understood solely by way of mutuality (*aññamañña*), and not by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth.

For even while being a co-nascent condition and the like, something may not be a mutuality-condition; yet, there can be no [condition] apart from those phenomena that are co-nascent conditions and the like.
This [mutuality condition] does exist. For instance, while being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth, something may indeed be a mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*).

Moreover, if the mere fact of being helpful to that which assists oneself were to constitute a mutuality condition, then the bases (*vatthu*) and aggregates (*khandha*) that assist by way of being prior-born or posterior-born would also have to be mutuality conditions; however, that is not accepted. Therefore...

It has been said: "The state of being a benefactor should be understood precisely through their mutual relationship. And this [relationship] should be understood as a benefactor for both arising and persistence.

Furthermore, this is to be understood as threefold: a wholesome phenomenon for a wholesome phenomenon, an unwholesome phenomenon for an unwholesome phenomenon, and an indeterminate phenomenon for an indeterminate phenomenon.
601. Just as the earth element is the support for the remaining elements in the manner of a foundation, like the ground for trees and so forth;

and just as the eye and other sense organs are the benefactors of eye-consciousness and the rest; so too, the aggregates and so forth are the supports for their respective dependent aggregates and so forth in the manner of a basis, like canvas and other materials for a painting.
For it is only by being established upon the earth element that the remaining elements and derived forms (upādārūpa) exist.
They perform their respective functions as if they were distinct entities.
"By way of determination" means by way of support. And here, the mode of support should be understood as their being pre-eminently dependent upon that [earth element] for their existence.
Since the primary elements (bhūtas) are thus said to be locations that cannot be pointed out as separate, and having established this, it follows that even the eye and so forth—
The state of being a support (upakārakatā) in the sense of being a basis (adhiṭṭhānākāra) is perfectly appropriate.

For, apart from the specific quality of dependence upon that [basis] as previously described, no other mode of being a basis for immaterial phenomena—which have no location—can possibly exist within the eye and so forth.

Even though all those phenomena that arise in dependence upon any given phenomenon possess the state of being dependent upon it, [the eye, etc., are called bases because they are the primary supports].

However, by means of that specific mode of being a condition through which visual consciousness and the rest proceed in accordance with the sharpness or dullness of the eye and so forth, this specific distinction of theirs is established here as their state of being dependent upon those [faculties].

For in this way, even though there is a commonality in their being conditions, the distinction between the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and the support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) is made clear. This same method was explained below...
It has indeed been explained. Regarding the phrase "But the sixth," here the statement "material phenomena [arise] at some time for immaterial phenomena" is not applicable.
However, as for what *is* applicable here—namely, "some material phenomena"—in order to point out those very phenomena, "the eye-base," and so forth, are specified.
That which is called "matter" (*rūpa*) is said with reference to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*).

This dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), however, is of thirteen kinds. How so? There are three wholesome roots (*kusala-mūla*) as co-nascent (*sahajātato*); likewise, there are three unwholesome roots.
Among the indeterminate roots (*abyākata-mūla*), however, the pre-nascent (*purejāta*) is obtained. For the indeterminate is a condition for the indeterminate both as co-nascent and as pre-nascent;
it is also a pre-nascent condition for the wholesome; likewise for the unwholesome. The wholesome and indeterminate [roots] are [conditions] through co-nascence and pre-nascence.
"Of the wholesome, [it is a condition] only by way of co-nascence; likewise for the indeterminate, and for the unwholesome and indeterminate"—thus there are thirteen.
602. Because it exists dependent upon that, it is "supported" (nissita) by its own fruit;

having stated that any cause whatsoever is a "support" (nissaya), he determines therein that which is a preeminent support as the "decisive support" (upanissaya). It is an assistance by virtue of being a powerful cause.

It is helpful by way of being an object, by way of its capacity to produce a corresponding state of consciousness immediately after it, and by way of being a powerful cause. Therefore he said, "He," and so forth.
In that context, "having given a gift" means having relinquished the object to be given; or rather, it refers to that volition by which it is given.

"Generosity": "having given" means having purified and made clean that volition. "Having undertaken virtue" means having taken up the constant virtue (niccasīla) by way of the fivefold or tenfold precepts.

By this, only the abstinence consisting in undertaking is shown; however, the abstinence consisting in possession and the abstinence consisting in eradication are not mentioned because they are not well-known in the world as "virtue.
Even though they are not mentioned here, they certainly do exist as object-conditions (ārammaṇapaccaya).
In this context, abstinence by eradication is the object of the wholesome state for those in training (sekkha) alone, and not for others. Regarding the "Uposatha ritual":
this refers to the Uposatha virtue as stated thus: "One shall not kill living beings, nor take what is not given.
Reflecting upon that with respect—both the person in training and the worldling reflect upon that aforementioned wholesome state; even the Arahant likewise reflects upon it.
For even in the case of an Arahant, wholesome kamma performed in the past remains wholesome. However, the consciousness by which he reviews it is called functional consciousness (*kiriyacitta*).
Therefore, [the Arahant] is not included in this section concerning "the wholesome [consciousness] of the wholesome.

As for the phrase "previously well-performed," those acts described as "having given" or "having done" refer to what was performed recently; by this term, those that were not performed recently are meant.
These [factors] are to be understood; or rather, this was said in order to show the remaining wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) by means of giving and so forth.
"Having emerged from jhāna" means having entered jhāna and then emerged from it. There is also a textual reading: "Having emerged from jhāna.
"The trainee's change-of-lineage" (*sekkhā gotrabhu*) is said with reference to the stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), for he reviews the change-of-lineage. However, "purification" (*vodāna*)—this...

This was said with reference to the once-returners and non-returners, for their consciousness is called "purified" (*vodāna*). "Learners" (*sekkhā*) refers to stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners.
"Having emerged from the path" means having emerged from the paths they themselves have attained by way of transcending the path, the fruit, and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*);
however, having emerged specifically from the pure path itself, there is the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
There is no [separate] name for it. By the word "etc.," it includes such passages as “insighting into the wholesome as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

Although it has been analyzed without making a distinction [between the two], nevertheless, the words beginning with “therein” (tattha) were stated in order to show that this too is a specific difference between objective predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and objective decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya).
There is a distinction in the presentation of the immediate condition (anantara-paccaya) and the immediate decisive support (anantara-upanissaya) for those consciousnesses and mental factors;
for while the former occurs by way of indeterminate states (abyākata-dhamma), the latter does so by way of wholesome states (kusala) and so forth.
Nevertheless, this distinction in presentation results in a single unity in meaning, because both are required in all instances of the arising of consciousness.

“Even though this is so,” and so forth, is a demonstration of the distinction between the immediately preceding and the proximate conditions (*anantara* and *upanissaya*). “Just as,” and so forth, is a demonstration of the possibility of the proximate condition.
Regarding the word *pakato*: here the prefix *pa-* indicates the state of being well-prepared by virtue of its capacity to produce its own fruit.
And since that which is thus prepared is performed within one’s own continuum, he says, “in one’s own continuum,” and so forth. Furthermore, the act of performing—

To show that accomplishment (*nipphādana*) and service (*upasevana*) are twofold, it is said: "or accomplished," and so forth. Therein, accomplishment is the production of a fruit through the convergence of causes and conditions.

Service, however, consists of service by way of application (*upayoga*), which is the act of clinging to the body, and service by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*), which is the acts of cognizing, perceiving, and so on. For this very reason, even for those [factors] yet to come...

It is stated that the seasonal conditions (*utu*), nutriment (*āhāra*), and so forth, when cultivated by means of attending to them as objects, possess the nature of natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*); how much more so, then, for those that are past or present.

For even in the case of the present, the status of being a natural decisive support is obtained from such statements as: "One generates jhāna depending upon present seasonal conditions, nutriment, and lodging.
The phrase "by way of nature alone" (*pakatiyā eva*) means by way of being free from any admixture with other types of conditions.

By its own intrinsic nature. "Strong support" (upanissaya) means acting as a powerful cause. Its various classifications should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Pañhāvāra* (The Chapter on Questions).
However, in the *Paccayavāra* (The Chapter on Conditions), it is stated:
"Preceding wholesome states are related to succeeding wholesome states by way of strong-support condition."
Condition: preceding wholesome states are conditions for subsequent unwholesome states in some cases, for wholesome or indeterminate states;
unwholesome states are conditions for unwholesome states, for wholesome states in some cases, or for indeterminate states;
indeterminate states are conditions for indeterminate states, for wholesome states, or for unwholesome states; this applies to persons as well as to lodgings.
"...is a condition by way of decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

In this context, those preceding states which serve as the proximity-decisive support (anantara-upanissaya) for subsequent states do so for all of them invariably, and not for some of them at certain times.
Therefore, in those instances where the proximity-decisive support is obtained, [the phrase] "for some" does not apply.

It is not said that [they] cannot be stated. However, those preceding [states] which serve as either object-strong-dependence (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) or natural strong-dependence (*pakatūpanissaya*) for succeeding [states] do so for those [specific ones], but not necessarily for all.
They do not exist for those for whom conditions obstructing their arising are powerful; they do exist for others. Therefore, in those instances where...
The condition of immediate succession (*anantarapaccaya*) is not obtained; therefore, it is said of them, "of some" (*kesañci*).
Regarding the established conditions (*paccayadhamma*), those for whom there must be corresponding conditioned states (*paccayuppanna*) are referred to here as "of some.
Because a designation (*paññatti*) such as a kasiṇa lacks the status of being an object-condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), every phenomenon [is included] together with certain designations.

The object-strong support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*); the immediately preceding aggregate of consciousness and mental factors (*anantarātīta-cittacetasika-rāsi*) as the immediate-strong support (*anantarūpanissaya*); and the natural strong support (*pakatūpanissaya*), which is fivefold according to the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material—this is the summary here.
The detailed exposition, however, should be understood from the *Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā*.
603. "Earlier" means prior to that which has arisen by way of condition. For this prior-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) applies only to material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).
It is obtainable. And that which arises by way of condition consists exclusively of non-material phenomena (arūpadhamma). Therefore, he said: "it is an assistant by way of its present state.

The state of being an assistant—without the distinction of support (nissaya), object (ārammaṇa), aspect (ākāra), and so forth, but solely by way of prior arising—to those bases (vatthu) and objects (ārammaṇa) which would not otherwise become assistants, is the state of being a pre-arising condition (purejātapaccayatā). Thus, by way of the bases and objects...

In the two-fold prior-arising condition (*purejāta-paccaya*), that which is stated as "the eye-base" and so forth is said by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*); that which is stated as "the visible-object-sphere" and so forth is said by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*).

The phrase "that which is material form" is said with reference to the heart-basis (*hadayavatthu*). In this context, "at some time" is stated by way of the period of its active occurrence (*pavatti-kāla*);
"at another time" is by way of the period of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-kāla*). Those [bases] which cannot exist without the object-prior-arising condition—

By demonstrating that for those [mental states] such as eye-consciousness, etc., there is object-prenascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*), it is already shown that in the mind-door (*manodvāra*) as well, whatever functions by way of object-prenascence—all that material form which serves as its object-condition—is indeed object-prenascent.
For it is said in the Pañhāvāra: "Object-prenascence: whether trainees (*sekkhā*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*), [they perceive] the eye..."
“...insighting into [them] as impermanent, suffering, and non-self,” and so forth. “An indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of pre-arising condition;
an indeterminate state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of pre-arising condition;
an indeterminate state is a condition for an unwholesome state by way of pre-arising condition. These are the roots based on the indeterminate.
These are the same three ways. Furthermore, each of these is divided into two types: object-prenascence (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*) and base-prenascence (*vatthu-purejāta*).

Regarding the phrase "of those that are prenascence" (*purejātānaṃ*): this is stated because the condition (*paccaya-dhamma*) arises subsequent to the conditioned state (*paccayuppanna-dhamma*), which has already been established beforehand.
Moreover, this method applies only to material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) and not to immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*).
It was stated: "of material phenomena. If the phenomena produced by conditions had already arisen prior [to those conditions], how could they function as conditions?

To this he said: "by way of providing support. For when phenomena—which, in the absence of what is posterior-born, would not attain the status of being causes for the non-interruption of the continuum—receive assistance from that which is posterior-born, their quality of being an assistant is distinguished from other modes of assistance, such as those characterized by dissociation.

the condition of being a postnascence-condition (*pacchājātapaccayatā*). In this way, the supportive efficacy of all conditions, as distinguished by their specific modes of conditioning, should be applied.

By the phrase, “like the volition of desire for food in the bodies of vulture chicks,” he shows how the material body is sustained by immaterial phenomena that proceed by way of the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*).
For that very reason, he did not say “like the desire for food,” [but rather specified it as volition].
The mention of "volition" (cetanā) has been made. "Of the body" means of the material body, which is comprised of the primary elements and their derived matter arising from the fourfold origination.
Briefly stated, excluding material phenomena, the non-material aggregate (nāmarūpa) that is undifferentiated [in its nature] is the postnascent condition (pacchājāta-paccaya).
It should be understood as being fourfold according to its birth: wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional.
605. The meaning of *āsevana* (repetition) is the repeated performance or occurrence of an action that is to be done through an application similar to oneself by way of being wholesome and so forth;
or it is the perfuming (*vāsanā*), which is the bringing about of a nature similar to oneself. "Like previous application" means like previous repetition such as learning, hearing, and memorizing.

Among these three [conditions], however, "the preceding ones" should be understood as those immediately past. Why, then, is this not included under the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-paccaya*)?
Is it not the case that, in such passages as "preceding wholesome states [are related] to succeeding indeterminate states," no description has been made together with those of a different class?
Because they are incapable of leading one another to their own destination.

For states of a different class, while bringing about a state of proficiency and strength in those of a different class through the quality of repetition (*āsevana-guṇa*), cannot lead them to their own destination, which is defined by their own nature as wholesome and so forth.

They are unable to lead [the mind] to their own state. Therefore, it should be understood that instead of providing a detailed exposition (niddesa) together with them, a detailed exposition is made for those who are capable of leading themselves to their own state—characterized as wholesome and so forth—which is distinguished by its proficiency, strength, and specific nature through the quality of repeated practice (āsevana-guṇa) known as "predisposition" (vāsanā).
They are thus grouped together with those of a similar kind.
Now, why is the resultant indeterminate (*vipākābyākata*) not included? Because it lacks the quality of repetition (*āsevana*).
For the resultant indeterminate, having attained the state of a result by way of karma and proceeding as something transformed by karma, is effortless and weak;
thus, even though it might grasp its own specific nature and cultivate it through the quality of repetition, it does not produce another result.
Nor does it arise by taking up the influence of a previous result; rather, it arises as if flung down by the force of karma and having fallen.
Therefore, in no way is there repetition (āsevanā) in the case of a result, and thus it is not included [among those states that can be repeated].

Even when arising immediately after wholesome, unwholesome, or functional [states], because its mode of existence is bound to its own specific karma, it does not take on the quality of repetition; thus, the wholesome and so forth [are also not included].
For that [consciousness], these do not serve as a condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*). Because they are of different classes, they do not even provide a basis for its repetition.

However, since there is no difference in class either by way of plane or by way of object, limited wholesome or functional states, and wholesome states having formations as their object, certainly serve as a condition of repetition for sublime wholesome states and for those having Nibbāna as their object respectively. This [wholesome state] is "wholesome" (*kusala*)...

"It is said in three ways: 'A wholesome state is a condition for a wholesome state by way of repetition-condition; an unwholesome state is a condition for an unwholesome state; and an indeterminate state is a condition for an indeterminate state by way of repetition-condition.
By the inclusion of the term 'indeterminate,' functional states (kiriyadhamma) excluding the advertence (āvajjana) are taken.
606. Mental application (cittapayoga) is mental activity (cittakiriyā); the meaning is 'exertion' (āyūhana). For just as bodily and vocal application are intimation (viññatti),..."

Thus, mental application (*cittapayoga*) is volition (*cetanā*). For it is by means of that [volition] that, within a continuum distinguished by the occurrence of an active process (*kiriyatā*), volition assists even the resultant states and the kamma-produced material phenomena (*vipākakaṭattārūpa*) as they proceed upon the convergence of the remaining conditions—precisely because of that specific distinction in the continuum, through its state as an active process.
Indeed, their occurrence takes place because that state of being an active process has come into operation, and not otherwise. As for the co-nascent [phenomena], however...
Since they function as supportive factors by way of the activity of accumulation (āyūhana), what need is there to say more?

By "kamma," only volitional kamma (cetanā-kamma) is intended; for kamma associated with volition, such as covetousness and so forth, does not serve as a kamma-condition. Even though they possess the nature of being resultants (vipāka-dhamma), because those [factors] excluding volition lack that specific nature, the resultant volition itself is indeed a conascent kamma-condition (sahajāta-kamma-paccaya). This, moreover—
It should be stated in its entirety that the kamma-condition is fourfold according to its mode of birth.

(607) By the phrase “by way of being effortless and tranquil,” he shows that although wholesome and unwholesome states accompanied by effort (*saussāha*) are similar to those possessing fruition (*vipākadhammadhamma*) in having objects and so forth, their state of fruition is dissimilar. For that [fruition] arises through application (*payoga*).

Because it cannot be accomplished through effort, or because it is accomplished solely by the mere performance of karma once the other conditions have been fulfilled, the state of peace is effortless;

it is not a state of the subsiding of defilements (*kilesa*). Indeed, it is precisely because of this state of being thus peaceful that the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth are difficult to discern.
For even in the five sense-doors, when the objects such as visible forms are apprehended through the occurrence of impulsion (*javana*), [the underlying state remains peaceful].
It is discerned; however, the resultant states consisting merely of adverting, receiving, and investigating are indeed difficult to discern.

"For the sake of being effortless and tranquil" means for the purpose of being effortless and tranquil. By this, he shows the occurrence of even non-resultant material phenomena—which possess those same conditions—in a manner conformable to resultants.

The passage beginning with "occurs," etc., is stated by adopting the method of the *Pañhāvāra* (Chapter on Questions). But in the *Paṭiccavāra* (Chapter on Dependent Origination), it says: "Resultants..."
It is stated [in the texts] as: “The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of the resultant condition (*vipākapaccaya*),” and so forth.
Here, it should be understood that the demonstration of the method is made with reference to those cases where the resultant is invariably a resultant condition;
for in the immaterial plane, unlike in the sense-sphere and fine-material planes, a resultant is not a condition for material form.
608. Although nutriment possesses the quality of producing [matter], its primary function is to support; thus it is said:

"by way of supporting both material and immaterial [phenomena]. For this supporting quality exists even when there is also a productive quality, in the case of the immaterial nutriments and in the case of the physical nutriment that originates the matter born of nutriment.
However, although there is a nutriment that supports the matter originated by the four causes, if the supporting quality were absent—

Since nutriment does not possess the quality of being a producer, its primary function is that of support. Alternatively, even while producing, nutriment produces by way of supporting through non-interruption; thus, the very state of supporting constitutes the state of being nutriment.
Therefore, it is said: "by way of supporting. However, some maintain that material nutriment is not a nutriment-condition for what is produced by itself, but rather for what is produced by another.

They say, "Therefore it is stated [as] 'by way of support. Others do not accept this, saying, "It is contradictory that nutriment, while being a condition for matter, should not be a nutriment-condition.
Furthermore, in this context, material nutriment (*rūpāhāra*) is a nutriment-condition only for material phenomena;
however, immaterial nutriments (*arūpāhārā*) are a nutriment-condition even for material phenomena.

[They] exist. And this is not only for the sake of showing that [this applies] to material phenomena originated by consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), but rather to show that it sometimes applies to material phenomena produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*) as well;
thus the passage beginning with "In the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), however... was stated.

Regarding the phrase "in the sense of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭhena*)," here it does not mean having overcome those things that act as obstructions to the occurrence [of a state], as is the case with the conditions of predominance (*adhipati-paccaya*).

The meaning of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭha*) is the state of being weighty by way of occurrence; for instance, in the functions of seeing and so forth, [the eye-faculty is predominant] over eye-consciousness and the rest;

in living, over the material qualities born of karma and the immaterial states that are living; in cognizing, over the associated states; in the states of being happy and so forth, over those who are happy and so forth;
and in resolve, exertion, establishment, non-distraction, and comprehension, as well as in the occurrence [of the thought], "I shall know the unknown."
In the case of the faculties of "knowing" (*ājānana*) and "having known" (*aññātāvibhāva*), [the dependence] is through the factors such as faith (*saddhā*) that arise simultaneously;
thus, in their respective functions, the eye and other [faculties] possess the quality of being followed by the factors that serve as their conditions.

For in those functions, the eye and others hold sovereignty, and the factors conditioned by them proceed therein by following those [faculties]. But why are the two faculties of female and male (*itthipurisindriya*) not included here?
But is it not the case that this [sex] also follows along with the gender-mark (liṅga) and so forth?

True, it does follow along, but not by way of being a condition (paccaya). For just as life and nutriment are the conditions for those [beings] they support, acting as their protectors and sustainers, and serving as the presence and non-disappearance conditions;
the female and male states do not assist the gender-marks and so forth in any such manner. Therefore...

They may indeed be conditions; however, the state of being a faculty and the state of being governed by the gender-signs and so forth is spoken of because, while these gender-signs and others proceed solely by their own respective conditions, they do not occur in any other mode within the continuum associated with them—just as there is a conditionality for the apprehension of "female" and so on.
Therefore, they do not possess the status of being "faculty-conditions."

It has been said: "The eye and so forth are only non-material phenomena. Herein, it should be understood that the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of pain are also included by the mention of the eye and so forth. 610.

Having approached the object by way of initial application (*vitakka*) and so forth—which constitute the close contemplation of the characteristic and the object—one [engages with] the object through the function of initial application and the rest.

Contemplation (*nijjhāna*)—meaning looking at, or reflecting upon—is the specific function of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the other [mental factors] alone; this is the sense of "contemplating" (*upanijjhāyana*).

Although it was stated that "apart from the two sets of fivefold consciousnesses, there are the two feelings of pleasure and pain," one should understand that by the subsequent statement "there are seven jhāna-factors," the exclusion of equanimity (*upekkhā*) and one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*)—which are not jhāna-factors—is effected. If...
Since it is already established by the phrase "seven jhāna-factors" alone, why was it stated, "excluding the pair of pleasant and painful feelings"?
It is for the purpose of showing that, among the five types of feeling, the pair consisting of pleasure and pain is absolutely not a jhāna-factor;
this is because they are specified in the context of jhāna-factors, or else because, even though the designation "jhāna-factor" applies to them, these two types of feeling are absolutely [excluded].

This is for the purpose of showing the absence of the condition of jhāna [for these factors]. As for equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, although there is an absence of the condition of jhāna for them, there is no absence of the state of being a jhāna-condition;
therefore, they are included here among "all seven jhāna-factors.

In that context, the expression "all" is intended to include all divisions such as the wholesome and so forth, but it is not intended to include everything occurring in every arising of consciousness.

It should be understood thus. However, for those who read the text as "the three feelings, excluding the two fivefold consciousnesses," the aforementioned investigation should be understood as occurring by way of one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*) alone.

"From whatever [source]" means either rightly or wrongly. As for the passage beginning with "But in the section on questions" (*pañhāvāre*), although it appears in the description of conditions (*paccayaniddesa*), [it is included here for the sake of completeness].

That meaning is indeed already indicated by the inclusion of their origination; however, it is stated here for the purpose of showing that they are taken in their own specific form within the section on questions (pañhāvāra).
Regarding the phrase "these two [conditions]... [are not found]," one should understand that the words "according to their respective order" (*yathāsaṅkhya*) are the ellipsis to be supplied.

But in the *Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā*, it is said: "Both [jhāna and path conditions] are not found as conditions in rootless consciousnesses (*ahetukacitta*). How, then, is there no contradiction between these two statements?

By way of intention. For this is the intention here: it is stated for the purpose of showing that the jhāna and path conditions are not obtained in rootless consciousnesses (*ahetuka-citta*), but are not non-obtainable in root-possessing consciousnesses (*sahetuka-citta*);
it is not stated for the purpose of showing that they are obtainable in rootless consciousnesses. For if the meaning were taken in this way, then in some rootless consciousnesses...
It is understood that the non-occurrence of [jhāna] in any [state of consciousness] is not prohibited.
By this, the possibility of the jhāna-condition (jhānapaccaya) in thought-moments that are with initial application but rootless (savitakkāhetuka-citta) is permitted.

For in that regard, it refers to that non-occurrence by which jhāna was not mentioned in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* within the sections on the inclusion of the mind-element (manodhātu) and so forth, and the emptiness section; and thus, even for the jhāna-condition, [its presence] in rootless thoughts is intended.

Non-attainment has been stated. For just as in the case of thought-arising with roots, the function of close contemplation—which, by gathering together initial application (*vitakka*) and the other factors that arise simultaneously, brings them to a state of unity—is powerful;

it is not so in the case of thought-arising without roots. However, here, even if the close contemplation is weak, if it exists to even a slight degree, there is no lack of its being a contributing factor; thus, it is present even in thought-moments without roots that possess initial application.
When permitting the jhāna condition, it was stated: "But these two [conditions]—jhāna and path—are not found in the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness or in rootless consciousness.
Indeed, the discussion of conditions is based on the *Paṭṭhāna*, not on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. 612.
*Sama* means even or level; it is the state of being endowed with modes correctly or together, as if attaining a state of unity, which constitutes helpfulness.

The state of being an associated condition (*sampayutta-paccayatā*). But in what sense are they "associated"? To this he says: "By way of what is termed having a single basis, a single object, a single arising, and a single cessation.

In that context, if it were merely stated that "those which have a single basis are associated," then among inseparable material phenomena, one great primary (*mahābhūta*) is the support-condition for the remaining great primaries and derived matter;
thus, those would also be "having a single basis. [This is not the case,] because the eyes and so forth serve as the bases [for consciousness].

If one were to conceive that those phenomena which have a single basis (*ekavatthu*)—meaning they are dependent upon the same physical base—are "associated" (*sampayutta*), there would be the consequence of their being associated even when they do not share the same object.

To prevent this, the inclusion of the term "single object" (*ekārammaṇa*) is made. Furthermore, if it were held that those which have a single basis and a single object are associated, then there would be the consequence of death-proximate consciousness, receiving-consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*), investigating-consciousness (*santīraṇa*), and so forth, being associated with one another. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "arising together" (*ekuppāda*) is made.

Regarding the inquiry: "Are those which have a single basis, a single object, and a single arising called 'associated,' or do those with different cessations also possess these three kinds of characteristics,
or only those with a single cessation?"— it is stated "with a single cessation" in order to show that only those with a single cessation possess such characteristics.

Or, if it were stated from the reverse order as "arising and ceasing together" (*ekanirodhā*), then it would follow that material and immaterial phenomena—which cease at the same moment—are associated (*sampayuttatā*).

Therefore, it is said "arising together" (*ekuppādā*). Even so, since inseparable material phenomena possess simultaneous arising and simultaneous cessation, it would follow that they too are associated;
to prevent this, the inclusion of the term "having a single object" (*ekārammaṇa*) is made. Those which have a single object...
The inclusion of the term "having a single physical basis" (*ekavatthuka*) is for the purpose of showing that this method—

namely, that those which arise together, cease together, and are associated are "associated"— is applicable only to those states that have a single physical basis, and not to those with different physical bases. Furthermore,

this mention of "single physical basis" is made with reference to existence in the five-aggregate realm (*pañcavokāra-bhava*), since in the formless realm (*ārūpa*), there is no physical basis at all.
Since [the two] do not exist [simultaneously], how could there be any occasion for grasping them as having a single basis?

613. Even though they are joined by mutual connection, because they are dissociated—being distinct through their state of non-intimacy and their attainment of diversity—their state of being a condition is that of a dissociation-condition (*vippayutta-paccaya*).
And this state of dissociation is not the same as the state of association-condition (*sampayutta-paccaya*).
They should not be understood as being related to one another by way of the relation of condition and the phenomenon arisen from that condition; rather, they are entirely distinct.

For in that case (the mental group), there is a commonality of burden due to the homogeneity of immaterial phenomena; here, however, there is a lack of such commonality due to the heterogeneity of material and immaterial phenomena.

Therefore it is said: "Even though they are conjoined... [there is] the state of dissociation-condition. This is because [the relationship] does not occur by way of the basis, co-nascence, or post-nascence.
There exists the state of dissociation-condition even for those dissociated factors that are helpful as objects and so forth to [mental states] associated with them; for example:
"The physical basis (vatthu) is a condition for the aggregates by way of dissociation-condition;
co-nascent wholesome aggregates are [a condition] for mind-originated matter; post-nascent wholesome aggregates are [a condition] for this pre-nascent body."

Because of such statements as, “it is a condition by way of dissociation-condition,” there exists the state of being a dissociation-condition for those things that are conjoined with the physical basis (vatthu) through the modes of co-nascence and post-nascence;

however, this does not exist for those that are not so conjoined. If this is so, why is a dissociation-condition not stated for material phenomena (rūpa) in relation to other material phenomena? [The answer is: although material phenomena are inseparable from one another, they do not possess association (sampayoga) in the same way [that mental states do].

Since there is no dissociation [between them], they do not possess the conditionality of dissociation (vippayuttapaccayatā). For it is said: "There is association with four [mental factors], and dissociation with four.

Indeed, because there might be a suspicion of association between immaterial states and material phenomena, or between material phenomena and those [immaterial states], their mutual conditionality of dissociation has been stated. However, for material phenomena, there is no association with material phenomena.
The relation of dissociation (vippayutta-paccaya) is not stated for those [material phenomena].

In the passage, “Material phenomena [are related] to immaterial phenomena, and immaterial phenomena [are related] to material ones,” the inclusion of the term “immaterial” should be understood by way of the four aggregates (khandha).
For among immaterial phenomena, it is only the four aggregates that [function as] conascent (sahajata) and prenascent (purejata) [conditions].

Material phenomena are related to [mental] states by way of dissociation-condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*). However, just as Nibbāna is not a concomitance-condition (*sampayuttapaccaya*) for immaterial phenomena, so too it is not a dissociation-condition for material phenomena.
For it is said: "Concomitance with four, dissociation with four. Therefore, among immaterial phenomena, the status of being a dissociation-condition belongs only to the four aggregates.
And it is said in the *Pañhāvāra*: “Co-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-produced matter by way of dissociation-condition,” and so forth.
As for the phrase “material phenomena,” this should be understood by way of both the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*) and the [physical] bases such as the eye.
For among material phenomena, only the six bases are the dissociation-condition for the immaterial aggregates; the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) and the rest are not.
However, although the objective phenomena (*ārammaṇadhammā*) are dissociated phenomena, they do not constitute the condition of dissociation (*vippayuttapaccaya*).

Why? Because there is no possibility of association (*sampayoga*) between them. For it might be suspected that since the immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandhā*) arise as if emerging from within the bases (*vatthu*) such as the eye, they might perhaps be associated with those [bases].

"Or are they dissociated? However, since objective phenomena (ārammaṇadhammā) merely serve as objects for those states that arise by depending on a physical basis (vatthu), there is no suspicion of association among them;
thus, they are not dissociated. Because the suspicion of association does exist [in the case of the bases], the physical bases themselves are dissociation-conditions (vippayuttapaccaya).
This has also been stated in the *Pañhāvāra*: "The physical basis is a dissociation-condition for wholesome aggregates..."
“...the basis is a condition for unwholesome aggregates; the eye-base is a condition for the eye-consciousness element,” and so forth. This dissociation condition [is classified as follows]:
the indeterminate is [conditioned] by the wholesome through the relations of co-nascence and post-nascence; likewise, the indeterminate is [conditioned] by the unwholesome;

the indeterminate is [conditioned] by the indeterminate through the relations of co-nascence, pre-nascence, and post-nascence; and [it is conditioned] by the indeterminate through the relation of the pre-nascent basis (*vatthupurejāta*).
It should be understood as fivefold: "the wholesome, likewise the unwholesome"—thus one wholesome root, one unwholesome root, and three indeterminate roots. 614.
By the characteristic of the present means by way of its present intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). By that [it is said]: "I have committed an evil deed."
In such passages as "there is a person practicing for his own benefit," it is the state of existence characterized by being produced and currently obtainable that is denied.
Although there is a sense of being a producer (*janakatta*), because the primary factor is the state of being a support (*upatthambhakatta*), it is helpful by way of its state of existence;
thus he says, "by way of being a support. And this state of being a support is common to bases, objects, and conascent factors alike.
It should be understood that [the meaning] is being helpful by way of its existence.
To show by means of the actual text (pāḷi) the point already stated—that "the matrix (mātikā) has been set forth in seven ways"—it was said, "As it has been said," and so forth.

Therein, the presence condition (atthipaccaya) is shown by way of co-nascence (sahajāta) through the passage beginning, "The four formless aggregates," and by way of pre-existence (purejāta) through the passage beginning, "The eye-base," and "Whatever form..."

By the words “nissāya,” etc., [it is shown] by way of the co-nascence and prenascence conditions. Thus this reading has come down solely by way of the co-nascence, prenascence, and presence conditions.
However, in order to show that it has been stated otherwise elsewhere, he said, “In the section on questions (pañhāvāra),” and so forth.
That demonstrates its status as a presence condition also by way of the postnascence, nutriment, and faculty [conditions]. But in the previous reading, it was incomplete.
It should be understood that the teaching has been given. Furthermore, regarding those things for which [the nutriment] is a condition:

because they lack the status of being co-nascent conditions (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth when arising together with it, before it, or after it, nutriment and the faculties do not receive the classification of "co-nascent" and so on.

And this absence [of such classification] should be seen as due to the intrinsic nature (*dhamma-sabhāva*) of those phenomena. This presence-condition (*atthi-paccaya*), moreover, [arises] from co-nascence...
By way of the wholesome, there is the wholesome; by way of conascence and post-nascence, the wholesome [produces] the indeterminate;
and by way of conascence alone, the wholesome [produces] both the wholesome and the indeterminate—thus there are three [results] from wholesome roots. Likewise for unwholesome roots.

Furthermore, by way of conascence, prenascence, post-nascence, nutriment, and faculty, the indeterminate [produces] the indeterminate; by way of base-prenascence and object-prenascence, the indeterminate [produces] the wholesome, and likewise the unwholesome.

“Wholesome and indeterminate [states] are related to the wholesome by way of co-nascence and prenascence; wholesome and indeterminate [states] are related to the indeterminate by way of co-nascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty;
unwholesome and indeterminate [states] are related to the unwholesome by way of co-nascence and prenascence;
and unwholesome and indeterminate [states] are related to the indeterminate by way of co-nascence, prenascence, postnascence, nutriment, and faculty. Thus it is said.
It is of thirteen kinds. Briefly, it is fivefold by way of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional, and material phenomena;
nibbāna is not [included]. For that which is non-beneficial through its mere presence, but becomes beneficial upon having attained presence, is a presence-condition (*atthipaccaya*).
And nibbāna is not non-beneficial to those things that take nibbāna as their object merely through its own presence or absence.

Having been offered, it becomes helpful by way of its presence; or rather, the state of being helpful—which is the opposite of the state of being unhelpful for those things associated with arising and so forth—is the "presence condition" (*atthi-paccaya*). Nibbāna is not a presence condition.
615. There is no coexistence of the many factors such as contact (*phassa*) and the rest, which occur by way of touching the object and so forth.
When one aggregate such as contact is present, a second does not exist; when it is absent, however, it does exist.

Thus, the state of being a condition through that absence is "non-existence-conditionality" (*natthipaccayatā*). Even though earlier moments of consciousness are in a state of non-existence, they are not assisted by that state of non-existence;
rather, it is by their own state of existence immediately following [the absence] that they find an occasion for their occurrence through that state of non-existence.

Because it is helpful as if it were granting space, he said: "They are helpful by granting the occasion for occurrence (*pavatti-okāsa-dānena*). "Of those presently arisen" means of those in the present.
By the phrase "those very [conditions]," he states that there is no difference in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*) between the conditions of absence (*natthi*) and disappearance (*vigata*).

Even so, the state of being a condition of absence consists in providing space through mere non-existence; whereas for those things not occurring due to the non-disappearance of their own-nature, [the condition of disappearance consists] in the disappearance of their own-nature.

The state of being helpful is the state of having departed as a condition. Non-existence (*natthitā*) and emptiness (*suññatā*) immediately following cessation, and the state of having departed as the attainment of cessation—this is the distinction between them.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "only the phenomena that are presence-conditions" has the sense of inclusion.

By this, it illuminates the following meaning: not only are the non-existence and departure conditions indistinguishable in terms of their nature, but so too are the presence and non-departure conditions. Even though these...

Although conditions are not distinguished from one another in terms of their intrinsic nature (*dhamma*), nevertheless, the distinction in their status as conditions should be understood even while the phenomena remain undifferentiated: the state of being a presence-condition (*atthipaccayatā*) consists in being an auxiliary factor by virtue of existence and possessing an intrinsic nature;
the state of being a non-disappearance-condition (*avigatapaccayatā*) consists in being an auxiliary factor by virtue of not having ceased and not having lost its intrinsic nature.
For [the Buddha] has fully awakened to all the specific capacities of phenomena exactly as they are.

Since twenty-four specific conditions have been taught by the Blessed One, one should—through faith in the Lord of Dhamma, having generated the knowledge consisting of what is heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*) that "these phenomena possess such distinctions"—apply oneself to their realization through the knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Furthermore, among these, the object (*ārammaṇa*), immediate (*anantara*), contiguous (*samanantara*), decisive support (*upanissaya*), prenascence (*purejāta*), repetition (*āsevana*), association (*sampayutta*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) conditions apply only to immaterial phenomena; the postnascence (*pacchājāta*) condition applies only to material phenomena; and the remaining fourteen apply to both material and immaterial phenomena.

The conditions of immediate succession (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), repetition (*āsevana*), post-nascence (*pacchājāta*), kamma, fruition (*vipāka*), jhāna, path-association (*sampayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) relate only to immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*).

The condition of prenascence (*purejāta*) relates only to material phenomena (*rūpa*). With the exception of the object-condition (*ārammaṇa*) and decisive support-condition (*upanissaya*), the remaining ones relate to both;
these two latter conditions also pertain to designations (*paññatti*) as well as to intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
The conditions of proximity (*anantara*), contiguity (*samanantara*), repetition (*āsevana*), absence (*natthi*), and disappearance (*vigata*) belong only to the past.

The conditions of object (*ārammaṇa*), object-predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), object-decisive-support (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), and decisive-support (*upanissaya*) belong to all three times and are also timeless. The condition of kamma belongs to two times, namely the past and the present. The remaining fifteen conditions belong only to the present.

Likewise, the conditions of proximity, contiguity, contiguity-decisive-support (*anantarūpanissaya*), natural-decisive-support (*pakatūpanissaya*), repetition, and asynchronous kamma belong [only to the present].

The conditions known as absence (natthi) and disappearance (vigata) are only productive (janaka), not supportive (upatthambhaka). The post-nascence condition (pacchājāta-paccaya) is only supportive, not productive.
The remaining conditions are both productive and supportive; this distinction should also be understood.
Commentary on the detailed exposition of the phrase "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]."

616. *Paccayesu* (in the conditions): this is the locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*). *Duvidhā*: in two ways, of two kinds. *Anekadhā*: in seventeen ways, by way of the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) and so forth. *Abhiññācittena*:
with a consciousness accompanied by the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), namely, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of future destinies.
*Samohacittajānanakāle*: at the time of knowing the deluded mind of others and one's own deluded mind. *Avijjāpubbaṅgamā*: preceded by ignorance.

The meaning is: "Whatever unwholesome occurrences there may be, whatever failures there may be, they all have delusion as their root"—thus, by seeing the danger in ignorance, one forms the aspiration for turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) in order to transcend ignorance. Of those two kinds of meritorious formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*).
"Because of being deluded by ignorance" means because of being deluded by ignorance which conceals the danger of existence (*bhava*). "Those very merits" refers to those same meritorious deeds.
These are precisely those aforementioned merits of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere. The connection is that they act as a condition by way of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
"Of lust and so forth" refers to lust, views, doubt, restlessness, and grief.

Because they are associated with ignorance, it should be understood that lust and the others arise with reference to ignorance at the times when one relishes lust and the rest. Relishing by way of esteem occurs through association with lust and views.
In this same way, it should be applied to ignorance (*avijjā*). Craving (*rāga*) is the gratification, and views (*diṭṭhi*) are inseparable from it;
thus, by the very mention of "gratification," it should be understood that both the aforementioned ignorance and the views—which honor that [ignorance]—are included.

Furthermore, by mentioning craving and the rest in their own form within the text, he shows that the formations associated with them have ignorance as their object and so forth. "Those who do not see the danger" means...

“Whatever” is said for the purpose of including everything— both that which has not been mentioned in the statements regarding the object-condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*), the predominance-condition (*adhipati-paccaya*), and the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) (namely, ignorance which lacks an object and the first impulsion), as well as that which has been mentioned (namely, the lack of vision of danger in killing living beings and so forth).
“In the manner stated” means in the manner stated for the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) by way of transcending [the world] and aspiring for existence.

617. By the words beginning with "What then does he intend," etc., the opponent’s intention is as follows: "In the statement 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise,' the restriction 'they arise *only* [from that]' is not tenable, because volitional formations would not arise in the absence of the concurrence of the remaining conditions.
Likewise, the restriction 'only volitional formations' is also not tenable. Why? Because of others..."

Because the arising of the phenomena that have arisen by way of conditions must be sought from that [ignorance]. Since a statement has the function of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), even if one were to take it as a restriction—namely, "only with ignorance as condition do volitional formations arise"—this same fault remains. Why?
Because other conditions, such as greed and so forth, the source of kamma, the bases of clinging, objects, and attention, are indeed obtainable.
In this context, "alone" means without companions; the sense is that it is independent of other causes. Other conditions exist as cooperative causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*).
Perceiving that the challenger asks with the intention of pointing out a fault here, the Teacher said:
"But what [is to be said] here?"—that is, regarding the state of ignorance being either devoid of or accompanied by other conditions, what indeed is there to be said? For it is incomplete.

This is what is meant by "those are the objections; now, please explain what remains. The phrase "it follows that there is a doctrine of a single cause" expresses an undesirable consequence (*dosappasaṅga*).

For a doctrine of a single cause is undesirable because it would entail the possibility of [all things] arising at all times and in all places, and because it would entail the attainment of a nature identical to that one [cause].
Since the three modes—such as "one is not from one"—are non-existent, by the method of elimination (*pārisesa*), [the conclusion is] "from the many, and only from the many."
While this fourth mode indeed exists for the purpose of illustrating a single cause and its fruit, it is therefore not untenable; rather, it is entirely tenable.

There is no single fruit from a single [cause], nor is there even a plurality [of fruits] from a single [cause]. The connection is that even from a plurality [of causes], a single fruit does not exist.

“Elucidation of single causes and effects” means that “with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise” is an elucidation of a single cause, and “with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises” is an elucidation of a single effect; thus, in various instances, the elucidation of single causes and effects is made.
“In accordance with the disposition of those to be trained” means in conformity with the inclinations of those to be trained.
This elucidation of either a single cause or a single effect is due either to the Teacher’s skill in teaching or to the dispositions of the individuals to be trained. [The elucidation] of both...
In this context, the reasons are as follows: the predominance, the clarity, and the uniqueness of the meaning to be taught in each respective instance;

and the fact that the Blessed Buddhas, having attained mastery in the art of teaching, teach the Dhamma by selecting from among many available methods according to their preference, which constitutes their conformity with such skill in teaching. Regarding these:
However, by whatever method those who are to be trained (veneyya) awaken, by that very means their awakening occurs; this is conformity with the disposition of those to be trained.

Regarding the determination of feeling according to contact (*yathāphassaṃ vedanāvavatthānaṃ*): it is as stated in such passages as, "Monks, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises," and so forth, and:
"Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; of these three..."

And because, through such statements as "conjunction is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises," there is a specific determination of pleasant feeling and so forth, and of feeling born of eye-contact and so forth, according to the corresponding pleasant-contacting contact and eye-contact, etc.;

for even when the eye, visible object, and so forth are common [to all], there is no absence of the distinction between pleasure and so on by way of contact, and even when the attention to the visible object and so forth are common, [the distinction exists] by way of the impact of the eye and so forth.
The meaning is: because there is no absence of the specific distinction [of cause] such as "born of eye-contact" and so forth;
and because, even when other conditions are common, there is no confusion regarding the grossness or subtlety of pleasant feeling born of eye-contact and so on by way of that specific eye-contact.

The non-erroneous state of contact being the condition for pleasant feeling and so forth, exactly as stated, is precisely the "determination of contact according to feeling. This is due to the distinction between cause and fruit.
Or, because there is a desire for a specific result as the cause, it is said that in both cases the "certainty" (nicchaya) refers to the manifestation [of the effect].
"Kamma and so forth" refers to kamma, nutriment, season, and so on; these are not manifest, since the subsiding of disease occurs through the counteracting of phlegm (*semha*).
And because of the sluggish state of the phlegm and so forth, phlegm itself is the manifest cause. This [ignorance] here [functions] as the causal state of the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

The connection is with the word "explained. Regarding the statement, "For one who contemplates gratification, craving increases," the meaning is that by this sutta—"Bhikkhus, for one who contemplates gratification in things that fetter, craving increases; with craving as condition, clinging arises;
with clinging as condition, existence arises"—it is stated that craving is the cause of volitional formations (saṅkhāra). Furthermore, of that [craving] also...
He said, "Because of the statement: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints (āsava),' in order to show that ignorance is the cause.

Alternatively, since craving—which constitutes the four types of clinging—and the taints of sensual desire and views are evident as the causes of volitional formations (saṅkhāra), he shows by means of these two suttas that ignorance is indeed the manifest cause of volitional formations. [The phrase] "for one who contemplates gratification" refers to...
Indeed, by this statement it is shown that ignorance (*avijjā*), whose function is to conceal the danger inherent in existence, is the cause of craving (*taṇhā*).

Since one who is ignorant performs formative volitions (*saṅkhāra*) such as those of merit and so forth, the state of being ignorant is stated as the cause of volitional formations because the status of ignorance as the cause of formations is thus made manifest.
This is because volitional formations do not exist for one whose taints (*āsava*) have been destroyed.

Furthermore, because the formative forces of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) and so forth have specific, uncommon causes, while their common causes are such things as the physical bases (*vatthu*) and objects (*ārammaṇa*), the meaning should be understood as follows:
ignorance (*avijjā*), which conceals the danger inherent in meritorious existence, is the uncommon cause of the formative forces of merit and the rest.

By this very principle, it should be seen that in the formula "with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness," [ignorance is mentioned first] because of its predominance, its manifest nature, and its uncommon character.

By means of the statement that avoids the [objection] regarding the illumination of individual causes and effects, one should understand that in all instances—such as "with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises"—the purpose is the illumination of the Dhamma, which is effected according to the inclinations of those to be enlightened.
By the phrase "having an exclusively undesirable fruit," its contradictory nature is shown; by the phrase "blameworthy," its heterogeneous nature is shown.

It illuminates ignorance. For meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations are opposed to that [ignorance] because they have desirable results and an irreproachable nature, and they are of a different class.

"How would it not be appropriate? and so forth is the resolution; by this, he shows the non-absolute nature (anekantikata) of that statement regarding the cause consisting in the fact of having exclusively undesirable results and so on. This is the intended meaning here.
This objection which was raised by you with the words, “Even if this were so,” and so forth, is appropriate with respect to the ripening of kamma.
For a cause that ripens as undesirable does not produce a desirable fruit, nor does one that ripens as desirable produce an undesirable one.

However, what is intended here is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of the relationship between conditions and the phenomena produced by those conditions; and in that regard, there is no such fixed rule, because of the manifold nature of things.
“Of that” means: thus he said, “And it is contrary,” and so forth.
Therein, “of phenomena” (dhammānaṃ) means of those phenomena possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva). “Station” (ṭhānaṃ) means persistence. Therefore, “contrary to station” means contrary to existence.
