Some, however, say: “The stations are rebirth-linking and so forth. This being so, [the phrase] “the preceding consciousness [is contrary] to the succeeding consciousness... [is explained].

The statement “a condition that is contrary in location” would not be absolute. For instance, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is a proximity-condition for the life-continuum, and javana is a proximity-condition for javana;
yet there is no such thing as a location for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and so forth in relation to crafts and the like. Therefore, that [type of condition] is not intended here.

Furthermore, kamma is contrary in intrinsic nature (sabhāvaviruddha) to matter because of the opposition between bending and being bent, and because of the opposition between having an object and lacking an object, and so forth.
Condition: Milk and such things [are conditions] for curds and such things due to the opposition between their intrinsic natures, such as sweet and sour tastes.

Light, whose function is non-cognition, [is a condition] for consciousness, whose function is cognition. And sugar and such things, whose function is non-intoxication, [are conditions] for fermented liquor, whose function is intoxication.

Regarding "cow-hair, sheep-hair, and so forth": in these cases, cow-hair and sheep-hair [should be understood as] *dubbā* grass; and "sheep" (*avī*) should be understood as a red-colored ewe. Horns...
Curd, sesame flour, and molasses are for *bhūtiṇaka*; duckweed is for *taṇḍuleyyaka*;
and a rough mare is for the mule—such things as these are included by the word "etcetera.

Since [ignorance] is not exclusively a result of kamma, the meaning is that it is not illogical for ignorance, even when its ripening is painful, to serve as a condition for meritorious and imperturbable volitional formations whose ripening is not painful.

Even though it has that same kind of ripening (*vipāka*), because it is faulty (*sāvajja*), it is a condition only for unwholesome formations (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*) that are not opposed to it and are similar to it, and not for others.
To prevent this possible objection, it was said: "The condition of phenomena is established as both opposed and non-opposed, and likewise as similar and dissimilar.
Therefore, making that meaning clear, he said: "Thus, this ignorance... and so forth.

619. “Not grasping at death” means not knowing as it truly is that death is the final dissolution of the aggregates—such as form and so forth—designated as ‘death’ within this or that state of existence (bhava).
[The phrase] “of a being who exists” means of one who is actually present. “Transmigration to another body” means the coming together with another physical frame.
"The manifestation of aggregates everywhere" means the initial arising of the aggregates here and there in various states of existence such as rebirth.
"The manifestation of a new body" means that, upon the casting off of this aged body, there is the arising of a new body included within the next world. As some say:
Just as a man, having discarded worn-out clothes, takes up others that are new, so too,
having cast off this body here when it is worn out, [he goes on].
"He grasps at a new self, seeking pleasure.
Here, "this being" (*satta*) refers to this "self" (*attā*), which is intended as the master, the inhabitant, the agent, and the experiencer.

The same principle applies here to the expressions "a being dies" and "a being is reborn. In all three instances, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes various conceptualizations such as being created by Īśvara or created by Brahmā.

"Specific characteristic" (*sabhāvalakkhaṇa*) refers to non-arising, experiencing, and so forth, or indeed to the intrinsic natures such as hardness and touching. "General characteristic" (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*) refers to impermanence and so forth. Regarding the notion that "the formations are the self" or "belong to the self": among form and the other aggregates, one takes a certain part as the self and the rest as belonging to the self.
Or, like the followers of Kapila and others, they conceptualize that "the self knows. Or, like the followers of Kaṇāda, the Ājīvikas, and others, they hold that "it does not know.
For even according to the followers of Kaṇāda, the self does not know by its own nature; rather, when it is conjoined with the quality of intelligence (*buddhi*), it then knows.

"He desires. "He himself both does and causes to be done" means that he who experiences pleasure and pain for the sake of another is the very one who personally performs merit and demerit and causes another to do them;
the intention is that it is not someone else. "Establishing" means by way of producing dyads and so forth, and by way of accomplishing [them] according to desire.
"He" refers to the being designated as a self. "Endowed with faculties" means by means of the faculties such as the eye and so forth.
Being thus endowed, he demonstrates the occurrence of the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*).

All this has been stated from the perspective of seeing that the theorist (*diṭṭhigatika*) is deluded when he attributes his own activity or agency to ignorance (*avijjā*) and the other factors as they proceed according to their respective conditions.
Just like gems strung on an unbreakable thread, there is a fixed order of priority and sequence; this is *niyati*, [the state] of *niyati*. *Niyati*.

"Union" (*saṅgati*) means meeting or coming together; "destiny-union" (*niyati-saṅgati*) refers to those things that have evolved through such union into various states, having attained the condition of humans, gods, birds, and so forth—thus they are called "evolved through destiny-union and state" (*niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā*).

Alternatively, some explain the meaning as follows: they are "evolved through destiny, through union, and through their own-nature (*sabhāva*) which is termed 'state' (*bhāva*)," having thus attained manifold varieties.

And showing the meaning that, by means of these conceptualizations, one makes the mind unwholesome through ignorance and causes sentient beings to engage in any of the formations such as merit (puñña), etc., he said:
"He is blinded by ignorance," and so forth. "Practices" (paṭipajjati) means approaches.
"Without a guide" means devoid of a good friend who would establish one in the path to Arahatship; [it refers to] that which culminates in the knowledge of the path to Arahatship.
Or, it is a "guide" because it leads beings to Nibbāna by showing what is even and what is uneven; one devoid of that is "unguided.
"Having known the Dhamma" means having known the Dhamma consisting of the Suttas and so forth which illuminates the Four Truths by relying on true persons;
or, having known the Dhamma of Nibbāna—the most excellent of all phenomena—by means of path-knowledge itself. And the realization of the remaining three truths depends upon that knowledge.

Even though it is simultaneous, it is spoken of as if it were a previous time. "He will wander having become tranquil" means that through the attainment of the supreme path, with the complete pacification of ignorance, he becomes tranquil;

then, remaining in the element of nibbāna with residue remaining, until the attainment of the element of nibbāna without residue, he will continue to wander, manifesting a personal existence for the sake of acting for the welfare of beings, and dwelling in happiness in this very life.
The meaning is "he will dwell.
Commentary on the detailed exposition of the passage concerning consciousness conditioned by formations (saṅkhārapaccayāviññāṇa):
That consciousness arising with the aforementioned formations as its condition must necessarily be produced by kamma.
“Thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses are included,” he said. However, in the *Dhātukathā*, in the exposition of the terms “included” and “not included” regarding dissociation, it is asked:

“By how many [factors] are those states which are dissociated from consciousness conditioned by volitional formations, those states which are dissociated from contact conditioned by the six sense bases, and those states which are dissociated from feeling conditioned by contact, included?”

"Are they included by the aggregates... [etc.]? "Those states, setting aside the unconditioned as an aggregate, are included by one aggregate, eleven bases, and eleven elements. By how many are they not included?
They are not included by four aggregates, one base, and seven elements. From this statement, there is the inclusion of all consciousness, contact, and feeling.
It is done so. For if consciousness, contact, and feeling were here limited (sappadesa), there would have been an answer similar to that for "resultant states" (*vipākā dhammā*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the intention is that consciousness and the rest, conditioned by formations (*saṅkhāra-paccayā*), are taken there according to the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*. And in the *Abhidhamma-bhājaniya*, the formation conditioned by ignorance (*avijjā-paccayā saṅkhāro*) is the wholesome formation belonging to the four planes.
It should be understood that since the unwholesome formation (*akusalasaṅkhāra*) has already been mentioned, it is precisely this that is included in the *Dhātukathā*.

However, in the *Dhātukathā*, "existence" (*bhava*) is not included according to the method of the *Abhidhammabhājanīya* for the purpose of showing the distinction between the existence of karma (*kammabhava*) and the existence of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
This being the case, instead of citing "with clinging as condition, existence arises," existence is cited there by way of the formula beginning with "the existence of karma."
He says, "It is twenty-two-fold," referring specifically to mundane resultant mind-consciousness (*lokīyavipākamanoviññāṇa*).
"By six consciousnesses" means by the six consciousnesses as previously specified, namely, eye-consciousness and so forth. But why is only the mundane resultant consciousness included here?
He replies: "But supramundane [consciousness] is not applicable to a discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*). If this is so, why...
In this *Dhātukathā*, in such passages as “those states dissociated from consciousness conditioned by formations,” is there an inclusion of supramundane resultants (*lokuttara-vipāka*) as well?

That is stated because the teaching of the Abhidhamma is a teaching according to the actual nature of phenomena (*yathādhamma-sāsana*); it is expressed by way of including all resultant states without exception, just as in the *Vipākattika*.

However, the teaching of the Suttas is a teaching according to what is appropriate (*yathānuloma-desanā*); therefore, in that context, the processes of occurrence and cessation are presented without confusion.

[They] must be shown. Therefore, having made [the point that] this is a commentary on that meaning, only mundane resultant consciousnesses are included in the discourse on occurrence (*pavattikathā*).
For this very reason it was said: "They are not included because they do not fit within the discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*).

Just as an action performed becomes capable of yielding a fruit when performed in such a way, it is called "accumulated" (*upacita*); thus, it is precisely that which is fit for the giving of a result.
When taking up the volitional formation (*saṅkhāra*), he says, "in the absence of accumulated karma. The term "cause" (*hetu*) emphasizes the negative concomitance (*byatireka*);
thus, the inclusion of the word "absence" implies that when karma exists, [the result] exists, and when it does not exist, it is absent.
However, while its status as a condition for consciousness is not established, its nature as a karmic ripening (*vipāka*) is. Since that is established, he says, "for this is a ripening."
By means of that [fact], he establishes that consciousness has the status of a result by way of being conditioned by volitional formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya*).
To establish that point, it was stated: "Because in the absence of accumulated karma there is an absence of result. Explaining that, he says: "And as for the result," and so forth.
"If it were to arise" means: if the result were to arise independently of karma. [Then] all beings would attain the state of a Brahmā.

The nose-consciousness and other [sensory] consciousnesses of those who have approached [their respective objects] are "great resultant consciousnesses," even when they abide in the absence of their specific corresponding resultants.
The term "resultants" (*vipākāni*) is used in the neuter gender in view of the word "consciousnesses"; the meaning is "all resultant consciousnesses.

The formations (*saṅkhārā*) are many, due to the division into twenty-nine types of volition (*cetanā*), and the consciousnesses (*viññāṇāni*) are also many, because they are of thirty-two kinds. And yet...
He said, "From all [formations], all [consciousnesses]" in response to the question, "If it is asked, 'Conditioned by which formations is which consciousness?
And this term "consciousness" is stated by taking the general category of consciousness.

Although these types of consciousness have indeed been described in the Exposition of the Aggregates (*Khandhaniddesa*), that account was extremely brief, and the fact that they are conditioned by formations was not clarified there; therefore, [it is explained] here in relation to their occurrence (*pavatti*).

In order to show in detail, by way of the mode of occurrence during rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and in the [subsequent] existences (*bhava*), the passage beginning with “conditioned by kāmāvacara wholesome volitional formations” (*kāmāvacarapuññābhisaṅkhārapaccayā*) is commenced.

In the phrase “in mind-consciousness” (*manoviññāṇe*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). In the expression “great resultants” (*mahāvipākāni*), the neuter gender is used in reference to consciousness (*viññāṇa*).
However, if the reading is “great resultants” (*mahāvipākā*), one should supply the words “mind-consciousness elements” (*manoviññāṇadhātuyo*) and connect them accordingly.
"By way of whatever volitional formations as condition" (*yaṃsaṅkhārapaccayā*) means by way of the conditionality of this or that volitional formation.
"Whatever consciousness" (*yaṃ viññāṇaṃ*)—here, in both instances, the elision of the repeated word (*āmeḍita*) should be understood.
By the word "arises" (*hoti*), only the mere existence of consciousness in its capacity as a cause is made known, not its specific mode of occurrence; demonstrating this, he says: "Thus it occurs..."

“It should be understood,” he said. Since even for Brahmās, unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness and the rest occasionally arise when undesirable forms and so forth come within their range, it is stated:

“These thirteen... proceed. In this context, “fivefold existence” (*pañcavokāra*) means that which has the expansion (*vokāra*) or detailed manifestation of the five aggregates; that itself is existence (*bhava*). In this fivefold existence (*pañcavokārabhave*), there is [existence].
For there is indeed a *aññapadattha-samāsa* (compound with a different referent) even for words with different loci, as in the example "urasiloma" (hairy-chested).

Alternatively, it is called the "fivefold plane" (*pañcavokāra*) because it is distinguished by the five aggregates that occur according to their respective conditions; that itself is "existence" (*bhava*), as explained entirely as before.
The passage beginning with "How... is commenced in order to elaborate upon the meaning stated in brief as "they occur only during the course of existence."
Regarding the phrase “mostly at the conclusion of a javana associated with greed”:

some say this is because [a javana] accompanied by mental joy does not arise immediately after one associated with aversion, doubt, or restlessness; however, that should not be accepted. [For it is said: “One relishes and delights in the eye;
taking that as an object, lust arises, wrong view arises... [and so on] ...doubt arises, restlessness arises.”
This is because of the statement: “When unwholesome [states] have ceased, the resultant arises as registration.
And if the object is desirable, joy accompanied by that object does not fail to arise.

Regarding the rule for registration following javana, others say that this was stated with reference specifically to those [javana states] associated with joy; however, that should be examined, since [registration] also occurs immediately after wholesome or unwholesome javanas associated with equanimity.

Because that object which is accompanied by joy is desirable. For they do not admit that the object accompanied by joy occurs immediately after a functional javana (kiriyājavana) associated with equanimity.
However, because at the conclusion of a javana with three roots (tihetuka), there is sometimes a rootless (ahetuka) registration (tadārammaṇa), he says "for the most part" (yebhuyyena).

It has been stated. Some say that because the object of impulsion (*javana*) lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, and at that time there is only one instance of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), it was therefore said, "or once.
Others, however, maintain that what is called registration is the function of experiencing the object of the impulsion;
this does not arise when the object is of such a nature as to perish within a single moment of consciousness due to its extreme proximity. Therefore, [the phrase] "or once" refers to this.
It should be understood that this is stated for the sake of euphony in speech, as in the case of *dirattatirattādi*;
however, it arises only twice. For in the expression *dirattatiratta*, since the particle *vā* is absent, it is logical that the mention of *diratta* is made merely for the sake of euphony.
But in the phrase, "Or for the purpose of showing continuous [occurrence] for three nights," here...
The word *vā* is stated here in the sense of an alternative; thus, it should be understood that the phrase "or once" (*sakiṃ vā*) is said with reference to its occurrence at a single time.
For this very reason, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, while demonstrating that the occurrence of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) is to be examined, it is stated:
"In the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness, however, only two instances of the registration consciousness are mentioned for all doors."

In that context, by the phrase "according to the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness," he speaks with reference to the reckoning of the occurrence of consciousness as stated in the *Vipāka-kathā* (Discourse on Resultant Consciousness) regarding a powerful object such as visible form.
For in that [text], only two instances of the arising of registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) are mentioned. It is precisely with reference to that same point that it is said here as well:
"In the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*, however, two rounds of consciousness are recorded for the registration [consciousness]. This refers to the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*.
It is stated thus without mentioning the door because they proceed having the function of occurring with indeterminate objects;
this is said with the intention of providing a similar commentary immediately following for the resultant consciousnesses with roots that are discussed later.
For the two types of rootless [consciousness] and so forth, which constitute the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), are themselves the doors, and those which constitute death and rebirth-linking—

Because they do not arise through the door designated as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) or through any other door, it cannot be said that "these have a fixed or unfixed door. However, for the two rootless [consciousnesses]—namely, investigation (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa)—a door is obtained, and that is unfixed; therefore, including those as well, he says: "They function having become the station, the object, and the function of an unfixed door. For this very reason, it is stated here: ... [the rest of the passage follows] ... Thus, because they are included within the category of the "unfixed," they are called "unfixed" by way of their doors, objects, stations, and functions. This is the meaning. Herein, the word "station" (ṭhāna) refers to the sense-base (āyatana). The word "function" (kicca) refers to the specific activity (kiriyā) of each consciousness. The word "object" (ārammaṇa) refers to the object itself. The word "door" (dvāra) refers to the sense-faculty (indriya). Regarding the phrase "having become the station": the station of the first [rootless consciousness] is the eye-base; its object is visible form; its function is seeing. The station of the second is the ear-base; its object is sound; its function is hearing. The station of the third is the nose-base; its object is odor; its function is smelling. The station of the fourth is the tongue-base; its object is flavor; its function is tasting. The station of the fifth is the body-base; its object is tangible object; its function is touching. The station of the sixth is the mind-base; its object is mental phenomena; its function is cognizing. The phrase "having become the function" means that the function of the first is seeing; the function of the second is hearing; the function of the third is smelling; the function of the fourth is tasting; the function of the fifth is touching; and the function of the sixth is cognizing. The phrase "having become the object" means that the object of the first is visible form; the object of the second is sound; the object of the third is odor; the object of the fourth is flavor; the object of the fifth is tangible object; and the object of the sixth is mental phenomena. The phrase "having become the door" means that the door of the first is the eye-faculty; the door of the second is the ear-faculty; the door of the third is the nose-faculty; the door of the fourth is the tongue-faculty; the door of the fifth is the body-faculty; and the door of the sixth is the mind-faculty. Therefore, because they possess these four characteristics—station, function, object, and door—they are called "unfixed" by way of their doors, objects, stations, and functions. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the statement "they are called 'unfixed' by way of their doors, objects, stations, and functions": the word "furthermore" (api ca) indicates that there is another reason why they are called "unfixed. What is that? It is because they are included within the category of the "unfixed. How so? Because they are included within the category of the "unfixed," they are called "unfixed" by way of their doors, objects, stations, and functions. This is the meaning. Herein, the word "furthermore" (api ca) signifies inclusion. The word "also" (ca) signifies conjunction. The word "by way of" (vasena) signifies the instrument. The word "called" (vuccati) signifies being spoken of. The word "unfixed" (aniyata) signifies that which is not fixed. Since even those [states] with great fruition obtain a door when they become objects, the designation "door" is also applied there.

Because the fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) resultant occurring in a single being occurs only upon a specific object such as the earth-kasiṇa, and does not occur upon any other, it is said that fine-material-sphere states have fixed objects. As for the others...
The resultant consciousnesses of the formless realm (*āruppa-vipāka-viññāṇa*). "Fixed with respect to their basis" (*niyata-avatthuka*) means having a fixed basis.

They have fixed objects (*niyatārammaṇa*) because they proceed only toward objects such as the space revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa. "Therein" (*tatra*) refers to the course of existence (*pavatti*). "Of this" (*assa*) refers to the thirty-two types of resultant consciousness.

"Those various formations" (*te te saṅkhārā*) refers to the aforementioned formations, such as meritorious volitional formations (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). "By way of the condition of kamma" (*kammapaccayena*).

By way of the condition of asynchronous kamma (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*). "By way of decisive support condition" (*upanissaya-paccaya*) means by way of the natural decisive support condition (*pakatūpanissaya-paccaya*).

Having thus shown the occurrence of consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatti*), he said "But as for what was stated," etc., in order to show it at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Therein, "by way of a corresponding rebirth-linking" (*anurūpāya paṭisandhiyā*) means by way of a corresponding function of rebirth-linking. That correspondence, however—

He himself will explain this later. Since the linking of one existence to another is what is meant here by "rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*), and taking into account that this exists even in mindless states, the question "How many rebirth-linkings are there?
was asked; yet, having asked that, the question "How many rebirth-linking consciousnesses are there?
was also posed. "By what, where? means by which consciousness and in which existence.

“Among those” means among those nineteen rebirth-consciousnesses (*paṭisandhi-citta*). It is connected with the phrase “to the rootless mind-consciousness element (*ahetuka-manoviññāṇa-dhātu*) that is a wholesome result.
The qualification “in the human world” is used because there are no rootless rebirths among the gods.

By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “neuter beings, etc.,” the inclusion of hermaphrodites (*mamma*) and others is intended. However, some say that certain individuals who possess rootless rebirth consciousness have unimpaired faculties.
Having offered [this], they are indeed by nature somewhat investigative; therefore, it is said that even such [consciousnesses] are included here by the word "etc.
"In brief" means concisely; the meaning is that no distinction is made as to which rebirth-linking has which object.
"Of the rest" refers to these seven remaining from those mentioned: the five of the fine-material sphere and the two of the first and third immaterial spheres.
Regarding rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*): there is no death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) that has a present object, because it functions only with the same object as the rebirth-linking.
"In two objects" means in two objects by way of not specifying the past.
"Those" refers to the kamma performed previously. "Of him" refers to the person whose death is imminent. "Hang down" means...
In the evening, like the shadows of great mountain peaks, they descend and settle upon the earth; so too, they descend and settle upon his mind.
"When that has ceased" means as soon as that death-consciousness has ceased, immediately following its cessation.

"That very same" refers to that very object which served as the objective support for the aforementioned javana-process. [This occurs] while the defilements such as ignorance and craving remain unsevered.

Because there is an attendance upon one's own karma, and with that as its object, the continuum of consciousness possesses a downward slope, an inclination, and a tendency toward another existence, he said: "directed by the power of unabandoned defilements.

For when the continuum is directed, the rebirth-linking consciousness—which is a single part of that continuum—is likewise directed; and without such direction of a single part, there can be no [direction] of the continuum.

“There is a state of being bent down. However, in all cases, they determine that for a death tending toward rebirth in an unhappy destination, the preceding javanas are unwholesome, and for the other [death], they are wholesome.
“Bhikkhus, consciousness, when standing, stands either clinging to the gratification in signs or clinging to the gratification in secondary characteristics; and if at that time one should die...”
For it is said: “It is possible that he might be reborn in one of two destinations—either in hell or in the animal realm.
Therefore, unwholesome karma is the decisive support for rebirth in an unhappy destination, and wholesome karma is the decisive support for rebirth in a happy destination.
However, because all defilements have been utterly severed in the case of an Arahant, and because all longing for existence has subsided, [there is no such rebirth].
If the sign of karma does not appear, then even though karma exists, it fails to produce rebirth-linking because it lacks an associate.
"By way of the aforementioned type of karma" means by way of evil karma; the intention is that [the sign] is produced by that.
The phrase "the color of flames of fire and so forth in the hells, etc. is stated by way of similarity, for the color of the hell-fire itself is not what appears.

Then it comes within his range of perception. In that context, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the color of the fire-flame etcetera," one includes the colors of the Vetaraṇī river, the *simbali* tree, the forest of sword-leaves, and so forth.
Furthermore, by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "in the hells etcetera," one includes the colors comprised within the fixed places of movement for hungry ghosts (*petas*) and animals.
It "comes within the range of the mind-door" means that for one seeing a dream, the sense-base of color (*vaṇṇāyatana*) is presented through the power of karma.
Just as with the divine eye, it becomes an object for the mind-door alone. There are three types of process-thoughts:
one adverting consciousness, five impulsion moments, and two registration moments.
An "inferior object" refers to an undesirable object that serves as the cause for greed and so forth, and is thus suitable to become the object of unwholesome-resultant consciousness.
For that too, by way of intention (*saṅkappana*), becomes a cause for lust.

Or rather, inferiority consists precisely in the state of being a cause for lust and so forth that are conascent with karma producing unwholesome result (*akusalavipāka*), or with the proximate death-moment javanas similar to that [karma].
For that [inferiority] is the object of karmas that produce subsequent remorse; it is undesirable by way of the karma itself, and it is the object of unwholesome result.
Otherwise, the result of unwholesome kamma that occurs with a desirable object would not have the sign of that unwholesome kamma as its object;
for it is not possible for an unwholesome result to have a desirable object.

And in the case of the five sense doors, the present sign of kamma—which has come into range—is [perceived] within the continuity of the stream of consciousness that had the object of the kamma performed recently.
That which has arisen and that which is similar to it should be regarded [as the object].
Otherwise, that very same [consciousness] would be both the establisher of the object for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the producer of rebirth-linking itself.

Furthermore, unlike those [states] which serve as the preparation for rebirth-linking, the states occurring near the moment of death (*cuti*) do not arise in such a way that "you must proceed in this manner," nor do they arise without producing an object for rebirth-linking.
The javanas would have to be the producers of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), for it is said: "Because of what has been done and accumulated.

And at that time, how could those [javana-cittas] be considered "done" and "accumulated" while they are occurring in the same cognitive process (*vīthi*) as that [rebirth-linking], as if they were identical to it? At that time, they have not yet been experienced with relish (*assādita*).

Furthermore, mundane (*lokiya*) states do not share the same process-result (*samānavīthiphala*) as supramundane (*lokuttara*) states. Or rather, that [kamma] must have been performed by him previously.

“Either a bad deed to be experienced as suffering has been committed by him, or that bad deed to be experienced as suffering was committed by him later on, or at the time of death he possesses and has adopted wrong view.

Because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell,” and so forth; thus it is stated in the Sutta regarding the time of death.
It is stated that the giving of rebirth-linking occurs through right view and the volition co-nascent with it when wrong view has been fully undertaken;
however, wrong view or right view does not become fully undertaken or adopted by means of the weak five-door impulsion moments.
For thus it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "All this, beginning with the discernment of wholesome and unwholesome states and ending with the process of death..."

“The function is performed by mind-door consciousness alone, not by five-door consciousness; therefore, in the performance of this entire function, the process-consciousnesses accompanied by conascent impulsions (sahajavana) are excluded.
For in that context, it is said, “Mind precedes all phenomena,” yet [the mind] does not discern even a single phenomenon. Thus, even that which was spoken of as such—[is here excluded].
It is also stated that [the mind] does not discern what is wholesome or unwholesome.
That process by which the occurrence of discernment leads to the following of either pleasure or pain is excluded from the five sense doors.

The undertaking of wholesome and unwholesome kamma is likewise [excluded]. However, death occurs immediately after that object, and rebirth occurs immediately after that [death]; these belong to the mind door.

It should be understood that with this intention—that it is not included within the sense-sphere javana-cittas—it is stated here that death occurs immediately after the five-door object-attending consciousness (*pañcadvārika-tadārammaṇa*), and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) occurs immediately after that.

In this context, with reference to rebirth-linking that arises in relation to matter and so forth that lasts for the remaining five mind-moments, [it is said]: "The rebirth-consciousness has a present object; [it is] for a present object..."

It should be understood that this was stated with reference to the rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi) that arises for the remainder of a single moment’s duration: "The present-object rebirth-consciousness is a condition for the past-object life-continuum (bhavaṅga) by way of proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya)."
624. Regarding the phrase "setting aside the bright side (sukkapakkha) in the case of the dark side (kaṇhapakkha)":

just as previously, when it was said "either a bad kamma or the sign of a kamma," the bright side was stated as "either blameless kamma or the sign of a kamma," so too here, [the dark side] refers to "rebirth-consciousness included in the miserable destinies, and the sign of a miserable destiny such as the color of a mass of flames in the hells and so forth."

And when this has been stated regarding the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*), having set aside the bright side (*sukkapakkha*)—namely, "the rebirth-linking consciousness included within a happy destination; in the human world, that which is called the color of the mother's womb, resembling a red blanket;

or in the world of the gods, that which is called the color of parks, celestial mansions, wish-fulfilling trees, and so forth, as the sign of a happy destination"—all the rest should be understood in the same manner as previously described. "With past and present objects" means by way of kamma and the sign of kamma (*kamma-nimitta*).
It has a past object by way of the mother’s womb, complexion, and other signs of a happy destination; it has a present object by way of such signs.

And as for that which was stated without specification—“either blameless kamma or the sign of kamma”—it is indeed the sign of kamma alone that comes into range, because the sublime resultant consciousness has exclusively one's own kamma as its object.
"Pure" means having as its object the sign of a sublime kamma; the meaning is that it is devoid of registration (tadārammaṇa).
Furthermore, that cognitive series of impulsion should be regarded as the proximate cause for a sublime resultant, though some say that this series concludes with the sublime [consciousness].
"Or having an indeterminate object" refers to the fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking.

This was stated with reference to the first and third [formless attainments] among the formless states (*ārūpya*). However, the second and fourth are included by the very mention of "having the past as their object.
By the passage beginning with "reckoned as the color of the mother's womb," it is color itself that is presented as the sign of the destination (*gatinimitta*).

In that regard, sound is not mentioned in the Commentaries as a sign of the destination, because it is not comprised within a happy destination (*sugati*) due to its being non-clung-to (*anupādinna*).
This is appropriate; however, the reason why odors and so forth do not arrive must be investigated.

In such cases as, "Dear son, this Buddha-pūjā is being performed for your sake," merit arises by way of the prior volition (*pubbacetanā*). They say that this applies even to one who is engaged in the very last gallop of the chariot.
626. Why was it said: "Following this sequence, the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) immediately after death in the formless realm (*āruppacuti*) should also be understood"?

Is it not the case that, according to the method beginning with "for one who has attained the sublime [states] by means of the earth-kasiṇa jhāna and so forth, and who remains in a happy destination," this rebirth-linking is also included therein?
No; because in that context, only rebirth-linking immediately following death from the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) is mentioned.
For there, it says: "The sign such as the earth-kasiṇa, or the sublime consciousness, [appears] at the mind-door..."

By that statement beginning with "it comes within the range of the eye or the ear," it is understood that rebirth-linking is stated as occurring immediately after death specifically in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*).

Furthermore, even if this rebirth-linking is included there according to its possible application, there is no rebirth-linking in the fine-material sphere immediately following death in the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*). In the immaterial sphere...
Furthermore, there is no lower rebirth-linking immediately following an upper death; thus, for a death in the fourth formless realm, there is no rebirth-linking with an indeterminable object.

Therefore, in that case, the rebirth-linking has a past object, whereas in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), it has past or present objects. And in other cases, as applicable, it has past or indeterminable objects.

The separate extraction [of this case] is made for the purpose of showing this distinction: that the rebirth-linking of the formless realm and the sense-sphere rebirth-linking with past or present objects should be correlated accordingly. 627.
Thus, from a single type of death in a fortunate sense-sphere existence by way of object, there arise two types of rebirth-linking in an unfortunate state.
There is a twofold rebirth-linking in a happy destination following death in an unhappy destination;

there is a fivefold rebirth-linking in a happy destination following death in a happy destination of the sense-sphere, by way of the two, one, and two types of rebirth-linking in the sense, fine-material, and immaterial realms respectively; there is likewise a fivefold [rebirth-linking] following death in the fine-material realm;

and there is an eightfold [rebirth-linking] following the twofold death in the immaterial realm, by way of the two and two types of rebirth-linking in each of the sense and immaterial realms respectively.
Rebirth-linking has been shown. However, regarding the single type of death in an unhappy destination (duggati), the two types of rebirth-linking in an unhappy destination have not yet been shown;
in order to show that, it was said: "But for one situated in an unhappy destination... and so forth. As it has been stated:
Two, two, then five, and eight—these are the two [types of rebirth] according to the distinction of the objects of existence (bhava).
“In such a death, there are twenty-four linkages.

(628) By the passage beginning with “Because of having performed wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere,” the manner in which kamma functions as a asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kammapaccaya*) has already been shown below; therefore, [the author] says “For this has been said,” etc., in order to demonstrate its status as a decisive support-condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).
Here, the mixing of consciousness with that [matter] is simply its co-occurrence with matter that serves as a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*); the absence of that [mixing] is...
*Amiṣṭā*: "Mixed. Those beings here who are mixed with one another by way of having a commonality of birth are *yoniyo* (wombs).
Because they are to be gone to and reached by means of good and bad conduct, they are *gatiyo* (destinies). That wherein something stands is a *ṭhiti* (station);

the station of consciousness is *viññāṇaṭṭhiti*. Because it is to be inhabited by beings, the very dwelling—beginning with "possessing diversity of body and diversity of perception"—is the *sattāvāsa* (abode of beings).
Because the abode of non-percipient beings is impossible here [in this world], it is said: "It is eightfold by way of the abodes of beings.

(629) Regarding the phrase "except for the rebirth-linking of those born blind and eunuchs," one should also add "and for the rebirth-linking of the beings of the first aeon," for that too arises without [the presence of] gender.
"Omatoti" means despised; the sense is "one who is held in low esteem. "Ādinā" refers to the beginning of this dyad: "mixed and unmixed."
By the aforementioned mixed consciousness (*missaviññāṇa*). It is said that two or three decads arise for those born from a womb;

however, elsewhere, many groups (*kalāpa*) arise together. For even in the state of a Brahmā, many groups arise simultaneously within a body measuring several hundred *gāvuta*, such that the material phenomena (*rūpa*) exceed thirty. This is as in the case of a lamb born on that very day.
Some say that "jātuṇṇa" refers to wool. Others say it is the wool of a wool-bearing sheep born in the Himalayan region. Still others say it is the wool of a sheep taken after splitting open its womb.
Regarding these destinies (*gati*), there is a classification of the occurrence of these birth-bases (*yoni*) according to whether they do or do not occur within them;
such is the distinction in the occurrence of birth-bases by way of destiny.
630. "Excluding the earth-dwellers" means the exclusion of the earth-deities (bhummadeva) with respect to the classification of birth (yoni), because they are similar to human beings.
By the negation of the first three modes of birth (yoni), it follows by implication that the final mode of birth is permitted.
"In the three destinations" (gatittiya) refers to the three destinations known as humans, ghosts (peta), and animals; for these were not previously mentioned here.
The phrase "by the word 'ca'" and so forth was stated to show that the word *ca* has the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*avuttasamuccaya*).

But why are the first three modes of birth (*yoni*) not present among the *nijjhāmataṇhika* pretas? Because they are impossible. For since those [pretas] are constantly afflicted by illness, there is no indulgence in sensual pleasure;
thus, they do not belong to the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and other categories. Furthermore, an embryo does not remain in their wombs because of the presence of a net-like membrane (*jāla*).

Some say: "Because their bodies are scorched by the flames of fire when they are reborn there, and because birth from moisture (*saṃsedaja*) is impossible in moist places or among flowers and the like, moisture-born beings do not exist among them.
Therefore he says: "For they are exclusively of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).

Regarding the phrase "among the material-brahmas who are of spontaneous birth," he distinguishes the material-brahmas by specifying that they are those of spontaneous birth. "Among the material-brahmas" means...

In this context, the locative case is used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*), while in the phrase "among those of spontaneous birth" (*opapātikesu*), it is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

Therefore, from the general category stated as "among those of the spontaneous birth mode" (*opapātikayonikesu*), the phrase "among the form-possessing Brahmas" (*rūpībrahmesu*) selects a specific subset thereof.
Regarding the phrase "of the decads of eye, ear, and physical base, and of the nonad of life," some say: "of the heptads of eye, ear, and physical base, and of the hexad of life."

Having stated the reason—“By way of four groups, twenty-seven material phenomena arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness in the fine-material existence (rūpabhava), because odors and tastes as nutriment are excluded therein”—they support that point by saying: “For in the Canon it is said:
‘At the moment of rebirth in the fine-material element, the five bases appear for other beings, the gods, excluding [odors and tastes].’”
It is said, "five elements become manifest. Likewise, it is said, "in the form element there are six bases and nine elements";
this was stated in order to show the bases and elements existing therein by way of a comprehensive inclusion.

And in the *Kathāvatthu*, the existence of the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) and so forth in that [form element] is rejected, just as the existence of the nose-base (*ghānāyatana*) and so forth is rejected, [with the words]: "There is not therein..."
"Is it the nose-base? "Yes. "Are there odor-bases therein? "One should not say so," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is impossible to maintain that odors and tastes—which lack the odor-base and taste-base—exist therein, just as the earth element and others exist in the non-tangible bases;
for the intrinsic nature of earth and the rest cannot be established apart from their capacity to be touched.
This is because there is no such thing as the intrinsic nature of odor or taste that is distinct from the state of being the sense bases of odor and taste.

Furthermore, if they were not called "bases" (*āyatana*) because they lack the status of being causes for olfactory contact and so forth, there would be no reason not to call them "odor element" (*gandhadhātu*) and "taste element" (*rasadhātu*), since the term "element" (*dhātu*) denotes that which is devoid of a sentient being or a living soul; moreover, their status as phenomena (*dhamma*) must be admitted without exception.

Because there is no other [nature] apart from the characteristic of maintaining its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and so forth. Furthermore, the status of phenomena as *āyatanas* is absolute, as stated in the *Yamaka*:
“Is a phenomenon (*dhamma*) an *āyatana*? Yes. Therefore, even though they lack the status of being the *āyatana*s of odor and taste, some sort of *āyatana*-status must be predicated of them.
And if, like the status of earth and so forth being distinct from the status of the tangible (*phoṭṭhabba*), the status of odor and taste were distinct...
If they were to have some other intrinsic nature (sabhāva), they would be included within the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana).

However, since they possess the intrinsic nature of odor and taste as well as the status of being bases (āyatanabhāva), it follows that "it is both an odor and a base, thus the odor-base; it is both a taste and a base, thus the taste-base.
Therefore, their status as the odor-base and taste-base cannot be denied. Furthermore, this is because of the statement: "There are three kinds of nutriment."

It is understood that edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is absent there. Therefore, the enumeration of material phenomena (*rūpa-gaṇanā*) should be made in such a way that it does not contradict the Canon (*pāḷi*).
For in this way, the nature of things (*dhammatā*) is not subverted—so they say. To this, it is replied:
Because the sense bases of nose and tongue are absent for beings in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), even though odors and tastes exist [there], [they are not included].
Because they do not perform the function of a sense-base (*āyatana-kicca*), those [nutriments] are not mentioned;

instead, it is said in the Canon, "five sense-bases manifest" and "six sense-bases," and so forth. Furthermore, because of the absence of edible food, the function of nutriment—which consists in the production of the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence—is not performed; however, this is not the case in every respect.

Because of the absence of odors, tastes, and nutritive essence (*ojā*). Thus, due to the absence of both the subject and its function, neither the object nor the phenomenon possessing that function is mentioned.
For in whatever existence a subject is absent, in that existence there is—strictly speaking (*nippariyāyena*)—no status as a sense-base (*āyatana*) for the object based on that subject;
thus, even though they exist, they are not mentioned, just as in that very same fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*).
[The earth, fire, and air elements possess] the state of being a sense-sphere of the tangible (phoṭṭhabbāyatana).

However, when there is mention of something in a particular place, its status as a sense-sphere (āyatana) in the primary sense (nippariyāya) is stated to be caused by the presence of the corresponding object, as is the case for the sense-sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) in that very context.
If the status of an object as a sense-sphere in the primary sense is caused by the presence of the corresponding subject, how [can this apply] to non-percipient beings?

Regarding the statement that "two bases (āyatana) manifest": since the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) does not exist for non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), and because of their lack of an eye-base, the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) is not an object for others—is this not a contradiction?

This is not a contradiction. For the same intention by which the odor-base (gandhāyatana) and so forth are not mentioned among those with perception in the form realm (rūpadhātu), by that same intention the visible-form base is also not mentioned; thus, for the non-percipient beings, there is only one [base].

The sense base (āyatana) must be stated. For when those things which possess the status of a sense base in the primary sense—considering their respective nature as the domain of the faculties—are being pointed out, [the odors and so forth] are not mentioned separately as distinct sense bases within the form element (rūpadhātu).

This is because they lack that [separate] status there, because they do not transcend the essential nature of phenomena (dhamma), and because they fall under the category of the sense base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) by becoming the objective domain of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa).
Having done so, it is stated in the Pāḷi as “the five bases. For this purpose, the designation “dhammāyatana” is applied in a general sense;
or alternatively, having grouped them together like the planks of a back-rib cage, they are called “the five bases.

And by whatever intention the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) was spoken of in relation to non-percipient beings, by that same intention the odors and so forth of percipient beings [are also included].
The phrase "they should be grasped separately" is stated for the purpose of showing this method: "For the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) gods, two bases (āyatana) become manifest.
For even though their own faculties (indriya) are absent there, there is no transcending of the essential nature of the visible base (rūpāyatana), which is the sphere of color;
therefore, it is called simply the "visible base. And by this demonstration of the method, having added the three [bases] beginning with odor (gandha), etc.,...
This demonstrates that there are eight bases for those possessing perception and five for those lacking perception. This must be accepted in this way;
otherwise, because it would be impossible to touch [objects] in the fine-material world (rūpaloka), even the vocal sound of the Brahmās consisting of earth and so forth would not exist.
For the production of sound does not occur without impact and friction, nor is there [sound] from things whose nature is to be touched.

In some cases, the state of not being tangible can be understood; furthermore, in the absence of the triad of primary elements (bhūta) designated as the tangible base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana), there could be no occurrence of the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) and so forth even in the form realm (rūpabhava).

Therefore, although earth and the other elements are capable of being touched, their status as tangibles is not mentioned therein because of the absence of the body faculty (kāyindriya). And having established it thus:
In the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu), their designation as "possessing resistance" (sappaṭigha) is thus justified. For it is said:
"In the case of non-percipient beings, depending on one invisible and resistant great primary (mahābhūta), two great primaries [arise]," and so forth.
Furthermore, "resistance" (paṭigha) refers to the state of being directed toward the sensitive body-faculty by means of the impact of the primary elements that serve as its support.
In this case, however, there is the state of having that same nature. And because there is no contact with that which has a nature incapable of being touched, it does not exist [there].

If, even though the objective factor is absent there, the sense-sphere of visible form is apprehended and it is said, "two spheres," then why is it not said, "five spheres," by apprehending the sense-spheres of odor and so forth? This is shown by way of the underlying principle (naya).

This meaning has already been stated as "the teaching proceeds. Alternatively, the mention there of the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) alone is intended with reference to its being the object of the sensitivity (*pasāda*) belonging to other planes;
it is not because of the non-existence of the others, nor because of the absence of the status of a base even in a figurative sense.

For the visible-form base of those in the non-percipient realm is [the object] for the inhabitants of the *Vehapphala* heaven who dwell on the same level, as well as for those in the higher planes of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*).
It becomes an object of faith (*pasāda*), but not of smell or taste; therefore, it is appropriate that these two alone are not mentioned there.
Furthermore, in the *Kathāvatthu*, the refutation was made with reference to one who asserts the existence of the odor-base (*gandhāyatana*) and so forth in an absolute sense (*nippariyāyena*).
Even if this statement does not clarify the non-existence of the odor-base and so forth there, it nevertheless illuminates their existence.
"But is it not the case that there is no other statement [to the contrary]? This is not so, because in the *Aṭṭhakathās* (Commentaries) their existence therein has been established and stated.

For whatever statement of the *Aṭṭhakathā* does not contradict the *Pāḷi*, that is authoritative just like the *Pāḷi* itself, because it has come down to the present day through an unblemished succession of teachers. In this regard, it might be argued: "That which..."
Is it not the case that the word of the Commentary does not contradict the Canon and is therefore authoritative, whereas this [other view] contradicts it?

This is not so, because it has been demonstrated that there is no contradiction. The Blessed One’s teaching on the elements (*dhātu*) was for the purpose of demonstrating the emptiness of beings in the sense bases (*āyatana*), such as the eye and so forth, and in the consciousnesses supported by them; thus, it refers precisely to those things spoken of as sense bases.
Since they illuminate the state of being elements (dhātubhāva), it is indeed appropriate that even the state of being elements is not mentioned for them.

Therefore, one should understand that there is no room here for suspicion of contradicting the nature of things (dhammatā), as the enumeration of matter is performed here by way of the "eye-decade" and so forth, in such a way that there is no conflict with the Pāḷi.
Regarding "other moisture-born and spontaneously born [beings]"—this refers to other spontaneously born beings, excluding the material Brahmās.

The connection here should be understood as "among the moisture-born" (*saṃsedajesu*). For in this context, the mention of "others" (*añña*) is a qualification of the "spontaneously born" (*opapātika*), not a qualification of the "moisture-born," because [the latter] are impossible [in that state].
Indeed, there is a relationship between a qualifier and a qualificand only when both possibility and deviation exist.

Among the sense-sphere gods (*kāmāvacara-deva*), at all times—both during rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatti*)—there are material phenomena (*rūpa*) according to the aforementioned continuity (*santati*).
It is said, "And these are always among the gods," because they never have deficient faculties nor are they non-existent.
Because the eye completes these ten, it is called the "eye-decade" (*cakkhudasaka*); or else, the decade is called the "eye-decade" because it is characterized by the unique eye.
"The rest are likewise" means that just as the eye-decade has been described, so too are the others.
The remaining decades should also be understood by applying [the same logic].

Expanding upon the meaning stated in brief as, “In the moisture-born and spontaneously born wombs, at least thirty,” he said, “But at least...,” and so forth; however, this does not accord with the canonical text (pāḷi).
For in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, the rebirth of moisture-born and spontaneously born beings of the sense-sphere realm who lack noses is not mentioned.
For it has been stated: "At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), for some eleven bases (āyatana) appear;
for some ten bases; for others another ten bases; for some nine bases; and for some seven bases appear.
It has not been stated that "eight bases appear. For if there were rebirth even for one who lacks the nose...
It might be said three times that "ten bases appear," and it might be said three times that "nine bases appear," yet this was not stated.
Therein, "at the moment of rebirth" means at the moment of *paṭisandhi* (relinking). "Eleven" refers to the eleven bases of one whose bases are complete, excluding the sound base (*saddāyatana*).
There are eleven bases (āyatana). For someone [who lacks eyes], there are ten bases—namely, for the blind, excluding the eye-base.
Another set of ten bases refers to those who lack ears—namely, for the deaf, excluding the ear-base. There are nine bases for one who is both blind and deaf—excluding the eye-base and the ear-base.
There are seven bases for a being born from a womb, by way of the bases of visible form, odor, flavor, body, tangibles, mind, and mental objects.
It has been stated [that one born with a deficiency in the eye, ear, or nose possesses eight bases]. If one deficient in the eye, ear, or nose could arise, he would possess only eight bases;
yet it was not stated that "eight bases manifest. Therefore, there is no such thing as being deficient in the eye, ear, or nose.
Furthermore, regarding birth without a nose, it should have been stated again that "for some, ten other bases also manifest."

It might be so. And that being the case, just as it was stated once—on account of one who is both blind and deaf—that "for someone nine bases appear," so too, on account of one who is blind but not deaf, and on account of one who is deaf but not blind, it would have to be said:
"for someone other [nine bases appear], and for someone else yet other nine bases appear. This is the meaning.
They say that questions such as those concerning the manifestation of the elements (*dhātu-pātubhāva*) should also be stated in this way.

And here, while the phrase "seventy at most, then material phenomena" is applied according to two modes of birth—namely, the moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) and the apparitional (*opapātika*)—this [phrase] "thirty at least" is not so applied.
Rather, this must be applied specifically according to the moisture-born mode of birth alone. This is because even that which is indicated by a single grammatical connection (*ekayoga-niddiṭṭha*)...

The statement that "a portion obtains a connection" means that for one born by moisture (*saṃsedaja*) who is blind from birth, deaf, noseless, and asexual, thirty material phenomena arise by way of the tongue-decad, body-decad, and base-decad;
it does not apply to one of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*). This is the intention of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) in this regard.
However, as for those who [hold that] "for one of spontaneous birth who is blind from birth, deaf, noseless, and asexual, [the tongue-decad, body-decad, and base-decad...]"
They say, "It is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* that thirty material phenomena arise by way of this [condition]," but that should not be accepted, for it is a reading resulting from negligence.

For if that were the case, it would contradict the commentary on the *Āyatana-yamaka*, which states: "In the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), however, there is no spontaneously born being (*opapātika*) who lacks a nose.
If such a being existed, one would have to say, 'For some, eight bases (*āyatana*) become manifest.'"
It has been stated. However, others say: "The passage from 'For some, eleven bases manifest' down to 'For some, nine bases' was spoken with reference to those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).
Therefore, there is established no contradiction between what precedes and what follows in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
Thus, this explanation of the meaning according to the aforementioned canonical text (*pāḷi*) is entirely consistent and harmonious. This is what [they say].
Some say: “By the mention of *opapātika* (spontaneously born beings), moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) beings are also included.

For instance, in the exposition of the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*, in the description of such passages as ‘At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm, eleven bases appear for some,’ only the term *opapātika* is used—as in ‘of spontaneously born *petas*’—and not the term ‘moisture-born.’”
It should be understood that this was stated by way of including those born of moisture (*saṃsedaja*) with complete sense bases among those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*).

For it is said in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "Those of the moisture-born womb are stated as being included within spontaneous birth according to whether their sense bases are complete or incomplete.
Or else, [it refers to] the entire womb of complete sense bases under the category of the primary type of womb.
And because it was stated [elsewhere] "of those born spontaneously (opapātika)" in order to demonstrate that, whereas here,
in order to reveal two modes of birth (yoni) by their very nature and to show the manifestation of form at its minimum even in the case of moisture-born (saṃsedaja) birth,
it was said "in the moisture-born and spontaneous modes of birth," excluding the other from the category of the spontaneous mode; all of this should be understood after careful investigation.
"In between the maximum and minimum" means in the midst of the limits of the maximum and minimum of material form as stated thus: "seventy" and "thirty.
The alternative [number] should be understood according to what is appropriate: because for one blind in the states of misery (apāya) there is an absence of the six decads of the eye;
likewise, for one deaf, there is an absence of the decad of the ear; and for one both blind and deaf, there is an absence of the five decads of the eye and the decad of the ear.
It should be understood by way of this method and others like it. Furthermore, whatever remains to be said here has already been stated.
631. Non-difference is the mutual similarity of the aggregates and so forth between death and rebirth-linking; difference is their dissimilarity.
They are also non-different in terms of the object for one who, having passed away from this or that state among the four formless realms, is reborn right there.
...so it is said. Likewise, however, there is no rebirth below in the fine-material plane (rūpabhava).

Rebirth below after falling from the immaterial plane (arūpabhūmi) occurs only in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), and even there, it is only a three-rooted (tihetuka) rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

They say, moreover, that one who has passed away from the fine-material plane may also have a two-rooted (duhetuka) rebirth. Immediately after a death consciousness with a non-lofty (amahaggata) and external object—
The second and fourth immaterial rebirth-linkings have sublime internal objects. Thus it was said because only the general method was shown;
and having included everything not explicitly mentioned, he said: "This, first of all, is the method for the immaterial planes alone.

Because the access concentration of the fine-material and immaterial realms is powerful, there is no rebirth in a miserable destination after passing away from them; hence, [he speaks of] "passing away from certain happy destinations."
He said: Regarding the phrase "rebirth-linking in some miserable states" (*ekaccaduggatipaṭisandhi*), the purpose of the inclusion of the word "some" (*ekacca*) must be sought.

However, the intended meaning here might be this: among those described as "diverse in body and diverse in perception," there are some beings in the states of ruin (*vinipātika*) who possess rebirth-linking with three roots (*tihetuka*) and so forth.
Taking their rebirth-linking as "rebirth-linking in a miserable state" by virtue of their being in a state of ruin, [this is stated] after all death from a happy destination.
And since that rebirth-linking does not occur only after death from some happy realm, the term "some unhappy realm" is used in order to exclude that possibility.
For rebirth-linking in the states of misery occurs only after death from some happy realm, not after death from every happy realm.
Alternatively, rebirth-linking in the unhappy realms is of two kinds: immediately following death from some happy realm, and following death from an unhappy realm. In this regard—
Having excluded the latter, it is stated that one should take only the former: “the rebirth-linking of certain miserable states.
Regarding “rebirth-linking with roots from death without roots,” this should be applied to both two-rooted and three-rooted [rebirths].
For, as in the case of the frog-devaputta and others, there can indeed be a three-rooted rebirth-linking following a death without roots.

"And by way of the opposite for each respective case, it should be applied as appropriate" means that among the specific distinctions such as "the death of some in a happy destination and the rebirth-linking of some in an unhappy destination," whatever is applicable—such as "the death of some in an unhappy destination and the rebirth-linking of some in an unhappy destination"—that should be applied.
The neuter designation is used in view of the mere fact of being applicable. "Should be applied" (yojetabbaṃ).

Or rather, the meaning of the terms should be understood as they are stated. However, in such cases as “for a death with a sublime (mahaggata) and internal object, there is a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) with a non-sublime (amahaggata) and external object,” one must not apply the terms in a reversed manner.

For there is no rebirth-linking with a non-sublime and external object in the formless planes following a death with a sublime and internal object. [Regarding] “immediately after a four-aggregate formless death...”
The reversal of the statement, "The five aggregates are the rebirth-linking [consciousness] of the sense-sphere," has been applied by oneself.
Furthermore, there is no reversal at all for the statement, "For a death with a past object, the rebirth-linking has a present object.

Thus, only the distinction regarding their differentiation has been shown in detail; however, the distinction regarding their non-differentiation exists within each individual differentiation in its respective place.
It should be understood by way of the linking of death and rebirth-linking: "From a five-aggregate death in the sense sphere, [there arise] five aggregates in the sense sphere... up to ...

from a death without applied thought and sustained thought, [there arise] [aggregates] without applied thought and sustained thought. However, for a four-aggregate death, four aggregates [arise] as already linked by themselves.
It can be understood through this very method; therefore, no distinction regarding non-differentiation among the five aggregates and so forth has been shown.
632. "Iti" means in the manner thus described. This consciousness has obtained its conditions through volitional formations (saṅkhāra) accompanied by co-operative causes such as ignorance (avijjā).
Because there is no presiding entity established by outsiders, it is merely a collection of material and immaterial phenomena (rūpa- and arūpa-dhamma).

Therefore he said: "Neither a being (satto) nor a soul (jīvo). It is called "approaches" (upeti) merely as a conventional expression; in actual fact, however, it is due to the completeness of conditions.
The intended meaning is "mere arising by way of another existence. Therefore he said, "And of that," and so forth.
"There, without a cause" means without a cause in that context. "By way of human death and human rebirth-linking" means from human death to human rebirth-linking;
for in this way, the mention of what is manifest serves as a qualification for both. And here, "manifestness" is by way of the aggregates immediately preceding [the rebirth].
It should be understood as in such passages as “passing away and being reborn.
Or, by the phrase “in the sequence of human death and rebirth-linking,” it means by the sequence of rebirth-linking for anyone following human death. For he will say accordingly:
“whether relishing the support or not relishing it.”

"Sarasenā" means by their very nature; the meaning is: because the formative forces of life have been completely exhausted. "By means of an effort" (upakkamena) means by an effort such as decapitation, etc., performed either by oneself or by another.
"All the bondages of the joints of every limb and member" refers to the binding of all the joints of the limbs and members;
[the phrase refers to] those who cut them. "Sannipāta" means falling down or occurrence. Even the region of the heart gradually dries up.
"Only a small remnant remains, let alone the body"—thus he said, "while the body is gradually drying up. For this very reason, he said, "dependent upon the heart-base that remains at that moment.

The phrase "when the eye and so forth have ceased" is stated with the intention that, just as the sense-bases (*āyatana*) of those dwelling in the womb arise successively, their cessation also occurs successively;
or else, it is said "have ceased" with reference to their having reached a state of extreme feebleness.
This was stated [with respect to] cessation, not total (anavasesa) cessation. For even immediately after the five-door consciousness, death was previously shown.
And in the *Yamaka*: "For whom the eye-base ceases, for that person does the mind-base cease? Yes.
Or, for whom the mind-base ceases, for that person does the eye-base cease? [Yes,] for those possessing consciousness."
"For those who are eyeless at the moment of death, the mind-base ceases, but the eye-base does not cease for them.
For those with eyes at the moment of death, both the mind-base and the eye-base cease," and so forth;
thus, the cessation of the eye-base and the other bases together with the death-consciousness has been stated.
"Merely the heart-base" means merely in the location of the heart-base. For the body-faculty does not function supported by the heart-base.
They say that it is stated as "supported by the heart-base remaining at that moment" because at that time even the heart-base has very little remaining, like a green palm leaf placed in the heat.
However, this is because the other bases are incapable of performing their respective functions.
It is said that at that time consciousness exists supported solely by the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*); thus it is stated: "supported by the remaining heart-base at that very moment.

"Weighty" (*garuka*) refers to such acts as matricide and so forth, or other sublime (*mahaggata*) states, or others of a similar nature. "Habitual" (*samāsevita*) means performed frequently. "Proximate" (*āsanna*) means performed at the time of death;

or even if performed at another time, it is that which has become manifest and is recollected. "Previously done" (*pubbakata*)— [...]* (The text continues with the definition of *pubbakata*) *Note: The provided source text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on the Abhidhammattha Sangaha, specifically the section concerning the five types of kamma.*

To be experienced in subsequent successions (*aparāpariyāyavedanīya*). "Condition by way of what remains" (*laddhāvasesapaccaya*) refers to the formative force (*saṅkhāra*), such as ignorance and so forth, which serves as the condition for consciousness by virtue of what remains [after the death-moment].
By this, he refers to wholesome or unwholesome volition that has been accumulated and for which the opportunity to ripen has been created.

"Kamma-sign" (*kamma-nimitta*) is that object-base (*vatthu*) which one takes as an object while performing an action at the time of accumulation; even if it occurred at the end of hundreds of thousands of millions of eons in the past.
Indeed, when a deed has been performed, at the time of its ripening, it comes and stands before one as either the deed itself or the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*).
As for the "sign of the destination" (*gati-nimitta*), it is a single image appearing in the place where one is to be reborn;

and that, for one destined to be reborn in hell, has already been described below as "the color of a mass of flames," and so forth. Regarding that object such as the deed, whose dangers are concealed by ignorance, the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*)...
[It occurs] by way of being an object and a basis for arising.

Because craving has not been abandoned, and because the previously arisen continuity has transformed accordingly, consciousness proceeds inclined, leaning, and tending toward the place of rebirth-linking;
thus it is said, "craving leads. "Concomitant formations" means...
Volition co-arising with the death-proximate javana-consciousness, or alternatively, all factors beginning with contact;

these "cast" consciousness toward its object, such as karma, at that stage of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). The meaning is that they function as the cause for the establishment of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking toward that object, as if they were casting it there.
"That" refers to that consciousness. [This concerns] the death-consciousness, the rebirth-linking consciousness, and the consciousness proximate to them.

By way of continuity, consciousness is brought to a state of unity. Being bent by craving... [as it is said] "...it proceeds"—this shows that the bending, the hurling, the abandoning of the former support, the seeking out of another support, and the proceeding devoid of a support—all these belong to that very same single consciousness by way of continuity, and not to any other.
And by saying "by way of continuity," he refutes this false grasp: "This very same consciousness runs on and wanders about, not another."
He rejects [the objection]. For when there is the principle of diversity (*nānattanaya*), there is the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*) by way of the continuity of the stream.
And here, the object of action and so forth, which is bound to the personal existence (*tattabhāva*) of the previous birth, should be regarded as like a rope tied to a tree on this side of a river;

consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is like the man; craving (*taṇhā*) is like his desire to cross over the boundary; the volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) that effect the crossing are like the act of throwing [the rope]; just as...
And just as that man, while establishing himself on the further shore, whether he finds some support from a tree on the further shore or does not find it,
establishes himself solely upon the earth by means of his own bodily efforts;

even so, this [consciousness], while finding support in the heart-base (hadayavatthu)— which is bound to the individual existence within another becoming— in the five-aggregate existence (pañcavokārabhava),...
In the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*), not finding gratification, it proceeds solely through kamma associated with the object.
In this context, "finding gratification" means reaching or obtaining.

"Because of the linking of the beginning of another existence" means because of the state of being the initial linking of another existence—that is, a different existence. "Another existence and so forth" [refers to]...
The meaning is: "the linking of those [beings] who are within the various realms of existence, wombs, destinies, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings.
This consciousness has not come from elsewhere, because it arises right here in this very existence. "Kamma" refers to the kamma that produces rebirth-linking.
"Formations" (saṅkhārā) refers to the projecting formations associated with the impulsion-consciousness immediately preceding death. "Inclination" (natī) is so called by way of bending.
Craving is that which proceeds. The object consists of karma and so forth.
633. Although there exists the relationship of condition and conditioned in the case of echoes of sounds and the like, the continuity of the stream is not evident;

therefore, without touching upon their state of identity or difference, [the author] demonstrates only the arising from causes that do not come from the future nor go to the past, saying: "In this regard..."
And so he said, beginning with “...and. Regarding the phrase “caused by sound, etc.,” here an echo is caused by sound;
a lamp is caused by another lamp, and so forth; finger-calculation (muddā) is caused by marking; a shadow is caused by a face facing a mirror, and so forth.
They exist without going elsewhere—that is, without reaching the location of the conditions such as sound—because they do not exist prior to that [location]. Thus, this too is [the same].
Rebirth-consciousness does not become caused by having gone to the place of its cause, because it did not exist prior to that.
Therefore, this [consciousness] has not come here from a previous existence by way of the location of its cause, as an echo and so forth do from sound and so forth;
