nor has it arisen there without a cause, as an echo and so forth do without sound and so forth. This is the meaning. Alternatively, they exist elsewhere...

"Having come" means that having been present previously at the location of the conditions, they do not become those conditions by going elsewhere from there, because they did not exist prior to their arising;
nor is it the case that the conditions such as sound do not exist. This [case] should also be applied in the same manner as stated.
There is no unity, because even when there is a single continuum, one distinct consciousness alone manifests. Nor is there plurality, because of the binding together of the continuum.

Like a lamp. For just as a momentary flame of a lamp is spoken of as "that very same [lamp]" by taking its continuity as a single unity, and it performs its functional purpose, so too should it be understood here.
By the words "If indeed," etc., he shows that within the connection of a continuum, there is no absolute identity or difference to be grasped, and he demonstrates the fault in grasping them as such.
"This is the method" is an extended application (atidesa) to all causes and effects produced from causes, such as seeds, sprouts, and so forth.

He shows that the application [of the analogy] should be made according to what is possible. For here too, if there were absolute identity between the cause and the consciousness produced by the cause, the divine realm could not have arisen from the human realm.
If there were absolute difference, there would be no fruit for one who possesses the karma;
therefore, just as in the case of the statement, "the seed is red, the fruit is red," and so forth, [it is said]: "Venerable sir, formerly I was Rohitassa..."
there would be an annihilation of conventional designations such as "this person was a seer" and so forth;
therefore, in this context, regarding the continuity of the stream and the relationship between cause and effect, one should neither exclusively assert nor grasp at either identity or difference.

And here, by the negation of absolute identity, he refutes the view that "pleasure and pain are self-made"; by the negation of absolute difference, [he refutes the view that they are] "made by another."
By stating that pleasure and pain arise from causes, he refutes the view that they are "fortuitously arisen" (*adhiccasamuppanna*).
634. *Tattha* means "in the place where the fruit arises. *Aññassa* means "from one other than the person by whom that karma was performed.
*Aññato* means "from something other than the karma that produced it. This is because it has been stated: "A mere phenomenon (*dhammamatta*) enters into another state of existence."
He investigates: "In the absence of one who enjoys the fruit, to whom would that fruit belong? In this context, "therein" (*tattha*) refers to the aforementioned inquiry.
"In that" (*tatra*) means within a single continuum (*ekasantāne*). The meaning is: within the very same continuum in which the action was produced within that mass of phenomena (*dhammapuñja*).
"Of this matter" (*etassa atthassa*) means: although the cause and the fruit are distinct in their actual nature, they are connected by way of that very relationship of cause and fruit.
The meaning of this is that the fruit cannot be said to be "of another" or "from another.
The cultivation of the four sweets, liquid lac, and so forth, is the preparation (*abhisaṅkhāra*) of the seeds of mangoes, citron trees, and the like.

In this context, the prepared seed is like the being (*satta*), the preparation is like the karma, and the continuity of the sprout and so forth from the seed is like the continuity of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-viññāṇa*) and so forth for the being.
Just as there is the existence of a sweet fruit with red filaments produced from that very seed and from that same formative process,
so too should the existence of the fruit be understood as arising solely from the karma of the sentient being who is the agent of that karma.
This applies to the mastery of knowledge, the training in crafts, and the application of medicinal herbs performed during the body of a child.
Nor do they go into an old body. Yet, for the sake of that [body], there is proficiency in knowledge, mastery of skills, and health in the old body;
and these do not belong to another, because they arise only in an old body included within that very same continuum (*saṃtati*).
Nor do they come from elsewhere without the application of such things as the acquisition of knowledge as previously employed, in the absence of which they would not exist.
Because of non-existence; thus, here too, regarding the continuum, whatever fruit there is, that belongs to none other. And it should be construed as "not from another.
By this, he demonstrates that in the absence of the formations (*saṅkhāra*), there is simply an absence of the fruit, but he does not intend to exclude other conditions.

As for what was said, "I shall speak on that point"—this is the ellipsis of the statement. Or rather, the connection is: "In the absence of the experiencer, the conventional designation (*sammuti*) of an 'experiencer' is established. "It bears fruit" is the conventional designation; hence, "the conventional designation of bearing fruit" (*phalatisammuti*).
"Of the phenomena designated as 'tree'" means: of the primary (bhūta) and derived (upādāya) phenomena that serve as the basis for the designation "tree.

"Therefore" means: because, just as in the continuum of the aggregates there is the conventional expression of an agent—saying "he performs merit" or "he performs evil"—upon the arising of wholesome or unwholesome volition, so too upon the arising of its fruit, there is the expression "he experiences pleasure" or "he experiences pain."
This is a conventional expression for the "enjoyer"; therefore, there is no such thing as an "enjoyer" here that exists apart from the aggregates. 635. "Even though this is so" means:
even when there is non-transmigration and manifestation, and when the aforementioned faults have been avoided;

the sense is "it is established. "At the very moment of occurrence" means precisely at the moment the formations are occurring. "Prior to their occurrence" means prior to the moment of the accumulation of kamma.
This was said because they are equal in their non-existence previously. "And afterwards" means after the attainment of ripening.

To dispel the apprehension that if conditions are productive of results by virtue of having been performed even when the result has not yet ripened, then those [conditions] whose results have already ripened would likewise be productive of results simply by virtue of having been performed, he says: "And they do not constantly bring forth a fruit.
By the phrase "neither by way of existing nor by way of not existing," he refers to both existence and non-existence as the basis.

It avoids the faults already mentioned. Regarding that act of standing as a guarantor, the act of purchasing goods, or the act of contracting a debt—the mere performance of those acts serves as the condition for the fulfillment of their purpose, namely, the delivery of the corresponding goods or the repayment of the debt;
this is the meaning of "the fruit consisting of the delivery of what was not previously produced," and so forth.

636. "For the purpose of dispelling delusion" means for the purpose of removing the delusion regarding the process [of consciousness] that arises when the conditioning state of the aforementioned formations—both in rebirth-linking and during the course of existence—has not been analyzed and understood among the thirty-two types of consciousness.
"In the case of meritorious formations" (*puññābhisaṅkhāre*) is the locative case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).

"Without distinction" (*aviseseṇa*) means generally, by way of a collective whole, without making such divisions as "a triple-rooted [consciousness] is the condition for a triple-rooted [consciousness]," and so forth. In all cases, the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*) pertains to powerful kamma.
It should be applied according to the [appropriate] method. For it is shown in the *Paṭṭhāna-ṭīkā* that "weak kamma does not function as an object-predominance condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

The distinction regarding the fivefold wholesome volition of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) should be stated by specifying "excluding that which has attained direct knowledge (*abhiññā*"), or it need not be so stated, because there is no occasion for discussing what is not subject to ripening (*avipāka*) within the discourse on the state of being a condition for ripening (*vipāka*).

For it has already been explained above that the volition of direct knowledge (*abhiññā-cetanā*) is not subject to ripening (*avipāka*). This same principle applies here as well regarding the phrase "without distinction.
The phrase "of the five resultant consciousnesses" (*pañcannaṃ vipākaviññāṇānaṃ*) should be brought forward and connected [to the previous context].

Regarding "of the five": these are the eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness, the receiving mind-element (*sampaṭicchana-manodhātu*), and the two investigating mind-consciousness-elements (*santīraṇa-manoviññāṇadhātu*).
Of these five. "In the same way" means in exactly two ways.

But how is it that wholesome resultant consciousnesses, which function only with desirable objects, function in a miserable destination? To this he says: "In hell, [as experienced] by the Elder Mahāmoggallāna," and so forth.
For the Elder, having created a rain there through his psychic power and having extinguished the fires of hell for a certain period of time, [remained there].
He teaches the Dhamma to them.

That very same [volition] is the meritorious formation pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). However, the term "meritorious formation" in general encompasses both types—the sense-sphere and the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*)—collectively as a single category.
Regarding the phrase "the twelvefold division of unwholesome volitions," no reason is apparent for including the volition associated with restlessness (*uddhacca*) therein.

This must be investigated. That there is a condition for only one consciousness at rebirth-linking, and not during the course of existence—that restriction regarding the state of being a condition for only one applies to rebirth-linking, not to the course of existence.
For the intention is that during the course of existence, it is a condition for all seven.
"In the fine-material realm, for four" refers to the unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving-consciousness, and investigating-consciousness.

Furthermore, those [objects] are exclusively undesirable objects; and as to how there can be a conjunction with undesirable objects in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*), he says, "But that," and so forth.
The statement, "Likewise, in the world of the sense-sphere devas (*kāmāvacaradevaloka*), there are no undesirable forms and so on," is said by way of general rule (*yebhuyyavasena*).
For, as a rule, only desirable forms and so on appear to them, though occasionally an undesirable one may do so.
For even among certain devas, there occurs at times such as when the appearance of a portent arises, a conjunction with undesirable objects like withered garlands and the like.

637. Since a detailed exposition has already been made elsewhere, wishing now to provide a mere summary from that point onward, he says, "Starting from the beginning. For this very reason, he states, "In two types of existence," and so forth. Some humans also...
Since there are those born from eggs (aṇḍaja) and those born from moisture (saṃsedaja), it is said "in the four modes of birth" with reference to them.

By virtue of the commonality of having a single body and a single perception, even those belonging to the plane of the fourth jhāna—excluding the non-percipient beings and the formless realms—belong to the fourth station of consciousness alone.
This is the formation of merit. "In the manner already stated" means: by way of the asynchronous kamma-condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) and the decisive support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya).

And it is according to the method already stated. "According to possibility" means as follows: among the twenty-one wholesome and resultant states of the sense-sphere and fine-material sphere, fourteen occur both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence;
seven occur only during the course of existence—this is what is meant by "according to possibility.
"In those very same [beings]" refers specifically to those designated as having diversity of body and unity of perception.

The phrase "of the four consciousnesses" is stated with reference to existence (*bhava*) and so forth. However, the conditionality of the three consciousnesses included within those four must be applied to the three stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*).

Even though consciousness conditioned by formations (*saṅkhāra-paccaya-viññāṇa*) cannot be found in the non-percipient realm (*aviññāṇaka-sattāvāsa*), its being caused by formations is indeed obtainable there. For instance, in that place, the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) [is present].
It is a condition for the material phenomena produced by past karma (kaṭattārūpa) by way of the asynchronous kamma-condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya).

And it should be understood that in this brief exposition of the general method, the fact that the volitional formations of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth serve as conditions for consciousness such as wholesome resultant (kusala-vipāka) in the occurrence of rebirths in miserable states (duggati) and so on,
is to be understood through the very same method already explained regarding the realms of existence (bhava), and thus has not been stated here.
Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of Name-and-Form Conditioned by Consciousness (638). "Of the divisions of name-and-form": this refers to the classification of name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*).
Therein, first, in order to show the division of name—although consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is indeed name itself—it is [treated separately] because it is both a condition and an arisen-from-condition.
However, in order to show them without confusion, it is said: "The three aggregates beginning with feeling [are called *nāma*] because they bend toward the object.
But in this context, regarding the discussion of its occurrence, there is no possibility [of including *nibbāna*] because it is without conditions and lacks the quality of bending.
For that is called *nāma* in the sense of being bent (*namana*), not in the sense of the act of bending (*namana*). Of those *nāma* and *rūpa*, by way of pleasure and so forth...
And there is a classification by way of earth and so forth.
"One abode of beings" refers to the abode of non-percipient beings (*asaññasattāvāsa*). [This applies] to the first four and to the abode of non-percipient beings—thus, to five.

By the mention of "those born from a womb," those born from a placenta (*jalābuja*) are included; therefore, it is said, "and of those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*). And of those born from eggs and those who do not exist.

It should be applied. "The beginnings of the continuity" means the roots of the continuity of the aggregates (kalāpa). Although the derivative material phenomena (*vikāra-rūpa*) do not exist at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the characteristic and delimiting material phenomena (*lakkhaṇa-pariccheda-rūpa*) do exist;
therefore, pointing out that these are not ultimately established (*aparinipphanna*) in the ultimate sense, he says, "from the perspective of material form.
Having brought contact and the rest into a unity by way of their being the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*), [he states] "twenty-three..."
"Phenomena (dhammā)" is what was stated. "Having excluded" means not including earth and so forth that have entered into another group because they share the same characteristic.
"Of those" refers to the Brahmakāyika deities and others. "In detail" means by not abbreviating the material phenomena within all four types of continuity.

Regarding the phrase "but in the sense-sphere existence, as for the remaining beings of spontaneous birth," although it is true that those of spontaneous birth in the sense-sphere existence were mentioned here—

It should be understood that the mention of "the rest" (*sesa*) would be purposeful if there were others; however, since the egg-born and those born from a womb are [already] included, the egg-born and those born from a womb are the exceptions to the spontaneously born (*opapātika*) and moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*).
Therefore, it should be known that the term "the rest" was employed for this reason.

Alternatively, having stated the spontaneously born such as the Brahmakāyika gods and so forth, he said "the remaining spontaneously born" with reference to those other than them. Since those [remaining ones] also exist as formless (*arūpin*), he specified "in the sense-sphere existence" (*kāmabhava*).

It has been stated [that this is not mentioned]. However, it should be understood that for those whose sense bases are incomplete, the mental and material phenomena (*nāmarūpa*) can be understood by way of the enumeration of factors according to the method explained in the exposition of consciousness mixed with matter as they occur; thus, it was not mentioned.
"Together with the temperature coexisting with the rebirth-linking consciousness" means from the fire element among the material phenomena arisen together with the rebirth-linking consciousness.
Because the heart-basis has arisen at that very moment, there is weakness of the basis for the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
When their bodies are sustained by ingested food, there is a strong production of matter originated by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*); this is the connection.

"A person" (*naro*) refers to one who is hidden by the very fact of being in the mother's womb. At the minimum, only two octads originate from temperature and mind; this is said with reference to a time when sound is present.

“At most, for two new [beings],” it is said. Regarding the phrase “previously”: having taken into account that the materiality previously mentioned—beginning with the two continuities and ending with the group of seven—was stated here as arising at each of the three moments of every single consciousness, he says, “previously...
seventy-fold. That twofold [materiality] consists of that produced by temperature and that produced by consciousness.
That sound is of two kinds.
"To persist" means to remain by way of durability; however, it remains for only its own momentary duration.
"Determined in the four directions" means that their tops are joined to one another, while they are determined in the four directions by their bases. [They are] mutually...
And it stands like a broken boat after being embraced.

(639) Regarding the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), this is said with reference to the time when the five types of consciousness born of kamma arise—which do not produce matter—and with reference to the condition of co-nascent consciousness.
For at that time, there is only name (*nāma*) arising from the condition of kamma-consciousness.
However, even then it can be said that both exist, for matter is supported by the condition of subsequently-arisen consciousness (*pacchājāta-viññāṇa-paccaya*).

The phrase "among those without perception" (*asaññesu*) and so forth is stated with reference to the condition of kamma-consciousness. And regarding the phrase "in the occurrence within the five-aggregate existence" (*pañcavokārabhave ca pavattiyaṃ*):

it refers to the time of the arising of matter other than the kamma that produces the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth, as well as the time of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the time of the arising of the life-continuum and so forth.
It is appropriate to say that this was stated with reference to another time.

For at the time of the arising of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and so forth, it can be said that the materiality arising through the karma that produces it, as well as that resultant [consciousness], is a condition for karmic consciousness.

Indeed, although during the course of existence (pavatti) materiality and mentality proceeding by way of karma do not depend on a co-nascent consciousness-condition, they are nonetheless not independent of karmic consciousness.
"In all cases" means in both rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and the course of existence (*pavatta*).
"Mind-and-body conditioned by conascent consciousness" and "mind-and-body conditioned by kamma-consciousness" should be applied according to what is possible.

Regarding the expression "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), here the term *nāmarūpa* is identical in form to the word *nāma* through its own component part *nāma*, and to the word *rūpa* through its own component part *rūpa*; therefore...

"Of those having the same form, there is a single remainder" (*ekasesa*) means a partial *ekasesa*; the meaning is that the word "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) remains in place while other words for "name-and-form" are not seen.
"Non-resultant" (*avipāka*) means other than resultant (*vipāka*). Since [the mind] is considered twofold from that [perspective], the phrase "this is indeed appropriate" should be connected to that.

In the phrase "at the moment of wholesome and so forth" (*kusalādicittakkhaṇe*), by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is implied that just as in the moments of unwholesome and functional minds, so too in the moments of resultant minds.
It should be understood that [the object] originated by kamma that does not produce a result (vipāka) is included.

However, at the moment of a resultant consciousness (vipākacitta), both [types of objects] are obtained through the condition of volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa) according to the method previously stated; therefore, in order to exclude such moments of resultant consciousness, it is said: "at the moment of wholesome and other types of consciousness.
640. "According to the Suttanta method" is stated because the decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya) for material phenomena is not mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*.

In the Suttanta, however, when something exists because another exists, and does not exist when that other is absent, the latter is considered its decisive support (*upanissaya*), source (*nidāna*), cause (*hetu*), and origin (*pabhava*);
thus, in the statement "name-and-form has consciousness as its decisive support," the fact that form has consciousness as its decisive support is stated.
And in the *Vanapattha-pariyāya*, the postures and abodes have the forest-thicket, village, town, city, country, and person as their respective decisive supports.
Furthermore, it is stated that the requisites for life, such as robes and so forth, arise both with difficulty and without difficulty;

yet forest retreats and the like do not serve as object-predominance conditions (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) or other types of conditions for the postures (*iriyāpatha*) or for the arising of robes and such things.

Therefore, according to the method of the Suttantas, the state of being a predominance condition (*upanissayabhāva*) should be understood as the absolute non-existence [of the effect] in the absence [of the condition].
It cannot even be said that the formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) of the mental (nāma) serves as a condition for the object at the time of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and so forth;
therefore, from the perspective of the discourses (suttanta-paryāya), the state of being a condition is stated to belong to matter alone in a single way.
For when it is said that this is a condition for matter, which is subject to doubt, it need not be said that it is a condition for the mental.

Because the [mental] process (*pavatta*) is well-known, he takes up the rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), which is not so well-known, and asks, "But how is this? and so forth. It should be understood that from the standpoint of the Sutta, the name (*nāma*) arises with consciousness as its condition, and from the standpoint of reasoning (*yutti*), the form (*rūpa*) does.
Having established it through reasoning, he strengthens it by means of the Sutta, saying, "And also of that produced by kamma," and so forth.
"Of that produced by mind alone" means just like that produced by mind. And here, by the Blessed One speaking thus, "With consciousness as condition, name-and-form," [he shows the meaning].

Because, when investigated by the wise, only name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is seen as occurring in the ultimate sense, and neither a "being" nor a "living soul" (jīva), therefore the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion, which cannot be turned back by anyone.
For the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma is the elucidation of emptiness (suññata). Alternatively, by the statement regarding the state of being merely name-and-form...
It is stated that within the process of existence there is merely the truth of suffering.

And by the exposition of the truth of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the practice leading to its cessation are likewise expounded. This is because there is no suffering that is causeless, nor any that does not cease through the cessation of its causes;
furthermore, cessation cannot be attained without a means. Thus, this is the exposition of the Four Noble Truths.
The Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma is to be established.

Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Section on the Six Sense Bases Conditioned by Name-and-Form (641): *Taṃ*: that [refers to] name-and-form. *Tassa*: of that [refers to] the six sense bases. *Tādisasseva*: of exactly that same kind [refers to] the residual compound (*ekasesa*).
"Here too, 'only'"—the reason for taking up only the triad of aggregates is as already stated.

"Necessarily"—this is said with reference to the fact that, as far as possible, the four great elements, the six bases, and life-force are invariably conditions for the sixfold sense base as it occurs, by way of such factors as co-nascence, support, pre-existence, and faculty. [This does not apply] to the visible-object base and so forth...
However, it should be understood that they are not included [in this context] because they lack the state of being co-nascent, supportive, and protective.

Furthermore, their status as objects, objects-of-objects, prenascent, and so forth, does not apply only to those factors included within one's own continuity (*sasantati*), nor do they function simultaneously like the eye-faculty and others;

thus, their conditionality is non-restrictive. "In a restrictive manner... up to the life-faculty"—here, by the word *evaṃ* (thus), the visible-form base (*rūpāyatana*) and the others are also [included].

The inclusion (*saṅgaha*) is to be understood as follows: regarding the expression "the sixth base and the six bases are the six bases" (*chaṭṭhāyatanañca saḷāyatanañca saḷāyatananti*), although there is no formal identity (*sarūpatā*) between the terms *chaṭṭhāyatana* and *saḷāyatana* from the perspective of their phonetic form, there is nevertheless a partial identity (*ekadesasarūpatā*) in terms of meaning, since the sixth base is merely one part of the six bases.

Thus, it should be understood that a "partial-identity single-remainder compound" (*ekadesasarūpekasesa*) has been formed. For indeed, a partial-identity single-remainder compound occurs among things that are identical in meaning.

They maintain that [the term] "crooked, bent, and curved" is a single-remainder compound (*ekasesa*). Therefore, in terms of meaning, there must be a single-remainder compound for those words that are partially similar in form.
Alternatively, the sixth base (*chaṭṭhāyatana*) and the mind-base (*manāyatana*) may be called either "the sixth base" or "the mind-base";
or, the sixth base and the sixth base may be called "the sixth base," and the mind-base and the mind-base may be called "the mind-base."
Having applied the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*ekasesa*), it is called "the sixfold sense base" (*saḷāyatana*) together with the eye and so forth.

To demonstrate the meaning of that very term "single remainder" by way of the mind-base (*manāyatana*)—which serves as the condition for both name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and name alone (*nāma*)—he said:

"The sixth base and the sixfold base [together] are 'the sixfold base'; thus it is when the single remainder has been made. For even this "single remainder" as described above is [to be understood] in terms of its actual meaning.
The sixth base and the six bases—thus it is called a "name" when so constructed.

And in all cases where a single remainder (ekasesa) is made, the use of the singular number should be understood as being made on account of the commonality of the denotation of the terms *saḷāyatana* and so forth once the single remainder has been effected.
By the phrase "not otherwise," he clarifies the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), showing that in the absence of this or that name and form, that respective base does not exist.

"Whatever name and form they go to": "of whatever" means of whichever base (*āyatana*). "In whatever way" means by whichever mode, such as co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and so forth. "To be known" (*neyya*) means that which is to be cognized (*ñeyya*).
"By way of that" means by way of that condition, such as the root-condition (*hetu-paccaya*) and so forth. Regarding "the maximum and minimum":
here, the maximum (*ukkaṃsa*) refers to the state of being a condition in seven ways, then in eight ways, then in nine ways, and then in ten ways; this is the maximum. The minimum (*avakaṃsa*)...
However, it should be understood that from tenfold conditionality there is ninefold conditionality, from that eightfold,
and from that sevenfold; but one should not apply both the maximum and minimum [counts] based solely on sevenfold conditionality,
because there is no minimum beyond that.

The connection is with the phrase "called resultant. "In the manner already stated" means by way of being co-nascent and so forth (in seven ways), and by way of the root-cause and so forth. "The other" refers to that which is called non-resultant.

By the phrase "acting as an associate to the heart-basis," he shows only this much: that, unlike in the formless realm, the name is not without an associate, and that the heart-basis serves as a condition for the sixth sense-base together with the name; however, it does not show [anything else], such as...
The meaning intended here is that the heart-base is a condition for mind, and likewise, name is also [a condition] for the base.

For the base is a dissociation-condition for mind, but mind is not [a condition] for the base. And mind is a condition for the base through such factors as the ripening-cause, but the base is not [a condition] for mind.
During the course of existence, immaterial phenomena are conditions only for material phenomena born of kamma that have reached the stage of subsistence, not for those that are currently arising.
The dissociated, presence, and non-disappearance relations—namely, the postnascent-dissociated and so forth—should be applied only to the eye-base and the others.
By the phrase "in that very [existence]," he refers back to "during the course of existence" (pavatte), as indicated by the words "for in that very course of existence.
Furthermore, the phrase "in the five-aggregate existence" is already illustrated by the word "of the five. This is the name for the eye-base and so forth during the course of existence.

It is not a result-condition (*vipāka-paccaya*); rather, it is only for the materiality produced by itself. However, at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), that which is originated by kamma is similar to that originated by consciousness;
therefore, even the physical basis (*vatthu*) is indeed a result-condition.

"From materiality" means among material phenomena. "Whichever sense base arises" means that at rebirth-linking, for those born from eggs or from a womb, only the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) arises among the five sense bases. For the others, the remaining bases arise as appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "of the remaining mind-base (*manāyatana*)," it should be understood that because the expression "in the existence consisting of the five aggregates" (*pañcakkhandhabhave*) follows here, it refers to the mind-base occurring specifically within the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), which remains after [the exclusion of] the five types of sensory consciousness.

Furthermore, the state of being a common condition— such as a co-nascent condition— for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), as well as the state of being an uncommon condition— such as an associated condition— are to be understood according to their respective applicability.
It should be applied thus: "With matter as condition, there are five bases. This method is also obtainable by way of those who have attained cessation (nirodhasamāpanna);

however, because it is not common and because the conditionality of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that serves as a condition for rebirth-linking is generally explained through its presence during the course of existence (pavatti), it is not shown here—it should be understood in this way.
Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Section on Contact Conditioned by the Sixfold Base (Saḷāyatanapaccayāphassapadavitthārakathāvaṇṇanā) 642.
"Associated with twenty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses" means associated with the twenty-two mundane consciousnesses. For that very reason, there are twenty-two [types of contact].

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in that sixfold base; the meaning is "in those six bases. "Internal" (*ajjhatta*) refers exclusively to what is included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*).
It grasps it; for that [object], being produced by kamma included within one's own continuity (*sasantatipariyāpanna*), serves as a condition for such a contact.
However, visible forms and so forth, which are external and unclung-to (*anupādinnāni*), are the objects (*ārammaṇa*) of contact;

they do not serve as conditions for contact in the same way that the eye and other faculties do, by virtue of their state as manifestations of the signs of kamma and defilements included within one's own continuity.

In the first teacher’s doctrine, these were not included; however, in the second teacher’s doctrine, they were included because it was held that as long as the state of being a condition exists in whatever way, they cannot be excluded.
"Therein" refers to the phrase "with the six sense bases as condition, contact [arises]. As for those teachers who were residents of the Mahāvihāra, just as with consciousness...
Thus, when explaining name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling as both condition and conditionally arisen phenomena included within one's own continuity,
they maintain that these are exclusively kamma-result (vipāka). Regarding the statement, "Contact has the sixth base as its condition," it is said,
"In accordance with the scriptural text 'contact has the sixth base as its condition,'" because this passage from the Abhidhamma-bhājanīya was spoken with reference to the formless realm (ārūpya).

The construction is: "All contacts do not arise. If a single contact were to arise from all the sense-bases (*āyatana*), then the statement "contact has the six sense-bases as its condition" would be appropriate;

likewise, even if all contacts were to arise from a single sense-base, there would still be no differentiation of contact according to the differentiation of the sense-bases because all contacts would arise from all sense-bases. Therefore, by virtue of that non-differentiation...
One might object that while the statement regarding a single [contact] would be logical, it is not tenable because such a thing is impossible;

thus he challenges it with the words, "Not from all sense-bases," and so forth. Alternatively, this was stated—"Nor do all contacts arise from a single sense-base"—in order to indicate another rule that is likewise impossible.
Furthermore, the phrase "Not from all sense-bases does a single contact arise" serves to demonstrate the illogicality of the claim concerning a single contact.
It should be understood as the cause; or rather, this was stated by way of illustration.
Nor do all contacts arise from a single sense-base, and likewise, a single contact does not arise from all sense-bases. Therefore, the statement regarding a single [base] is inappropriate.
However, showing that a single contact can arise from multiple sense-bases, he said, "In this regard, the answer is as follows," and so on.
The remaining associated factors are the sense-sphere base consisting of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana) and those mental concomitants associated with it, excluding contact.
One [base] may arise from many bases, and one [base] may also arise from many bases.

Regarding the conditionality, one should analyze five [bases] in six ways and one [base] in nine ways; the connection is that the six external bases should be analyzed according to their respective modes of conditionality, such as being the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), and so forth.

“Anekabhedassa” means of the manifold variety of resultant contact associated with the two sets of fivefold consciousness, excluding [the mind-door], according to the divisions of the wholesome-resultant and so forth, and the five doors and so forth.
“Tāni ca” refers to the sense-base of visible form and the rest; for it has been said: “And the mind experiences their range and domain.
“Tathā ca” refers to present visible forms and so forth, as well as that which is included within the present base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana).

This was said with reference to "form-form" (rūpa-rūpa). The phrase "merely by way of the object-condition" (ārammaṇa-paccaya-mattena) was said with reference to all that is not present, as well as other factors of the mental base (dhammāyatana).
[End of] the commentary on the detailed exposition of the passage concerning feeling conditioned by contact (phassa-paccayā vedanā).

643. "Six from the door" (*dvārato saḷeva*): although they are of one kind by way of their commonality as sources, they are said to be "only six feelings" because there are exactly six doors of arising.

Although there are eighty-nine types through the differentiation of consciousness, it is stated "but among the feelings" (*vedanāsu pana*) and so forth in order to show that only those intended here are meant.

Regarding the phrase "of the rest" (*sesānaṃ*), although the five—eye-contact and so forth—which are associated with the [feeling] of reception (*sampaṭicchana*), are indeed [included] by way of the immediate [condition] and so on...

They are conditions; however, because the proximate (anantara) and other types are included within the decisive support (upanissaya), and because of that common factor shared by both investigation (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa), it is stated as "in one way.

For in each door—such as the eye-door and so forth—the contact arising together with the eye-consciousness and others is a condition for the feelings associated with the respective functions of reception and so on within their own cognitive series; and in the mind-door...
It should be understood that for the resultant feelings of the three planes which arise by way of having that [feeling] as their object, that contact—
consisting of the co-nascent mind-contact— is a condition in eight ways.
This applies to the resultant feelings of the fine-material and immaterial planes which arise by way of rebirth-linking and so forth, and also to some of those of the sense-sphere plane.
It is said: “And also for the resultant feelings of the three planes.

For even for those [feelings], the conascent mind-contact is a condition in eight ways. Since some maintain that a condition may be non-clung-to (*anupādinnaka*), the state of being a condition for the contact associated with mind-door adverting is stated by the words “But as for that which...,” and so forth.
And this should be regarded as a mere illustration. By this method, [the same applies] to all that is immediately preceding.
And the state of decisive support (*upanissaya*) for that very contact and for each respective resultant feeling should be applied.
This concludes the commentary on the detailed exposition of the section on craving conditioned by feeling.

644. "Here" (*idha*) means in this world, or in this teaching; six kinds of craving are illustrated. Alternatively, "here" refers to this phrase: "craving conditioned by feeling. "Therein" (*tattha*) means among those six types of craving.

The mode of occurrence regarding form and so forth, which accords with the delighting in those [objects] through craving accompanied by either the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*) or the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*), is threefold because it is a distinct mode of occurrence when it proceeds solely by way of sensual gratification (*kāmassāda*), as distinguished from the aforementioned modes of occurrence.
"By way of 'mine-ness'" means by way of endearment; that is to say, by way of craving for enjoyment (*assādana-taṇhā*). In this context, it is like a son...
Feeling (vedanā) is to be seen [as the recipient]; the forms and so forth that serve as conditions for feeling are like the milk and so forth;

the six types of consciousness-makers who provide the six objects such as form are like the nurse who provides the milk and so forth. Among these, the weaver is the provider of the object-base for pleasant contact;

the physician [is the provider] by way of the taste-sphere and the nutritive essence, and by way of the life-faculty supported by that. And [there is the provider] of the mental-object sphere (dhammārammaṇa).
It should be understood as "the giver.

All these [conditions], even though they are divided into one hundred and eight types, are merely the object for that which arises; they are not "arising-makers" like the decisive support (upanissaya).

Therefore, it is stated as "of one kind" by way of the decisive support alone, which is the arising-maker. Or, among the decisive supports, it refers to the object-decisive-support (ārammaṇūpanissaya).
It is included. And by that state of being an object (*ārammaṇabhāva*), it is indicated that other similar states of being object-conditions (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) also exist;
thus, it should be understood that the state of being a condition is stated specifically by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
By the words "Or because," etc., it is shown that not only is there resultant pleasant feeling (*vipākasukhavedanā*), but all three types of feeling are resultants, especially so.

This shows that craving is a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*), and by extension, so too are the others. However, because equanimity (*upekkhā*) is peaceful, it is spoken of as "pleasure" (*sukha*);
therefore, the intention is that it too is a decisive support for craving by way of being further desired.

Furthermore, equanimity that is the result of unwholesome kamma (*akusala-vipāka*) must be classified under suffering (*dukkha*) because it is undesirable; the other kind, however, is pleasure because it is desirable.
It can be said that both suffering and pleasure serve as decisive support conditions (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

Regarding the statement “with feeling as condition, craving arises,” since this would imply that craving must arise for everyone who possesses feeling because such a condition exists, the text says “and with feeling as condition” and so forth, in order to preclude that consequence.

Is it not the case that, because there is no statement saying "feeling accompanied by underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) is a condition for craving," one cannot prevent this over-extension (*atippasaṅga*)?
No; because this is occurring within the context of a discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Since the cycle of existence does not exist in the absence of underlying tendencies, it is effectively stated by implication that [feeling] is a condition only when accompanied by underlying tendencies. Alternatively, [the phrase] "with ignorance as condition" (*avijjāpaccayā*)...
Because it occurs in accordance [with them], it is understood that the condition is indeed accompanied by latent tendencies (*anusaya*).

Regarding the statement "with feeling as condition, craving arises," the intended restriction here is that craving arises *only* with feeling as its condition and not without feeling; it is not meant that craving must necessarily arise from feeling as a condition.
Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) in this case.

"Vusīmato" means "of one who has lived [the holy life]," that is to say, of one who has completed the dwelling in the life of purity (*brahmacariya*). Alternatively, "vussati" (he dwells) refers to the path, which is called "vusī";
one who possesses that which has been traversed is "vusīmā. By way of the highest description, this refers to the Arahant.
Or else, because the final fruit is the completion of the dwelling, it is called "vusī"; one who possesses that is "vusīmā."
Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Section on Clinging Conditioned by Craving (Taṇhāpaccayāupādāna):

645. *Atthavibhāga* means the analysis of the meaning. By "sensual pleasure" (*kāma*), which is reckoned as the basis, he refers to the objects such as visible forms, etc., known as the strands of sensual pleasure.
"Clinging" (*upādiyati*) means one grasps by way of sensual pleasure; the meaning is that one relishes it firmly. Regarding the phrase "clings to sensual pleasure": here...

The word *kāma* is used instrumentally (*kamasādhana*), as in "desire" (*kāmo*). But here, in the phrase "and that is desire" (*kāmo ca so*), it is used nominally (*kattusādhana*), because it is intended to mean the defilement of desire (*kilesakāma*).
The word *upādāna*, however, is used nominally in both instances. The sense of "firmness" (*daḷha*) is the sense of "intensity" (*bhusa*).

Just as intense exertion is "over-exertion" (*upāyāsa*) and intense leprosy is "secondary leprosy" (*upakuṭṭha*), so it is here as well; thus he said, "as in the case of *upāyāsa*, *upakuṭṭha*, and so forth."
"The later view takes up the earlier view" means that it takes it up by grasping the earlier view as being eternal;
or else, the later view, arising in the very same manner as the earlier view, strengthens that earlier view and is thus said to "take it up.
Alternatively, "the later view takes up the earlier view" refers to [the view] "the self is eternal."
This was stated in order to demonstrate the subsequent view while one is still adhering to the preceding view.

For just as this [subsequent view] adheres to the preceding one by way of strengthening it, so too does the view beginning with "there is no giving" and so forth. However, the inclusion of the term "self" refers to the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*);

thus, this should not be regarded as a demonstration of the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*). Alternatively, the phrase "and the world" refers to an apprehension distinct from the apprehension of a self.
It should be understood that what is called "clinging to views" here is expressed by the terms "prior view" and "subsequent view.

Regarding the phrase "one clings to rules and observances": here, "virtue" (*sīla*) refers to the undertaking of cow-virtue and so forth as a path to purification; "observance" (*vata*) refers to non-transgression.
Alternatively, both may be considered "virtue," while they are "observance" because they are grasped as ascetic practices (*tapokamma*), such as the cultivation of the nature of cows and so forth.

Or, one's own virtue (*sīla*) is the resolve upon being a cow or the like; the vow (*vata*) is the performance of the activities of a cow and so forth, such as by saying, "While walking I eat, while standing I urinate," and so on.

Alternatively, virtue is the abstention from what is considered improper for each [status], while the vow is the specific practice of performing the duty of eating and so forth, which is undertaken through the formal adoption of that very vow.
Regarding that virtue and vow, which are not a path to purity, [one regards them] as "the path to purity."
Grasping [them] and likewise adhering to them, one clings; the meaning is that one takes hold of that grip firmly.
Having taken the misapprehension associated with rules and observances (sīlabbata) as being "rules and observances," he said: "And that is both rules and observances and clinging.
And by the phrase "cow-virtue, ox-virtue, etc.," he refers to such a view. For this very reason he said: "They themselves are the clingings. From "adherence" means from the state of adherence.

Or, from the standpoint of adherence. "Grasping at a doctrine of self" (attavādupādāna) means: views that serve as the cause for the propounding, the establishing, and the grasping of the doctrine "self.
"Merely a doctrine of self" (attavādamatta): because of the non-existence of a self, this is merely the verbal expression "self.
"They grasp" (upādiyanti) means they seize firmly. How? By saying "self. For those who adhere [to it] as "self," it is merely a verbal expression.
The meaning is: "grasping firmly. Thus it is said: "clinging merely to the doctrine of self" (*attavādamatta*). Or, "merely the doctrine of self" refers simply to the basis for speech.
For they cling to what is merely the basis for speech as "self," because of the non-existence of a self.

However, regarding the concise and detailed classification of the aggregates of phenomena (*dhamma*), clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is, in brief, the intensification of craving; the remaining three types of clinging—

"Only by way of view, but in detail..."—thus, from the combination of the summary and the detailed exposition of the Dhamma, he distinguishes the summary and the detailed exposition which constitute its parts.
In the phrase "in the summary and detailed exposition of the Dhamma," the locative case should be understood in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇe*).
"In sensual pleasures" means in the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) refers to desire consisting of sensual objects, not the desire for the wish to act.
And there is no desire for the Dhamma. By way of longing and by way of coloring, "kāma" itself is lust;
thus, having understood the meaning of "kāma" in all these instances: in the sense of delighting, "kāma" itself is delight in sensual pleasure (*kāmanandi*);

in the sense of craving, "kāma" itself is craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*); in the sense of endearing, "kāma" itself is affection for sensual pleasure (*kāmasneha*); in the sense of burning, it is the fever of sensual pleasure (*kāmapariḷāha*); and in the sense of infatuation...
Craving for sensual pleasures (*kāma-mucchā*) should be understood as clinging to sensual pleasures (*kāma-ajjhosaṇā*) in the sense of swallowing and digesting them.

Craving (*taṇhā*) is the longing for objects not yet attained, because it involves agitation toward the object; grasping (*upādāna*) is the seizing of objects already attained, because it involves a firm grip on the object.

Craving is the opposite of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), because it is directed toward sense objects; grasping is the opposite of contentment (*santuṭṭhi*), because it is the intensification of craving.

Because of the absence of non-desire, having sacrificed [the root of suffering]. Craving (*taṇhā*), being the root of the suffering of seeking, exists because of the absence of longing for objects not yet attained;
clinging (*upādāna*), being the root of the suffering of guarding, exists because of the grasping of objects already attained.

Regarding the phrases "there is no giving" (*natthi dinnaṃ*) and so forth: "giving" refers to the act of giving (*dāna*); since that has no fruit, it is said that what is called "giving" does not exist, just like a material form (*rūpa*).
He rejects it. "Yiṭṭha" refers to a great sacrifice similar to the Mahāvijita sacrifice. "Huta" refers to offerings made for the sake of guests, hospitality, and auspicious rites.
In this context, "āhuna" is the offering or gift given after having invited [the recipient]; "pāhuna" is the hospitable service rendered to guests (*pāhunā*) or visitors;

"maṅgalakiriyā" is the giving of gifts for the purpose of auspiciousness during weddings and other such occasions; and the ten courses of wholesome action (*kusalakammapatha*) are called "well-performed deeds."

The ten unwholesome courses of action are called "wrong deeds" (*dukkaṭakamma*); the construction [of the sentence] is that there is no fruit, no ripening (*vipāka*), meaning neither the outflow-fruit (*nissandaphala*) nor the literal ripening-fruit (*nippariyāyavipāka*).
And just as it is here, so too in such statements as "there is no giving," etc., one should understand that there is only a negation of the fruit and the ripening.
"There is no this world" means that one standing in the next world says of this world, "it does not exist."

He grasps it. For, having observed this world, there is a "world beyond"; and having observed the world beyond, there is this world, insofar as they are respectively to be gone to and to be come from.

Thus, because there is no coming here from the world beyond, and because [the self] is annihilated right there, he who stands in the world beyond with his mind grasps this world as "non-existent. This is the meaning. Indeed, this view does not [apply to] the world beyond.
"It remains for one who stands still" means that while standing in this world, one grasps the view that "there is no other world.
Here too, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. Or rather, the meaning here is this:
this world is the sphere of wandering; there is no such thing as an "other world," because in the absence of wandering, there is merely a cutting off right there and then.
"Upapāta" (rebirth) is the arising in a subsequent existence from a previous existence; those whose nature is this are "opapātika" (beings of spontaneous birth).
However, showing that there are no beings who undergo such death and rebirth, he said: "There are no beings of spontaneous birth.

"In the world there are no recluses... and so forth... "...who proclaim [the truth]," because they have entered upon the conformable practice, they are those who have gone rightly and practiced rightly.
This shows that there are no righteous ascetics or brahmins in the world who,
having personally known this world and the world beyond through their own preeminent knowledge, are capable of proclaiming it— namely, those called omniscient Buddhas.
Regarding such statements as "one regards form as self," what is to be said has already been stated below.

The view of self (attaggāha) sometimes arises with the thought that there exists some permanent or perishable self which is the master of those views—such as the eternalist views of primordial nature (pakati), atoms (aṇu), and so forth, or the annihilationist views regarding the body;

hence it is said, "for the most part" (yebhuyyena). This view of self, in its actual meaning, should be understood as having the aggregates (khandhā) as its object for the most part. For the most part.

The connection is precisely with the phrase "first, clinging to a theory of self," and so forth. Although the cognitive process (vīthi) of the impulsion of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) occurs first—
because it must arise in one who has already taken rebirth-linking due to a latent tendency toward existence—

the author does not state that craving for existence arises first as clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), thinking that such craving for existence does not constitute an intensity of craving (*taṇhādaḷhatta*).

If the distinction were not made—that craving is *kāmupādāna* (clinging to sense-pleasures)—then all craving would be *kāmupādāna*. Or, even if the distinction were made, craving other than sensual lust that has reached a state of firmness would be called *kāmupādāna*; thus it is stated that this [firm craving] is to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship.
The mental states (*cittuppāda*) which serve as the basis for its arising are the "object" (*visaya*). The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandhā*) are the "attachment" (*ālaya*).

One who delights therein is "one who delights in attachment" (*ālayarāmā*), namely, the generation of beings (*pajā*). For this very reason, that delight in attachment is manifest both in one's own continuum and in the continua of others. Regarding "of sense-pleasures" (*kāmānaṃ*):
Regarding sensual objects: without grasping the fact that "pleasure and pain arise through karma," one becomes full of superstitious omens, auspicious signs, and the like.

That is the state of being full of superstitious omens, auspicious signs, and so forth. Of this person who possesses clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), there is the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).
Its subtlety is stated because it is a clinging to more subtle phenomena, consisting of the false adherence to the mere collection of phenomena—which are not-self—as being "self."

By the term "decisive support" (*upanissaya*), the object-support (*ārammaṇa*), proximity (*anantara*), and natural support (*pakatūpanissaya*) are stated; thus, the inclusion of the proximity-condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and others is also effected.
**Commentary on the Detailed Exposition of the Section on the Condition of Clinging as Existence (Upādāna-paccayā-bhava):** 646.

*Atthato*: from the standpoint of the meaning of the words. *Dhammato*: from the standpoint of the phenomena of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). *Sātthato*: from the standpoint of being purposeful (*sātthaka*); previously...
Because even that which has already been stated may be spoken again for a specific purpose. "By way of analysis and synthesis" means by way of analysis and by way of synthesis;

that is to say, by way of classification and by way of the condensing of what has been analyzed. "Whatever condition for whatever" means whatever clinging is a condition for whatever existence, and from that [it follows].
"It comes to be" (*bhavati*) is "existence" (*bhava*); by way of the conventional designation for the fruit, it refers to *kamma-bhava*.

For the very etymological definition of *upapatti-bhava* (rebirth-existence) has been stated as common to both, or alternatively, it is called *bhava* because "from this [kamma] rebirth-existence comes to be. However, the second, *kamma-bhava*, is specifically called *bhava* because it exists as the state of renewed existence (*punabbhava*) for a being. For that very reason, it does not apply to every other form of existence.
Or else, from that cause, there would follow the consequence of the existence of becoming (*bhava*). "In two ways" means it proceeds by way of two modes.
Alternatively, "in two ways" is the instrumental case used in the sense of identity; thus, it is said to be "twofold. "Exists" means it is found. 647.
It is called "kamma" because it is made by its own conditions; some say it is called "kamma" because it produces its own fruit. Thus, "kamma."

Thus they are to be described as comprised within kamma. "Pertaining to the limited plane" means pertaining to the sense-sphere plane (*kāmabhūmaka*). "Pertaining to the great plane" means pertaining to the sublime plane (*mahaggatabhūmaka*).

"All" means without exception. It "goes to existence" (*bhava*) and causes it to go; thus it is "leading to existence" (*bhavagāmi*). As for "goes," it is by way of its capacity to produce [the result];
the meaning is that during its own period of occurrence, it proceeds facing toward existence, or alternatively, "going" simply means being produced.

This is what is intended. By the term "leading to existence" (*bhavagāmi*), he excludes the karma that brings about the destruction of karma. For this is a discourse on the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭakathā*), and that [karma] is dependent upon the turning away from the cycle (*vivaṭṭa*).

As for "meritorious volitional formation" (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), it should be understood as including all twelve types of volition (*cetanā*), just as in the case of "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance" (*avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā*), where even volition accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*) is included. In the phrase "birth conditioned by existence" (*bhavapaccayā jāti*),...
However, just as in the case of the phrase “with volitional formations as condition, consciousness,” that [term] too should be excluded here.
“Small and great fruition” means having little and great results. By the statement “all karma leading to existence,” covetousness and so forth associated with volition are expressed;

thus, by saying they are designated as “karma” because they lead to accumulation, he speaks of their inclusion within the “kamma-process existence” (kammabhava) figuratively, whereas in the literal sense—
However, volition alone is the kamma-process existence (*kammabhava*). For it is said: "The kamma-process existence is associated with three aggregates, one base, and one element;
it is associated with some [of the factors] of one aggregate, one base, and one element.

The rebirth-process existence (*upapattibhava*) is stated by all three triplets (tikas) to be exclusively the appropriated aggregates (*upādinnakkhandha*). As it is said: "The rebirth-process existence... the sense-sphere existence..."
“Perception-existence … five-aggregate existence is comprised by five aggregates, eleven bases, and seventeen elements,” and so forth.
For if there were an inclusion of even those things not clung to, it would have had to be said: “by twelve bases and eighteen elements.
Just as enjoyments are objects of desire because they are desired through craving for sensual pleasures, and because they serve as a basis for such desire; [so too is the case here].
Because they are accompanied by sensual desire, as in the expression “the spears are moving”; because they have sensual objects as their referent, as in “pleasurable form”;

and because they are the locus for the condition of sensual desire, as in “heaven is pleasant”—thus the term “sensual desires” (kāmā) refers to the aggregates of clinging delimited by the realms from the Avīci hell up to the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven.
By way of metaphorical designation based on that which is dependent upon them due to non-detachment from form, it is said: “The beds are shouting.”

Just as [beings] are called "trembling deities" (*phandanadevatā*), so too the appropriated aggregates (*upādinnakkhandhā*) delimited by the Brahmakāyika and Akaniṭṭha realms are called "form" (*rūpa*).

Form itself is existence; thus, "existence in form" (*rūpabhava*) refers to the four appropriated aggregates delimited by the peak of existence, the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatanabhavagga*).
Formlessness itself is existence; thus, "existence in formlessness" (*arūpabhava*). Desire itself is existence; thus, "existence in desire" (*kāmabhava*).
Since that [existence] must be called "kama" (sensual desire) in the sense already stated, it is therefore said: "existence consisting of kama.

Alternatively, existence designated as "belonging to the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) is called "existence consisting of kama. Likewise, regarding "existence of form" and "formless existence," he says:

"this same method applies to the existences of form and the formless. In the phrase "existence of those possessing perception" (*saññāvatam bhavo*), the suffix *-vant* should be understood as having been elided.
Alternatively, by inserting the letter *a* into the sense of the word, there is also a reading as “*saññābhavo*. Therefore he said, “one possessing perception,” and so forth.
By the word “mixed” (*vokiṇṇo*), he indicates that the term *vokāra* has the sense of the object (accusative). It is called *vokāra* because it is scattered (*vokiṛīyati*), spread out, or expanded;
or else, *vokāra* is the act of scattering. Because it proceeds by way of only a single aggregate (*khandha*), it is called “one *vokāra*.”
The meaning is "the arising of passion.

648. Although, in the exposition of existence (*bhava*), it was stated that "all karma leading to existence is karmic existence," which includes factors associated with volition (*cetanā*), nevertheless, the phrase "meritorious formations, etc.
is a restriction intended to show the specific distinction in meaning even among those factors that serve as conditions.
This was stated in order to show that there is indeed a distinction between the grasping of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*) and becoming (*bhava*). Therefore, he said:

"Even though this is so," and so forth. If it is argued that this repetition is inappropriate—on the grounds that since volitional formations and becoming are distinct phenomena, volitional formations were not already mentioned [by the previous term]—we say no;
for "becoming" was mentioned again because volitional formations constitute a portion of becoming. By the opponent...
Or, without grasping a specific distinction in the Dhamma, the repetition was prompted; thus, according to the expression of the prompter, it is said: "This repetition is indeed purposeful.

649. In the Commentary, the state of being the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and so forth for the karma that produces sense-sphere existence and so forth is expressed by way of the terminology of the fruit (phalavohāra).

It has been stated. By the inclusion of "volitional formations" (*saṅkhāra*), any kind of karma previously mentioned—which serves as a condition even for co-nascent consciousness and is rooted in ignorance—is intended here;

however, because of the statement "all karma leading to existence," what is meant by "existence" (*bhava*) is specifically that which produces existence, is rooted in clinging (*upādāna*), and has already been given the opportunity to ripen. That [karma] which, with the condition of clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*)...
Kamma that produces existence in the fine-material realm and kamma that produces existence in the immaterial realm is "kamma-existence" (kammabhava);
the aggregates produced by that [kamma] are "rebirth-existence" (upapattibhava). This point is extended by the phrase, "This method applies to the fine-material and immaterial existences.

Regarding "two kinds of sense-sphere existence": there are two kinds of sense-sphere existence, namely, sense-sphere kamma-existence and sense-sphere rebirth-existence. Likewise, "two kinds of fine-material existences" and "two kinds of immaterial existences" [should be understood].

"Even here. For, not taking them separately as distinct entities, but rather including them within [the aggregates] themselves and doubling the categories such as sense-desire existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth by way of *kamma*-existence (*kammabhava*) and rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), he said, "six existences.

"Without distinction" means without making a division according to the types of clinging (*upādāna*). And because they are subsumed by way of the inclusion of the twelvefold classification through that very non-making of distinctions among the types of clinging, it is stated as "six existences. "Not approaching" means without depending upon, or without touching; this is the meaning.

650. Some say that because it is stated that companionship with cattle and dogs results from the complete undertaking and observance of the cow-vow (*gosīla*) and the dog-vow (*kukkurasīla*), meditative development (*jhānabhāvanā*) does not succeed for one who clings to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*);

thus, they maintain that through such clinging, rebirth in the fine-material and immaterial realms (*rūpārūpabhava*) does not occur. However, this should not be accepted, because—as will be explained later—it serves as a condition [for those realms].
He said: "The adherence to a path of purification where there is no path of purification is the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
Thus, it is not unreasonable that the production of fine-material and immaterial-sphere jhānas occurs through such adherence to a path of purification.
"By way of hearsay" means by way of hearsay such as, "One desiring prosperity should offer a white horse sacrifice," and so forth. Just as...
These sensual pleasures in the human world are abundant; likewise, those in the deva-world are seen to be even more abundant according to one’s adherence to views.
Hearing the *Purāṇas*, the *Mahābhārata*, the abduction of Sītā, the ritual of animal sacrifice, and so forth, constitutes hearing what is not the true Dhamma.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes reliance upon unworthy persons, the failure to perform merit in the past, and one's own wrong aspirations. "And bodily misconduct, etc. refers to these as well.

The intention is that one performs bodily misconduct and so forth—even though these are not the means for attaining the sensual pleasures one desires—by way of war and the like, for the sake of long-lasting sovereignty and so on.
Or, it refers to sensual pleasures comprised within visible things, such as the status of a king or a general.
"Included therein" means they are included within that sense-sphere existence produced by misconduct and that produced by good conduct.

This is the meaning. And the phrase "included within" is stated because the realms of perception-existence (*saññā-bhava*) and five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokāra-bhava*) are included as partial portions within sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*);
for they are not entirely included within sense-sphere existence.
"Possessing its divisions" means possessing the divisions of happy destinies, miserable destinies, humans, and so forth.

In the fortunate existence of the sense-sphere realm (*kāmāvacara-sampatti-bhava*), by way of the first and second annihilationist views; in the fine-material realm (*rūpa-bhava*), by way of the third annihilationist view;
and in the immaterial realm (*arūpa-bhava*), by way of the remaining annihilationist views—one thinks, "This self has been completely annihilated," and thus performs karma leading to rebirth there.

Therefore, it is said: "This is what is called 'self,'" and so forth. In that context, "completely annihilated" (*su-ucchinno*) means thoroughly [destroyed] through the total eradication of the suffering of the entire cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa-dukkha*).
The meaning is that [existence] is cut off, such that there is no further arising of renewed existence.
The phrase "in the fortunate existence of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara-sampatti-bhava*) is stated according to the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life as seen first;
the remainder is according to the doctrine of Nibbāna in this very life as seen otherwise. In that regard, although in the Canon it is indeed by way of the fine-material-sphere jhānas alone—

Above, four theories of Nibbāna in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammanibbānavāda*) have been presented. However, since a proponent of wrong views (*diṭṭhigatika*) clings to anything whatsoever in whatever way, there is the mention of "existence in the formless realm" (*arūpabhava*).
Alternatively, the mention of "existence in the formless realm" is because the formless meditative absorptions (*arūpajjhāna*) are included within the fourth jhāna.
Or else, it is because of its peaceful happiness, due to the commonality of the state of being happy for one who possesses it. It is "free from fever" (*vigatapariḷāha*).
The meaning is that one has attained Nibbāna in this very life, having pacified the fever of sensual lust through the relinquishing of, and by offering up, the objects of desire as they were craved.
Whatever mundane virtue and meditative absorption (jhāna) is practiced by way of clinging to a path to purity is called "virtue and observance" (sīlabbata).
He says, "This is what is intended here," beginning with the words, "This is called virtue-and-observance (sīlabbata)," and so forth.

Instead of stating [the sequence] in order, the statement that the clinging to virtue-and-observance is a condition for existence (*bhava*) at the end [of the list] is because it does not frequently manifest—just like the clinging to a self-theory (*attavādupādāna*)—and because it is the cause for the clinging to a self-theory.

In the phrase "in kamma-existence" (*kammabhave*), the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "by means of the divisions of the root-condition and the condition," the path-condition (*maggapaccaya*) should also be mentioned here.
For views and the other forms of clinging serve as path-conditions for co-nascent kamma-existence;
therefore, it should be understood that by removing the root-condition from among the co-nascent conditions and adding the path-condition, they become sevenfold conditions.
Furthermore, all [clinging] are conditions by way of the proximity, contiguity, proximity-strong-dependence, presence, absence, and repetition conditions.

They do not serve as a condition for what is immediate by way of the decisive-support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). Sometimes they may also serve as conditions by way of the object condition (*ārammaṇa-paccaya*) and so forth;
however, since those are included within the decisive-support condition itself, it is stated: "But for what is dissociated, [they serve] only by way of the decisive-support condition.
This concludes the commentary on the detailed exposition of the phrases beginning with "birth from the condition of existence" (*bhava-paccayā jāti*).

651. Regarding the phrase "in 'birth' and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the entire passage: "With birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Therefore, he says "of birth and so forth," etc.

Since birth is precisely the arising of the rebirth-existence (upapattibhava), he says "not the rebirth-existence. However, because birth belongs to that which is being born, even the rebirth-existence [is included] under "birth."

It can be said that non-existence is a condition for birth. For the state of being the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) of the category of form (*rūpa-jāti*) while it is being born is also stated [in the texts]:
"Accumulation (*upacaya*) has accumulated form as its proximate cause; continuity (*santati*) has uninterrupted form as its proximate cause.

Inferiority and excellence are the states of being despised and being esteemed respectively regarding the aggregates that have been born. For what is undesirable is inferior, and what is desirable is excellent.
"Exquisite. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes such qualities as beautiful and ugly, inferior and superior, and so forth.
"Even among twins" means even among those who are identical, having been produced as twins. And that is the distinction between beings.
Because there is an absolute absence of any distinct cause for [such] difference within a separate continuum, it is said: "within one's own internal continuum. [This refers to] another cause.
"By way of non-existence" means that no other specific cause is found apart from what belongs to one's own continuum;

and because if such a cause were present, it would follow that everything would exist at all times for everyone—a consequence difficult to avoid—and because a distinction in the fruit is untenable when the cause remains undifferentiated.
Therefore he said: "Or else, it has kamma-existence as its cause."
"By this or that" means by some other painful phenomenon than aging and death, such as the loss of relatives and so forth.
For the sorrow and other states that arise with aging and death as their cause are directly connected to aging and death; those other than these are not so connected.

"By way of decisive support" (*upanissaya-koṭiyā*) means by way of being a decisive support, or by way of the essence of a decisive support—this is the meaning. For that which exists when [a certain condition] is present and does not exist when it is absent is what is not mentioned in the *Paṭṭhāna*.
And non-existence is a decisive support (upanissaya) according to the method of the Suttas; that is called the "limit of decisive support" (upanissayakoṭi).
This, namely "decisive support," is indeed the Great Authority on Conditions (paccayamahāpadesa).
Commentary on the Discourse on the Wheel of Existence (Bhavacakkakathāvaṇṇanā).

652. It is begun with the words “But because,” etc., in order to show that birth is not only a condition for sorrow and the rest, but is also a condition for ignorance itself by virtue of being a condition for sorrow and the rest.
“In this context” means in the teaching on dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
In the phrase *aviditādimidam*, the letter *m* is used as a euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*). “Constantly” means at all times, until the attainment of the supreme path.
*Samitaṃ* means joined together; the meaning is "uninterrupted.
*Tesu* refers to sorrow and the rest. *Siddhesu* means when they are present or occurring. Ignorance (*avijjā*) is established because it is inseparable [from those states].
*Kāmayānassa* means of one who desires; or, one for whom desire (*kāma*) is the vehicle (*yāna*) is *kāmayāno*, [meaning] of one who is driven by desire.

The meaning is as follows: "Of one in whom desire has arisen" means of one in whom the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*) has arisen. "They perish" means they disappear. "Is afflicted" means it is disturbed by sorrow and so forth.
"One who stands in obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī*) refers to one whose nature is to persist in obsession;

alternatively, the reading is *pariyuṭṭhaṭṭhāyino*. In that case, the meaning should be understood as follows: "obsessed" (*pariyuṭṭhaṃ*) refers to the obsession of views (*diṭṭhi-pariyuṭṭhāna*); one who stands by means of that is "one who stands in obsession."

"The five portents" means the five signs of death mentioned as: "the garlands wither, the clothes become soiled, sweat breaks out from the armpits, a change of color comes over the body, and the deva finds no delight in his celestial throne.
Having seen these, [one passes away] through the power of desire for existence (*bhavacchanda*) into the rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), which consists of the aggregates produced by karma.
"A powerful sorrow arises for the gods.

"Foolish" means ignorant; by this, he shows ignorance to be the cause. "Threefold suffering" refers to the suffering consisting of hearing talk about the formless realms, witnessing the execution of one's karma, and the arising of sorrow and so forth caused by the presence of death at the time of dying.
"They settle the taints" means they bring the taints to rest or clarify them.
"Such being the case" means such being the case when the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) is beginningless due to its unknown beginning.
