The primary elements (*bhūta*) are earth, water, fire, air, and space, which are initiated by odors and so forth; their intrinsic nature is volition (*cetanā*).
"Person" (purisa): thus, nature (pakati) and the others should be understood according to their own characteristics.

For therein, first, "nature" is a name for the mere state of pleasure, pain, and delusion; by undergoing states of evenness and unevenness, it becomes subject to impermanence, suffering, and being conditioned (saṅkhata).
As for "the Great One" (mahā), it is said: "Therefore, from that which is without gender, the Great One arises as a mere distinction of gender."
By virtue of its verbal expression and by virtue of its admission as the state of intellectual awareness, "name" (nāma) is indeed established as impermanent and conditioned.

As for the statement, "Therefore, six distinctions arise from the great [mind]," it is possible [to explain it thus]: by virtue of its verbal expression and by virtue of its admission as the state of being the cause for the apprehension of "I am," it is termed "egoity" (ahaṃkāra) and "conceit" (abhimāna);
for that very reason, its attainment of the state of being impermanent and conditioned is proven.
The other fivefold set of "mere-ness" (tammattapañcaka) is called "form" (rūpa) because it is understood as the mere states of odor, flavor, visible form, tangibility, and sound;
however, the claim that it is "non-form" (arūpa) is merely the false dogmatic adherence of the followers of Kapila.

For they hold that the sixteen specific qualities consist of the five primary elements (bhūta), the eleven faculties, and the specific qualities of the elements—namely, earth, water, fire, air, and space—which are the supports for those [faculties] consisting of the mere states of odor and so forth.

The primary elements (bhūta) are desired [as the basis]. According to the statement, “And the specific qualities derived from them are of various kinds, as well as the sense-faculties (indriya) arising from the conceit of ‘I’,” there are eleven faculties:
namely, the ear, body, eye, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, as well as the mind (mano).
Among these, the mind is name (nāma), while all the others are form (rūpa). Furthermore, in this context, “speech” (vācā) refers to a collection of syllables that makes manifest the intended meaning.

[This refers to] grasping. However, since for these [schools] it is accepted that the phenomenon (dhamma) is not distinct from its nature (dhammin), impermanence is established in the case of transformation (pariṇāma).
Even in the case of manifestation (abhivyakti), if manifestation is established by the arising of the knowledge regarding that object, then impermanence is indeed established;

or else, if knowledge already exists prior to that [manifestation], then impermanence is likewise established. But the theory of the manifestation of the unmanifested (akkhabyattivāda) might still be possible—this is what is meant here.
A mere direction. Substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence are the categories beginning with substance.
Among these, there are nine substances: earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind.
Sound, form, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, [and effort are the qualities].
Effort, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, and velocity are seen as the [five] formations; thus, these are the twenty-three qualities (*guṇas*).

Lifting up, lowering, contracting, extending, and moving—these are the five actions (*karmas*). A designation that is undifferentiated among things differentiated from one another serves as a condition.

Because the prefix *saṃ-* exists in such a way that it is present in substances, qualities, and actions, this is the "great generality" (*mahāsāmañña*). [This applies] to earth and the other [elements].

The cause for the cognition of recurrence and exclusion is "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth; these include substantiality, quality-ness (*guṇatva*), action-ness (*karmatva*), pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), and the like.

This is the "particular universal" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*). Here, in the sense that "there is cloth in the threads" and "there is a pot in the potsherds," the relation between cause and effect is called "inherence" (*samavāya*);
thus, these [categories] such as substance and the rest are [related] by way of inherence.
In this context, earth, water, fire, and air are derived matter (*bhūtarūpa*). Space is merely the absence of those [elements], or it is their delimitation;
time is a mere designation based on the revolution of the moon, sun, and so forth, as well as the occurrence of phenomena.

Likewise are the directions and the self. Mind is name (*nāma*). Sound, visible form, taste, and odor are matter alone. Similarly, contact is matter because its intrinsic nature consists of the three primary elements.
Number, beginning with one and so forth, is a mere designation (paññatti-matta) based on this or that [object].

Likewise, in a collection of parts, by way of a specific quality or a specific shape, there is "large" or "long," and by way of its opposite, "minute" or "short. In places with distinct characteristics, there is "diversity" (puthutva).

When things existing in distinct locations are together, there is "conjunction" (saṃyoga); when they depart from that, there is "disjunction" (viyoga). This applies to those situated in the same direction and location.
"Far" and "near" are mere designations based on material forms that occupy extensive space. Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, hatred, and effort are merely name.
Heaviness, liquidity, viscidity, and momentum are modes to be grasped through specific variations in the activity of material phenomena.

The other [type of] formation is a specific variation in the activity of knowledge. Although unseen, it is merely name because of its status as either merit (*dhamma*) or demerit (*adhamma*). Lifting up...

Throwing down, contracting, extending, and going are merely the occurrence of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*). The designations "generality" and "particularity" refer to similarity and dissimilarity;
the designation "inherence" refers to an improper connection. Thus, it should be understood that even substances (*dravya*) and so forth are included within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Living beings, non-living beings, bondage, merit, demerit, influx, restraint, shedding, and liberation are the categories beginning with "living beings. Therein, "living being" (*jīva*) means the self (*attā*).

The perception of non-living (ajīva) applies to the person (puggala), dhamma, adhamma, space (ākāsa), and time (kāla). Among these, sound, touch, visible form, taste, smell, configuration, cohesion, disintegration, subtlety, priority, posteriority, resistance, radiance, shadow, and lightness are the characteristics of the person (puggala-rūpa);
the person is merely the mode of occurrence of material phenomena (rūpadhamma).
Dhamma and adhamma are not distinct from that [person], as they are merely the movement and stability of living beings and persons. Space and time are mere designations (paññatti). Cohesion...
Because of the statement, "the conjunction of karma and the person," [karma] is not other than them. That merit and demerit are indeed names is quite evident.
Because of the statement, "the influx (āsava) of karmas and persons," the designation "influx" applies to the arising of merit and demerit; therefore, the influx is not distinct from that.
Because of the statement, "restraint is the cessation of the influx," restraint is the cessation of merit and demerit by means of their opposites.
Because of the statement, “The non-occurrence of the natural process of the manifestation of kamma-results is nibbāna,” nibbāna is the cause for the cessation of vipāka.
Liberation (*mokkha*) is also the dissociation from kamma, the person (*puggala*), and the life-principle (*jīva*), because of the statement, “Liberation from all kamma.

In that context, the state of being mere form (*rūpa-matta*) consists in the fact that kamma and the person have the characteristics of sound and so forth; their state of being immaterial (*arūpa*) consists in the fact that they are mere merit and demerit. As for the life-principle...
And "only formless" (arūpamattam eva) refers to this liberation as substance (dravya-mokṣa). However, liberation as state (bhāva-mokṣa) is the non-transformation of the soul's states such as passion;
since passion and so forth are merely names, even the soul and other categories are included within name-and-form (nāma-rūpa).
Bodies, their activities, destinies, births, bonds, and liberation consist of the body and so forth. In that regard, among earth, water, fire, air, self, pleasure, and pain—

The conventional designation "body" (*kāya-samaññā*). Since it is stated that "existence, occurrence, destiny, birth, bondage, and liberation are not distinct from that," and according to the statement, "the meaning is 'state' (*bhāva*);
'body' (*kāya*) is not a different thing," there is nothing whatsoever other than the body.

According to the statement, "The notion of 'occurrence' (*pavatti-saññā*) applies to conjunctions and disjunctions of action," occurrence is merely a metaphorical designation for earth and the other elements as they occur in the form of destinies and so forth. "There is nothing other than that."
In terms of speech and body, there are no states of rebirth other than those among gods, humans, ghosts, animals, and those fallen into hell.

Among these destinies, even the conviction that one born in each successive state is superior to the preceding one is merely a mental occurrence; therefore, there are no births other than those designated as black, blue, red, yellow, white, and extremely white.

These births, which become progressively more distinguished, consist respectively of ignorance, delusion, passion, hatred, truth, and lack of vision; the "white birth" is characterized by the abundance of truth.
It is the "white class" because it is utterly liberated and because it has been fully penetrated.

According to the statement, "The designation 'bond' applies to the humors," there is no difference between the living being and the bond characterized by ignorance and so forth. Since ignorance and other defects are absent, liberation is established;
thus, even the body and so on are merely name-and-form (nāmarūpa).

Furthermore, whatever referent for "self" is expressed here and there through various modes such as "a person," "the self," or "the soul," that too is designated either by depending upon mere name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as appropriate, or it is merely name-and-form itself.
Therefore it was said: "Those [terms] are also determined solely by way of their inclusion within, or exclusion from, name-and-form.
[End of] the commentary on the discussion concerning the correlation with many suttas.
672. "He" refers to that practitioner of yoga who is engaged in insight (vipassanā). "'Thus'" refers to the aforementioned mode of grasping.

"'In accordance with its true nature'" means according to its actual intrinsic being (yathābhūtasabhāva). The connection [of the sentence] is: having defined name-and-form (nāmarūpa), he defines this matter by synthesizing it.
This is for the sake of abandoning even worldly conventional designations (lokasamaññā), let alone the false adherence (micchābhinivesa) that occurs as "a being" or "a soul" (jīva).

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). Because there is no determination of [the world] as being merely name-and-form (*nāmarūpamattatā*), and because the distinctions such as the density of the continuity (*santāna*) and so forth have not been made, the delusion that proceeds by grasping at a collective unity without clinging (*abhinivesa*) is "delusion regarding a being" (*sattasammoha*). The stage of non-delusion (*asammohabhūmi*) is the suppression of that [delusion].
"By way of many suttas" refers to those stated here with the words "Just as... (*yathāpi*) and so forth, as well as those not explicitly stated.
“Mahāli, if this form were the self, this form would not lead to affliction,” and so forth—this is by way of many such suttas.
With reference to the very meaning stated in the passage beginning with “mere name-and-form,” he says, “this is the meaning. “A collection of parts” means for the sake of a collection of parts.
With that as its cause, and not relinquishing it, when that [collection] exists, there is the conventional designation “a being.”
The construction is as follows: "But in the case of the house" (*agārantveva*) means that just as, depending upon and taking as its basis materials such as wood and so forth,
their individual names are set aside and it comes to be designated by the conventional term and name "house," so too, depending upon and taking as its basis bones and so forth,
their individual names are set aside and it comes to be designated by the conventional term "form" (*rūpa*) or "body" (*sarīra*).
"Only suffering arises" means that only the threefold suffering, distinguished as the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*) and so forth, comes into being;

it arises according to its conditions. That very suffering both persists by way of momentary duration and continuity of duration, and ceases by way of momentary cessation, the exhaustion of the life-span, and so forth—this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show the meaning excluded by the particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only suffering," [the text says] "not otherwise," and so on.
This has been stated. Its meaning is as follows: apart from the aforementioned suffering, no other class of phenomena exists that could be called a "being" or a "living soul";
since such a thing is entirely non-existent in every respect, how could there be its cessation?
[End of] the commentary on the discourse explaining the simile for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

673. "In those things established in a single mode" means: by whatever manner they are situated in the axle and so forth that the designation "chariot" is applied, in that same single mode—being thus assembled and gathered together into one mass. "In just this way" refers to a collection of parts distinguished by its specific arrangement, occurring as a continuum;
just as [one speaks of] a "chariot," a "house," a "fist," a "lute," an "army," or a "city."
“Tree” is merely a conventional designation; in the ultimate sense, however, there is nothing such as a chariot or the like—just so it is here.

Regarding the “aggregates of clinging”: when the material and immaterial phenomena designated as aggregates of clinging have arisen and are occurring by way of a continuum, “a being” or “a soul” is merely a conventional designation;
in the ultimate sense, however, neither a being nor a soul exists—this is according to reality.
Knowing this is the vision of things as they truly are;
it is called "purification of view. 674. "Of that" means of the self grasped as a "being. "Destruction" means the cessation of what has perished.
"Non-destruction" means non-perishing; the meaning is "permanence. For those who maintain the doctrine of self stand on these two positions alone: "the self is eternal," or "it is annihilated."
Or rather, even the doctrine of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*) is included right here.

"Admitting non-destruction" means that even one who desires the destruction of phenomena such as consciousness (*buddhi*), while admitting the absence of destruction for himself by claiming "the self (*dhammī*) is eternal and immutable," falls into the eternalist view (*sassata*).

The intended meaning is that he falls into the fallacies of attributing destruction to what has not been destroyed and attributing the state of what has not been done to what has been done, and so forth.

“Of the nature of milk” means being a consequence of milk; the meaning is: being its fruit. “Of that same nature” means because there is no other thing whatsoever that is a consequence of that [milk] itself.

“It is called ‘shrinking back’” means that, through the dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*) that “the self is eternal,” having become one who delights in existence (*bhava*), it undergoes contraction away from the cessation of existence and thus remains hidden (*nilīyati*) in existence itself. “It runs too far”...

Regarding the term "merely" (nāma): in that context, they say that one who holds to annihilationism—grasping the view that "the self is annihilated"—and thus overreaches by asserting that "there is no existence" after death when there actually is an existing state of being, is said to be "merely" overreaching.
However, since the cessation of defilements entails the non-ripening of karma, the cessation of existence must be sought; yet, failing to grasp it in that way, [they overreach].
One who grasps [the view] that "by coming to such and such a particular state of existence, the self is annihilated, and thus there is the cessation of existence" is said to overreach.
"Overwhelmed" means overcome.
"Possessing eyes" means possessing the eye of knowledge, which is defined as seeing things as they truly are.

"Bhavārāmā" means those for whom existence (*bhava*)—divided into the realms of sense-desire (*kāma*), fine-materiality, and so forth—is a "pleasure-grove" (*ārāma*) in the sense that it is to be resorted to. "Bhavaratā" means those who delight in and take pleasure in that existence.
"Bhavasammuditā" means those who have reached a state of jubilation regarding existence. By all three terms, what is expressed is simply their being bound by the gratification of existence.
"The mind does not leap forward" means that because they are bound by the gratification of existence, the mind [does not leap forward] toward the states that lead to the cessation of existence.

“Does not enter into”: it does not settle. “Does not become confident”: it does not resolve. “Does not become established”: it does not find a footing. “Does not become convinced”: it does not adhere. “Being distressed”:

being pained by suffering. “Being ashamed”: feeling shame. “Being disgusted”: loathing. “Non-existence”: annihilation. “They delight in”: this is a demonstration of the manner of delighting mentioned [in the text], beginning with “From what indeed, sir,” and so forth.

“Bhūta” refers to the pentad of aggregates (*khandhapañcaka*). For it is called “bhūta” because it has arisen from its respective conditions and because it exists as an ultimate reality (*paramattha*). “Bhūtato” means according to its actual nature, its specific characteristic (*salakkhaṇa*), and its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*).

Having thus shown, by means of the Sutta itself, the faults of shrinking back and over-reaching due to the grasping at a being, as well as the virtues such as disenchantment (*nibbidā*) through seeing things as they truly are, [the author] now says “Therefore,” etc., in order to show that even in mere name-and-form (*nāmarūpamatta*), the functions of going and so forth, as well as the activity of a self, are accomplished.

It has been stated. Therein, "therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because there is no so-called "being" (*satta*) that serves as the objective basis for the grasping [expressed as] "I am" or "I," and in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), there is only name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); therefore.

Anticipating the objection, "If there is no such thing as a self (*attā*), how can the functions of a self, such as going and so forth, be established here in what is merely name-and-form?", he says: "Like a wooden puppet," and so forth. "Appears" (*khāyati*).
By this it is shown that, just as in the case of a lifeless wooden doll,
there is merely the appearance of effort and activity on the part of the life-principle existing within it due to specific conditions, so too in the case of the lifeless mere name-and-form,
the performance of its own functions such as going and so forth occurs due to specific conditions; thus, there is merely the appearance of effort and activity.
"Truly" means according to reality; "ultimately" is the meaning. The intention is that it is empty of a soul (*jīva*), being conditioned and proceeding by way of conditions like a machine.
It is a mass of suffering because of constant affliction, resembling grass and wood due to its emptiness of self (*atta*);
this is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Yamaka" means a pair. And this state of being a pair is due to their mutual dependence; thus he said, "both are dependent on one another.
For that very reason, when one is broken, both are broken.
Indeed, it never happens in the five-aggregate existence that while the form [aggregate] ceases, the non-form [aggregate] does not cease, or while the non-form ceases, the form does not cease.
There is that which does not cease. This "breaking up" (bhaṅga) occurs through the cessation of the condition by means of the cessation of the conditioned;

the meaning is the cessation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Alternatively, "conditions" (paccayā) refers to those things that have become conditions; the meaning is that even while acting as mutual conditions for one another, both [name and form] indeed break up. 676.
By the qualifying term "struck by a staff," [the text indicates] the staff, the condition for the impact of the staff, and the human effort.
[The text] shows this; however, the drum (*bherī*) is specified because it is the unique cause of the sound.

For that very reason, in the phrase "another drum," it is the drum itself that is taken, not the stick or other factors. Having treated the sound—which is invisible in form—as the object of the designation, [the author] effects the connection with the simile by means of the words "just so" (*evameva*), and so forth.
“They do not arise from the eye” means they do not arise by way of emerging from the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*).

For prior to the attainment of the status of being a condition for the eye-base, the [aggregates] beginning with contact as the fifth are not obtainable; nor do they possess a location from which they might emerge.
Therefore he said: “There is no heap in the future. Regarding “not from form,” the same applies here as well.
This is the method. As for the phrase "nor between the two," this is stated because, being immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), they lack spatial location.
However, since they merely arise at the very moment the convergence of conditions occurs, it is said: "Conditioned things come into being dependent on a cause.
This means that depending upon a collection of factors—such as the eye, visible forms, light, and attention—which serve as the conditions...
The meaning is that conditioned phenomena such as contact arise because they have obtained their causes and have been produced through coming together and combining.
In order to show the manifestation of the occurrence of material phenomena (rūpadhamma) for the arising of those phenomena, he said:
"Just as sound [arises] from a struck drum. And here, the mention of "contact as the fifth" is a demonstration of the manifest immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma).
The same method applies to the *Sesagāthā* as well.

Regarding "material bases" (*vatthurūpa*), this refers to the heart-base (*hadayavatthu*). Because the immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) that depend upon it are of many varieties, they are indicated by the general term "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*).
677. "Lacking brilliance" (*nitteja*) means devoid of heat or lacking in majestic power. To show how it is thus lacking in brilliance:

The passage beginning with “it does not eat” has been stated. For otherwise, it would not be possible to say that name (nāma) is “devoid of power” (nitteja) in regard to such functions as faith and exertion, nor would it be possible to say so of matter (rūpa) in regard to such functions as supporting and binding.
It is for this very reason that, having stated “matter is devoid of power,” it was said: “for it has no desire to eat,” and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of the method of exclusion (*vyatireka*) in the passage beginning with “but rather,” [the distinction] between name and matter is shown.

It reveals only their lack of brilliance. For the demonstration that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is individually incapable of accomplishing its own function even through mutual dependence is itself the revelation of their lack of brilliance.
Thus, the emptiness of name-and-form of a self, its lack of agency, and its freedom from activity become much more clearly manifest.
But how can there be capacity when combined for those things that lack capacity individually?
[This would imply] that even non-causes, which lack the nature of a cause in their state of disharmony, would attain the status of a cause when in harmony. Anticipating the objection:
"For even a hundred or a thousand blind people, who are unable to see individually, cannot see when combined," he says: "But regarding this matter... and so forth.
The masters of the commentaries cite this simile because even by means of a simile, a meaning that has not yet been established must be proven.
For this very reason it was said: "I shall give you a simile; for by means of a simile, some wise persons understand the meaning of what is spoken. "Tuṭṭhahaṭṭho" means:
even if I am unable to perform what is to be done with the eyes, I can nevertheless perform what is to be done with the feet.

"I am able, and you too have need for eyes; therefore, through the cooperation of us both, the attainment of the desired destination will be accomplished"—thus the one born blind is filled with joy and delight.
Therein, the passage beginning with "the one born blind" is the correlation between the simile and that which is illustrated by it.
It must be said that there is no such thing as the acquisition of self-nature (*attalābha*) for phenomena being dependent on another, because such a nature does not exist prior to that [acquisition].
To show that even for one who has obtained such a gain, the duty of purpose remains dependent upon others, it is said:
"It does not arise by its own power, nor does it proceed in various activities.
It has been established through the simile of the man born blind and the cripple that the arising or the proceeding of those name-and-forms does not occur without mutual dependence.

The refutation— "because even in the case of a combination [of causes], there would result a state of causelessness for those that are not causes"— clarifies the inconclusiveness (*anaikantika*) of the reason stated above.
"Those who follow the power of other phenomena" refers to those who conform to other phenomena— those things reckoned as causes and conditions— which are distinct from oneself.
[They are] of a nature to follow along by way of [that]. "Weak in themselves" means weak or incapable by their own nature.

"By reason of other conditions" means because of the state of being a condition for the phenomena of others; by this, he speaks of the producing condition (*janaka-paccaya*). For that very reason, he says "they arise.

"By reason of other objects" means because of the state of being an object for the phenomena of others; by this, he speaks of the supporting condition (*upatthambhaka-paccaya*). [The inclusion of the word] "condition" (*paccaya*)...
Or, the apprehension of an object depends on form, and it depends on name. The phrase “by other phenomena” is a qualification of the object-conditions (*ārammaṇapaccaya*).
For that very meaning already stated by the former term is made clear by the latter term. “Produced” means brought into being.
By the passage beginning with “Just as,” etc., three verses are given to clarify that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are not subject to one's own mastery, using the simile of the ship’s mast.

"Dependent" (*nissāya*) means having established oneself upon. "They go" (*yanti*) means they proceed. "Dependent on people" means relying on people such as the steersmen, sailors, and laborers who act as guides;
for without their actions—such as seizing the oars, maintaining the rigging, and bailing out water—the ship does not reach its desired destination.
"Both" means that people depend on the ship and the ship depends on the people; this is the meaning.

"In this manner" means by the way already described. "By various methods" refers to the fourteen ways of discerning the formless, consisting of the seven jhānas beginning with the first and their respective access stages;
and the thirteen ways of discerning the elements taught in the *Analysis of the Four Elements*—namely, by way of the elements, the bases, the aggregates, and the primary elements;
as well as the faculties, the truths, and dependent origination, both those mentioned here and those not mentioned.
By way of these [twenty], there are twenty modes for discerning materiality;

each of these, when multiplied by three due to the presence of the three immaterial phenomena—contact, feeling, and consciousness—becomes sixty, resulting in fourteen modes for discerning the immaterial.
Thus, by means of these seventy-four methods for discerning name-and-form...

By means of the similes of the many-threaded cloth, the chariot, the house, the handful of chaff, the lute, the army, the tree, the wooden machine, the bundle of reeds, the clay pot, the deaf man, the cripple, and the boat;

and by means of the methods for establishing the delusion regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). "Having overcome the perception of a being" means having suppressed the grasping at a self within the five aggregates that has been cultivated since beginningless time. "The seeing of name-and-form as they truly are" means: "This is name..."
“Name is just this much, not more than this; form is just this much, not more than this”—this is the demonstration of the mere nature of phenomena by way of discerning their characteristics.
It should be understood as “purification of view” because it cleanses the stain of the view of self.
“Of this very same” means of the very same seeing of name-and-form as it truly is.
The commentary on the Description of Purification by View is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the eighteenth chapter.
19. Commentary on the Description of Purification by Overcoming Doubt.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Investigation of Conditions (Paccayapariggahakathāvaṇṇanā) 678. It is said, "of this very [insight]," because it has been shown as the objective domain for the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi) just described;
it is not for the sake of qualifying it from something else, since there is nothing other than that. For the application of insight (vipassanābhinivesa) is indeed internal.
Whether it be external, all name-and-form (nāmarūpa) whatsoever is indeed grasped without remainder by way of its characteristics within the establishment of the internal.

"By means of the discernment of conditions" (*paccayapariggahena*): here, the instrumental case is used for the cause (*hetu*), for the overcoming of doubt regarding the three periods of time occurs through the cause that is the discernment of conditions;
or else, this instrumental case is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the discernment of conditions.
It is by way of being the most effective means for the act of overcoming doubt.
For when his discernment of conditions becomes perfectly purified—free from roots and free from tangles—then doubt is overcome by him. "Having overcome" means having transcended;
the meaning is "having suppressed. Furthermore, that knowledge, once thus attained and brought to mastery, is like jhāna.
It is said that "knowledge is established" because it proceeds in a continuous stream within the continuum of the yogi.
The word "that" refers to the purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*). The connection is: "one undertakes [the practice] desiring to accomplish that.
Name-and-form, seen as they truly are, are like a disease because of their association with the three kinds of suffering; and their conditions are the origin of that disease.
Showing the meaning of "appearing as if [he were there]," he said: "Just as if... pe... he would search.

Since the state of being worthy of compassion is obtained through the desire to liberate from it the continuum of existence submerged in the suffering of *saṃsāra*, the passage beginning with "Or just as" was stated to demonstrate that point.
Such being the case, when some say: "By seeing the boy who is to be pitied..."

"The mental advertence (*āvajjana*) toward his mother and father is not cited here as an example, because there is an absence of the need for compassion for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that is to be ceased"—this [position] is refuted.

And this must certainly be accepted in this way; otherwise, one would have to investigate only the occurrence of the Teacher’s great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) within the continuum (*santāna*) of a person to be trained.
"Mandam" means "slightly," due to dullness of intellect. Even someone who is older...
Because one might [otherwise] be considered dull-witted, the term "youth" (*kumāra*) is stated for the purpose of qualification.
Since anyone existing in the first stage of life is called a "youth," the term "tender" (*dahara*) is stated for the purpose of further qualification.
Even so, since a young child who runs about and wanders would also be called "tender," the term "lying on his back" (*uttānaseyyaka*) is used to exclude such a person.
It has been stated. By all four phrases, he demonstrates precisely that which is to be felt with compassion (*karuṇāyitabba*). "He incurs" (*āpajjati*) means he performs [the action].
To show how his offense arises through the search for causes and conditions, the passage beginning with "he" (*so*) was stated.
In this context, since the meaning is established by way of contrast (*byatireka*), it is correctly established; thus, first rejecting the state of being causeless (*ahetuka*):
Having stated, "This name-and-form is not indeed without a cause," he provides the reason for this with the words beginning "In all places" (*sabbattha*).
If things could exist without a cause, then the absence of a cause would be common to all phenomena; thus, there would be a universal uniformity (*sabbasamānatā*).

And if that were the case, there would be an absence of causes for eye-consciousness and so forth both within the spheres of the ear and other sense bases, as well as externally—thus, "in all places"—from the arising of the eye and the rest.

Previously, regarding the absence of a cause due to disintegration and upward [transmigration], and the absence of a cause at all times for those who are blind and so forth, and for those who are formless (*arūpin*), and for those who are non-percipient (*asaññin*)—if there were no cause, then visual consciousness and the rest would have to arise for everyone;
yet because they do not arise specifically due to the absence of a cause, it is said:
"Because of the consequence that everything would be identical everywhere, at all times, and for everyone. This is merely an illustration.
This refers to the phrase "in eye-consciousness and so forth. The intention is that whatever distinctions exist in the world, all [mental factors] must possess them at all times.
Or rather, it should be understood that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those [distinctions] are indeed included.
Therefore, because they would attain a state identical in every respect at all times, there is no possibility of distinction in their being rootless (*ahetuka*). Thus, at all times...
The connection should be understood as follows: "due to the attainment of a state identical to one [another]," and "due to the attainment of a state identical for all.
Thus, when the absence of a cause has been refuted, the proponent of an unequal cause might say: "This is not causeless;
on what account then is it caused? It is caused by a creator god (Issara) and so forth."
By the word "etc. (ādi), it should be understood that the inclusion of the Primordial Man (Pakatipuruṣa), Pajāpati, Time (Kāla), and so forth is intended. Rejecting that [view], he said:

"Not caused by a Lord (Issara) and so forth," etc. Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is not caused by a Lord and so forth, because nothing other than name-and-form is perceived, and because a Lord, Primordial Matter (pakati), and the like do not exist at all.
If, however, name-and-form were to arise from a non-existent Lord and so forth, then...
If it exists, it follows that it must be identical in all respects, at all times, and for everyone.

Furthermore, if name-and-form alone were caused by a Lord (Īśvara) and so forth—since name-and-form is seen arising after not having existed and perishing after having existed—then those causes, such as the Lord, must also be of the same nature.
And thus, they too would be conditioned and dependently arisen; therefore, even that [Lord]...

The discernment of conditions must be performed. If that [consciousness] does not arise, it follows that it is without a cause. Therefore he said, "because of falling into the state of being causeless.
Furthermore, name-and-form is not caused by a Lord (Īśvara) or other such causes. What is the reason? Because they arise successively.
For if there were such a thing as a permanent cause designated as a Lord, independent of karma, defilements, faculties, objects, and so forth, then for all beings...
There could be their simultaneous arising, as many as are required to arise from it. Why? Because the cause is present.
But if they were to postulate its arising according to the power of desire, what would be the obstacle to the simultaneous arising of those desires?
Or else, something else—such as karma, defilements, faculties, or objects—must be expected [as a condition].
If you say, "It exists," then that very thing is the cause and the reason; what is the use of postulating anything else whose efficacy has not been seen?
For the efficacy of karma and so forth is indeed seen, since [the result] is absent when those [causes] are absent, even though other conditions are present.
Just as, for example, even when visible form, light, and attention are present, visual consciousness is absent if the eye is absent, but [present] when it is present.
And having seen the phenomenon, it is understood that there exists in the eye the capacity to produce visual consciousness.

Furthermore, just as this distinction between the inferior and superior qualities of beings is observed— even when the external conditions such as the father, mother, semen, and blood are equal for twins—
this is because of the absence of any other such cause within their own respective continua (*saṃtāna*).
It is understood that karma has the capacity for that [result] there because it is caused by both action and defilement; this is not the case for a Creator God and so forth.
For the capacity of a cause is understood through the presence or absence of the effect when the cause is present or absent.
And nowhere is it seen that name-and-form—which, even when present, lacks that [specific] cause—fails to arise due to the absence of a Creator God and so forth.
Therefore, Īśvara is not the cause.
Furthermore, if heaven were said to be caused by Īśvara and so forth in this manner, then that type of heaven would have to be produced from him at all times;
for it is not logical that an effect whose causes are present should fail to arise. And since the cause is eternal and independent of anything else, [the result would likewise be constant].
It is not even appropriate to begin with heaven, because as long as a cause such as Īśvara (the Lord) is posited, it follows that everything must exist [simultaneously].

Furthermore, if one were to say, "Other conditions also certainly exist according to their respective roles, and Īśvara and the rest serve as their cooperative causes (*sahakārī-kāraṇa*)," whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated above. If the opponent were to say, "In this case, preceded by intelligence..."
"A specific arrangement of entities is observed, as in the case of pots, houses, and so forth. And there exists a specific arrangement of internal and external things, such as bodies and lotuses;
therefore, that too must have been preceded by intelligence.
And he by whom it was preceded by intelligence is the Lord (Īśvara) and so on; therefore, he must be the cause of the world designated as name-and-form."
That [reason] is unproven (*asiddha*), because the body, lotuses, and so forth are "composed" precisely because they arise in that very way.
For the arrangement of what has already arisen, established in such and such a manner by way of its configuration, is called "composition.

Furthermore, this reason is inconclusive (*anaikantika*), because composition is seen even in things not preceded by intelligence; for instance, the specific arrangement of sinews and the like through contact with fire, and likewise the arrangement of the skin and so forth as they dry up.
If, however, this Lord and so forth were to paint the dung-pits of cows, horses, goats, rams, and other animals, he would be as distracted as one who is insane.
Furthermore, when preparing the world, would he prepare it for his own sake or for the sake of the world?
In that regard, if the former were the case, his effort would be in vain, because there is no benefit to be accomplished by the world.

Now, as for the second [alternative]: why would he cling to evil—which brings harm and suffering to the world, such as hell and so forth, as well as aging, death, and so on—or why would he cling to both of these merely for the sake of play? For play, by its very nature, exists for the sake of delight.
To one who begins play for the sake of delight without knowing what delight is apart from play, he would be a master of delight only in name; he would not be a true master of delight. Now...
If one who is independent of any purpose were to produce [an effect] at all times, then this capacity of his to produce it would be either causeless or caused.
If it were causeless, it would belong to everyone; if it were causeless, it would belong to all.
But if it is caused, then that cause of his must have arisen either from another or from himself. In that regard, if it were from another...
[He is] like a servant for that which has arisen and been obtained by him.
Now, as for what this world was like prior to its arising from oneself—this entire matter is muddy and turbid, confused and disordered, like a mass of foam following the path of a herd of cattle;
it is unable to withstand being pressed, lacking essence. Let the digression rest; we shall describe only what is relevant. Therefore:
Because this name-and-form is neither causeless nor produced by an unequal cause such as a Creator God (Issara), therefore—“those” refers to the causes and conditions.

Since form is gross and clearly manifest, the discernment of its conditions is easy; thus, beginning with the words “of this physical body,” he first commences the method for discerning its conditions.
In that regard, the discernment of the conditions for name-and-form is as follows:

It serves to turn one away from the doctrines of no-cause and irregular cause; likewise, because it brings about disenchantment and dispassion, it is intended to turn one away from delighting therein.
Showing this by way of the womb-dweller, he said, "This body," and so forth, in order to clarify its impurity by means of refuting the notion that the place of birth is pure.
In this context, even though lotuses and the like grow in impure places, [they are not considered impure].
The inclusion of the term "internal" is for the purpose of demonstrating that these [lotuses] are indeed considered pure. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Just as a lotus might grow there in a heap of refuse discarded on the great highway—pure-scented and delightful."

"Is born" (nibbattati): this is stated by taking the commonality of the production of the material body during the occurrence of rebirth-linking within the mother's womb, and not merely its initial manifestation.

And by doing so, the statement that nutriment is a supporting condition, the statement regarding the making of the abdominal membrane behind [the embryo], and the statement regarding its foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive nature are all rendered consistent.
This being the case, when it was stated that "since some [factors] act from behind and others from the front, what would be the point at the time of rebirth-linking?

and so forth, that is refuted. By the phrase "because they are productive causes," he shows that ignorance and the rest are causes because they are the specific (asādhāraṇa) conditions for the material body, just as a seed is for a sprout. By the phrase "because they are supportive causes," however...
It shows that nutriment is a condition by way of being a common cause, just as earth, water, manure, and so forth are for a sprout.
"Five factors are the root-condition" means that the five factors beginning with ignorance are, as appropriate, both roots and conditions.
The longing that conceals the defects existing in the various states of existence functions, through its state of firm grasping, as the cause for volitional formations and becoming.
Being a cause by way of assisting the producer, it is a formative condition (*abhisaṅkhārika*) because it is a proximate cause co-arising with that [craving];
and being a support, it is said to be "the decisive support (*upanissaya*) like a mother for a child.
Just as a father is the progenitor because the semen produced by him leads to the birth of the son, so too karma is called the "progenitor" because it brings about the arising of a being.
Just as a nurse (*dhāti*) is called a "sustainer" (*sandhārikā*) by virtue of nourishing a newborn child, so too is nutriment called a "sustainer" (*sandhāraka*) of the arisen body.

Although ignorance and other factors are indeed conditions for the mental body (*nāmakāya*) as well, the phrase "dependent on the eye" and so forth was stated in order to demonstrate the method of discerning its conditions in a more manifest manner.
In that context, the word "and" (*ca*) in "the eye and" (*cakkhuñca*) has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

By this, he includes all internal conditions for eye-consciousness, beginning with adverting. Furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "in visible forms" (*rūpe ca*), he includes other external conditions as well, just as external visible form is generally the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for eye-consciousness.
"Dependent" (*paṭicca*) means having obtained that which has become a condition.

By this, he demonstrates the state of being a condition for the eye by way of its being a support-condition (*nissaya-purejāta*), faculty-condition (*indriya*), dissociation-condition (*vippayutta*), presence-condition (*atthi*), and non-disappearance-condition (*avigata*); for visible form, by way of its being an object-condition (*ārammaṇa-purejāta*), presence-condition, and non-disappearance-condition;
and for the other included factors, by way of proximity-conditions (*anantara*) and so forth, and co-nascence-conditions (*sahajāta*) and so forth.

As for the reason for the difference in wording, it has already been stated below. And by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [he includes] ear-consciousness and the rest together with their co-nascent conditions, just as in the case of contact and the rest.
Inclusion should be understood because the passage beginning with “dependent on the ear,” etc., is included within the passage beginning with “the meeting of the three is contact,” and so forth.
Thus, all name that comes under investigation is included together with its conditions. Therefore he said:
“He discerns the conditions for the mental body.”
"Having seen the present occurrence" means having seen the occurrence at this time.

By the word "thus," it should be understood that not only is mere conditionality being referred back, but also the similarity of conditions: that by whatever kinds of conditions it occurs now—namely, by conditions such as ignorance (avijjā) and so forth—it likewise occurred in the past.
680. "The past" (*pubbanta*) refers to the portion consisting of the continuity of the aggregates (*khandha*) in the past. "With reference to" (*ārabbha*) means aiming at that.

Relying on the mode of eternalism (*sassata-ākāra*) and the mode of spontaneous origination (*adhicca-samuppatti-ākāra*), one doubts whether one existed in the past or did not exist, [wondering] about one's own presence or absence in the past.
"Did I exist?"—this is based on birth, gender, and rebirth, [thinking], "Was I a kṣatriya... [and so forth].

One doubts: "Did I exist? Was I one among the brahmins, among householders, or among the gods? One doubts: "In what manner did I exist?"—this refers to the mode of physical form, doubting: "Was I tall?
Or was I one among those who were short, fair-skinned, dark-complexioned, large-statured, or small-statured?
One doubts: "By what means was I produced?"—this refers to the mode of origination, such as through the creation of a Supreme Lord (Issara-nimmāna) and so forth.
And they say, "he doubts. Based on birth and so forth, he doubts his own successive rebirths, thinking:
"Having been a khattiya, was I a brahmin... [and so on] ...having been a deva, was I a human?
And in all these cases, "addhāna" is a designation for time. "Will I exist? refers to the mode of eternalism (*sassata*).
Relying on the aspect of annihilation, one doubts whether one’s own self will exist or not exist in the future. The rest here is exactly as previously stated.
"Or else, regarding the present time" means either now, or the entire duration of the present moment beginning from rebirth-linking and ending with death.
"One is full of doubt about the internal" refers to one's own aggregates (*khandha*).
There is doubt (*vicikicchā*). One doubts the existence of oneself, thinking, "Do I perhaps exist? [The commentary notes: "But this is improper.
What consideration can there be here as to whether it is proper or improper? For the foolish worldling is like one who is insane.
One doubts the non-existence of oneself, thinking, "Do I perhaps not exist? Or, while being a kshatriya, one doubts one's own status as a kshatriya, thinking, "What indeed am I?"
He doubts. This same method applies to the remaining cases. As for the phrase "How indeed am I?": it is exactly as previously explained.

However, here one should understand that having grasped the notion that "there exists within what is called a soul (jīva)," and doubting its longness and so forth, he doubts, thinking, "How indeed am I?
Indeed, there is no one who does not know the present configuration of their own body. From where has [the soul] come?
"Where will he go?"—thus one doubts regarding the place of arrival and departure for this personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"All that is abandoned"—all that aforementioned sixteenfold doubt is abandoned by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*).
(681) It is the common condition for all modes of mentality (*nāma*), categorized as wholesome and so forth; therefore, it proceeds from that [condition].
It should be connected thus: "attention and so forth are the uncommon conditions for every type of mentality (nāma), according to the classification into wholesome and so on.

"According to the classification into wholesome and so on" means according to the division into wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional. And "of every type" refers to its further division into those accompanied by joy and so forth.
Whatever is exclusively of the six doors is also included by the very mention of the "six doors," just as...
It is also stated that "the sixfold object" means by way of grasping the six objects; thus it says, "even of every kind. "From that" means from the eye, visible forms, and so forth.
"Beginning with attention" means beginning with wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and unwise attention (*ayonisomanasikāra*), as well as beginning with kamma and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
Although here, by way of the six doors and wise attention and so forth, both common and uncommon conditions for name (*nāma*) have been stated, [it should be understood accordingly].
That, however, was stated without distinction. Specifically, kamma is the common condition for resultant mentality and for matter originated by kamma;
consciousness is the common condition for mental factors and mentality, as well as for mind-originated matter.
Furthermore, it is the uncommon condition for the aforementioned mentality and matter in relation to other mentality and matter. Likewise, it is of the same class (sabhāga).
Nutriment, which shares its function with the material phenomena produced by it, is a common condition for them; yet, in relation to other factors, it is an uncommon condition.
Thus, both the common and uncommon conditions for material phenomena must be determined as appropriate.

Since the discernment of conditions must be undertaken by one who has not yet attained Arahantship, it is said that, in consideration of this, [the practice] begins with systematic attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), hearing the true Dhamma, and so forth.

"Only of the wholesome," it is said. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of reliance upon true persons (sappurisūpanissaya) or the four wheels of prosperity (sampatticakka) should be understood.

From the statement that the opposite is a condition for the unwholesome, the meaning is that just as the opposite of wise attention (yonisomanasikāra) and so forth is a condition only for the unwholesome, so too wise attention and so forth are conditions only for the wholesome.
Or rather, for whomsoever wholesome [states] arise, unwholesome [states] arise, or both wholesome and unwholesome [states] arise—for such a person; this is established by the sense of the word.

By the word "beginning" (*ādi*) in the phrase "beginning with kamma," it should be understood that just as ignorance (*avijjā*) and so forth are included, the destination (*gati*), time (*kāla*), and other factors are also included.

By the phrase "beginning with the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅga*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), investigation (*santīraṇa*), limited functional (*paritta-kiriya*), and the state of an Arahant are meant. Among these, the life-continuum belongs to the five-door adverting consciousnesses and the functional consciousnesses of the mind-door.

It should be understood that investigation is a condition for determining; limited functional consciousness is a condition for both limited and sublime functional consciousnesses as appropriate; and Arahantship is a condition for all functional consciousnesses with the exception of adverting.
By "kamma," it is volition alone that is intended, and that is both wholesome and unwholesome. For this has been said: "Wholesome and unwholesome volition..."

“It is a condition for resultant aggregates and for the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa) by way of the kamma-condition. It is not like consciousness, which is accompanied by its associated states;
for here, consciousness is intended as being accompanied by its associated states, according to such statements as:
“Roots are a condition by way of the root-condition for states associated with roots and for the matter originated by them. Therein: in those [factors], namely, kamma and so forth.

Regarding the conditions that produce material form: it is stated that "the fruit arises from karma only when it is past, not while it is present," thus, "karma is a condition for the material form originated by karma only when it is past.
For if the fruit were to arise from karma while it is present, the fruit would have to arise at the very moment of the effort (the *āyūhana*-moment); however, that is neither seen nor desired.
Or rather: for in the world, an action being performed is never seen to give its fruit immediately, nor is there any such scriptural authority [to that effect].
But is it not also the case that this too is not seen—namely, a fruit arising from a cause that has already perished, or a hen laying eggs after she is dead?
True, it is not seen in the case of material phenomena (*rūpa-dhamma*) when their continuity is severed; however, this [is different].
The analogy does not apply because even for the formless, there is a continuity; for it is precisely from past kamma—due to its having been performed and accumulated—that the fruit arises.
Indeed, this has been stated: "Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness arises," and so forth.
This is because [the fruit arises] through the acquisition of conditions such as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*).
Because it is strong at the very moment of the mind’s arising, it generates the materiality that is itself arising; therefore, it is said:
“Consciousness [is the cause] of consciousness-originated [materiality] while it is arising. The connection is: “it becomes a condition for materiality.
However, because it is strong at the moment of materiality’s presence due to its acquisition of conditions such as post-nascence, it is stated: “temperature and nutriment... [etc.]”
“...exist”: the meaning is that, having obtained external conditions such as temperature and nutriment, temperature and nutriment generate material form at the very moment of its own persistence.
“In this way”: by the manner described in the passage beginning with “by way of common and uncommon [conditions]” and so forth.
682. “Of formations” (saṅkhārānaṃ): of conditioned formations. “Dissolution” (bhaṅgaṃ): death. Aging-and-death is [the result] of birth.

The phrase beginning with "When there is" (*satīti*) is presented after having shown that the discernment of the conditions of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is easy to perform by means of the sequence for demonstrating the cause following the sequence for demonstrating the fruit.
Therein, "when there is existence" (*bhave sati*) means when there is kamma-existence (*kammabhava*).
This was previously demonstrated in detail by way of dependent origination in forward order (*anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda*), starting from the end.
Having been shown in detail by way of the reverse order starting from the beginning, it is now shown by way of the direct order of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
For when the mode of conditions is shown in the reverse order by such statements as, "When there is no birth,

there is no aging-and-death," it is easy to discern the condition for name-and-form through both the method of negation (vyatireka)— that "from the absence of which there is the absence of another, that is the condition for the latter"— and the method of affirmation (anvaya).

684. "In the previous kamma-existence, delusion... and so forth has already been explained according to its literal meaning. Because it is an associate of kamma, the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) is included within the cycle of kamma (*kammavaṭṭa*), and thus it is said: "by way of the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*). 685.
"The present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the manifest, presently existing personal existence (*attabhāva*).

Kamma whose fruit is to be experienced therein is "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*). Kamma whose fruit is to be experienced immediately after the present existence is...

To-be-experienced-upon-rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*). "In another successive becoming" (*aparāpariyāye*) means in a succession of personal existences (*attabhāva-pariyāye*), that is, in a turning of personal existence other than the present life or the immediately following one.
"Lapsed karma" (*ahosikamma*) means karma that has simply been; its result has not yet occurred. It is karma about which it can only be said, "It exists" or "It will exist.
This is due to its being unoverpowered by opposing factors and through specific conditions.

Furthermore, the first impulsion volition (paṭhamajavana-cetanā), having attained a state of strength through the acquisition of specific qualities and having proceeded with exceptional intensity due to a similar prior karmic formation (pubbābhisaṅkhāra),
is called "to be experienced in this very life" (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) because it yields its fruit within that very same existence.
For, in the manner described, it is powerful within the stream of impulsion and proceeds by way of benefit or harm toward those endowed with distinguished virtues.

Because of its lack of repeated practice, its lack of acquisition, and its weak ripening, the volition of the first impulsion does not—unlike the other two—depend on the cessation of the ongoing stream of existence nor depend on the acquisition of a [suitable] occasion;
thus, it yields a fruit that is merely a result of the process itself, like a mere flower right here.
"Being unable to do so" means that the giving of a result by karma occurs only through the convergence of other conditions, such as the physical basis (upadhi) and the application (payoga).
"It occurs" means that, due to the absence of those [other conditions], it is unable to give its result within that very same personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"Accomplishing the purpose" means effecting the purpose of giving and so forth, or of killing and so forth. If one asks, "What is that?", he says:

"The seventh impulsion-consciousness (*javana-cetanā*). For that is the consciousness of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*), which has acquired distinction according to the method already stated, and has gained repetition (*āsevana*) through the preceding impulsions.
And that which is equal [in weight] and yields its result in the immediately following existence is called *upapajjavedanīya-kamma* (kamma to be experienced upon rebirth).

By the phrase "as long as the cycle of existence continues," he indicates that in the absence of the continuation of the cycle of existence, such kamma remains on the side of *ahosi-kamma* (kamma that has been), because there is no opportunity for it to ripen.
686. "That which is grave" refers to unwholesome kamma that is highly reprehensible, or wholesome kamma that is of great power. "That which is habitual" refers to...
"That which has been done frequently and habitually" means that it was recollected at the time of death with clarity as death approached;
for it is said that there is nothing at all to be said regarding what is done when death is imminent.

By the phrase "repeatedly cultivated," he distinguishes this from the karma described as "done frequently. Likewise, [he distinguishes] the karma to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).

It turns back [the process] because it does not permit the drawing forth of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For the fourfold set of kamma beginning with the "weighty" (*garuka*) is stated by way of its producing rebirth-linking.
Among these, the weighty ripens first of all; for it is said that it is "weighty. In the absence of the weighty, the habitual (*bahulīkata*) [ripens];
in its absence, the proximate (*āsanna*); and in its absence, that which was performed in previous births, as stated in the phrase "or else [kamma] stored up" (*kaṭattā vā pana*).

Karma that has been performed ripens. Furthermore, among those actions that are frequent, proximate, or previously performed, one must understand their relative strength or weakness: namely, evil following evil, or wholesome [following evil];
and likewise, evil following wholesome, or wholesome following wholesome; as well as what was frequently practiced, what was great, or what was performed in the past, compared to what is slight.
Because [an unwholesome deed] generates remorse and so forth through frequent recollection, and because its counteragent is incomplete, its result begins to manifest.

Because of the non-exhaustion of karma or residual karma (*kammasesa*) to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyāya-vedanīya*), there is a specific transformation of the continuity (*santati*);
thus, by those various causes, that which has acquired strength first ripens.
The examples here are Alāta, the general of King Videha; the slave Bījaka; and the princess Rucā, as found in the *Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka*. For it was said by the Blessed One: [as follows].
“In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person here who destroys life... [and so on] ...up to:
being of wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
Either previously he has performed that evil deed to be experienced as suffering, or later he has performed that evil deed to be experienced as suffering, or at the time of death—”

Or else he has adopted and taken up wrong view; because of that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. Furthermore, whatever killing of living beings he has done here...
[and so on] ...up to whatever wrong view he has held, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.

“In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who here has been a taker of life... [and so on] ...up to one of wrong view, yet at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world:

either a wholesome deed to be experienced as pleasant was done by him previously, or a wholesome deed to be experienced as pleasant was done by him later, or at the time of death, he had a wholesome thought.”

If he possesses right view that is fully undertaken and maintained, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, a heavenly world. However, as for his killing of living beings here...
[and so on] ...up to his wrong view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
“In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who here abstains from the destruction of life...
[and so on] ...who possesses right view and, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world:
either that wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasant was performed by him previously, or that wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasant was performed by him later, or at the time of death.”

If he possesses right view that is fully undertaken and adopted, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Furthermore, as for his abstention from taking life here...
[and so on] ...up to his possessing right view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
“In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who here abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...who possesses right view, yet after the breakup of the body, after death...

is reborn in hell: either an evil deed to be experienced as suffering was done by him in the past, or an evil deed to be experienced as suffering was done by him later on, or at the time of death he possessed wrong view.
"Because he has fully undertaken [these unwholesome deeds], with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation... even in hell.
But as for the fact that he here abstains from taking life... and possesses right view, he experiences the result of that either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period."

In short, this is the domain of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the Great Analysis of Kamma (*mahākammavibhaṅgañāṇa*): namely, the capacity for the prior and subsequent ripening of various kamma through various causes.
It is "productive" (*janaka*) because it brings about the production of the stream of ripening-result by way of giving rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and so forth. Therefore he said:

"It produces the material and immaterial resultant aggregates both at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence. [It is productive] of the stream of pleasure and pain, that is, of the continuity of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Or it is the supporting [condition] that serves as the cause for a much longer duration. Therefore he said: "It supports pleasure and pain;
it causes them to proceed for a long time. The obstructing [condition] gradually diminishes pleasure and pain while they are proceeding in a continuous stream.
Therefore he said: "It oppresses and afflicts pleasure and pain; it does not allow them to proceed for a long time."
"Having destroyed" means having cut off. Since the cutting off of karma is precisely the warding off of its result, he said, "having warded off its result.
And that is the making of room for the arising of one's own result; thus it is said, "he makes room for his own result. Karma for which room has been made for ripening is indeed called "ripened."
He said: "But when such a space has been made by karma, that result is said to have arisen.
The obstructive (upapīḷaka) [karma] cuts off the result of another, but does not itself give its own result. The destructive (upaghātaka), however, cuts off a weak karma and produces its own result;
this is the distinction between them. [This occurs] through the occurrence of conditions such as being subject to much illness.
It is an obstructer and a pressurer of the result (vipāka), and likewise an interrupter and a destroyer of the very same result.
When an action (kamma) ripens by destroying [the opposing force] and thereby making room for its own result, it may indeed be a "producer" (janaka).

Since the status of being a producer and so forth must be understood in relation to the result, and not in relation to the action, it is logical that the action possesses the quality of being a destroyer specifically of the result.
It is seen; it should be investigated.

"Difference in kamma" means a distinction among kamma, the differentiation between the strength and weakness of kamma. "Difference in result" means a distinction among results, its differentiation according to inferiority, superiority, and so forth.
According to another method: when a certain kamma has been performed, [it produces] resultant aggregates, kamma-produced matter, and [other matter] in the rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
That which arises [as a cause] is the producer (*janaka*).

However, that by the performance of which there occurs the non-arising of conditions that obstruct or interrupt the desirable or undesirable fruit produced by another, and by which there occurs the arising of conditions that foster its growth, such that the nourishment and the long-term continuity of that fruit correspond to the power of the producer—that is the supporter (*upatthambhaka*). The wholesome fruit produced by the producer—
That which, acting as an adversary, afflicts [the fruit] by way of the signs of the equilibrium of the elements of disease and so forth—
whether it be wholesome fruit or unwholesome fruit— is the *upapīḷaka* (afflicting). However, that karma by which the fruit— even though it is capable of a long-continued succession—
is impaired and interrupted through the arising of interrupting conditions by virtue of its generative power, is the *upaghātaka* (impairing).
In this regard, some describe the wholesome nature of the second [kamma] by way of its leading to freedom from illness and long life for a person of such-and-such a name,
and they describe the unwholesome nature of the latter two by way of their leading to much illness and short life.

Furthermore, for Devadatta and others, for Nāgas and others, and for hungry ghosts who subsist on what is not given from here, these [kammas] act as supports for unwholesome kamma-result, or as oppressors and destroyers in the hells and other realms.
It is not the case that the unwholesome nature of even those four [factors] is contradicted by their non-existence.
Because it is the object of a knowledge that is unique to Buddhas and not shared with others, "kamma, its result, and so forth" is said to be "unshared with disciples. It can be known only partially;
it cannot be known in its entirety because it is beyond the scope [of such knowledge]. If one does not know everything in its totality, the discernment of conditions is not fulfilled.

688. Since only that karma which has been described as the cause for the continuity of presently occurring results is intended here, it is stated that "twelvefold karma is included within the cycle of karma" by virtue of being a portion of karma.
Furthermore, because the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) acts as an auxiliary to karma, it is likewise categorized under the cycle of karma;
thus he says, "by way of the cycle of karma and the cycle of result. From whatever kind of condition...

Showing how the method [of analysis] applies to the past and future just as it does to the present— namely, that the occurrence of name-and-form in the present time is exactly the same as in the other two times—

he says, "This," and so forth. In this context, the word "only" (*eva*) used in the phrase "even in the future, by way of the round of kamma and the round of result" should also be brought over to the phrase "at present and in the past," so that it applies to all three times.

Because the exhortation is intended to show that there is merely the fruit of action and non-action. Thus, the passage beginning with "And what is karma... is stated as a conclusion to the very meaning already explained.
It is called the "round" (*vaṭṭa*) in the sense of revolving again and again. Its "occurrence" (*pavatta*) is its proceeding in such a manner.

It is a "continuity" (*santati*) because it connects by way of cause and fruit; it is a "series" (*pabandha*). It is an "action" (*kiriyā*) in the sense of doing, or because it is produced by conditions.
“From karma” means from action (*kamma*). It is called an “origin” (*sambhava*) because it originates from this; since its origin is karma, it is “karma-originated,” namely, the result (*vipāka*).
Because the designation of an agent is applied to the mere cause when the activity accomplished by giving and so forth is occurring within the totality of causes, he said:
“He does not see an agent apart from the cause. For one who acts is an “agent” (*kāraka*). [The text refers to] the experiencer of the result.

The connection is with the word "does not see. Granted that even fools, when they say "the doer" or "the experiencer," are speaking from the standpoint of meaning merely of a conceptual designation (*paññatti-matta*);

however, since they speak so through the influence of a distorted adherence (*viparītābhinivesa*), that [view] is not authoritative. Therefore, he said: "The wise employ [terms] by way of mere conventional designation (*samaññāmatta*)."
689. "Evetan" means this kind of seeing; it means right seeing, non-perverted seeing. Regarding the phrase "of seeds, trees, and so forth":

just as from a seed comes a tree, and from a tree again a seed—since the continuum of seeds and trees is beginningless, there is no prior limit—so too, with karma as a condition for fruition and fruition as a condition for karma, [the cycle] is beginningless.

No prior limit is discernible for the continuum of kamma and its result. By the word "beginning" (ādi), such things as "the hen from the egg, the egg from the hen, and again the hen from the egg" are included.

Regarding the future round of existence as well: just as in the past, so too in the future period, within the cycle of existence described by the phrase "the succession of the aggregates," there exist kamma and its results.
“Non-occurrence is not seen” means that the non-occurrence of the fruition of kamma is not seen; the sense is that it simply continues to occur.
“This matter” refers to the matter stated in the passage beginning with “there is no doer of kamma. “Not self-dependent” means not having mastery over oneself;
the sense is that they are dependent on wrong adherence. “Mutually contradictory” means being opposed to one another; [this refers to] views.
They are "contradictory" because they are mutually opposed by way of their views.

They are "profound" because they are the domain of profound knowledge; likewise, they are "subtle. They are "empty" because of the emptiness of sentient beings and the emptiness of mutual intrinsic nature.
"Condition" means the condition for name-and-form; and through the penetration of that very condition, everything is penetrated.
"Exists," etc. Regarding such statements as "there is no karma in the result," that which ought to be said has already been stated above.

To clarify by means of a simile the meaning already explained—that the fruit is empty of conditions—it was said, "Just as not in the sun," and so forth. "Of them" refers to the sun and the rest. "He" refers to the fire. "By means of the requisites" refers to the causes such as heat and so on.
If the cause and the fruit were mutually devoid of one another, how could the fruit be produced from the cause? To this he says:

“And yet, it is dependent upon karma. This is stated to show that not only is the fruit of karma empty and devoid of an agent, but every category of phenomena (dhamma) is likewise devoid of a doer; thus, the verse beginning with “There is no god here” was spoken.
“Causes, requisites, and conditions” means the cause for the collection of causes, or the cause for the condition of causes.

690. "They are known by way of death and rebirth-linking" means that because the investigation of conditions has been performed by way of the round of kamma and the round of result, they are said to be known by way of death and rebirth-linking.

However, according to the method already stated, for one who has abandoned doubt regarding the three periods of time through the vision of name-and-form together with its conditions, the phenomena included within those three periods—in past, present, and future existences—[are clearly understood].
They are known by way of the falling away and the rebirth-linking, but not by way of the successive states (anupada-dhamma), because such an investigation has not been performed.
This is his "full understanding through knowledge" (ñāta-pariññā). By means of this, he performs the investigation of name-and-form and the investigation of its conditions;
for that yogi, [he understands] by way of "this is name, this much is name," and so forth, and "this is its condition, this much is the condition," and so forth.
And because it is wisdom that knows by way of discernment, it is called "full understanding through the known" (*ñātapariññā*).
Now, in order to show the reason why the phenomena included within the three periods of time are understood by way of death and rebirth-linking, it is said:
"He understands thus," and so forth. By this, what is called the "transition between states of existence" of phenomena is demonstrated.
He shows that it never exists [elsewhere], because it ceases right there where it arose.

With the similes of recitation, the drinking of mantra-water, the decoration of the face, and the flame of a lamp, he says "But furthermore" (*apica kho*) and so forth to clarify that very absence of transition between phenomena.
