"Immediately after the mind-element" (*manodhātuanantaraṃ*) refers to the eye-consciousness obtained immediately after the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*). Nor indeed...
"It has not come" means it has not come from the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*), because visual consciousness does not exist within that functional mind-element.
"Nor has it not arisen immediately after" means that although it does not come from the functional mind-element, by obtaining the convergence of conditions, it arises immediately after it;
thus, it has indeed arisen. This is just like the occurrence of consciousness during the course of existence (*pavatti*).

In the same way, the continuum of consciousness proceeds through rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). Although the rebirth-linking consciousness does not come from the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), it is nevertheless not non-arisen immediately after it;
rather, the meaning is that it arises precisely by way of the convergence of conditions.

Furthermore, by the mention of "continuum" (*santati*) here, he clarifies the absence of any arrival from anywhere. For the progression of phenomena (*dhamma-pavatti*) is a connection established by way of the relation of cause and fruit.

Regarding the term "continuity" (*santati*): therefore he said, "The preceding consciousness ceases," and so forth. "Preceding" refers to the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*). "Ceases" means it passes away.
"Subsequent" refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). "From that" means it arises immediately after the death-consciousness.
For even though the rebirth-linking consciousness arises at a distance from the death-consciousness or after a long interval of time, it arises immediately [after it].

It is said, "it arises. Therefore, there is no interval between them; there is nothing that intervenes between those death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) and rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*).
"There is no gap (*vīci*) between them" is a synonym for this. "From here"—that is, immediately after the death-consciousness—no other consciousness proceeds.
For that [death-consciousness], together with its associated mental states (*sasampayuttadhamma*), ceases right then and there. Rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Thus, by showing that both the rebirth-linking consciousness and [the subsequent states] arise and are produced as something distinct according to their respective conditions,
he concludes the demonstration of name-and-form with its conditions, further clarifying the very absence of transmigration.
By the inclusion of "name-and-form" and the inclusion of its conditioning factors, there is no dhamma of the three planes that remains ungrasped.
Because of their non-existence, it is said, “one who has known all phenomena. And herein, supramundane phenomena have not been realized.

This [lack of realization] persists because the method for discerning the conditions of the manifold bases in their various aspects has not been performed. It is abandoned more thoroughly because of the absence of delusion regarding the occurrence of phenomena throughout the three times.
“That very same” refers precisely to the sixteenfold doubt. Since, in this context, [there is doubt regarding] the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha...
"Training" refers here to mundane phenomena that serve as the objective domain for doubt.
For defilements are not able to arise with reference to supramundane phenomena. "The past" refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements of the past.

"The future" refers to those of the future. "The past and future" refers to both of these; or alternatively, it refers to the present in terms of duration (*addhā*), because it is connected to both of those portions.
Thus, by the inclusion of the Buddha and so forth, and by the inclusion of dependently arisen phenomena, the eighth object of doubt—mere name-and-form—is already grasped;
however, by the inclusion of specific conditionality (*idappaccayatā*), its condition is also grasped.
Therefore, when the sixteen-based doubt is abandoned, the eight-based doubt becomes entirely baseless. Thus he said: "Not only... but it is indeed abandoned."

Because doubt (*vicikicchā*) is closely associated with views (*diṭṭhi*), just as a view is completely eradicated together with doubt when it is being eradicated, so too doubt is suppressed together with a view when it is being suppressed;
thus he said, "suppressing the sixty-two types of views. For the underlying tendency toward the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa-upanissaya*) is [the cause of the thought]: "Did I exist..."
The sixteen bases of doubt proceed according to the method beginning with "I am," and that very same [doubt] is stated as having the prior limit (*pubbanta*) and so forth as its basis.

Furthermore, there are sixty-two types of views based on the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*), and the doubts regarding the Buddha and so forth are included therein as being of the same category. They are called *dhammas* because they are sustained by their own conditions; [the world] stands upon them because its existence depends upon them.

"Abiding" (*ṭhiti*) means they bear fruit. The "abiding of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhiti*) is the condition-phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*). Alternatively, "phenomenon" (*dhamma*) here means cause, as in the expression "analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).

The "abiding" of a phenomenon is its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*); since there is no intrinsic nature other than the phenomenon itself, the state of being a condition for condition-phenomena is the "abiding of phenomena.
Knowledge regarding this abiding of phenomena is "knowledge of the abiding of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
Knowledge regarding the actual nature of formations—such as impermanence and so forth—exactly as it is, is "knowledge of things as they really are" (*yathābhūtañāṇa*).
Seeing correctly is "right seeing" (*sammādassana*).
Ignorance as a condition means that ignorance is the appropriate condition for formations by way of being their cause and so forth; for that very reason, there are formations.

"Arising by way of conditions. "Both of these" means that since ignorance (*avijjā*) also arises solely through conditions such as the taints (*āsava*), therefore both these phenomena—ignorance and formations (*saṅkhāra*)—are "arisen by way of conditions. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way.

"Wisdom in the discernment of conditions" is wisdom that functions by grasping conditions after having delimited them. By the method already stated, it is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
The "sign" (nimitta) is the sign of formations; in meaning, it is the five aggregates.
For they are the "sign" because they serve as the basis for the occurrence of the perception of solidity, or because they appear as having a substantial form.

Since what is called impermanence is the non-erroneous mode of formations—and because therein not even a trace of permanence exists—one who sees [them] as impermanent knows them as they truly are. And that knowledge...

Right seeing consists in grasping things without error. For one who possesses that [seeing], by applying the same method to the past and the future as to the present, those [phenomena] become well-understood.
Furthermore, since impermanence belongs to that which has arisen, and arising occurs by way of conditions, impermanence is established for conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).
Showing the meaning that establishing conditionedness leads to the abandoning of the aforementioned doubts, he said:

"By way of impermanence... [it] is abandoned. Therein, "by following upon that" means by following what has been seen through direct perception. "In this regard" refers to the phenomena as they have been seen.
The same method applies to the phrases "contemplating as suffering," and so forth. It occurs thus:
The occurrence of the acquired aggregates. For that indeed appears with an excessive degree of suffering because it is set in motion by defilements and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Others say:
"It occurs" means the occurrence of formations by way of standing, sitting, and so forth, and by way of the suffering of suffering (*dukkha-dukkhatā*) and so forth.
And when both "the sign" (*nimitta*) and "occurrence" (*pavatta*) are mentioned, they refer to everything that is conditioned, known as the internal and external continuity.
The single wisdom that proceeds with respect to name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as it truly is, is called by way of synonyms "knowledge of things as they really are" (yathābhūtañāṇa),
"right seeing" (sammādassana), and, by the suppression of doubt therein, "crossing over doubt" (kaṅkhāvitaraṇā).
Just as one might say "tree," "foot-stayer," or "woodland" to show this same meaning, so he said, "and that which is knowledge of things as they really are," and so forth.
In the ultimate sense, according to the Dispensation, "consolation" (assāsa) is the Noble Fruit (ariyaphala), and "foundation" (patiṭṭhā) is the Noble Path (ariyamagga).

However, although this person has not yet attained the Path and its Fruit, because he stands in the practice that is the means for attaining them, he is as if one who has gained consolation and as if one who has gained a foundation;
thus it is said: "one who has gained consolation, one who has gained a foundation. He is one whose purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi) is not lost.

Because the practitioner of insight (vipassaka), being endowed with mundane perfection in virtue, concentration, and wisdom, does not penetrate further but has a happy destination as his ultimate goal, it is said that he is "one whose destination is fixed.
For this very reason, he is called a "lesser stream-enterer" (cūḷasotāpanna). Indeed, a stream-enterer has exhausted rebirth in the states of deprivation, miserable destinies, and the fallen realms.
Alternatively, he has "found breath" through the attainment of purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).

For by discerning name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), having observed the aggregates and so forth according to their intrinsic nature and essence, he finds breath through the acquisition of gladness associated with the Dhamma within the Teaching.
He has "found a foothold" through the attainment of purification by overcoming doubt (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi*), by seeing name-and-form together with its conditions.

For one who has thus rubbed away the thorns of wrong views and discarded the doctrines of no-cause and false cause, having understood that phenomena arise solely from their respective conditions and having gained faith established in the Teaching, is said to have "found a footing. Through the analysis of name-and-form, the truth of suffering is discerned;

through the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, the truth of the origin [of suffering] is discerned; and subsequently, by means of the method of mental attention to those very things as impermanent and so forth—

Having directly known the truth of the path and seen the state of suffering in continued existence, one possesses an inclination directed exclusively toward cessation—the non-occurrence [of suffering].

Because the four noble truths have been realized even by means of mundane knowledge, one becomes incapable of rebirth in the states of misery and capable of rebirth only within the stage of stream-entry;
thus it is said, "one whose destination is fixed. Therefore it is said, "one is called a minor stream-enterer."

Therefore, because this knowledge of things as they truly are possesses such great benefit, therefore: "Always" means at all times, both by night and by day. "In every way" means in every manner, by way of comprehending the causes for rebirth and so forth.
The commentary on the description of Purification by Overcoming Doubt is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth chapter.
20. Explanation of the Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is the Path and What Is Not the Path; Explanation of the Discussion on Knowledge of Comprehension (692).
Thus, "knowledge that stands having known what is the path and what is not the path" refers to that which has emerged from the defilements and entered the right path.
Insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) is the preliminary path to the Noble Path;

it is the knowledge established after having correctly determined, as they truly are, both the path and the non-path, [recognizing] that these ten kinds of defilements—such as illumination (*obhāsa*) and so forth—are not the path.
Comprehension by condensing into groups those phenomena that are divided into many categories according to the past and so forth is "comprehension by groups" (*kalāpa-sammasana*).
This, it seems, is the expression used by those dwelling in Jambudīpa. For insight into phenomena according to the method beginning with "Whatever form...

is called *nayavipassanā* (insight into the method); this, it seems, is the expression used by those dwelling on the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Therefore he said: "by means of insight into the method known as the comprehension of aggregates.
The word *tāva* has the sense of "extent"; by it, he illustrates the great variety of the modes of comprehension.
Because there are many [aspects] to them, he first instructs on the commencement of the practice of insight into the method, saying:

"First, the practice of insight into the method must be performed. The question "Why? is the challenger's statement. His intention is this: "If the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path is to be accomplished, then why is it said that 'the practice of insight into the method must be done from the beginning'? The other [responds] with this:
Showing that this is the means for attainment, he said, "For one who has initiated insight," and so forth. By this he demonstrates:
"When insight exists, there arises the knowledge of arising and passing away; when the knowledge of arising and passing away exists, the adventitious defilements such as the 'aura' (obhāsa) arise;

from that comes the discernment of what is the path and what is not the path. Therefore, since its commencement does not occur at the very beginning [of the practice], insight must first be undertaken."
Thus, to the question "Why is it that insight according to the method (nayavipassanā) is undertaken first?", he said: "And for insight, the comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana) is the beginning.

For that is the beginning because it is easy for a beginner to comprehend, as it proceeds by way of defining phenomena that are otherwise divided into categories such as past and so forth, having condensed them.
"Therefore" means because it is the beginning. Alternatively, "therefore" means because for one who has begun insight (*vipassanā*), the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*) is the beginning;

therefore [it is called the beginning]. "This" refers to the comprehension of groups. Furthermore, the phrase beginning with "Moreover" shows the reason for the accumulation [of merit] regarding the status of the comprehension of groups as the beginning of insight.
The full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*) culminates in the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*); even before that [knowledge] is reached...
And because the discernment of what is the path and what is not the path occurs through the knowledge of arising and passing away, he said, "while the full understanding by scrutiny is taking place.

As for the instruction that "one should first apply oneself to the comprehension of groups," the reason for beginning with that very practice should be understood here in the same manner as previously stated.
This is because the so-called comprehension of groups is not even included within the single purification, and some...
They praise the practice of insight (vipassanā) without even mentioning that [foundation]. Even so, this has been shown in the Suttantas both partially and in its entirety.
In the *Paṭisambhidā*, it is established as the starting point of insight because it is easy for beginners to attend to it.
Furthermore, when illumination and other signs arise for one practicing insight, there occurs the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that this investigation was undertaken by the passage beginning with, "by one who desires to accomplish that. 693.

*Tattha* (therein) means: either in that state of being immediately subsequent to the full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) within the full understanding through scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*), or in those [other] full understandings.

*Vinicchayo* (determination) is a definitive conclusion regarding their essential nature, function, and plane. Even supramundane states associated with the Path [are included] in the first two truths.
Since all three kinds of full understanding (pariññā) are obtained by way of function, it is stated with qualification as "mundane full understanding" (*lokiya-pariññā*).
Wisdom that is directed toward the knowable through the discernment of the characteristics of phenomena possessing intrinsic nature is "insight-wisdom" (*abhiññā-paññā*).

It is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) because it is the cause for knowing—that is, for the purpose of making known—that which is to be fully understood. "Full-understanding wisdom" (*pariññā-paññā*) is so called because it delimits the characteristics such as impermanence.
*Jānanapaññā* (wisdom of knowing) is so called because it has the nature of comprehension as its cause. *Pahānapaññā* (wisdom of abandoning) is the wisdom that abandons what is to be abandoned.
Because they are devoid of characteristics such as being felt (*vedayita*), the characteristic of being affected (*ruppana*) is stated as their individual characteristic (*paccattalakkhaṇa*).

This refers specifically to those phenomena grasped by way of observing their own individual characteristics. Just as earth, contact, and so forth have the characteristics of hardness, touching, and so on.

In all three moments, these [particular characteristics] are grasped as being established by their own nature through their specific individuality (*paṭiniyatarūpatā*), unlike the general characteristics such as impermanence.

However, because those [general characteristics] must be grasped by way of the modes of dissolution, arising, decay, and liability to oppression, they are grasped as if they were superimposed forms; thus it is said: "having superimposed the general characteristic."

Since only mundane full understanding (*pariññā*) is intended here, it is specifically insight that has the characteristics as its object which is called "full understanding as abandoning" (*pahānapariññā*).
"From the cutting off of formations" means from the defining of mind-and-body (*nāmarūpa-vavatthāna*), which is called "purification by view" (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*). However, some say:
"Because the aggregates and so forth constitute the ground for insight, the entire investigation of the aggregates and so forth is the 'cutting off of formations.'"
They say: “The predominance belongs only to the penetration of individual characteristics.
By this, he shows that the wisdoms which comprehend the conditions of name-and-form are incapable of scrutinizing or abandoning [defilements].

However, because those [wisdoms] also proceed by way of observing a common mode of appearance—namely, that “name has the characteristic of bending” and “form has the characteristic of being affected”—there is a manner of scrutinizing them in a single aspect.

It might be argued that a mode of abandoning is obtained through the suppression of views and doubt; thus, some say that the functions of scrutinizing and abandoning also have predominance [in the path].

However, according to the highest exposition, just as the delimitation of formations occurs only through the purification of view, so too the functions of scrutinizing and abandoning should be understood to belong only to insight that has general characteristics as its object. For in this way, all three kinds of full understanding [are accounted for].
They are established; otherwise, there would be confusion. This is the ground for full understanding by scrutiny, because wisdom scrutinizes the characteristics such as impermanence therein.

Therefore he said: “In this... [and so on] ...sovereignty. Granted that even the knowledge of rise and fall abandons certain types of wrong adherence, yet because it has not reached the path, its abandonment is not preeminent. Thus he said: “Contemplation of dissolution...”

“Starting from this as the beginning, there are the stages leading up to the full understanding through abandoning. “Contemplating as impermanent” means contemplating and comprehending formations by way of their aspect of impermanence.
“The perception of permanence” refers to the wrong perception that occurs in the form, “These are permanent and eternal.
It should be understood that under the heading of “perception,” views and consciousness are also included. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. “Becoming disenchanted” means...
He sees by way of becoming disenchanted with formations through the contemplation of disenchantment, which has arisen from the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.

"Delight" (*nandi*) refers to craving accompanied by rapture. "Becoming dispassionate" (*virajjanto*) means contemplating in such a way that passion does not arise toward formations by way of the dispassion of the contemplation of fading away;
for one who has become thus is said to abandon passion. "Causing to cease" (*nirodhento*)...
Contemplating cessation means contemplating in such a way that formations cease and do not arise again in the future through the process of renewed becoming (*punabbhava*).
One who has become thus is said to "abandon" the arising of formations by bringing about their state of non-arising.
"Relinquishing" means relinquishing in such a way that, through the contemplation of relinquishment (*paṭinissaggānupassanā*), formations are no longer grasped.
Therefore he said, “he abandons grasping”; the meaning is that he relinquishes the apprehension [of things] by way of [viewing them as] permanent and so forth.
“Because it has been accomplished” means because it has been brought to completion. “The other” refers to the full understanding of abandoning through investigation (*tīraṇapahānapariññā*).

Having thus demonstrated full understanding, in order to conclude the point previously stated—that following the overcoming of doubt, “application to the comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpasammasana*) must be practiced”—according to the sequence of full understandings:
Recalling [the source], he said, "Thus it was stated," and so forth; that has the same meaning as what was already stated.
694. *Tattha* (therein) means: either in that which is to be clarified through the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*), or at the beginning of that comprehension of groups.
*Ayaṃ pāḷīti* (this is the text) refers to the text of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* being shown. In that regard, regarding the determination by way of abbreviation:

"Wisdom" (*paññā*) refers to the wisdom that accomplishes the discernment (*vinicchaya*) of phenomena—classified according to distinctions such as the past and so forth—by grouping them together under aspects such as impermanence and so on;
it is the wisdom that effects that accomplishment. "Knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) is said to be the investigation (*tīraṇa*) by way of impermanence and so forth during the stage of comprehension (*sammasana*).

The meaning is: how does that [wisdom] come to be? In the phrases "in the defining" (*vavatthāne*) and "in the comprehension" (*sammasane*), the locative case is used because these are the stages to be brought to completion. "Whatever form," and so forth...

The words have meanings already explained below. As for the phrases "he defines all materiality as impermanent," and so forth, since they will be described later, we shall clarify their meaning in those very places.
The analysis of the text, however, should be understood as follows: herein, it is for the sake of the ease of insight-attention for beginners that—
First, by the passage beginning with “whatever form,” the five aggregates are taken up by way of their classification into the past and so forth.

Since those aggregates receive their classification in conjunction with the doors and objects through the phenomena that arise at the doors, ten hexads are taken up immediately thereafter by way of the six doors and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the characteristics...
The characteristic of non-self is the analysis of suffering; therefore, the six elements are taken for the purpose of clarifying that.

Then, the ten kasinas are taken to show that those objects upon which outsiders fixate as a self are, for these meditations, merely modes of appearance existing as objects of concentration. Following that, there is the contemplation of suffering.
The thirty-two parts are included by way of their being a retinue and by way of their repulsive aspect.
The phenomena (dhammas) previously taken up briefly by way of the aggregates (khandhas) are to be attended to by a method that is neither too brief nor too detailed;
for the purpose of showing this, the twelve bases (āyatanas) and eighteen elements (dhātus) are included. Among these, even though these phenomena...
The faculties (*indriyāni*) are included for the purpose of revealing the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*),
in the sense that they function by way of predominance according to the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena (*dhamma*) which are empty, inactive, and devoid of agency. Furthermore,

the three elements (*dhātuyo*) are included to show that although these phenomena are divided into many categories, they are nonetheless only threefold by virtue of being comprised within the three planes (*bhūmi*).
To this extent, having shown the sign (*nimitta*), nine types of existence (*bhava*)—beginning with sensual existence (*kāmabhava*)—are taken up in order to show the occurrence (*pavatta*).

The jhānas, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), and the formless attainments (*arūpa*) are taken up for the purpose of showing that, through skill in attention regarding these specific objects of direct knowledge (*abhiññeyya-visesa*), attention should be applied to the subtle, delicate, and sublime states produced therein. Among those, the jhānas...
The remaining objects mentioned by name are the fine-material-sphere jhānas.

The factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādanga) are included here for the purpose of showing that these phenomena must be attended to by distinguishing them according to the analysis of conditions and the conditionally arisen.
For the attention to the mode of conditions (paccayākāra-manasikāra) easily and more thoroughly clarifies the three characteristics; therefore, it is taken up last. Thus, these...
When taken by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth as objects of comprehension, they are twenty-fivefold according to their divisions.
However, when taken without regard to the distinctions of past and so forth, there are one hundred and ninety-eight.

Among these, the first section on the determination of characteristics begins with "He defines [them] as impermanent," and so forth; the second begins with "Impermanent in the sense of destruction," and so forth.

The second section on causes is so called because it describes the causes of the characteristics. The section beginning with "Impermanent, conditioned," however, is the section establishing the cause, because it observes the manifest state [of those characteristics].

"In the sense of destruction" means that because its intrinsic nature is destruction—since form, having arisen, goes to destruction, fall, and breakup—it is therefore impermanent. "In the sense of terror" means because it is a state that ought to be feared.
Because form is terrifying due to its perishable nature, it is therefore suffering. Thus the Blessed One said: "That which is impermanent is suffering.
By the phrase "in the sense of being coreless," the meaning is: because of the state of being coreless, that is, because it is devoid of a self as its core.
In the third section, however, having stated "form is impermanent," the words beginning with "conditioned" are spoken in order to establish the reason for that. Because...
Having come together and having been produced by conditions, it arises in dependence upon appropriate conditions, not without them, nor apart from them, and it arises rightly;
therefore, it is "subject to destruction, vanishing, fading away, and cessation. For there is no such thing as that which is produced by conditions and yet does not cease.
Thus the Blessed One said: "That form which has been born, become, conditioned, and is subject to dissolution..."

“Indeed, that it should not perish—that situation does not exist. By this, he shows that the earth element is impermanent because it is produced by conditions, just like anything else produced by conditions.
This same method applies to the remaining phenomena as well.
Now, in order to establish the impermanence of conditioned phenomena through both positive and negative concomitance, [the text says] “with birth as condition,” and so forth.

It has been stated. And here, the establishment of the characteristic of impermanence alone [is intended], because once that is established, the establishment of the other two characteristics is also accomplished.
By this elliptical expression, the connection is that these groups of phenomena (*dhammarāsi*) have been condensed. "Together with the doors and objects, those proceeding through the doors..."

In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, under the exposition of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), after showing the phenomena occurring at the doors together with the doors and their objects by means of the passage beginning "Bhikkhus, the eye is to be directly known," it is stated [as follows] in order to show that these are included within the five aggregates:
"Form is to be directly known... consciousness is to be directly known. Thus it was said. In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*...

However, after first showing the five aggregates with the words "whatever form," etc., the phenomena occurring at the doors are shown together with the doors and their objects by means of the words "the eye," etc.
The reason for showing them in this way has already been stated above. Why, then, are these heaps of phenomena abbreviated here?
[The author] shows that they are presented in detail in the Pāḷi:
He said, "For it has been said," and so forth. Therefore he said, "That therein... [etc. ...is condensed. Therein, "that" refers to what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*).

"Therein" refers to the exposition of what is to be directly known. By means of such passages as "consciousness, mind, mental objects," etc., those supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*) that have appeared here and there in various sections are included. Some, however, say, "Therein means in the *Paṭisambhidā*"; that is not correct.
For in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, only those phenomena that are subject to comprehension (*sammasanupagā*) are included, because the section on comprehension (*sammasanavāra*) is intended;

they are not all phenomena that are to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), as is the case in the exposition of what is to be directly known. Regarding "those" (*ye*): these are the material and immaterial phenomena. Regarding "for whom" (*yassa*): for the practitioner (*yogī*).
He should begin the comprehension of them according to their manifestation, taking this as the basis for insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*). Afterwards...
However, even if they do not appear, one should cause them to appear by means of a skillful method and contemplate them without exception.

(695) Because the distinctions such as "past" and so forth serve as the basis for the occurrence of the contemplation of impermanence—as in "Past form is impermanent," etc.—he says, "by way of eleven instances.
"Definition" (*vavatthāpana*) means reaching a conclusion. And here, the conclusion is reached in terms of impermanence.
“‘Impermanent’ is insight-knowledge,” thus he said, “he comprehends as impermanent.
Since the manner of comprehension was asked about, he answers it briefly by means of the very method stated later in this same text during the second section.
Now, in order to make that meaning clearer, he says, “For this has been said,” and so forth.

In this context, *hi* is a particle used in the sense of a reason (*hetuatthe nipāto*). Because it has been stated that "form—past, future, and present—is impermanent in the sense of destruction," the construction is:
"therefore, one comprehends it as impermanent according to the method thus described.
To show by way of analysis that even in this way it is merely a summary, the words beginning with "this" (*esā*) were spoken. "In the past" (*atīte*) means in a past existence.
For this method of comprehension is intended for a beginner; therefore, the division of time is intended by way of existence (*bhava*).
Thus he said: "This does not reach this existence. Here, the word *iti* has the sense of a reason. This is what is meant:
whatever material form was included in a past existence, that has already been exhausted in that very past existence; therefore, it does not [reach] this existence.
"Attained," therefore, he comprehends as impermanent in the sense of destruction because its nature is destruction. This same method applies to the phrases "whatever is future," and so forth.

Whatever is external, that too perishes right there externally and does not become internal; thus it is impermanent in the sense of destruction. Whatever is gross, that too perishes right there; thus it is impermanent in the sense of destruction—and so on, the construction should be applied accordingly.

"All this" means that because one comprehends material form—divided into the past and so forth—all eleven kinds of comprehension are treated as a single comprehension, namely, comprehension by way of impermanence.
"That" refers to those eleven kinds of material form. "By way of being fearful" means by way of being terrifying.
"It brings fear" means it produces fear in one who has not abandoned the perversions and thinks, "I am perishing; what belongs to me is perishing."
It occurs. "As in the case of the gods in the *Sīhopama-sutta*" means as it was for the gods when the *Sīhopama-sutta* was being taught. For therein it is said:
"When a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One...
he teaches the Dhamma thus: 'Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away. Such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations...'"
‘Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.

And even those gods, bhikkhus, who are long-lived, beautiful, abundant in happiness, and dwell for a long time in lofty palaces—even they, upon hearing the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part fall into fear, a sense of urgency, and terror, thinking: ‘It seems that all things are indeed impermanent...’
‘Friends, we thought we were permanent; but alas, we are indeed impermanent...

[and so on] ...alas, friends, though we thought we were eternal, we are indeed non-eternal; we too, friends, are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and included within identity (sakkāya).’—In this way, the arising of fear among the gods is described.
The five aggregates, or a portion thereof, is conceptualized as "self" by those who propound a self-doctrine;

and since that is absolutely impermanent and suffering, it is said: "For whatever is impermanent, that is suffering," and so forth. Among the three types of suffering, the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) alone is all-pervasive, and it is this which is intended by the statement, "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. Thus it was said: "Or rather, impermanence is the oppression by arising and passing away..."
“Or,” [it means]: “The self will come to be”—the intention being that the self will exist as such, namely, as “the agent, the experiencer, and the one who is self-ruling.

For if this were so, the fact that form leads to affliction would be untenable. Just as there is a threefold comprehension of the aggregate of form by way of non-differentiation and a thirty-three-fold comprehension by way of differentiation, so too it is with the aggregates of feeling and the rest; such is the meaning.

“This is the method” refers back [to what precedes]. By this, first of all, one hundred and sixty-five modes of comprehension have been shown by way of the analysis according to the aggregates (*khandha*).
According to this method, the various types of comprehension should be understood as appropriate for the six doors and so forth. 696.

“It is definitely characterized by the distinction of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and so on” means that it possesses, with certainty, the specific qualities of being conditioned and so forth, while having the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) and so forth.
Because of its impossibility in the case of impermanence. "Assa" means "of the impermanent. "For the purpose of showing synonyms" means for the purpose of showing alternative expressions;
that, moreover, should be understood by way of [terms] such as "subject to destruction," and not by way of the preceding three.

For that very same term cannot be its own synonym, nor do the terms "conditioned" and "dependently arisen" serve as synonyms because they illuminate non-existence or illuminate the state of being cooked (i.e., transformation).
However, by way of illustrating the state of being cooked (pākabhāva), they stand on the side of proving impermanence.
For that very reason, because there is no redundancy among all the terms, the alternative option "or in various ways" is taken.
"For the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention" means for the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention that cultivates impermanence.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Contemplation of the Forty Aspects (Cattārīsākāra-anupassanā-kathā-vaṇṇanā) 697.
"He" refers to the practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*). "Of that" refers to the comprehension of impermanence and so forth, which has been analyzed as previously described.

"For the sake of firmness" means for the sake of stability; it is because of the state of repeated cultivation (*bahulīkāra*), similar to the repeated mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward the aspects of impermanence and the rest. That which...
The connection is that the discernment of impermanence and so forth was taught by the Blessed One in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of this [term].
"Conformable" (*anulomika*) means suitable for the attainment of the noble path (*ariyamagga*). "Acceptance" (*khanti*) refers to the acceptance of knowledge (*ñāṇakhanti*);

for knowledge is called "acceptance" because it accepts—that is, endures—when it has penetrated and determined the intrinsic nature of its object. "The certainty of rightness" (*sammattaniyāma*) refers to the noble path; for it...
Right view and the rest are called both "rightness" (sammatta) and "the certainty" (niyāma) because they possess the nature of not turning back.
By the phrase "by way of the beginning method," there is an ellipsis of the text such as: "One who sees the five aggregates as suffering acquires the conformable acceptance;
one who sees the cessation of the aggregates as the bliss of Nibbāna enters the certainty of rightness."

It should be expanded by way of connecting it with the opposites of disease and so forth. By the statement, “The cessation of the aggregates is the permanent Nibbāna,” the fact that Nibbāna possesses the nature of happiness, health, and so on—which is the opposite of the suffering, disease, and so forth of conditioned phenomena—is indicated here by the inclusion of the word “and so forth” (*ādi*).
Thus, the entire remaining text is already explained.
Granted that this comprehension by way of forty aspects is the method for developing conformity knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*);
therefore he said, “By one analyzing conformity knowledge... [as] stated. However, from this point onward, it brings about its function only for one who has already gained proficiency;
thus it should be understood that it is also stated here. “Of that too” means not only of the comprehension of groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*), but also of... [the rest].
It is indeed desirable that one should definitely desire even the contemplation of impermanence and so forth, which has forty-four modes as already shown.
For that leads to the attainment of conformity-acceptance (*anulomikā khanti*) and to the entry into the certainty of rightness (*sammattaniyāma*). As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, surely that bhikkhu who regards any conditioned phenomenon as permanent [cannot] possess conformity-acceptance..."

It is impossible that he will be endowed [with these qualities]; it is impossible that one who is not endowed with the conformable acceptance (anulomikā khanti) will enter the fixed course of rightness (sammattaniyāma);
and it is impossible that one who does not enter the fixed course of rightness will realize the fruit of stream-entry... or even arhatship. Indeed, he—
“Monks, a bhikkhu contemplating all conditioned phenomena as impermanent”—beginning with this, the "bright side" (sukkapakkha) should be expanded upon.
Likewise, it should be expanded upon thus: “Indeed, monks, that bhikkhu [would not regard] any conditioned phenomenon as pleasant or as painful, nor any state as self or as non-self.
698. The connection is: “He comprehends each aggregate by means of the comprehension of impermanence and so forth. Furthermore, of that...
Because the five aggregates are common to the act of comprehension (*sammasana*), it is said, "each individual aggregate.

"Non-eternality" (*anaccantikā*) means the absence of eternality; that is to say, the lack of permanence. For what is eternal (*sassata*) is "ultimate" (*accantika*) because it lacks a further limit. "Having a beginning and an end" means having limits at both the prior and subsequent ends;
that is to say, being subject to the nature of arising and passing away. Thus, one comprehends them as impermanent.
The connection [is as follows]. This method applies everywhere.

"Impermanent" (*anicca*) means because it is unstable (*addhuva*). For this is not permanent; because it is momentary or because it does not persist constantly, it is not permanent and should not be approached as such—thus it is "impermanent.
"By being oppressed by arising and passing away" means by each respective arising and passing away.
Because they have the nature of afflicting those who possess them at every moment, or because they must themselves be afflicted by them;
for phenomena subject to arising and passing away are constantly oppressed by these [characteristics]. This oppression is what is called "the suffering inherent in formations" (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*).
As for "being the basis of suffering," it is because they serve as the foundation for all three kinds of suffering and for the suffering of the round of existence (*saṃsāradukkha*).
"By way of being maintainable by conditions" means by way of having to be sustained by conditions as appropriate.

"By way of being the root of disease" means because, like a primary disease, it serves as the root for subsequent diseases; by these two phrases, he shows that it is similar to a chronic (maintainable) illness.

For a chronic illness is called a "disease," while the other is called an "affliction. "By way of being possessed of the sting of suffering" means by way of the afflicting characterized as the threefold suffering.

"By way of being joined": because of the trickling out of the impurities of the defilements—namely, lust and so forth—according to their respective objects and by way of their possession [of those objects].
"From arising after not having been": this refers to the state of swelling due to its production.
"By way of internal piercing": because of piercing within; for these formations, like painful feelings and the rest, [cause] the personal existence...

They pierce [the heart] precisely from within by way of their arising and passing away. Their "difficulty of removal" is due to the fact that they cannot be extracted without the tongs of the Noble Path (ariyamagga), because of the firmness of the adherence to craving and views.
It is called "misery" (agha) because it is to be censured by the Noble Ones, just like evil;
and it is "bringing about non-prosperity" because it produces harm for beings, being the basis for evil—the five aggregates (khandhapañcaka).
He said: “...reproaching... [and so on] ...from calamity. “By way of producing a state of non-independence” means by way of generating a state of being subject to another’s power.

Just as a sick person is not independent because their bodily existence is dependent on others for such things as being laid down and being helped up, so too these [defilements] produce a state of non-independence.
“By way of lack of mastery” means by way of the inability to exercise control. Just as a man who is in another’s debt does not come under his own power, so too...
Because it is impossible to bring [the body] under one's control through states such as beauty or pleasure;

because of its uncommandability, meaning that it cannot be directed by such commands as "do not grow old" or "do not die"; because of its perishability, meaning that it is broken up and destroyed by various modes such as disease, or because of its ruin by those very same factors.
For the word *loka* has the sense of "ruin," while the prefix *pa-* has the sense of "intensity."
It should be seen. Regarding "the ruin of the aggregates through disease and so forth": it is called *īti* because it comes (*eti*) as that which brings about ruin;

this is a designation for adventitious factors on the side of unwholesomeness that are causes of ruin. Since the aggregates are of such a nature, he says: "Because they bring about manifold ruin, [they are] from *īti*.
It is an *upaddava* because it afflicts (*upaddavati*); the meaning is that it overcomes and overwhelms by producing harm, such as royal punishment and the like.
This is a designation. And because the aggregates are of such a nature, it is said: "Because they are unknown... [etc. ...because they are a calamity.

Because they bring about fear pertaining to the present life and the future life, and because they are the opposite of fearlessness, the aggregates are "fear"; thus he says: "Because they are all fears... [etc. ...because they are fear.

In the sense of afflicting with external misfortunes such as the loss of relatives, and with internal misfortunes such as lust, and by virtue of being similar to an affliction (*upasarga*), [they are called "afflictions"].
And there is "affliction" (*upasagga*). "Affliction" refers to misfortune such as disease that occurs through the intervention of deities.
This must not be overlooked for even a moment by one who desires their own welfare. Therefore it is said: "From many... [etc. ...by way of affliction.

"Being beset by faults" means being possessed of faults such as lust and so forth, both by way of the object and by way of association. "Worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) are the tendencies of attraction and aversion caused by gain and the rest.
By those [factors] such as disease and so forth, there is instability and wavering.
"By means of an effort" refers to one's own or another's application. "By its own nature" refers to its intrinsic character.
The state of being prone to disintegration is its fragility. "Falling in all places" means, like the fruit of a tree, from the very time it is extremely tender, in all [stages].

Because of the nature of falling away during various stages. Even for one who does not fall away, because of being entirely without essence and lacking the state of stability—indeed, that which is stable is called "constant" (dhruva).
Because it is incapable of protecting or guarding, it is "not a refuge" (atāyana); the state of being such is "the lack of refuge-ness" (atāyanatā).
It is the unobtainable security for one who has approached with the hope for refuge. [It is so] by means of the intention to cling out of fear of suffering.

"To resort to" means to take refuge. "The cessation of suffering" is the function of a shelter. "The destruction and dispersal of the fears of birth and so forth" is the quality of providing security from fear.
"By those imagined as such" means by those who do not exist in the ultimate sense, but are of the kinds imagined by fools.
"By way of emptiness" means by way of being secluded; the meaning is "by way of being devoid. Emptiness is the absence of internal essence. And that very [absence] is vanity; thus he said.
“Emptiness (rittata) is indeed vanity (tucchata). “By way of meagerness” means by way of limitedness or by way of inferiority.
Having stated the absence of a self-essence (*attasāra*) along with the absence of a stable essence and so forth by means of the term “empty” (*rittapada*), the phrase “by way of being void...

voidness” (*suññato*) is said in order to show specifically the absence of an essence produced [only] as a mere conceptual construct (*nibbattitamatta*). Just as it is void of a self characterized by such qualities as ownership and so forth...
Since these are likewise of a nature that is not-self, he said: “And themselves... as non-self. For “non-self” (*anattā*) means “not self” (*na attā*).

“By way of the suffering of the process of existence” means because of the state of suffering inherent in the process of becoming (*bhava-pavatti*). And the process of becoming is simply the occurrence of the five aggregates in modes such as impermanence;
and that is a disadvantage (*ādīnava*). As it was said: “Bhikkhus, whatever there is of the five aggregates of clinging...”
“Impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. This, monks, is the danger in the five aggregates of clinging.
Thus he said, “and because of the danger of suffering. *Ādīnaṃ* is a neuter noun used adverbially, as in the expression “to one side” (*ekamantaṃ*);
the meaning is “extremely wretched. For this prefix *ā-* has the sense of intensity, just as in the expression “torn in two, rent apart” (*dvidhā chiddakaṃ vicchiddakaṃ*).
Here, the word *vi-* has the sense of the word *dvi-*, and thus he says, “Because it is of a nature subject to transformation in two ways, it is characterized by change (*vipariṇāma-dhammatā*).
And transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the attainment of an opposite intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). “Due to weakness” means due to the absence of strength, because of its inherent fragility.
Even something weak might be difficult to overcome due to its being soft and pliable; however, these [elements] are indeed easy to overcome, and thus he says:
“And because they are as easily broken as wood. The state of being a cause of misfortune (agha) is *aghahetutā*. For all evil (*kibbisa*) is indeed bound up with the aggregates (*khandha*).
It is so called because it has the nature of striking down those who have conceived the confidence that these forms and so forth are causes of happiness, not causes of suffering.
For through the grasping of the aggregates as “this is mine,” beings meet with calamity; or rather, it strikes down their confidence.
"Deceivers of trust," because of that state.

"From the absence of becoming" (*vigatabhavatāya*) means from the departure of increase. "Non-becoming-craving" (*vibhavataṇhā*) and "non-becoming-view" (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*) are [called] "non-becoming" (*vibhava*) through the elision of the final member of the compound;

therefore, it is "from non-becoming. Alternatively, it is because they have arisen from destruction (*vināsa*), which is the cause of their own nature similar to that of a father. Of the taints (*āsavānaṃ*).

The state of being a condition by way of object and so forth is the footing for the taints (*āsava*). A seed and the like are the specific cause (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*), while the elements, water, and so forth are the common conditions (*sādhāraṇa-paccaya*).
This same method applies internally as well. That which is made by those [conditions] coming together and combining is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*).
It is "become food" (*āmisabhūta*) because it serves as the domain of the Mara of Death and as the condition for the Mara of Defilements to grow; this also applies to the aggregates (*khandha*).

The aggregates are "bait" because they nourish [craving] by way of being its condition; the volitional formations are included within them. Furthermore, for the Māra who is the son of a deva, they constitute bait through the conceit "this is mine";
thus, it should be stated that these [aggregates and so forth] are likewise of the nature of bait, as appropriate for each of the various Māras.

In the word *dhamma*, the sense is that of "nature," as in "subject to the nature of birth" (*jātidhammānaṃ*), and so on; whereas in "the analytical knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*) and so on, [it has a different sense].
And because it has the sense of a cause, he said: "By reason of being subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death; and by reason of being the cause of sorrow, lamentation, despair, and anguish.
By the inclusion of the three types of defilement (saṃkilesa), the inclusion of the ten bases of defilement (kilesavatthu) which are associated with them should also be understood.
For even those phenomena that take those [defilements] as their object are indeed defiled, because they do not transcend them. Likewise in the cases of *khuddā*, *taṇhā*, *jaṭā*, and so forth.
The inclusion of both the body and its defilement should be understood.
Since all forty modes of comprehension are included within the three contemplations (*anupassanā*), the phrase beginning with "For here" was stated to demonstrate that they are contained therein.
The contemplations of impermanence are so called because they reveal the state of impermanence both by way of their essential nature and by way of synonyms.
This same method applies to the others as well. "By way of being without essence" (*asārakato*) is an elucidation of the absence of any permanent essence.

Up to this point, having grouped phenomena into clusters, only the mere comprehension by way of method has been shown; since insight into phenomena one by one (*anupadadhammavipassanā*) has not yet been established, this is called "the instruction for beginning comprehension. Thus it was said.
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Nine Causes for the Sharpening of the Faculties* (*Indriyatikkhakāraṇanavakathāvaṇṇanā*)

699. For some person of keen faculties and great wisdom, the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) arises by means of insight into the method (*naya-vipassanā*) alone, while for another it does not arise. With reference to that, it is said: "But for whom... [it] does not succeed.
For here, the intended meaning of "success" is the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away through insight into the method. By this, [the text says]: "In nine ways..."
The connection is as follows: having made the faculties sharp by means of the nine modes thus described—“the faculties become sharp...
[and so on]... even before the completion”—one should contemplate while cultivating what is suitable.
“By him” means by the yogi. “By nine modes” means by the nine modes that will be explained. “Faculties” refers to faith and the others.
The faculties. "Sharp" means keen, clear, and resolute. "Of those that have arisen" means of those that arise moment by moment.
"Formations" refers to material and immaterial phenomena as they are being observed through insight.
"Only their destruction" means that having first seen their arising, one lets go of that and sees only their destruction—that is, their dissolution. For one who is thus intent on seeing destruction:
Insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) is sharp, heroic, and carries [the burden], as do the other faculties. "Therein" means in the vision of exhaustion (*khayadassana*).
"By doing with care" means by acting with reverence; that is, one accomplishes it with such reverence that insight-knowledge proceeds solely for the sake of the vision of exhaustion.
"By doing continuously" means by acting without interruption, so that insight-knowledge proceeds by way of the vision of exhaustion.
It proceeds without interruption; thus, one who is properly engaged accomplishes it.

"By means of suitable action" means by means of appropriate action—that is, by means of the practice of the seven kinds of suitability, such as the dwelling place and so forth. "By grasping the sign" connects to the following:
by grasping the sign of serenity through the observation of the specific mode in which insight-concentration arose for one who was attending to the object.

"By way of non-contrariety" means by proceeding in accordance [with the state of mind]; the meaning is: by the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of rapture, energy, and investigation-of-dhammas when the mind of development is sluggish, and by the strengthening of the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity when it is agitated.
"Without regard for body or life" means regarding one's own body as being impure like an external, unconscious corpse, and regarding life as an adversary that brings about harm.

He establishes a mind that is, as it were, indifferent. And therein, "having overcome by means of renunciation" means that, through the state of being indifferent toward body and mind, he accomplishes the meditation by overcoming each successive arising of suffering with vigor, having brought about sharpness of the faculties.
"In the interval" means precisely in the interval before the intended success of the meditation is achieved.
"By non-contracting" means by not shrinking back.
"Thus stated" refers to what was stated in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) in such passages as, "The faculties become sharp in nine ways.
And here, just as when piercing fine objects such as pearls or coral, [one uses] something even finer...

Just as one must have a sharp tool for piercing, so too one must possess keen knowledge when grasping the subtle and delicate phenomena of the material and immaterial realms, as well as their conditions;
moreover, it must be even keener when seeing their destruction and fall.
This greater keenness is produced by honing it upon a whetstone—just as the edge of an axe is sharpened by being rubbed against its smooth, polished surface.
It is to be accomplished by bringing the faculties to a state of sharpness. And that occurs through nine aspects;
among these, first stated is the seeing of the mode of moment-by-moment dissolution of formations that arise momentarily, expressed as: "He sees only the destruction of formations as they arise.
For in the absence of such sharpness of knowledge, because that [sharpness] is lacking, there is no sharpness of the remaining faculties.

It is so stated because it constitutes its equipment (*sambhāra*), or because of its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). The mention of "performing with diligence" and so forth, however, shows the means for that [development].
By avoiding unsuitable food and other things through such methods as non-consumption, and by partaking of what is suitable in moderation;
because material and immaterial phenomena are utterly distinct and therefore cannot be considered as one, likewise...
And because contemplation (*sammasana*) is not intended here [in the sense of the specific meditation subject], it is said: “At one time form should be contemplated, at another time the formless.
Even there, because of the grossness of form and its ease of comprehension, its status as the first thing to be contemplated is stated.
First, its arising should be seen by means of inference according to the scriptures; after that—
When one has gradually attained strength in the knowledge of development (bhāvanā-ñāṇa), it is seen even through direct perception.
This concludes the commentary on the section concerning the exposition of the mode of contemplation on the production of form.
(700) "Of all" means of all beings, distinguished by categories such as those of the sense-sphere realm and those born from eggs, and so forth. "Firstly, from kamma..."
It arises because it is the root-source of material phenomena born of temperature (*utuja*) and so forth.

The phrase "by way of the three continuities" is said either with reference to the continuity consisting of the body-decad (*kāyadasaka*) and so on that occurs subsequently, or else with reference to the "summit of the continuity" (*santatisīsa*).
It is called "slowly ceasing" (*dandhanirodha*) because its cessation is sluggish, weak, and delayed, owing to its lifespan of seventeen mind-moments.

Therefore he said, "with a heavy turn. "Therefore" means for that reason; because of the statement, "Monks, the life-formations cease even more quickly than that," material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are indeed short-lived, while immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) are even more exceedingly short-lived than those.
Therefore, this is the meaning of what the Blessed One said. As for what ought to be said here, that has already been investigated above.

"Similar to those" means similar to the moments of arising and dissolution of consciousness. For there is no dissimilarity among the moments of arising and dissolution of any conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
they are all of equal duration. "Reached the moment of presence" means reached the moment of stability (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*). "By that" refers to the second life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅgacitta*).
The physical basis (*vatthurūpa*) serves as the support for one consciousness and not for another, with the exception of the consciousness immediately preceding death.
Therefore it was said: "Together with that," and so forth.

Having thus shown [the process] from the moment of rebirth-linking up to the arising of the death-consciousness, the passage beginning with "Of the rebirth-linking consciousness" is now commenced in order to show its cessation.
In that context, "at the moment of its occurrence" refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness.

"At the moment of stability" (*ṭhitikkhaṇe*). "As long as there is so-called occurrence" means as long as there is so-called occurrence of *saṃsāra*, or as long as there is so-called occurrence of consciousness.
For in the rebirth of non-percipient beings (*asaññūpapatti*), there is no occurrence of consciousness.

Regarding "in the rebirth of the material realm," since moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) are similar to spontaneously born beings (*opapātika*), only the spontaneously born are included. By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "of spontaneously born beings also," [moisture-born beings] are likewise included.
He summarizes. "By way of the seven continuities" means by way of the seven series of decads, beginning with the eye-decad.

Regarding the phrase "therein," it refers to the occurrence of materiality through kamma. Since "kamma" here is intended specifically as that which serves as the asynchronous kamma-condition, he says:
"Kamma is wholesome or unwholesome volition. The life-nonad is included within the eye-decad and the others.
Having done so, it is stated as "seventy-one types of materiality. Alternatively, that [materiality] does not constitute a clear grasp of pleasure in the same way as the eye-decad and so forth.
"That very [materiality]" refers to the aforementioned resultant aggregates and the materiality produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa). For kamma is the producer of what is born of kamma;
it is also the ripener of the life-faculty, because of the presence of protection through the power of the fires born of kamma.
It is because it is the cause for obtaining food and so forth, and because it is a supporting sign. Therefore he said: "It is also a supporting condition.
Its status as a supporting condition should be understood precisely by way of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*).

That which has kamma as its condition is "kamma-condition"; that very consciousness is what originates this, thus it is "originated by consciousness with kamma as its condition" (*kammapaccaya-cittasamutthāna*).

It should be stated whether resultant mental factors (vipākacetasika) are also produced by mind with kamma as their condition; or rather, it need not be so stated, because they are already included by the inclusion of "produced by kamma" and "kamma-condition.
It should be understood that nutritive essence (ojā), when it has reached its functional state, produces another octad of nutritive essence within a body sustained by nutriment.
"There too" refers to the octads of nutritive essence produced by kamma and produced by nutriment. Therein, there are either four or five occurrences.
"It connects" means that it continues four or five occurrences of material groups by way of a homogeneous continuity (*sabhāga-santati*).
However, they say that it connects even many dissimilar occurrences due to specific external conditions.

Just as there is a connection of the lineage (*paveṇighaṭanā*) in the case of what is originated by kamma-condition and nutriment, so too is there such a connection in the case of what is originated by kamma-condition and temperature; to show this, [it says]: "Kamma-condition-originated temperature..."

The passage beginning with “nāmā” has been stated. And here, just as in those various sections the successions of the second [moment] and so forth that are not born of karma were shown without distinction by one who demonstrates their successive occurrence, so too [should they be understood] by way of the kamma-born, nutriment-originated, and temperature-originated;

by way of the kamma-born, temperature-originated, and nutriment-originated; and by way of the kamma-conditioned, consciousness-born, nutriment-originated, temperature-originated, temperature, and nutriment.
And they say that the occurrence of matter should also be shown by way of its division.

In this regard, it cannot be said that, when there is the acquisition of specific conditions from kamma-born and nutriment-born [matter], the occurrences do not connect with occurrences beyond the aforementioned limits.
For indeed, it is said: "It connects the occurrence for ten or twelve rounds," and likewise, "Thus, even for a long time..."
And he will say: "Even while standing on the side of the non-clung-to (*anupādinnapakkha*), the temperature-born (*utusamuṭṭhāna*) [matter] indeed continues to arise.
702. "Those considered productive and non-productive": those included in the first three sections are considered productive;

those belonging to the final section, called "the sixteen," are known and understood as non-productive. "From the wholesome and the functional": from both the wholesome (*kusala*) and the functional (*kiriya*). Regarding "posture" (*iriya*):...
The postures (*iriyāpatha*)—walking and so forth—are so called because they serve as the pathways for the occurrence of bodily activity;

in their actual sense, they are the manifestation of matter in those specific states. While it is true that in this context there is no posture nor intimation (*viññatti*) apart from matter, nevertheless, not every consciousness that originates matter necessarily supports the postures or produces the modifications of intimation.
Furthermore, that consciousness which generates intimation (viññatti) invariably generates the other [the postures] because of their inseparable connection;
likewise for matter that supports the postures (iriyāpatha). To demonstrate this distinction, the conjunction "matter, posture, and intimation" is employed.
Regarding the phrase "excluding the resultant," it should be stated here as "excluding both the resultant and the two types of direct knowledge (abhiññā)."

Because they must be understood as included by the mention of "the rest" (*sesa*) among others; or rather, it need not be stated [separately], since the mention of "the rest" itself excludes the consciousnesses of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
They do not produce intimation (*viññatti*) because states such as sublime wholesome consciousness are tranquil and lack diffusion.
For only that which is diffused originates intimation belonging to the sense-sphere wholesome consciousness and so forth, which supports the postures (*iriyāpatha*).

However, even though there is a state of tranquility, because they possess effort due to the momentum of jhāna, they perform the function of impulsion (*javana*). This is connected with the phrase "five life-continuum consciousnesses" (*bhavaṅga-citta*).
They produce only material form, not the postures (*iriyāpatha*), because of their extreme weakness due to the state of effortless tranquility.
At the time when the life-continuum proceeds unmixed with functional consciousnesses (*kiriya-maya-citta*), [it does not produce] the bodily parts such as the aggregates (*khandha*).
It is the state of remaining steady through its immobility. For when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) flows on uninterruptedly, the limbs become slack as if they have sunk down.

However, when the thirty-two types of wakefulness consciousness mentioned by the phrase "thirty-two," etc., are occurring, the limbs remain firm and proceed precisely according to their respective postures (iriyāpatha). [The two fivefold sense-consciousnesses...]

Due to extreme weakness, they do not produce [mental] form (*rūpa*). The rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*) [does not produce it] due to the weakness of the physical basis (*vatthu*). Regarding "the death-consciousness of those whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavānaṃ cuticittaṃ*):

here—“At the moment of arising of the final consciousness of those belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), immediately after which [consciousness] of theirs [there follows another] of the sense-sphere... [etc.]

“For those whose final consciousness is about to arise, for those in the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere who are in their final existence, and for those who, having been reborn in the fine-material or immaterial sphere,
will attain final Nibbāna at the moment of death— the verbal formation will cease for them,
but the bodily formation will not cease for them.”
From this statement, it is understood that the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) does not produce material form (*rūpa*) for others either.

For there is no reason why the consciousness that produces material form would fail to produce the bodily formations (*kāyasaṅkhāra*) simply because of the absence of obstructions such as being in the womb;

nor is it logical that material form produced by consciousness should continue to occur in one who has already passed away; nor indeed can it be said that "the death-consciousness produces material form."
The Pāli text contains the qualification "of those whose taints are exhausted" (*khīṇāsavānaṃ*);
however, it should be understood that this was included because the production of matter by their death-consciousness (*cuticitta*)—which ceases through non-relinking cessation—is made manifest.
The specific limitation to "sixteen consciousnesses" must be established as an absolute rule regarding their generation of matter; for otherwise, there are many others.
Those [mental states] arisen in the formless realm do not produce matter at all because they have reached a state where there is no room for it.

The connection is that they do not produce matter either at the moment of presence or at the moment of dissolution; however, at the moment of arising, they are powerful due to the acquisition of conditions such as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*).
Just as material phenomena such as earth and so forth are mind-rooted (*citta-hetuka*) and mind-originated (*citta-samutthāna*), so too are feeling and the rest; thus it has been said.
“Mind-originated (cittasamuṭṭhāna) means the three formless aggregates and the sound-nonad,” and so forth. For this very reason it was said:
“Which phenomena are mind-originated? The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, the formations aggregate, bodily intimation, and verbal intimation.
In this context, it should be understood that the status of bodily intimation and the others as being mind-originated is stated figuratively (pariyāyato).

Because they are not produced [by that mind]. By the phrase "thus described as matter originated by the four [factors]," it is shown that only the mind-born matter (*cittaja-rūpa*) which is not originated by itself has the mind as its condition (*cittapaccayatā*).

However, if the mind-condition were understood in the same way as the kamma-condition was shown, then matter originated by that [mind] itself, as well as co-nascent feeling and so forth, would also have the mind as their condition. [This is the case] regarding the mind-condition for mind-originated matter.
However, it should be understood that the mind-condition (cittapaccaya) is mentioned here specifically by way of the postnascent condition (pacchājātapaccaya) in order to show it without confusion.
Since the temperature and nutriment produced by kamma are stronger than those produced by mind, the joining of four or five occurrences is stated with reference to them;
whereas the joining of two or three occurrences is stated with reference to those produced by mind.

That [occurrence] should be understood by way of ordinary (pākatika) consciousness; however, by way of exalted (mahaggata) and supramundane (anuttara) consciousness, even more numerous occurrences should be expected, because the mind-born material phenomena produced thereby are sublime and refined.
By the phrase, "having obtained a condition consisting of clung-to (upādinna) kamma-born matter," the function of bringing in external, non-clung-to nutritive matter is indicated.
This shows that [the body] does not act [itself]. Its acquisition of conditions occurs by way of its dependence upon the primary elements born of karma; thus he says, "being established therein.
In this context, since material form originating from consciousness (citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) and so forth is also rooted in karma, it might be subject to the designation "born of karma" (kammaja);
therefore, to exclude that, he specifies it as "clung-to" (upādinnam). As for the condition of nutriment (āhāra-paccaya)...
To show that nutriment is not only a support but also a producer, it is said, "matter produced by the four [nutriments].
Having stated, "ten or twelve times," he says, "food consumed on a single day," and so forth, with reference to the inquiry:
"How is it that this very [food] occurs in ten or twelve instances? "Pervading the body of the child" means...
Having pervaded [the body] by means of the nutrient-carrying channels (rasaharaṇī) that follow from the base of the navel, otherwise there would be no proper utilization of food for the body,

which is like an interior water-jar. Regarding the two kinds of nutriment— appropriated (upādinnaka) and non-appropriated (anupādinnaka)— the nutriment that serves as a condition for nutriment (āhāra-paccaya-āhāra) was previously shown to be the non-appropriated one.

To show the other [type], the passage beginning with “nutriment born of kamma” was stated. That follows the same method as what was explained regarding the nutriment-originated by the condition of kamma.
Therefore he said: “It joins together four or five occurrences.

It should be understood that for the temperature-originated by the condition of nutriment, as well as for the nutriment-originated by the condition of temperature, there are ten or twelve rounds of joining together in occurrence. They say it is not redundant because it follows the stated method.
"Of the rest" refers to the three types of material phenomena produced by kamma, consciousness, and temperature within the continuity (*santati*).

For edible food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), acting as a producer, becomes a condition for other material phenomena produced by nutriment and for the three types of material phenomena produced within the continuity, by way of being a support (*upatthambhaka*).
Thus, while being a nutriment condition, it also acts as a condition by way of presence (*atthi*) and non-disappearance (*avigata*); however, its status as a support—

According to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*, there is no [such category]. However, it should be understood that this is stated according to the method of the Suttas, on the grounds that material phenomena occurring with nutriment as their condition are called "supported by nutriment.
The same principle applies to the subsequent explanation of the support for temperature (*utu*).
704. This is because all four types of the fire element—beginning with those produced by kamma—are equally capable of generating material phenomena.
“It is said that ‘temperature (utu) is the fire element (tejodhātu) arising from the four [causes]. This is twofold:

although there is no difference in its nature as the fire element, it is twofold—hot and cold—due to the distinction between intensity and dullness. Whatever else needs to be said on this point has already been investigated below.
Even though temperature produces matter even without what is clung-to (upādinnaka), nevertheless, in that which is bound to the faculties (indriyabaddha)…”
Because there is no arising of that [material] form without it, he said, "having obtained a condition consisting of what is clung-to.
Therefore he said, "temperature has four origins. For temperature itself, when originating from temperature, produces material form without what is clung-to.
That which is called the "condition of temperature" is material form originating from all four [causes]. For that fifteen-fold material form which originates from temperature—
And whatever other materiality belonging to the continuity of relatives there may be, for all of that, temperature is the similar supporting condition (*sabhāga upatthambhaka-paccaya*).
Because dissimilar temperature—such as frost and so forth—is like a cause for the arising of dissimilar materiality in lotuses and the like, acting as if it were destroying the preceding materiality;
therefore, taking both the similar and the dissimilar together, it is said: "Temperature [is the condition] for materiality arisen from the four [sources]."
"It is a condition for both occurrence and destruction.
"For a long period" means for a long time—ten or twelve cycles—beyond the limits mentioned by others.
For temperature (utu), having obtained its conditions through a homogeneous continuity (sabhāga-santati), maintains the occurrence of material form (rūpa) in a similar mode for even a very long time.
It continues [the stream] without the support of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*), let alone otherwise. Therefore he said:
