"Even while standing on the side of the unclung-to. The intention is that this refers to the flesh-free hair, body hair, nails, skin, moles, freckles, and so forth within a living body, as opposed to the corpse and such elsewhere.
When the arising of form is seen, its dissolution too is necessarily seen.
Because the occurrence of phenomena lasts only for a short time, he said: "One who perceives arising contemplates material form at the appropriate time, and likewise name.
For the mere perception of arising is not called "contemplation" (sammasana); rather, the perception of rise and fall is what is required.
This same principle applies to all subsequent mentions of "arising."

Commentary on the Exposition of the Modes of Contemplation for Rebirth in the Formless Realm (Arūpanibbattipassanākārakathāvaṇṇanā) 705. The restriction "only by way of mundane states of consciousness" is made because the other [the supramundane] is not its object.
It is reborn according to the respective realms of existence (bhava). That very same consciousness, consisting of nineteen varieties, is reborn as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
The connection is thus: "by way of death" and "by way of that object" apply here as well. "Therein" refers to those nineteen types of consciousness-arising.
By the phrase "starting from the immediately preceding consciousness," etc., it is the very process of occurrence (*pavatti*) that is described.

However, since that is the mode of occurrence specifically for rebirth-linking consciousnesses during the course of existence, [it does not apply] to pure process-consciousnesses (*suddhappavatticitta*).
Showing its arising, he said, “But in the course of existence,” and so forth. “Because of being undisturbed” means because of not having perished.
To explain in detail the meaning stated in brief by the phrase “because of the eye’s being undisturbed,” etc., it was said, “For the eye-sensitivity,” and so forth.
By the phrase “only reaching the state of persistence,” he shows that just as matter in the process of ceasing does not serve as a condition for anything, so too...
This shows that it arises as well. The connection is: "eye-consciousness arises. The same applies to the others. The connection is:
"it arises having become one, five, or seven impulsion-moments (*javana*) within the wholesome, unwholesome, or functional consciousnesses of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).

The phrase "or a rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity" should be connected by bringing forward the word "or" (*vā*). For this was said with reference specifically to the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*).

That, moreover, should be understood by way of the second section on the "floods" (moghavāra). Five impulsion moments are to be understood as occurring at times such as when one is asleep or unconscious, while seven are to be understood as occurring during normal states. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the impulsion and its object":

this refers to the impulsion, such that if the impulsion is triple-rooted, it is either triple-rooted or double-rooted, and so forth; and regarding the object, such that if the object is desirable, the impulsion is accompanied by joy, and so forth.
And it is in accordance with the object. "In the remaining doors" means in the remaining doors such as the ear-door and so forth.
"In due order" means that by following the sequence of attaining the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*), one accomplishes the development of wisdom and attains Arahantship.
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Comprehension of the Set of Seven Material Phenomena* (*Rūpasattakasammasanakathāvaṇṇanā*)
706. The "sevenfold attention regarding forms" (rūpesu manasikārasattaka) is the sevenfold [contemplation] of form; the meaning is that one attends to form-phenomena in seven ways.

The "sevenfold [contemplation] of the formless" (arūpasattaka) should be understood in the same way. "By these modes" means by these various types such as attention to taking up and laying down, or by these aforementioned sections.
"Having applied" means having applied the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa).
"From taking up and putting down" means from the grasping and relinquishing of existence; that is to say, from birth and from death.
"Leading to decline and old age" means because it leads to the state of one who has grown old in years; the meaning is simply "leading to destruction. "From nutriment" means by way of nutriment;
the meaning is "by way of nutriment which serves as a condition for material form. [It refers to] various colors and shapes, such as copper, iron, and so forth, or earth, stone, and so forth.
Materiality that is independent of kamma and established by its own nature is *dhammatārūpa*. "Sevenfold" means in seven ways or by way of seven aspects.
"He contemplates" means he contemplates—that is, he scrutinizes—by applying the three characteristics to each respective component.
Because of the statement, "The taking up of the burden is suffering in the world," it is considered the initial grasping of the burden of the aggregates; thus, "taking up" (*ādāna*)...
He said, "rebirth-linking. However, because of the statement, "All beings in the world shall lay down their physical frame," it is considered the laying down of the burden of the aggregates;
thus it is said, "'Laying down' means death. Because of the statement, "Whoever lives long, lives for a hundred years," the fact that [the lifespan] may be less or more than that is not the measure;
therefore it is said, "having delimited it as one hundred years."

"All formations within this interval" means all formations—comprising the various categories of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)—that occur within this interval between taking up and laying down [the body].
For among material phenomena, this is the method of comprehension. The phrase "beginning with 'Why?

is stated for the purpose of establishing in the heart the mere fact that they have been grasped as "impermanent" through logical reasoning. Therein, "because of being subject to arising and passing away" means by way of their process of arising.
And because it proceeds by way of cessation—the meaning being that it comes into being after not having been, and passes away after having been.
Regarding "by way of change," they say it is because the continuity consists of successive states that are dissimilar.
This may have been stated with the intention that this is the comprehension [of impermanence] regarding matter delimited by a hundred years; for [matter] is subject to change through aging and death.
This is the meaning. Even though there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*dhamma*) of the phenomenon, a difference in its states (*avatthā*) must be admitted.
For it is not logical that the state of arising itself is the state of dissolution. Thus it has been said: "Because of both aging and death, it is of a dual nature of transformation.

Alternatively, here "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) refers simply to the departure from one's own inherent nature (*sabhāva*). "Momentariness" (*khaṇikatā*) means being temporary. The negation of permanence is simply the absence of an eternal intrinsic nature.
For indeed, things characterized by impermanence (aniccadhammā) deny permanence for those who know them by their own intrinsic nature.

Since they are not permanent, they are "impermanent" (anicca). It is understood that the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) which exist at the moment of arising do not exist at the moment of stability, because they reach another state;
thus, their mode of exhaustion is expressed as "they are exhausted by aging during their stability."

This meaning should be understood by means of manifest aging. As for those who do not accept the stability of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*), what must be said regarding that has already been stated below. The intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena is indeed difficult to transcend;
since destruction follows immediately after aging, it is said: "Having reached aging, they necessarily break up. Therefore, because [they exist] by way of arising, aging, and destruction...
Because formations are subject to constant affliction, and because they are difficult to endure, they are characterized by suffering;

and because they are the basis for the three types of suffering as well as for the suffering of saṃsāra, they are the "substratum of suffering. Therefore, the construction is: "frequently... [are] suffering.
The phrase "by way of the negation of pleasure" is exactly according to the method already stated. May they not reach stability, but rather [be understood] in the very mode of their arising.
The intention is: "May they continue to proceed. By the word "arisen" (*uppannā*), possession of the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) is expressed.
Why was it said, "May they not grow old upon reaching stability"? Is it not the case that, in terms of meaning, stability itself is aging (*jarā*)? This is true;

however, it should be understood that here, by the inclusion of "aging," the exhaustion (*kilamatha*) resulting from the process of aging is what is intended. "May they not break" refers to permanence (*niccatā*).
He wishes. Even for the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, there is no mastery over anything; for it is impossible for anyone to alter the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) [of phenomena].
Indeed, the domain of supernormal power (*iddhi*) consists only in the alteration of state (*bhāva*). "Formations are empty" means they are empty in the sense of non-mastery over the three points.
"Therefore" is a reference to the reason already stated. "By way of emptiness" means by way of being devoid of an inhabitant, a maker, an experiencer, and a controller.
"Empty" means empty of any intrinsic nature (sabhāva) imagined by some; it is not empty of its own lack of essence. "Ownerless" means because there is no owner whatsoever.
By this, he shows the state of being non-self (anattan). "Not subject to mastery" means because of the absence of the state of being subject to mastery as previously described.
"By way of the negation of self" means by the rejection of a self imagined by others. For, by the words "empty," and so forth—
The absence of a self conceived by outsiders is stated regarding phenomena; however, by this [definition], because it lacks the nature of a self, there is no self.

707. And herein, matter-phenomena are established as impermanent by four reasons beginning with "because of the nature of arising and passing away," as suffering by four reasons beginning with "because of being constantly oppressed," and as non-self by four reasons beginning with "because of being empty."
Having observed the three characteristics previously unobserved by himself, he is said to be "superimposing them there" while contemplating.
Furthermore, because he contemplates by way of taking up and laying down, it is said: "having superimposed the three characteristics upon form.

And therein, since the apprehension of the characteristic of suffering is preceded by the apprehension of the characteristic of impermanence, and the apprehension of the characteristic of suffering is preceded by...

or the grasping of the characteristic of non-self. Herein, since the characteristic of impermanence, when demonstrated through the various divisions of form, ought to be illustrated starting from the most obvious, it is first shown by way of the hundred-year limit;
having analyzed that which lasts for a hundred years as "ten or twenty," and so forth, it is demonstrated gradually down to the stage of extraction and so on, according to the divisions of form.
Having seen that dissolution, one then applies the three characteristics—“impermanent, suffering, non-self.

To show that this is the method of comprehension (*sammasana*) by way of the passing away of youth and maturity, the procedure for comprehending matter by way of its stages of decay is commenced with the words, “That very hundred years,” and so forth.
In this context, since this classification of matter is first grasped by way of its grossness, [the text does not say] “a hundred years”...
It is analyzed by way of equal divisions; or, because it possesses such a nature during the middle stage of life, one year is added to the middle age.
708. A decade of years that proceeds with a predominance of dullness is a "dull decade" (*mandadasaka*). This same method applies to the others as well.
"Then" (*tadā*) means in the first decade of years. "He" (*so*) refers to the person. "Fickle" (*capala*) means unsteady due to the instability of his actions.
By this, he distinguishes [him] from the state of extreme dullness (*momūhabhāva*). For he is not dull through the state of extreme dullness as in the ninth decade;

rather, he is so through restlessness (*capalatā*). Therefore, he said, "a youth" (*kumāraka*). In the third decade, because of the fullness of flesh, the complexion of the skin becomes clear according to its natural state;
thus he said, "the sphere of color (*vaṇṇāyatana*) reaches fullness. In the fourth decade, [there is the fullness] of bones and sinews.
Through the attainment of stability, strength and power reach fullness.

In the fifth decade, due to the distancing of the intoxication of youth and the general attenuation of the defilements, wisdom becomes very clear according to its respective capacity. "Delight in play" (*khiḍḍārati*) refers to the pleasure derived from play.
Just as the purity of a lamp depends on its specific support—such as a bowl or other vessel—so too [the nature of delight] depends on its specific support.
In the fifth and sixth decades, one should understand that there is a decline in wisdom and intellect. The body becomes stooped due to the joints of the waist and the neck;
this occurs even in those who are short, let alone those who are tall. "Stooped" means hanging down due to the weight [of the body].
One becomes utterly bewildered because of the absence of mindfulness and wisdom. One spends much time lying down, being unable to bear the burden of the body through standing and other postures.

"Of three years each" is stated by way of the majority; for there is also one section consisting of four years. It should also be understood that this is said by dividing [the period] into two hundred sections according to each individual year.
The connection is "the form occurring during the rainy season.
However, that rainy season is completed in two months, not as before in four months; thus he says "two months. [This indicates] absolute duration (*accantasaṃyoge*).
This is a term used for application. Furthermore, the seasons (*utu*) should be understood as follows: the rains (*vassāna*) consist of the months of Sāvaṇa and Poṭṭhapāda;

autumn (*sarada*) consists of the months of Assayuja and Kattika; winter (*hemanta*) consists of the months of Migasira and Phussa; the cool season (*sisira*) consists of the months of Māgha and Phagguṇa;

spring (*vasanta*) consists of the months of Citta and Vesākha; and summer (*gimha*) consists of the months of Jeṭṭha and Āsāḷha. "Having divided into six parts" means having divided them into six parts by way of ten-day periods (*nāṭikā*).
710. Moving forward toward the front is *abhikkama*. Moving back by way of turning around is *paṭikkama*.
Looking straight ahead is *ālokana*. Looking here and there in various directions is *vilokana*.
Contracting and bending the hands and feet is *samiñjana*. Stretching them out is *pasāraṇa*.

"At the time of lifting the foot" means at the time of lifting the second foot. "Of the foot" means of the foot that has been lifted. "Deficient" means smaller in measure than seven [finger-breadths].
Therefore he said, "sluggish. "The others" refers to the fire and air elements.

Just as the lifting of the foot is accomplished, so too there is an absolute predominance of the fire and air elements among the material phenomena originated by the consciousness occurring at that moment.
Their lightness of nature is to be desired; for that very reason, the others are inferior due to their heavy nature.
However, because of their connection with those [light elements], the remaining material phenomena originating from the three [mental] origins belong to that same category.
It should be understood that the predominance of air and earth during the occurrence of bodily and vocal intimation is the illustration of this point. In carrying forward, backward...
And since the occurrence of matter with a nature that is very light is like [the process of] lifting up and carrying away, it must be admitted that those same two elements are predominant;
thus he said, "so too in the cases of bringing forward and carrying away.
Just as in the case of lifting up and so forth, because of their nature of being very light, the function of the latter two elements is superior while that of the others is inferior, [so it is here].

Thus, because there is a greater degree of gravity (garusabhāva) in the three [stages] beginning with relinquishing (vossajjana), he said "in relinquishing" and so forth, showing that for the first two the duty is more extensive, while for the others it is less.

"Derived matter dependent on those" (tadupādāyarūpāni) means the derived material phenomena (upādārūpa) that arise depending upon those elements (dhātu). "In this very [context]" (ettheva) means in the context of extraction (uddharaṇa) itself.
Therefore he said, "without reaching the carrying across. "Iti" means "thus. "Tattha tattha" means "in each respective section," such as the section on extraction and so forth.
"Section by section" and so on is a demonstration that there is no confusion between the different sections of those phenomena.
"Taṭataṭāyanti" means "as if they were rattling"; by this, he shows the brevity of their moment of occurrence.
711. *Assā* means of comprehension (*sammasana*). *Dārutiṇukkādīsu* means among wood-fires, grass-fires, and so forth.
With the underlying intention, “O blind fool, do you imagine this to be a single solid mass, permanent, eternal, and unchanging?

he said, “What is there that is pleasing here? *Idampi* refers to what was stated regarding the non-appearance of the lamp due to the exhaustion of the oil and the wick; this too [is impermanent]. *Aṅgulaṅgulantare* means between every finger’s breadth.
"Measured by a finger" (*aṅguli-mita*) means a place of the measure of a finger; this is the meaning.
He says, "having released the thread," referring to a fiber (*aṃsu*) that is a constituent part of the yarn and has reached a state of extreme subtlety.

The passage beginning with "Therein... and so forth is the application of the simile. In this regard, just as in the object of comparison (*upameyya*), the distinction of time is evident in the simile as well.
There is no [separate] entity; rather, it should be understood as a metaphor insofar as one part does not reach another part.

Or, since even in a metaphor a mere distinction of time (*kāla*) can be found by means of "for so long" (*yāva*), the metaphor should be applied even according to the distinction of time when grasping that [metaphor]. 712.
Previously, the fourfold continuity of matter was shown by way of its taking up and laying down; now, it is shown by way of its origination from nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna*), and so forth.
Having broken it down and demonstrating it, he said, “That very form, having been decomposed,” and so forth. Therein, *visaṅkharitvā* means having analyzed or divided.
Alternatively, the reading is *visaṅgharitvā*, which has the same meaning. *Āhāramayaṃ* means produced by nutriment. *Jhattaṃ* means withered.
*Kilantaṃ* means exhausted. *Dhātaṃ* means bitter. *Pīṇitaṃ* means nourished by the excellence of the accumulation of flesh.
For that very reason, it is soft (*mudu*). "Glossy" (*siniddha*) means smooth due to the glossiness of the skin; for that very reason, it is possessed of touch (*phassavanta*). 713.
"The form arisen at the time of heat" refers to the form heated by the torment of heat. "By a favorable cold season" means by a cold season that is suitable. 714.

"By way of the doors of the sense bases" (*āyatana-dvāra-vasena*) means by way of the doors designated as sense bases (*āyatana*). The term "sense base" (*āyatana*) is used in order to exclude the door of kamma.
"At the body-door" means at the sensitive-body door. The "mind-door" refers to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) accompanied by adverting.
It is called the "mind-door" by way of a metaphorical designation for that which is supported—referring to the heart-base as its support—at which point the arising of the mind-door occurs.
715. "By way of being joyful or sorrowful" means either by way of a person who is joyful or sorrowful, or by way of the time when one is joyful or sorrowful.
"This meaning" refers to the meaning now being stated, which consists in the extremely brief duration of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*).

"Life" is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "Pleasure and pain" are the feelings of pleasure and pain; for equanimity (*upekkhā*) is also included within pleasure and pain, by virtue of its being either desirable or undesirable.
"Personal existence" (*attabhāva*) refers to the remaining phenomena, excluding life, feeling, and consciousness.
They are so called. Some say "perception" (*saññā*). "Exclusively" (*kevala*) means unmixed with its own state of permanence.

"Associated with a single consciousness" (*ekacittasamāyutta*) means accompanied by each individual consciousness. "The moment proceeds swiftly" means that, according to the method already stated, because it lasts for only a single moment of consciousness, the moment of life and so forth proceeds very briefly.
“Eighty-four thousand aeons” (*kappāni*) means an aeon measuring eighty-four thousand;
this is the accusative case used to express continuous duration. Furthermore, the singular number is used in a generic sense. “Marūs” refers to the gods.
“They do not remain with two minds” means that even though they live for such a long time, they do not persist while accompanied by two simultaneous thoughts. This is what was said.
It is so: even in their continuity, the life-faculty and other factors do not persist together with two consciousnesses;
because they arise together with one consciousness and cease together with that very same one, they do not persist until the second [moment].
Those which have ceased for one who is dying—meaning for a being passing away—should be said to have ceased along with the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).

Regarding "the aggregates": for one who is staying here, or for those aggregates that have ceased through reaching dissolution while staying and persisting here during the course of existence—all of them are alike;

all are exactly the same in having gone to their end, being without rebirth-linking, and having departed because there is no further returning to link with a new birth. For just as the aggregates of death do not re-arise, so too...
Therefore, the aggregates existed even prior to that; thus, the intention is that the life of sentient beings lasts for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*).
And "those which have been broken immediately after" refers to those formations (*saṅkhāra*) that have just been broken—that is, ceased—immediately following.

And "those which are to be broken in the future" refers to those formations that are to be broken in the future, whose nature is to break, and which will disintegrate. "Between those [two], they have ceased."
Of those past and future [phenomena], having reached the present state in the interval between them, they have ceased and are broken.

Regarding the phrase "there is no unevenness in their characteristic": there is no irregularity or dissimilarity in the cause of the characteristic of dissolution for these three types [of phenomena].
By "not born by that which has not arisen," it means one is not born by a mind that has not yet arisen; thus, one is said to be "unborn. By the present...
One lives by means of a mind that is currently occurring; thus, one is said to be "living. When the mind has ceased, this world is "dead";

for just as with the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), when any such mind reaches its dissolution, this world is in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*) called "dead," because that which has ceased lacks re-linking (*appaṭisandhika*). Even so, this is a designation based on the ultimate reality. By means of this...

Taking that peaceful mind together with its basis as the foundation, there is a conceptual designation of continuity (*santānapaññatti*) which serves as the object for the occurrence of such expressions as "Tissa lives" or "Phussa lives.
This [designation] is, in this context, ultimate in the sense of being an ultimate reality (*paramatthiyā paramatthabhūtā*).
For it is said: "Name and clan do not decay."
"Those that have perished and gone to non-deposit" means that those which have perished have not gone to any place as a deposit; rather, they have simply gone to non-existence (*abhāva*).
There is no heap in the future from which they could return to a state of existence. "And those that have been produced" refers to those present beings who have acquired a physical form;
even these stand like a mustard seed on the point of an awl. Just as, for example, a mustard seed placed upon a needle—
Just as a drop of water thrown onto her [hot] head vanishes upon contact and does not remain, so too conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) arise and then break up;

there is no stability for them. "Their breakup is placed before them" means that for those produced phenomena, what is called their breakup is already established beforehand; the meaning is that it is certain to happen and does not recede. "By the ancient ones" means by those of the past.
“From non-appearance” means from being unobservable. “They come” means they arrive. By the phrase “they arise,” too, he expresses precisely the absence of coming from some heap.

“The broken go to non-appearance” means that even when broken, because there is no approaching anywhere, they go to a total non-existence of appearance. He provides an illustration for this: “The arising of light... and they pass away.”

716. By the phrase “matter that arises from the beginning of the eon of dissolution” (*vivaṭṭakappato paṭṭhāya uppajjanakarūpa*), he shows that it has the descriptive name “matter of natural law” (*dhammatārūpa*) because of its inherent quality of arising by itself.
Among iron, copper, and so forth, “iron” (*ayo*) refers to black iron. “Copper” (*loha*) is fourfold:
copper by genus (*jātiloha*), copper by species (*vijātiloha*), artificial copper (*kittimaloha*), and copper of the Pisācas (*pisācaloha*). Among these, “iron” (*ayo*) and “silver” (*rajata*)...
Gold, tin, lead, copper, bronze, and iron—these are the seven metals by birth (*jātiloha*).

Copper-nose metal is a metal of mixed origin (*vijātiloha*). Brass, round metal, and *hārakūṭa*—these three are metals of artificial origin (*kittimaloha*). The "fiendish metal" (*pisācaloha*) consists of emerald and so forth.
Therein, together with the two metals by birth, namely copper and bronze, everything else here [is included].

“Metal” (loha) is what has been taken up. “Tin” (tipu) refers to white tin. “Lead” (sīsa) refers to black tin. “Gold” (suvaṇṇa) is of various kinds, such as that produced from mines or refined by chemical processing.
“Pearl” (muttā) refers to sea-pearls and the like. “Gem” (maṇi) refers to every other variety of gemstone, excluding beryl (veḷuriya), ruby (lohitaṅga), and cat’s eye (masāragalla).
“Beryl” (veḷuriya) is a gemstone the color of bamboo. “Conch” (saṅkha) refers to the sea-conch. “Stone” (sila) is of various kinds, such as black stone and yellow stone.
All these are stones reckoned as gems. *Pavāḷa* is coral, both round and perforated. *Lohitaṅga* is a red gem. *Masāragalla* is a *kabara* gem.
The earth and so forth are well known. "That belongs to him" means that this form of the Dhamma-tārā belongs to that yogin.
"The color of young sprouts" means having a color equal to the young sprouts of mango trees and the like. "A continuity of similar forms."
A continuity of matter that shares the same characteristics, such as color and so forth. "Causing it to follow on" means it proceeds by way of connecting through a succession of cause and effect.
"He" refers to the yogi. "That" refers to the leaf of the *asoka* tree. "Having grasped" means having delimited and apprehended it with knowledge. By this...
"By this method" means by the method stated in the *Asokapaṇṇa*. All material form classified as iron, copper, and so forth, is a "form of natural law" (*dhammatārūpa*).
For even that is cool during the cold season, and during the hot season it becomes hotter through the heat of the sun.

In that regard, the material form occurring with the quality of coldness does not reach the state of heat, nor does the material form occurring with the quality of heat reach the state of coldness; it remains right there.
It should be connected with the passage beginning, "it breaks with a *taṭataṭa* sound," and so forth. 717.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse on the contemplation of the immaterial septad:
"From the aggregate" means from the aggregate of immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammakalāpa*).

Because in that context the phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth are common to all mental arisings, being well-manifested and easy to understand, he said, "As a 'group' (kalāpa), they are the phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth," showing them by way of those [phenomena]. The connection is:
"All these phenomena consisting of contact as the fifth, which have arisen in the course of comprehension, have perished."
"Mind occurring" means mind occurring by way of comprehension (*sammasana*) in seven instances.
"Comprehending" means comprehending by taking [them] together as one. "That is more appropriate" means that what was stated in the discourse on the Noble Lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*) is more appropriate;

for it is said that comprehension occurs by taking the sevenfold materiality together, because of its proximity and because it is more manifest due to being stated along with the comprehension [of the immaterial]. Furthermore, in the sevenfold materiality...

Because contemplation (*sammasana*) proceeds by effecting an especially thorough analysis of the compactness of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), the contemplation of the immaterial (*arūpa*) directed toward that same object proceeds with particular efficacy for the penetration of the characteristics such as impermanence; thus, this is more appropriate.

However, it does not proceed by first performing a contemplation of the hair and so forth, and then proceeding toward that [immaterial] object. If that were the case, it would not be a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"It would be ever new" means that one discards the previously grasped object of comprehension (*sammasana-visaya*) and takes up another object of comprehension.

"The rest as well" refers to the methods of comprehension such as the "pairing" (*yamaka*) and so forth. "By that very same method" means by the method of the discourse on the Noble Lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*).
"That too is consciousness" refers even to the arising of consciousness occurring through the mode of comprehension by way of taking up and putting down; it is designated by the term "consciousness."
This is the exposition. This same method applies everywhere. "Comprehending by way of pairs" means that comprehension proceeds by way of dyads with reference to the phenomena of mind and matter.

For although he previously stood having comprehended by way of the sevenfold materiality, he now comprehends that very same [matter] by way of its taking up, laying down, and so forth. The same method applies to "comprehension by moments" and the others as well.
719. *Etampi* means this fourth contemplative consciousness as well.

*Paṭhamacittaṃ* (the first consciousness) refers to the consciousness that has contemplated material form by way of its taking up and laying down, etc., which is intended here as the consciousness that discerns material form.

Because it clarifies their momentary nature through the contemplation of the consciousness that has already contemplated and the consciousness that is currently contemplating, this contemplation is called "contemplation by way of the momentary."
And this very same comprehension, when doubled, is called "comprehension by way of sequence" because it arises through a series of many successive acts of comprehension.
"It would turn out" means it would be possible. If that were so, meditation would consist only of comprehension by way of sequence;

it would not be helpful for the fundamental meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), nor would it be the course leading to attainment (samāpatti). And because [the goal] is not achieved by that much alone...
The characteristics of impermanence and so forth become very clear regarding both material and immaterial phenomena; therefore it is said:
"Up to the contemplation of the tenth consciousness... [etc. ...it should be set aside.

As for the phrase "it should be set aside," this is intended to show the limit of the sequence of contemplation—that the eleventh [consciousness] is not to be contemplated by means of the twelfth—and not that one should stop contemplating after that point.

Since the seeing of the repulsiveness of the mouth is paramount, one should therefore again grasp the form and continue to devote oneself to development until the contemplation of the mind by way of the ten contemplations.
"It is said" means it is stated in the *Ariyavaṃsa-kathā*.
There is no such thing as a method of contemplation separate [from that]; there is no other attention of insight-meditation apart from the attention directed toward impermanence and so forth.
There is none. Here, the suppression of views and so forth by means of insight (vipassanā) is what is intended by "the uprooting of views" and so on.

For it is by means of insight itself, through its specific modes of operation, that the uprooting of views and other such results are accomplished; showing this, he said, "But as for this... and so forth.
In that context, "perception of beings" (sattasaññā) is the perception arising from the thought, "beings exist. It is also the perception associated with the weak view of self (attadiṭṭhi).

They say: by means of a mind that has discarded the perception of a being—that is, by means of a mind occurring through the suppression of the perception of a being—wrong view does not arise; because of the absence of that [perception], the mental perversions of view which arise with the perversions of perception as their cause do not occur.
As for what is called "conceit" (*māna*), that which is supported by wrong view and leads to rebirth in the states of misery is suppressed when wrong view is suppressed.
Thus it is; because views have been eradicated and are being eradicated, he said: "When views are uprooted... conceit does not arise.
Conceit, when suppressed, prevents the occurrence of craving, because craving occurs only toward objects that are desired;
thus it was said: "When conceit is uprooted... craving does not arise. Craving—
"Here, subtle attachment is intended," he said, "thus it is called 'completely overwhelmed by craving'... and so forth.
"This method" refers to the procedure of comprehension (sammasana) which is now being described.
Regarding the phrase "my insight": even for this insight characterized as "mine-ness," the self that acts as its owner is misapprehended.
"Because of the immersion in views": it is said thus because "for one who grasps, there is no such thing as the uprooting of views.

Granted, he has purified his view through the attainment of purification of view and purification by overcoming doubt; however, this is stated with reference to a view that is not yet gross, since it has not been uprooted by the Path.

“Suṭṭhu” means rightly (*sammā*). “Manāpaṃ” is an adverbial modifier of the action; the meaning is “in a manner that increases the mind. By both terms, he expresses his high resolve (*adhimāna*) regarding the object of insight (*vipassanā*). Therefore it was said: “There is no such thing as the eradication of conceit (*māna-samugghāṭo*).
“I am able to see with insight” shows the worthiness of being relished in insight due to its association with specific qualities, by way of stating one’s capability therein:
“I am able to see with insight; therefore, I shall pass my time practicing insight alone.”
The construction is: "of one who relishes insight.

Since the uprooting of views here occurs specifically through the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*), he therefore stated the method for the contemplation of non-self with the words, "If formations...
and so forth; and because [this is achieved] by one contemplating [them] as non-self...

Formations (saṅkhārā) must indeed be contemplated as impermanent and as suffering because they nourish that [insight]; therefore, it is said: "in the sense of having been and then not being," and so forth.

For the uprooting of conceit occurs through the contemplation of impermanence. When one sees formations that break up moment by moment, what opportunity is there for conceit? Indeed, it is said: "The perception of impermanence should be developed for the purpose of uprooting the conceit 'I am'.
For the exhaustion of attachment occurs through the contemplation of suffering; for [suffering] is not [exhausted] by its own nature, nor by the basis of suffering.
And for one who sees formations as suffering, there is not even the slightest delight in them.

For craving would arise toward that which is viewed as gratifying. The rest is exactly as explained under the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*). This, however, is the summary of the meaning here:
when the contemplation of non-self becomes sharp for the yogi who is intent on comprehension in the sequence described above...
When the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) proceeds sharp, brave, and clear, the other two [contemplations] follow suit;

at that time, the uprooting of views has been accomplished. For all views are rooted in the view of self (attadiṭṭhi), and the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) is the direct antidote to the view of self.
But when the contemplation of impermanence proceeds sharp, brave, and clear, the other two follow suit.
At that time, the uprooting of conceit (*māna*) has been accomplished by this [contemplation].

For when there is a grasping at permanence, the prattle of conceit occurs—such as "this is permanent," "this is eternal"—just like the Brahmā Baka. And the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is the direct antidote to the grasping at permanence.
But when the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*) proceeds keenly, courageously, and clearly, the other two [contemplations] follow along with it.
Thus, by this, the exhaustion of attachment is accomplished. For when there is a perception of pleasure, there is indeed the grasping of craving;
and the contemplation of suffering is the direct opposite of attachment. In this way, through the specific functions of the three contemplations, there occurs the uprooting of views and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "Thus this insight stands right in its own respective place. Regarding the contemplations:

The intention is that since performing one's own respective function is itself "abiding in one's own place" (*sakaṭṭhāne ṭhāna*), it should not be said that there is no separate method of comprehension (*sammasana-naya*). 722.

"In all aspects" (*sabbākārato*): unlike here [in the previous section], this means not by way of a partial aspect, but in all aspects—that is, in its essential nature (*sarūpato*) and in its function (*kiccato*), without exception.
It should be stated: "Right here" means precisely within the full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).
He says, "penetrating a portion," because the attainment of only certain contemplations occurs here; he will, however, show those [contemplations] by their own nature later on.
"The states opposed to that" means he abandons and suppresses the states opposed to the contemplations that are possible here, such as the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*) and so forth.
Contemplation of dissolution (*khayānupassanā*) is the contemplation of the momentary destruction of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*). "Developing" means increasing it.

"The perception of compactness" (*ghanasaññā*) is the grasping of unity by way of continuity, mass, function, and object. They say that "contemplation of dissolution" is the contemplation of non-existence after having been.
That wisdom by which one effects the resolution of the compact and sees [it] as "impermanent in the sense of dissolution"—that is [the contemplation of dissolution].

Contemplation of vanishing (*khayānupassanā*). From the point of starting with contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) onwards, there is the fulfillment of that [contemplation], which is the abandoning of the perception of compactness (*ghanasaññā*);

prior to that, because it is not yet fulfilled, that [abandoning] does not occur. Thus, in other cases as well, the state of being fulfilled or unfulfilled should be understood in terms of the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*) regarding the full understanding through abandoning and investigation.
[This applies] to the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) both through direct experience and by way of inference.
Seeing dissolution, the inclination toward cessation—which is designated as dissolution—right there is the contemplation of fall (*vayānupassanā*);
by means of that, one abandons the accumulation (*āyūhana*). One’s mind does not incline toward craving for that process, nor for the purpose for which, or by means of which, one accumulates.
Therefore it is said: "Developing the contemplation of fall, one abandons accumulation. For that which is born, there are two ways [of suffering] through aging and death.

The contemplation of change (*vipariṇāmānupassanā*) is the seeing of a different state beyond each respective delimitation of that which has been grasped by way of the "sevenfold set of form" and so forth;
through this, one abandons the perception of permanence (*dhuvasaññā*), which is the grasping of a stable state.

The contemplations of the signless (*animittānupassanā*) and so on are simply the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so on. "Sign" (*nimitta*) refers to the notion of unity within a continuity or within a collection.

When grasped, it is merely a manifestation appearing as if possessed of a physical form, due to the conditioned phenomena’s persistence over time and their apparent permanence, and because they are delimited by their own specific functions.
"Aspiration" (*paṇidhi*) means a longing for pleasure, or an aspiration such as lust and so forth;
in actual fact, it is the inclination toward conditioned phenomena by way of craving. "Adherence" (*abhinivesa*) means adherence to a self. For these signs and so forth—

Since the contemplations of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth are described by names such as "signless" (*animitta*) and so on by virtue of being their opposites, one should understand that the grasping of signs (*nimittaggāha*) and so forth are the opposites—just as the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*) and so forth are to be abandoned by the contemplations of impermanence and so forth.

Having known the object, such as form (*rūpa*), and having seen the dissolution of the consciousness that had that as its object, one sees that it is only conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) that dissolve; this is the death of conditioned phenomena.

Insight that proceeds by grasping emptiness through the mode of dissolution—thinking "there is nothing else whatsoever"—is higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*), and because it is insight into phenomena (*dhammesu vipassanā*), it is called "higher wisdom and insight into phenomena" (*adhipaññādhammavipassanā*). By means of this, one abandons the adherence that proceeds by way of grasping at permanence, essence, and so forth, as well as the view accompanied by craving.
What is called "knowledge and vision according to reality" (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*) is the vision of name-and-form together with its conditions.
By means of that, one abandons such dogmatic adherence to delusion as “Did I exist in the past? and so forth, as well as “The world originates from a Creator,” and so forth.
Contemplation of danger is the knowledge that sees the peril in all states of existence and the like, which has arisen by way of the appearance of fear;
through it, because no basis or support for clinging is seen anywhere, one abandons dogmatic adherence to clinging.

In that way, one abandons craving as it occurs. Contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*) is the knowledge of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhāñāṇa*), which serves as the means for the relinquishing of formations;
through it, one abandons ignorance, which is the opposite of reflection because of the lack of reflection upon impermanence and so forth.
Equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) and conformity knowledge (*anulomañāṇa*) are contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*); for by means of that—
Just as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, his mind recoils and shrinks away from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*);
therefore, by means of that [contemplation], he abandons attachment to union—the manifestation of defilements such as the bond of sensual desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*).

The seven contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), have been analyzed in meaning below and will be further commented upon later; thus they are not mentioned here.
"In those" means in the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*). "By this" means by the practitioner (*yogī*).

"Because of that" means because he has seen conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) by way of the three characteristics, such as impermanence (*anicca*). For the vision of them is indeed the contemplation of impermanence and so forth. "Penetrated" means acquired.
For at the very moment an object is penetrated by knowledge (*ñāṇa*), at that same moment it is said to be acquired. It is merely a matter of terminology.
Just as [the synonyms] for "tree" are "rukkho," "pādapo," and "tarū. These too are the contemplations of the signless (animitta), the desireless (appaṇihita), and the empty (suññatā).
All insight (vipassanā) is thus included; therefore, the intention is that they have been penetrated in part.

They are already comprised within the purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi); therefore, the meaning is that they are established even beforehand. Hence he said: "This pair, too, is indeed penetrated."

...arises. Regarding the remaining ten [insight knowledges], beginning with the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*): by the phrase “some have been penetrated, some have not been penetrated,” he refers to their partial penetration.

For when the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is established, the contemplation of cessation (*nirodhānupassanā*), the contemplation of destruction (*khayānupassanā*), the contemplation of fall (*vayānupassanā*), and the contemplation of change (*vipariṇāmānupassanā*) are said to be established in part.

When the contemplation of suffering is accomplished, the contemplation of disenchantment and the contemplation of danger are accomplished; when the contemplation of non-self is accomplished, the others are accomplished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 723.

In the subsequent discourse on the Knowledge and Vision of the Way, [it is said that] just as the sky appears through the clearing of clouds and so forth, or as water appears through the removal of mud and impurities...
Just as water is purified by the removal of mud, or gold by the removal of impurities, so too is knowledge purified by the disappearance of defilements;

thus it is said: "one whose knowledge is purified by the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth. Because he has performed the comprehension that discerns the three characteristics within formations consisting of manifold modes and bases, it is said:
"having reached the further shore of comprehension-knowledge (*sammasana-ñāṇa*). In this context, "of comprehension-knowledge" refers to that which is termed method-insight (*naya-vipassanā*).
Regarding the knowledge of comprehension by groups (*kalāpasammasanañāṇa*): they say that the other specific types of comprehension exist for the sake of stabilizing that very [knowledge].

Or, "of the knowledge of comprehension" means of the knowledge of comprehension such as comprehension by groups and so forth; for that is similar to insight into phenomena one by one (*anupadadhammavipassanā*).
For by means of that [latter], the uprooting of views and so forth become possible. This is the method of development in detail.
Desiring to speak further, he said, "First, one begins with a summary. For a beginner, beginning with a summary is easy.
Therein means in the summary-beginning. "How?
is a question expressing the desire to explain. That which is called "the knowledge of contemplating rise and fall in regard to presently arisen phenomena... and so forth.

The meaning is: "How is that to be known? One should apply the focused attention on seeing the arising and passing away of phenomena either in their continuity as present or in their momentary present, but not in the past or future; thus it is said, "of present phenomena.
And here, the seeing of arising is solely for the purpose of seeing the passing away, so as to emphasize the primacy of seeing the passing away.

In order to show this, having stated "wisdom in the contemplation of change," he further said "knowledge in the contemplation of rise and fall," because that vision of passing away is preceded by the vision of arising.

"Born" (*jāta*) means produced, having acquired an individual existence (*attabhāva*). For this word "born" is used with reference to the possession of the three moments [of arising, presence, and dissolution], as in such passages as "those phenomena which are born, become," and so forth; it does not refer to the past.
“As those who have been born do not exist, and those who have not been born likewise do not exist;

only those who have acquired a personal existence and have not yet perished exist by way of their own nature”—as in such passages, nor is there mere birth, as in such passages as “that which is born, become, and conditioned. Therefore he said:
“‘Born materiality’ means ‘present’”: the meaning is that present materiality is that which has been born and is included within the three moments.
However, since that is difficult to discern from the beginning, the application of insight (*vipassanā*) should be made by way of the present as a continuity (*santati*).
“Of that” refers to materiality. Without touching upon the conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) of the characteristic of conditions, the characteristic of arising is “origination.”
"Arising" (*udaya*) is the characteristic of the conditioned known as "birth," which is emergence (*uppāda*). "Passing away" (*vaya*) is the characteristic of change;

it is the passing away and destruction known as "dissolution. "Knowledge of contemplation" (*anupassanā-ñāṇa*) is that knowledge which consists in the close observation of both arising and passing away.
Although, in the context of the Compendium of Groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*) and so forth, phenomena possessing birth, aging, and death are treated under the heading of "birth, aging, and death,"...
However, here in the exposition of the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbayañāṇa*), when it is stated, "Birth is present;

its characteristic of production is 'rise,' and its characteristic of transformation is 'fall,'" and so forth, it would seem as though the possession of birth, aging, and death by those very factors, as well as their actual production, were being admitted.
To avoid this [misunderstanding], the teaching regarding the factors of dependent origination was presented ending with existence (*bhava*).
"Sā" refers to the yogi. "By this method of the Pāḷi" means by this manner of the text shown in the passage beginning, "Form that has been born is present.
"Born" (jātaṃ) does not mean produced [from a womb], nor merely the first moment of manifestation; rather, it means arising, which is a transformation consisting in origination.
Since this transformation is, for conditioned phenomena, like aging—the departure from a state of novelty—he says, "the aspect of novelty" (abhinavākāraṃ).

"He contemplates" is the connection [to the following]. There is no mass or accumulation of what has not yet arisen from which that which is arising might come, because it is entirely non-existent, having not yet acquired its own-being. Therefore he said: "That which is arising...
there is none. Just as these phenomena are entirely non-existent in the future period, so too they are in the past period.
Having stated "even for that which is ceasing," and so forth, he spoke the passage beginning with "Just as...

in order to clarify—by means of a simile that constitutes a part of the whole—the collective meaning that there is an arising of even non-existent material and immaterial phenomena when causes and conditions coincide, and that having arisen, they reach a state of total non-existence.
In that context, "from a heap" (*rāsitō*) means raised by way of being a heap.
A "heap" (*puñja*) is a mass. It is a collection formed into a single lump in whatever way. A "treasure-store" (*nidhāna*) is that which has been placed and set down by being buried in the ground.
"Lute-playing" (*upavīṇa*) is so called because one plays the lute (*vīṇā*) with it; it is the playing of the lute. 724.
Having thus shown the method of attention to rise and fall in brief, he now shows it in detail.
“Furthermore, ‘from the arising of... and so forth was said. Therein, ‘from the arising of ignorance’ (avijjāsamudayā) means from the production of ignorance; the meaning is ‘from its existence.
It has already been stated that ‘arising’ (uppāda), being an antonym of cessation, also denotes existence. Therefore, the meaning is:
when ignorance established in a previous existence exists, there is the arising of form in this present existence. [This is] in the sense of the arising of conditions.”
The meaning is "by way of the state of existence" (atthibhāvato), that is, by way of the condition's having arisen.

It should be understood that by means of the three beginning with ignorance (avijjā), their cooperative causes—namely, clinging (upādāna) and the rest—which belong to the past time, are also included.

Among the conditions for the process of existence (pavatti), edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) alone is taken because of its preponderance, as in the phrase "from the arising of nutriment. In that regard...

However, since temperature and consciousness are already included by virtue of the commonality of being "conditions for the maintenance of existence" (*pavattipaccayatā*) once [nutriment] has been grasped, it should be understood that the demonstration of the arising of matter through its conditions—namely, the fourfold origination (*catusamuṭṭhānika*)—has indeed been clarified.

The material body (*rūpakāya*) is produced solely by karma accompanied by the decisive supports (*upanissaya*) of ignorance and craving. And in the absence of the decisive support of ignorance—the craving for existence (*bhavanikanti*)—there is no possibility of birth.
Thus it is said. Just as ignorance and craving are the decisive supports (*upanissaya*) for material form, so too should they be understood for feeling and the other aggregates.

However, nutriment is the nourisher of material form that has already arisen, because edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) is intended here, and because the teaching is based on the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Alternatively, the mention of nutriment is by way of its preeminence. [The phrase] "the characteristic of production," etc., is according to time.

He speaks of "seeing the arising. In that context, having previously seen the arising by way of the duration [of the process], one who stands firm here sees it by way of the continuity, and subsequently sees it by way of the moment.

"The five characteristics" refers to the characteristics consisting of the existence of these conditions—namely ignorance, craving, karma, and nutriment—as well as the characteristic of the production of matter.

There are five characteristics. Their existence is such that material form (*rūpa*) is characterized by them; thus they are called "characteristics. However, arising (*nibbatti*) is simply a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*).

Regarding the statement "with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of material form": through the non-arising cessation of ignorance by means of the knowledge of the supreme path, [there is the cessation] of that which is yet to come.

The non-arising and cessation of form occurs because of its absence when conditions are absent. "By way of the cessation of conditions" means by way of the ceased state of the condition for form that would otherwise arise in the future, namely ignorance.
The same principle applies here to the statement, "With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of karma.
"With the cessation of nutriment" refers to the absence of edible nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), which is a condition for the continuation [of existence]. "Cessation of form" [means the same].

There is an absence of the material form originated by that [consciousness]. The rest should be understood according to the method explained below. "The characteristic of change" is the observation of their decline by way of the time of dissolution.

Therefore, having first seen that by way of the [three] periods of time (*addhā*), one who stands [in meditation] here sees it by way of the continuity (*santati*) and then gradually sees it by way of the moment (*khaṇa*). "The five characteristics" refers to this [context].
The non-arising and cessation of the four conditions beginning with ignorance, and the momentary cessation of material form—

these are the five characteristics. For they are called "characteristics" because by means of them the non-arising cessation of those [conditions] and the absolute cessation of material form are characterized.
Change is indeed the characteristic of the conditioned. This same method applies to the aggregate of feeling and the others. However, this is the distinction:
because of the statements, "Touched, one feels; touched, one perceives; touched, one wills," and "With contact as condition, there is feeling;
feeling born of eye-contact; perception; volition," contact is the condition for the occurrence of the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations.

And with the cessation of that, there is the cessation of those [feelings], as stated in the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* and the *Mahānidāna Sutta*, and in the Abhidhamma, in the section on mutual conditionality (*aññamaññapaccaya-vāra*), by the statement "consciousness has name-and-form as its condition" (*nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇaṃ*). Thus, name-and-form is the condition for the occurrence of consciousness, and with its cessation, there is the cessation of that;
hence it is said: "With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling," and so forth.
And here, some first say: "The observation of the rise and fall of the immaterial aggregates is only by way of the continuity of the life-span (*addhā-santati*), not by way of moments (*khaṇa*).
According to their opinion, there could be no observation of rise and fall from the standpoint of moments. Others, however, say:

"In the observation of rise and fall from the standpoint of conditions, without taking into account the classification into past and so forth, [one observes] in a manner common to all [factors], beginning with ignorance as a condition..."
"It sees the occurrence of feeling as its being obtained, not its arising; and in the absence of ignorance and so forth, it sees its non-occurrence as its being unobtainable, not its dissolution.
When seeing rise and fall from the perspective of the moment, one sees the arising and dissolution of present phenomena"—this is logical.
For, by way of continuity (*santati*), material and immaterial phenomena are seen in terms of arising and passing away...

And for one who attends to this, when the power of meditation has gradually been attained, the arising and passing away appear from moment to moment due to the attainment of a sharp and clear state of knowledge.

For he, first attending to the arising and passing away by way of conditions, sets aside the conditioning factors such as ignorance and grasps the aggregates that possess arising and passing away; [he then observes] their arising from conditions...
By way of seeing rise and fall, he also brings to mind the rise and fall even in terms of the moment.
When his knowledge proceeds having become sharp and clear, then material and immaterial phenomena appear as they arise and break up moment by moment.
Therefore it was said: "In this way too, there is the arising of form," and so forth.

In this context, "the arising of form" (*rūpassa udayo*) means that, according to the method already stated, there is the production of form through the arising of ignorance, craving, karma, and nutriment.

Likewise, "the passing away of form" (*rūpassa vayo*) means that, by the same method stated above, there is the cessation and non-arising of form through the cessation of ignorance, craving, and nutriment. This is the detailed attention to the condition (*paccaya*).

"It does. Likewise, when one sees the characteristic of arising according to the method thus stated—thinking, "In this way materiality arises"—one understands that both kamma-originated materiality and nutriment-temperature-consciousness-originated materiality arise, emerge, and come into being.

Similarly, when seeing the characteristic of change according to the same method stated above, one understands that both kamma-originated materiality and nutriment-temperature-consciousness-originated materiality pass away and cease.
The construction is: "He gives attention in detail by way of moments.
(725) When one attends in this manner, until the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) arises, the arising and passing away do not become clearly manifest;
taking this into account, it is said: "Thus, indeed, these phenomena... pe... experience [the result]," by way of showing the method (*naya*).
Or it is stated thus: first, having seen the arising and passing away of present phenomena, one then applies that method to the past and the future.
These consist of the classifications of the Truths such as suffering; the classifications of dependent origination such as the direct order (*anuloma*);

the classifications of methods such as unity (*ekatta*); and the classifications of characteristics such as impermanence (*anicca*). By the very mention of dependent origination, [all these are included].
And here, "phenomena arisen through dependence" (*paṭiccasamuppannadhammā*) are also included, because even they arise dependently with respect to their own fruit.
(726) *Yaṃ* is a nominative singular form used in the sense of the instrumental; they explain the meaning as "by which knowledge. Or, *yaṃ* is a reference to the action.
In the passage, "He sees the arising of the aggregates, he sees the cessation of the aggregates," that which is called "seeing" is—
The meaning is as follows. Regarding the phrase "But that which...," the same method applies here as well.

Furthermore, in this context, while a distinction in expression is made—such as "the arising of form from the arising of ignorance"—because the arising and cessation of the aggregates are distinct from the arising and cessation of ignorance and so forth, there is no such distinction between the rise and fall of the aggregates according to their characteristics of production and transformation; for they share an identical substratum (*abhinnādhikaraṇatta*).
This was stated without making a distinction in the phrasing, such as: "One who sees the characteristics of arising and the characteristics of change sees the rise and fall of the aggregates.
For the word *hi* (for/indeed) has the sense of a reason;

because the characteristic of arising exists only at the moment of origination, and the characteristic of change exists only at the moment of dissolution, therefore, one who sees these [characteristics] from the perspective of the moment...
"He sees the arising and passing away of the aggregates" (khandhānaṃ udayabbaye passati) means that he makes even clearer the very meaning already stated by the passage beginning with "But what...

(yaṃ panā). 727. Regarding the phrase "And thus for him" (iccasseva): here the word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). The meaning is: because the seeing of the arising and passing away of the aggregates is, from the perspective of conditions, as stated in "With the arising of ignorance... (*avijjā samudayā*) and so on;
and from the perspective of moments, as stated in "The characteristic of production" (*nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ*) and so on; therefore [he sees it]. "For him" (*assa*)...

[This refers to] the yogis. Thus, "evam" is a reference to the aforementioned mode of grasping (*parāmasana*). However, for those who read "icc'assa paccayato," "iti" is a reference to the aforementioned mode of grasping.
"From the awakening to the producer" means from the awakening to the conditions such as ignorance (*avijjā*) that produce the aggregates (*khandha*).
"From the awakening to the suffering of birth" means from the awakening to the suffering characterized by birth. [This is] the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*).
It becomes clear through seeing a single part, just as for those who see mountains, oceans, and so forth. The same principle applies here regarding "the realization of the suffering of death.
By the phrase "through the non-arising of conditions," it is shown that the cessation of conditions—namely their non-arising—is what is meant here by "the cessation of conditions.
"Possessing conditions" means [those things] that arise from conditions. And as for "his vision of rise and fall": whatever...
For that yogin, there is the vision of the arising and passing away [of phenomena] by way of conditions and by way of moments.

Non-delusion regarding this, or the collection of states such as applied thought (*vitakka*) dominated by that [vision], is the mundane path. Because it conforms to the outlet (*niyyāna*), this is indeed the mundane path.
Thus, for that reason, the truth of the path becomes manifest through the realization of its own nature. Therefore he said: "Because of the destruction of delusion therein."
The meaning is "by way of being its constituent part. Alternatively, the path—consisting of right view as previously described—is the means to the Noble Path;
having the nature of non-delusion, it reveals itself just as a lamp [reveals objects], and thus the Truth of the Path becomes manifest.
This manifestation occurs through the dispelling of the darkness of delusion; hence he says: "Therein, by the destruction of delusion."
“‘With ignorance as condition’ and so forth is the forward order of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), because it follows the forward sequence of the process of existence (pavatti).

By the phrase ‘from the arising of ignorance’ and so forth, the meaning stated is ‘when ignorance and the other factors exist. Thus he says: ‘Because of the realization that when this exists, this comes to be.
Because it reverses the sequence of the process of existence, ‘with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance itself,’ and so forth, is the reverse order of dependent origination.”
And these are conditioned and dependently arisen, because of such statements as: "Bhikkhus, aging-and-death is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen.

Furthermore, the manifestation of what is dependently arisen occurs precisely through the manifestation of the mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*), since one understands: "This is the fruit of that. 729.
This meaning—that the cessation of each preceding factor is followed by the arising of each succeeding factor—is established by way of condition (*paccayato*).

That which is established by the vision of arising leads to the realization of the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*), because there is no room for the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) that asserts conventional successions such as "one acts and another experiences [the result]. Therefore, he said: "By way of the connection between cause and fruit," and so forth.

The meaning that "formations (*saṅkhārā*) arise moment by moment" is established by the vision of arising from the perspective of the moment (*khaṇa*), leading to the realization of the principle of diversity (*nānattanaya*).

...there is. Because of the realization of the difference in intrinsic nature between the condition and the conditionally arisen, there is no room for the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) that proceeds in such a manner as "he acts, he experiences [the result]. Therefore, he said: "By seeing arising from the momentary," and so forth.

Through the vision of arising and passing away from the perspective of conditions, the meaning—that when the condition exists, the fruit exists, and when it does not exist, the fruit does not exist—is established; thus, by the mere fact of its existence...

The method of non-agency (abyāpāranaya) becomes evident through the fact that those phenomena are the cause, since there is no room for a self-view and because [a self] cannot be found as one who exercises mastery.
Therefore it is said: "Of phenomena," and so forth. The state of not exercising mastery is dependence on others, and that is to be understood as being conditioned (sappaccayatā).
By seeing their arising from conditions, these phenomena [are seen] by means of this or that condition.

Since things arise, and in arising they arise only in accordance with their conditions, the non-actionist view (akiriyadiṭṭhi) finds no footing because the correspondence between cause and fruit is established through the conformity of the cause to its effect; thus he said, "But as for conditions," and so forth.
When a cause exists, how can there be a doctrine of non-action? For that which acts is indeed a cause.
730. For one who sees arising from conditions, it is understood that when a condition exists—and thus when its own-nature (sabhāva) exists—the fruit comes to be;

that there is assistance by way of mere existence; that conditioned phenomena are devoid of agency (nirīhatā); and that their occurrence is dependent on conditions, such that they do not exist when conditions are absent.

Thus, this reveals the emptiness of self (*attasuññatā*). Therefore, he said: "And for him, from conditions... [etc. ...from the understanding of that much. This is the characteristic of impermanence (*aniccalakkhaṇaṃ*).
It becomes evident because, through the vision of rise and fall from moment to moment, formations are understood as being delimited by their rise and fall.
Therefore he said: "Because of the realization of non-existence after having existed. For cessation after having arisen is indeed "non-existence after having existed.
Separation from the past and future limits is the emptiness of past and future states; for formations do not [persist] beyond three moments.
"Exist before and after" means that because one awakens to the seclusion of the past and the future, the sense is that one penetrates their having a beginning and an end.
The connection is: "The characteristic of suffering also becomes manifest through the seeing of rise and fall.
Having arisen, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) break up; from the moment of their arising onwards, they are incessantly oppressed by the occurrence of successive stages of aging and destruction.
And since that state of being oppressed by them is dispelled by the correct vision of arising and passing away, he said: “from the understanding of suffering...

[etc. ...of awakening. “The characteristic of intrinsic nature as well”: not only the characteristics of impermanence and suffering through the vision of arising and passing away, but also the characteristic known as intrinsic nature—such as hardness in the case of earth and contact in the case of touch—is broken down by the state of ripening.
It becomes manifest as delimited by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāva). Therefore, he said: "from the realization delimited by arising and passing away.

Regarding "the characteristic of intrinsic nature" (sabhāvalakkhaṇa): it refers to the characteristic designated as intrinsic nature, that is, the specific characteristic (salakkhaṇa) of each respective phenomenon (dhamma).

"Even the temporary nature of the conditioned characteristics" means that even the conditioned characteristics such as arising have a limited duration—such as the moment of arising—because they do not persist beyond that particular moment.

Regarding that, he said “at the moment of arising,” and so forth. And here, the grasping of merely the arising and passing away is because this knowledge proceeds by way of seeing arising and falling away, not because of the absence of the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is not only ever-new, but also lasts for a brief duration. To explain how, he said “at the rising of the sun,” and so forth.
In that context, a line made with a stick in water is a "stick-line in water.
Although the five examples beginning with a drop of dew are all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), they are cited in ascending order to demonstrate their increasingly brief duration;

nevertheless, they are cited as having relatively slow cessation, because conditioned phenomena cease even more rapidly than those. For instance, among the sons of gods who delight in wandering, [the lifespan] proceeds from the lowest to the highest...
It is said that for material phenomena (rūpadhamma), their cessation is even swifter than the collision of the sharp edges of a horse's hooves as it gallops headlong toward them;
how much more so for immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma). They are not only ever-new, nor do they endure for even a brief moment, but rather they are devoid of substance.
To explain how this is so, he says: "Illusion" (māyā), and so forth. For illusions and the like, when perceived through gems and such means, lack their own true intrinsic nature (ataṃsabhāvatā).
They are without essence. In this context, "illusion" refers to magical deceptions such as Indra’s net, cultivated through mantras and medicinal herbs.
"A mirage" is the thirst for water in a deer. "A dream" is merely a dream. "A firebrand-circle" is simply a firebrand being whirled in a circular form.
A "city of the gandharvas" is a mere appearance in the sky, like a city that arises from the desire of gandharva-devaputtas to play.

"To this extent" means: to the extent that the method of development has been undertaken up until the penetration of rise and fall, either according to the sequence of the text beginning with "Materiality that is born is present," or according to the sequence of the text beginning with "Whatever materiality there is, whether past, future, or present.
For indeed, the entire method of development, including the comprehension by groups and so forth, is solely for the purpose of producing the knowledge of rise and fall.
"Not the binding of hands by those standing around. "Subject to decay" means having the very nature of breaking up.
It goes to its destruction according to its own inherent nature (*dhammatā*).

For even that which is said to perish through an external effort perishes only by its own inherent nature, because destruction is without cause. External effort, however, results in a dissimilar arising. In this manner...

For it has been said: "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation. Therefore, even without taking [the object] as a focal point, one should apply this aforementioned mode of direct realization to both arising—thinking, "What arises is indeed subject to falling away"—and to falling away—thinking, "And what has arisen approaches falling away.
[This refers to] that which has just arisen and has not yet reached full maturity.

He said, "It is 'the knowledge of nascent insight' (taruṇavipassanāñāṇa). Contemplation proceeding by way of the comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana) and so forth does not receive the designation of "insight" in the primary sense;
rather, it receives that designation only when it proceeds by way of the contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā) and so forth.
Therefore, he said, "By the attainment of which one comes to be reckoned as 'one who has commenced insight'."
Commentary on the Discourse on the Imperfections of Insight (Vipassanūpakkilesakathāvaṇṇanā) 732. By means of this nascent insight known as the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*),

and not by means of the nascent insight known as the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) and so forth for those who have already begun insight, nor by means of that known as the contemplation of disenchantment (*nibbidānupassanā*) and so forth.
The meaning is: "by way of powerful insight. For at that time, the defilements of insight do not arise.
Regarding the phrase "of one who has commenced insight," the particle *eva* (only) is indicated by elision; thus he says, "for the defilements of insight," and so forth.
They are called "defilements of insight" because they defile insight by serving as the basis for the grasping of views and the like. "Of a noble disciple" (*ariyasāvakassa*).
This is stated by way of the highest possible case (ukkhaṭṭhaniddesa), because [the defilements] do not arise even for one who has attained powerful insight (balavavipassanā).
"Of one who has practiced wrongly" means of one who has practiced in whatever manner through a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti) and so forth.

He said "of one who has practiced wrongly" in order to show that his practice is to be censured. The word "and" (ca) should be construed with the two subsequent phrases as well. "Of one who has abandoned the meditation subject" (nikkhittakammaṭṭhāna).
For one who, having begun insight (vipassanā), falls into despondency midway;
for a lazy person—that is, one who, despite being endowed with virtue, does not apply himself to meditation due to indolence;

or alternatively, for one who has practiced wrongly—that is, one whose practice is censurable due to the absence of the right practice known as the cultivation of insight. For the practice of insight itself, together with its requisites, [is what is meant].
In the preliminary stage, there is right practice, while anything other than that is wrong practice; and this [wrong practice] belongs to one who has abandoned the burden [of the task].
