Abandoning the burden occurs through laziness, as it is said: "of the lazy person who has cast aside the meditation subject.
"One who is devotedly engaged" means one who is intent upon development through yoga and knowledge. Furthermore, that state of being devotedly engaged—

He said, "for one who has initiated insight," because it occurs by way of serenity (samatha) as well. They certainly arise and do not fail to arise, for otherwise the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇa) would be impossible.

Regarding the light and so forth, the restlessness that occurs [thinking] "this is the noble state" (ariyadhamma) is agitation; that agitation regarding the state is *dhammuddhacca*. By means of that *dhammuddhacca*...
By departing from the course of insight (vipassanā), the mind that has grasped and engaged with what is unwholesome is a mind seized by agitation regarding phenomena (dhammuddhacca).
He says "the radiance is a phenomenon" by way of figurative usage for its cause; the meaning is that such a radiance being emitted is "my Noble Path.
One adverts to the radiance as "Nibbāna," or "the Path," or "the Fruit. When grasping it as "Nibbāna":

In that context, one grasps the phenomena occurring therein by way of the state of the path and its fruit; however, one grasps knowledge and so forth specifically by way of the state of the path and its fruit.
From that, distraction is restlessness (*uddhacca*); the meaning is that the distraction which has the appearance (*obhāsa*) as its cause is restlessness.
To explain in detail the meaning stated briefly in the phrase "with a mind agitated by restlessness," it is said: "as impermanence," and so forth.

In this context, [one] does not understand impermanence... because there is an absence of even the attention directed toward impermanence and so forth through the perception that "I have attained the path. And this is the meaning:
"Friends, whatever monk or nun declares the attainment of Arahatship in my presence, all of them do so by means of the four paths, or by one of these. Which four? Here, friends, a monk..."
He develops insight preceded by serenity. As he develops insight preceded by serenity, the path arises in him;
he pursues, develops, and cultivates that path. As he pursues...
[and so on] ...cultivates it, the fetters are abandoned and the underlying tendencies are brought to an end.
“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu develops serenity preceded by insight… he develops serenity and insight in conjunction… Furthermore,
friends, a bhikkhu’s mind is seized by restlessness concerning the Dhamma;
yet there comes a time, friends, when that mind becomes internally steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated.”

"The path arises for him... [and so on]... the underlying tendencies (anusaya) come to an end"—this is to be understood from this very passage of the Sutta. For here, in the exposition of the fourth path, the phenomena consisting of the path, its fruit, and Nibbāna as previously described are "dhamma.
In that context, agitation regarding dhamma (dhammuddhacca) is the distraction toward what is not the path and so forth, thinking, "I am one who has attained the path and so on."

Afflicted by that, the mind becomes agitated. Attachment (*nikanti*)—that is, longing or craving (*taṇhā*) for luminosity and so forth, which consists of subtle forms—presents itself in the manner of a delight in insight (*vipassanā*).
Because it is grasped as "the Dhamma" by one who is conceited (*adhimānika*), he says:
"He adverts to attachment as 'Dhamma'."

733. "Illumination of insight" (*vipassanobhāsa*) refers to the radiant material form (*rūpa*) originating from the mind of insight (*vipassanā-citta*), which belongs to one's own continuity (*sasantati-patita*) and is temperature-originated (*utu-samutthāna*).
Among these, that which originates from the mind of insight remains luminous only within the body of the practitioner;
the other, however, leaves the body and spreads out in all directions in accordance with the power of his knowledge.

They say that this must be investigated: "Is it seen by eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) or by mind-consciousness (*manoviññāṇa*) when one sees even a form in the space touched by that [light] which is known only to oneself?
It appears as if it were stated that, like those who possess the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*), this [form] is cognizable solely by mind-consciousness.
As for what is called the "path of insight" (*vipassanāvīthi*), it proceeds in successive order.

It is insight itself that is called "cut off" because it has been abandoned by the yogi through overweening conceit (*adhimāna*) thinking, "I have attained the path," or because the yogi’s insight is thus said to be "cut off from the path. "The basic meditation subject" refers to insight itself.
"By way of difference" means by way of dissimilarity due to being small or extensive. "Of this" refers to the illumination (*obhāsa*). [The phrase] "delimited by two walls" [is used].
A "double-walled house" (*dvikuṭṭageha*) is a house with one wall on the inside and another on the outside, with a walkway between the two.

In the evening, five-colored flowers are strewn there; and in a place permeated by the radiance of clear knowledge, all forms appear as if to the divine eye. Therefore it was said: "Venerable sir, mine... and so forth.
Having thus shown the basis for the diversity of illumination, the passage beginning with "But this... is stated to show the basis for long-term deception.
Therein, "this defilement of insight" is said with reference to the specific type that will be described hereafter, not to every kind.
"He" refers to that person who possesses serenity and insight but is conceited.
"Divāsaneti" means the seat upon which one should sit in the daytime resting place. He said, "Venerable sir, I have come to ask a question," because he had first thought, "I shall ask a question.

He said, "I have come indeed to be a refuge," because he subsequently thought, "By means of a skillful method, I shall make him understand his state as an ordinary person (puthujjana) and then direct him toward a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)"; and since that was his primary purpose, he spoke with this restriction.
“This is the Dhamma” means that this is the Dhamma of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) following the Noble Path; he says this according to the elder’s own inclination.
“Concentration” refers to the concentration of direct knowledge (abhiññāsamādhi). “With ears pricked up” means with the ear-cavities held motionless. He began to flee out of fear.
Therefore he said, “The elder, it is said, was of a temperament prone to hatred. For even in one of a hateful temperament who is brave, there is [a tendency to act] impulsively.

Fear arose in him. Thereupon, the Elder Khīṇāsavatthera, knowing his underlying disposition, thought, "By this means I shall make him recognize his state as an ordinary worldling (puthujjana)," and he performed the manifestation of an elephant and so forth.
For the Elder, being of a temperament characterized by hatred (dosacarita), penetrated [the truth] quickly;
for one of a hateful temperament is one who attains dispassion quickly.
734. "Of him" refers to the yogi who has brought the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) to its culmination.

Here, "weighing" and "investigating" should be understood as the very contemplation of rise and fall in the manner of: "In this way material form arises; in this way material form passes away," and so forth.
Just as the thunderbolt hurled by Devānaminda is unfailing and unimpeded, so too is this knowledge subtle.
Regarding the phrase "seeing rise and fall," it is said: "Like a well-aimed thunderbolt," and so forth. In this context, "sharp" means unblunted.
"Valiant" means possessing brilliance. "Extremely clear" means that through its state of being whetted, an exceptionally acute knowledge arises.
Likewise, by means of this, the yogi thinks, "I have attained the path."
“Insight rapture” (vipassanā-pīti) means rapture associated with the mind of insight. The minor and other types of rapture have already been described above.
Since the five kinds of rapture arise in succession when the contemplation of rise and fall has entered its proper course, it is said:
“This [rapture]... arises in five ways. However, by means of the knowledge of rise and fall that has reached its culmination—
It is indeed accompanied by pervading joy (*pharaṇā-pīti*). For pervading joy occurs not only at the moments of access and absorption, but at other times as well.
Therefore, he said: "It arises filling the entire body.
As for the six pairs beginning with tranquility (*passaddhi*), they are inseparable from one another; thus, when tranquility has arisen, the others have also arisen.
Showing all of these by way of demonstrating their function—that they "are thus"—he said: “There is neither distress nor heaviness of body and mind,” and so forth.
In this context, it should be understood that by the mention of “body,” the material body (rūpakāya) is also included, not merely the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling.
For the tranquility of the body and so forth are what suppress the distress and other afflictions of the material body as well. “Body and mind are tranquil…” and so on.

They become truly straight because, by means of dispelling the defilements such as restlessness and torpor, views and conceit, the remaining hindrances, lack of faith, deceit, and fraud—those states that serve as causes for the state of non-tranquility and so forth—the arising of insight-consciousness proceeds at that time.
"At that moment" means at the moment of the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall.

It is called *mānusī* (human) because it belongs to humans; it is the delight in sensual pleasure appropriate for humans, since it cannot be surpassed by the experiences of even those distinguished among humans.
"Divine delight" (*dibbā rati*) is included [here] because it is similar to human [delight] in its nature as sensual pleasure;
or else, "divine delight" is so called because it transcends that [human pleasure], and thus is not human—hence "non-human" (*amānusī*).
"An empty place" (*suññāgāra*) refers to any secluded lodging, or indeed to insight (*vipassanā*) itself; for that too is "empty" by virtue of being devoid of permanence and other such qualities.
And because it is the basis for the happiness of the yogī, it receives the designation “empty house.
It is for one whose mind is peaceful through the disappearance of those defilements that cause the non-contemplation of the mind; for a bhikkhu who sees the fear in saṃsāra;

for one who possesses insight by means of right method through the contemplation of the arising and passing away of material and immaterial phenomena; and for one who is practicing comprehension [but] has not yet commenced insight.

Because it is not within the domain of human beings, it is "non-human. "Delight" refers to the perception of the bliss of the joy of insight (*vipassanā-pīti-sukha*). This is the summary meaning of the verse here.

The second verse, however, was spoken specifically with reference to the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*). In that context, "whence, whence" means from whatever form or formless state.
"Vipassanā-sukha" (the bliss of insight) is the mental happiness associated with the insight-consciousness.
Because the entire body is suffused and nourished by the extremely refined material qualities (rūpa) originated from that [bliss], it is said: "pervading the whole body."
“Resolve” (adhimokkha) here means faith (saddhā); the intention is that it is not the resolve that is merely a concomitant factor (yevāpanaka).

And in this context, it does not occur by way of trusting in the fruit of action or the Triple Gem; rather, it is that which, through the removal of the turbidity of the defilements, becomes the cause for the state of extreme clarity in the associated mental states. Therefore he said: “Faith associated with insight... arises.”

Energy that has been perfected through the power of prior cultivation and proceeds evenly is called "exertion" (*paggaha*) because it exerts the associated states away from the side of defilement and from laziness. Thus he said: "Exertion is energy," and so forth.
"Well-established" (*supaṭṭhitā*) means well-settled upon the object by means of the clear discernment of its intrinsic nature.

"Well-founded" (*supatiṭṭhitā*) means well-established because of its immovability due to the departure of opposing factors. For that very reason, it is unshakable like something dug into the ground. By virtue of this immovability...
By all three phrases, "like the king of mountains," he shows that [the mind] is well-established. "He" refers to the practitioner (*yogāvacara*).
"Whatever place" means whatever place of his own station, whether form (*rūpa*) or formless (*arūpa*). "Having leaped down" means having entered into it.
"Having plunged in" is a synonym for that same act. Of the divine eye, which serves as its surrounding ornament...
With reference to beings known as "the other world" who appear to the knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*), it is said:

"The other world is as if [seen] by the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*). This is not because the divine eye has the other world as its object; for that [divine eye] has the sphere of visible form (*vaṇṇāyatana*) as its object.
When that [knowledge] exists, [the other world] appears, manifests, or stands present—this is the meaning. For to the extent that the object is present...
Having plunged in, it stands near; for that very reason, it is said that even the object plunges in and stands near.
Because formations are objects to be investigated, insight-equanimity (vipassanupekkhā) abides in a state of neutrality during investigation.

In terms of its actual meaning, however, it is simply equanimity regarding the specific (tatramajjhattupekkhā) as it occurs in that manner. It is associated with the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana-citta).
Volition (cetanā) is called "adverting equanimity" because it occurs by way of adverting and looking on.

Here, however, it is called "insight equanimity" because it is a state of neutrality toward the contemplation of those [phenomena] due to the very clear manifestation of their arising and passing away.
Since that arising and passing away belongs to all conditioned formations, he says: "it is a state of neutrality toward all conditioned formations. Regarding adverting...

The resemblance to Indra’s thunderbolt, a true iron arrow, and the quality of being both gentle and sharp should be understood as the state of the knowledge that follows the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), just as attendants follow their leader.
"Craving for insight" (vipassanānikanti) means the longing for or the expectation of insight. The radiance and other qualities are manifestations of insight.
He says, "adorned with radiance and so forth," because these [qualities] are like ornaments for her. *Ālaya* means attachment or longing.

*Sukhumākārā* means having subtle aspects; they are both subtle aspects and peaceful aspects. And that state of having subtle and peaceful aspects arises through the preeminent manifestation of meditation, whereby even her state of defilement (*kilesabhāva*) becomes difficult to discern.
Therefore he says: "That which is attachment is a defilement... and so on.

“Even these” means even among those [defilements] such as knowledge already mentioned. The phrase “when any one has arisen” is stated for the purpose of showing the apprehension that “I have attained the path,” etc., when any one [of them] has arisen; it is not because they arise one by one alone.
For indeed, the defilements do not arise even at the same moment, but the reviewing occurs separately for each.

“Indeed, never before has such a craving arisen in me”—this was said by way of seeing the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), and not by way of the arising of such a state of mind in the practitioner at that time. For he did not then perceive it as “craving”;
if that were the case, there would be no possibility of his apprehending the object of that [insight] as “I have attained the path,” and so forth. Therefore...
Thus he might think: "Indeed, such delight in development has never arisen in me before; surely I have attained the Path. Regarding "as the basis for the defilements":
in the direct sense (*nippariyāyato*), here the defilements are views, conceit, and craving; it is "by way of being their basis," that is, by way of being the place of their arising.
He said "not because of its unwholesome nature" to mean that it is not unwholesome in its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). However, just as with the illumination and so forth, so too—
It is said that "attachment is also a basis for the grasping of views and so forth," which is why it is called "a ground for defilement.
By the phrase "by way of the basis alone," it means without referring to the specific graspings themselves, but rather by way of their being the basis for those graspings.

For the self postulated by the proponent of self—the self conceived as "the substrate of the notion of 'I'"—is grasped as the object of the genitive case "mine" (mamā), appearing as the owner of the illumination; thus he says: "mine..."
"‘A light has arisen’: for one who grasps thus, there is the grasping of a view. By way of grasping the light as agreeable, one regards oneself as superior and so forth;
therefore it is said: "‘A light has arisen that is indeed agreeable’: for one who grasps thus, there is the grasping of conceit. "Experiencing" means relishing with delight.
"Of these" refers to the defilements designated as the grasping of views and so forth. "In the light and so forth" means for the sake of the signs of the light and so forth.

Showing that wavering (*kampana*) occurs when one does not abide in insight (*vipassanā*) as it has been undertaken, but falls into distraction—and that this consists in the grasping of craving for such things as the aura—he said:
"It wavers regarding the aura... [etc. ...it regards [them].
The connection is: "The mind wavers toward the sign of the aura. Or, when the aura has become the object, the mind [wavers] due to the defilements.
The construction is: "it trembles. Therefore he said, "by which the mind quivers. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"In establishing" means in mindfulness. "And by equanimity" means by insight-equanimity (*vipassanupekkhā*).
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the determination of the path and the non-path.

736. Regarding the passage beginning with "But one who is skilled," etc.: he is "skilled" (*kusala*) through his application of skill in the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). He is "wise" (*paṇḍita*) because of the ripeness of his knowledge.

He is "proficient" (*byatta*) due to his proficiency in the scriptures (*āgama*). He is "endowed with intelligence" (*buddhisampanna*) because of his application in awakening to the dangers and benefits in the purification of the defilements.
"This indeed is he" refers to that [person] who arises at the time when the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbayañāṇa*) arises for him at the moment the teacher gives the meditation subject.
Having shown the determination of the state of being a basis for the defilements by saying, "This indeed is that light which has arisen," he now speaks the passage beginning with "But as for that...
in order to show the method for bringing it within the range of insight (*vipassanā*).

Therein, in the first method, only the manifestation of the characteristic of impermanence (*anicca-lakkhaṇa*) was shown; once that is established, the other two characteristics are also necessarily established.

[It] exists. However, in the second method, in order to show the procedure of mental attention by way of the uncovering, uprooting, and exhausting of the adoption of views and so forth that arise depending on the "aura" (obhāsa) and other such phenomena, it was said:

"If the aura were the self," and so forth. In the section on the immaterial beings (*arūpasattaka*), the statement beginning with "If formations (*saṅkhārā*) were the self" was spoken in a general sense, encompassing all formations; here, [it is stated specifically].

Having analyzed the formations by way of the illumination and so forth, it was stated [previously]. As for the remaining method of attention, since it follows the same procedure explained therein, he said:
"All of this should be elaborated according to the method stated in the *Arūpasattaka*.
By contemplating the illumination as "this is not mine," one purifies the mind from the grip of craving; [and by contemplating it] as "I am not this."

Observing it from the perspective of grasping at conceit, one observes: "This is not my self," thus observing it from the perspective of grasping at views. Therefore he said: "This radiance is not mine," and so forth.
This same method applies to knowledge and the other [qualities] as well.
"These ten points" refers to these ten causes of defilement, beginning with radiance, as previously described. Wisdom (*paññā*).
"Of which one it is well-practiced": for that yogin, wisdom has become well-practiced by way of grasping impermanence and so forth amidst the illuminations and other signs;

having encompassed them and investigated them, it remains established. By knowing the state of composure regarding agitation about phenomena (*dhammuddhacca*), he is skilled in agitation about phenomena.
"Entered upon the path": entered upon the path of insight (*vipassanā*) by way of contemplating rise and fall.

"In the purification of view" means: when purification of view has been attained, or through the knowledge of purification of view, the definition of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*) is accomplished by way of defining the mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) included within that truth of suffering.
Since the conditions for mentality-materiality belong to the side of the origination of mentality-materiality, he said: "Doubt... [etc. ...of the truth of origination."
"...has been defined. For according to the method of the Abhidhamma, all defilements and kamma constitute the truth of origination (*samudayasacca*).

"Of this" means "by this. "Correctly" means without error. "Of the path" refers to the Noble Path, the path that serves as the means. The commentary on the description of the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the twentieth chapter.
21. Commentary on the Exposition of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away Freed from Imperfections.
737. Equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) is insight that has reached its culmination (*sikhāppattā vipassanā*) through the attainment of the summit of the practice of insight.
Its culmination, however, arises by way of the eight knowledges beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall; thus it is said:
"Insight that has reached its culmination by way of the eight knowledges. [This refers to] the coarsest of the coarse darkness of delusion that conceals the Truths.

Because it is conducive to the penetration of the truths through its departure [from defilements], "knowledge in conformity with the truths" (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) refers to the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
To show those knowledges according to their specific nature, the passage beginning with "and eight" is commenced.

Therein, the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*) is precisely that which clarifies the characteristic of impermanence of formations through the seeing of their arising and passing away, and by following that, the other characteristics as well.
Some say that because it "occurs," it is called "the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall, which is known as insight that has entered the path.
However, this was said by those who consider that [knowledge] to be entirely devoid of the full comprehension through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*).

For although the knowledge of rise and fall is indeed included within the full comprehension through investigation, it is so in the sense of knowing rise, fall, and so forth, and in the sense of direct experience.
In the sense of seeing, they are "knowledge and vision," such as the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*) and so forth.

Because these very things are purified by way of their opposition to defilements, they are "purification by knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*). And because one proceeds by means of this, it is the "way" (*paṭipadā*); thus it is called "purification by knowledge and vision of the way.

However, that was said with reference to what has merely arisen and is not yet proficient. For when it is proficient, through the accomplishment of the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so forth, it is...
It is the foundation for the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). For, through its absence, some of the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*) are indeed attained.
Indeed, without the direct penetration of rise and fall (*udayabbaya*), the mere examination of the general characteristics cannot result in the superior abandonment of opposing factors.
And if there is no abandonment of opposing factors, from where [could it come]?
The state of having unimpeded momentum, or being sharp and clear, like a diamond (vajira) among knowledge and the other factors.
Therefore, the knowledge of rise and fall that has reached proficiency should be regarded as belonging to the side of full understanding through abandoning (pahānapariññā).

The contemplation of the dissolution of all conditioned formations is "contemplation of dissolution" (bhaṅgānupassanā); that very knowledge is "knowledge of contemplation of dissolution. One who sees things as they truly are...

It is called "fear" (*bhaya*) because one fears it; it refers to the phenomena of the three planes. When these phenomena appear as fearful, the knowledge that apprehends the aspect of what ought to be feared is "knowledge of the appearance as fear" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*).
It is called "desirous of deliverance" (*muñcitukamyam*) because it desires to be liberated; this refers either to the mind or to the person.

The state of that [mind or person] is "desire for deliverance" (*muñcitukamyatā*), and that very knowledge is "knowledge of desire for deliverance" (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*). Furthermore, it occurs in the mode of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*).

Knowledge is the knowledge of contemplation by reflection. Knowledge that occurs by way of equanimity toward formations through their lack of concern is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).

"Therefore" means: because the ninefold knowledge beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away, when freed from imperfections, is the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (*paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*), therefore [it is so called].
738. Not understanding the meaning already clarified by the qualification “freed from imperfections,” the questioner asks:
“What is the purpose of further application to the knowledge of arising and passing away? In this context, “what is the purpose” means what is the motive;

it is useless, because it has already been produced, like cooking what is already cooked—this is the intention. Alternatively, [the question may be asked] by way of grasping the sequence of causes such as the discernment of characteristics and so forth.

Desiring to make this matter known, the teacher himself asks, "For what purpose? by way of wishing to speak. "The purpose of discerning characteristics" means the purpose of correctly ascertaining the characteristics of impermanence and so forth.
Showing the reason for this, he says, "Knowledge of arising and passing away," and so on.
But is it not the case that knowledge of arising and passing away sees only the arising and passing away of formations, and not...

Regarding the three characteristics beginning with impermanence: how, by means of that [knowledge of rise and fall], does the discernment of the three characteristics beginning with impermanence come about?
This should not be viewed as follows: "The knowledge of rise and fall has the three characteristics as its object.
Rather, when rise and fall have been penetrated, the characteristic of impermanence becomes manifest and stands out. Then: "Whatever is impermanent is suffering."

"Whatever is suffering, that is non-self"—this is the other characteristic as well. Alternatively, by means of the apprehension of rise and fall, the mode of non-existence after having been, the mode of constant oppression, and the mode of lack of mastery become more manifest;

thus, it should be understood that the purpose of the meditator's practice in the knowledge of rise and fall is the discernment of the three characteristics by way of their causal relationship, not by way of direct confrontation.
"Below" refers to [the stage] prior to the purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.

Below. For although that [wisdom] proceeds having become sharp and clear by virtue of being the cause for the arising of illumination and so forth, it becomes blunt and indeed not clear because it is defiled by views and the like.
Therefore he said: “By ten... pe ... he was unable. 739.
*Amanasikārā* (due to non-attention) is an ablative expression used in the sense of a cause. For this [phrase], “Due to non-attention to what? is equivalent to “Because of being concealed by what?”
For one who conceals what has been asked about, there is an inquiry into the cause. Because continuity (*santati*) is concealed for him, the characteristic of impermanence does not become manifest;
and that continuity becomes concealed through a lack of attention (*amanasikāra*) to its arising and passing away.

Because the postures (*iriyāpatha*) are concealed, the characteristic of suffering does not become manifest; and those postures [become concealed] through a lack of attention to their constant oppression.
They become concealers. Because they are concealed by density, the characteristic of non-self does not appear;

and those densities become concealers through the failure to attend to the resolution of the various elements. For one who sees rise and fall, the stage of rising does not reach the stage of falling, nor does the stage of falling reach the stage of rising. The moment of rising is one thing, and the moment of falling is another.
"Even a single phenomenon appears through its division by way of moments, let alone those that are past and so forth"; thus he said, "But arising and passing away...

appear. In this context, "when the continuity is disrupted" means when the continuity of phenomena occurring in a prior and subsequent sequence is broken by the observation of their mutual difference.
For it is not the case for one who correctly observes arising and passing away [that the continuity remains unbroken].

When phenomena appear as being connected, the characteristic of impermanence is not as clearly evident; however, when they appear as disconnected—like iron rods—the characteristic of impermanence becomes much more manifest.
"By attending to constant oppression" means by way of the rise and fall of formations as they have been defined.
Having brought to mind the state of being incessantly oppressed and afflicted.
"The postures are laid bare" means that the capacity of the postures to conceal the suffering experienced within them is laid bare.
For when suffering arises in one posture, another posture serves as its dispeller, acting like a cover for it; and so it is with the others as well.

When the manner in which the various postures conceal suffering is known as it truly is, their status as concealers of suffering is said to be "uncovered," because the formations are manifest as being incessantly pierced by suffering. Therefore he said:
"The characteristic of suffering appears according to its true nature. "Various elements" means the various kinds of elements, such as earth and so forth.

"Having analyzed the various constituent phenomena": having separated them individually, such as "the earth element is one, the water element is another," and so forth, and "contact is one, feeling is another," and so forth. "When the analysis of the compact has been made":

when the compactness of the aggregate, and the compactness of function and object, have been distinguished. For this [analysis] applies to the material and immaterial phenomena that arise together, mutually supporting one another.
The density of the mass [of formations] is grasped by means of undifferentiated formations through the adherence to their unity;
likewise, the density of function is grasped as a single unit despite the distinctness of the functions of those various phenomena due to their fixed nature;
and likewise, the density of the object is grasped as a single unit despite the distinctness of the way objects are apprehended by phenomena that possess objects.
And when these [elements] are analyzed by means of knowledge regarding the elements, they dissolve like a mass of foam being rubbed with the hand;

as they proceed according to their respective conditions, it becomes more evident that "these phenomena are empty, mere phenomena," and thus the characteristic of non-self becomes clearer. Therefore it was said: "The various elements... appear."
740. Because it rejects the state of permanence, it is "impermanent" (*anicca*), namely the five aggregates (*khandha*).
As it was said: "Form, Rādha, is impermanent; feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is impermanent. Stating the reason for this, he said:
"Because of the nature of arising, passing away, and change. Here, arising has the characteristic of production, and passing away has the characteristic of transformation.
“Alteration is aging; the meaning is that it is the presence of these [characteristics]. ‘Having been, it is no more’ means because of perishing after having arisen.
And here, by the first [definition], he shows that it is impermanent due to the presence of birth, aging, and death; by the second, due to the absence of the state of ripening and destruction.
To show that the characteristic of impermanence is that state by whose existence the pentad of aggregates is called ‘impermanent,’ [he says:]”
“Arising, passing away, and changeability,” and so forth, has been stated. By that, it is characterized as “impermanent. “Modification of mode” means a transformation of mode.

For the mode of non-existence is obtained in the form of a transformation; because it is a disfigurement, it is not the mode of arising. Alternatively, “modification of mode” means a distinction of mode.

For the state of having existed and then being non-existent is distinct from the state of ripening (or cooking), due to the absence of destruction; and therein lies the characteristic of impermanence.

This is well-established. For the aspect of impermanence (*aniccākāra*) is indeed distinct from the aspects of suffering (*dukkhākāra*) and non-self (*anattākāra*), as well as from the aspect of arising (*uppādākāra*).
Thus, the absence of disintegration in sound is also established by its conditioned nature (*saṅkhatabhāva*).
And conditioned nature, in its actual meaning, is the state of possessing arising. Furthermore, arising is the state of existing, established by the fact of being subject to ripening (*pākabhāva*).

In this same manner, the characteristics of suffering and non-self are to be understood. Furthermore, just as "impermanent" is the negation of permanence, so the aspect of impermanence—described as the mode of non-existence—is the characteristic of impermanence through the negation of the aspect of permanence;

likewise, "suffering" is the negation of pleasure, and the aspect of suffering—described as the mode of constant oppression—is [the characteristic of suffering] through the negation of the aspect of pleasure.

The characteristic of suffering (*dukkha-lakkhaṇa*) is thus to be understood; likewise, from the negation of a self, "non-self" (*anattā*) refers to the characteristic of non-self defined by the mode of being subject to lack of mastery, which results from the negation of the mode of a self—that is, the characteristic of non-self (*anatta-lakkhaṇa*).
These three modes are not included within the aggregates (*khandha-pariyāpanna*), because they are phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature (*asabhāva-dhamma*).
Yet, because they cannot be apprehended apart from the aggregates, they are also not separate from the aggregates. However, regarding the aggregates...

These specific designations arising therefrom should be understood as the specific causes for discerning the danger inherent in those [aggregates], which are obtained by way of conventional usage based upon them.

"All this" refers both to the three characteristics already mentioned and to the five aggregates that are to be characterized. The statement, "He observes according to their actual nature through the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall," is expressed using that conventional designation for the sake of that meaning; for it is for the purpose of the knowledge of rise and fall that—

Insight that has the characteristics as its object is called "knowledge of arising and passing away" (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*). For knowledge of arising and passing away does not have the characteristic of suffering and so forth as its domain.

If it were to have those as its domain, it would no longer be knowledge of arising and passing away. However, one who wishes to make knowledge of arising and passing away sharp and clear should indeed investigate the three characteristics;
this is like a preliminary exercise for it. This same method applies to the remaining types of knowledge as well.
The knowledge of arising and falling away freed from imperfections is finished.

Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution (Bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): "It flows" means it proceeds. The sharpness of the knowledge is due to the proficiency of the cultivation. And the cultivation is proficient.
Because there is no distraction, it proceeds as if fixed upon the object; thus, by means of the sharpness of knowledge, the quick appearance of formations is shown.

When formations appear quickly and repeatedly by way of their arising and passing away, the observation of their arising is for the sake of observing their passing away—since the observation of arising leads to disenchantment through the realization that "that which has arisen must perish."

Only when there is an application of attention, a coordination, and a mental orientation toward its passing away (*vaya*) does knowledge arise directed specifically toward that passing away, setting aside its arising and so forth.
Therefore it is said: "or arising," and so on. In this context, "arising" (*uppāda*) refers to the transformation of manifestation.

"Stability" (*ṭhiti*) refers to having reached the state of stability; the meaning is "aging" (*jarā*). "Occurrence" (*pavatta*) refers to the occurrence of what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*). "Sign" (*nimitta*)...

The sign of formations (*saṅkhāranimitta*). That appearance of formations which, by way of their accumulation and so forth, and by way of the delimitation of their own functions, presents itself as if they possessed a physical body—that is the sign of formations.
Some, however, say: "What is called 'occurrence' (*pavatta*) is the continuous proceeding of formations, which is simply their arising;
what is called the 'sign' (*nimitta*) is the continued existence of those that have arisen, a succession of stations."
Therefore, they say: "If one grasps only arising, one is said to grasp at occurrence; if one grasps only stability, one is said to grasp at the sign.

But this contradicts the statement beginning with "or arising," for an alternative (vikappa) is not appropriate when there is no distinction. [The mind] does not reach [the object] because it does not grasp it.
To the question, "What then does it reach? he says: "It reaches destruction... [and so on]... it comes to rest."

In this context, since the word "cessation" (*nirodha*) is seen to refer even to non-arising, it is qualified by the word "breaking up" (*bheda*); since the word "breaking up" can also denote a specific [kind of] distinction, it is qualified by the word "waning" (*vaya*);
and since that [word "waning"] can also signify non-cessation, it is qualified by the word "destruction" (*khaya*). Thus, the meaning is:
in momentary cessation, which is characterized as destruction, waning, and breaking up. By the phrase "mindfulness stands firm," he speaks of knowledge by way of its primary aspect, mindfulness.

"In this state" means at the time when, through the attainment of sharpness in the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) which is free from defilements, one—according to the method already described—relinquishes even the arising and attends only to the passing away.
"Reflecting on the object" means reflecting upon the objects such as form and feeling precisely by way of their exhaustion and passing away; [the *yakāra* is omitted] due to elision.
For this is an exposition [of the term], as in the phrases "by his own direct knowledge" (*sayaṃ abhiññā*) and so forth.

Alternatively, the contemplation of the object (*ārammaṇa-patisankhā*) is the reflective discernment (*paṭisankhā*) of the aforementioned object by way of its destruction and fall. "Contemplation of dissolution" (*bhaṅgānupassanā*) refers to the contemplation of the dissolution of the consciousness that has that [object] as its support.
"Wisdom" (*paññā*) is knowing in various ways. Whatever else needs to be said regarding this matter will be explained right now in the commentary.

742. "Whatever object" refers to everything included within the range of formations (*saṅkhāra*), from material form up to aging-and-death, taken as the state of what is to be seen through insight (*vipassanā*).

"Reflective contemplation" (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) means knowing; and since that [knowing] is intended here as the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*), it is simply the seeing of things from the perspective of their dissolution.
Thus he says: "The meaning is: having known, having seen them as subject to destruction and vanishing. This is to be connected with "of that knowledge."

"Having visible form as its object" (*rūpārammaṇa*) means "the state of having visible form as its object" (*rūpārammaṇatā*). To show this meaning—that it is like saying "a god is itself a deity"—it is said, "consciousness has visible form as its object.

Alternatively, showing that the term "having visible form as its object" is used in the nominative case to express the locative sense, he says, "or else, in the state of having visible form as its object.
"He contemplates the dissolution with another consciousness" refers to the object of insight (*vipassanā*).
He speaks of the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*). For in this way, the contemplation of dissolution becomes proficient, and the object appears to him with even greater clarity.
"Known" refers to the object, because it is known by way of contemplation. "Knowledge" refers to the knowledge of contemplation.
"He contemplates both" means that he contemplates both of these as subject to destruction and vanishing. This is the summary meaning here.
The vision of the destruction and fall of form, up to aging-and-death, as an object is "reflection on the object.
The vision of the destruction and fall of the knowledge of seeing is "contemplation of dissolution" through reflection on the object. In both cases, it is wisdom (*paññā*).

Alternatively, since the former does not exist in the absence of the latter, one may include the former within the latter; thus, it is the latter alone that is "wisdom in insight-knowledge" (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*).

“In this” means in the passage: “He contemplates the dissolution of that consciousness... [etc]...”. “In many ways” means by way of many modes such as contemplation of impermanence and so forth. He says “he sees again and again” because the prefix *anu* has the sense of “furthermore.
Here, a conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhatadhamma*) is characterized by birth, aging, and death; of these, birth is the initial limit, aging is the middle limit, and death is the final limit.

In this regard, although the threefold characteristic of arising and so forth is the characteristic of impermanence by virtue of being a conditioned characteristic, [it is here specifically the dissolution that is intended].
Nevertheless, when birth and aging are seen, the characteristic of impermanence does not appear as clearly manifest as it does at the moment of dissolution (*vaya-kkhaṇa*).
Thus he said: "Dissolution is the ultimate limit of impermanence. The meaning is that it is the highest limit, the final limit.
For just as that which is subject to aging and subject to death is born, birth is the initial limit of impermanence.
Likewise, that which is subject to birth and subject to death decays; thus, decay (*jarā*) is the middle limit. That which is subject to birth and subject to decay breaks up;

thus, breaking-up (*bhaṅga*) is the ultimate limit. "He contemplates as impermanent" means he does not do so by way of inference—such as "it is impermanent in the sense of destruction"—as one who is merely comprehending by groups (*kalāpa*), nor does he do so like one who has already begun insight meditation (*vipassanā*).

It is not by way of first grasping at arising and then seeing passing away; rather, through the power of the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*), as arising and passing away present themselves directly to perception, one contemplates impermanence by way of seeing dissolution alone, having let go of arising according to the method already stated.
And for one who contemplates in this way, there is not even a trace of the grasping at permanence; thus it is said: "not as permanent."
For it is said that "he thus abandons the perception of permanence. And here, in the phrase "he contemplates only as impermanent," the particle *eva* is indicated by elision;
therefore, to show the meaning excluded by it, "not as permanent" is stated.
Nor should one suspect here an exclusion of contemplation as suffering and so forth, because the particle *eva* functions to exclude its opposite (*paṭiyogī*).
And because they have already been treated in the teaching above. The same method applies to such passages as "he contemplates them as suffering" and so forth.
First, contemplation as impermanent is appropriate for one who contemplates dissolution, since it is said, "Dissolution is the ultimate limit of impermanence.
But how can this be said regarding suffering and the rest? To answer this, he says, "Because that which is impermanent is suffering," and so on. By this, whatever is impermanent...
That [form] is exclusively suffering and non-self, and therefore it is not something to be delighted in and so forth.
Thus, he shows that one contemplates it by way of the other six contemplations as well, for the purpose of preparing the knowledge for its subsequent production.
However, some here maintain that there is no separate function of seeing such as "one contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent," and so on.
When they say, "By seeing dissolution alone, everything has been seen," that is appropriate for the culmination of the contemplation of dissolution;
however, prior to that stage, the contemplation of the manifold aspects and formations must certainly be undertaken.
Otherwise, the Pāli text beginning with "he contemplates as impermanent," and its commentary which states, "he sees again and again in many ways," would be contradicted.
And there would be contradiction. That very same state of all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) has been seen as impermanent.
"It is not to be delighted in" means that this state of conditioned phenomena is not to be delighted in by way of delight through craving and views, thinking, "This is mine;
this is my self. "One should not be infatuated with it" means one should not be infatuated with that state of conditioned phenomena by way of passion.
"It should not be set in motion" means that sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) or lust for existence (*bhavarāga*) should not be set in motion.

"He brings about the cessation of lust" means he brings lust to the cessation of suppression (*vikkhambhana-nirodha*); the sense is that he suppresses it. Therefore he said: "First, by means of mundane knowledge alone.
And as to how there is an origin [of suffering] when there is suppression, he said: "It does not originate; it does not produce an origin."
"Thus detached": thus detached by way of the contemplation of dissolution. He brings to cessation the range of formations that has just now appeared as it was seen, and he attends to its cessation;

and even regarding what has not been seen—the past and the future—he brings them to cessation by means of inferential knowledge (*anvaya-ñāṇa*), inferring: "As this is now, so too were the others," while attending to their cessation.
"He does not. Regarding "it does not arise," the same method applies here; the meaning is that he does not attend to its origin (*samudaya*).
"Practicing in this way" means practicing by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth, in the manner described.

"By completely abandoning the defilements together with the aggregates and the formative forces" means by the relinquishing of the defilements along with the aggregates (*khandha*) and the formative forces (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
For one who abandons defilements, it is said that they abandon the kamma caused by those defilements as well as the aggregates produced from that kamma.

"By seeing the fault in the conditioned" means by seeing the disadvantage in conditioned phenomena, such as their impermanence, suffering, and so forth. "In their opposite" refers to the nature of permanence, pleasure, and so on.
"Tending toward them" means being inclined toward them. The word *paṭinissagga* has the sense of relinquishment.
And the phrase "the sense of leaping forward" expresses the twofold nature of relinquishment. Therein, "leaping forward" means resolute confidence (*adhimuccana*).

"In the manner already described" refers to the modes of abandoning such as "by way of its own constituent" (*tadaṅga*) and so forth, and the mode of being inclined toward that. "By way of producing" means by way of generating.
For one who produces [them] takes up the defilements; therefore, one who does not produce them does not take up the defilements.
"By way of seeing the absence of fault" means by way of not perceiving faults. The construction is: "one grasps conditioned objects.
For it is because one sees the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) that one grasps at formations; therefore, by seeing the disadvantage, one does not grasp at them, one does not take them up.

(743) "His" refers to the practitioner. "By those knowledges" refers to the knowledges of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth. "That" refers to the abandoning. "Perception of permanence" [is what is abandoned].
The expression "perception of permanence" is a designation by way of its characteristic mark (saññā-sīsena). The same method applies here to "perception of pleasure" and "perception of self.
"Craving accompanied by rapture" refers to a longing that is full of excitement (sauppilāvita). 744.

Regarding the phrase "transference of the basis" (vatthu-saṅkamana): because it is the locus where insight (vipassanā) proceeds, the objective supports such as form and so forth are termed "bases" (vatthu).
Showing what is intended, he says "of form," and so forth. Therein, "transference" is stated by way of the method of unity (*ekattanaya*) due to the commonality of the state of insight (*vipassanā*);

otherwise, since the knowledge whose object is the dissolution of one form would be different from the knowledge whose object is the dissolution of the consciousness that takes it as its object, how could there be any transference?
The same principle applies to the turning away of wisdom (*paññāvivaṭṭanā*). "By wisdom" means by way of seeing arising and passing away (*udayabbaya*).
This refers to the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā) as it proceeds. Turning away from arising by means of grasping at passing away is what is meant by the statement:

"Abiding in passing away after abandoning arising. By the phrase "the capacity for adverting immediately thereafter," he expresses the state of proficiency and strength of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā).
745. "Both" refers to the two objects by way of being seen and not seen. "Defining as one" means defining them as equal due to their momentary perishability (*khaṇabhaṅguratā*).

"While it is existing" means while it is being apprehended through direct perception in the present. "One whose vision is purified" means one whose knowledge is purified by the removal of obstacles to the vision of dissolution;
the meaning is "one who has a perfectly purified vision of dissolution. "He leads [the mind] following that" means...
He brings forth a knowledge that follows upon and conforms to that knowledge which perceives the dissolution of present formations.
To the question, "Where does it operate? he says, "In the past and future," meaning in the past and future categories of formations.
The phrase beginning with "all" is a demonstration of the manner in which it operates.
The intention is that [this insight] pertains to cessation reckoned as dissolution, not to Nibbāna.

"This" refers to that discernment which, by means of the continuity of the object, establishes both the seen and the unseen as a single unity through their momentary perishability; the meaning is that this is the insight into dissolution within the characteristic of vanishing and the characteristic of change.
746. "And he reflects upon the object," and so forth, is a strengthening of the very same meaning already stated, because the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) is difficult to penetrate.
This vision of dissolution leads to the penetration of the characteristic of non-self through the realization that formations do not admit of one's will;
showing this, he said, "and its appearance as empty. For the object of the mind that has the dissolution of the object as its focus—
And for one who contemplates dissolution, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) appear specifically as empty. Therefore he said, "Of that very [person]," and so forth.
"There is no other" means that in this world there is no so-called self (attā) whatsoever apart from the aggregates (khandha).
"He sees their destruction" means he sees the dissolution of those phenomena as it manifests moment by moment.
He is diligent through the practice of diligence as previously described. How so?
Just as a skilled person, when piercing a gem with a diamond using the proper method, attends to and observes only the hole in the gem and not its color or other qualities;
even so, he wisely attends to the continuous dissolution of conditioned phenomena.
The intended meaning is that it does not form [new formations], nor does it volitionally construct them.

Or, just as the pierced spot of a gem struck by a diamond does not heal again, so too, when dissolution is seen by the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution—which is like a diamond—the grasping at permanence does not grow again;
thus, the meaning is that one sees only dissolution.

And as for "reflection on the object": this refers both to the reflection on the object that has come down in the passage, "Having arisen with a visible form as its object, the consciousness breaks up;
one reflects upon that object," and to the contemplation of dissolution spoken of thus, "He contemplates the breaking up of that consciousness.
[It is understood that] "only formations break up; their dissolution is death, not..."
The meaning is that this appearance as empty—spoken of in three ways as "Is there anyone else?

and so forth—is what is called "insight into higher wisdom" (*adhipaññā-vipassanā*). (747) "In the contemplations of impermanence, etc. means in the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. "In the contemplations of disenchantment, etc. means in the contemplations of disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment.
"Three modes of appearance" refers to the threefold appearance by way of impermanence and so forth. For appearance as destruction and passing away is appearance as impermanent;
appearance as fearful is appearance as suffering; appearance as void is appearance as non-self.
"In views" means that he does not tremble at the sign of views; for, being unshakable, he does not waver.
748. “Like a fragile vessel” means that one sees only its breaking, like a raw clay vessel filled with liquid;

this is the connection. And here, the simile of the fragile vessel is for the purpose of showing its inherent tendency toward destruction; the simile of the fine dust being scattered is for the purpose of showing the lack of mutual connection between the parts;
and the simile of the sesame seeds being broken is for the purpose of showing the state of breaking moment by moment.
They are to be seen as subject to dissolution alone; that is, one sees only their destruction because of the non-perception of their arising and so forth.

"In this very way" means: just as water bubbles, having arisen in dependence on conditions such as the surface of the water, do not endure for long but break apart very quickly, even so all material and immaterial phenomena, having arisen in dependence on conditions such as karma, have only momentary duration.
"Breaking up very quickly, very quickly" means that one sees only their breaking up.
Indeed, the repetitive expression "they break up, they break up" is used for the purpose of showing their breaking up with great urgency.
Even a mirage lasts only for a short time, yet because it persists through its dependence [on a support], it appears for a longer duration; thus, "as one might see... [is said].
It is called a "mirage," not merely because it appears as something other than what it truly is. "The world" refers to the world of the aggregates (*khandhaloka*).
The King of Death does not see [the Arahant], because through the attainment of Arahatship there is no further becoming. 749.
"The abandoning of the view of existence" is the suppression of the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*); for there is no uninterrupted dissolution alone.
For one who has seen [this], there is no occasion for the eternalist view (*sassatadiṭṭhi*). Precisely because of that lack of attachment to life, there is the relinquishing of craving for life.

"Always" means at all times, day and night. It is the state of being devotedly engaged in spiritual cultivation (*bhāvanā*). It is a pure livelihood (*visuddhājīvitā*) due to being far removed from improper conduct.
It is the abandoning of anxiety and the lack of preoccupation with what must or must not be done, owing to intense spiritual urgency (*tibbasaṃvega*). It is the state of being free from fear.
Fearlessness toward anything arises from the absence of attachment to oneself. The attainment of patience and gentleness results from having clearly seen impermanence.

"Endurance of non-delight and delight" refers to the endurance and overcoming of aversion toward secluded lodgings and superior wholesome states, as well as the delight in the strands of sensual pleasure.

These are called "the eight supreme qualities"; this is stated with a change in grammatical gender (using the masculine *guṇā* for the feminine *guṇāni*). The letter *m* serves to join the words; the meaning is: "These eight are the supreme benefits, beginning with the abandoning of the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*). "Therein" means: therein, in the contemplation of dissolution (*bhaṅgānupassanā*).
The knowledge of contemplation of dissolution is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Appearance as Terror (Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā):
"Of all formations" means of all formations belonging to the three planes. For, by virtue of the context, the scope of "all" refers here to a specific portion [of all formations].
Here, the word "all" (sabba) refers to everything. "Of one who practices" (āsevantassa) means of one who practices with diligence, of one who causes [the practice] to proceed.

"Of one who develops" (bhāventassa) means of one who increases and expands it. "Of one who cultivates repeatedly" (bahulīkarontassa) means of one who performs it again and again, of one who applies oneself to it.

"Destructive" (pabhedakā) means destructive in the sense of breaking apart moment by moment. "Livelihood" (ājīvikā) refers to those who desire to die due to illness and so forth, as well as those who do not desire to die.
"Even that which ought to be feared from the sun does not appear as a source of fear," thus it is said: "for a timid person who wishes to live in comfort.

Just as lions and the like are a cause of terror for one of a timid nature because of their terrifying state, so too do formations (*saṅkhāra*) appear as fearful to the meditator when they are seen in the process of dissolution;
hence he says: "lions... appear [as fearsome]. "Present" means present in terms of time (*addhā-paccuppanna*).
The gross [states] are long-lasting continuities; those that are momentarily present are more subtle and short-lived; those that are continuously present are intermediate.

Here, one should first comprehend them from the beginning. Knowledge regarding the things that stand near as being fearful and terrifying is "knowledge of the appearance as fear" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*).
Just as a woman’s head being cut off or being in the process of being cut off is terrifying when perceived by her children, so too for the practitioner.
In order to show the meaning of "being grasped through the cessation of formations belonging to the three times," the passage beginning with "Of a certain woman" was spoken.
Just as spoiled rice and the like do not remain in their own nature but perish, so too for that woman who has given birth repeatedly...
Sons do not live; they surely die. Thus she is called "one whose offspring are putrid.

And here, the mention of "putrid offspring" is specifically for the purpose of showing the meditator the determination regarding the cessation of future formations, by way of demonstrating the contemplation of death even for those still in the womb.

For the cessation of past and present formations is already perfectly evident to him, and thus it does not need to be established by means of this simile. [This applies] to one in their final existence...

Furthermore, for the sake of showing that for a yogi who will attain the supreme state after seven more births, there was an abundance of suffering in the past and a scarcity of suffering in the future,

a woman with many children is used as an illustration. In this context, just as her nine sons have died, so too have the conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) of the past— distinguished as internal and so forth— been previously lived through.
Or, the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) are to be seen as present formations (saṅkhāra), like a son who is currently being measured;
or the abode of beings that is currently occurring is to be seen as such. Future formations are to be seen like a son not yet born, or as a future abode of beings.
This being the case, some [criticize] the inclusion of the mother of nine sons while excluding the mother of ten sons, claiming it is purposeless.
What they say is refuted. Because death for children occurs after a long time, it is called "recollection of death.

With the intention that one who has entered the womb remains only as a future potentiality because it is not yet directly perceived, one who has gone into the belly is described as being in the state of a future formation (*anāgata-saṅkhāra*).
"At this moment" refers to the moment when formations appear in their terrifying nature by way of showing their dissolution.
751. It does not fear because it does not function in the manner of fear. For fear occurs by way of the arising of a mind of aversion (*paṭighacitta*);

knowledge, however, knows the object to be feared as "this is to be feared" according to reality. Therefore he said: "The past... [etc. ...is merely an investigation. The three heaps of coals are intended to be distinguished as sharp, medium, and mild by their respective heat. For among the realms of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*)... [etc. ... [Note:

The inclusion of those three [types of trees] is by way of being an illustration for the three states of existence (bhava), just as the three qualities of the *khadira* tree’s trunk—such as its being unyielding and so forth—are illustrative.
Therefore he said, “Only,” and so on. “Of it” means of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). “Fallen into calamity” means fallen into various kinds of extensive misfortune.
“From fear” means from that which is to be feared.

"The sign of formations" (*saṅkhāranimitta*) means, as it has been stated: "The appearance of formations as if they were possessed of a physical form, by way of their density as a collection and so forth, and by way of their delimitation of their own functions.
However, since such an appearance of formations is not separate from the formations themselves, he said:
"It is a designation for the past... [and so on]. "Death itself" means precisely dissolution. "By that" means by the seeing of dissolution.
For one who sees only dissolution moment by moment, the conditioned state known as the "sign" appears as something fearful, according to the method already described for impermanence.
While it is true that "occurrence" refers to the entire process of existence in all realms of being,
nevertheless, through the attainment of the highest stage of contemplation of dissolution, occurrence appears even more clearly as a constant oppression within all states of existence.

It is said, "The occurrences of existence in the realms of form and formlessness proceed," and so forth, in order to show that even existence, though regarded as peaceful happiness, presents itself as fearful due to its inherent nature of suffering.
"Both" refers to the sign (nimitta) and the occurrence (pavatta);
for both of these present themselves as being empty of self.
The knowledge of appearance as terror is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Disadvantage (Ādīnavānupassanāñāṇa):

"Protection" means guarding against [the self] as non-self due to the cause of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). It is not perceived because all states of existence and so forth possess disadvantage.
"Similarity with one" means being like that [self]. "A shelter" (leṇa) is its being a place of refuge and concealment. "A resort" (gati) is the place to which one must go for that purpose.
"An asylum" (paṭisaraṇa) is the very place of refuge for that [self]. "Aspiration" (patthanā) does not mean a longing;

by this, he expresses the absence of the grasping of craving, namely, "This is not mine. "Misapprehension" (parāmāsa) refers to the misapprehension of views. By this, he expresses the absence of the grasping of views, namely, "This is my self."

And here, by the very absence of the grasping of craving (*taṇhā*), the absence of the grasping of the conceit "I am this" (*esohamasmi*) is also already stated, either explicitly or by the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*).
Now, in order to show the reason for the absence of aspiration and so forth, it is said: "The three states of existence," and so on.
Therein, the three states of existence are like heaps of glowing coals because they possess great heat due to being the basis for the suffering of birth and so forth. The four great elements...

They are like fierce venomous serpents known as the Wood-mouthed, the Putrid-mouthed, the Fire-mouthed, and the Weapon-mouthed, specifically because they inflict the sufferings of stiffness, spreading, burning, and cutting upon the body;

and generally, because of their abode, their poisonous transformation, their infliction of harm, their difficult approach, their unassailability, their ingratitude, their indiscriminate action, and their manifold dangers and calamities.
As it is said: "Four venomous serpents of fierce power and terrible poison..."

For it has been said: "Monks, this is a designation for these four great elements. The five aggregates are so called because when one aggregate is distinguished, the others do not remain as that same aggregate;
and because they strike one another and bring about the suffering of death, they are like executioners with raised swords.
And this has also been said: "Monks, 'an executioner with raised sword' is a designation for these five aggregates of clinging."
“Designation. Even though the six internal sense bases are grasped as being self or belonging to a self, because they are empty of that [nature], they are like an empty village;
and because the objects of enjoyment such as food and so forth exist therein, they are like a village entered by people. For it has been said:
“‘An empty village,’ monks, is a designation for these six internal sense bases. From the perspective of the eye...”
“Even if, monks, a wise, competent, and intelligent person were to examine it, it would appear as empty, it would appear as hollow, it would appear as void”—and so forth.
The six external sense bases are like thieves who plunder a village, because they are destroyers in every respect. For this very reason, he said:
“‘Thieves who plunder the village,’ monks, is a designation for these six external sense bases.
The eye, monks, is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms,” and so forth. [It is also afflicted] by the eleven fires, beginning with the fire of lust.

For this has been said: “The eye, monks, is ablaze. By what is it ablaze? By the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion; by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.”

*Ādi*. The fact that formations (*saṅkhārā*) are like boils and so forth has already been stated below. "Lacking enjoyment" (*nirassādā*) means devoid of anything to be relished, because their intrinsic nature is suffering.
"Lacking sap" (*nirasā*) means devoid of excellence, because they end in misfortune. In all instances, the connection is as follows:
just as it was stated below that they appear as being devoid of enjoyment and lacking sap, having become a great mass of calamities, so too it is above.
In such passages as “like a forest thicket full of brambles,” that [phrase] should be brought in and connected.

“With tigers” means with leopards (*byaggha*). “Crocodiles” refers to *kumbhila* and others. “Rākṣasa” refers to a water-rākṣasa. By the phrase “devoid of essence, devoid of enjoyment,” he shows the uninterrupted nature of the danger (*ādīnava*).
For thus, for that practitioner, in all states of existence (*bhava*) and so forth, all...
Volitional formations (saṅkhārā) appear continuously as being full of peril due to their nature of relinquishment. And that which is full of peril is fraught with danger (sādīnava).
Therefore he said, "Of that very [peril]," and so forth.

"Yam" refers to the knowledge of danger. "This has been stated" means that this exposition of the terms, consisting of ten bases and adorned with twelve rounds, has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* by way of positive and negative concomitance.
"Arising is fear": the arising of formations is "fear" in the sense of being a ground for fear by way of insecurity. For everything that has arising as its root has that [arising] as its basis;
thus it is accompanied by calamity. The same method applies to the phrases "occurrence is fear," and so forth.
"Non-arising" (*anuppāda*) means that there is no arising of this, or that once this is attained, there is no future arising of formations; it is Nibbāna.
And because it is entirely free from fear and has become the supreme consolation, it is called "secure" (*khema*) in the sense of being fearless.
By the term "state of peace" (*santipada*), he refers to the deathless state (*amatapada*) which consists in the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

With the words "non-occurrence" (*appavatta*) and so forth, he speaks of Nibbāna itself by way of negating occurrence and the like. Having seen the danger in occurrence, one immediately thereafter perceives the benefit in cessation.
The third section, "Arising is danger, non-arising is security," is stated with reference to those who are striving to accelerate their insight (*vipassanā*).
This same method applies to the sixth section and the others as well. Here, "arising" (*uppāda*) is the qualifier (*visesa*), and "danger" (*bhaya*) is the thing to be qualified (*visesitabba*);
because it possesses the nature of a general term (*sāmaññabhāva*), the difference in gender is maintained despite the two words being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Just as:
“‘The noble truth of the origin of suffering’—this same method applies to ‘destinies are fear’ and so forth.

Regarding the phrase ‘arising is formations,’ here the arising of all formations is taken as a general whole, while formations are then set forth by way of their specific divisions; thus, because they are to be clearly seen through insight according to their various classifications, this distinction in expression is made.
The connection is: one sees the accumulation [of kamma] and rebirth-linking as ‘suffering. Knowledge regarding danger is ‘this’ in the context of danger.”

When this has become the object, this fivefold knowledge should be understood. "Knowledge in the state of peace" means that this knowledge stands by way of being inclined toward, and so forth, the state of peace. 753.
The arising of formations occurring in the present existence due to kamma-conditionality becomes more manifest.
It is said, "it arises," meaning "arising here due to past karma as a condition. "Occurrence" (pavatta) refers here to the occurrence of phenomena during the course of existence;
thus it is said, "the occurrence of what has arisen. "All" means all form and non-form belonging to the three periods of time, including the internal and external divisions.
"Karma" refers to the karma occurring at present. And herein, by the mention of arising, occurrence, and accumulation—
Formations included in the present portion are grasped; by the grasping of rebirth-linking, those included in the future portion are clung to.
And by the grasping of arising, formations of kamma included in the past portion are indicated because they have already manifested. However, by the grasping of the sign, all are grasped.
That destiny in which that rebirth-linking occurs—be it the various types of destinies such as hell and so forth—is determined by way of good and bad conduct.

Because they are to be gone to; furthermore, in actual meaning, they should be understood as the resultant aggregates (vipākakkhandhā) that are subject to the designation "existence" (bhava) as determined by their respective kamma, as well as the matter produced by kamma (kaṭattā-rūpa).
"The arising of the aggregates" means the production of all aggregates whatsoever.

They are "evident" because they have been demonstrated in the *Saccavibhaṅga* by way of their characteristics and so forth. "By way of the basis" means by way of the station of occurrence, which is designated as the object (ārammaṇa).
If only those five are intended as the actual bases, then why are the others mentioned? To this he says: "The others are [included] by way of being synonyms for them.
By this, he shows that the teaching was expanded for the purpose of increasing the range of objects for the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇavipphāra*) of those practicing insight (*vipassaka*).

The presentation of the knowledge of the opposite side is for the purpose of showing the negative consequence (*ādīnava*) of the knowledge already shown by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), through its contrapositive (*byatireka*).
“Where there is no arising, there is absolutely no fear.

By first showing the process of occurrence with the words “or by the manifestation of fear,” etc., he demonstrates that it is the custom of the Buddhas and their close disciples (Anubuddhas) to show cessation after having shown the two preceding truths, just as in the world [one might say] of someone...
The vision of danger can also be purposeless, but this is not so; rather, it is indeed purposeful.

To show this meaning, the passage beginning with "Because... was stated. The mind inclines toward its opposite, just as one overcome by heat inclines toward coolness, because there is a state of absolute desire for liberation from that [danger] once its peril has been clearly seen.
"Bhayanti" means one should fear. By the phrase "necessarily suffering," it is shown that because of its nature as suffering, it is an object of fear;
thus, the state of being an object of fear does not deviate from the state of suffering. They say that "the bait of the round" refers to the aggregates subject to clinging.
The "bait of the round" consists of both the threefold round itself and that which is dependent upon the round, because it can be grasped by the defilements.
The bait of the world (*lokāmisa*) consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇā*). The bait of defilements (*kilesāmisa*) consists of the defilements themselves.

In the phrase "merely formations" (*saṅkhāramattam eva*), the word "only" (*eva*) excludes the state beyond formations (*visaṅkhāra*); for there, even the slightest trace of being "with bait" does not exist.

By the word "mere" (*matta*), however, it indicates incompleteness; for not every category of formation is "with bait. Therefore, regarding that which was called "fear," by way of its nature as suffering and so forth—

Because of their fixed nature (*niyatattā*). If that which is fear were of the very same nature as suffering and so forth, then in that case, the purpose would be accomplished by just one of them—fear, for instance.
With this objection in mind—asking why all [three] are included—he says, "Even though this is so," and so forth.
This is because, within those very same formations (*saṅkhāra*), there is a diversity of aspects (*ākāranānatta*) due to their occurrence as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Regarding the diversity of contemplation: thus, the diversity of knowledge here is due solely to the mode of its occurrence, such as through the mode of fearfulness and so forth.

In this context, it should be understood that knowledge occurring in the mode of fearfulness is "knowledge of appearance as terror" (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa*), while that occurring by way of other modes is "knowledge of danger" (*ādīnava-ñāṇa*).
