Since the fifteen meanings mentioned as the objects of the knowledge of danger are included within the five [factors] beginning with arising,
and since the knowledge regarding them is tenfold because it proceeds by way of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), he therefore said,
"he understands ten kinds of knowledge. And this understanding is preeminent, being unconfused due to the removal of delusion concerning its object.
“Even oneself is indeed undeluded”: this is said because one regards oneself as if one were understanding [it]; thus he said, “one penetrates and realizes. Regarding the word “of two” (*dvinnam*):
since it is joined with the word *kusala*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative, as in “skilled in dance and song” (*kusalā naccagītassa*).
As for “skillfulness” (*kusalatā*), the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; hence he said, “by the skillfulness of the two.”

"Of two" means either "of two persons" or "by way of two kinds of knowledge. Because the process of existence has been seen as it truly is, the state of peace—which is its opposite—stands out as being well-determined.
Consequently, his mind does not waver through false attachments such as the view that Nibbāna occurs only in this very life (*parama-diṭṭhadhamma-nibbāna*).
Regarding this, he says, "He does not waver among various views," and so forth, because he has clearly seen the danger [in those views]. The rest here is of plain meaning.
The knowledge of contemplation of danger is finished.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment (Nibbidānupassanāñāṇa): 754.
"In regard to formations" means in all formations belonging to the three planes. "He becomes disenchanted" means he attains disenchantment through the disenchantment of knowledge.

He enters [into that state]. Being thus situated, he is said to be "discontented" (*ukkaṇṭhanto*) and "not delighting" (*anabhiramanto*) therein; hence it is said, "he is discontented and does not delight.
To illustrate this lack of delight with a simile, the passage beginning with "just as if" (*seyyathāpi*) was spoken.

Regarding the mountains—namely, Gandhamādana, Kāḷakela, Sudassana, and Cittakūṭa—which stand encircling Lake Anotatta and are respectively two hundred *yojanas* in height, composed of rock, aloe-wood, silver, gold, and the seven precious gems:
Among the five great peaks of the Himālaya, the western one is named Cittakūṭapabbata. Regarding the seven great lakes, such as Sīhapapāta and others:

"In a golden cage" means in a cage made of gold fashioned like a lion. "Placed within" means obstructed. "Established on seven points" means established by not touching the ground with the seven parts—the two hands, two feet, tail, and two knees—within the threefold existence of happy rebirths, such as the fortunate realms of the sense-sphere and so forth. In the middle of the city...
He does not take delight because of the fear of oppression by the door-frames, bars, shafts, and so forth. "Seen" means seen through the observation of general principles preceded by conviction.
Therefore he said: "His mind is inclined toward that, slants toward that, and tends toward that.
The knowledge of contemplation of disenchantment is completed.

755. "But that" refers to the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*). "By means of the two kinds of knowledge" means by means of the two knowledges of the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*) and the contemplation of danger (*ādinava-anupassanā*).

Since it is precisely when formations are seen as terrifying that they appear as great dangers and as objects of disenchantment, therefore even that single knowledge—having reached the power of such cultivation—is associated with a specific stage and possesses the capacity for its threefold function.
"It is said to be 'one in meaning' because it occurs [in both contexts]. Therefore he said, "all formations," and so forth.

This has been stated by way of these contemplations reaching their culmination; however, at the beginning, they indeed proceed with distinct intrinsic natures (*sabhāva*). "He caused to arise" means he manifested; the sense is that he made them manifest.
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance* (Muñcitukamyatāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)

756. It does not cling because it is seen as having many disadvantages. It becomes desirous of being released and desirous of escaping because the aggregates, which have existed since beginningless time, are being fully understood.
This "desire for release" is the desire to extricate oneself from that [bondage], the desire to escape, the desire to depart.
"Confined in a cage" means obstructed by a cage. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...
The inclusion of such things as places beset by glowing embers, and forests thick with wild beasts and creeping creatures, should be understood.
The knowledge of desire for deliverance is finished.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection.
757. Having stated, "Desiring to be released from all states of existence...
and so forth, the repetition of the word "all" in the phrase "from all that pertains to formations" is an additional statement intended to demonstrate a preeminent release;

it makes known another meaning. For that release which belongs to one who is no longer followed by formations is a preeminent release. And that occurs through the aforementioned contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*).

To demonstrate that, it was said: “Furthermore, those very formations... and so forth. The word “furthermore” (puna) is used because the grasping of formations by applying the three characteristics was already performed previously.
The word “those” (te) is used because there are no formations existing in states such as existence (bhava) that have not yet been scrutinized.
The word “very” (eva) is used because there exists a mode of contemplation (anupassanākāra) that has not been encountered before. [This refers to] by means of the mode that is now being described.
This is the meaning. Since the grasping of formations occurs only by way of their complete characteristics, it is said, "having applied the three characteristics.

Regarding the phrases beginning with "because of non-eternality," that which ought to be said has already been stated above. By the first word "beginning" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such [phrases] as "because of having a beginning and an end" and "because of the negation of permanence.
By the second [word "beginning"], there is an inclusion of such [phrases] as "because of being oppressed by arising and passing away" and "because of the negation of pleasure."
“From the unrefined” means from the unpleasant, or from the unsightly. “From the loathsome” means from that which should be felt with disgust, thinking, “Shame!
“From the repulsive” means from having a state of repulsiveness due to being the opposite of what is pleasing. “Not destroyed by adornment” (*amaṇḍanahatā*) means not struck down by decoration;
the meaning is that it is possible to destroy their beauty through lack of adornment. Or else, it is by lack of adornment that their foulness becomes manifest.

"Unmarred by adornment": either because it is not destroyed by adornment, or because its nature is such that it cannot be destroyed by adornment—just like the term "not to be seen by the sun" (*asūriyapassā*).
He speaks thus with reference to the formations of form (*rūpa-saṅkhāra*) because of this state of being unmarred by adornment. "Ugly" (*virūpa*) means unsightly.

Because it serves as the basis for the fetter of aversion (*paṭigha-saṃyojana*), it binds itself to the one who looks; thus it is "loathsome," exceedingly ugly—that which is a cause for the arising of mental distress even upon mere sight.
It exists. For that which is to be despised by the wise is loathsome, like excrement, and must be abandoned. Here, by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such terms as "from the impure" and "the unpleasant.
By the fourth "etc.," there is an inclusion of such terms as "from the lack of a guide" and "from the rejection of self."

758. *Ayanti* refers to the practitioner of yoga (*yogāvacara*). *Muñcanassa* means for the sake of not following after [the object] again; it refers to one who has well-released and is letting go. *Upāyasampādanatthaṃ* means for the sake of accomplishing the means; the means is the thorough grasping and rubbing [of the object] by way of its impermanence and so forth, and it is for the purpose of achieving that.
*Khippaṃ* means that which is thrown here and there in the water for the purpose of catching fish;
it is a fish-catching trap. *Oḍḍāpesi* means he cast down; the meaning is "he threw. *Sappaṃ* means a black snake. *Gahaṇe* means regarding the snake as it was caught.
"Having released [him] from the grasp. "Having uncoiled the hand" means having uncoiled and freed the portion of the hand wrapped around by the snake’s coils.
"Having wriggled" means having moved about by casting off the coils. "Having relinquished" means having abandoned it. The passage beginning with "Therein," etc., is the correlation of the simile.
"Therein, from the very beginning" means at the time of reaching the age of discretion (*viññutā*). "The analysis of the compact" (*ghanavinibbhogaṃ*)...
"Having done" means having taken up the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and having broken through the grasping of a solid mass, such as a collection [of parts].
"Well-freed" (*sumutta*) is a neuter noun used adverbially, as in expressions such as "the moon and sun revolve unevenly.

The inability of formations (*saṅkhārā*) to appear in modes such as permanence is due to the attainment of an especially superior state of strength by insight (*vipassanā*), which is distinguished by the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*) and so forth; and that—
"By means of thoroughly observing the aspects of formations such as impermanence," he says, "by applying the three characteristics...

having brought [them] to [that state]. For just as in a wrestling match, when one wrestler is overwhelmed here and there by a stronger opponent with blows from the fists and so forth, the other is rendered incapable of contending with him; it is not merely that he is rendered incapable—
Just as one who has been brought to a state of extreme weakness reaches either suffering equal to death or death itself,
so too these formations, having been brought to such a state of frailty by the power of higher knowledge, reach a state of non-functioning and total dissolution.

"By this much" means by this reflective contemplation— which proceeds by way of discerning the impermanence and other characteristics of formations through forty-four modes, beginning with "from the non-absolute nature."

Regarding what should be said concerning the passages beginning with "contemplating as impermanent" (*aniccato manasikaroto*), that has already been explained in the method set forth in the *Bhayatupaṭṭhāna-kathā* (Discourse on the Appearance of Fear).

However, this is the distinction: having stated that the word "reflecting" (*paṭisaṅkhā*) means "having known," he shows that because the act of reflecting and the arising of [the knowledge] occur at the same moment, even though there is no sequence of prior and subsequent time, it is spoken of in this way by mere verbal convention.

He says, “‘Sensual pleasure’ (kāma), etc. By this, it is shown that this linguistic usage is based on simultaneity, as in such passages as: “Dependent upon a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises by way of the root-condition (hetupaccaya), having dispelled all darkness, like the risen sun,” and so forth.
Likewise, it is not the case that first the mind and mental objects arise, and subsequently the mind-consciousness [arises].
In order to show that it is the same here as well as in the case of [the arising of consciousness], the passage beginning with “dependent on the mind” was stated.

Since such a grammatical construction is generally seen in the world according to the sequence of prior time, he said, “or by way of the method of unity... should be understood,” in order to show that it is likewise here according to the sequence of prior time.
Its meaning is as follows: with respect to the cognitions that arise one after another, by way of the preceding one—
The act of reflection and the act arising by way of something other than that should be applied;

yet they are not to be regarded as distinct, because they are taken as a unity according to the principle of oneness due to their inclusion within a single continuum. Regarding the "other two phrases," this refers to the pair of phrases:
"reflection upon occurrence" and "reflection upon both the sign and occurrence."
The knowledge of contemplation by reflection is finished.
Commentary on the Knowledge of Equanimity Towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā): 760.
Although the knowledge of contemplation by reflection proceeds by way of grasping the modes of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, regarding formations...

In particular, it is said that the primary effort is the grasping of the aspect of non-self, as expressed in the passage beginning, “having grasped that all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are empty,” and so forth.

For when that [grasping] exists, the penetration of the Truths succeeds; it does not succeed when it is absent. Indeed, because of its absence, even the teachings of teachers such as Sarabhaṅga—which demonstrate the characteristics of impermanence and suffering—turned out to be non-leading to liberation.
Or else, [it is because they lacked this grasping] regarding [the notion of] permanent essence and so forth.
It is with reference to what is empty that it was said, “having discerned that ‘all formations are void. For whatever is empty of something, that is void of it.

Because the voidness of formations regarding a self is difficult to discern, even though voidness-contemplation has been penetrated many times, the passage beginning “Again, this is void” is commenced for the purpose of strengthening its realization. Therein:
To the extent that formations are non-self, to that same extent they are not belonging to a self.
For it has been said: "This is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self," implying that if there were a self, there would have to be something belonging to a self.
"Two-sided" means having two parts; the intention is that one does not see a self through the eye of knowledge by direct perception, nor is it apprehendable through inference.
The construction is: "He does not see another being, or a formation, standing in the state of being an accessory (*parikkhāra*) or as a means for his own pleasure and pain.
This connects further with the word "he again grasps" (*pariggaṇhāti*). "In this" (*ettha*) refers to this section on the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*).
"Anywhere" (*kvaci*) means in some place, time, or phenomenon; or alternatively, "anywhere" means internally or externally.

“His own self” (*attano attānaṃ*) means his own person. By saying, “This indeed is the venerable Brahmā, the Great Brahmā… the best, the creator, the controller, the father of those who have been and who are to be,” he shows that one does not see either a self imagined by others or anything belonging to anyone;
thus he says, “of anyone” (*kassaci*), and so forth. In that context, “another’s” (*parassa*) refers to [the notion of] “another birth” or “another person.”

And thus it is for one who has grasped [this view]. Regarding the phrase "and not mine anywhere," he says, "setting aside the word 'mine' for a moment," because here the word *mama* is used in an inappropriate sense.
"Of another" means of one other than oneself. When there is such a meaning as "another person," [one thinks] that person stands for my sake, and by virtue of him, everything is accomplished for me;
this is according to the conceptualization of certain proponents of wrong views.
Showing that one does not perceive either a self or anything belonging to a self, he says, "And nowhere," and so forth.
Herein, "I am nowhere" means one perceives the non-existence of one's own self.

"Not as anything belonging to anyone" means one perceives that very same self as not belonging to anyone else. And the two phrases, "nor is there 'mine'," should be connected respectively to these two.
"It exists" refers to each [aggregate] individually. "And nowhere does another's self exist" means he sees the non-existence of another's self.
"In that other's self there is no 'mine' for me" means he sees the non-selfhood of another's self.

Thus, by means of grasping the emptiness of the fourfold limit—the emptiness of self and what belongs to self regarding the aggregates both internally and externally—he perceives them as a mere heap of formations.
It has been seen. Therefore it was said: "In this way," and so forth.

By the passage beginning with "In six ways," he demonstrates—summarizing—the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*) as it appears in various places throughout the Niddesa and other texts.
In that context, "in six ways" means by six modes of apprehension, that is, by the modes in which [emptiness] is to be apprehended.
Or: "By the permanent" means by a self—whether one's own or some other—that is imagined to be "permanent. Or, "by the permanent" means by way of the state of permanence (*niccabhāva*).

The terms "stable" (*dhuvā*) and so forth are the modes to be grasped for that very thing which has been grasped as "permanent. For it is through its differentiation from that [permanence] that this [set] constitutes a group of six.

In this context, "permanence" (*niccatā*) means immutability (*kūṭaṭṭhatā*). "Stability" (*dhuvabhāva*) means firmness (*thiratā*). "Constantly existing" (*sadābhāvitā*) means eternal persistence (*sassatatā*). "Unchangeableness" (*nibbikāratā*)...
The state of being subject to changelessness (*avipariṇāmadhammatā*). Instead of providing the full repetition up to "old age and death," he shows only the concluding phrase.

762. *Na sāram* means "without essence" (*asāra*); it is "coreless" (*nissāra*) because there is no core (*sāra*) in it. It is "devoid of essence" (*sārāpagata*) because it is removed from essence, or because essence has departed from it.
However, some here [interpret] it as "by way of the essence of permanence" or "by way of the essence of happiness."

According to the intention that "or by the core-essence of oneself" is the canonical text (*pāḷi*), they say that the three terms—"insubstantial," "coreless," and "devoid of essence"—constitute one mode of discerning emptiness; otherwise, there would be only seven modes, not eight.

Others, however, maintain that since the phrase "by the core-essence of the beautiful" also exists in the text, these three terms—“insubstantial,” “coreless,” and “devoid of essence”—[are to be understood accordingly].
They say that [the term] should be applied individually in such phrases as "with constant essence" (*niccasāra*) and so forth. *Setavaccha* means the white *varuṇaka* tree;
some also call it the *minarukkha*. *Pālibhaddaka* is the *kiṃsuka* tree.

Because of the absence of constant essence and so forth, he sees it as empty (*rittato*). Because it is limited, or because it is inferior, he sees it as void (*tucchato*). Due to the absence of an essential self (*attasāra*),...

It is "empty" (*suññato*). It is "not-self" (*anattato*) because it is itself devoid of selfhood. It is "without mastery" (*anissariyato*) because of the absence of sovereignty and because it is impossible for anyone to exercise mastery over it.

It is "not subject to one's will" (*akāmakāriyato*) because, just as one who wishes to make a vessel or the like out of a lump of foam cannot achieve it, so too with regard to form; one cannot effect anything according to one's own desire.
Because it cannot be obtained by saying, "Let it be thus," or "Let it not be thus. Because it does not act under the control of another, nor does it bring another under its own control;
thus, it is due to the absence of mastery (*avasavattaka*). Because within its own continuity it is not subject to the influence of another, like another person;

thus, it is due to being other-dependent (*parata*). Because it is devoid of causes such as a creator and so forth, as well as being devoid of a fruit; for there is no fruit [produced] by a cause, nor [is there a cause produced] by a fruit.
Or the cause remains pregnant [with potential]. This same method applies to feeling (vedanā) and the other aggregates as well.
Regarding the passage beginning "Form is not a being" (rūpaṃ na satto), the meaning intended here is not that "whatever is called a 'being' by worldly convention, form is not that";

for such a point is already established by what has been said previously. Indeed, the world does not conventionally designate mere form as a "being," [but rather a being] as imagined by outsiders (bāhiraka).

But here, "self" (*atta*) is intended as "a being" (*satta*). For it is called a "being" because it is attached and bound to those [aggregates] such as form, in the sense of causing others to perceive it;
the meaning is that it is not form itself. "This is the grasping of emptiness"—this same method applies to the phrases "not a soul" (*na jīva*) and so forth.
In that context, it is a "soul" (*jīva*) in the sense of living; it is a "person" (*nara*) in the sense of leading, by way of being a leader. "I am"—[this is the conceit].
It is called *mānavo* because conceit (*māna*) moves or proceeds there, being the basis for its arising. It is called *itthī* because the womb is situated (*thiyati*) therein.
It is called *puriso* because he lies (*seti*) before (*puri*) others by virtue of his preeminence. It is called *attā* because the conceit "I" (*aham-māna*) is placed (*āhita*) therein.
Furthermore, because each individual is the objective basis for the conceit "I," it is called "self" (*attā*) as "I" by those who hold to views; however, material form (*rūpa*) is not such [a basis].
The passage beginning with “Form is not a being” was stated in order to show the method for grasping emptiness (*suññatā*).
Therefore, by all eight terms, the emptiness of form of a self (*attasuññatā*) is shown; by the other four, its lack of anything belonging to it (*kiñcanatābhāva*) is shown.
In that context, “not mine” means it is not my own possession, nor is it the possession of another self.

Nothing whatsoever belongs to oneself because of the very non-existence of a self. This same meaning, which is expressed by the phrase "not belonging to a self" (*na attaniya*), is also expressed by three other synonymous terms.
This method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates as well. 765.

By means of the method of comprehension (*sammasana-naya*) taught below for the purpose of strengthening the comprehension of the aggregates (*kalāpa-sammasana*), one also engages in the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatā-anupassanā*).
Showing that these lead to firmness of being, he said, "By way of full understanding through investigation," and so forth.
Therein, it is because of not harming fear that it is "without refuge" (*asaraṇa*). Because it is unfit to be grasped as a "refuge" (*saraṇa*), it has become "without refuge" (*asaraṇībhūta*).

The phrase "because of non-nourishment" (*anassādata*) does not appear in the Pāḷi; if it were included, there would be forty-three modes. This is because of the perception of all dangers within the manifestation of form.

“From the perspective of danger. Regarding the pair “from the perspective of origin and from the perspective of passing away,” this is stated because, just as the contemplation of impermanence serves as a conduit for the manifestation of emptiness by demonstrating the absence of a permanent core, so too do these two serve to manifest emptiness.
Likewise: “Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on form—this is the gratification in form.”
The vision that discerns emptiness by way of discerning the conditions and the conditioned nature [of phenomena] is as follows:
the vision that “whatever form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in form,” because it cultivates the emptiness of permanence and so forth.
Likewise, [the vision that] “the removal of desire and lust for form, the abandoning of desire and lust for form—this is the escape from form. Thus...

The cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*) should be understood as applying to the visions of the origin [of suffering] and so forth, as well as to the others, as appropriate.

Furthermore, although the vision of [suffering] as a disadvantage was mentioned previously, its mention again here should be understood as referring to the vision that rejects gratification (*assāda*).
The remainder is exactly according to the method explained below. [This applies] to the forty-two [factors] beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) as well.
"The modes are to be brought forward," he said: "He sees feeling... pe... consciousness as impermanent... pe... as an escape.

And this was stated in the *Niddesa* as a demonstration of the discourse on the grasping of emptiness; it is for the purpose of showing that "this is the commentary on such-and-such a text," and for the purpose of demonstrating its fruit.
(766) Thus, by way of the full understanding through investigation, emptiness is [seen] in each of the aggregates through forty-two modes.

Showing that for one who applies himself to meditation even after having grasped [the object] by means of the threefold contemplation alone, there arises the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*), he says:
"Thus, through emptiness," and so forth. Therein, "grasping" means comprehending. "Having abandoned both fear and delight" means:
due to the state of equanimity, having abandoned both the fear that arises based on the failure of formations and—

Having abandoned both the rapture (*pīti*) that arises dependent on those attainments, or alternatively, having abandoned both the fear that arises through the manifestation of terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*) and the delight (*nandi*) termed rapture that arises through the process of comprehension (*sammasana*).
For when emptiness (*suññatā*) is seen in its entirety, there is no occasion for either fear or delight; rather, there is only equanimity (*upekkhā*).
It settles. Therefore he said, "He remains indifferent toward volitional formations.
In that context, showing the absence of that wrong grasp by which indifference would not occur, he said, "He does not grasp at 'I' or 'mine'.
Now, showing a simile for his state of indifference, he said, "Like a man whose wife has been released," and so forth.

In this context, in order to show that the state of indifference preceded by non-indifference—which is being described—applies here to the purpose of the simile, the passage beginning with "desirable and lovely" was stated.
He would cherish her excessively because he does not understand the deceit, guile, crookedness, and so forth, of women.
"Being desirous of release" means being indeed desirous of release; he would let her go through his lack of regard for her.
The intention is "by means of that very [desire]"; this refers to the practitioner (yogāvacara).

He says, "grasping formations by means of the contemplation of reflection" (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā), because the insight (vipassanā) occurring until the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa) arises—due to the desire for deliverance—is indeed the contemplation of reflection.

“*Patilīyati*” means it hides away on one side; it becomes as if concealed. “*Paṭikuṭati*” means it shrinks back. “*Paṭivaṭṭati*” means it turns away. “*Na sampasāriyati*” means it does not spread out; the meaning is that it does not leap forward due to delight.
“*Iccassa*” means “thus for this” yogin. 767.
When equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) is being accomplished through the state of being sharp, clear, and resolute, that indeed is the knowledge of equanimity toward formations.
When Nibbāna, which has been occurring many times, reaches full maturity and becomes a condition for conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa), one is said to "see it as peace.
Having relinquished the entire occurrence of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) in such a state, one is said to "launch into" Nibbāna itself.
This knowledge here is identical with the knowledge of conformity and the knowledge of the lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa).

This has been stated by way of the principle of unity (*ekattanaya*). "If one does not see Nibbāna as peace" refers to the very immaturity of the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*).
"Crossing the ocean" means those who belong to the sea, namely, sailors. A crow that knows the directions is a "direction-crow";
this is merely a descriptive term for any such bird whatsoever. "A foreign land" (*videsam*) means a place without a [known] location, an unfamiliar region in the ocean.
"Having followed along" means having followed along step by step.
This is the knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). "Like kneading dough" refers to the fine flour-like dust being squeezed out by way of separating it from its coarsest parts.
"Cotton with the seeds removed" refers to cotton from which the seeds have been extracted. "Beating it" [refers to the process of cleaning].

It is like a bird being struck by a bowstring. By means of these two similes, he describes how, through repeated contemplation, the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa) reaches a state of extreme subtlety.

For just as insight becomes sharp, clear, and courageous through the power of its cultivation, so too does it become increasingly subtle. "In the discernment of formations" refers to the attainment of the pinnacle of investigative analysis (pavicaya).
Just as with the formations themselves, one remains indifferent even toward their investigation, standing by way of the threefold contemplation because there is no other mode [of contemplation].
For although the modes of contemplation are analyzed as "sevenfold, eighteenfold," and so forth, these modes of contemplation are included within the three—contemplation of impermanence and the rest;
thus, when insight has reached its culmination, it stands by way of those three alone.
768. *Tatra*: in that attainment of the state of the doors to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*), and in the sense of being a condition for the classification of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).

This is insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*). "Of the three faculties" means of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).

"By way of predominance" means by way of their being the dominant factors over the associated states (*sampayuttadhamma*). For one who is frequently practicing the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*)...

For when the faculty of faith is strong, the faculty of concentration belongs to one who frequently contemplates suffering, and the faculty of wisdom belongs to one who frequently contemplates non-self;

thus, these three faculties, having attained a state of greater strength by way of these three contemplations, bring about the state of being doors to liberation. Therefore it is said: "The threefold contemplation... he comes to attain."

Regarding the phrase "the state of being the threefold door to liberation": here, in response to the implicit inquiry as to what the three liberations are or what the three doors to liberation are—since the attainment of liberation is dependent upon the doors to liberation—he first shows the doors to liberation by saying, "For there are three...
they are so called. Then, showing that this meaning is understood from the canonical text itself, he says, "As it has been said," and so forth.

"For the sake of going forth from the world" (*lokaniyyānāya*) means for the purpose of emerging from the world, or for the purpose of the world of beings (*sattaloka*) emerging from the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*).
"By way of delimitation and circumscription" (*paricchedaparivaṭumato*) means by way of both delimitation and circumscription through [observing] arising and passing away.

The connection is: "they conduce to the state of contemplation" (*samanupassanatāya*), that is, to right and successive seeing. For the contemplation of impermanence [contemplates] conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
He sees them as delimited by their arising at the beginning and their passing away at the end; for it is because they possess a beginning and an end that they are impermanent.
And "in the signless element" means in the unconditioned element which has acquired the name "signless" due to its being devoid of all signs of conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
"By the mind's leaping forward" means by way of the state of conformity knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) and so forth, having correctly delimited [the formations].

For the purpose of entering into higher consciousness (*adhicitta*). "As the wishless" (*appaṇihita*) means having acquired the name "wishless" due to the absence of longing for sensual passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
"As the void" (*suññatā*) means having acquired the name "void" due to being void of a self (*atta*).
"Destination" (*gati*) means rebirth. The mind, being stirred by the discernment of the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), [is established] in right practice.

Regarding the phrase "it is called 'encouraged' (*samuttejitaṃ*)," he said: "By means of mental encouragement (*manosamuttejanatāya*), that is, by means of causing agitation in the mind (*cittasaṃvejanatāya*).
First, the self, which is the owner of the object perceived as "mine" through the notion of "I-am-ness," is grasped; thereafter, it is [grasped] as "belonging to the self. Thus he said:
"By means of contemplating as non-self (*anattato*) in this way: 'not I, not mine. "Three phrases" refers to the delimitation and enclosure.

They say that "the incitement of the mind" refers to the phrases for contemplation; however, it should be understood that the three statements beginning with "all conditioned phenomena" constitute the three terms.
"Precisely because of that" means precisely because those three terms have been stated by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.
Regarding the answer to the question: "When one attends to things as impermanent, how do conditioned phenomena appear?"
In the answering of the question:
Having thus shown the doors to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*), the passage beginning with “But which ones? is now stated in order to show the liberations (*vimokkha*).
“Attending to [them] as impermanent” means practicing the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*). “Abounding in resolve” means abounding in the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
For one whose contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) is particularly sharp and keen, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) becomes predominant. For,
having initially set out by means of mere faith with the thought, "Conditioned phenomena are impermanent," when insight has reached its peak,
one perceives their impermanence directly and with extreme clarity even in jewels, gold, and so forth, just as one does in young shoots and the like.
“Indeed, that Blessed One is a perfectly enlightened Buddha”—thus strong faith in the Teacher arises;

therefore, he is one who abounds in resolve (*adhimokkha*) and possesses supreme faith (*adhimatta-saddha*). Because of his abundance in the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), there is an emergence from the aspect of impermanence;
thus it is said: “He attains the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*)”. “Abounding in tranquility” (*passaddhi-bahula*) refers to the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*).
By applying himself with the mental attention, "Formations are suffering;

cessation is blissful as their opposite," and by resolving upon the peaceful and sublime blissful nature of Nibbāna, he becomes abundant in tranquility due to his frequent association with rapture and gladness.
Then, through the attainment of the faculty of supreme concentration and the distancing of longing for sensual passion, there comes the realization of the signless liberation (appanihita-vimokkha).
It is said: "He acquires [the perception] as suffering... [and so on]... he acquires it.

One who is "abundant in wisdom" (vedabahula) is one who, by devoting himself to the contemplation of non-self, becomes abundant in knowledge because the emptiness of self is the domain of subtle knowledge.

And because delusion is distanced through the acquisition of the preeminent faculty of wisdom, there is the attainment of the liberation of emptiness; thus it is said: "He acquires [the perception] as non-self... [and so on]... he acquires it."

One who, having discerned formations by way of their sign through the contemplation of impermanence and is devoted to insight, resolves upon that which is entirely devoid of this sign of formations as "the signless Nibbāna" by way of the signless aspect;
he then joins it with the path leading to emergence. It is said that for him, the path realizes Nibbāna as signless.
He said: "The Noble Path proceeds having made Nibbāna its object by way of the signless aspect (animittākāra).
This signless aspect of Nibbāna was neither produced by the Path nor by insight; rather, it is established by its own intrinsic nature (sabhāvasiddha).
And showing that the Path is called "signless" because it has that as its object, he said: "It is signless because it has arisen in relation to the signless element (animittāya dhātuyā)."
One should apply the same logic as follows: "He who, by means of contemplation of suffering, becomes detached from aspiration and thus resolves upon the wishless;
he who, by means of contemplation of non-self, becomes detached from the apprehension of a self and thus resolves upon emptiness," and so forth.
Therefore, he said, "In this very manner," etc.
770. If the Noble Path receives all three names of "liberation," then why is only a pair of liberations mentioned in the Abhidhamma?
Addressing this objection, he says, "But as for that... and so forth. Therein, "that" refers to the statement regarding the pair of liberations in the Abhidhamma.
"With reference to the arrival at insight in its direct sense" means the arrival of the name of the Path from insight in a straightforward manner.
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). Why? Because insight into the signless (*animittavipassanā*), while standing at the stage of arrival, is unable to give its own name to the path.
Granted that in the Sutta it is said, "Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit," thus describing insight into the signless;
nevertheless, although that [insight] removes the signs of permanence, the signs of stability, and the signs of self, it itself [remains] among the phenomena that possess signs (*nimittadhammesu*).

"One who practices in this way possesses signs" means that he still has objective signs. Furthermore, the Abhidhamma is the teaching on ultimate reality (*paramattha*), and for the signless path (*animitta-magga*), there is an actual deficiency of causes from the perspective of ultimate reality.
For the signless liberation (*animitta-vimokkha*) is explained by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
In that state, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is predominant, yet it does not constitute even a single factor of the noble path (*ariyamagga*), because it is not a factor of the path.

It is unable to give a name to its own path. Among the others, the wishless liberation (*appaṇihita-vimokkha*) occurs by way of the contemplation of suffering, and the emptiness liberation (*suññata-vimokkha*) occurs by way of the contemplation of non-self.
Among these, the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*) is predominant in the wishless liberation, and the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*) is predominant in the emptiness liberation.

Some say that because they are factors (*aṅga*) of the Noble Path, they are able to give their own names to the path; however, the signless path (*animittamagga*) cannot do so because it lacks those factors.

But according to those who maintain that "the signless path, although not receiving its name from its approach (*āgamanato*), does receive its name from its qualities (*saguṇato*) and its object (*ārammaṇato*)," then by their view, the wishless and emptiness paths would also [receive their names] from their qualities.
...and that they should receive their names solely from their objects? That is incorrect. Why? Because a path receives its name for two reasons:
from its own essence (*sarasato*) and from its opposite (*paccanīkato*). This means: from its intrinsic nature and from its counteragent.
For the desireless path is free from the longing of lust and so forth, and the emptiness path is empty of lust and so forth; thus [they are named].

They receive their names from their own intrinsic nature (*sarasato*). Likewise, the desireless path (*appaṇihita-magga*) is the opposite of desire (*paṇidhi*), and the emptiness path (*suññata-magga*) is the opposite of the adherence to a self (*attābhinivesa*); thus, they receive their names from being the opposites (*paccanīkato*).

However, the signless path (*animitta-magga*) receives its name solely from its own intrinsic nature due to the absence of signs such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth, or of signs such as permanence (*nicca-nimitta*) and so on; it does not receive its name from being the opposite. For it is not [the case that] it...

The path of the signless (animitta-magga) is not found in any way according to the Abhidhamma method, because it is the antidote to the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) which has the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) as its object, and yet that [contemplation] remains in a state of conformity (anuloma) to it. Therefore it was said:
“That refers to the approach to insight (vipassanā-gamana) in the non-figurative sense (nippariyāyato).”
Because, according to the method of the Suttas, the signless path is obtained.
For insight leading to emergence, as it emerges by comprehending whatever [object] it is contemplating, gives its own path a name by standing in the place from which it has come;
therein, for one emerging from the perspective of impermanence, the path is signless (*animitta*); from the perspective of suffering...
For one emerging [from the attainment], it is the wishless; for one emerging by way of non-self, it is the void.
Therefore, considering that this is a commentary on the Suttanta, all three liberations have been extracted here.

However, in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the state of the three contemplations—and by extension, of the path that follows them—as being the void liberation and so forth, is based on their release from misapprehension, signs, and wishes.
To show that there is nothing further to be said regarding its status as a synonym, it is stated: "Vipassanā-ñāṇaṃ hi... and so forth.

The connection is that although *vipassanā-ñāṇa* is described in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* as "the wishless liberation" (*appaṇihito vimokkho*), [it is here identified with the knowledge of impermanence].
"Knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence" (*aniccānupassanā-ñāṇa*) is the knowledge that arises by way of contemplating, "Formations are impermanent. From [the perspective of] permanence...
"It relinquishes adherence" means by way of destroying the false adherence that occurs through the aspect of permanence, thinking "those [things] are permanent";
however, the path-knowledge that follows it relinquishes it by way of total eradication. "Thus" (iti) means therefore.
The void liberation is so called because of its emptiness and its state of being liberated from the adherence to permanence. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

That is the threefold knowledge of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*). In this context, in order to show that for which there is the acquisition of a name both figuratively (*pariyāyato*) and non-figuratively (*nippariyāyato*), it is said:
"of the sign of formations" (*saṅkhāra-nimittassa*), and so forth. The meaning is: not non-figuratively, but rather figuratively.
"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because of the absence of non-figurative discourse. The intention is that only the two liberations (*vimokkha*) are mentioned in the Abhidhamma.
"In this" means in this section on insight (*vipassanā*), or in this statement of the summary: "having attained the state of being the three doors to liberation.

"For the purpose of their classification" means for the purpose of classifying those seven noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) already mentioned according to their specific natures as followers by faith (*saddhānusārī*) and so forth.
"He acquires the faculty of faith" means he acquires the preeminent faculty of faith which serves as the cause for the state of being a follower by faith.
He attains it. The reason for this—namely, the abundance of resolve (*adhimokkha*) and the preponderance of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*)—has already been stated above.

Furthermore, this is the summary of the meaning here: because the observation of the aspect of impermanence (*aniccākāra*) serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the increase of faith, faith becomes sharper on the path that follows it; therefore, the person at the eighth stage is called a "faith-follower" (*saddhānusārī*). As for the others...
"In seven places" means in seven locations starting from the first fruit up to the highest fruit (*aggaphala*). Why was it said "in seven places"?

Is it not the case that in the remaining six places one is "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*), while in the highest fruit, if one is an attainer of formless jhāna, one is "liberated both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), and if one is not an attainer of formless jhāna, one is "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*)?
He is not one liberated by faith. For in the Abhidhamma it is said:
"And what kind of person is one liberated by faith? Here, a certain person understands as it really is:
'This is suffering,' 'this is the origin of suffering,' 'this is the cessation of suffering,' 'this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.'"
He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata have been seen by him through wisdom;
having seen them through wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed, though not to the extent of one who has attained through vision.
This person is called one liberated by faith.”

From the statement regarding the destruction of certain taints (*āsava*), it is understood that one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) is still a trainee (*sekha*), not one beyond training (*asekha*).
And since the Commentary states, "There are two burdens, two fixations, and two heads," does this mean there is no such thing as one liberated by faith who is an arahant?
This is true from the standpoint of the direct method (*nippariyāya*). For the Abhidhamma is discourse according to the direct method, whereas here [in the Suttas]...

However, this was stated by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*). If it is by way of a figurative method that an *arahant* is "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*), what then is that figurative method?

It is the state of being a follower of one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimuttānvayatā*). For he who is liberated by faith at the moment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*) is likewise called "liberated by faith" at the moment of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) due to being a follower of that [state];
thus it is stated figuratively in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, and here too it is exactly the same.
It has been said. Alternatively, the Arahant is called "liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutta) because of his similarity to one liberated by faith.

What is the similarity here? Just as for the trainee (sekkha) liberated by faith, the destruction of the defilements is like cutting a plantain tree with a blunt sword—as stated in the words, "but not as it is for one who has attained through vision"—so too is it for the Arahant who follows after him. This is the similarity in this context.

There is equality. But is there any difference between them regarding the abandonment of the defilements? No. Then why does the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) not reach the level of the one who has attained through vision (diṭṭhippatta)? It is due to the difference in their progress.
For the one who has attained through vision is able to suppress the defilements during his progress with ease and without fatigue, whereas the one liberated by faith does so with difficulty.
One is able to suppress them with difficulty. Moreover, there is a difference among them in terms of wisdom (*paññā*) as well;

and they say that this [wisdom] is indeed obtainable to whatever extent it may be found. And by taking it thus, even the statement regarding the sharpness of faith (*saddhā*) and the other faculties, despite their equality in the first path and so forth, becomes justified.
773. "He" refers to one who has emerged from suffering. "In all places" means in all eight locations. But is it not stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*)...?

Because it is restricted by the statement "there are two types of those who bear the burden," could one at the moment of the first path be either a *saddhānusārī* (follower by faith) or a *dhammānusārī* (follower by Dhamma)?
Here, being a *saddhānusārī* is not applicable; furthermore, even the state of a *kāyasakkhī* (body-witness) does not exist for an *arahant*.

For in the Abhidhamma it is said: "And what kind of person is a *kāyasakkhī*? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight liberations with the body, and having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are completely destroyed. This is called a person who is a *kāyasakkhī*."

Is it not the case that from the statement regarding the destruction of certain taints (*āsava*), only the state of being a trainee (*sekha*) who is a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhin*) is understood? This is true from an absolute standpoint (*nippariyāyato*);
however, here it is stated by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyena*). What, then, is that method? It is the similarity to a body-witness.

For, having obtained a contact with formless concentration (*arūpasamādhi*) that is far superior to the access-concentration and the fine-material-sphere jhāna-concentration, one is born [in the formless realm]; thus, based on the destruction of certain taints, [the designation "body-witness" is applied].

Regarding the term "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*): when applied to a person who possesses an especially distinguished contact with concentration and its basis—the commonality of which is the destruction of the taints (*āsava*)—the Arahant is called a "body-witness" just like [others] who are body-witnesses. This is stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, and here too, by adopting that very method, the state of being a body-witness is attributed even to the Arahant.
For this is an exegesis of the Suttas; it is not according to the direct, literal method (*nippariyāyena*).
However, from the first fruit onwards, one is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī) in six respects;

yet this refers specifically to one who has attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti), not to a dry-insight practitioner (sukkha-vipassaka) who follows the path of insight (vipassanā-yānika), nor to one who has merely attained access concentration (upacāra-matta), or merely the fine-material jhānas (rūpa-jhāna).

Furthermore, since "abounding in tranquility" (passaddhi-bahula) refers to concentration by way of its primary aspect of tranquility, it is intended here as referring specifically to one who follows the path of serenity (samatha-yānika) and has attained preeminent concentration.
And it was stated above that the status of being a "body-witness" belongs only to one whose vehicle is serenity (*samatha*). Regarding "formless jhāna": there are four kinds of formless jhāna.

However, in this context, the term "formless jhāna" alone is used—not "the four formless jhānas"—in order to show that even if one has attained only a single one of them, having reached Arahantship, one is indeed "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Therefore, this [refers] to the four...
It is fivefold by way of the formless attainments and the attainment of cessation. This same method applies to the body-witness as well.
One who is liberated in both ways is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*) because he is liberated twice by means of two portions.
For one possessed of wisdom, subtle and profound meanings appear clearly and manifest; thus, they are seen as non-self.

For one who attends to the mind, an abundance of wisdom and the acquisition of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) are stated. One becomes a follower of the Dhamma (dhammānusārī) because of the predominance of the faculty of wisdom.
For here, "wisdom" is intended by the term "Dhamma," as in such passages as "truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity.

To show the scriptural passage (pāḷi) by virtue of which the state of being a person of noble lineage (ariyapuggala) such as the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) and so forth is described here, the passage beginning with "For it is said" is commenced; that is indeed easy to understand.
776. Another statement has also been given to establish the meaning of such terms as "one liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*) due to the predominance of the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
By the phrase "liberated while having faith," it demonstrates that one who is not liberated in every respect is designated as "liberated by faith" merely through faith;
thus, it clarifies that the one liberated by faith is indeed a trainee (*sekkha*). Alternatively, "one liberated by faith" means one who is intent upon faith.
"Realized at the limit of what is touched" (*phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikato*) means: immediately after what is touched (*phuṭṭhānaṃ anantaraṃ phuṭṭhanto*);
the intended meaning is "the time immediately following the immaterial jhānas. This is the accusative case used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoge*).

What is meant is that he realized, by means of the method of realization, that which is to be realized precisely at the time immediately following what is touched. Alternatively, this is a neuter abstract noun (*bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ*).

As in the phrase "to one side. For one who is liberated from the material body by means of formless jhāna, and from a portion of the mental body by means of suppression-liberation (vikkhambhana-vimokkha), liberation—which is termed cessation—becomes as if observed and manifested by him;
yet it is not personally realized by the body. However, when certain taints have been exhausted by taking cessation as an object, he has indeed realized it.
Therefore, because he has realized with the mental body (*nāmakāya*) that which was to be realized exactly as it was observed, he is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasakkhī*);
yet he is not yet "liberated" because some of his taints (*āsava*) have not been fully exhausted.

"One who has reached the goal" means that he has attained immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimaggañāṇa*), which is designated as "seeing. For [this applies] from the first fruit onwards until—
“Attained to vision through the highest path. Alternatively, the reading is *diṭṭhiyā patto*;
the meaning is that he has attained cessation by means of the vision consisting in the seeing of the Four Truths.

And since these three—those liberated through faith and so forth—have not yet completed the function of knowledge in the ultimate sense, the statement beginning with “one who believes is liberated” was spoken in order to show that method. “Jhāna-contact” means preeminent jhāna-contact.
By that, the contact of the formless jhāna is included.
By the statement, “It is known that formations are suffering,” he speaks of the penetration of the truth of suffering;
by the statement, “Cessation is blissful,” he speaks of the penetration of the truth of cessation. And by both of these, the penetration of the truths of origin and the path is implied.
Not because of the state of being an immediate (ānantariya) result. By the phrase "it is known" (ñātaṃ hoti), the function of the second path is indicated;

by "it is seen" (diṭṭhaṃ hoti), the function of the third path; by "it is understood" (viditaṃ hoti), the function of the fourth path; by "it is realized" (sacchikataṃ), the function of the first fruit;
and by "it is touched" (phusitaṃ), the function of the remaining two fruits. Thus, for one who has attained through vision (diṭṭhippatto):
They say these words show the activity of the knowledge of the path and its fruition (maggaphalañāṇa).
"In the others" refers to the terms such as *saddhānusārī* (faith-follower) and so forth. "He follows faith" means he follows the faith established in the stage of arrival;
just as that [faith] was sharp and resolute, he exercises it in a corresponding manner even at the moment of the path.

The meaning [of *saddhānusārī*] is as follows: "He follows by means of faith" (*saddhāya vā anusarati*) means that, with faith acting as the cause, he remembers, proceeds, and practices in a manner corresponding to the penetration of the Truths; this is the meaning. By both interpretations of the term, he clarifies precisely the preeminence of faith.
The same method applies here for the term *dhammānusārī*. Regarding the term *ubhatobhāgavimutto*: by two parts...
"Released in both ways" means released from both the material body (*rūpakāya*) and the mental body (*nāmakāya*), by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and by way of eradication (*samuccheda*).
One is released from the material body and a portion of the mental body through formless jhāna, while one is released from the mental body through the Noble Path;
because of being released in both ways from both sides, one is "released in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Knowing...

"Released" (*vimutta*): one who, through the contact of the first jhāna, knows and penetrates the Four Noble Truths by way of full understanding and so forth, is "released" in the sense of being specifically liberated because his task is finished due to having reached the culmination of those duties.
This, however, is the concise explanation according to the direct method: he for whom there is an emergence from the aspect of impermanence...
One who abounds in resolve (adhimokkha) becomes a "follower by faith" (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the first path due to the sharpness of the faculty of faith;
in the middle six stages, he is "liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutta); and at the moment of the highest fruit, he is "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta).
Likewise, for one whose emergence occurs from the aspect of suffering (dukkhākāra), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) [predominates] due to an abundance of tranquility (passaddhi).

It becomes excessive due to the intensity of even his faith because it is accompanied by suffering, and because it is a primary obligation. At the moment of the first path, he is a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*);
in the middle, during the six stages, he is one liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*); and at the end, he is one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*).
However, for one whose emergence occurs from the aspect of non-self (*anattākāra*), he is abundant in knowledge (*vedabahula*) due to the sharpness of the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*).
At the moment of the first path, one is a follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī); in the middle, during the six stages, one is one who has attained vision (diṭṭhippatto);
and at the end, one is liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutto). However, these [three types] do not possess the eight liberations;

whereas one who possesses the eight liberations may, at the moment of the first path, be either a follower by faith (saddhānusārī) or a follower by Dhamma. In the middle, during the six stages, such a person is a body-witness (kāyasakkhī).
"At the conclusion, one is 'liberated in both ways'":
this is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*).
(778) That which, having entered the state of being an entrance to liberation, is also a condition for the classification of the seven noble persons (*ariyapuggala*).

It is said that "it occurs," and this refers to the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*). By the phrase "by the two previous knowledges," the intended meaning is that they are one in substance—namely, the two knowledges of desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*) and contemplation of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*)—but different in their modes of manifestation.

To establish the aforementioned point through both the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) and the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the passage beginning with "Therefore it was said" was stated. This also includes the knowledges of desire for deliverance and the application of the means for deliverance.
Because it proceeds with a state of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhāra*), they receive the designation "equanimity regarding formations" (*saṅkhārupekkhā*); thus it is said:
"This knowledge of equanimity regarding formations receives three names for one and the same thing.
By this, he shows that the conventional term *saṅkhārupekkhā* refers to the entire collection of knowledges beginning with the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*).
780. "Arising and so forth" refers to the formations spoken of by way of such designations as arising and occurrence.
"The desire to relinquish" is the desire to let go through the abandoning of the will and lust that obstruct that relinquishing. "Reflecting" is repeated investigation.

"Having released" means having let go by way of relinquishing concern through the attainment of a state free from attachment. "At the end" means after the time of acting in that manner, until the leaping forward into Nibbāna.
It does not succeed; therefore, even while investigating, with reference to the continuity of knowledge proceeding in a state of equanimity, he says:
"Equanimity is the settling. "In this way" means by way of the commonality of the mode of equanimity, in the manner described as: "the desire for deliverance and that settling."

781. "These states" (*ime dhammā*) means these states known as knowledge; here the word *dhamma* is used in the sense of knowledge, and thus the meaning is "these knowledges. "Unity" (*ekatta*) means having a single nature. 782.

It "leads to emergence" because it goes toward emergence. "Of the triad of knowledges beginning with equanimity towards formations" refers to the triad of knowledges termed equanimity towards formations, conformity, and change-of-lineage.
It is said [to be supramundane] because it stands above mundane knowledges both by way of its function and by way of its position.
"Because it has reached the state of being supreme. "From that which serves as the sign" means from the pentad of aggregates that have become the object of insight (vipassanā).
Therefore he said, "from the basis of adherence. For that is called the "basis of adherence" by way of the adherence known as making [the aggregates] the domain of insight.
And although this [basis] is included within one's own continuity (sasantatipariyāpanna), because of the view held toward what is other...
"External" (bahiddhā) has been stated. For that very same thing is referred to in various places as "all external signs" (sabba-nimittāni).

"From the occurrence within oneself" means from the occurrence of wrong view and so forth within one's own continuum (sasantāne), and from the aggregates of defilements (kilesa-khandha) that follow upon it.

This is because [the latter] consists in the occurrence of defilements within one's own continuity, and because [the former] consists in the occurrence of the appropriated aggregates (upādinnakkhandha) that arise when there is no cultivation of the Path (maggabhāvanā) to serve as their antidote.
And it has been stated thus. Their emergence consists in both making [the object] the mental object and bringing about the state of non-arising in the future.
It is "struck" because the Path arises immediately after itself.
783. Therein: in that concise statement, "from the basis on which one is fixed and from the emergence therefrom. Internal and external.
This summary of the matrix is presented by way of the three characteristics of the aggregates of form and the formless.
"Having become intent upon the internal" means having established insight (*vipassanā*) regarding the aggregates included within one's own continuity.

The statement "he emerges from the internal" is said figuratively because the path leading to emergence takes internal phenomena as its object; however, in the non-figurative sense, it is the Path itself.
One emerges from everything. The same method applies to such phrases as "one emerges externally," and so forth. "All at once" means simultaneously;

however, that should be understood as occurring through the process of the path leading to emergence, without making internal and other such divisions, but rather by way of the undifferentiated [contemplation]: "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
This was taught according to the instruction received directly from the Teacher.
They say that for one who directs knowledge, the arising of supreme knowledge occurs. 784.

The emergence from the path does not occur by the mere seeing of the pure internal [mind] alone, because even the objects of the "mine-making" (mamaṃkāra) must be fully understood; thus, there is an emergence reckoned as the path, or an emergence by means of the path, which is "emergence from the path.

785. "Having made into a heap" means that although it is twofold by way of the primary elements and derived matter, and manifold by way of its internal subdivisions, it is [designated as such] in the sense of being subject to deformation (ruppana).

"Form" is taken as a whole. Just as there is generally an adherence to insight regarding form for one whose vehicle is insight (vipassanā-yānika), so too there is generally an adherence to insight regarding the formless for one whose vehicle is serenity (samatha-yānika).
"Adherence" should be understood here as the discernment of mind-and-body (nāma-rūpa-pariccheda) to be performed prior to insight. Therefore, first comes the grasping of form.
Adherence to form. This same method applies to the remaining [aggregates] as well.

(786) Although it has been shown that adherence consists in grasping at arising and passing away—namely, "whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation"—nevertheless, having grasped the phenomena of form and the formless as they actually appear, and their conditions...

Briefly stated, one who possesses supreme knowledge, while practicing insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*), penetrates the Truths very quickly through the sequence of knowledges even while remaining seated;
thus, it is said that he "emerges" from the five aggregates all at once.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for the comprehension and full understanding of the five aggregates to occur within a single mundane state of consciousness. For [a single mind] cannot [simultaneously perceive] that which is visible and resistant, and so forth.
It is possible to make them a single object. However, they say that this was stated with reference to those for whom what has once been touched by knowledge must necessarily be touched again. 788.
And here, insistence is not the cause; rather, emergence itself is the criterion. Therefore, the classification of the liberations and noble persons mentioned below [also applies].
The passage beginning with “And here, whoever... has been commenced in order to show that [the distinction] arises by way of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*).

In that context, the statement “these three persons” is said by taking a distinction obtained merely through dogmatic adherence (*abhinivesa*), even though no such distinction exists by way of emergence.

(789) “Together with the preceding and succeeding knowledges” means together with the preceding knowledges such as the appearance as terror (*bhayatupaṭṭhāna*) and so forth, and together with the succeeding knowledges such as the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) and so forth. “Summary” (*uddāna*) means a table of contents (*uddesa*).
"Anywhere... [etc. ...is said because a suitable object for comparison can be found for each respective stage of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
"In this place," however, means in this context of insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*).
"All" means all knowledge, or rather, the entire function of knowledge becomes manifest because it is being analyzed while standing in the middle. This has been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
790. *Nilīyitvā* means having sat down. *Parāmasitvā* means having investigated.
*Adisvā gayhūpagaṃ* means not seeing anything fit to be grasped, such as a permanent core or essence.

Through the thorough suppression of deceit (*māyā*) and other factors that cause crookedness of mind, the state of conformity (*anuloma*) is like a straight branch. This is because the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) has nibbāna as its object.
It is like looking upwards. Because it is established in the supportless Nibbāna, the knowledge of the path (maggañāṇa) is like leaping into the sky. 791.
The knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhuñāṇa) is like the expulsion of a snake, because it casts off the entire realm of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) and takes Nibbāna as its object.
The knowledge of the path is like the position of one looking back at the road traveled, by way of penetration through non-delusion.
Because of seeing even oneself. "Standing in a place of fearlessness" refers to having reached the state of fearlessness, not the practice for attaining it.
(792) Because one does not comprehend one's own welfare and so forth, the grasping at "I" and "mine" is like falling asleep.

By the mention of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatā*), both reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhā*) and composure (*santiṭṭhanā*) are also included. These three [factors] are [the means of escape] from saṃsāra.
Because it is intent upon departure, the state of conformity (anuloma) is like the searching for the path of departure.

Just as the practice of the path is undertaken once the path has been seen, so too, when conformity is established, the path is considered established; thus, conformity is similar to the seeing of the path.

Because it has departed from the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta), the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa) is like departing from a burning house. The knowledge of the path (magga-ñāṇa) is like traveling with speed.
Because of the connection with specific functions of proof regarding points that are to be rejected or accepted;
and because of the fact that they are not to be cherished by others, the grasping of the aggregates as "I" and "mine" is said to be like a king’s grasping of his own oxen.
Because it is the cause for seeing safety where there is danger, the grasping of the aggregates as "I" and "mine" is [like] that of a female *yakkha*.
Similarity in co-residence: Just as one leaves a cemetery, so too, having left the cemetery of formations, the change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) consciousness occurs by taking Nibbāna as its object.

795. "Lusting after her son" means being fond of her son. "Being afraid" means being filled with trepidation. Because it abandons formations by suppressing the coarse aggregates of greed and so forth, the conformity (anuloma) consciousness has a similarity to planting a sapling right there. 796. [The states] leading to emergence...
are mentioned for the purpose of showing [the path], not for the purpose of [showing] the appearance of terror and so forth as in the preceding [stages].
The intention is that this is for the purpose of showing the manner of fear and so forth for one who stands [in the world].

Because it arises again and again, because it persists for a long time, and because it is difficult to endure, the suffering of hunger is similar to the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha); thus he said, "the hunger of the cycle of saṃsāra.
Mindfulness directed to the body itself is the food of mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsatibhojana). Furthermore, in this context, it is right mindfulness associated with the Path.

Because it accomplishes the tasks such as the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) and because it is the enjoyment of the taste of the Deathless (amatarasa), it is called "the food of mindfulness directed to the body, which has the taste of the Deathless.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, those who enjoy mindfulness directed to the body enjoy the Deathless," and so forth.
It consists of many constituent parts, such as the fruits of the *phala*, *rasa*, *āmalaka*, *siṅgīvera*, and *mugga* beans.

The moisture of craving (*taṇhāsineha*) is like cold because it produces a state of wretchedness, servitude, and so forth. "The fire of the path" refers to the forest fire known as the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Nibbāna is "the allaying of the eleven fires," because therein the eleven fires, beginning with the fire of lust (*rāgaggi*), are extinguished.

"Overcome by darkness" means being overwhelmed by a darkness endowed with four factors, such that one is rendered incapable of accomplishing any purpose for oneself or for others. "Consisting of the light of knowledge" (*ñāṇālokā*) refers to the cultivation of the path, for this [cultivation] possesses the light of knowledge.

The "deathless medicine" (*amatosadha*) is the medicine that is itself deathless, or that accomplishes the state of being deathless; it is Nibbāna. By way of conclusion, he says "Therefore it was said," etc., showing the very function of equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) that he himself had previously described.
One who "lives withdrawn" (*patilīnacara*) is so called because, through the absence of a home, his disposition does not spread out toward existence and so forth by way of craving;
rather, with a mind thus contracted, he moves and proceeds in a state of withdrawal. [This refers to] the fear within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

For a monk who possesses integrity (*ikkhanatā*) and who frequents secluded lodgings due to the accomplishment of physical and mental seclusion (*kāyacittaviveka*), it is fitting—that is to say, appropriate—for that non-appearance [of defilements] to be his "conformity" (*sāmaggi*).
"In existence" (*bhavane*) refers to the threefold existence, beginning with the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*);
for here, it is called "existence" in the sense of "becoming. "He would not show" means he would not manifest them by way of their non-arising. That non-appearance of theirs is his conformity.
The construction is: "the Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddhas, have said.
"Having determined" means having made it certain and one-sided. The word "distinction" (*visesa*) should be applied to each [term]:

the distinction of the enlightenment factors, the distinction of the path factors, the distinction of the jhāna factors, the distinction of the modes of practice, and the distinction of the liberations. "Distinction" refers to the state of being sixfold or sevenfold.

The states of "seven" and "eight," and the state of "five" and so forth—this refers, respectively, to the divisions found in the Noble Path among the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and the rest.
"Foundational jhāna" (pādakajjhāna) means the jhāna that serves as the proximate basis for insight (vipassanā) leading to emergence, which is close to the Path.
"Being the object of insight" means being the objective domain of the very same insight leading to emergence that is proximate to the Path.
"Vipassitā" means one who possesses insight. "Puggalajjhāsayo" (the inclination of the person) refers to the inclination of the one possessing insight when there is a distinction between the two.
Here, the first "some say" refers to the Elder Cūḷanāga of the Tipiṭaka; the second "some say" refers to the Elder Mahādatta, resident of Moravāpi;
and the third "some say" refers to the Elder Cūḷābhaya of the Tipiṭaka.
It should be understood that even in their doctrines, this insight leading to emergence in the prior stage is likewise determined. Why?
Because by the very determination of insight, even in the first Elder’s doctrine, paths based on the first jhāna without a basis (apādaka) are themselves of the first jhāna;
and other paths, such as those of the second jhāna and so forth, are of their respective jhānas due to the determinations of the basis-jhāna and the insight.
This is because, for the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) arising from each respective second and subsequent supporting jhānas,

there is an absence of the desire not to attain the factors that transcend the supporting jhāna due to the cultivation of dispassion (*virāga-bhāvanā*), whereas for the other [knowledge], such a state does not exist.

For just as when insight proximate to the path is accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), the path is characterized by the first jhāna and so forth, and when it is accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), [the path is characterized by the higher jhānas].
Furthermore, it possesses the state of being a fifth-jhāna attainment, and from that comes the distinction of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) and so forth;
thus, the proximate cause for their determination is insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*), and not the foundational jhānas and so on.
For without the foundational jhāna, insight alone is unable to determine this aforementioned distinction; however, by the method already stated, the primary cause is insight.
It indeed exists; therefore, instead of saying "it is only insight leading to emergence that determines [the fruit]," it is said, "insight leading to emergence certainly determines it.
In the same way, the determination by insight should be applied to the remaining statements as far as possible.

For just as there is insight leading to emergence—which consists in the cultivation of dispassion and the lack of desire to attain the factors that transcend the foundational jhāna—so too [should it be understood].
The path’s factors, such as the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), become determinative of its specific qualities through the distinction imparted by the foundational jhāna serving as a basis;

likewise, the path becomes determinative of its specific qualities through the distinction imparted by the jhāna of comprehension, which consists in the cultivation of dispassion in the form of revulsion toward the factors that have transcended the jhāna used as the object of comprehension;
