and when both are present, it becomes determinative of its specific qualities through whichever one is emphasized according to the practitioner's inclination.
And insight leading to emergence determines the specific qualities of the path, such as the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and so forth.

798. In that context—namely, in the determination of those specific qualities such as the factors of enlightenment—the "dry-insight practitioner" (sukkha-vipassaka) is one who has not attained jhāna and is solely a follower of pure insight.
For he is called a "dry" or "rough" insight practitioner because his insight is not moistened by the moisture of jhāna.

“Of this one” refers to one who is called a “dry-insight practitioner” (*sukkha-vipassaka*). “Miscellaneous formations” (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra*) refers to formations other than those of the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna*).
By this, he shows that there is nothing at all to be said once the formations of the foundational jhāna have been comprehended;

for it has been stated: “having made the first jhāna the foundation. And here, the mention of the dry-insight practitioner and so forth is for the purpose of establishing the necessity of insight (*vipassanā-niyama*).

This is for the purpose of showing its absolute nature. For it is not observed that the basic jhānas and so forth, taken alone, are the causes of such a restriction without the path leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*).

However, the path leading to emergence is the cause for the state of having the first jhāna as its constituent even in the absence of the basic jhānas and so forth, as in the case of those who practice bare insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
Therefore, it is the absolute cause for the specific restriction of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) and so on. Now...
In order to make the meaning already stated even more clear, the passage beginning with "Of these" was spoken.

This distinction means that this distinction of the jhānas and so forth—such as having four factors and so on—is not, as before, restricted solely by insight (*vipassanā*), but rather by both the restriction of the foundational jhāna (*pādaka-jjhāna*) and the restriction of insight.
"Of these too" refers to the second, third, and fourth jhānas in the fivefold system, which serve as the foundations.

"Even for those who have produced the path," by the phrase "in a proximate location," he shows that there is no difference [in this case] due to the attainment entered into from time to time by the practitioner of insight (*vipassaka*). 799.

"And there too" means even in the second Elder’s doctrine. The similarity to each respective attainment is due to the constraints of insight into formations (*saṅkhāra*) as they are respectively comprehended.

It exists. For even there, insight—by way of the cultivation of fading away and non-fading away from this or that [object]—becomes accompanied by joy and accompanied by equanimity, thereby establishing the fixed order of the jhāna factors and so forth for the path; thus the fixed order of insight should be understood in the manner already described.
(800) "That" refers to a state resembling each respective jhāna. And this meaning [is established] through the basic jhāna, the jhāna of comprehension, and the decisive support.

The failure to achieve results through mere intention (*ajjhāsaya*) alone—without a decisive support (*upanissaya*)—and the failure to achieve the fruit of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmiphala*) and so forth through mere resolve (*saṅkappa*) alone, should be illustrated by the discourse to Nanda.

For in that context, while the Blessed One spoke of even a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) having fulfilled resolves, he stated: "In each case where a decisive support exists, it is that very support which determines the intention."
The phrase “not for another” indicates that the fulfillment of one’s intention occurs through each respective [attainment] and not beyond that, because even when the intention is present,
it does not succeed [beyond its limit]. Likewise here, for whichever path belonging to the second jhāna and so forth there exists the aforementioned decisive support (upanissaya),
the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of that very path alone is the determining factor, and not of another, even though that support may be present.

"Because it does not succeed. However, in this position, when the supporting condition of the jhāna attained through preliminary reflection (*pādakasammasita*) is present, the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) is necessarily present;
just as when the supporting condition for a particular fruit is present, the corresponding resolve (*saṅkappa*) is present. Because [the fruit] is absent when that [intention] is absent, it is said:
"The underlying intention determines [the result]. "In this case too" means even in the third Elder’s position. "In the same manner as stated" refers to: "From whichever attainment..."

...by the method stated in the passage beginning with "having emerged" (*vuṭṭhāya*). Therefore, its meaning should be understood here by the method stated in the passage beginning with "for there too is insight" (*tatrāpi hi vipassanā*).
801. Having thus shown that insight is the regulator of the enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) and so forth, he now says "But if this...

and so on, in order to show that it is the regulator of the path (*paṭipadā*) and so forth. Therein, "this" refers to equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) which was mentioned; for even that—though indeed...

Regarding the phrase "choose this time," they say that "this time" refers to the "difficult practice" (*dukkhāpaṭipadā*) because, at the conclusion of the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*), when the contemplation of rise and fall (*udayabbayānupassanā*) is occurring, the defilements of insight (*vipassanupakkilesa*) arise; since these must be suppressed three times, it is called "with difficulty.
However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, it says: "When insight-knowledge is sharp, keen, clear, and flowing..."

Because it is said, "One who is suffering, with difficulty and toil, overcomes the arisen craving for insight," equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), which occurs in the prior stage through the state of desiring liberation and so forth,

remains on the side of the painful way of practice (dukkhāpaṭipadā) as it suppresses its own opposites with difficulty and toil. Therefore he said, "Suppressing the defilements from the beginning," and so forth.

Some, however, say: "This knowledge is described as 'suppressing defilements from the very beginning' by making it one with that knowledge which suppressed the imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) through the method of unification. "With application" means with exertion, which is termed the application of the mind.
"With effort" is a synonym for the same. By both terms, they mean that the suppression of defilements was accomplished only with difficulty.

It says: "By way of reversal" means without suffering, without effort, and without volitional formation (*asaṅkhāra*). Because one dwells having followed the desired place designated as the Path, it is called *parivāsa*;
since insight (*vipassanā*) has this *parivāsa* as its characteristic, it is "insight-parivāsa," which is the manifestation of the Path.
Furthermore, because it brings that about swiftly, it is called "swift direct knowledge" (*khippābhiññā*).
It is said, "gradually. The construction is: "This equanimity regarding formations is what is being performed. "From where the path comes" refers to that place from which it arrives;
[the phrase] "in that place from which it arrives" is used. The connection is: "Having stood at the source of the path, he gives it its name.
The method of insight such as the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge is one thing, and the path itself is quite another.
He said: "Of each respective path. Thus, it receives the four names beginning with "the painful way with sluggish direct knowledge" according to the name acquired from its approach;
for such a name does not exist for the path by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (*sarasato*).
Furthermore, this aforementioned classification of ways is distinct—that is, it is separate—for each individual bhikkhu.

There is no fixed rule that there is only one [type of practice] in all four paths, because they are subject to fluctuation. It is said, "they were," but it should rather be said, "they are," referring to our Blessed One.
For for all perfectly enlightened Buddhas, all four paths are indeed of pleasant progress and quick direct knowledge.
In connection with the discussion of the modes of progress (*paṭipadā*), in order to show the dominant influence (*adhipati*) as well, [it says]: "Just as..."

And so it was said, beginning with the words "and... The term *adhipatayo* refers to the predominances such as desire (*chanda*) and the rest. For the path conforms to previous volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*);
thus, each path may have desire as its predominance, or one of the others such as energy (*vīriya*), and there is no fixed rule for any one [predominance].
Therefore he said, "for some bhikkhu," and so forth.
802. Having emphasized what was stated previously, the phrase beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) is spoken in order to show the reason for the path receiving its name in its entirety.
Therein, "by its own force" (*sarasena*) means by its own intrinsic nature or its specific mode of occurrence;
"by its opposite" (*paccanīkena*) means by way of its counter-agent; and "by its own quality" (*saguṇena*) means by way of its own excellence.
In this context, it is true that just as the designation of the Path is not established without its arrival, its qualities, and its object,
so too its designation occurs through its own inherent nature (sarasena) even without its opposite; nevertheless, the word "or" (vā) is used in every instance—
such as "or by its inherent nature"— to show that each factor, including the inherent nature and the rest, is indeed a cause for the attainment of the designation.

And in order to show these [factors] without confusion, the passage beginning with "If indeed" (*sace hi*) was commenced. Therein, "having comprehended" (*sammasitvā*) means "on account of comprehension.
For this particle *tvā* has the sense of a cause, as in such examples as "Having drunk the potion, strength arises; having seen the lion, fear arises.

Thus, equanimity toward formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*), which is the absolute cause for the act of emergence performed by the path as its agent, is [referred to] by way of a metaphorical designation of the fruit.

"He emerges" is what is said. Or rather, since "equanimity towards formations" is a characteristic mark of that which leads to emergence—and the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) is included therein, for it emerges from the sign—therefore, according to the method of unity, it is said: "having comprehended, he emerges.
"He is liberated by way of the signless liberation" means he is liberated by a liberation characterized as signless.
The word "path" (*magga*) should be supplied and connected [to the preceding terms]. Or, "is liberated" refers to the noble person (*ariya-puggala*) who possesses that [path].

The same method applies to the other two as well. This is called the name by its own essence; that is, because it is devoid of signs and so forth, this threefold designation—signless (*animitta*), wishless (*appaṇihita*), and empty (*suññata*)—is the name established by the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of the path.
"Esā" means the path. And this is spoken of as one with the preliminary path by way of the principle of identity.

This set of three names for the path—beginning with "signless" (animitta)—obtained through the abandoning of aspiration for permanent signs and so forth, and of the perception of a self, is called a name established by way of its opposite; that is, it is named from the perspective of its counteragent.
"Emptiness" (*suññatā*) means the state of being secluded. For lust and the other defilements do not exist on the path.
"Of the signs of form, etc."—the intention is that these are the signs of form, feeling, and so forth, which are to be grasped. The same principle applies here to "signs of lust, etc.
Here, what is intended by "sign" (*nimitta*) is its appearance as if it were something graspable. "This is its name according to its quality" refers to its being secluded from lust and the rest.
The name of this Path is established by way of its own qualities through the absence of aspiration for signs such as form and so forth.
It is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*) because it is empty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) and empty of a self (*atta*).

It is "signless" (*animitta*) because of the absence of the signs of all conditioned phenomena. It is "wishless" (*appaṇihita*) because of the absence of craving, aspiration, and so forth. This is its...

Regarding the name "from the object" (*ārammaṇato*): just as a material form that has happiness as its object is called "happiness," so too, because it takes as its object Nibbāna—which possesses names such as "emptiness" (*suññatā*)—this name of the path, distinguished as emptiness and so forth, is established from the perspective of its object.
(803) The contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*) is called "emptiness" by its own nature (*sarasato*), because it sees the emptiness of self. Of that insight into emptiness...
The path is "void" (*suññata*) by way of its approach through insight (*vipassanā*). It is called "signless" (*animitta*) because it has dispelled the signs of permanence and so forth.
However, this name "signless" for the path is not obtained according to the method of the Abhidhamma. What is the reason?

Because in the Abhidhamma, names are obtained from the perspective of opposition rather than by grasping the intrinsic nature (*sarasa*). For any name obtained from qualities and objects is primarily based on intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, if names were acquired by means of their own inherent essence (*sarasena*), there would be no definitive determination that all paths possess the nature of emptiness (*suññatā*) and so forth.

Therefore, although in the Abhidhamma names are acquired through both causes, the establishment of names is understood as being performed precisely by way of opposition; thus, because that [inherent essence] is absent, it is not applicable.
Alternatively, "it is not applicable" refers to those objects possessing qualities (*saguṇa-ārammaṇa*) that are independent of anything else.
It is not obtained. What is the reason? Because in the Abhidhamma, names are not obtained in association with the "opposites of the essence" (*sarasapaccanīka*).
For in the Abhidhamma, there is no status as a cause for the name of the mere essence without regard for the establishment of the opposite; this is because it would result in a lack of definition.
Therefore, even though the paths that are the counterparts to the inclinations and aspirations toward a self (*attābhinivesapaṇidhi*) and are in conformity with insight (*vipassanānuloma*) exist...

They receive their name from the "arrow" (sara) because they are accompanied by an arrow that is its opposite within the stream of consciousness. However, for the signless path (animitta-magga), insight (vipassanā) is not the opposite of the sign (nimitta), as it itself grasps the sign;

nor is the path conforming to that (tadanuloma-magga) the opposite of the sign, since it does not prevent the grasping of the sign. If it were [the opposite], it would also be the opposite of the insight directed toward the sign.

It might be so; therefore, although the "essence" (sārassa) exists, it is not included in the Abhidhamma as a designation for the "signless" (animitta), because there is no factor that establishes its definition [in that context].
If this is so, would it follow that the path conforming to the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanānuloma-magga) is not included in the Abhidhamma?
No, because it is included within the system of the "pure way of practice" (suddhika-paṭipadā-naya). For that very reason it is mentioned there. However, in the Suttanta...
Because it is taught by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyadesanā*), the name is applied even on account of its having a quality as its object;
thus he said, "It is obtained according to the method of the Suttanta. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated above.

To show that the name "signless" (*animitta*) is indeed applicable to the path by way of its arrival (*āgamana*), he said, "For there," and so forth. "In the place of arrival" means in the state of the path of arrival (*āgamanapaṭipadā*).
The remainder is clear because it follows the method already stated.
The knowledge of equanimity towards formations is finished.
This concludes the commentary on the discourse on the knowledge of conformity.
804. *Adhimokkha-saddhā* (resolute confidence): Resolute confidence (*adhimokkha*) is a decision regarding the objective basis that has become clarified.
Therefore, through a specific mode of cultivation, it arises as more powerful due to its intensity (*adhimatta*) in terms of its function.
*Supaggahitaṃ*: well-exerted. *Asallīnaṃ*: energy (*vīriya*) that, by way of being more active, is capable of dispelling opposing factors.
"Well-established" means that mindfulness is firmly established by way of being directed toward the object with greater sharpness.
"Well-concentrated" means that, due to the excellence of the bliss of tranquility, it is well-concentrated, properly placed upon the object, as if fixed there.
"More sharp" means possessing a state capable of becoming a condition for the arising of conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
They are sharp and keen. Even in the discernment of formations, equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) arises as a state of neutrality.
Having comprehended [formations] as "impermanent," and so forth... it descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Thus, while comprehending by way of one aspect among impermanence and the rest, having occurred seven times and then ceased, it is said to have "descended" into the life-continuum; after that, [there is] the life-continuum.

Having taken "turn" (vāra) in this sense. "By the very method used for equanimity toward formations" means by the method of making the object [of meditation] such as impermanence and so forth, not by the method of full comprehension (sammasita).
Therefore he said, "making it its object. "Having turned back" means having diverted [the mind], not allowing it to proceed by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
It is "without interval" (avīcikā) because of the absence of an interval (vīci) consisting in the occurrence of dissimilar states of consciousness.

“Continuity of consciousness” (*cittasantati*). For when the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*) turns back toward the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), there is an interruption in the flow of the functional consciousness and the arising of resultant consciousness;

it is not so with the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*). Thus it is said: “maintaining a continuity of consciousness that is uninterrupted” (*avīcikaṃ cittasantatiṃ anuppabandhamānaṃ*).

“In the same way” means just as, in the thirty-two past cognitive processes of the impulsion stage (*javana-vīthi*), equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) [arises] as either “impermanent” or “suffering.”
Or likewise, if one takes formations as the object, thinking "non-self," it is the same.

It is called "preliminary work" (*parikamma*) because it is the preliminary work for the path and because it performs the function of reflection. It is called "access" (*upacāra*) because it is near to the path or because it moves in its vicinity.
Its conformity is stated by itself.

And although this method is stated to be appropriate—wherein the first impulsion has the sense of "reflecting," the second the sense of "being close to that," and the third the sense of "conformity" between the preceding and succeeding moments—it is nevertheless said, "But without distinction...
and so forth, in order to show that these designations apply to all of them as well. In that context, "repetition" (āsevana) means...
"Attentive service" means serving with respect. "Of the prior and posterior portions" refers to the lower and upper sections of the factors of the Dhamma.
"Of the eight" refers to the eight beginning with the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*). All insight (*vipassanā*) has the function of comprehending the three characteristics;

this [knowledge] is likewise, which is why it is said, "by virtue of having that same function. "Above" refers to the Path (*magga*). Of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*).

It conforms to its function because it dispels the opposition to mindfulness and so forth. Now, in order to show in detail the conformity to those two functions of the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), the passage beginning with "For that" (*tañhi*) was stated.

Therein, the knowledge of conformity reaches the ultimate limit of excellence among mundane knowledges by means of its superior dispelling of the mass of delusion (*moha-khandha*) and other factors that conceal the Truths;
for that very reason, it [surpasses] even the knowledge of arising and passing away (*udaya-bbaya-ñāṇa*) and others produced previously.
The function proceeds by accomplishing its purpose in the sense of distancing itself from its opposite;
and as it proceeds in that way, it is as if it conforms to their function. Thus he said: "Of those possessing arising and passing away... it conforms through having such a function.
In this context, by the phrase "manifested as fear," he speaks specifically of the operation of knowledge under the heading of the object, regarding those things that are fearful.
This is because it illustrates the seeing of formations according to their true nature. In the remaining seven instances, however, only the activity of knowledge is shown.

Since this knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa) occurs by taking formations as its object through one of the characteristics such as impermanence, it is therefore said: "because it occurs by taking formations as its object through the characteristic of impermanence, etc. By that...
"By way of practice" means by that practice which suppresses the defilements that obscure the grosser aspects of the Truths for one possessing conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
For if conformity-knowledge has not arisen in such a manner, change-of-lineage-knowledge (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) is unable to take Nibbāna as its object;
and if change-of-lineage-knowledge has not arisen, path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) does not arise.
In order to make the matter already stated more evident by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as" was spoken.

Therein, just as the eight judges abandon improper conduct and carry out their respective judicial decisions, so too do the eight knowledges abandon their respective opposites and engage in the observation of the arising and passing away of formations; this is like the king’s state of neutrality.
It is like the conformity of the preceding and succeeding portions of a dhamma to knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).
"By that very [fact]" means precisely because the higher factors conducive to enlightenment conform by way of the conformity of the lower knowledges.
It is called "conforming to the truths" because it conforms to the truth of the path (*magga-sacca*).
The knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse on insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-gāminī-vipassanā*):

although some knowledge has the unconditioned as its object, it is included within the category of "insight leading to emergence" by being grouped together with that which has formations as its object; thus, it is said, "[insight] having formations as its object."
An qualification has been made. For that [insight] is called "leading to emergence" because it specifically goes toward and approaches the Noble Path as its emergence;

thus he said, "in every way," and so forth. "For the sake of non-confusion" means for the purpose of removing confusion regarding what has been stated through various synonyms in this or that discourse (*sutta*). "Connecting the discourses" refers to those discourses...
The sequence of those sutta passages:

that craving which, depending upon and bound to those mundane formations (*saṅkhāra*) for which insight leading to emergence proceeds in forward order until its conclusion, is called "consisting of that" (*tammaya*) because it does not occur without them;
the state of consisting of that is simply "consisting of that. It is *tammaya*.

Or, it refers to the aggregates associated with craving; their state is "being made of that" (*tammayatā*), which is itself craving. The insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā*), being the opposite of that, is "not being made of that" (*atammayatā*).
Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "Being made of that is craving;
because of its complete exhaustion, the insight leading to emergence is called 'not being made of that'. "Depending on" means depending on that [state of] not being made of that.
The meaning is: having made [them such], having developed them. Regarding the term "variety" (*nānattā*): here the text says, "Bhikkhus, there is equanimity regarding forms...
up to... tangible objects; this equanimity, bhikkhus, is varied, based on variety. The meaning is that it itself possesses various intrinsic natures and is dependent upon various objects.
That, however, should be understood as the equanimity of insight (*vipassanupekkhā*) associated with concentration (*samādhi*).
“Bhikkhus, there is equanimity based on the base of infinite space... [and so on] ...equanimity based on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This, bhikkhus, is equanimity that is unified and based on unity. For whatever equanimity is included within those various immaterial states of consciousness, it is called “unified” and “based on unity” because of its uniform nature and its single object; and furthermore—
They say that this consists of both the equanimity associated with the feeling accompanying each respective jhāna and the equanimity of insight having that as its object.
"Abandon that" means abandon it by abandoning the defilements that have that as their object. Therefore he said, "Transcend that.

"Disenchantment" refers to that which leads to emergence. For in that sutta, "he becomes dispassionate" expresses the function of the Path, while "he is liberated" expresses the function of the Fruit.

The *Susimasutta* is in the *Nidāna-vagga*. Therein, "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is called "leading to emergence" because it proceeds by way of non-delusion regarding dependent origination within the stability of phenomena. "Knowledge of Nibbāna" refers to path-knowledge.

Regarding the passage, "Perception, Poṭṭhapāda," although it is simply called "perception" here, he says, "it is called the 'summit of perception,'" because it was previously stated that "one touches the summit of perception."

"Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way" refers to the "emergence-leading" state, which constitutes a portion of that [purification]. For conventional designations applied to a whole also apply to its parts. "The factor of striving for complete purification" means the primary cause for complete purification.
"By three names" means by the three names known as conformity, change-of-lineage, and the signless (or emergence).

"Kittita" means praised because of his steadfastness in the Noble Path. "By the Great Seer" (Mahesi) refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), in the sense of seeking after the great aggregates of virtue and so forth. "Peaceful" (santa) because of the pacification of the defilements. "Yoga" means meditative development (bhāvanā), or perhaps application to meditative development.
The commentary on the description of purification by knowledge and vision of the way is finished. Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-first chapter.
22. Explanation of the Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision (Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesavaṇṇanā). Explanation of the First Discourse on Path-Knowledge (Paṭhamamaggañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā):
Now, as the description of purification by knowledge and vision has been reached, [it must be stated] which knowledge arises immediately after it.
Demonstrating that, he said: "Beyond this, there is the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). "Beyond this" means above this conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa).

"That" refers to the knowledge of change-of-lineage. It does not belong to the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi) because it does not grasp formations as impermanent and so forth.
Nor does it belong to the purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), even though its object is Nibbāna.

Because it does not expel the defilements. For that very reason, while it points out the object of the consciousness-elements and performs the function of seeing, it is called the "substitute for adverting" (*āvajjana*) of the Path, just like the functional mind-element (*kiriyamanodhātu*).

"In between" means in the interval between the sixth and seventh purifications. It is indeed indeterminate (*abbohārika*), because it lacks the specific characteristics of both types of purification. Nevertheless, regarding the [purification] leading to emergence...
Because it is at the conclusion [of the path], it belongs to the side of insight (vipassanā). For that very reason, it is included within that stream.

Therefore he said: "It goes by the name... pe ... of the stream of insight. By this, he shows its classification under the purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).
Stream-entry (sotāpatti) is the reaching of the noble stream from the beginning; that itself is the path. Or alternatively, one reaches—that is, attains—the noble stream from the beginning.
Stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) is the first [fruit]. Its path is the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
One who returns to this human world only once more by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*); his path is the path of once-returning (*sakadāgāmimagga*).

One who does not return to the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) by way of rebirth-linking is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*); his path is the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). [The term "path" is used] because of the slaying, etc., of the defilements and so forth.
An *arahant* is one who stands at the summit of the path. The state of being such is *arahatta*; that itself is the path, hence it is called the "path of *arahant*-ship" (*arahattamagga*).
Taking the knowledge of the four paths together as one is what is called "purification by knowledge and vision.

The phrase "by those three" is stated because the three preceding types of conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) have already been mentioned; or alternatively, because two of them are included within the [remaining] three.
The word *pi* (also) has the sense of combining other alternatives; by it, it is meant "by three or even by two.
"According to their own strength" means in accordance with their respective power. For the first knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) is relatively coarse;
the second is not so coarse as that; and the third dispels the darkness that is not so coarse as the former. Alternatively:
"According to the strength [of the power] acquired" means according to the strength acquired previously during the stage of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

For indeed, by virtue of previous formations, there exists a specific distinction between the degrees of pliancy and sharpness in the occurrence of even the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*)—just as in the case of the knowledge of the path (*magga-ñāṇa*)—among those who are liberated through faith (*saddhāvimutta*) and those who have attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*).
It "stands as an impediment" because it is the darkness that conceals the state of being an impediment.

Because it has been made to disappear. By the phrase “at the end of repetition,” he shows that the arising of the change-of-lineage knowledge (*gotrabhu-ñāṇa*) occurs immediately after the second or third conformity knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), and not after the first, because that [first] lacks repetition.

For change-of-lineage knowledge cannot arise without having attained repetition. Because it is devoid of signs (*nimitta*) and so forth, and because it is the opposite of those, it is called “signless” (*animitta*) and so on.
Nibbāna is distinguished [as follows]: "The lineage of worldlings" (puthujjanagotta) refers to the common designation of worldlings, unmixed with that of the noble ones (ariya).
For "lineage" (gotta) is a common appellation for those born of a single clan; so it is here as well. "The category of worldlings" (puthujjanasaṅkhā) is a synonym for that very same thing;
"the plane of worldlings" (puthujjanabhūmi) refers to the basis of worldliness. It is "not subject to returning" because it arises only once due to its absolute finality.

“Emergence and turning away from the external” (*bahiddhā vuṭṭhāna-vivaṭṭana*) refers to the wisdom that arises when the turning away—which constitutes the emergence from the conditioned—is being accomplished; it is called “external” because it exists outside the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).
“Overcomes” (*abhibhuyyati*) means he overcomes. “Enters” (*pakkhandati*) means he penetrates.
And here, by the phrase “he overcomes arising,” etc., the overcoming and transcending of the lineage of worldlings (*puthujjana-gotta*) is expressed.

“‘He leaps into non-arising,’ etc.: because of the cultivation of the lineage of the Noble Ones (ariyagotta) through the manifestation of both [non-arising and cessation], there is no need for the term ‘single cognitive series’ (ekavīthi) to exclude multiple cognitive series among those with a single adverting consciousness;
rather, it should be understood that the term is used to show that even for those with a single adverting consciousness, there is no diversity of cognitive series when the objects are diverse.”
*Mahāmātikaṃ* means a great watercourse. *Laṅghitvā* means having crossed over without descending. *Ullaṅghitvā* means having leaped across by way of the upper part alone.
*Ninnapoṇapabbhāratā* is simply the state of being sloping, inclining, and tending downwards, each succeeding one being more distinguished than the preceding.
*Anulomañāṇa* (conformity-knowledge), which has acquired distinction through the eight successive knowledges, is the condition for the knowledge that has Nibbāna as its object.
He said, "having run with speed by means of the contemplation of rise and fall, etc.," because it is born capable of becoming [such].
It is said, "or a rope of form," because form, due to its connection with many successions, is like a rope woven from many rounds of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Since the individual existence (*attabhāva*) has been described as standing in the place of a tree, among feeling and the other aggregates, only one stands in the place of the staff connected to it.
It is not [the object] of the aggregate of feeling and so forth; thus it is said: "or a single factor among feeling and the rest.
"By means of the adverting of conformity" means by the adverting of conformity. That object is apprehended by that very adverting through which the knowledge of conformity arises.
The phrase "having leaped over by means of the first consciousness of conformity" refers to its being the commencement of the crossing over of that "ford of personality" (sakkāyatīra).
It was said: “With a mind inclined, leaning, and bent towards Nibbāna by the second [jhāna].

This was said because, having become exceptionally unattached to all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it clings to the unconditioned (*visaṅkhāra*). The practitioner falls toward Nibbāna by way of making it his object (*ārammaṇa*).
“In a single object” means in an object grasped only once. Therefore he said: “Because of not having practiced it repeatedly.”
This shows that repetition [of the mind] upon a single object is beneficial, whereas it is not so when the objects are diverse.

(808) "Therein" means in the case where the *anuloma* and *gotrabhū* do not perform their respective functions for one another. "The conjunction with a lunar mansion" (*nakkhattayoga*) means the moon’s conjunction with a lunar mansion, or the time determined by the *nakkhattayogavibhāvanī*; the meaning is "the day.
The passage beginning with "Therein" (*tattha*) and so forth is the correlation of the simile.

"Thus they have arisen" means that, like the knowledge of conformity (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), they do not take conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as their object, but rather proceed with Nibbāna as their object, as if saying "I [am here].
This refers specifically to the Path's relinquishing of the perception bestowed by the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) and its subsequent following through by making Nibbāna its object.
809. "Therein" means in that very object grasped by it, as if not having relinquished the perception bestowed by the change-of-lineage.

Having turned [the mind] toward the penetration of the mass of greed and so forth on the path, one is called an *issāsa*, meaning an archer, because he shoots an arrow. The range of the arrow is said to be eight *usabhas*.

Now, for a man of medium stature who shoots far, one *usabha* consists of twenty staff-lengths (*yaṭṭhi*), with each staff being four cubits (*hattha*) long; thus, the area of eight *usabhas* is measured by the hand.
In a space of six hundred and forty hands. "A hundred planks" means a hundred planks made of the heartwood of the *āsana* tree. "On a wheel-base like a potter’s wheel" means on a rotating base.
"Having whirled" means having caused it to revolve. The "perception of the handle" is the sound that must be produced by the striking of the handle.

Just as the perception of the handle serves as the condition for the piercing through of the hundred planks, so too does the knowledge of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) serve as the condition for the piercing through of the mass of greed and the other [defilements].
Because it serves as a condition for the knowledge of the path; because, like an archer, it pierces through that which is to be pierced by the knowledge of the path.
From the eighth existence onward, it dries up the ocean of suffering in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra.
[It consists of] the wealth of faith, the wealth of virtue, the wealth of moral shame, the wealth of moral dread, the wealth of learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom.
Of these seven noble treasures. "Manifestation" (*sammukhībhāva*) means establishment through direct perception.

All enmities and fears, namely the five enmities beginning with the destruction of life and the twenty-five great fears, as well as [the obstacles] for others who possess faith and the other virtues established in the Triple Gem—the word *sotāpatti-magga* (stream-entry path), which functions in reference to the whole collection, is also used for its individual parts; thus he said, "by the stream-entry path..."
“Knowledge associated [with the path].
The explanation of the first path-knowledge is finished.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion of the person who has entered the stream (sotāpanna).

811. Of that very same stream-entry path-consciousness. Although here, for one of not very sharp wisdom there are two fruition-consciousnesses, and for one of sharp wisdom there are three, it is nevertheless stated as "two or three" by way of the path that has been taken without distinction.
"They call concentration 'the immediate' (ānantarika)" means that which, immediately following its own occurrence, necessarily bestows the fruit.
"Ānantarikasamādhi" means "called immediate concentration. *Anantara* refers to the fruit that occurs immediately;
that which is connected to it, or that which has it as its purpose, is *ānantarika*, namely the Path (*magga*).

"At the end of repetition" (*āsevanante*) means at the conclusion of repetition; the meaning is "immediately after the knowledge of adaptation (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) obtained through repetition. It is precisely that which has obtained repetition.
It produces the conformity (anuloma) and the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). However, six or seven subsequent impulsion (javana) moments proceed;
therefore, one might say that there are four fruition-consciousnesses (phala-citta). To this, it is said: "And the single-adverting cognitive process has seven consciousnesses at most.
The construction [of the sentence] is: "But that should not be accepted as the essential truth. Whatever else needs to be said here has already been stated below.
"812. 'To this extent' means at the moment of the arising of the fruit immediately after the first path.

'Even though he be greatly negligent' means even if he has become greatly negligent by resorting to grounds for negligence such as divine sovereignty or the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
The intention is that through the arising of those aforementioned advertence (*āvajjana*) and impulsion (*javana*) consciousnesses, this stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) indeed performs the reviewing."
In this very context, the passage beginning with "And as" was stated in order to show the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) of the remaining noble ones.
The meaning is that this is merely the highest limit, namely, the demonstration of five and four reviews.
By the phrase "or even by non-existence," it is indicated that some possess the capacity for reviewing the defilements that remain after having been abandoned.
He shows that it does not exist for anyone. "Lobha-dhamma" means greed itself.
Commentary on the Discussion of Knowledge of the Second Path (813):
"For the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will" means for the purpose of attenuating these defilements. Therein, by two...
The attenuation [of defilements] occurs due to two causes: their non-frequent arising and the weakness of their obsession.

For in the case of a once-returner, the defilements do not arise frequently as they do for the common multitude who follow the cycle of existence; rather, they arise only occasionally and in a sparse manner.
Even when they do arise, they do not arise as trampling, covering, or creating darkness; rather, they are abandoned by means of two paths.
Because they have been abandoned, they arise very slowly and in a thin form. Some, however, say:
"Even for a once-returner, defilements arise only after a long time, and even when they do arise, they arise thickly; for instance, his sons and daughters are seen.
That is not a valid reason, because conception can occur even without the actual indulgence in the physical object. Therefore, it is according to the method already stated.

The attenuation of those [defilements] should be understood by way of two reasons. "In the second" means both in the sense of being the second in numerical order and in the sense of being the second stage (*bhūmi*) in terms of its arising.
"For the attainment" means for the sake of obtaining the fruit of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).

For that [stage] is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*) because the associated states exist therein by virtue of its being their support; or alternatively, because even while sharing the same supramundane nature, it itself comes into being.
It arises; it is not unmanifest like Nibbāna, and for that reason also it is called a "ground. "He practices yoga" means he practices the application of insight (vipassanā).

Just according to the method stated in such passages as, "The faculties become sharp in nine ways," by the very same degree that he brings about the sharpness of the faculties, by that same degree the powers (balāni) and the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgāni) attain a state of greater clarity.
Bringing forth the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, he rubs [the object] with knowledge by way of investigating the three characteristics.
Therein, by moving knowledge back and forth, he turns it over. Therefore it is said: "He enters the path of insight.
"In the manner already stated" means in the manner stated for the arising of the knowledge of rise and fall and so forth. Regarding the phrase "immediately after the change-of-lineage": here,
"Change-of-lineage" (*gotrabhū*) is so called because it is like the change-of-lineage itself.

For the knowledge that precedes the first path is called "change-of-lineage" in the primary sense, because it overcomes the lineage of the worldling (*puthujjana*) and brings about the lineage of the noble ones (*ariya*).

This [knowledge], however, is "change-of-lineage" in a secondary sense due to its similarity to that. Furthermore, it is so called because it takes as its object a certain purification from defilement and absolute purification.
And it is called "cleansing" (*vodāna*). Therefore, it is said in the *Paṭṭhāna*: "Conformity (*anuloma*) is a condition for cleansing by way of the proximity-condition" (*Paṭṭhāna* 1.1.417).
Furthermore, because in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, with reference to the overcoming of arising and so forth, it is stated:
"Eight states of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*) arise by way of concentration; ten states of change-of-lineage arise by way of insight," and so on...
This has come down by way of the name "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū); therefore, it should be understood that here too it is called "immediately following change-of-lineage.
The second knowledge is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the discussion of the third path-knowledge.
814. *Sakideva* means "only once. By the phrase "having come to this world," four out of the five types of once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) are excluded, and only one is included.
One attains the fruit of once-returning here and attains final nibbāna right here in this world;
another attains it here and attains final nibbāna in the heavenly world; another attains it in the heavenly world and attains final nibbāna right there.
One person, having reached the world of the devas and then being reborn here, attains final nibbāna. These four types are not included here.

However, it should be understood that only this one type is included here: he who, having reached this world, dwells in the world of the devas for the full span of his life, and then being reborn here once more, attains final nibbāna.

"For the complete abandonment of sensual lust and ill will" means for the total relinquishment of those very fetters which were attenuated by the path of the once-returner. Because he does not return to the sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*) by way of rebirth-linking, he is a non-returner (*anāgāmī*).
The third knowledge is finished.
Explanation of the discourse on the knowledge of the fourth path.
"Of spontaneous birth" (*opapātika*) means one whose mode of birth is spontaneous. By this, his lying in a womb is rejected.
"One who attains final nibbāna there" means one who attains final nibbāna in that very Pure Abode (*suddhāvāsa*).

"One whose nature is not to return from that world" means that by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), he has the characteristic of not returning here from that world; however, there is indeed coming for the purpose of seeing the Buddhas and hearing the Dhamma.

"For the sake of the complete abandonment of attachment to the fine-material realm, attachment to the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance" means for the purpose of relinquishing these five higher fetters (*uddhaṃbhāgiya-saṃyojana*) without remainder.

Therein, "attachment to the fine-material realm" (*rūparāga*) is the desire and lust for existence in the fine-material realm. "Attachment to the immaterial realm" (*arūparāga*) is the desire and lust for existence in the immaterial realm.
"Conceit" (*māna*) refers to that which is abandoned by the path of Arahantship. Likewise for restlessness and ignorance.
The fourth knowledge is completed.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Person Who is an Arahant (816):
"One whose taints are utterly destroyed" (*mahākhīṇāsava*) is a term of veneration based on his great majesty; it is not a term used with reference to [the aggregates].

Just as in the case of “Mahāmoggallāna. For there is no such thing as a “Cūḷakhīṇāsava” (a Lesser One whose taints are destroyed). He bears his final body, thus he is “one who bears his final body” (*antimadehadhārī*).
Because the burdens of the aggregates, the defilements, and volitional formations have been laid down and set aside, he is “one who has laid down the burden” (*ohitabhāra*).

He has attained his own goal, his personal aim, thus he is “one who has attained his own goal” (*anuppattasadattha*). And by “own goal,” one should understand *arahatta* (Arahatship); for that, in the sense of being bound to oneself, is...
Because he does not abandon himself and because his own ultimate goal is his own welfare, he is called "one who seeks his own welfare" (*sakattha*).
One for whom the ten fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*) have been completely destroyed is "one whose fetters of existence are destroyed" (*parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojana*).

One who is liberated through having rightly understood the meaning of the aggregates and so forth is "liberated by right knowledge" (*sammadaññāvimutta*). He is both supreme and worthy of offerings; thus, he is the "supreme object of offerings" (*aggadakkhiṇa*).
Or, he is called "the one worthy of the foremost" because he is the most worthy of offerings.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiyakathāvaṇṇanā):

817. "By means of the four knowledges of the paths" refers to the four knowledges. "For the purpose of discerning his majesty" means for the purpose of awakening to his majesty, such as the fulfillment of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.

That which has the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*) complete is "one whose factors conducive to enlightenment are complete" (*paripuṇṇabodhipakkhiya*); this refers to the Path (*magga*). The state of being such is "the state of having complete factors conducive to enlightenment" (*paripuṇṇabodhipakkhiyabhāva*).

The conjunction with the powers of emergence (*vuṭṭhānabala*) is simply the association with those powers; these are the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth that are to be abandoned by the first path and the others.

Alternatively, "enlightenment" (*bodha*) is so called in the sense of awakening; it is the arising of the mind of the Path. Because they are favorable to that act of awakening, they exist on its side (*pakkhe bhavanti*), and thus they are "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*).
819. Regarding those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*): "In the objects" means in the objects such as the body and so forth. "Having plunged in" means having entered into them.

"Having leaped into" is a synonym for that same term. "By way of establishing" means by way of approaching and remaining fixed through the apprehension of the aspect of foulness (*asubha*) and so forth.

The apprehension of the aspect of foulness and so forth regarding the body and other objects is accomplished as the function of abandoning perceptions of beauty and the like, by way of the preliminary foundations of mindfulness (*pubbabhāga-satipaṭṭhāna*).
It should be understood by way of the foundations of mindfulness of the path.
For therein, a single mindfulness functions by accomplishing the fourfold task. Or, "striving" means making an effort, or exerting the body and mind.

"Beautifying" (sobhana) means the act of beautifying through the abandoning of defiled states that are causes of ugliness, and through the cultivation of purified states that are causes of beauty; the meaning is "excellent."

"By bringing about the state of excellence" means by accomplishing the state of being most praiseworthy. "By being the cause of the state of pre-eminence" means by being the reason for the highest state. 821. "As stated previously" refers to what was stated in the exposition of the knowledge of the various kinds of supernormal power (*iddhividhañāṇa*).

The sense of "success" (*ijjhana*) is the sense of accomplishment, or the attainment and perfection; or, that by which they succeed, become successful, and reach the pinnacle—that is success (*ijjhana*).
Here, the path factors headed by the volitional formations of concentration (*samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra*) are intended by the term "success" (*iddhi*).
The sense of being a precursor is the state of being a dominant condition (*adhipati-paccaya*). Therefore, because the stream-entry path succeeds, it is "success";

thus, the associated factors such as desire (*chanda*) are the "foot" in the sense of being a precursor. For that very [path], which is the fruit consisting of the emergence-tending [concentration], desire and the others are the cause in the sense of being the preliminary factor.
“Pādo” means “basis. “So” refers to the basis for spiritual power (iddhipāda).
“These are supramundane” means that these aforementioned factors—desire and the rest—are to be understood as supramundane according to the method presented in the *Uttara-cūḷa-bhājanīya*.

The meaning is that even phenomena such as contact and so forth, when acquired by way of desire and the other [bases] acting as dominant influences (*adhipati*), become bases for spiritual power. Although it may be the case here that the basis for spiritual power is not the dominant influence, or the dominant influence is not the basis for spiritual power.

There is no such thing; rather, it should be understood that just as in a single kingdom among four princes worthy of sovereignty, at one time only one of them governs the kingdom and not all of them,
so too in each single arising of consciousness, there is only one dominant factor (*adhipati*) and one basis of psychic power (*iddhipāda*).

822. Lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) consists of unwholesome states that are the opposites of faith, or it is a false resolve resembling confidence that has reached a state of stability. Laziness (*kosajja*) is an unwholesome mental arising characterized primarily by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

Heedlessness (*pamāda*) is the loss of mindfulness (*satisammosa*), as well as the unwholesome aggregates (*akusala-khandhā*) proceeding in that manner. It is said "in the sense of predominance (*adhipati-ṭṭhena*)" because it is designated as such in the sense of overcoming, namely, by way of overcoming lack of faith and the other [hindrances].

It is called "overpowering" (abhibhavana) in the sense that it possesses a single characteristic—namely, resolution, exertion, establishment, and non-distraction—and thus acts as the dominant factor (adhipati-ṭṭhena) among the associated states.
As for the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and by lack of faith, etc.," it has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya) and is used in the sense of a reason (aṭṭhānappayutta).
Therefore, the intended meaning here should be understood as follows: it is called "power" (bala) in the sense of being unshakable and in the sense of stability among the associated states.
"Of a being who awakens" means of a being who penetrates the four noble truths.
For he, at the moment of the supramundane path, awakens by means of the collection of states beginning with mindfulness— which acts as the instrument—
and thus rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or penetrates the four noble truths, or [penetrates] Nibbāna itself.
One who realizes [this] is called an "enlightened one" (*bodhi*), namely, the noble disciple;

the factors of that enlightenment—that is, of the being who awakens—are the "factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*). "In the sense of leading out" means in the sense of escape from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

824. The connection is: "They are found in various states of consciousness in the prior stage. "In fourteen ways" refers to the sections on mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, clear comprehension, attention to repulsiveness, and attention to the elements.

And the nine cemetery contemplations (*śivathika*); thus it is fourteenfold. Mindfulness of the body as a foundation of mindfulness (*kāyānupassanā-satipaṭṭhāna*) is obtained by one who comprehends the body, not by one who comprehends feelings and so forth.
This same method applies to the rest as well. Or, it is ninefold: as "pleasant feeling" and so forth;

or as "worldly" (*sāmisa*) and so forth; or as "unworldly" (*nirāmisa*) and so forth. [The nine objects of liberation are] the terms for liberation with lust, hatred, and delusion; contracted; exalted; concentrated; and surpassed.
By way of sixteenfold [classification] according to the factors together with their opposites;

by way of fivefold [classification] according to the hindrances, the aggregates of clinging, the bases, the factors of enlightenment, and the truths. "In this present existence" means in the present personal life.

"Never arisen before" means not having occurred for oneself previously. Having seen unwholesome states arisen in another, as well as the signs thereof, such as being subject to execution, imprisonment, and so forth.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Of that" means of such a kind. For the designation of a thing is applied even to what resembles it, as in the expression, "those very same medicines.
The same principle applies here in the phrase "for the abandoning of that. It may be that jhāna and vipassanā have arisen previously in another existence;
therefore, it is said, "not previously arisen in this existence," referring specifically to the basis of zeal (*chandiddhipāda*) and right speech (*sammāvācā*).

The inclusion. When these have been stated, the remaining bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), and the abstinences (*virati*) are already included by implication;

thus this meaning should be understood by way of the "mode of characteristics" (*lakkhaṇahāra*). In this way, these foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), and bases of psychic power are obtained among various states of consciousness during the preliminary stage.
"Of the four knowledges" means of the four noble path-knowledges (*ariyamaggañāṇa*). Granted that all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) are [included therein]...
Although they are indeed included within the arising of the path-consciousness, nevertheless, the activity of the right efforts (sammappadhāna) is especially predominant at the moment of the path;

thus it is said: "Excluding the four right efforts at the moment of the fruit. The remaining thirty-three factors are obtained, but these are so only by way of a figurative approach (pariyāya), not in the primary sense (nippariyāya); this is the intended meaning.
825. "But in the remaining [factors]" refers to the five sections beginning with the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda).

The meaning is that there is no such reduction or expansion as there is in the case of mindfulness and energy—where there is reduction by way of abbreviation, as in "foundations of mindfulness" or "right efforts," and expansion by way of showing divisions, as in "contemplation of the body" and so forth.
There is no such reduction or expansion here.
826. Now, the passage beginning with “Furthermore” (*apica*) is commenced in order to show the divisions as they are applicable to all [the factors] respectively.
Therein, “among them” (*tesu*) refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*).
“In six ways” (*chadhā*) means that they exist in six modes: namely, in one way, two ways, four ways, five ways, eight ways, and nine ways.

"By way of zeal, the basis of psychic power, and so forth": zeal is indeed by way of the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal; consciousness is indeed by way of the basis of psychic power consisting of consciousness;

zest, tranquility, and equanimity are indeed by way of the factors of enlightenment; and intention and the others are indeed by way of the path. Thus, these nine become of one kind. They are fourteen indeed when undivided:
mindfulness, energy, zeal, consciousness, wisdom, faith, concentration, zest, and tranquility.

Equanimity, right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these are fourteen distinct intrinsic phenomena (sabhāvadhammā) when taken together without being conflated by the inclusion of other categories.
The number "fourteen" is stated according to the maximum limit;
however, this is in reference to the arising of consciousness in the path associated with the first jhāna, for in the second jhāna, right intention is absent.
In the third, fourth, and fifth jhānas, there are twelve factors because of the absence of the enlightenment factor of rapture (*pītisambojjhaṅga*).
As for the phrase "classified as thirty-seven," this too is stated by way of the maximum;

however, by way of the minimum, according to the method already explained, there are thirty-six or thirty-five factors in a single moment, because the four predominances (*adhipati*) do not arise together in one moment, and thus only one [of them] occurs at a time.
It should be understood that there are thirty-two [factors] arising from the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda).
To explain how they are divided into thirty-seven, he says: "Because of the accomplishment of their respective functions," and so forth;

the meaning is that each one, by its own nature, accomplishes its particular function—such as the contemplation of the body—in accordance with its own specific power. [This is stated] according to their individual forms.
And it is called "maintenance" (*vutti*) because the factors of enlightenment, such as the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), proceed in their own specific forms without distinction.

"In this context" means in the purification by knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*). But why is the jhāna factor not included among the wings of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*), given that there is no noble path (*ariyamagga*) devoid of jhāna?
It is true that there is none; for that very reason, however, it is not stated thus.

It should be understood that "jhāna is not included among the factors conducive to enlightenment" because jhāna characterized by the contemplation of characteristics is already included by the inclusion of the path.
For it is with reference to this that it was said: "At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna," and so forth.
However, there is no possibility here for jhāna characterized by the contemplation of the object. Another method:
But why is the factor of jhāna not included among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya*)? Is it not the case that there is no noble path (*ariyamagga*) devoid of jhāna?
Nor is it exclusively a preliminary stage like the practice (*paṭipadā*), nor is it an outflow of the path (*magganissanda*) like certain analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*);
rather, it is comprised within the arising of the path-consciousness, since it is said, "he develops supramundane jhāna. [This refers to] the states that accompany both the path and its retinue.

And what about the "states conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya-dhamma*)? It is said: Regarding the statement that "there is no noble path devoid of jhāna," it is not by mere association with the noble path that jhāna acquires the status of being a state conducive to enlightenment;
for if that were so, there would be the over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) of even the nutriment and other factors also being states conducive to enlightenment.
By this, it is shown that the status of being a state conducive to enlightenment consists in being included within the arising of the path-consciousness.
Thus it is shown that [the former] is not the cause.

As for what was stated, "The factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā) are both the path and the surrounding factors (parivāra)," in this context, does the meaning of "surrounding" (parivāra) signify co-arising, or rather the sense of requisites (parikkhāra)?
If the first alternative is held, that has already been refuted.
Now, as for the second point, this must be investigated: In what way is jhāna a requisite of the path while it is occurring?
If it is by way of being a co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) and so forth, then in that case, even contact (*phassa*) and the other factors would follow as being requisites of the path.
If, on the other hand, it is by way of destroying the opposing factors (*paṭipakkhavidhaṃsana*), not all dhammas of jhāna are capable of destroying opposing factors; for indeed—
Investigation and feeling function as direct opposites to certain defiled states.

As for what is stated in the *Peṭaka*—namely, that "pleasure is the opposite of restlessness-and-worry, and investigation is the opposite of doubt"—that is said by way of a figurative method (*pariyāyena*). For pleasure itself is not the direct opposite of restlessness-and-worry; rather, it is the [factor] that is its opposite...

However, [vicāra] is the opposite of concentration by way of being its condition. Vicāra is not the direct opposite of doubt in the same way that wisdom (paññā) or resolve (adhimokkha) are; rather, it is called the opposite because it resembles the opposite.
Likewise, joy (pīti) is not the direct opposite of ill-will (byāpāda) in the same way that non-hatred (adosa) is; nevertheless, it is called the opposite because of its association with non-hatred.

Therefore it was said: "That was stated by way of a figurative method. However, among the factors of jhāna, it is precisely applied thought (vitakka) and concentration (samādhi) that are directly capable of destroying their opposites.
Since this [jhāna] lacks a complete constituent of jhāna capable of destroying its opposite, it has not been included among the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya).
This is because right intention (sammāsaṅkappa) and right concentration (sammāsamādhi) [are already accounted for elsewhere].
And because the factors of jhāna included within the path are intended here, or because the others are also included by virtue of being associated with them, it is stated figuratively in the Pāḷi:
"At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna that is leading to liberation," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the conjunction with the power of emergence.
827. Emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) is emergence from the sign (*nimitta*) and from occurrence (*pavatta*).

The conjunction of powers (*balasamāyoga*) is the state of being associated with the powers of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Since path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*) is also called "insight" in the sense of seeing the specific characteristics of suffering and so forth by way of the full understanding (*pariññā*), clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*), and so on, it is stated as "mundane insight" (*lokiyavipassanā*) for the sake of distinction. For this very reason, he said: "in the sense of emergence..."
“He develops serenity and insight conjoined. Because it has the sign as its object, it “emerges from the sign”;

because it cuts off the process [of existence], it “emerges from the process”—this is the construction. In this context, emergence from the sign is the taking of Nibbāna as the object by relinquishing the sign of formations.
Emergence from the process is the non-arising of future resultant process through the cessation of its cause.
It is the bringing about of the state of non-occurrence. Therefore he said: "Because it does not cut off the origin, one does not emerge from the process.
"From both" (*dubhato*) means from both sides; it is stated thus by adding the letter *da*. Alternatively, *dubhā* is another word with the same meaning as the word *ubhaya*.
"In the sense of seeing" refers to the sense of seeing the Four Noble Truths, characterized by the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññā-abhisamaya*), and so forth.

"By wrong view" means by wrong view of the sixty-two-fold variety. "By the defilements that follow it" means by the defilements such as doubt and so forth that follow that wrong view because it leads to the states of misery (*apāya*).
Regarding the phrase "by the aggregates," here too the word "that which follows it" (*tadanuvattaka*) should be brought in and connected;
and those [aggregates] should be understood as being liable to arise with wrong view and the rest as their conditions. This also applies to the cases beginning with "wrong intention."
One emerges from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; one also emerges from all external signs—thus the text is abbreviated.
Just as wrong view and wrong intention, so too wrong speech and the others should be understood as leading precisely to the states of misery (apāya).
Wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood have volition as their essential nature. Wrong mindfulness is likewise [volitional] in its occurrence; these four...

The aggregates. In the three higher paths, right view emerges from the conceit [of "I am"] which is to be abandoned by each respective path. For that [conceit] is a basis for views because it occurs as "I am.

However, here, instead of mentioning emergence from the wrong path itself, the emergence is stated specifically in terms of the fetters and underlying tendencies (anusaya) to be abandoned by each respective path.
"Subsisting in a subtle state" means having reached a subtle condition; the sense is that they have become attenuated.
828. Having thus shown the emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*), he now says "of the mundane" (*lokiyānañca*) and so forth in order to show the conjunction of powers (*balasamāyoga*).

The power of serenity (*samathabala*) is predominant because of the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*). The power of insight (*vipassanābala*) is predominant because of the supremacy of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) resulting from the cultivation of insight.
They are called "conjoined" (*yuganaddhā*) because they exist in a state of equality, as if bound together by a yoke. Therefore he said:

"In the sense of not overstepping one another" means by way of function (*kicca*) there is neither deficiency nor excess. For that very reason, "conjunction" (*samāyoga*) means a conjunction of equal delimitation (*samapariccheda*).

It is stated as "by defilements accompanied by restlessness" (*uddhaccasahagata-kilesa*) for the purpose of showing the opposites of concentration (*samādhi*); [it refers to those] in which restlessness is predominant.
The intention is "by means of the defilements. "Non-distraction is concentration" means that concentration is the direct opposite of distraction by way of its total eradication.

"Having cessation as its domain" means having Nibbāna as its object. "In the sense of emergence" means by way of emerging from both the sign and the occurrence, through the state of being that which emerges. "Of a single flavor" means having an identical function.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of States to be Abandoned (829):
"Those states" refers to those defiled states (*saṃkilesadhamma*). Among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, they are called "fetters" in the sense of binding and in the sense of constraining;
they are called "defilements" (*kilesa*) in the sense of afflicting or in the sense of burning; and they are called "perversions" (*micchatta*) because their intrinsic nature is wrong.
In the world, those phenomena included within the world are "worldly phenomena" (*lokadhammā*). Stinginess is "stinginess" (*macchariya*), meaning its state or its action.

In the sense of being inverted, they are "perversions" (*vipallāsā*); in the sense of binding, they are "bonds" (*ganthā*). An improper course is "wrong course" (*agati*). They flow out, thus they are "taints" (*āsavā*);
they carry away, thus they are "floods" (*oghā*); in the sense of yoking, they are "fetters" (*yogā*); they obstruct, thus they are "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇāni*). [The nature of] the phenomena...
They are called *parāmāsā* (perversions) because they grasp excessively beyond [the object]; they are called *upādānāni* (clinging) because they take hold intensely;

they are called *anusayā* (latent tendencies) because they lie down (*sentī*) repeatedly (*anu-anu*) within the continuum due to their state of being unabandoned; they are called *malā* (stains) in the sense of making one soiled;

and they are called *akusala-kammapathā* (unwholesome courses of action) because they are unwholesome karmas that serve as the paths for rebirth in happy or miserable destinies, as well as for the pleasure and pain produced therein.

"Cittuppāda" means that which arises as mind; it is a collection of mind and mental factors. By bringing forward the word "unwholesome" (*akusala*), it should be connected thus: "an unwholesome state of mind arising" (*akusalacittuppāda*).

In the phrase "from aggregates to aggregates," this refers to the aggregates of this world [leading] to the aggregates of the next world. For "to whatever extent those" refers to those [defilements] such as lust for form (*rūparāga*) and so forth.
"As long as they proceed and are not cut off, so long there is no cessation and no interruption of these aggregates, fruits, and sufferings.
By this, he clarifies their meaning as fetters (*saṃyojana*). "Above" (*uddhaṃ*) means in the fine-material and immaterial realms, or above [the desire realm] upon the arising of the third path.

They "partake of what is above" (*uddhaṃbhāga*), namely the fine-material and immaterial realms; because they are the cause for the non-interruption of those [realms], [they are called "above-partaking"].
The "benefits" (hitāni) are those pertaining to the higher realms (uddhaṃbhāgiyāni).
To show both meanings—that they are defiled and that they cause defilement—he said, “Because they themselves are defiled,” and so forth.

“Wrong liberation” (micchāvimutti) refers to the wrong liberation that occurs in relation to worldly monuments and the like. “Wrong knowledge” (micchāñāṇa) is indeed delusion (moha), because it proceeds wrongly and perversely through such means as misapprehension, rather than proceeding rightly.

"In the process of the world" means when there is the process of the aggregates (*khandha*). "Having the nature of not ceasing" means because of proceeding from one state to another without interruption by way of merit and demerit. The phrase "gain caused by gain," and so forth, is stated through the metaphorical designation of the cause as the effect.
"Avarice regarding a dwelling" (*āvāsamacchariya*) refers to avarice with respect to a dwelling, or avarice caused by a dwelling.
The word "three" is stated without breaking down the basis; however, if it were stated by breaking it down, there would be twelve.
"Binding" (*ganthana*) means making something bound by way of being a cause; that [binding] is found even in the material body (*rūpakāya*), which is why it is said:

"of both the mental body (*nāmakāya*) and the material body. In this context, the sense of binding should be understood as applying to ill will (*byāpāda*) as well, because it proceeds by way of resentment and grumbling;
for that reason, its status as the fetter of aversion (*paṭigha-saṃyojana*) has been stated.
"By way of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear" means by way of the causes of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear. "That" refers to doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done.
"From flowing" is because they set things in motion. "From trickling" is because they flow out as the impurity of the defilements. "Again, from flowing" is because they pour forth.
By the phrases "in the sense of dragging along" and "in the sense of being difficult to cross," he shows that they are like floods (*ogha*). By way of the object...
He shows that they are "yokes" (*yoga*) in the sense of being joined to suffering—which is defined as non-separation—and in the sense of causing defilement;

this is the meaning. "Of those very same" refers to sensual lust and the rest. For when these operate by way of a stream, like a river, they cause beings who have fallen into that stream to enter the ocean of the states of misery (*apāya*), and they do not allow them to lift their heads out of the ocean of *saṃsāra*, nor do they let go of what has been grasped.
They do not allow the object to be relinquished; having committed such evil that one has fallen into suffering, they again yoke one to the like thereof.
"Of the mind" means of the wholesome mind, specifically of the meditative (jhāna) mind. "Obstruction from the beginning" is *āvaraṇa*.

Having led to the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the defilements, it is an obstruction (*nīvaraṇa*). It is a closing up or a concealing, as if by walls, doors, and so forth; furthermore, that [concealing] [obstructs] the wholesome and other [states].
It should be regarded by way of gathering together, full understanding, and knowing through non-bestowal.

"The intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of each respective phenomenon" refers to the impure nature, etc., of each respective phenomenon such as the body. "An unreal intrinsic nature" refers to an intrinsic nature such as beauty, etc.

"In the sense of being firmly established" means by way of its state of being firmly established. And "firmly established" refers to that which is not shared with others, [namely] of sensual lust and so forth.

The intrinsic nature (sabhāva) must be observed. That by which they were called "latent tendencies" (anusaya) by the Blessed One is their state of being ready to arise when the conditions assemble, due to not having been abandoned by the Path.
Therefore he said: "They indeed lie latent (anusenti) by way of being the cause for the repeated arising of sensual lust and so forth."
He says, "like oil, collyrium, and mud," with reference to their occurrence as things that cause one to be deluded. 830.
"The rest" refers to those who do not go to the states of misery (*apāya*). The connection is that they are subtle and counteract sensual lust and aversion.

By the restrictive phrase "only to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge," the fact of being abandonable by the first knowledge and so forth is excluded. This demonstration of restriction applies elsewhere as well.

Showing that [these states] are to be abandoned, he said, "from another," and so forth. In this context, by the phrase "we shall not make a restriction," it is implied that if no restriction is made, even the state of being subject to abandonment by the lower paths is permitted.
Regarding the phrases "those to be abandoned by greed... up to ...
