those to be abandoned by the fourth knowledge," the intended meaning should be understood as follows: by means of the first knowledge and the others, the states of being subject to rebirth in the woeful planes and so forth are destroyed. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), grossness and subtlety are included.
"Yasa" means retinue.

Although zeal and the other [hindrances] are to be abandoned by the higher paths, nevertheless, because performing what should not be done and failing to do what should be done—which are rooted in them—lead to rebirth in the states of misery, they are to be abandoned by the first path.
As for remorse, which consists of regret regarding what has been done or left undone, whether wholesome or unwholesome, that is to be abandoned here by the third knowledge.

It has been stated. However, regarding that which was said, "One falls into an offense due to being overcome by remorse (*kukkucca*)," it was with reference to that specific kind of remorse that the *Aṭṭhasālinī* states, "Remorse and doubt are abandoned by the path of stream-entry.
Therefore, the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) of these two statements must be understood. In other similar instances as well, the intended meaning should be sought; one should not...

It should be understood that this is to be inferred from the contradiction [in the texts]. Alternatively, it should be known that the fact that remorse (*kukkucca*) is censurable by the first and third knowledges was stated with reference to the abandoning of gross and non-remaining [remorse].

Furthermore, the remorse mentioned in the passages, "Having stayed repeatedly, one should eat alms-food from a guest-house," which was censured by the Blessed One, and "Being full of remorse, he did not accept it," is not an *nīvaraṇa* (hindrance).

Because it arises in an Arahant, what is called "Vinaya-worry" (vinayakukkucca) is merely a semblance of the hindrances; it consists of the investigation as to whether something is "allowable" or "unallowable," and its nature is simply the arising of such a thought-moment.

The underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will remain in a subtle state and are to be abandoned by the third knowledge. As for their coarse forms, however, they are to be abandoned by the second knowledge, according to the method already explained below.
And here, by the inclusion of "arising of consciousness" (cittuppāda), it should be understood that hypocrisy, flattery, deceit, fraud, negligence, stubbornness, hostility, and so forth are included.
831. Regarding the phrase "exertion is fruitless": let exertion be fruitless for the abandoning of past states, since they have already ceased;
but how is it so for future states? For one who does not understand the unerring meaning of those [future states] which will be explained, there is merely the notion of their non-existence.
Having grasped this, he challenges [the opponent]: Even so, the challenge was previously made on the grounds that there is no "fruit" because of the non-existence of those things to be abandoned;
now, however, it concerns abandonment itself. For if abandonment exists, how can there be things to be abandoned? Or if things to be abandoned exist, how can there be abandonment?
That "things to be abandoned exist and abandonment occurs" is a contradiction. Why? Because regarding those things to be abandoned...
Since abandonment is impossible while [defilements] exist, the effort directed toward that end is fruitless, just as light is fruitless when darkness remains present simultaneously.
Moreover, if abandonment were somehow possible, it would follow that the cultivation of the path is defiled, because the object to be abandoned and the abandoner would exist simultaneously.
Or else, one would have to accept that defilements are dissociated from the mind, according to those who maintain that formations are dissociated from consciousness.

The intention is that it is like [the relationship] of dissociated formations (*vippayutta-saṅkhāra*). However, showing that this case here is just as it is according to the mere opinion of those proponents, he said:
"And there is no such thing as a present defilement (*kilesa*) that is dissociated from consciousness (*citta-vippayutta*).
For immaterial phenomena (*arūpa-dhamma*), existing by way of having a single basis (*ekavatthu*) and so forth, and included within the three moments, are "present."
How could they be called dissociated from the mind? Therefore, there is no such thing as dissociation for the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Individual" (*āveṇika*) means not shared; the intention is that [these] arise by themselves and are not recorded in the Canon (*pāḷi*). For the connection is: "it is rejected in the Canon itself.
This refers to the person (*puggala*). "If" (*hañci*) means "if."

"Bound" (*vinibaddha*) means having a mind made rigid by conceit (*māna*). "Misapprehended" (*parāmaṭṭha*) means wrongly adhered to. "Firmly established" (*thāmagata*) refers to defilements that have become firmly rooted, meaning the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) have reached a state of stability.

For this reason, there is no cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*); because the abandonment of defilements is not tenable at any of the three times, and defilements exist across these three times, therefore there is no cultivation of the path.
The meaning is that there is no task to be accomplished by her. This is a refutation of the fourfold negation stated in the passage beginning with “For there is no cultivation of the path.
One should connect this by bringing forward the words “For it is in the Pāḷi itself,” and so forth.
“In the same way” means just as, when the root of a young tree is cut before its fruit has been produced, those fruits which would have arisen in the future are prevented from arising.

Just as things that do not arise due to cutting [off their causes] are said to be "destroyed," even so, when the development of the Path is absent, those defilements fit to arise are called "abandoned" because they do not arise through the development of the Path; this is how the application of the simile should be understood.
"Arising" refers to the aggregates possessing arising, spoken of by way of the headword "arising. "In non-arising" means in Nibbāna.
"Those that have not yet arisen do not arise; therefore, they are said to be abandoned. This negation made by the opponent—"there is no abandoning of defilements"—is refuted with "No, it is not so.

He shows that one cannot say "one abandons past defilements," and so forth, because those [defilements] have neither arisen and passed away, nor will they arise, nor are they currently arising. "By the cessation of the cause": [this refers to the cessation of the cause].
From the cessation of the defilements that are the causes of suffering. "Cessation of suffering" means the cessation of suffering that would otherwise arise in the future.
Accumulation (*āyūhana*), which is the cause for the arising and occurrence [of suffering], is understood here by way of present existence. 832.
By this—that is, by the statement beginning with "The unborn do not arise"—[is meant] the pentad of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) which serves as the object of insight (*vipassanā*).
Those who have obtained the state of existing on a plane are "plane-obtainers" (*bhūmiladdha*), just as one is called a "fire-obtainer" (*aggiāhita*);

the meaning is "those who have obtained a plane. It is said that because they lack the stability of being presently occurring and so forth, they are indeed called "arisen from having obtained a plane" (*bhūmiladdhuppanna*).

833. That which has departed after having been experienced and having come into being is "departed from what has become" (*bhūtāpagata*). For those things that have been experienced and have come into being [are so designated] by virtue of the commonality of their "having become" (*bhūtatā*).

They are expressed by the word *anubhūta*. For it is the common noun itself that is qualified by the prefix. And because there is no desire to express the object (*karman*) [of the experience], the word *anubhūta* should be understood as denoting the experiencer (*anubhāvaka*).
By way of grasping various alternatives, one experiences the flavor of the object through greed and so forth, as well as through their opposites—the unwholesome and the wholesome.
But the result (*vipāka*) does not [experience it] because it is projected by the force of karma, nor does [the mind-element experience it].

This is because functional states (*kiriyā*) are extremely weak when they arise in those with root-causes (*sahetuka*), and because they are exceedingly tranquil when arising in one whose defilements are exhausted (*khīṇakilesa*) and who possesses the sixfold equanimity.

Furthermore, in the first method, it was stated as "departed from the elements" (*bhūtāpagata*) by way of intention, referring specifically to the wholesome and unwholesome. That which [was said] for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome states...
In the phrase "for the stability of wholesome states," by taking the word "arisen," the abandoning of things similar to it and their increase are stated.

And in the latter method, by drawing in both the wholesome and the unwholesome through the word "and" (*ca*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*) are stated with the intention of expressing their state of having passed away after having existed.
That which has arisen by way of making room for maturation is the past.
And the karma has begun to arise from that, while the result is yet future;
it is called "arisen by way of making room" (*okāsakatuppanna*) based on two meanings: "room has been made by this" and "room has been made for this.
This refers to what is understood as "arisen" even without the word *uppanna*, with reference to which it was said: "I do not [say], monks, of intentional karmas... and so forth.
"In those various planes" means in the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) comprised of the personal existences of humans, devas, and so forth.

It is "unabandoned" because it has not been brought to a state where its future arising in this or that continuum is precluded. Indeed, precisely because it is unabandoned, there arises the conventional designation "it exists," as it cannot be said that it does not exist.
834. In order to dispel the doubt, "What is the plane? Or who has attained the plane?", the passage beginning with "And here" is commenced.

By the phrase "having become the object of insight," he shows that the aggregates are not fully understood (*apariññāta*); it does not merely indicate their status as objects, since that is already established by the inclusion of the three planes (*tebhūmaka*).
For it is the aggregates, when not fully understood, that are intended here as the "plane" of the defilements.

"When the aggregates have become the basis" means when they serve as the foundation. "By way of being an object" means by way of making them an object. The intention is that this applies even to past and future [objects], let alone the present.
"That" refers to that collection of defilements existing within another continuum. The connection is:

"If, merely by making it an object in another continuum, it were to be said that [the defilement] has 'gained ground' (bhūmiladdha) from that [other continuum]. "Of that" refers to the collection of defilements.
Because they would fall within the continuity of another, no one at all could abandon the root of existence (*bhavamūla*).

For the intention is that what has reached the ground is called "latent" (*anusayita*). "By way of the basis" means by way of the place of arising; that is, in whichever existence (*bhava*) or in whichever continuity (*santāna*).
They are called "not fully understood" because they have not yet become a ground for full understanding. "From their arising onwards" refers to those aggregates (*khandha*).
From the moment of their arising, because there is no other cause except for the state of the defilements being unabandoned,

the class of defilements lies latent within those aggregates; therefore, that latent class of defilements should be understood as "having gained a footing" by way of that very sense of being unabandoned, which is designated as *anusaya*.
835. Furthermore, among the aggregates that have become the "ground," not all serve as the basis for all;
rather, there is a distinction. To demonstrate this, he said, "For whom, in which," and so forth. Therein, "for whom" means for whichever person.

"In which" refers to those aggregates—which, despite the commonality of their internal nature—are divided into categories such as the past and so on, or the sense-sphere and so on. It is precisely these [that are the basis].
Just as the aggregates are so disposed. But do these defilements, while taking an object, adhere by delimiting it one by one?
Since those very aggregates are said to be the basis (*vatthu*) for those defilements, there is no occurrence of the adherence of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) by way of delimiting the basis.
However, according to the distinctions of the past and so forth, or the sense-sphere realm and so forth, they adhere in whatever way they have been delimited.
Regarding the object (vatthu), that which is the state of the defilements not yet abandoned proceeds as if it were delimited; thus it is said, "in the past aggregates," and so forth.
By this, he shows that since [the defilement] has acquired its plane by way of the object, there may be a differentiation of it according to the differentiation of the object.
For it is precisely because of its being thus established that there is such a statement as: "A certain person of a greedy nature tasted that earth of flavor with his finger."

It clarifies that the latent tendencies such as craving for flavor (*rasataṇhā*), which have been latent within the aggregates of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), have transcended the aggregates of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*) and have once again become based upon the aggregates of the sense-sphere.
Therefore, he said: "In the same way, in the aggregates of the sense-sphere," and so forth.
And just as they proceed here having transcended the aggregates of the fine-material and immaterial spheres, so too [they proceed] in the aggregates of the sense-sphere.
Having transcended [the lower realms], there is occurrence; thus he said, "This is the method regarding the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

Furthermore, the state of underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of the defilements is inferred by way of their obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and their overcoming, because in the absence of those [obsessions], they are absent.

For one whose underlying tendencies toward a particular object have been abandoned, that object-base has been transcended by him through full understanding (*pariññā*); so how could these [tendencies] exist?
The phrase "sotāpannādīsu pana" and so forth is stated in order to show the conventional designation of the stages (*bhūmi*).

Here, "defilements rooted in the round of existence" (*vaṭṭamūlakakilesā*) refers to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), not ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*). "Whatever" refers to anything distinguished by volition and mental factors, or by the body and so forth.
"Iti" means "thus"; the intended meaning is "because the underlying tendencies have not been abandoned. "Assa" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*). These, moreover, are the underlying tendencies.
Showing that even while they underlie their respective objects as delimited by way of the past and so forth, or the sense-sphere and so forth,
those various underlying tendencies nevertheless underlie the five aggregates of clinging by making them their object without distinction, he said:
"This is the root of that round," and so forth.
836. Now, in order to clarify that matter by means of an analogy through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is said:

“Like the essence of the earth,” and so forth. The “essence of the earth” (*pathavī-rasa*) is the sap of the earth together with its constituent parts, which serves as the condition for trees, shrubs, creepers, and the like.

The same principle applies to the essence of water (*āpo-rasa*). A “branch” (*sākhā*) refers to a small branch; a “twig” (*pasākho*) is a spreading branch (*viṭapa*). “The lineage of trees” (*rukkha-paveṇi*) means the succession of trees from one to another.
"Continuing the stream" means connecting one after another in succession.

"Maṇḍūkakaṇṭaka" (frog-thorn) is what some call the "macchakaṇṭaka" (fish-thorn). "Without clinging" means one who has abandoned the four kinds of clinging, or one who does not grasp at anything among form and the other aggregates. 837.
Here, "manifestation" (*samudācāra*) means having attained its own acquisition; thus it is said to be "arisen as a manifestation" when it possesses the three moments.
He said: "That which has arisen in the present is itself what has arisen as active manifestation.
"Even though it does not arise in the prior stage" means even though it does not arise during the initial rounds of the impulsion (javana) that proceed when the object has come into range.

"Because it has been seized" means because it has been mounted upon and grasped by improper attention (ayoniso-manasikāra); the meaning is that it has been firmly grasped. "In the subsequent stage" means in a later [moment].

"At a certain time" means at another time. "Arising exclusively" means that when the collection of conditions is present, [the state] arises there with necessity because of the occurrence of improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*).
"In the village of Kalyāṇī" refers to a village of that name.
It is said that in Rohaṇa, that village was called by that name because it was a place where beautiful women were born. "Not having entered into the continuity of consciousness" means...

It negates the state of being present (*paccuppannatam*). By the phrase "due to the absence of a cause that would prevent its arising," it shows that the designation "arisen" applies to that which is not suppressed, because it is capable of arising when the conditions are present and the collection of conditions is complete.

But is it not the case that even what is arisen without having been eradicated is simply capable of arising when conditions are present? True, this is so; however, [the distinction is made] on account of the specific nature of its abandonment.

However, there is this distinction between them: just as mindfulness that has not been suppressed, not eradicated, and has arisen by way of its own plane is capable of arising when the conditions assemble, so too is that which has arisen by way of having seized an object;
thus, all three types are said to be included within the category of "arisen by way of its own plane.

(838) Unwholesome [states] that have arisen by way of being dissociated from the primary elements are not to be abandoned because they are past; likewise, certain [states] that have arisen by way of making room [for other states].

The other [fetters] are not to be abandoned; the remaining two [fetters] possess the state of being present during the three moments [of the path]. Therefore, he said, "because they are excluded from the paths.
"By any" means by any one among the four types of path-knowledge. "Of that" refers to the aforementioned fourfold [defilement] that has arisen.
"Destroying its state of having arisen" means destroying its fitness for arising by bringing about the quality of non-arising (anuppatti-dhammata).

The inclusion of the term "mundane" (*lokiya*) is made because mundane knowledge first abandons [defilements] according to its own power, and subsequently supramundane knowledge (*lokuttara-ñāṇa*) abandons them.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Functions of Full Understanding, etc. (839).
"At the time of the realization of the truths" (*saccābhisamaya-kāle*) means at the moment of penetrating the four Noble Truths. "Are stated" (*vuttāni*).
These have been stated in such passages as “Suffering is to be fully understood,” and so forth, and “He who, monks, sees suffering,” and so forth.
By “in accordance with their true nature” is meant by way of their non-erroneous nature.

Having said, “They are to be known,” the commentary first shows the method of knowing them by way of a simile according to the manner already explained, beginning with the words, “For it has been said.”
In this regard, one might raise the objection: "How can four functions of a single knowledge occur simultaneously, as in the passage beginning 'just as a lamp' and so forth?
For nothing such as that is seen in the world, nor is there any scriptural authority for it.

Keeping such an internal objection in mind, it is said: "By the clear realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*). This refers to the act of knowing by way of delimiting [the object] without remainder.

One realizes through penetration; that is, one penetrates by way of non-delusion. "By the realization of abandoning" means one realizes through penetration characterized as the abandoning of eradication, due to non-delusion.

"By the realization of the development of the path" means one realizes the knowledge of the path—the remaining factors of the path such as right intention—by way of the realization of development through the conditionality of co-nascence and so forth.
One realizes [this] by means of that which has arisen from prior-stage development.
He realizes the Eightfold Path through penetration, which is known as the cultivation of the Noble Path;
he penetrates it without delusion. For the knowledge of the path, while destroying delusion regarding associated states, also destroys its own delusion.
"Cessation" means Nibbāna. "By the realization of direct experience" means by that which is termed making [the truth] manifest to oneself.
"By penetration. "Attains" means he reaches. This attainment is a penetration by seeing; thus it is said, "he sees, he penetrates.

By the phrase "he penetrates cessation... [etc.]," it is explained according to its logical connection that through the penetration of the object, one penetrates the Truth of Cessation alone, while through the penetration of non-delusion, one penetrates all four Truths via path-knowledge.
To establish that there is a single penetration even by means of the scripture (*āgama*), it was stated, "And this has also been said," and so forth.

By the phrase "all that is to be known," the application based on the truth of suffering and the other truths— such as the passage beginning, "He who sees the origin of suffering sees suffering as well"— is included.
And this was not stated with reference to seeing at a different time; rather, in order to show that it is indeed a single penetration, another passage from the Sutta is cited:
"The knowledge of one who possesses the path is knowledge regarding suffering... [and so on]... the way leading to cessation. For likewise it is said:
"Friend, whoever sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering... [and so on]... the practice."

Thus, in order to establish that meaning by investigating whether one who possesses the vision of one truth can simultaneously possess the vision of other truths, the Venerable Gavampati Thera spoke [the verse beginning with] "he sees"; and he has applied the vision of each of the three truths individually.

Otherwise, in the case of gradual realization (*kramābhisamaya*), since what was previously seen would not be seen again, the vision of suffering and so forth would not occur for one who is seeing the origin and the rest.

Furthermore, it might be argued that if [the path] were to be repeated, then since every subsequent vision would be surpassed by a further vision, there would be no cessation of seeing at all. Because it serves as a basis and a cause, the full understanding of suffering (*dukkha-pariññā*) is like the kindling of a fire; because it destroys its opposite, the abandoning of the origin (*samudaya-ppahāna*) is like the dispelling of darkness; and because it nourishes the light of knowledge, the development of the path (*magga-bhāvanā*)— [The text continues: ...is like the rising of the sun. Because it brings about the attainment of the fruit, the realization of cessation (*nirodha-sacchikiriyā*) is like the arrival of the harvest. Because it is the supreme state of security, the cultivation of the fruit (*phala-bhāvanā*) is like the enjoyment of the harvest. Because it is the supreme state of peace, the final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*) is like the total extinction of the fire. Thus, the sequence of the truths is established according to their respective functions. As for the order of the faculties (*indriya*), they are listed first because they are the primary factors for the attainment of the path. Among them, faith (*saddhā*) comes first because it precedes the others in the process of entering the path. Energy (*viriya*) follows because one who has faith exerts energy. Mindfulness (*sati*) follows because one who exerts energy maintains mindfulness. Concentration (*samādhi*) follows because one who is mindful attains concentration. Wisdom (*paññā*) follows because one who is concentrated discerns with wisdom. This is the sequence of the faculties according to their functional priority. As for the sequence of the powers (*bala*), they follow the same order as the faculties, but they are called "powers" when they are unshakable by their opposites. This concludes the explanation of the sequence of the truths, faculties, and powers. Now, regarding the sequence of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*): mindfulness (*sati*) is placed first because it is the foundation for all the other factors. Investigation of phenomena (*dhamma-vicaya*) follows because one who is mindful investigates phenomena. Energy (*viriya*) follows because investigation of phenomena leads to exertion. Joy (*pīti*) follows because one who exerts energy experiences joy. Tranquility (*passaddhi*) follows because one who experiences joy becomes tranquil. Concentration (*samādhi*) follows because one who is tranquil attains concentration.

Equanimity (*upekkhā*) follows last because one who is concentrated dwells in equanimity. This is the sequence of the factors of enlightenment according to their functional priority. As for the sequence of the path factors (*magga-aṅga*): right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is placed first because it is the precursor to the rest of the path. Right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*) follows because it is the mental concomitant of right view. Right speech (*sammā-vācā*), right action (*sammā-kammanta*), and right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) follow because they constitute the virtue aggregate (*sīla-kkhandha*). Right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*), right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*), and right concentration (*sammā-samādhi*) follow because they constitute the concentration aggregate (*samādhi-kkhandha*). This is the sequence of the path factors according to their functional priority. Thus, the sequence of the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and path factors is established. As for the sequence of the fruits (*phala*): stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) is placed first because it is the first fruit to be attained. Once-returning (*sakadāgāmi*) follows because it is the second fruit. Non-returning (*anāgāmi*) follows because it is the third fruit. Arahantship (*arahatta*) follows last because it is the fourth and final fruit. This is the sequence of the fruits according to their order of attainment. Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, and fruits is established. As for the sequence of the knowledges (*ñāṇa*): knowledge of the meaning of the truths (*sacca-attha-ñāṇa*) is placed first because it is the foundation for all other knowledges. Knowledge of the penetration of the truths (*sacca-paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) follows because it is the penetration of those very truths. Knowledge of the path and fruit (*magga-phala-ñāṇa*) follows because it is the realization of the path and its fruits. Knowledge of the reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*) follows because it reviews what has been realized. Knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa*) follows last because it is the ultimate knowledge. This is the sequence of the knowledges according to their functional priority. Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, fruits, and knowledges is established. This concludes the explanation of the sequence of the Dhamma. As for the sequence of the persons (*puggala*): the person of dull faculties (*mudindriya*) is placed first because they enter the path slowly. The person of medium faculties (*majjhindriya*) follows because they enter the path moderately. The person of sharp faculties (*tikkhindriya*) follows last because they enter the path quickly. This is the sequence of the persons according to their faculties. Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, fruits, knowledges, and persons is established. This concludes the explanation of the sequence of the Dhamma. As for the sequence of the teachings (*desanā*): the teaching on the truths (*sacca-desanā*) is placed first because it is the foundation for all other teachings. The teaching on the faculties (*indriya-desanā*) follows because it shows the means for attaining the truths. The teaching on the powers (*bala-desanā*) follows because it shows the unshakability of those means. The teaching on the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga-desanā*) follows because it shows the development of the path. The teaching on the path (*magga-desanā*) follows because it shows the actual path to be traversed. The teaching on the fruits (*phala-desanā*) follows because it shows the goal to be reached. The teaching on the knowledges (*ñāṇa-desanā*) follows last because it shows the final realization. This is the sequence of the teachings according to their functional priority. Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, fruits, knowledges, persons, and teachings is established. This concludes the explanation of the sequence of the Dhamma. As for the sequence of the texts (*pāḷi*): the Sutta Piṭaka is placed first because it is the foundation for all other texts. The Vinaya Piṭaka follows because it is the means for the preservation of the Suttas. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka follows last because it is the analytical exposition of both the Suttas and the Vinaya. This is the sequence of the texts according to their functional priority.

Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, fruits, knowledges, persons, teachings, and texts is established. This concludes the explanation of the sequence of the Dhamma. As for the sequence of the recitations (*saṅgīti*): the First Council (*pathama-saṅgīti*) is placed first because it was the first recitation. The Second Council (*dutiya-saṅgīti*) follows because it was the second recitation. The Third Council (*tatiya-saṅgīti*) follows last because it was the third recitation. This is the sequence of the recitations according to their chronological order. Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, fruits, knowledges, persons, teachings, texts, and recitations is established. This concludes the explanation of the sequence of the Dhamma. As for the sequence of the lineages (*vaṃsa*): the lineage of the Buddhas (*buddha-vaṃsa*) is placed first because they are the source of the Dhamma. The lineage of the Dhamma (*dhamma-vaṃsa*) follows because it is the teaching of the Buddhas. The lineage of the Sangha (*saṅgha-vaṃsa*) follows last because it is the community that upholds the Dhamma. This is the sequence of the lineages according to their functional priority. Thus, the sequence of the truths, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, fruits, knowledges, persons, teachings, texts, recitations, and lineages is established. The similarity to the destruction of light is as follows: in whatever manner the realization of cessation occurs through each respective path, in that same manner there comes to be the exhaustion of the moisture of the defilements; thus, the similarity between the realization of cessation and the exhaustion of moisture is stated by way of figurative designation of the cause.

840. *Obhāseti* means "it illuminates" or "it makes manifest. *Kilesapaṭippassaddhiṃ* refers to that which has become the subsiding of the defilements because of the state of the pacification of all the distress and feverish agitation (*pariḷāha*) of the defilements.

841. *Appeti* means "he attains. Because it brings about the crossing over the shore of the self-identity (*sakkāya*) through the full understanding of suffering (*dukkhapariññā*), it is like the abandoning of the near shore; because the cultivation of the path (*maggabhāvanā*) brings along the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), it is like the carrying of a load.
842. That which possesses knowledge of occurrence (*pavatta*) is "one with knowledge of occurrence," namely, the Path (*magga*). Of this Path...

*Taṭhaṭṭhena* means by way of its true nature; the meaning is: by way of its non-erroneous nature such as oppression (*pīḷanā*) and so forth. *Ekapaṭivedhāni* means those aspects that are to be penetrated all at once.
Regarding what should be said about "the sense of oppression of suffering" and so forth, that has already been stated below in the commentary on the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*).
*Ekasaṅgahitāni* means comprised by one alone. By what? By the sense of being thus (*tathaṭṭhena*), which is to say, by the sense of truth (*saccaṭṭhena*). That which...
The passage beginning with “comprehended as one” (*ekasaṅgahita*) is a demonstration of the single penetration of knowledge.

For although path-knowledge takes only cessation as its object, it proceeds by penetrating and making manifest that very reality (*saccaṭṭha*)—which consists in the true nature of suffering and the rest, free from distortion—as it actually is, by means of destroying the delusion that conceals it.
Consequently, [the aspects of] oppression and so forth [arise] subsequently.
All sixteen aspects of the truths present themselves exactly as they are to the Noble One, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
(843) "Meanings" (*attha*) refers to the modes (*ākāra*) that have received this conventional designation because they are to be sought after (*araṇīya*) by means of knowledge.

"By way of seeing other truths" means by way of seeing the remaining truths, such as the truth of origin and so forth. "By way of manifestation" means by way of their becoming evident. This is what is meant:

Those aspects which manifest in relation to suffering and the rest by way of their intrinsic nature and by way of the vision of the other truths are only these four—namely, oppression and so forth—and thus only sixteen have been stated, and no others. How is it to be understood that this is the meaning intended here?
To this he says: “In this context, what is knowledge regarding suffering? and so on. By this he shows that because [the aspects] are listed individually in the Canon...

Knowledge of the truths (saccañāṇa) has been described both by way of making them its object and by way of the accomplishment of its function; therefore, it is understood that "the aspects of the truths become manifest through their intrinsic nature and through the seeing of one truth in another.

Since the manifestation [of aspects] occurs through the accomplishment of the function, and thus resembles the act of seeing itself, that [seeing] is not mentioned here; rather, only the other [knowledge] is intended.
Demonstrating this, he said, “In that regard,” and so forth. “In that regard” means in those two modes of seeing.
“Accumulated” (āyūhita) means produced by way of a mass. For whatever is called “dependently arisen,” all of it is produced only through a combination [of factors].
“Conditioned” (saṅkhata) means made by coming together and uniting through other conditions. “Heaped up” (rāsikata) means formed into a pile. It is indeed manifold.

For that which has arisen through conditions, being produced all at once, is as if gathered into a heap by its own conditions. Therefore (*tasmā*): because it is accumulated (*āyūhitatta*) by way of origination (*samudaya*).
*Assa*: of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). It removes the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-santāpa*) in whichever continuum (*santāna*) it arises;
it is itself very cool due to the absence of the burning heat of the defilements. Thus, the sense of "cooling" (*santa*) becomes manifest.
Showing that, by means of sublime vision, the state of being non-sublime in others is likewise revealed, he said, "of the Venerable One," and so forth.
For that which is of an unchanging nature and eternal essence, there is nothing at all to be said, because its mode of manifestation as the opposite [of suffering] is established as happiness.
The sense of "source" (nidāna) is manifested in the sense that "this gives it [the fruit]. By way of its opposite, it stands as the obstacle of bondage.
Showing the mode of manifestation, he said: “Of that which has become dissociated,” and so forth. The sense of being bound by the defilements and sufferings is the sense of bondage (*saṃyoga*).
The sense of being obstructed within the prison of *saṃsāra* is the sense of impediment (*palibodha*).

For one who has become non-secluded due to the company of defilements and the like, the sense of seclusion (*viveka*) is the state of seclusion from the substrates of existence (*upadhivivekatā*), which is the state of being detached from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
Regarding the "unconditioned nature": although the Noble Path possesses such a marvelous and extraordinary nature, it is indeed conditioned;

thus, the fact that this alone is the one unconditioned thing makes the unconditioned nature of cessation clearly evident. Suffering is like poison because it is subject to death, while Nibbāna is the deathless, acting as its antidote.

“Path”: although it has attained the state of being cultivated and appears as something subtle and peaceful, and although it is characterized by attachment, this is not the origin or cause for the attainment of Nibbāna.
By the method explained in the *Ñāṇadassana* (Knowledge and Vision) regarding what is the path and what is not the path, the fact that this Noble Path is the cause becomes manifest.
By the vision of cessation (*nirodha*), [the nature of] that which is exceedingly subtle and supremely profound...
By the vision of the truth of cessation. Therefore he said, “extremely subtle,” and so forth.

“By the vision of suffering” means by the vision of the truth of suffering, which possesses an even greater disadvantage due to its having reached an extreme state of peril. Its meaning as “sovereignty” (ādhipateyya) is because it is the opposite of that [suffering].

Therefore he said, “afflicted by many diseases... like a state of excellence. Thus, these [meanings] are [explained] according to their respective order through positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (byatireka).
And the modes of manifestation regarding the truths have been analyzed.

"Of each one" means of each individual meaning; this is said with reference to the meanings of oppression, accumulation, escape, and departure. "Of three and three" refers to the meanings of the conditioned and so forth.
As for those proponents who [assert] "realization through various [means]," they mean realization by means of various types of knowledge.
The meaning is that the four truths are penetrated by various knowledges at different moments.

For if there were a separate realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four truths for the knowledge of the path, it would follow that the three fetters and so forth—which are to be abandoned by the first path and the others through the vision of suffering and so on—are abandoned only partially.
And if that were the case, it would entail the undesirable consequence of being only a partial stream-enterer and so forth.
Furthermore, immediately following each respective vision, there must be its corresponding fruit;

thus, as with the paths, there would be four fruits corresponding to the subsiding of the specific defilements to be abandoned by each. If that were the case, it would follow that one could be a "stream-enterer" and so forth only in part.
Moreover, if there were a separate realization for the knowledge of the path, one would see suffering through one kind of knowledge [and the path through another].
If origination were seen by one [cognition], cessation by another, and the path by yet another, then the function of the path would remain incomplete.
For the vision of the path involves two possibilities: either it is the vision of that [path] by that very same [cognition], or by another.
Of these, the first alternative is not tenable, because it is impossible for a cognition to operate upon itself. Indeed, a finger-tip cannot...
It is possible to grasp that very [path]. Otherwise, there would follow the fallacy of instability: "That by which one sees the path is itself the path;

and that by which one sees that [instrument] is also the path. Therefore, because of the single realization (*ekābhisamaya*), only the aforementioned penetration through non-delusion (*asammoha-paṭivedha*) is appropriate.
Furthermore, this pertains to the two truths—the truth to be delimited and the truth to be completely severed—concerning which [the path] proceeds.
Limitation and eradication are not possible for the knowledge of the path because there is no escape from it.
For the full understanding of suffering and the abandoning of its origin cannot be accomplished by a knowledge that takes the truths of suffering and its origin as its object.
However, they can be accomplished by means of a knowledge that takes Nibbāna as its object, thereby shattering delusion regarding those two truths as well.
Only a single realization (ekābhisamaya) is logical. However, since this matter has already appeared in the Canon, it is said: "Their answer is stated precisely in the Abhidhamma, in the Kathāvatthu.
This concludes the commentary on the discussion concerning the various classifications such as full understanding (pariññā).
845. The meaning of *abhiññāpaññā* (specialized wisdom) and so forth has already been stated above.

Furthermore, they are "well-known" (*abhijñāta*) because they are known by means of a highly distinguished wisdom consisting of that born of hearing, that born of reflection, and certain [levels] of that born of cultivation. Their ground is unique because it is not within the domain of those who possess full understanding through penetration (*pariññantara*).
For there is no occurrence of the full understanding by scrutinization (*tīraṇapariññā*) and so forth by way of discerning name-and-form and grasping conditions.
846. Even conformity knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*) proceeds by taking conditioned phenomena as its object precisely through the aspects of impermanence and so forth;
how much more so, then, [the stages] beginning with reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*). Therefore, he said: "Up to the stage of conformity, which is unique (*āveṇika*).

Although, in this context, the stage of the full understanding of scrutiny (*tīraṇapariññā*) also provides an opportunity for the full understandings of knowing and abandoning (*ñātappahānapariññā*), the term "unique" is used because, while the full understanding of scrutiny performs its function there preeminently, the others do not.

847. In the non-figurative sense, the full understanding of abandoning (*pahānapariññā*) is the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*); thus it is said, "The stage extends as far as the knowledge of the path.

This is what is intended here; that is, at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), when considering its function, this full understanding of abandoning is intended here because the other types of full understanding have that as their purpose.
Therefore he says, "Or because," and so forth.
“For the sake of that alone” means for the sake of full understanding as abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*) alone. Alternatively, “for the sake of that alone” means for the sake of abandonment alone.
Or alternatively, “for the sake of that alone” means for the sake of the Path (*magga*) alone.

For full understanding as the known (*ñāta*) and as scrutinized (*tīrita*) occurs only for the purpose of attaining the Path. This is because, by necessity, things are both known and scrutinized; for there can be no abandoning in the absence of the states of being known and scrutinized.
And because the state of being known and fully understood is established through the accomplishment of abandonment.

For when the knowledge of the path proceeds by way of the clear comprehension of suffering, it is said that it penetrates its general characteristic as well as its specific characteristic, owing to the destruction of the delusion that conceals them. Therefore he said: "The threefold full comprehension... should be understood."

"Like full understanding" indicates the commonality of being threefold; it does not indicate the commonality of being abandoned by full understanding, because suppression-abandonment (*vikkhambhanappahāna*) is not the function of final knowledge (*ariyapaññā*).

Just as sensual desire and the other [hindrances] do not remain by obsessing over the mind, so the prevention of such obsession—the making of non-occurrence—is suppression; suppression itself is abandonment.

It is abandonment by suppression. "Because it is manifest" means because it is manifest even to others in such ways as, "This person has a mind free from ill will, is devoid of sloth and torpor," and so forth.
The statement, "They do not suddenly overwhelm the mind," is said with reference to jhāna that has merely been attained;
however, when the jhāna is well-developed and mastered, they do not overwhelm it even up until the final moment of consciousness.

Alternatively, "even in the preliminary stage" (*pubbabhāge*) refers to the preliminary practice for the attainment of jhāna. "Even in the subsequent stage" (*pacchābhāge*) refers to one who, having attained jhāna, is occupied with other duties.
"Applied thought and so forth" (*vitakkādayo*) refers to applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), bliss (*sukha*), perception of form (*rūpasaññā*), and so on.
These are the adversaries of the second jhāna and the others; they are suppressed precisely when the second jhāna and the rest are entered. However, for one who has merely emerged from them...
However, they proceed by way of the limited (paritta) consciousness itself, because of emerging [from cessation].
The phrase “as darkness by means of a lamp” is stated for the purpose of showing that [cessation] has been abandoned by its opposite;
for a lamp is the opposite of darkness, whereas striking with a jar is not the opposite of moss, being merely [an agent of its removal].

It merely effects the prevention of their occurrence. Therefore, even though there is no direct opposition [to the jhāna factors], that illustration is even more appropriately applicable to the suppression of applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth in the second jhāna and beyond.

The phrase "by means of that which is a constituent part of insight" is stated here for the purpose of showing the abandonment through the factor of predominance (*adhikatadaṅgappahāna*). For the abandonment through the factor of predominance occurs also by means of the purification of virtue (*sīlavisodhanādi*) and other such methods.

"It certainly exists. By the factor of knowledge means by the cause designated as "knowledge. Abandoning a factor by means of that same factor is "abandonment by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅgappahāna*).

When the body, designated as the five aggregates, exists, or when there is a view regarding that very [body], it is the "personality-belief" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), which is the view of self described in such passages as "one regards form as self," and so forth. It has sixteen bases and eight bases.
And "the stain of doubt" (*kaṅkhāmala*) is the stain consisting of doubt. "Of the grasping at a collection" means:

by means of the contemplation of groups (*kalāpasammasana*), one abandons the grasping at a collection that occurs as "self" and "belonging to self" by including it within the eleven instances and seeing the aggregates through the method of dispersal.
"Of the perception of gratification" means: of the false perception that occurs by way of finding gratification in the five aggregates. "Of non-reflection" means...
[It is] of delusion, which is the opposite of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*). "Non-contemplation" means the absence of contemplation.
The grasping at formations as permanent and so forth is a "grasping contrary to the truth," because it opposes the attainment of the Truth of the Path.

Furthermore, they say that perceiving what is fraught with danger as being without danger, and perceiving what is without danger as being fraught with danger, is also "grasping contrary to the truth."

Having thus shown the abandonment by means of that factor (*tadaṅgappahāna*) through the sequence of purification, the passage beginning with “Or else, whatever... is now stated in order to show it also by way of the eighteen great insights (*mahāvipassanā*). Therein, the connection is “or else, whatever... abandonment.
(850) It has already been stated [in the *Visuddhimagga*] by such passages as “He contemplates the entire field of formations as impermanent,” and so forth.
“Solid grasping” (*ghanaggahaṇa*) refers to the perception of solidity (*ghana-saññā*) by way of continuity, collection, function, and object; [the phrase refers to] “of that perception of solidity.”

"Devotion to cessation": by means of this, it is the wisdom that functions by way of resolving upon the cessation of formations belonging to the three periods of time, having seen only that cessation.

"Of the accumulation": of the volitional formation. "Each respective delimitation": each respective delimitation such as taking up, laying down, and so forth. "Seeing the occurrence in another manner":
seeing the occurrence in a different mode prior to and subsequent to the aforementioned delimitations; that is, seeing the occurrence of specific states.
"Perception of stability" (*dhuvasaññā*) means the grasping of a state of firmness.
"Adherence to the apprehension of essence" (*sārādānābhinivesa*) means the adherence to grasping an essence in things that are essenceless.

Delusion (*sammoha*) is the confusion arising from doubt and wrong knowledge; that itself is an adherence, hence "adherence through delusion" (*sammohābhinivesa*). The grasping of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) as a refuge and protection is "adherence to a home" (*ālayābhinivesa*); in terms of meaning, it is craving for existence (*bhavanikanti*).

Because it proceeds in such a way that the mind, having released itself from formations, leaps into the turning-away (vivatta) of Nibbāna, equanimity regarding formations and conformity (anuloma) are called "contemplation of turning away" (vivattānupassanā).
The "adherence to defilements" refers precisely to the defilements such as the fetters that are active by way of being established and deeply embedded.
By "concentration partaking of penetration," he means insight-concentration (vipassanāsamādhi).
851. “The thunderbolt-wheel, the thunderbolt-circle”: thus he speaks of the bringing about of the state of non-arising as abandonment.
It is called "leading to destruction" (*khayagāmī*) because it goes toward the exhaustion and cessation of both karmic defilements (*kamma-kilesa*) or all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).

Although this is already established by the mention of the supramundane (*lokuttara*), the inclusion of the term "leading to destruction" is for the purpose of praising it. The restriction “only the abandonment by cutting off” (*samucchedappahāna*) is used.
This is stated from the perspective of the non-figurative sense (*nippariyāyato*). "Only for that purpose" means only for the purpose of abandoning by eradication (*samucchedappahāna*).

By this, he indicates that suppression (*vikkhambhana*) and abandoning by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga*) are merely requisites for the Path, because without them, [the Path] cannot be accomplished. Alternatively, "only for that purpose" means only for the purpose of the Path itself.
By this, he shows that because they have that purpose, they possess that specific function. Therefore, he says "Therefore," and so forth. He illustrates that very point with a simile:

To demonstrate this, it is said: "Having slain the rival king," and so forth. As for "whatever was done prior to that": this refers to whatever was done before attaining that kingship, such as the subduing of border regions and the destruction of difficult terrain.

Just as one says, "This and that were done by the king," likewise, even those things accomplished through mundane knowledge—namely, suppression and abandonment by means of its factors—are [regarded] in terms of abandonment by cutting off (*samucchedappahāna*).

They are called "functions" because they constitute the activity of the path that has arisen; they should be understood as belonging to the path because they have that as their purpose and because they fall within its continuity. 852.
*Lokiyasacchikiriyā* means either the mundane realization (*lokissa*) or the realization that is mundane (*lokiyā*). In the same way, there is supramundane realization (*lokuttarasacchikiriyā*).
It should be understood. "I am a possessor" means "I am one who possesses. The same applies here to the phrase "I dwell thus.
"By the touch of knowledge through direct experience" means by the touch of knowledge characterized as making [the object] a direct object of perception.
By the word "directly," he excludes making it an object through inference; rather, it refers to knowing directly by way of reviewing it as "this is such-and-such."
Here, "contact of knowledge" (*ñāṇaphassa*) is intended. "Touched" means touched by knowledge.

Although the jhānas, paths, and fruits do not arise within one's own continuum [in this context], the knowledge that functions by destroying the delusion obscuring them—by way of destroying that [delusion]—is "knowledge independent of others.
"Seeing" means knowing through direct perception. "Plunged into the Deathless" means included within the Deathless; the meaning is "reckoned as the Deathless."

The path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*) is "seeing" (*dassana*) because it is the first seeing of Nibbāna. The "realization through seeing" (*dassanasacchikiriyā*) is the realization by means of that seeing.

Although the knowledge of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū-ñāṇa*) sees Nibbāna even earlier than that, it is not called "seeing" because, despite making it its object, it does not perform the function that must be performed after having seen.
That [realization] is twofold, namely, by way of seeing and by way of development (*bhāvanā*).
There are two kinds of realization (*sacchikiriyā*). "By way of seeing and development" means by way of the path of seeing and the path of development.
By this, he excludes the realization through reviewing that occurs with respect to *nibbāna* when it is not yet the path.
"Of *nibbāna*" refers here to the realization through reviewing with respect to the paths and fruits. "Of this knowledge" refers to this supramundane knowledge as it has been attained.
853. "Abhimata" means intended. "Bhāvanā" (development) refers both to production and to the cultivation of a continuity;

showing these two, he says, "of the mundane," and so forth. For to the extent that mundane wholesome states and the like have been produced and increased, to that same extent his mundane development of virtue (*sīla-bhāvanā*), development of body (*kāya-bhāvanā*), development of mind (*citta-bhāvanā*), and development of wisdom (*paññā-bhāvanā*) have been accomplished.

And by that [cultivation], the continuum is also permeated. Among those mundane and supramundane cultivations, in this discussion on the purification of knowledge and vision, supramundane cultivation is intended, not the other, because the latter serves as its prerequisite.
This fourfold knowledge also—that is, this fourfold noble path-knowledge—gives rise to the supramundane virtues (sīla) and so forth, distinguished as right speech and the rest.

How so? By way of being a co-nascent and other types of conditions. Regarding the phrase "virtue and so forth" (*sīlādīni*), here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes concentration (*samādhi*), but not wisdom (*paññā*).
For that [wisdom] does not produce itself; rather, it is the arising of the path-consciousness (*maggacitta*) that produces it.

Right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is included within that [path-consciousness]; for they say it is comprised within the five aggregates. Alternatively, "virtue and so forth" refers even to the virtue of the fruit (*phala-sīla*) and so on.
"Grasping" is indeed appropriate as grasping by means of wisdom (*paññā*). Regarding the phrase "by way of being a co-nascent condition, etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) should be understood to include being a proximate condition (*anantara-paccaya*), and so forth. And "it perfumes the continuum with those":

by means of those supramundane virtues such as morality (*sīla*) that proceed by way of cutting off [defilements] and pacifying them, the noble person (*ariya-puggala*) cultivates his own mental continuum (*santāna*). Depending upon which...

They say it is "the transcendence" (*parāvutti*). Just as it was stated that the three types of full understanding (*pariññā*) and the three types of abandoning (*pahāna*) are functions of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*) by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*), it is not so here.
Here, however, only supramundane cultivation (*lokuttara-bhāvanā*) is the function of this path-knowledge.
The emphasis is placed on the fact that no figurative application of "cultivation" is found here; by this, mundane cultivation is excluded.

"Thus, to that which has come in its own form" means: unlike concentration, which does not come under the heading of "mind" (*citta*) when one says "develop the mind," wisdom comes in its own form when one says "develop wisdom. This refers to what was stated by way of summary.
At this point, it has been explained in detail; and the connection is that this question has now been answered.
The commentary on the Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-second chapter.
23. Commentary on the Description of the Benefits of the Development of Wisdom.

Commentary on the Exposition of Benefits (Ānisaṃsapakāsanāvaṇṇanā): 854. It possesses many hundreds of benefits because it brings about the vast and noble distinction of qualities such as the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi) and so forth.

"In detail" means that, rather than providing an illustration of the method, it is shown in detail by pointing out each benefit individually, saying, "This too is a benefit of the development of wisdom; this too... and so on.
It is not easy to explain [it] because of its extreme abundance. "Assa" means by means of the development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).

"The destruction of various defilements" refers to the abandoning of the manifold defiled states—such as the view of a self-identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*)—by way of their respective factors (*tadaṅga*) and so forth.
"The experiencing of the flavor of the noble fruits" refers to the relishing of the bliss of the fruits, such as the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) and the others.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Destruction of the Various Defilements (855):
By the phrase "experiencing the taste of the noble fruit" itself, the subsiding and abandoning of the defilements is indicated;

thus, the specific term "at the moment of the noble path" is used, either because [the fruit] exists through the presence of that [path], or because the abandoning by way of complete eradication has already been established. For when eradication by cutting off is accomplished...
The abandonment through subsiding is indeed established.
"Pursued by a terrifying force" means they were suddenly overtaken by a fierce and fearsome speed as if shattering the entire world.
"Upon a mountain mass" means on a mountain with broad rocky surfaces. "A circle blazing with sparks" refers to [the fire] flourishing during the autumn season.

By its own splendor, it makes the circle of the directions difficult to gaze upon. It brings about all manner of evils, such as killing, imprisonment, miserable rebirths, secondary defilements, birth, and so forth.
"Visible here and now" (*sanditthika*) means present before one's eyes. "One should know" (*jaññā*) means one should understand. "Here" (*idha*) refers to this cultivation of wisdom.
[This concludes] the commentary on the discussion of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*).
856. The fruit of the noble path is the "noble fruit" (*ariyaphala*). It is called the "noble fruit" because it is both noble due to its purity and a fruit.
Its "taste" is the bliss of liberation through subsiding; its "experience" is the relishing of that [fruit] which has Nibbāna as its object.
"Therein" refers to those two aspects. "Its" refers to the noble fruit.
857. Since all defilements (*kilesa*) are indeed abandoned when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned, only the fetters are mentioned.
The intention is that the fruit of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) consists solely in the abandoning of the fetters; there is no other separate entity existing as a result (*vipāka*).
Therefore he said: "There is no other dhamma whatsoever called 'fruit'. But who says this?
Andhakas and others. For they, having misunderstood the meaning of the Sutta passage—“‘Arahatship, friend, is called Arahatship...
it is the destruction of delusion’”—claim that, according to the literal sense, “there is no such thing as Arahatship; it is merely the abandoning of defilements that is so designated.
Thus, while rejecting the remaining fruits [of the path], they reject this Sutta as well. By saying “this Sutta too,” he refers to the Pāḷi of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

"Exertion" (*payoga*) means a strenuous and intense application; it is the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). The "subsiding of exertion" (*payogappaṭippassaddhi*) is the subsiding of the defilements that arose through that application.

Furthermore, that wisdom which arises when the fruition-wisdom (*vipākapaññā*) is being produced—this wisdom being produced due to the cultivation of the Noble Path—is called "wisdom of subsiding" (*paṭippassaddhipaññā*), because it is the wisdom to be accomplished within that state of subsiding.

It has been stated: "Right view emerges from wrong view. Having spoken thus by way of showing right view as the direct opposite of wrong view, the phrase "from the defilements that follow upon it" is said in order to show emergence from other factors as well—from the defilements that follow upon that wrong view by way of association (*sampayoga*) and decisive support (*upanissaya*).
By this, he expresses the abandonment of those [defilements] belonging to the same category. "From the aggregates" means...
The meaning is: by means of the aggregates that follow it, by the aggregates associated with that wrong view, and by the aggregates that will arise in the future conditioned by it.

And "from all external signs" means from all signs of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) that serve as the objective range for insight (vipassanā), which are external to the aforementioned defiled aggregates.
Having thus shown the function of the path, the passage beginning with "Because that application has subsided" is now stated in order to show the fruit by way of that path.
Therein, "because that application has subsided" means because that application—consisting of emerging from both internally and externally, and so forth—has subsided.
For the path abandons defilements while emerging from both the sign and from occurrence.
At the moment of its own arising, it is said that this application is active; however, at the moment of the fruit, that application is said to be subsided and stilled.
Therefore it is said: "Because of the subsiding of that application. It arises means that immediately after the path, it arises either twice or thrice.
But at the time of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), it arises many times, [and likewise] from cessation...
It arises twice for one who is emerging [from the attainment].
Since all of it arises as the sign of the subsiding of the aforementioned application, it is said: "It arises because of the subsiding of that application.
"This is the fruit of the path" means that the aforementioned resultants, called right view, should be understood as the fruit of the Noble Path. This is to be elaborated.
“In the moment of the stream-entry path, right intention in the sense of directing [the mind] is the abandoning of wrong intention,” and so on;
this should be understood in detail by way of intention and the other factors, as well as by way of the remaining paths.
And the four fruits of recluseship—these states have immeasurable objects; thus, by virtue of having immeasurable objects, they are [included] with the paths.

By way of its excellence. Likewise, the sublime state (mahaggata-dhamma) known as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) is a condition for the immeasurable state (appamāṇa-dhamma) by way of the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) at the moment of emergence from cessation; thus, it illustrates the status of the noble fruit (ariyaphala) as a proximity-condition.
These and other such points are proofs here that the noble fruit exists as a state possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma).
The intention is that it is not as shown in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* text itself.

(858) Regarding "in the attainment of fruition" (*phalasamāpatti*): this refers to the attainment characterized by the occurrence of the fruit. "Of it" (*assa*) means of the noble fruit (*ariyaphala*). This formulation of questions is based on the aspects of its own nature, its agent, its cause, its mode, its stability, its emergence, and its immediate succession.
(859) "Absorption (*appanā*) in the cessation of the noble fruit": this is the occurrence of the noble fruit-jhāna in the manner of absorption with Nibbāna as its object.
860. "All worldlings" (puthujjana) includes even those who have attained the meditative absorptions (jhāna-samāpatti); such worldlings do not enter [the attainment of fruition], let alone others.
It is certainly a general statement that "all noble ones" (ariya) enter the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), yet it applies specifically to those distinguished [by their stage].
The phrase "because they have realized" (adhigatattā) is a statement of the reason. This same [reason] applies to the higher [stages] by virtue of the lower.
He says "But the higher ones... and so forth, in order to exclude [the possibility] that they remain as if accomplishing the attainment just as one does with a worldly attainment (*lokiyasamāpatti*).
Therein, "the higher ones" refers to the once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) and so on; "the lower" refers to the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) and so on.
They do not attain it, even though it has already been reached. If one asks why, he states the reason: "by way of having entered the state of another person (*puggalantarabhāva*)."

"Because of its subsided state. By this, it is shown that the higher noble one enters the lower attainment of fruition because it has been attained by himself, just as one enters a mundane attainment;

thus, it excludes any deviation from the cause. For in mundane jhānas, there is no such thing as "entering the state of another person," due to the absence of any distinction [in the attainment itself].
But here, by means of the cessation [of defilements] through the non-eradication of karma and the defilements, [the distinction exists].
Just as there is a difference between worldlings and stream-enterers, so too for those such as stream-enterers and once-returners, there is the attainment of the status of distinct individuals.
For this reason, each lower fruit-state is turned back by the successive higher path-states;
like being overcome by adversaries, they reach a state of non-occurrence. Therefore, it was said: "Because of their subsiding."
Furthermore, the occurrence of wholesome functional states (*kiriya*) is of one kind, while the occurrence of fruition (*vipāka*) is of another.
Moreover, because supramundane wholesome states have an immediate fruit, that which is higher than the lower stage is as if it has gone to another existence.

Indeed, it is by way of their respective fruits that Noble Ones obtain the names of stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) and so forth. Even if they possess other fruits, they still retain the names of stream-enterer and so on.
It may be stable for them, as if they had taken rebirth through that particular jhāna; thus, for each respective noble one, that respective fruit is similar to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
Therefore, not even a trace of the attainment of a lower fruit by one possessing a higher fruit is possible, let alone the actual entering into it—this is how it should be understood.
And "the lower and the higher" refers to the lower ones, such as stream-enterers and so forth.
The connection is that noble ones do not attain the higher fruits, such as the fruit of once-returning. Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Because they have not yet attained it. For it is not possible to attain a meditative attainment (samāpatti) that has not been previously acquired.
By the phrase, "But each noble one attains his own respective fruit," [it is shown that] all noble ones [attain their own fruits].
When the sense that they "enter the attainment of fruition" (phalasamāpatti) arises, the passage beginning with "But some...
is stated to show a difference of opinion among certain teachers regarding that point. For these are "perfected in concentration" (samādhismiṃ paripūrakārino);
since those mentioned as "the two above"—namely, non-returners (anāgāmin) and arahants—are perfected in concentration, whereas the others are perfected in virtue (sīlesu).

Therefore, only two [types of persons] enter the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). The intention is that the utilization of an attainment is not possible without the perfection of concentration (*samādhi*).
"That" refers to the reason stated by them, namely, "those who have brought concentration to fulfillment.

"It is indeed no reason" means it is simply illogical. Why? He says: "Even for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*)," and so forth. The meaning of this is: for one whose defilements (*kilesa*) are not entirely severed.
Even for an ordinary person (puthujjana), it is possible to attain the mundane meditative attainments (lokīya-samāpatti) they have themselves acquired;

how much more so, then, for noble ones (ariya) of the lower stages who have eradicated certain defilements? Therefore, their failure to fulfill concentration is not the reason why they do not attain the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
This is what is called "considering the logical connection" regarding matters not explicitly mentioned in the canonical texts (pāḷi).
[The commentary] says, "But this matter is established in the Pāḷi," and in order to show the Pāḷi by way of disregarding the stated reasons, it says, "What then here?
and so forth. "For the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry" means for the acquisition of the path of stream-entry.

"For the sake of entering the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry" means for the purpose of entering into the fruition-attainment of stream-entry. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.

And here, because they are extracted in their own form by the phrases "for the sake of attaining the dwelling in emptiness" and "for the sake of attaining the dwelling in the signless," the sections on the path and fruit that precede them are stated by way of the wishless (*appaṇihita*). Among those,

the change-of-lineage states (*gotrabhu-dhamma*) which precede the attainments of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*)— which proceed by way of the contemplation of non-self (*anattā*) and by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*anicca*)— exist in nine or ten modes.

They should be understood as "stated. However, because a teaching identical for all four fruits is found in such passages as "for the purpose of attaining the fruit of stream-entry," it is understood that even stream-enterers and once-returners attain their own respective fruits.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that this was stated by way of the fruit immediately following the path (*maggānantara-phala*), for [the attainment] occurs by way of insight (*vipassanā*) for all ten [types of noble persons].
Because the teaching was commenced by way of showing the states of the lineage (gotrabhū), and because that purpose is accomplished by the section on the Path itself;

and because the fruit does not follow immediately after the Path and is not called "fruition attainment" (phalasamāpatti) as a separate entity due to the absence of a specific preliminary stage (parikamma).
Therefore, by the very mention of fruition attainment, the attainment of fruition by stream-enterers and others is also established. Thus he said, "Therefore," and so forth.
The purpose (*payojana*) is also the cause for the practice for that end, since one practices for the sake of that [purpose].
Therefore, having asked the question regarding the cause—"For what reason do they attain?"—the purpose is answered:

"For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihār’atthaṃ*). Alternatively, *kasmā* is an ablative form used in the sense of a dative; it means "for what [purpose]? "For the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life" means:
It is for the sake of dwelling in a peaceful abiding of happiness through the subsiding of the distress and fever of the defilements in this very life.
Although they possess the nature of fruition, because they do not arise without preliminary preparation, the attainment of the fruits occurs solely by the inclination of each respective Noble One;
therefore, since these are accompanied by mastery, he said: "They enter... for the duration... and so forth.
"By two aspects" means by two reasons. For just as the attainment of mundane jhānas— which is accomplished through the state of being endowed with association—

is described by way of the transcendence of the factors of abandoning because it is to be attained in that manner, so too the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), while being accomplished through the mental attention to Nibbāna,
is described by way of the non-attention to other objects than that, [namely] from all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra).
Because it succeeds by way of the turning away of the mind. Therefore he said, "From Nibbāna," and so forth.

For, through the succession of knowledges beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall, every fruit-consciousness proceeds for one whose mind is entirely disenchanted and detached from conditioned formations, having as its object Nibbāna which has issued forth from them.
And while proceeding in this way, because of the non-attention to any object other than Nibbāna, [it is directed] toward Nibbāna...
And it is said that [the mind] proceeds by way of mental applications (*manasikāra*).

"To the signless liberation of mind" means to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) consisting of the two signless liberations, or to the attainment of fruition that is to be entered by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).
"For the sake of attainment" means for the purpose of entering that attainment. "Of all signs" (*sabbanimittānaṃ*)...

"Of all the signs of formations (saṅkhāra), such as form and so forth": non-attention means not directing the mind or not attending to them because one has seen their disadvantage and has abandoned them.
"And attention to the signless element": it is signless because of the absence of any sign of formations;

and it is called "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata) because it is not conditioned by any conditions. [Attention] to this unconditioned element occurs together with the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
“Attention by means of attention” means paying attention to that element, or paying attention to what is termed the fruit-attainment consciousness.
(863) “By way of rise and fall, etc. refers to the activity of all nine knowledges as they proceed by way of rise and fall, dissolution, fearfulness, appearance as terror, and so forth.
Therefore he said: “Of insight proceeding in successive order. Immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge which has formations as its object...
Immediately after the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu-ñāṇa), which has formations as its object and receives the name "cleansing" (vodāna), [the path arises].
But why is it that here the knowledge of change-of-lineage does not have Nibbāna as its object, as the knowledge of the path does as its precursor?
Because resultant states are not leading-out (aniyyānika). For only the states of the Noble Path are leading-out. Indeed, this has been said: "Which states..."

“Are they leading out? The four paths that are not included [in the mundane sphere]. Therefore, since path-knowledge—which has the nature of being exclusively leading out and which proceeds by way of emerging from both sides—must be preceded by a knowledge that serves as its immediate condition and has emerged from the sign, it is logical that it has Nibbāna as its object;
however, this is not so because of the cultivation of the Noble Path itself.
Because the knowledge that precedes the fruition-knowledges— which, by their very nature, do not eradicate the defilements existing as karmic results, lack the quality of leading to liberation,
and are by nature non-emergent— never takes Nibbāna as its object, this is due to the dissimilar mode of both types of conformity-knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa). For, within the sequence of the Noble Path,
the conformity-knowledges [do not take Nibbāna as their object] because they [only suppress] the gross aggregates of greed and so forth that have not yet been previously pierced through.
Through their exceptional power of penetration, these [consciousnesses] arise in accordance with path-knowledge, having reached the highest perfection among mundane knowledges.

However, in the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), because those respective defilements have already been eradicated by each respective path, they are effortless in suppressing those defilements;
