they serve solely for the purpose of providing the Noble Ones with the experience of the bliss of the attainment of fruition.
Since they arise merely as preliminary stages (*parikamma*), there is no possibility of emerging from them anywhere;
for it is only from the emergence from the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*) that their concluding knowledge (*pariyosāna-ñāṇa*) can have Nibbāna as its object.

And having established this, [it is said]: "For the sake of the trainee’s own enjoyment of the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*), [he contemplates] formations by way of their arising and passing away... and so forth.
And this statement from the Aṭṭhakathā is thereby supported: "For one who is reviewing, only the fruit arises through the sequence of insight-knowledge, not the path.
Therefore he said: "Even for a trainee (sekha), only the fruit arises, not the path.
Attainment (samāpajjana) is the continuous occurrence of the fruition-consciousness alone for as long as the time has been delimited, by way of absorption-jhāna having Nibbāna as its object.
Regarding the phrase "attainment of fruition," it is said: "By means of the attainment of fruition, consciousness enters into cessation.

If the attainment of fruition occurs by way of gradual insight (*anupubbavipassanā*), then one might raise the objection that, according to that same method, there ought also to be a higher path for the trainee (*sekkha*). Anticipating this inquiry, he says:

"Because of being inclined toward the attainment of fruition," and so forth. By this, he shows that the practice of insight which leads to the Noble Path is indeed distinct [from the practice leading to fruition].
This shows that another [type of insight] leads to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); this classification of insight has already been explained.
The phrase "But those who... refers to the inhabitants of the Abhayagiri monastery. For they speak by mixing together the path, the fruit, and insight.
It is for this very reason that the words "If this were so," and so forth, were stated. [The question arises: "Will he become an Arhat or a Paccekabuddha? if there is also insight in the other case.

The intention is that it would conduce to that purpose. Furthermore, one should not take it to mean that their statement was rejected solely on the basis of the canonical text (pāḷi) because it contradicts the text—specifically the passage stating, "Ten change-of-lineage states arise by way of insight"—wherein insight for the sake of the path and insight for the sake of the fruit are treated separately.
Otherwise, the statement "ten change-of-lineage states" [would be untenable].
“Would it conflict?”—this is the conclusion of the very point already stated, namely, that this alone is what should be accepted.
“And its fruit,” etc., is a demonstration of the similarity between supramundane resultants and sublime resultants in their resemblance to the wholesome state.
It should be understood that by demonstrating the similarity through the jhānas, the similarity by way of the enlightenment factors and the path factors is also demonstrated therein.

864. "By way of stability" means by way of continuous persistence. For here, "stability" refers to the continued presence of the attainment (samāpatti) by way of its persistence for as long as the time has been delimited.

"Volitional formation" (*abhisaṅkhāra*) is the mental preparation consisting in the grasping of a temporal limit, such as: "I shall emerge when the moon or the sun has reached this much of its course."
865. “All these indeed”: he does not attend to all these—the sign of visible form and so forth—simultaneously because that is impossible.
“By way of including everything” means by way of taking them without remainder. For collective terms (samudāya-sadda) also apply to the individual parts;
and since a whole cannot be found apart from its parts, even an operation pertaining to the parts is expressed by way of the whole.

It has been stated. Therefore, because there is no simultaneous attention to all the signs of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), and because one is said to have emerged from the attainment of fruition (*phala-samāpatti*) when the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*) arises, it is said:
"That which is the object of the life-continuum," and so forth. "He attends" means by means of an act of attention accompanied by the life-continuum.
[This occurs] for one who is attending to that object, or for one who is attending to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) with respect to that object. 866.
For each preceding [consciousness], the subsequent one follows immediately after its own fruit, or else the life-continuum follows the very last one.
[The life-continuum arises] immediately after the fruit in the cognitive process of the Path (magga-vīthi) and in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).
“By means of which fruit there is emergence from cessation”—this is stated because of the state of emerging from cessation through the arising of that fruit.
“That” refers to either the non-returner fruit or the supreme fruit (arahantship) mentioned by way of the state of emerging from cessation.

“Immediately after the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception” means immediately after the wholesome or functional [consciousness] of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even though a period of seven days has elapsed.
Because it is separated by a dissimilar [state].
"With the distress calmed" means with the distress of the defilements entirely stilled. "Having the deathless as its object" means having Nibbāna as its object.
"Beautiful" means beautiful because even the defilement of ugliness is absent. The worldly bait known as craving has been vomited up.

"Cast off by him" means having vomited out the worldly bait (*lokāmisa*). "Peaceful" (*santa*) is due to the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*) and the state of being well-composed (*susantatā*).

"Fruit of recluseship" (*sāmaññaphala*) is the fruit of that which is called "recluseship" (*sāmañña*), namely the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), because one becomes a recluse (*samaṇa*) through union with that Dhamma.

"Possessing nutritive essence" (*ojavanta*) means endowed with its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). "Pure" (*suci*) means completely purified by being free from the impurity of the defilements. "With ease" (*sukhena*)...
“By unsurpassed bliss. “Moistened” (*abhisandita*) means made supple by the complete departure from all harshness.

“With sweetness exceeding sweetness” means with an exceedingly sweet and delicious [flavor] compared to the sweetness of the sublime (*mahaggata*) and the sweetness of the supramundane wholesome (*lokuttarakusala*).

For the bliss of the fruit (*phalasukha*) is more refined than the bliss of the path (*maggasukha*) due to its greater tranquility. “Rejoiced in by the Deathless” (*amata*)—by this [phrase], [the text says] “like honey.”
He clearly discerns it as ever more pleasant.
The construction is: because the wise person, having developed wisdom, finds—that is, obtains—that bliss which is the flavor and the essence of that noble fruit.
*Commentary on the Discussion of the Attainment of Cessation*

867. *Tatra* means in that [context], namely, in the abbreviated statement: “the capacity for attaining the attainment of cessation. This is an inquiry (*pañhākamma*) by way of its specific form and so forth. *Kattha* means in which existence (*bhava*). 868.

*By way of successive cessation* (*anupubbanirodhavasena*) means by way of the successive cessation of the three formations as one ascends through the eight attainments accompanied by insight, by means of the cessation of their respective opposites. For as long as the time is delimited, [there is the absence] of mind and mental factors...
The meaning is: "non-occurrence" is this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). As for who enters it and who does not:
although those capable of entering it were asked first because of their preeminence, the answer to that was deferred until later due to its importance;
therefore, first showing those who do not enter it, he said: "All... [do] not enter it."
Just as it is said, "Release the left hand; take hold of the right. In that context, the phrase "all of them" is a qualification of the three types beginning with the worldling (*puthujjana*).

For even those who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), like those who have not, are unable to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) because they do not fulfill their function regarding concentration.
Indeed, the fulfillment of one's function regarding concentration comes about through the complete eradication of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and the other hindrances.

Not by the mere attainment of *jhāna*. Regarding the terms "non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) and "arahant," the word "dry-insight practitioner" (*sukkha-vipassaka*) should be applied separately to each: "dry-insight non-returners" and "dry-insight arahants.

Both of these, despite possessing the power of insight (*vipassanā-bala*), do not enter cessation (*nirodha*) due to the absence of the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*). It is precisely because of the possibility of successive dwellings (*anupubba-vihāra*) that this is so.

"The power of concentration (samādhibala) must be desired. However, although the first three [arahants] possess the power of concentration, because they lack the power of insight (vipassanābala), they are unable to attain [the higher jhānas] due to its incompleteness.
And this incompleteness is due to their not having thoroughly mastered the mental formations (saṅkhāras).
Having stated, 'They attain the eight attainments...,' the reason for this is given there:"
In order to show this by way of the canonical text (pāḷi) itself, it was said: “By two powers,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “and three formations”:
here, *tayo* is a nominative plural used in the sense of a genitive, meaning “of three. “By the modes of knowledge” (*ñāṇacariyāhi*) means by the occurrences of knowledge.

“Knowledge of the attainment of cessation” (*nirodhasamāpattiyā*) refers to the knowledge for entering the attainment of cessation. And this “accomplishment” (*sampadā*) consists in the possession of the two powers and so forth, which brings about the aforementioned attainment of cessation.
*Sampanna*. "Non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed" (*anāgāmikhīṇāsavā*) refers to both non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*).
869. *Samathabala*: It is called *samatha* because it calms (*sameti*) adverse states such as sensual desire;

that very thing is a power (*bala*) in the sense of being unshakable by opposing factors. It is called *vipassanā* because it sees in various ways (*vividhehi ākārehi*) by way of impermanence and so forth; that very thing is...
"Power" in the manner described refers to the power of insight (*vipassanā-bala*). Regarding the phrases "by way of renunciation," and so forth:

the non-distraction consisting of one-pointedness of mind—which arises by way of the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) that suppresses sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), or by way of the arising of a wholesome state of consciousness proceeding in that manner characterized primarily by non-greed (*alobha*)—is the power of serenity (*samatha-bala*). [This applies likewise] to the suppression of ill-will (*byāpāda*).
It is by way of a wholesome state of consciousness that proceeds thus, characterized by thoughts free from ill-will or dominated by non-hatred;
by way of the perception of light established through mental attention that has rendered torpor and drowsiness suppressed;
by way of non-distraction, which is the concentration that suppresses restlessness; and by way of the suppression of all unwholesome thoughts.

The construction of the meaning is as follows: non-distraction, characterized by one-pointedness of mind through in-breaths and out-breaths that observe relinquishment—accomplished by means of mindfulness of breathing with the head-hair as the limit—that is the power of serenity (*samathabala*).
Having thus shown the power of serenity by way of access concentration (*upacāra*) and absorption (*jhāna*), [the text now proceeds] to that of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*).
The phrase beginning with “by the first jhāna” is stated in order to show the attainment of strength by virtue of being unassailable by opposing factors.

In this context, “in regard to the hindrances” means for the sake of the hindrances, or on account of the hindrances. Neither does the person possessing the jhāna nor the concentration associated with the jhāna waver.
For it is specifically this that is intended here as the “power of serenity. Likewise...
In what sense is it called the "power of serenity"? This asks about the meaning of "power. "Restlessness" refers to the sign of restlessness.

"Defilements accompanied by restlessness" refers to the causes of defilement such as delusion, shamelessness, and so forth, which are associated with restlessness. "Aggregates" refers to the sign of the four aggregates associated with restlessness.
"Does not waver," and so forth, are synonyms for one another. Alternatively, "wavering" is the departure from one's position; "shaking" is the state of being agitated or wandering about.
"Vedhanaṃ" means "sandhāvanaṃ" (stretching). It should be construed as follows: it does not tremble in agitation (*uddhacca*); it does not waver in the defilements accompanied by agitation;

or it does not stretch out toward the aggregates accompanied by agitation. And here, the mention of agitation is for the purpose of showing that, because it is the direct opposite of serenity (*samatha*), it attains power by overcoming it.
Thus, this is a demonstration of the preeminence of its function common to all eight attainments.

It should be seen. This is the power of serenity (*samathabala*): that state of being unshakable by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth due to one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*) obtained through renunciation (*nekkhamma*) and the like, and its persistence having overcome those [hindrances]; this is the power of serenity.
Now, in explaining the power of insight (*vipassanābala*), since insight is comprised, in brief, of seven contemplations (*anupassanā*):
Therefore, having emerged from each respective attainment, contemplation should be practiced by means of those [attainments];
for by that much alone, the function of contemplation is fulfilled here. Thus, after showing them in their own form as "contemplation of impermanence is a power of insight...
up to ...contemplation of relinquishment is a power of insight," they are shown again according to the method explained below, by way of the classification of their objects.

“Contemplation of impermanence in form,” and so forth, has been stated. Here too, in order to show that the state of being unassailable by opposing factors is indeed the sense of “strength,” the passage beginning with “In what sense is it the power of insight (vipassanā-bala)?
is commenced. Therein, “due to ignorance” refers to the cause of ignorance within the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arising.
“To the defilements accompanied by ignorance” refers to the objective signs of the bases for defilements such as greed and hatred associated with ignorance.

The rest is easy to understand because it follows the method explained below. And here, the inclusion of "ignorance" (avijjā) is for the purpose of showing that it has attained power by its direct opposition to insight (vipassanā) and by its overcoming of it.
Therefore, this should be seen as a demonstration of the preeminence of the function common to all seven contemplations.
This is called the "power of insight," which—by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth—

The state of being unshakable by the signs such as the perception of permanence regarding the insight-knowledge already attained, and the steadfastness that remains after having overcome them—this is the power of insight (vipassanā-bala).
Thought and examination are verbal formations because they form and set speech in motion; therefore he said: "Previously..."

"Friend Visākha, having applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one subsequently breaks forth into speech; therefore, applied and sustained thought are the verbal formation (*vacī-saṅkhāra*).
But since these two have subsided in the second jhāna, he said: "The second jhāna... [they] have become tranquil.
They are bodily formations (*kāya-saṅkhāra*) because they are formed by the body; they are inhalation and exhalation. For it has been said: "Inhalation and exhalation..."
“Friend Visākha, these states are bodily and bound up with the body; therefore, in-and-out breathing is a bodily formation.
Since they have subsided in the fourth jhāna, he said: “…the fourth jhāna … they have become tranquil.
They are formed by the mind, thus they are mental formations: namely, perception and feeling. For it has been said: “Perception…”
“Perception and feeling are mental factors; these states are bound to the mind. Therefore, perception and feeling are formations of the mind.
Since, however, they subside for one who has attained cessation, it is said: “Perception and feeling...
[as before] ...have become tranquil.”

By the inclusion of the contemplation of turning away (*vivaṭṭānupassanā*) among the modes of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*), the remaining contemplations that constitute its beginning are also included, because they are inseparable from it.
The statement that both the path and the attainment of fruition are modes of knowledge is made because the phenomena of the path and fruition are dominated by knowledge;
or else, it is because through knowledge [they function] as the dominant faculty, the cause, the path-condition, and so forth.

It is stated thus because, considering that the remaining path and fruition states have been practiced and set in motion by means of that which has become their preeminent condition, it is described in that way.

This same method applies to the practice of concentration as well. "By these sixteen" refers to these sixteen occurrences of knowledge by way of the eight contemplations and the eight knowledges of the paths and fruits.
"By means of the nine modes of practice for concentration (*samādhicariyā*). The eight attainments (*samāpatti*) are the eight modes of practice for concentration;

their access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) is one mode of practice for concentration by virtue of its commonality with the development of access concentration. Thus, it is "by means of the nine modes of practice for concentration. Therefore he said:
"The first jhāna is a mode of practice for concentration," and so forth. "And the applied thought (*vitakka*) for the sake of attaining the first jhāna," and so on.

It should be understood that this is stated by way of the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) consisting of various adverting (*āvajjana*). This is because the preliminary stages of the higher attainments (*samāpatti*) are likewise described in that same manner.
Indeed, in a single act of adverting (*ekāvajjana*), such as the preliminary stage of the fourth jhāna and so forth, joy (*pīti*) and the other factors do not occur.
Furthermore, by the statement "for the sake of attaining the first jhāna" and so on, it should be understood that the fulfillment of even access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) is intended here.

This is what is shown. But what here is the distinction between the power of serenity (samatha-bala) and the practice of concentration (samādhi-cariyā), or between the power of insight (vipassanā-bala) and the practice of mundane knowledge (lokiya-ñāṇa-cariyā)?

Just as even within the power of serenity, by the phrase "by way of renunciation" and so forth, only absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) among the eight attainments is mentioned along with access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), so too it is in the case of the practices of concentration, and likewise in the practices of mundane knowledge through the power of insight.

Is it only insight (vipassanā) that is mentioned? Although it is indeed mentioned, the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā)—which is not explicitly stated among the powers of insight such as the "preceding knowledge" (purecarañāṇa) and so forth—is nevertheless included within the "modes of knowledge" (ñāṇacariyā).
Furthermore, the meaning of "power" (balaṭṭha) is the state of being unshakable by opposing factors;

the meaning of "conduct" (cariyaṭṭha) is the state of being well-practiced by way of the five masteries (vasībhāva). By this very principle, the distinction between the power of serenity (samathabala) and the conduct of concentration (samādhicariyā) is also established.
It should be understood as "fully described.

Regarding the phrase "wisdom as mastery" (*vasībhāvatā paññā*): here, one who possesses mastery (*vaso*) is called a "master" (*vasī*); the state of being such a master is "mastery" (*vasībhāva*), and that itself is "the state of mastery" (*vasībhāvatā*).
However, because the word "masters" (*vasiyo*) is used in the Pāli text in the feminine gender, in order to show those [mastery-factors], he says: "Mastery... (*vasīti*).

The passage beginning with “five masteries” has been stated. Therein, the capacity to direct the mind continuously toward the factors of jhāna when one is reflecting upon them is the mastery of adverting (āvajjana-vasī).
The capacity to enter jhāna quickly when one desires to attain it is the mastery of attainment (samāpajjana-vasī).
The capacity to maintain the jhāna for the duration of a finger-snap or for several finger-snaps is the mastery of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-vasī).

Likewise, the mastery of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasī*) is the capacity to emerge quickly [from absorption]. However, the mastery of review (*paccavekkhaṇa-vasī*) is accomplished through the mastery of adverting (*āvajjana-vasī*) alone;
for in that case, the reviewing javanas themselves follow immediately after the adverting consciousness.

This is the summary here; the detailed explanation has already been given above. And this state of mastery is described by way of the modes of practice of concentration (*samādhi-cariyā*). Regarding the modes of practice of knowledge (*ñāṇa-cariyā*):
However, for supramundane modes of knowledge, there is no need to achieve mastery;

since their opposites have been thoroughly eliminated, mastery is established by their very nature. But for mundane modes of knowledge, mastery is indeed attained by bringing them to a state of proficiency and strength.

870. "The description by way of the highest" (*ukkaṭṭhaniddesa*) means a description that leaves nothing out. It is stated [there] that there are fourteen modes of knowledge (*ñāṇacariyā*) because the highest path and fruit have not yet been attained.

If it is so—that is, if it was stated "by sixteen modes of knowledge" according to the description by way of the highest—then it should also be accepted by way of the lowest. This being the case, why is it that one does not enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). It is "possessing the five strands of sensual pleasure" (*pañcakāmaguṇika*) because it has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its basis;

[this refers to] sensual lust (*kāmarāga*). Because it is not abandoned and not cut off. For the mere suppression (*vikkhambhana*) of sensual lust is not capable of being the foundation for cessation (*nirodha*).
Therefore: because sensual lust, which is an obstacle to concentration (*samādhi*), has been thoroughly abandoned. By this, [it is said]: "Granted that..."

The practice of the knowledge of the paths and fruits (*maggaphalañāṇacariyā*), like the practice of mundane knowledge and concentration (*lokiyañāṇasamādhicariyā*), does not function in its own form during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpajjana*), because they do not operate at that time;

rather, it shows that by means of severing their respective opposites, these powerful practices serve as specific conditions for the attainment of cessation, and thus become its basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*). "He" refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmī*). For this—

The statement beginning with “for one emerging from cessation” (*nirodhā vuṭṭhahantassa*) is spoken specifically with reference to the emergence from cessation by a non-returner (*anāgāmī*), because of the expression “wholesome [state] of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception” (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakusala*);
otherwise, it would have been called “functional [state] of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception” (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanakiriya*).
Why was it stated “in the five-aggregate existence” (*pañcavokārabhave*)? Is it not the case that even in four-aggregate existence, by way of formless jhāna...
Is it that successive attainment (anupubbasamāpatti) is obtained according to what is appropriate? Certainly it is obtained;

however, that [individual attainment] is not called "successive attainment" because it exists only as a single part [of the whole]. Since it is by way of the eight attainments alone that the term "successive attainment" is used, he said:
"There is no arising of the first jhāna and so forth," [meaning] due to the absence of the physical basis (vatthu), namely, the heart-basis (hadayavatthu).
They say it is "non-existence" (abhāva); however, the meaning is that there is an absence of the physical basis (vatthu) known as the body born of karma.

For if one were to attain cessation (nirodha) in the formless realms, then due to the absence of mind and mental factors, as well as anything else, one would become unmanifested, like one who has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). But what is this cessation dependent upon?

If it were said that he has "attained" [the attainment], what is the use of this investigation into the basis? Because of the deficiency of factors, there is no attainment of the attainment of cessation in the formless realms.
Regarding "in the differentiation of the occurrence of formations": this refers to the arising and breaking up of conditioned phenomena moment by moment;
or, to the distinction in their occurrence as they are afflicted by the three kinds of suffering, according to their respective classification into wholesome and so forth.

Although the suffering inherent in formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) is present within material phenomena due to the absence of mind and mental factors, it does not come to be designated as such [in that context].
"Becoming weary" means becoming disenchanted. "Having reached Nibbāna" is like having reached Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*). "Happiness" means being free from suffering.
873. "By way of serenity and insight" means by way of their being conjoined, mutually supporting one another, like a pair of yoked oxen.

"Having ascended" means having reached the pinnacle, having climbed up as far as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) and as far as the knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*).
"Ceasing" refers to one who, having entered the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is bringing that to cessation.

Thus, by the non-arising of any other consciousness whatsoever, there occurs the entry into this attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This is shown by the passage beginning with "For he... and so forth.
The phrase “by way of serenity and insight” explains the aforementioned meaning by means of a negative formulation (*vyatireka*).
Having reached the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one remains there, because beyond that there is an absence of pure serenity and insight.
If a noble one (*ariya*) who seeks the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) exerts himself by way of insight alone, he remains having reached his own respective attainment of fruition.
Now, if an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), or one in training (*sekha*) seeking the path, having reached the path through that very insight (*vipassanā*), stands in the fruit (*phala*);

he too is said to "stand having attained the attainment of fruition" (*phalasamāpatti*). Such a person is one who has practiced by way of both [the path and the fruit]. "That" refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
874. The method by which one becomes capable of entering cessation—namely, by being endowed with the two fruits and so forth—is as follows.
By saying "already fully developed," he shows the very manner of attainment; thus he says, "having finished his meal duties," and so forth.

For that is the preliminary duty common to all forms of meditation. Therein, "formations" refers either to that first jhāna or to the formations in the arising of the consciousness of the first jhāna.
It was said, “He sees with insight” (*vipassati*). But what kind of insight is intended here?
To determine that, the author divides that very insight into three types by means of the passage beginning, “But this insight,” and so forth.

If the insight is dull, it accomplishes a path of slow direct knowledge; if it is sharp, [it accomplishes] a path of quick direct knowledge. This is the distinction based on its dullness or sharpness.
However, insight that has reached the stage of characteristic-acquisition (*lakkhaṇappatta*) certainly becomes a condition for the Path. Demonstrating this point, he said:

"Formations... [etc] ...it certainly does. Even when formations are the object, it is appropriate that it be sharp, because it proceeds solely in the mode of turning away from all formations, and because, like the Path, it serves as a condition for the Fruit which has gone beyond formations (*visaṅkhāragata*).
Therefore he said, "resembling the development of the path. Because calmness (*samatha*) and so forth that are too weak are incapable of ceasing formations and thus culminate in calmness itself;
whereas knowledge (*ñāṇa*) and so forth that are too sharp result in an excessive perception of defects in formations and thus culminate in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*);
for this reason it was stated, "neither too weak nor too sharp is appropriate. This is the one who enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
He conditions those; those are the formations of the first jhāna.
By the phrase "just so," he draws in the meaning of "neither too weak nor too intense. This same method applies to the others as well.
It should be stated: "Having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it, he likewise contemplates the formations therein through insight."
However, because it has already been explained according to the method stated below, some say that [the Buddha] did not mention it here and simply said, "He performs the fourfold preliminary duty.

That is merely their own opinion. For the practice of concentration follows the practice of insight; therefore, having emerged from the attainment, the preliminary duty must be performed. Indeed, later on as well, [it is said]: "Having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it, this..."
He will say, "having performed the preliminary duties," and so forth, but not "having likewise practiced insight (vipassanā) upon the formations (saṅkhāra) therein.
"Not disturbing what is not tied up" means not destroying requisites that are not connected with oneself;
it is the resolve that they shall not be destroyed. "Honoring the Saṅgha" means the act of paying honor to the Saṅgha by bringing it to mind. "Calling out to the Teacher" means...
The teacher’s summons is the act of adverting [the mind]. "The delimitation of the duration" refers to the connection that one performs the preliminary duty of delimiting the duration of life. 875.
"That which is to be resolved" means the mind should be generated; for here, the resolution itself consists precisely in the generation of the mind.
Because of the non-arising of mind-born matter and so forth, and because of the absence of support from postnascent conditions and the like, [it lasts] only for seven days.

They say that because the body continues to function in such a way, it becomes exhausted thereafter; thus, they enter the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) by delimiting the duration to exactly seven days.
"By means of the attainment itself" means by means of the attainment of cessation itself. One who has entered the attainment protects it from obstacles such as fire and the like.

The intention is "by way of resolution. Regarding the passage beginning with "of the Venerable Sañjīva," whatever is to be said has already been stated below in the discussion on supernormal powers (iddhi). 876.

"Of this" means of one who is entering the attainment of cessation, or of the act of entering the attainment of cessation. "At that time" means at the moment that monk approaches; [the attainment] emerges right then. This is similar to the delimitation of time.

"Thus it is weighty" means that the Saṅgha’s command is indeed so weighty that even one who has entered the attainment of cessation— which cannot be overcome even by fire and the like— must emerge from that attainment [in obedience to it].
Therefore, the intention is that one who desires their own welfare and happiness should not transgress the Saṅgha’s command, even for the sake of life itself.
877. He does not call out, "Friend, the Teacher summons you. The connection is that one should reflect, "I shall arise.
878. "Of the duration of life" means of one's own lifespan, the occurrence of life. Life itself is the "life-formations" (āyusaṅkhārā).
And they say, "Life, heat, and consciousness"—these become the object of his natural mind at the moment of internal cessation.

There is no death [during this process], because one dies by means of the final *bhavaṅga* consciousness. One should enter [the attainment] only after having adverted [to it], thinking, "May there not be a sudden death.

For if death were to occur suddenly, one would be deprived of the opportunity for the declaration of another's spiritual status (*aññabyākaraṇa*), the giving of exhortation to monks, the manifestation of the power of the Dispensation, or the non-attainment of the highest path by a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). "The remainder" refers to the three types [of actions], such as those that are bound to various objects and those that do not disturb [the attainment].
The preliminary duty (*pubbakicca*). This is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.
Although it is stated as if without restriction—"one or two"—they nonetheless specify that there are exactly two occasions.

"In the section on consciousness" means in the section on consciousness pertaining to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*). "He touches cessation" refers precisely to the state of being without consciousness (*acittakabhāva*).

"Because it is the application for cessation" means that it is the state of being an application for the cessation of consciousness; the meaning is that the application consisting of the accumulation of the two powers and so forth results in the cessation of consciousness.

Furthermore, the possession of the powers of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), as well as mastery over the practice of knowledge and concentration (*ñāṇa-samādhi-cariyā-vasī*), must be understood here precisely in the sense of their not overriding one another; thus he said: "the two factors of serenity and insight..."

"Having brought about the union. This refers to the "application for successive cessation," which is the application for the successive cessation of the first jhāna and so forth, as well as their respective contemplations.
According to the method already stated, this is the ascent through the eight attainments, not the actual entering into the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Therefore, the construction is: "Consequently, no further consciousnesses arise beyond those two [final] consciousnesses."
"He cannot remain without consciousness for the full duration as determined" means that he is unable to remain without consciousness for the entire period specified.
This is due to his failure to perform the honoring of the Saṅgha, the summoning by the Teacher, the delimitation of time, and the act of adverting;
it is not due to his failure to avoid shaking what is tied separately. For by failing to do those [latter], at times only such [a person]—
There would be no loss of requisites, nor would there be an obstruction to the attainment of cessation. This point is indeed clarified by the case of the Elder Mahānāga.
Such being the case, it follows that emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs in three ways;
therefore, that [previous position] should not be accepted as authoritative. Turning back, he establishes himself once again in the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).

By this, he shows that such occurs only when an obstruction to the attainment has arisen; however, in the absence of an obstruction, emergence occurs through the arising of the fruition-consciousness upon the passing of the predetermined time.
And by taking it thus, some say that the illustration of the man climbing out of a deep ravine and being struck by a heated rock is also made consistent.
Others, however, [say] that because the preliminary task was not performed, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...

They say: "Because it is stated that 'as soon as he has attained [the base of nothingness], he turns back and establishes himself in the base of nothingness,' the attainment of the attainment of cessation does not succeed if certain prior duties—such as honoring the Saṅgha—are omitted, due to the deficiency of a necessary factor.
This performance of prior duties for the attainment of cessation is similar to the routine observances (vatta). Therefore, in that regard, of whatever is most important...
Others say that the non-performance [of the preliminary duties] hinders the attainment. This should be understood after investigation.
Furthermore, the statement "he becomes established in the base of nothingness" is said because the base of nothingness must be attained again;
for having emerged from the attainment, the former duty must be performed.
The phrase "Just as... and so forth constitutes a comparison based on the commonality of having previously performed the necessary tasks.
(880) "Of this" refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). By the words "by way of delimiting time," etc., he shows the duration of the attainment of cessation through four aspects.

(882) "Inclining toward seclusion" means inclining toward the seclusion of escape; it should be understood that this is all the more so because of the turning away from formations (*saṅkhāra*) and because of the arising of the fruit-consciousness (*phalacitta*).
883. Taking no distinction between those who are dead and those who have attained cessation, the question is asked:
"What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has attained [cessation]?
Granted that there is no distinction between them due to the subsiding of the three formations and so forth, yet because of the fact that only material phenomena remain, [the distinction is made].
However, in order to show the distinction between the disappearance and non-disappearance of the faculties (*indriya*), the passage beginning with “yvāyaṃ” was stated. 884.
“By way of intrinsic nature” (*sabhāvato*) means by way of a phenomenon possessing its own nature; the meaning is “from the perspective of ultimate reality” (*paramatthato*).

For it is only those things existing from the perspective of ultimate reality that can be described in terms of being conditioned (*saṅkhata*) and so forth, not what does not exist. “By way of one who enters [the attainment]” is said because...
For a noble person entering [the attainment], having coupled serenity and insight (*samatha-vipassanā*) and ascending through the eight attainments,
the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is said to be "accomplished" by means of the production of the application that causes the subsiding of formations (*saṅkhāra*);
therefore, it is appropriate to call it "accomplished" with reference to that production of the application.

It is "peaceful" because of the subsiding of formations (*saṅkhāra*) and because it is endowed with the state of peace (*santa-dhamma*). It is "cultivated by the Noble Ones" because it is to be practiced exclusively by the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
It has attained the designation "Nirvana" because of the extinguishing of all three kinds of suffering (*dukkhatā*).
"Noble wisdom" refers to the thoroughly purified wisdom of the paths and fruits. "Of this too" refers to this attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). "Capability for attainment" means...
The capacity for attaining meditative absorption.
885. Commentary on the Discourse Establishing the State of Being Worthy of Offerings, etc.:

"The establishment of the state of being worthy of offerings, etc. refers to the establishment of the states of being worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*), worthy of hospitality (*pāhuneyya*), worthy of gifts (*dakkhiṇeyya*), worthy of reverential salutation (*añjalikaraṇīya*), and being an unsurpassed field of merit (*anuttara-puññakkhetta*).

"By distinction" means without the distinction of the wisdom of the path of seeing and so forth; [it refers] to this supramundane wisdom (*lokuttara-paññā*). "That which is to be brought and offered" is *āhuna*;
it is a gift to be given after being brought even from afar. One who is worthy of receiving that is "worthy of offerings" (*āhuneyya*). "A guest-gift" (*pāhuna*) refers to a gift for a visitor;
one who is worthy of receiving that is "worthy of guest-gifts" (*pāhuneyya*). One who is worthy of the sacrificial fee (*dakkhiṇā*) is "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
The act of joining the palms is *añjalikamma*; one who is worthy of that is "one to whom the palms should be joined" (*añjalikaraṇīya*).
It is the unsurpassed, supreme place for the growth of merit among beings; thus, it is the "unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the summary here.
The detailed explanation, however, has already been stated above.
"Having come through weak insight" means that by means of weak insight, having developed the wisdom of the first path,
he has attained the state of a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). Although he is one of "weak faculties" due to the dullness of his faculties such as faith and the rest,
he is "one who has seven births at most," meaning that his maximum number of rebirths and assumption of individual existence (*attabhāva*) is seven times.

Beyond that, one does not take an eighth existence; thus, one is "one who has seven births at most. "Having wandered" means having gone from one state to another by way of taking rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"He makes an end of suffering" means he brings about the limit and the conclusion of the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
This refers to "seven existences in the happy destinies" by way of a mixed existence, taking sometimes the world of the gods and sometimes the world of humans.
Having been told, “having wandered through saṃsāra,” [the term] *kolaṅkolo* means one who goes from family to family.
From the moment of realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), there is no rebirth in a low family; the meaning is that one is reborn only in families of great wealth.
“Two or three families” refers to two or three existences (*bhava*) by way of gods and humans. Thus, this person also [attains liberation] only through mixed existence.
This has been explained. And this [phrase] “two or three times” is merely for the sake of instruction.

Even while wandering through existence up to the sixth birth, he remains a *kolaṃkola* (one who goes from family to family). He is called an *ekabījī* because he possesses only a single seed of the aggregates, which is defined as the grasping of a personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Furthermore, the phrase “human existence” is also merely for the sake of instruction; one could also say that he produces a divine existence.
It is indeed appropriate. But what determines this distinction among them? It is the insight (vipassanā) pertaining to the three lower paths.
For if the insight pertaining to the three higher paths is powerful, one is called an "ekabījī" (one-seeder).
If it is weaker than that, one is a "kolaṃkolo" (one who goes from family to family); if it is even weaker, one is a "sattakkhattuparamo" (one who has seven births at most).
887. One who comes back once by way of rebirth-linking is a *sakadāgāmī* (once-returner). "Only once" means just one time.
By the phrase "having come to this world," one of the five types of once-returners is selected, excluding the other four.
For some, having attained the fruit of once-returning here, attain final nibbāna right here; another, having attained it here, attains final nibbāna in the world of the devas.
One person, having reached the world of the devas, attains final nibbāna right there; another, having reached the world of the devas, is reborn here and then attains final nibbāna.

These four types are not included here. However, one who, having reached this world, dwells in the world of the devas for the full span of their lifespan and is then reborn here again before attaining final nibbāna—this one is included here.
888. He is called a non-returner (*anāgāmī*) because he does not come back here by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"By way of diversity of faculties" means by way of the relative superiority or inferiority of the faculties that bring about the maturation of liberation, such as faith and the rest.

"Having departed from here, he reaches his goal in five ways" means that this non-returner, having abandoned this world, attains final nibbāna in five modes, namely, as one who attains nibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyin*), and so forth.

He exists. Because he attains final nibbāna through the nibbāna of defilements (kilesaparinibbāna) in the very midst of his lifespan, he is one who attains final nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyī).
"Upahacca" means having approached the time of death. "Without great effort" means without excessive exertion, easily and with little difficulty due to his sharp faculties.
"With effort" should be understood here as the opposite of what was stated [in the previous case].

Because his stream of craving or the stream of the round flows upwards through his state of being, he is an "upstreamer" (*uddhaṃsota*). Alternatively, because the stream of the Path must be attained by going upwards, his stream is directed upwards;
thus he is an "upstreamer. Because he goes to the Akaniṭṭha existence by way of rebirth-linking, he is a "goer to Akaniṭṭha" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*).
"Wherever he is reborn" means wherever among the Aviha and other [pure abodes] he is reborn.
Furthermore, in order to understand the classification of these non-returners (*anāgāmī*), the fourfold group of those who go upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm should be known:

for one who, starting from the Aviha heaven, purifies the four divine worlds and, having gone to Akaniṭṭha, attains final nibbāna, this is called "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha. But as for one who...
Having purified the three lower deva-worlds and remaining in the Sudassī deva-world, one attains parinibbāna;
this is called an "upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota) who does not go to Akaniṭṭha. One who goes from here directly to Akaniṭṭha and attains parinibbāna is called an "upstreamer" who goes to Akaniṭṭha.
However, one who, among the four lower deva-worlds, attains parinibbāna right there in each respective place—
This is called the "Upstreamer who does not go to the Akaniṭṭha realm. However, among those born in the Aviha heaven, there are five types:

three who attain Parinibbāna in the interval—namely, one who attains Parinibbāna before reaching the midpoint of the lifespan, one who attains it after reaching it, and one who attains it upon landing; one who attains Parinibbāna after landing (upahacca-parinibbāyī); and the Upstreamer.
These become ten when divided into those who attain Parinibbāna without exertion and those who attain Parinibbāna with exertion. Likewise...
In Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī, there are four decades, making forty. However, in Akaniṭṭha, there is no one who goes upstream (uddhaṃsota).

There are three who attain nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin) and one who attains nibbāna upon arrival (upahaccaparinibbāyin), making four; these become eight when divided into those who attain nibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāra) and with exertion (sasaṅkhāra).
Thus, there are forty-eight non-returners (anāgāmin).

As for the stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), there are four who have seven births at most (*sattakkhattuparama*), four who go from family to family (*kolaṃkola*), and four who have one seed remaining (*ekabījin*). Thus, there are twelve who have practiced with faith as their primary quality (*saddhādhura*), and likewise twelve who have practiced with wisdom as their primary quality (*paññādhura*), making twenty-four in total.

As for the once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), there are four who are liberated by way of the emptiness liberation (*suññatavimokkha*) according to their mode of practice (*paṭipadā*), and likewise four each for the signless (*animitta*) and desireless (*appaṇihita*) liberations, making twelve.
(889) Likewise for the arahants: there are twelve who are liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*) and twelve who are liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*), making twenty-four.

There are sixty-three [arahants]: thirty who possess the threefold knowledge (*tevijjā*), twelve who possess the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), and twelve who have attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidāppatta*).
Thus, together with the paccekabuddhas and the sammāsambuddhas, there are one hundred and forty-six noble ones (*ariya*).

Since their status as noble ones is established through the development of noble wisdom (*ariyā paññābhāvanā*), it is said: "The attainment of the state of being worthy of offerings (*āhuneyyabhāva*) and so forth also belongs to this..."
“The benefit of developing supramundane wisdom. Even without mundane sciences and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), there is liberation in both ways;
thus, the one liberated in both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutto*) is mentioned separately. “With reference to which it was said”:
this refers to the development of the wisdom of the fourth path, which was stated briefly above in the commentary on the verses; that manner of statement is now concluded by way of a summary.

To demonstrate this, it is said: "At the moment of the path," and so forth. Granted that in all four moments of the path one is said to "untangle that tangle," and even in the moments of fruition one has untangled the tangle as appropriate;
yet it is only at the moment of the supreme fruit (agga-phala) that the tangle is untangled in its entirety, because beyond that there is no further tangle to be untangled.
Therefore, herein [the benefit] of the cultivation of wisdom through the lower paths is [described] below.
Because it has already been stated, the meaning is explained by way of the development of wisdom pertaining to the fourth path.
"Rati" means delight; the sense is "delightful preference. "Therein" refers to the development of noble wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "of this verse": it is in this verse that [the path] is spoken of as the support for the Path of Purification, which constitutes its own meaning. Alternatively, this is a genitive case used because the meaning is related to that [verse].
The commentary on the exposition of the benefits of the development of wisdom is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the twenty-third chapter.
Commentary on the words of the conclusion.

891. The meaning of these verses beginning with "Of this [verse] now" has already been stated below. The connection is as follows: this *Visuddhimagga*, which was thus promised by the words "I shall speak the Path of Purification," has been spoken up to this point.

892. Regarding the passage beginning with "Therein," etc., this is the summary of the meaning according to the grammatical construction of the words: of those meanings—such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth—which were mentioned in the verse "Having established oneself in virtue," and which consist of the five Nikāyas, according to the method of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), that is, within the lineage of the commentaries...
Since this definitive exposition has been presented— having for the most part collected and synthesized all the various explanations stated here and there,
and having freed them from the confusion of the faults of sectarianism and internal inconsistency—
it follows that those practitioners seeking purification should indeed apply themselves with diligence to this *Visuddhimagga*.
The Concluding Verses:
And to this extent—
He whose conduct is perfectly pure, adorned with the purified method;

The Great Seer, whose mind was stirred by the impulse of compassion and who possessed vast, noble, and pure proficiency of wisdom, spoke the *Visuddhimagga* for the sake of the world’s ultimate purification.
In order to elucidate its meaning, I have undertaken this commentary on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*),
relying upon the ancient path of exposition,
at the request of one who dwells in the Siddhagāma Pariveṇa.
By the Elder Dāṭhanāga, wise and of pure conduct,
this [work]— which contains the ultimate meanings (paramattha) as they appropriately belong here and there—
is called by the name *Paramatthamañjūsā* ("The Casket of Ultimate Meanings") because it is a repository for them.
Having reached completion, with its classifications free from confusion,
it consists of eighty-eight measures of text according to the recitation sections.
Thus, whatever has been attained by me while compiling this, [may it be for the welfare of all].
By the power of that merit, may all embodied beings, having entered the pure practice of virtue and the rest within the teaching of the Lord of the World,
partake in the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world;
may all living beings always have reverence for it.
May the King, the lord of the earth, cause the rain to fall properly in its season.
"May he, delighting in the true Dhamma, rule the world by the Dhamma alone.
Thus ends the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā* named *Paramatthamañjūsā*, composed by the teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery.
The Great Commentary on the Path of Purification is completed.
